The issue of hospital readmissions has been addressed in a number of studies [22], [23], [24]. Among the numerous works developed to provide supportive decisions in ICU is the prediction of mortality, LOS, and ICU readmission. This section summarizes the state of the art that utilized ML and DL to predict ICU readmission inside and outside hospitals.

First, some studies utilized ML to predict the readmission probability after the patients move from ICU to ward in the same hospital (same visit).

In [25], the authors explored the performance of eight classification algorithms, including NB, DT, rule-based approaches, and ensemble methods applied to various sets of attribute data, and the effectiveness of each algorithm was assessed using six criteria. There were 185 variables in the 9926 individuals analyzed in the dataset from three ICUs in a Brazilian university hospital. These included demographics, duration of stay before admission to the ICU, comorbidities, severity indexes, treatments, organ support care during ICU stay, and laboratory results. In [22], the authors applied a boosted C5.0 tree as the base classifier and combined it with SVM as a secondary classifier to predict ICU readmission. 20321 anonymized admission data were used to induce and validate the models at Veterans Health Administration (VHA) hospitals in Pittsburgh between fiscal years 2006 and 2014. In [26], ML models were predicted to be differentiated between patients who were unplanned ICU readmissions or deaths from those who were not. The models trained on 3326 ICU episodes that were collected from MMIC and tested on the target hospital’s data. In [14], the authors used a gradient-boosted model based on real-time risk scores to predict readmission using 24885 patients collected from hospitals in the United States (US). The gradient-boosting ML model performed the best since each DT is sequentially trained. In [27], rule-based algorithms: DT, RF, XGBoost, and LASSO models were used using the 2016 Nationwide Readmissions Database (NRD) database from a US hospital. Data resampling techniques were used to provide more balanced data to effectively address the readmission and non-readmission groups. In [28], the authors selected the most important features from the dataset using the LASSO feature selection algorithm. Then the authors studied the effect of applying ML models to predict readmission based on the selected features. A hospital registry system was used to collect data on 5791 COVID-19 hospitalizations retrospectively. In [29], LR, DT, SVM, XGB, extremely randomized trees (ET), light gradient boosting machine (LGBM), and extreme gradient boosting (XGB) were used to predict ICU readmission using 58036 patients collected from hospitals in Southeast Asia. LR recorded the highest AUC. In [30], the authors applied ML models with different feature selection methods to predict ICU mortality risk. A large hospital in Anhui provided data for 1628 patients with cardio-macrovascular disease in the ICU. In terms of performance, RF achieved the best results. In [31], the authors applied fuzzy modeling with tree search feature selection using 26655 patients from MIMIC-II to predict ICU readmission between 24h and 72h. The results showed that fuzzy modeling achieved the highest performance. In [32], the authors applied LR, SVM, RF, GBDT, and NB using text data for 40000 patients from MIMIC-II. They represented features using Bag-of-words and Term frequency-inverse document frequency (tf-idf). The results showed that LR achieved the highest AUC.

Others developed a deep-learning model to predict ICU readmission. In [33], the authors proposed heterogeneous long short-term memory (LSTM) and convolutional neural network (CNN) (CNN-LSTM) architecture for readmission risk measurement using the MMIC dataset. The architecture combined three stacked bidirectional LSTM layers, a CNN layer, and a dense decision layer. These layers were preceded by a preprocessing stage of categorical encoding using a MIMIC-III database. In [34], to incorporate the multivariate aspects of EHRs and catch abrupt and sudden fluctuations in chart event features like glucose and heart rate. The readmission prediction model was developed using three categories of features: chart events, ICD-9 embeddings, and patient demographic data. The authors conducted deep-learning models using the MIMIC-III dataset. They studied each feature that contributed to the prediction model over ten years. In [35], the authors applied CNN models and RF to the discharge summary notes in the MIMIC database and trained models were utilized to categorize and identify potentially high-risk admissions/patients. The CNN approach achieved the highest f1-score.

input: The proposed system introduces a clinical monitoring fog-computing framework for remote prognosis and monitoring of intensive care patients using health symptoms. The system uses machine learning to generate real-time alert signals for doctors, accelerating e-healthcare decision-making and remote health system control. As shown in Figure 1, the system consists of three layers: data acquisition, fog computing, and cloud server. To minimize delay and accelerate decision-making, the machine learning model is deployed on fog nodes within the computing layer, rather than transferring data to a cloud server. These fog nodes utilize a practical swarm optimization algorithm to select the most vital signs relevant to specific pathological conditions. This approach enables medical experts to speed up decision-making with higher accuracy and faster convergence.

FOG-COMPUTING-BASED SYSTEM

The main objective of this section is to introduce a clinical monitoring fog-computing-based system for remote prognosis and monitoring of the state of intensive care patients using their health symptoms. This proposed monitoring system uses the advantages of ML approaches for generating a real-time alert signal to doctors for supplying e-healthcare, accelerating decision-making, and monitoring and controlling the health systems remotely. As shown in Figure 1, the fog-computing-based system consists of three proposed layers: data acquisition, fog computing, and cloud server. To avoid delay time and accelerate decision-making, the proposed ML model has been deployed on the fog nodes residing at the fog computing layer instead of the traditional data transferring methods that use straightforward data uploading to the cloud server. The fog nodes hold an enhanced performance using the practical swarm optimization algorithm. This optimizer can select the most vital signs according to the nature of each pathological condition within the care unit. So, it helps medical experts to speed up decision-making with higher accuracy and faster convergence.

Medical Information Mart Intensive Care III is a benchmark dataset created by MIT [36]. It includes EHR data for 53,432 patients admitted to different ICUs (SICU, MICU, CRCU, CSRU, etc.). A total of 4750 measurements and 470 laboratory tests are included in MIMIC III tables. In our study, we only consider adult patients (age>15) which were admitted to both Surgical ICU (SICU) and surgical recovery (SR ICU). All data is stored as comma-separated values (CSV) files that could be converted to a relational database through PostgreSQL. Table 2 details the tables used in the current study. A total number of 10,465 patients were included in this study after applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria that could be summarized as follows: (1) exclude patients aged less than or equal to 15 years, (2) exclude patients that died inside ICU, (3) exclude patients who were admitted inside ICU rather than SICU and SRICU, (4) exclude patients that did not have at least one value in each measurement, (5) exclude some patients from making the data balanced. Inclusion and exclusion criteria detailed in Figure 3.

B. PRE-PROCESSING

Several challenges appeared at this stage and heavily affected model performance, including missing values, removing outliers, and data imputation.

• Irregular time interval: An irregular interval sampled time series is a series of samples with irregular intervals between observations. When the time gaps between observations are wide, this data introduces a time sparsity factor. Most machine learning techniques take observation order into account since they need more time comprehension. As a result, it is more challenging to learn the time dependencies included in time series problems [37], [38]. With MIMIC-III, vital signs are measured irregularly. Some took measurements every few minutes, whereas others took measurements every few seconds. Some ML methods could handle time series data when sampled with the same interval unless most are not equipped to handle it. To address this issue, we averaged all measures throughout an hour to produce a single record of the patient’s vital signs observations. As a result, each record has consistent values.

• Outlier removal is defined as values that deviate too much from the norm and are considered outliers [39], [40]. According to the judgments of medical experts, a normal range is defined. To identify outliers, first, we specify the normal range for each feature according to the medical expert, then remove the data that considers outliers from the medical expert’s perspective.

• Filling missing value: a dataset’s missing values are typically replaced by new values reasonably similar to those that would have been recorded if they had been observed. This procedure is known as data imputation.

FIGURE 2. The architecture of the proposed system.

TABLE 2. MIMIC III Dataset description.

Imputation techniques can often be divided into two groups: single imputation and multiple imputation. Single imputation substitutes plausible values for missing values only once, whereas multiple imputation methods perform imputation many times to produce a range of imputed values for each missing item. This gives information about the degree of uncertainty in the imputed values for imputation techniques with some stochastic elements. Missing values are frequently present in medical data. This raises several factors, such as sensor failure, data recording at various times, etc. Removing missing values is the most straightforward technique to handle them. However, doing it this way could result in losing important information. As a result, numerous methods, such as expectation maximization [41] and hot deck encoding [42], have been devised to infer missing values based on the other records. Large portions of data (40-55%) in crucial features were lost during the preprocessing step of MIMIC-III, but we could not eliminate them because they were essential to the prediction process. In light of this, we chose scenarios where each measurement has at least two values before using expectation maximization [43] to impute further missing values.

The practical swarm optimization scenario is designed
to select the optimal features (most vital signs) that
directly affect the decision of the machine learning model.
Figure 4 shows the flowchart of the standard PSO. Practical swarm optimization (PSO) is a meta-heuristic feature
optimization algorithm inspired by swarms. It was developed
to find the optimal solutions among solution spaces [47].
The mathematical model of PSO could be summarized in
the following points (1) each practice has a position, fitness
value, and velocity. (2) each practical search for the optimal

instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: GA is a randomized evolutionary algorithm for feature extraction and selection, based on biological evolution and natural genetics [49], [50]. GA optimizes functions by encoding them as bit arrays mimicking chromosomes, using genetic operators to find near-optimal solutions [51]. The process involves: coding goals and cost functions; establishing a fitness function; creating a population of individuals; evaluating fitness; forming a new population via crossover, mutation, and fitness-proportionate growth; substituting the old population; and decoding outcomes to resolve the problem [51]. The three primary genetic operators are crossover, which swaps solution parts to provide convergence and mixing; mutation, which randomly modifies solution parts to increase diversity and evade local optima; and selection of the fittest, which transmits high-fitness alternatives to future generations [51].
output:
GA is one of the enormously advanced evolutionary algorithms for extracting and selecting appropriate features. This randomized method for optimizing functions is based on biological evolution and natural genetics concepts [49], [50]. GA has been proven capable of exploring a huge space of solutions and dealing with many input characteristics. GA encodes the optimization function as bit arrays that mimic chromosomes, and Genetic operators customize strings to find a close-to-optimum answer to the situation at hand. This is performed using the method depicted in the following steps as in Figure 5 [51]:

• Coding the goals or cost functions.
• Establishing a fitness function.
• A generation is creating a population of individuals (solutions).
• Evaluating individuals in the population’s fitness function.
• Forming an entirely novel population through crossover and mutation, fitness-proportionate growth, and then substituting the old population and looping with the new population.
• Decoding the outcomes to resolve the problem.

The main steps of GA are shown in Figure 5. The three primary genetic operators in genetic algorithms are crossover, mutation, and selection [51]:

• Crossover: It is the swapping parts of a solution represented by chromosomes or other solutions. The main purpose is to provide convergence and solution mixing in a subspace.

• Mutation: It is the haphazard modification of a single solution’s constituent parts, which increases population diversity and offers a way to elude a local optimum.

• Selection of the fittest: it is the practice of transmitting alternatives with high fitness to future generations, which is usually done in the form of some selection of the most suitable solutions.

instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Ensemble learning combines multiple base models to improve performance. Each model addresses single-model issues like low accuracy or high variance, mapping features to output via distinct decision boundaries [63]. The three main types are bagging, boosting, and stacking. Bagging reduces variance and overfitting by averaging predictions from several models [64]. Boosting sequentially adds models, focusing each on the errors of the previous model and using a weighted average for the final prediction [64]. Stacking uses a secondary model to combine predictions from base learners [65], [66].
output: Ensemble learning is a learning approach that aims to achieve enhanced performance by combining predictions from several models. These models are known as base models. Each model solves single-model challenges such as low accuracy, high variance, and feature bias. The weak learner could be from the same type of various types, and each weak learner maps the features input to the final output with different decision boundaries [63]. The three main types of ensemble learning are bagging, boosting, hard voting, and stacking. There are differences in the learning and the aggregating results; these methods can be summarized in the following points [64]. Bagging: the main idea in bagging is to build several models, then average the whole prediction; bagging is used to reduce variance and overfitting. Boosting: the main idea is to add several models sequentially, while each model concentrates on the errors produced by the previous model, out a weighted average of the total prediction. Stacking involves utilizing several models in the base learning and another model to combine the prediction [65], [66].

1) Selection bias: The dataset that includes in that study only includes patients from a MIMIC III dataset aggregated from patients admitted to intensive care units (ICUs) at the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, Massachusetts, USA. Therefore, when testing the proposed model in the real-world, if certain laboratory tests or vital signs were not recorded for some patients, the model may not be able to accurately predict their risk of readmission.

IoT medical sensors collect data, which is locally processed in the fog layer using feature selection via PSO and stacking models to generate real-time alerts for physicians. The model, trained on 10,644 MIMIC III patients, achieved 98.42% accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score using PSO-selected features with a stacking model. The study provides local and global explanations to ensure model trustworthiness and plans future work on dataset generalization, unstructured data integration, and real-system deployment.

Due to healthcare devices’ heterogeneous and dynamic
nature, real-time monitoring and timely decision-making
have become crucial problems. This study introduced a clinical monitoring fog-computing-based system for remote prognosis and monitoring of the state of intensive care patients
and predicted unplanned readmission outside the ICU within
the next 30 days of discharge. The proposed system has
three layers: data acquisition, fog computing, and a cloud
server. First, a set of IoT devices called medical sensors
are scattered to collect the vital signs of the patient’s health
conditions in real-time, in addition to the data aggregated
through lab tests and medical histories. Then, data is locally
processed in the fog computing layer and predicts unplanned
patient readmission. The results are then sent to the cloud
layer, offering sizable storage space for patient healthcare.
The e-healthcare monitoring system can generate a real-time
alert signal for doctors supplying e-healthcare. This proposed
monitoring system used the advantages of ML approaches
for developing a real-time alert signal for doctors to provide
e-healthcare, accelerating decision-making, and monitoring
and controlling health systems. The proposed model was
trained and evaluated based on 10,644 patients extracted from
the MIMIC III dataset. Feature selection methods: Genetic
algorithm (GA) and practical swarm optimization (PSO) are
used to choose the optimal feature subset from detests. Moreover, Different traditional ML models, ensemble learning
models, and the proposed stacking models are applied to
full features and selected features to predict readmission
after 30 days of ICU discharge. The study results showed
that the proposed stacking model with features chosen by
PSO outperforms other traditional and ensemble ML, with
an accuracy of 98.42, a precision of 98.42, a recall of 98.42,
and an F1-Score of 98.42. In addition, we provide local and
global explanations of the developed model to ensure its efficiency, effectiveness, and trustworthiness. The development
of interpretable models such as the proposed model is necessary to improve the generalization ability of the proposed
model and enhance the integration of the predictive model
in the clinical process. Future studies will concentrate on
ensuring the generalization ability of the proposed model by
validating it using various datasets and different diseases.
They will also use unstructured data from MIMIC datasets
such as clinical notes, images, etc. To gain valuable information and improve the model’s overall performance. In
our future work, we plan to aggregate more data to ensure
the model’s generalizability. Additionally, we intend to analyze the model from a computational complexity perspective
to ensure efficiency. Furthermore, we plan to deploy the
developed model in a real clinical system to evaluate its
performance in a practical setting.

ABSTRACT Cyber threats are rapidly developing, necessitating more adaptable and intelligent security
frameworks for intrusion detection systems (IDS). Conventional Machine Learning (ML) methodologies,
although proficient in identifying recognized attack patterns, frequently falter against unexpected threats,
such as zero-day assaults, owing to their dependence on labeled datasets. Deep Reinforcement Learning
(DRL) addresses this limitation by independently learning and adapting to novel dangers via trial-anderror interactions with the environment. This study rigorously assesses the efficacy of Random Forest (RF),
Decision Tree (DT), and Deep Q-Learning (DQL) models utilizing the CIC-IDS2017 dataset, contrasting
their capacity to identify both known and unknown (zero-day) attacks. The experimental results indicate that
DT and RF attain the maximum accuracy in identifying known attacks, whereas DQL displays enhanced
generalization ability for unknown threats. Furthermore, comparative evaluation of the DQL model across
the CIC-IDS2017, NSL-KDD, and AWID datasets offers important insights into its robustness and generalization capacity under heterogeneous experimental conditions. In this study, we investigate the influence of
hyperparameter tuning on the efficacy of deep reinforcement learning, demonstrating that modifications to
the learning rate, exploration strategy, and experience replay buffer substantially improve detection accuracy.
This study systematically compares classic machine learning techniques with deep reinforcement learning,
demonstrating the viability of reinforcement learning-based intrusion detection system models and providing
insights into adaptive and autonomous cybersecurity solutions.
INDEX TERMS Deep reinforcement learning, cyber-attack, intrusion detection, machine learning.

section: I. INTRODUCTION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Cyberattacks are increasingly sophisticated, exposing the limitations of traditional Machine Learning (ML) models in detecting novel threats like zero-day attacks [1]. While Reinforcement Learning (RL) enables proactive security through continuous environmental interaction [1], recent data indicates 62% of attacks cause substantial damage before discovery [3], highlighting the need for autonomous Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) [2]. Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) integrates RL and Deep Learning (DL) to enhance decision-making in dynamic, adversarial settings [4]-[7], unlike conventional ML which relies on static labeled datasets. Although ensemble models offer accuracy, their fixed structures hinder adaptability to evolving attack patterns [8]. Deep Q-Learning (DQL), a DRL variant, integrates decision paths under uncertainty, outperforming static models [9]. This study evaluates the Random Forest (RF), Decision Tree (DT), and DQL models using the CIC-IDS2017 dataset [10], [11], systematically testing performance on both known and unfamiliar threats. Results show RF excels at known pattern detection, while DQL demonstrates superior generalization for zero-day and known attacks. Hyperparameter optimization—specifically learning rate, exploration strategy, and experience replay—significantly improves DRL flexibility and accuracy [12]. Despite these advantages, real-time application is challenged by long training times and high computational costs. The proposed DQL model achieves a 10.7% higher F1-score than DT and 7.5% higher than RF in zero-day attack detection. This work provides a reproducible framework for assessing DRL-based IDS under evolving network conditions, balancing detection performance with practical computational constraints.
output:
Cyberattacks are becoming more sophisticated and common; therefore, security systems need to be smarter and more adaptable to keep up. Although traditional Machine Learning (ML) models are good at identifying known attack patterns, they often struggle to generalize to new threats, particularly zero-day attacks. This drawback is reduced by Reinforcement Learning (RL), which allows proactive security measures by continuously learning from its interactions with the environment [1]. There is an urgent need for more autonomous and adaptable Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) [2] because recent studies show that 62% of cyberattacks are only discovered after they’ve done substantial damage [3]. By facilitating proactive threat mitigation, Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) could fortify cybersecurity frameworks, enabling systems to tackle emergent threats before their escalation [4]. DRL integrates RL and Deep Learning (DL), augmenting an agent’s capacity to function in dynamic and adversarial settings [5]. In contrast to conventional machine learning techniques that depend on labeled datasets, DRL independently acquires optimal behaviors via reward-based feedback mechanisms, enhancing its decision-making capabilities over time [6]. The incorporation of DL into RL frameworks facilitates intricate feature extraction and function approximation, rendering DRL an attractive option for cybersecurity applications, where attack patterns are progressively sophisticated, quick, and adaptive [7]. Ensemble and hybrid models have shown good predictive accuracy in intrusion detection, but their static structure and offline training limit them. Fixed combination weights or batch learning make these models less responsive to changing attack patterns or zero-day threats. Studies have revealed that static ensemble techniques cannot adapt to time-varying complex environments and lose prediction power in new scenarios [8]. DRL allows agents to interact with the environment, learn from delayed feedback, and adjust their policies in real time. Deep Q-Learning (DQL) integrates numerous decision paths under uncertainty, surpassing static ensemble models [9]. These qualities make DRL ideal for hostile cybersecurity because threat surfaces change quickly. The methodological foundation for adaptive and autonomous intrusion detection in this study is DRL.

The Random Forest (RF), Decision Tree (DT), and DQL models are carefully tested to see how well they work. The CIC-IDS2017 dataset is used as a standard for intrusion detection [10], [11]. Unlike many prior studies that focus only on detecting known classes, this work systematically evaluates model performance under both familiar and unfamiliar threat conditions, thereby highlighting the generalization power of DRL. The tests evaluate model effectiveness against both recognized attack types and novel zero-day attacks. The results show that RF is the most accurate at finding known attack patterns, while DQL is better at finding unknown attacks, such as zero-day threats and known attacks. The study also examines the influence of hyperparameter optimization on the efficacy of DRL-based IDS. The experimental results show that improving factors such as the learning rate, exploration strategy, and experience replay buffer makes the DRL model much more flexible and accurate at detecting things. This multi-perspective evaluation also contributes a reproducible framework for assessing DRL-based models under evolving network conditions. Despite this, real-time applications face problems like long training times and high computing costs that make them impractical in high-speed network settings.

The main contributions of this paper are as follows:

• The DRL model employs a reward function that dynamically adjusts to evolving intrusion patterns, improving its responsiveness to novel threats. Unlike traditional ML models, DRL supports online learning, allowing continuous parameter updates as new threats emerge in real-time network environments.

• DRL enhances intrusion detection accuracy and real-time response capabilities by autonomously learning from network interactions and optimizing security policies over time. The proposed DQL model achieves 10.7% higher F1-score than DT and 7.5% higher than RF in zero-day attack detection on the CIC-IDS2017 dataset. This quantifies the model’s superior generalization capacity over widely used ML baselines.

• By systematically evaluating the strengths and limitations of DRL, RF, and DT models in intrusion detection, this study provides valuable insights into the potential of reinforcement learning-based security systems for future autonomous and adaptive cybersecurity applications.

• Unlike most existing DRL-based IDS frameworks, this study explicitly targets the detection of previously unknown, zero-day attacks using the CIC-IDS2017 dataset, emphasizing DQL’s generalization capability. A comprehensive hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, spanning 27 configurations of learning rate, epsilon decay, and batch size, offers practical tuning insights. Additionally, this study evaluates the trade-off between detection performance and computational cost, providing a balanced perspective on real-time applicability.

Here is the outline of the paper: In Section II, we examine studies on IDS that use DRL methods. After RL algorithms are introduced in Section III, the preferred model, DQL, is examined in Section IV in further depth. In Section V, we detail the experimental results and compare the models that were considered. This document concludes with Section VI.

section: II. RELATED WORK
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Alavizadeh et al. [12] developed a DQL-based IDS achieving 90% intrusion detection with fewer false positives, designed for consistent updates against evolving threats. Kim and Park [13] proposed a hybrid DRL framework combining supervised learning and Q-learning to reduce training time and eliminate manual feature extraction, though it lacks testing on zero-day attacks. Our study uses a pure DQL framework to assess autonomous generalization to new attack types, conducting a full comparison with traditional ML models (RF, DT) and a hyperparameter sensitivity analysis. Beyond detection, Reference [14] used off-policy Q-learning to improve real-time response latency, while [15] introduced a multi-agent DQN with attention mechanisms for scalable threat pattern recognition. This study provides a comprehensive comparison of DQL against RF and DT using datasets with known and unknown attacks, examining hyperparameter impact on generalization to bridge the gap between theoretical RL advancements and practical IDS needs.
output:
New research has looked into how well DRL and DQL work in IDS, focusing on their benefits in constantly changing cybersecurity environments [5], [12]. Alavizadeh et al. [12] made a DQL-based intrusion detection system that found 90% of unauthorized intrusions and had a lot fewer false positives. They developed the model as a framework that allows for consistent updates, making it effective against the ongoing evolution of cyber threats. In the same way, Kim and Park [13] built a hybrid framework that combines DRL with supervised learning using deep autoencoders and Q-learning. The goal was to shorten the training time and make the learning process more stable. Their method focuses on eliminating manual feature extraction and speeding up convergence, but it hasn’t been tested on new attack types, such as zero-day threats. On the other hand, our study uses only a DQL framework without any supervised aspects, focusing on the agent’s ability to generalize to new types of attacks on its own. Our investigations also include a full comparison with traditional ML models and a sensitivity study of hyperparameters that affect generalization. Kim and Park’s study mostly looks at how well convergence and classification function on existing data. Our study, on the other hand, focuses on adaptive detection in the context of evolving cyber threat scenarios.

In addition to detection, certain research has incorporated DRL with adaptive response mechanisms. Reference [14] presented an off-policy Q-learning methodology to improve real-time intrusion response, facilitating swifter and more flexible responses against cyberattacks. Unlike traditional static response mechanisms, this model constantly changed protection techniques based on the state of the network. This greatly reduced reaction latency. At the same time, [15] introduced a multi-agent Deep Q-Network (DQN) model that uses attention mechanisms to find important threat patterns more quickly. By using a lot of agents, the system was able to grow across large network infrastructures, making the security framework more resilient and spread out.

While these studies in the literature demonstrate the potential of DRL-based IDS, they primarily focus on detection accuracy over a given dataset or the adaptability of response mechanisms [16]. However, this study provides a comprehensive comparison of DQL with two machine learning methods that have demonstrated great performance for threat detection in IDS: RF and DT. To facilitate a direct performance comparison among these models, adjustments have been made to the dataset to include both known and unknown attacks. Additionally, our study examines the impact of hyperparameter tuning on the effectiveness of DQL, highlighting how the method can be optimized for adaptive attack detection when properly configured. Unlike previous studies that rely on predefined datasets, our approach evaluates the generalization capabilities of DQL, shedding light on its strengths and limitations in real-time cybersecurity applications. By comparing DRL with ML techniques, this research offers new insights into the feasibility of reinforcement learning for autonomous IDS development, bridging the gap between theoretical advancements and practical cybersecurity needs.

input: Reinforcement learning (RL) aims to identify the maximum value (max-value) of actions [17, 18]. In chess, a piece moves forward one square with certainty, unlike stochastic actions that lack 100% likelihood [17]. A fundamental unit is the action; in Q-Learning (QL), actions are drawn from a discrete set with deterministic outcomes [18]. The objective of QL is to select a single deterministic action to acquire knowledge and optimize reward [18]. For example, a robotic vacuum cleaner must determine the most efficient route to its charging station [18]. Key concepts include environment, state, action, reward, and agent [18]. The environment provides feedback to the agent [18]. Observation relates to data from the environment [18]. An agent occupies a state, such as being 2 meters from a door [18]. Transitioning between states executes an action, and the environment provides rewards or penalties as feedback [18].
output:
III. REINFORCEMENT LEARNING

In RL algorithms, the principal aim is to identify the Maximum Value (max-value). This process is undertaken under deterministic conditions, signifying that the selected action is performed with absolute certainty [17]. In a chess game, a piece moves ahead by one square with complete certainty; it cannot move sideways or backward. Conversely, stochastic (non-deterministic) actions pertain to scenarios in which an action lacks a 100% likelihood of occurring as anticipated.

A fundamental idea in RL is action. In the context of the chess analogy, advancing a piece by one square is regarded as an action for the agent. In Q-Learning (QL), the term “set of actions” denotes the potential motions an agent may execute [18]. A chess piece can advance, shift left, or shift right. The algorithm determines actions based on the probability of their outcomes. Examine a dice roll; there exist six distinct outcomes, each clearly delineated. In Q-Learning, actions are derived from a discrete set, with each action yielding a distinct, deterministic result. The objective of QL is to choose a singular deterministic action from the set and acquire knowledge during the execution of that action to determine the maximum value. This allows the agent to optimize the reward and identify the most advantageous route. For example, if an autonomous vacuum cleaner employs a RL algorithm with the objective of traversing from one side of the room to its charging station, it must ascertain the most direct and efficient route to do this task expeditiously. To accurately comprehend RL algorithms, it is crucial to possess a thorough understanding of the following fundamental concepts: (1) Environment, (2) State, (3) Action, (4) Reward, (5) Agent.

The environment refers to the situation in which artificial intelligence (AI) operates. For an agent (e.g., a robot) utilizing a RL algorithm, the environment must provide feedback to aid the agent in achieving its reward. In the QL process, the environment must furnish the agent with observation and reward.

The idea of observation relates to data obtained from the environment, which may vary across different environments. In the QL algorithm, an agent occupies a certain state, which denotes an element within a collection of potential states. For instance, if the agent (e.g., a robotic vacuum cleaner) is positioned 2 meters from a door, that represents the agent’s state. When the agent shifts from one state to another, an action is executed. As the agent transitions between states, the environment administers penalties or reward points as feedback inside the environmental matrix. The feedback system is the environment, which provides rewards or penalties contingent upon the agent’s activities.

section: III. REINFORCEMENT LEARNING — A. REWARD FUNCTION AND OBJECTIVES
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: In reinforcement learning, a reward is a scalar value provided periodically by the environment to inform the agent of its performance. The objective of the reward is to furnish feedback regarding the agent's accomplishment, serving as the fundamental driver of the learning process [19]. The term "reinforcement" originates from the notion that the reward an actor receives should positively or negatively reinforce its behavior; a reward is a localized, instantaneous value indicating the efficacy of the agent's most recent activity rather than aggregate success [20]. An agent interacts with the environment through actions and observations; actions range from discrete, such as moving left or right, to continuous, such as steering a car [20]. Observations are data supplied by the environment reflecting occurrences surrounding the agent, which may include reward information, though the reward itself must not be regarded as ancillary [19]. The environment encompasses all external factors, and the interaction is confined to rewards, actions, and observations. RL is intended to facilitate learning in circumstances where comprehensive environmental measurement is unattainable [19].
output:
In RL, a reward is a scalar value acquired periodically from the environment. The reward may be positive or negative, substantial or minimal; it is merely a numerical value. The objective of rewarding is to inform the agent of its performance level. The frequency with which the agent will obtain this reward in the environment is established. Rewards may be administered every second or only once over the agent’s lifespan; nevertheless, for the sake of simplicity, it is customary to provide rewards at regular intervals or following each interaction with the environment. The primary function of a reward is to furnish the agent with feedback regarding its accomplishment, which is a fundamental idea in RL [19].

The term “reinforcement” originates from the notion that the reward an actor receives should either positively or negatively reinforce its behavior. A reward is a localized, instantaneous value, indicating the efficacy of the agent’s most recent activity rather than the aggregate success of all prior acts. Nonetheless, obtaining a substantial reward for an action does not guarantee the absence of significant repercussions stemming from prior acts shortly thereafter. An agent is the entity that engages with the environment, such as a robot or AI, executing activities, making observations, and receiving rewards for its interactions. In the majority of practical RL scenarios, the agent is anticipated to address difficulties with considerable efficacy. The environment encompasses all external factors to the agent. The interaction between the agent and its environment is confined to rewards (obtained from the environment), actions (executed by the agent and conveyed to the environment), and observations (comprising the reward combined with other information acquired by the agent). Actions are the activities that the agent can perform inside the environment. Actions may range from straightforward, such as advancing a pawn one square in a game, to intricate, such as completing a tax form for the following day. In RL, activities can be categorized as either discrete or continuous [20]. Discrete actions constitute a finite collection of mutually exclusive options, such as moving left or right. Ongoing actions possess a related value; for instance, the rotation of a car’s steering wheel or its angle, where varying degrees may result in distinct scenarios shortly thereafter. Consequently, merely rotating the wheel is often inadequate, it necessitates meticulous contemplation of the specific action executed.

The observation of the environment constitutes the second source of knowledge for an agent, the first being the reward. Furthermore, an additional data source is necessary, as it offers ease. Observations are data supplied by the environment, reflecting the occurrences surrounding the agent. Observations may pertain to the impending reward (e.g., viewing a bank statement that verifies a payment), or they may be unrelated. They may also encompass reward information in an ambiguous or intricate manner, such as the score metrics exhibited on a computer game’s display. The numerical scores are merely pixels, although they may be transmuted into reward values. Conversely, the reward must not be regarded as ancillary or trivial; it is the principal catalyst that propels the learning process. An inaccurate, noisy, or somewhat misaligned reward poses a danger of misdirecting the training process. It is essential to differentiate between the condition of the environment and the observations made. The environmental state may encompass every atom in the universe, rendering comprehensive measurement unattainable. Even in a sufficiently constrained setting, it may remain impossible to acquire comprehensive information, or the measurements may be compromised by noise. Nonetheless, RL is intended to facilitate such circumstances locally.

section: III. REINFORCEMENT LEARNING — B. IMPROVEMENT OF THE RL WITH THE Q-LEARNING

input:
QL is a preferred reinforcement learning algorithm where the agent learns an optimal policy through state changes, with expected rewards documented in a table for each state-action pair [12], [17]. As state and action dimensions increase, table storage and updating become complicated. The QL algorithm is an improved iteration of the Bellman equation; the stochastic formulation incorporates expectations over probabilistic transitions and rewards, enabling better generalization and robustness under uncertainty compared to the deterministic formulation, which assumes fixed transitions and may overfit specific scenarios [12], [17]. In dynamic environments like network security, the stochastic Bellman formulation ensures policies remain effective despite uncertainties [12], [17].

The deterministic Bellman equation is:

V(s) = max_a(R(s, a) + γV(s′)) (1)

In a reinforcement learning context, the Bellman equation calculates uncertain probabilities appropriate for stochastic environments, leading to the Markov Decision Process (MDP) when supplemented with randomization [21]. MDP operates as a stochastic control process in discrete time, where the future depends solely on the present state and action (Markov property). A novel probabilistic equation combining MDP and the Bellman equation is used by reinforcement learning to allow agents to navigate and make decisions in the environment:

V(s) = max_a[R(s, a) + γ ∑_{s′,a′} P_{s,a,s′} V(s′)] (2)

The Q-Learning algorithm developed from this formula. The updated Q-value is calculated as:

NewQ(s, a) = Q(s, a) + α[R(s, a) + γ max_{s′,a′} Q′(s′, a′) − Q(s, a)] (3)

NewQ(s, a) represents the updated Q-value for a state-action pair after learning from an experience. The equation starts with the current Q-value, to which the learning rate (α) multiplied by the temporal difference error is added. The reward for taking an action in a state is R(s, a). The discount rate (γ) multiplied by the maximum expected future reward, max_{s′,a′} Q′(s′, a′), where s′ is the next state and a′ is the best possible action, estimates future potential. This whole expression updates the agent’s knowledge about the quality of taking a certain action in a certain state.

Future rewards possess diminished worth relative to immediate rewards, guaranteeing the agent prioritizes both immediate and enduring rewards to maximize overall benefit [21]. The discount rate γ ∈ [0, 1] directly impacts the agent’s decision-making timeframe. A reduced γ (e.g., 0.1) compels the agent to prioritize immediate gains, leading to myopic policies that may neglect long-term hazards. A higher γ (e.g., 0.9 or 0.99) allows the agent to assess long-term ramifications, promoting tactics that optimize cumulative rewards over time. In intrusion detection, long-term planning is crucial for identifying slow-evolving or covert assault behaviors [21].

Temporal Difference (TD) is a model-independent learning approach where the model is trained by bootstrapping, relying on the existing estimate of the value function [21]. As the agent navigates the environment, it must determine which action will produce the greatest reward. TD denotes the agent’s capacity to revise predictions without awaiting the anticipated outcome. TD data are utilized in the construction of the Q-table. The TD value at time t+1 is computed by multiplying it by a constant known as the learning rate, which subsequently determines the Q value at time t+1. The learning rate should be adaptive. The agent autonomously executes its new state and action inside the environment. However, the agent will be unable to explore if it solely navigates by referencing the highest values in the Q-table. To sustain this equilibrium, the Epsilon-Greedy (ϵ) value is utilized rather than exclusively relying on the Q-Table values [4]. Epsilon-Greedy is a straightforward technique for balancing global (exploration) and local (exploitation) search by random selection between the two approaches. Prior to the agent’s action, a probability value is produced. If this value is less than the epsilon value, a random move is executed; otherwise, the course previously pursued is selected [4].

action at time t = { maxQ_t(action), probability of 1 − ϵ; any action, probability of ϵ } (4)

In the Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) method, adaptive epsilon-greedy is employed instead of a singular epsilon value [4]. Adaptive epsilon-greedy is initialized with a value and subsequently diminished at a specified rate. If Epsilon equals 1, exploration is at 100%. NewQ (s, a) represents the updated Q-value for a specific state-action pair after learning from an experience. The equation starts with the current Q-value, denoted as Q (s, a). To this, we add the learning rate (α) multiplied by the difference between the obtained reward and the current estimate. The reward for taking an action in a state is expressed as R (s, a). To estimate the future potential, we add the discount rate (γ) multiplied by the maximum expected future reward, represented as maxQ′ s′, a′, where s′ is the next state and a′ is the best possible action in that state. Finally, we subtract the current Q-value again, completing the temporal difference calculation. This whole expression updates the agent’s knowledge about how good it is to take a certain action in a certain state.

When an agent executes a certain action, the consequences of this action manifest after a delay, and these outcomes are met with a specific reward or punishment. Nonetheless, a future reward possesses diminished worth relative to an immediate reward. This scenario guarantees that the agent prioritizes both immediate and enduring rewards. The agent consistently evaluates the future ramifications of its present actions to maximize overall benefit. This equation, which aids in ascertaining the new state and action, employs the discount rate constant to equilibrate future rewards with present rewards. The reward emerges and fluctuates based on the objectives of the environment. When assessing the outcomes of an agent executing a certain activity, a method is employed to discount future rewards to their current worth.

The selection of the discount rate γ ∈[0, 1] directly impacts the agent’s decision-making timeframe. A reduced γ (e.g., 0.1) compels the agent to prioritize immediate gains, leading to myopic policies that may neglect long-term hazards. A higher γ (e.g., 0.9 or 0.99) allows the agent to assess the long-term ramifications of its actions, promoting tactics that optimize cumulative rewards over time. In the realm of intrusion detection, long-term planning is crucial for identifying slow-evolving or covert assault behaviors that may not yield rapid, readily detectable fingerprints.

Temporal Difference (TD) is an approach for learning that is independent of any specific model. The model is trained by bootstrapping, which relies on the existing estimate of the value function. Methods are extracted from the environment, and modifications are implemented based on the prevailing estimate. As the agent navigates the environment, it must determine which action will produce the greatest reward. TD denotes the agent’s capacity to revise its predictions without awaiting the anticipated outcome inside the environment. TD data are utilized in the construction of the Q-table. The TD value at time t+1 is computed by multiplying it by a constant known as the learning rate, which subsequently determines the Q value at time t+1. The learning rate should be adaptive. The agent autonomously executes its new state and activity inside the environment in this manner. Nonetheless, the agent will be unable to explore if it solely navigates by referencing the highest values in the Q-table. In this instance, it may fail to recognize that the path it is on is the proper one. Occasionally, the agent is required to investigate. Local search (exploitation) pertains to consistently adhering to a singular trajectory and progressing according to the maximum reward. By diverging from its established trajectory within the environment and conducting a more extensive search, the agent engages in a global search (exploration). If the agent consistently engages in local search, it may forfeit the opportunity to get greater rewards. Furthermore, there may be a temporal loss. To sustain this equilibrium, we utilize the Epsilon-Greedy (ϵ) value rather than exclusively relying on the values from the Q-Table. Epsilon-Greedy is a straightforward technique for balancing global and local search by random selection between the two approaches. Prior to the agent’s action, it produces a probability value. If this value is less than the epsilon value, it will execute a random move. Otherwise, it will perpetually select the course it has been pursuing.

In the DRL method, adaptive epsilon-greedy is employed instead of a singular epsilon value. Adaptive epsilon-greedy is initialized with this value and subsequently diminished at a specified rate. If Epsilon equals 1, exploration is at 100%. The epsilon value is updated by multiplying it with the epsilon decay, which is presumed to be 0.018, in each iteration. From this viewpoint, a substantial epsilon value is originally proposed, and the entire environment is examined. As experience accumulates, the agent acclimatizes to the environment, resulting in a diminished epsilon value. In this manner, the agent might utilize the acquired values and proceed from them. The pseudocode for the Epsilon-Greedy algorithm is presented in Table 1.

To check if the epsilon-greedy method works properly, we show the real-time changes using graphs created from Python code based on the pseudocode. Anaconda Spyder was used as the coding tool. Figure 1 shows the graph of data for various epsilon values from the code that was run. A comparison was conducted by presenting all scenarios on a singular graph. The epsilon-greedy values were sequentially established at 0.02, 0.002, and 0.0002. The graph indicates that as the epsilon value diminishes, the reward value escalates following a specific number of trials. The epsilon value must be calibrated to the most precise parameter for the agent to facilitate correct computations. Smaller epsilon values resulted in more stable and higher cumulative rewards over time. This is because reduced exploration enables the agent to increasingly exploit learned high-value actions, leading to improved performance once a reliable policy has been established. Even though Figure 1 presents just one example, we saw the same patterns of improvement in many separate tests for each epsilon value, which confirms that the reward trends are trustworthy. In these experiments, a system was developed to attain the maximum reward value of 3 in a limited number of attempts. The values’ results are presented below, respectively:

Since the discount rate (set to 0.9) progressively reduces the weight of future rewards, the agent assigns higher importance to immediate and accurate actions than to uncertain exploratory steps. Under such conditions, a smaller epsilon parameter minimizes unnecessary randomness and enhances policy stability, allowing the agent to consistently exploit high-value actions once they have been identified. While Epsilon-Greedy is 0.02 initially and exhibits faster reward growth, it stabilizes at a lower cumulative reward compared to smaller epsilon values. In contrast, epsilon-greedy is 0.002 and epsilon-greedy is 0.0002; both converge to the maximum reward value of approximately 3.0, as reflected in the final trials (e.g., 2.9969 and 2.9993). These results confirm that reducing exploration improves convergence and long-term performance once the Q-network has sufficiently learned the environment.

Another significant element in conjunction with the epsilon-greedy value is the living penalty (LP) value. LP value denotes the penalty incurred by the agent for each additional unit of time spent in the environment. LP is a parameter that must be judiciously selected. Based on the chosen LP parameter, the agent will either engage in risk-taking or go without risk. The optimal equilibrium of this parameter is essential, as insufficient or excessive amounts can inflict considerable harm on the reward system. The agent’s objective is to attain the maximum reward value. An elevation in the LP value necessitates that the agent generate a solution expeditiously. The agent may be compelled to choose the most perilous route to achieve the objective instead of the safest one. The LP parameter has a direct effect on the reward structure, which in turn affects how the agent makes decisions. An LP that is too high makes the agent act quickly, which can damage accuracy. On the other hand, an LP that is too low has the agent make decisions that are careful but take a long time. So, it’s important to carefully tune LP to find the right balance between speed and accuracy in decision-making, which will lead to strong and efficient policy convergence.

From a policy learning standpoint, the LP value directly affects the updating of Q-values during training. An elevated LP predisposes the agent to prioritize short-term incentives, resulting in swift although potentially poor policy convergence. On the other hand, a very low learning parameter impedes convergence, as the agent partakes in extended cautious exploration. Accurately calibrated LP values equilibrate these influences, facilitating steady and efficient policy learning over time.

This study favors Deep Q-Learning (DQL), which employs a deep neural network to estimate the Q-function, enabling scalable reinforcement learning where tabular approaches are infeasible. Our DQL framework is based on the DQN architecture, enabling efficient policy learning in complex, real-world intrusion detection scenarios.

Two primary justifications exist for selecting DQL over Q-Learning. First, as the number of states increases, preparing a Q-table becomes increasingly challenging, approaching impossibility; the addition of states poses hardware challenges, and retrieval and updating of Q-values is difficult. Second, the magnitude of the state space presents a practical challenge; for instance, a technique feasible for 500 states is impractical for 10,000 states, such as in gaming applications where each pixel signifies a state.

In DQL, approximation is employed instead of directly computing Q-values, enabling the technique to converge towards the ideal Q-value rather than constructing a Q-table. The number of neurons in the input layer varies contingent upon the study. The algorithm performs forward prediction; it analyzes Q-values generated for each action and selects the maximum value. The DQL algorithm trains the model utilizing states and Q-values. $$loss = \left( r + \gamma \max_{a'} \hat{Q}_{s, a'} - Q(s, a) \right)^2 \quad (5)$$

The agent aims to choose the best action based on information from the environment; a higher Q-value indicates better results. The pseudocode in Table 2 shows the step-by-step learning process from own experiences without a dataset. In the DQL method, the environment has action options $A = \{up, down, right, left\}$. input:
V. RESULTS

This section evaluates RF, DT, and DQL models on the CIC-IDS2017 dataset to analyze their efficacy in identifying known and zero-day threats. Results report accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 scores. Computational overhead is measured via training time (wall-clock to convergence) and inference time (average per-sample latency). DQL uses a fully connected feedforward network with three hidden layers (128, 64, 32 neurons) and ReLU activation, with a linear output layer for Q-value estimation trained via Adam optimizer and mean squared error loss. All models were implemented in Python under identical conditions using an Intel Core i9 CPU, NVIDIA RTX-4070, 32 GB RAM running Windows 11.

V. RESULTS

This section presents the test outcomes from evaluating the performance of the RF, DT, and DQL models utilizing the CIC-IDS2017 dataset. The assessment sought to analyze the efficacy of each model in identifying both recognized and unknown (zero-day) cyber threats. The results are organized to illustrate the accuracy, precision, recall, and enhanced F1 score of each model. We record the time necessary for computations during training and prediction to demonstrate the models’ practical applicability. We meticulously examine the impact of hyperparameter modifications on the DQL model’s generalization capability. This aids in comprehending its application in evolving cybersecurity scenarios. This comprehensive comparison delineates the advantages and disadvantages of ML and DRL in adaptive intrusion detection contexts.

This study used the DQL model, which comprises a fully connected feedforward neural network with three hidden layers. The hidden layers have 128, 64, and 32 neurons. After each hidden layer, the ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit) activation function is employed to make things more non-linear. The output layer utilizes a linear activation function to guess the Q-values for every conceivable action. The Adam optimizer and a mean squared error loss function are used by the network to train.

All experiments were conducted on Intel Core i9 CPU, NVIDIA RTX-4070, 32 GB RAM, running Windows 11, with all models (DQL, RF, and DT) implemented in Python under identical conditions to ensure comparability. Computational overhead was measured primarily in terms of time: training time was defined as the total wall-clock time to convergence and recorded using the Python time function, while inference time was defined as the average per-sample prediction latency across the test set. Each inference measurement was repeated five times, and consistent results were reported; resource consumption such as CPU/GPU utilization was not separately recorded, as the identical experimental setup made time-based measurements sufficient.

section: V. RESULTS — A. INTRUSION DETECTION DATASET
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
The CIC-IDS2017 dataset from the Canadian Institute for Cybersecurity serves as a benchmark for intrusion detection [11]. It contains normal traffic and various cyberattacks, allowing testing of machine learning and deep learning models. The dataset comprises real network traffic, including web surfing, email, file transfers, and streaming. Simulations of Denial of Service (DoS), Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS), brute-force, penetration, botnet, and port-scanning attacks were conducted. To optimize model performance, a feature selection method eliminated redundant and nonessential elements. Data cleaning addressed missing (NaN) and infinite (inf) values; absent values were replaced with column averages. Categorical labels were converted to quantitative representations. Statistical techniques removed highly correlated features to mitigate multicollinearity, and low-variance features were removed to retain impactful properties [10].

Seventy-eight features capture network traffic aspects such as packet sizes, flow durations, protocol types, and connection counts. Attack strategy investigation revealed mostly benign traffic, making DoS and DDoS attacks common, while botnet, brute-force, and port-scanning attacks occur less frequently. This diversity allows models to learn from varied attack strategies, enhancing generalization.

This study used CIC-IDS2017 to recreate a zero-day attack scenario by excluding a specific attack type (e.g., PortScan) from training despite its presence in testing. This evaluated models’ ability to extend beyond known patterns. Stratified sampling preserved class distribution, resulting in 80% training and 20% testing splits. StandardScaler normalized numerical features to zero mean and unit variance. Identical partitioning across all models maintained internal equity, facilitating a controlled assessment. While this deviates from traditional evaluation practices, it reflects a deliberate design to assess generalization to novel attacks rather than benchmarking against known patterns. The objective was to examine models’ ability, especially DQL, to respond to novel threats, a necessity for real-world systems.

The processed dataset trained DQL, RF, and DT models. Performance was examined on distinguishing known versus novel attacks, clarifying machine learning and deep reinforcement learning capabilities in adaptive threat detection. Feature selection reduced dimensionality, lowering computational load and improving efficiency. Selecting optimal features ensures models distinguish normal from attack traffic, improving classification accuracy and efficiency.

This work applies three main criteria for feature selection. Attack frameworks track basic network flow characteristics like packet sizes, connection durations, data flow rates, and protocol types, which distinguish network activity. Statistical investigation of attribute-label links identified and eliminated high-correlation elements, reducing overfitting risk and minimizing redundancy. The process ensured models focused on distinctive, instructional characteristics. Features with low predictive power were removed to maximize training time and enhance adaptability to various attack patterns, reducing complexity and improving scalability. These techniques made the DQL model more effective at finding previously undetected attacks (zero-day attacks).

DQL was used assuming full observability, utilizing manufactured statistical and temporal features from CIC-IDS2017. Although the environment may exhibit partial observability, the Markov Decision Process (MDP) assumption serves as a practical simplification. Engineered statistical and temporal features enhance effective observability of the state space and reduce uncertainty from incomplete information, enabling the DQL agent to learn effective policies despite incomplete observability.

Additional datasets corroborated findings. NSL-KDD and AWID were employed due to their distributional and feature complexity disparities [24], [25]. NSL-KDD assesses classifier robustness across varying train-test label distributions. AWID enables evaluations in large-scale, significantly imbalanced wireless intrusion environments.

Our aim in creating this dataset was to offer a reasonable environment in which to assess intrusion detection techniques in the framework of an always-shifting cybersecurity situation. Data preprocessing involved replacing missing and infinite values with column means and converting labels to numerical format (Non-threatening: 0; Service Interruption: 1; Distributed Service Interruption: 2; Port Examination: 3). The dataset was split 80/20 using stratified sampling. Features were standardized using StandardScaler.

Machine learning models (RF, DT) and deep reinforcement learning (DQL) were trained and compared. RF used 100 trees (n_estimators=100), Gini criterion, and parallel processing (n_jobs=-1). DT used entropy splitting with a tuned maximum depth. DQL used a three-layer ANN (128-64-32 neurons) with ReLU activation. The output layer had four neurons corresponding to BENIGN, DoS, DDoS, and PortScan attacks. Training used the Adam optimizer (learning rate=0.001), epsilon-greedy exploration, a discount factor of 0.95, and epsilon decay from 1.0 to 0.01 (decay rate=0.995). Experience replay stored 2000 samples with a mini-batch size of 64 over 10 epochs.

Random Forest achieved 99% accuracy. DQL achieved 94% accuracy. RF outperformed DQL in known attack detection, as RF excels at memorizing labeled patterns while DQL prioritizes generalization for zero-day threats. RF is highly accurate and fast for conventional IDS. DQL remains valuable for dynamic threat identification despite higher computational costs.

V. RESULTS — D. KNOWN ATTACK DETECTION

Using different preprocessing methods on the CIC-IDS2017 dataset improves the training process and makes this part of the model more accurate. To ensure data consistency, we initially identified and addressed missing and infinite (inf) values by replacing them with the mean of their respective columns. To ensure compatibility with ML techniques, we converted the target variable label from its original format into a numerical representation. The converter implemented this mapping: Non-threatening; Service Interruption; Distributed Service Interruption; Port Examination; 0; 1; 2; 3.

We divided the dataset into 80% for training and 20% for testing, maintaining a class balance through stratified sampling. This phase was crucial to ensure that both the training and testing stages accurately reflected the diverse range of attacks. After feature scaling, we implemented the StandardScaler method, which transformed all features into a zero-mean, unit-variance scale. DQL, known for their sensitivity to feature scaling, rely heavily on this preprocessing stage. Standardizing the features improves learning efficiency and performance, contributing to a more stable model training process.

We taught different ML models, such as RF and DT, and DRL models, such as DQL. Then, we compared how well these models worked to other models. For training, the DQL model used a deep neural network architecture based on reinforcement learning. RF and DT, on the other hand, were made using standard machine-learning techniques. The hyperparameters for the machine learning models were automatically optimal. The Random Forest model is configured with 100 decision trees (n_estimators=100) and employs a predetermined maximum depth, utilizing the Gini index as the criterion for splitting. Furthermore, parallel processing was initiated (n_jobs=-1) to fully utilize all available CPU cores. We developed the decision tree model with a self-determined maximum depth, utilizing an entropy-based splitting criterion.

A three-layer ANN was used to build a DQL model. The number of neurons in the input layer was set to match the number of features in the dataset. The initial layer employed ReLU activation functions and consisted of 128 neurons, followed by a second layer with 64 neurons and a third layer comprising 32 neurons. There were four neurons in the output layer. Each one represented one of the four types of attacks in the CIC-IDS2017 dataset: BENIGN, DoS, DDoS, and PortScan. During the training phase, we employed the Adam optimization algorithm, setting the learning rate at 0.001. We used an epsilon-greedy exploration method to let the model first look into random actions and then get better at making decisions by getting rewards.

A reward discount factor of 0.95 was employed to develop the reward-based learning process. Epsilon was initially established at 1.0 and underwent a decay rate of 0.995 with each iteration, ultimately reaching a minimum value of 0.01. The addition of an experience replay mechanism significantly improved learning efficiency by retaining 2000 experiences in a replay memory buffer. Throughout ten epochs, the model was trained using a mini-batch size of sixty-four samples for every iteration. The reward mechanism of the DQL model consisted of offering positive reinforcement for accurate predictions while implementing negative consequences for inaccuracies. The test dataset was used to see how well RF, DT, and DQL models sorted intrusion detection results into groups after the training phase was over.

RF model demonstrated superior accuracy in comparison to all other models assessed, as evidenced by the experimental results. Although DT model demonstrates notable computational efficiency [27], its performance is significantly inferior to that of the RF model.

Random Forest (99%) outperformed DQL (94%) in identifying known assaults. Because the two learning approaches are so different, this is expected. The supervised learning model Random Forest learns from labeled attack data. It is quite good at memorizing and finding patterns. DQL prioritizes generalization over memorization with long-term reward optimization and interaction-based learning. DQL is stronger at finding new or changing risks like zero-day assaults than it is at determining the past.

The results show that, when established attack patterns are present, machine learning models, especially RF, work rather well for IDS. A strong candidate for conventional IDS, RF is highly accurate and trains rapidly in settings free of unidentified attacks. With a 94% accuracy rate, the DQL model demonstrated that it could train on its own devoid of a specified dataset. In dynamic cybersecurity contexts, where traditional ML models would not be able to handle threat types not yet addressed, this demonstrates its value. However, the computational complexity and extended training length of DQL render it unsuitable for real-time applications without further advancements. DQL can be used instead of adaptive intrusion detection when dynamic threat identification is needed [28]. This is done by improving hyperparameters and training effectiveness. So, even though RF is better at quickly and accurately finding intrusions in known attacks, DQL works just as well and is a good way to take the next steps forward in cybersecurity.

V. RESULTS — F. DQL MODEL PERFORMANCE ON DIFFERENT DATASETS AND HYPERPARAMETER TUNING

As shown in Figure 5, the comparative evaluation of the DQL model across the CIC-IDS2017, NSL-KDD, and AWID datasets offers important insights into its robustness and generalization capacity under heterogeneous experimental conditions. On CIC-IDS2017, the model achieved an accuracy of 0.9407, with precision of 0.9187, recall of 0.9325, and an F1-score of 0.9256. These results demonstrate strong predictive capability on modern, complex traffic scenarios, where multiple attack families coexist.

In contrast, the NSL-KDD dataset posed a more demanding challenge due to its intentional divergence between training and test label distributions. In NSL-KDD dataset, performance decreased to an accuracy of 0.8172, precision of 0.8073, recall of 0.8172, and an F1-score of 0.8076. This reduction underscores the inherent difficulty of generalizing across non-overlapping attack distributions and highlights the necessity of adaptive exploration strategies in RL approaches.

On the AWID dataset characterized by extreme imbalance and a huge sample size, the DQL model demonstrated competitive results, with an accuracy of 0.9400, precision of 0.9484, recall of 0.9400, and an F1-score of 0.9434. In intrusion detection experiments, this kind of validation is very important because models need to work well not only in controlled experiments but also when they have to deal with new and unbalanced traffic patterns. The results thus illustrate both the capabilities and constraints of DQL; it demonstrates considerable accuracy and adaptability in intricate situations, yet its pronounced sensitivity to distributional shifts, as evidenced in the NSL-KDD dataset, poses a substantial obstacle for practical implementation. Also, it should be noted that the comparative evaluation reported here was done on known-attack instances from all three datasets to ensure that the experimental conditions were the same. This constraint was imposed because heterogeneous attack taxonomies and attack dynamics (for example, a port scan in one dataset versus a volumetric DDoS in another) introduce confounding factors that can substantially alter feature distributions, temporal patterns, and class imbalance, thereby biasing cross-dataset comparisons.

Figure 6 shows that the hyperparameters you choose especially the learning rate, exploration-exploitation strategy, batch size, and dimensions of the experience replay buffer have a big effect on how well the DQL model works.

We investigated two different configurations to see how they affected the model's generalizing capability and classification accuracy in spotting zero-day threats. The first configuration used a high learning rate of 0.99, an epsilon decay rate of 0.99, a large batch size of 256, a limited experience replay buffer of 1000, and a brief training time of 3 epochs. Under these conditions, the DQL model obtained an accuracy of 0.5465 and an F1 score of 0.5229, indicating that it suffered when generalizing to foreign attack patterns. The fast epsilon decay may have made it harder for the model to explore enough before using patterns it had learned. Also, the high learning rate probably made the model change its weights too quickly, which stopped steady convergence.

In the second setup, the learning rate was slowed down to 0.001 and epsilon decay was slowed down to 0.995. This gave the model more time to look for the best policies before they were found. Using a smaller batch size of 64 and a larger experience replay buffer of 2000 lets the model recall more past experiences for better decision-making. We added ten training sessions to enhance the learning process. This configuration produced an F1 score of 0.90 and an accuracy of 0.89, therefore indicating that a controlled learning rate and extended training period improved performance and generalization. The findings show that for intrusion detection models that use DRL, a lower learning rate, more exploration, and a batch size that is pretty evenly spread out make the models more stable and accurate.

Figure 7 shows the Accuracy performance of the proposed DQL model under 27 distinct hyperparameter configurations involving variations in learning rate (lr), epsilon decay (ed), and batch size. Each x-axis label represents a unique parameter combination in the format lr, ed, enabling direct interpretation of the tuning conditions. The results demonstrate that lower learning rates (e.g., 0.001 or 0.01) and higher epsilon decay values (e.g., 0.99 or 0.999) lead to a marked improvement in classification accuracy. Among the evaluated batch sizes, 64 generally yields the most stable and high-performing configurations.

Figure 8 depicts the F1-score performance of the DQL model across the identical 27 hyperparameter configurations assessed in Figure 8. The results confirm the accuracy patterns depicted in Figure 8, with optimal performance attained at lower learning rates and elevated epsilon decay values. The uniformity across measures highlights the essential function of systematic hyperparameter adjustment in improving model resilience and generalization.

section: I. INTRODUCTION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: BCI systems translate brain signals into device control commands. EEG-based BCIs are divided into exogenous types, which rely on externally evoked signals like P300 and SSVEP, and endogenous types, which use self-regulated signals such as motor imagery (MI). Most endogenous BCIs require users to learn MI control, a process often lasting weeks or months, with 15%–30% of subjects unable to achieve control, known as BCI illiteracy. Effective control requires the user to generate discriminative brain signals and the decoder to accurately map these to commands. The learning process involves machine learning to train the decoder and human learning to train the user, often using feedback. Coadaptive methods iteratively update both the decoder and subject, but assume the subject can learn effectively at every stage. This study proposes a joint human-machine learning framework where both processes are optimized simultaneously using a shared loss function. The framework treats human learning as a trial-and-error process, guiding subjects to copy "good" brain signals or modify "poor" ones. The decoder adaptively reweights signals to focus on successful samples. Experiments with 18 healthy subjects showed the framework improved average control accuracy from 69.1% to 74.5% compared to traditional coadaptive approaches.
