B
RAIN–COMPUTER interfaces (BCIs) act as an intermediary between the brain and external devices, translating
brain signals to control signals [1], [2]. BCIs employing electroencephalogram (EEG) signals have been developed successfully for many applications, including neural rehabilitation,
prosthesis control, and emotion recognition [3], [4], [5], [6],
[7], [8], [9], [10]. Most existing BCI systems can be divided
into endogenous and exogenous BCIs [11], [12]. Exogenous
BCIs such as the P300 and SSVEP systems, rely on brain
signals evoked by external stimuli [13], [14], such as visual
flashes or audio events. Conversely, endogenous BCIs, such
as based on motor imagery (MI), rely on self-regulated brain
signals often induced by users’ covert attention or mental
tasks [15], [16]. Thus, endogenous BCIs can provide more
flexible and natural brain control, resulting in high potential for a wide range of applications [17], [18], [19], [20].
In the remainder of this article, we will only focus on
endogenous BCIs.
Effective BCI control relies on the close collaboration of
the brain (the subject) and the machine (the decoder) [21]. The
user should generate discriminative and sufficient brain signals
as different control commands, while the decoder should identify different brain signal patterns and robustly interpret/map
them into control commands. For endogenous BCIs, the main
challenge lies in the difficulty for the user in generating
effective and stable brain signals. To achieve robust online
control, the BCI user should be able to accurately replicate at
least two discriminative and stable patterns for basic control,
such as going left and right. A typical endogenous BCI is
based on MI, where the user is asked to imagine movements,
for example of the left/right hand. However, generating MI
is challenging for most users, and a typical user usually
requires a long and difficult training process to learn the MI
control. Commonly, training for MI lasts several weeks or even
months [22], [23]. Furthermore, there are at least 15%–30% of
subjects across the population who cannot control BCI systems
through learning, a case called BCI illiteracy [24]. For these
reasons, the facilitation of the learning process in endogenous
BCIs is a very relevant problem.
The learning process in BCIs includes two parts: the learning of the decoder (machine learning), and the learning of the

See https://www.ieee.org/publications/rights/index.html for more information.
user (human learning). Here, we briefly review the existing
approaches.
1) Machine Learning: Traditional BCI training processes
start with a static subject learning process where the
subject tries to generate brain signals without feedback.
Then a decoder is trained with the initial data to
learn discriminative features from different brain signals
[as shown in Fig. 1(a)]. The discrimination of different
brain signal patterns can be regarded as a typical classification problem. Thus, linear and nonlinear classifiers
have been proposed for the decoding problem. For linear
methods, decoding in MI can be separated into feature
extraction and classification. Common spatial pattern
(CSP) is a widely used linear approach for extracting
discriminative features from different brain signal patterns. Filter bank CSP (FBCSP) [25] extends CSP with
a set of bandpass filters to enhance features, and it
can also be applied in neural networks [26]. However,
traditional CSP is not suitable for multiclass problems.
Joint approximate diagonalization (JAD)-based methods
are used to improve CSP [27]. Moreover, modifications have been made to enhance CSPs to deal with
the nonstationarity in EEG signals. Fuzzy covariance
matrices are deployed in DivCSP-WS to extract steady
features [28]. Channel selection methods could also
improve stability between sessions, improving the classification accuracy [29].
In terms of classification methods, linear discriminant
analysis (LDA) is commonly used for extracted features [30]. To enhance robustness on nonstationary EEG
signals, variations of LDA such as regularized LDA
(rLDA) and Bayesian LDA (BLDA) have been introduced [31], [32], [33]. Support vector machines (SVMs)
with flexible kernel design are with feature extraction
methods in some studies [34], [35]. Recently, deep
learning approaches including long short term memory (LSTM) [36], [37], [38] and convolutional neural
networks (CNNs) [39], [40], [41], [42], [43], such as
EEGnet [44], have demonstrated effectiveness in MI
classification. Combining the feature extraction methods and the deep learning approach, neural structured
learning (NSL) has been proposed to train deep neural
networks with feature inputs and the structured signals,
which enhances the robustness [45].
2) Human Learning: After the initial decoder is trained, the
subject can learn to control the BCI with the feedback
of the decoder, where the design of the feedback plays
an important part [see Fig. 1(b)]. Traditional feedbacks
usually directly reflect the decoding result, using a
moving cursor or a falling ball [46], [47]. To improve
the efficiency of subject learning, new paradigms with
different types of feedback have been introduced. For
example, Hwang et al. [23] proposed an intuitive feedback that uses a surface topography of EEG signal,
where the real-time spectrogram is presented to enhance
the MI [48]. Wang et al. [49] proposed a neurofeedback
training paradigm, in which the performance of MI
was transferred into the distance between a needle and
hands on the screen. Alternatively, auditory feedbacks
of different sounds have been presented to subject
depending on their MI performance [50]. Nevertheless, Shu et al. [51] and Yao et al. [52] proposed tactile
stimulation to help subjects improve the MI activation.
Also, Ono et al. [53] adopted exoskeleton attached to
subjects, making feedbacks more sensible.
3) Coadaptive Learning: The aforementioned approaches
mostly focus on one side of the learning, either the
signal generation by the user or the algorithm training
by the machine. However, coadaptive methods have also
been introduced [54], [55]. Instead of using a fixed
decoder after the initial training process, coadaptive
approaches retrain both the decoder and the subject
iteratively in sequential learning sessions to cope with
each other [54], [56] [see Fig. 1(c)]. To this end, different
decoder recalibration algorithms have been proposed
using machine learning approaches such as LDA [57],
SVM [58], probabilistic graphical models [59] to update
the decoder with newly collected data to cope with
changes in brain signals during the subject learning process. By considering the interaction between the subject
and the decoder, coadaptive approaches demonstrated
superior performance in BCI learning than separate
learning approaches [60], [61]. To provide a mathematical basis of coadaptive learning processes, previous
work has modeled the process with mathematical formulations. For example, in
[62], an encoder–decoder
model was proposed, in which the coadaptation was
described by the optimization of the user’s control.
With the assumption of two linear learning systems,
a theoretical formulation was derived by the stochastic
gradient descent method in [63].
In Fig. 1, we illustrate and compare the aforementioned
learning process in an intuitive way. Suppose there is a global
optimal point for the human–machine BCI learning process.
With the machine learning model alone [see Fig. 1(a)], where
the human model is static, the optimal performance is highly
limited by the boundary of brain signal patterns. With the
human learning model alone [see Fig. 1(b)], where the decoder
is fixed, the subject can learn with the guidance of the
decoder’s feedback. The performance highly relies on the
effectiveness of the decoder. Since the decoder is usually
trained with the initially imperfect brain signals of the subject,
it can be suboptimal and can degrade the human learning
process. The coadaptation model [see Fig. 1(c)] considers both
machine learning and human learning, where the decoder is
iteratively updated along with the human learning process.
Specifically, it contains an iterative process where the machine
and the human learn alternately, which improves the theoretical overall performance. However, it assumes that the subject
can effectively learn at every human learning stage, which can
be difficult, especially at the beginning rounds of the training
process.
This study proposes a novel BCI learning scheme for
efficient and effective BCI training. As shown in Fig. 1(d),
we aim to construct a joint learning model between humans
and machines, where human and machine processes can be
optimized simultaneously. To this end, we propose a novel
human–machine joint learning framework for effective BCI
training. Specifically, we assume the human learning behavior
in sequential training is a trial-and-error process, and let the
decoder determine whether a brain signal is “good” or “poor”
by its discrimination ability according to the distribution of the
feature space. The contribution of this study is summarized in
threefold.
1) We formally formulate the human–machine joint learning model and propose a human–machine joint loss
function, where the subject is encouraged to generate
Fig. 1.
Illustration of BCI training with different strategies. (a) Process of
decoder learning (machine learning model) gives a set of subject-generated
data (indicated by the red circle). (b) Subject learning (human learning model)
process with feedback from a fixed decoder. (c) Coadaptation learning process
is where the subject and the decoder learn in an alternate manner. (d) Proposed
joint learning process is where the subject and the decoder share the same

more discriminative brain signals, and the decoder optimizes the classifier to separate the different brain signal
modes.
2) From the human side, we formulate human behavior
in a sequential trial-and-error learning process. A novel
paradigm is proposed to guide the subject to optimize
brain signals. Specifically, if a “good” signal is generated, the system encourages the subject to “copy” the
state; otherwise, if a “poor” signal is generated, the
subject is encouraged to change the brain signal.
3) From the machine side, we propose a novel adaptive
learning algorithm to learn an optimal signal distribution
along with the subject’s learning process. Specifically,
the decoder reweighs the brain signals generated by the
subject to focus more on “good” samples to cope with
the learning process of the subject.
Online BCI experiments with 18 healthy subjects demonstrated that the joint learning framework can efficiently
guide the subject learning discriminate brain signals for
effective BCI control. Compared with traditional coadaptive
approaches, our method significantly improved the average
control accuracy from 69.1% to 74.5%.

section: II. HUMAN–MACHINE JOINT LEARNING FRAMEWORK — A. Modeling of the Human–Machine Joint Learning
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
BCI learning treats the subject and decoder as joint learners aiming for accurate intention decoding. The human learning model generates signals x based on label y and parameters θH, while the machine model decodes label y′ from x using function h and parameters θM. The mutual goal minimizes the distance between true label y and decoded label y′, defined as L_H−M = ||y′ − y||. Joint optimization minimizes L_H−M = ||h(θ_M, g(θ_H, y)) − y|| over θ_H and θ_M.

Human learning models the subject as a Markov process where the objective is to maximize the probability of generating "good" samples (x_G) and minimize "bad" samples (x_B). The learning objective is arg max_θ_H P(x_G)/P(x_B). A transition matrix defines state transitions between x_G and x_B, with steady-state probabilities derived as P(x_G)/P(x_B) = (1−P_BB)/(1−P_GG). Effective learning requires high P_GG and low P_BB.

Machine learning proposes a sample reweighting algorithm to adapt the decoder. Sample quality q_i is evaluated inversely proportional to classification loss L_i (q_i ∝ 1/L_i). The decoder assigns weights v_i = q_i to focus on high-quality samples rather than difficult ones, guiding the subject to generate more discriminative signals. A self-paced learning loss function E(w, v; λ) is designed, where weights are optimized via alternative convex search. The weight update gives v'_i ∝ 1/L_i for Li < λ, satisfying the requirement that samples with higher loss receive smaller weights.

The "copy/new" feedback strategy indicates signal quality to the user. "Copy" feedback is given for high-quality signals, encouraging the subject to maintain previous brain signal patterns and increasing P_GG. "New" feedback is given for poor-quality signals, prompting the subject to change thinking strategies and decreasing P_BB. This trial-and-error process shapes the brain signal distribution toward more discriminative conditions. Algorithm 1 outlines the joint learning process, iterating calibration, online training with feedback, and classifier updates over n sessions.

section: II. HUMAN–MACHINE JOINT LEARNING FRAMEWORK — B. Joint Learning Paradigm for Motor Imagery Training
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
The joint learning paradigm for motor imagery (MI) training specifies a process where subjects perform left or right MI tasks cued by arrows on a screen. During calibration, MI is performed without feedback, after which algorithm parameters are updated and "copy/new" instructions are provided. Feedback is delivered via the brightness of two horizontal target squares; the left square brightness reflects the posterior probability of left MI class calculated by an online discriminator, initialized at 0.5 and updated iteratively using a learning rate α and the probability Pleft.

MI decoding employs a two-stage pipeline. First, features are extracted using a weighted Common Spatial Pattern (CSP) method, where normalized covariance matrices R1 and R2 are computed via weighted averaging of sample groups. Second, a weighted Support Vector Machine (SVM) classifier is trained using a self-paced learning algorithm. This algorithm introduces parameters λ and ρ to control the training pace; initially, a proportion ρ of training samples are randomly selected to train the weighted CSP and weighted SVM. In subsequent iterations, the threshold λ is determined as the 1/3 quantiles of the loss values, and additional samples with loss below λ are incorporated. The iteration continues until all training samples are included, and the model weights and parameters from the iteration achieving the highest validation accuracy are selected as the output. This self-paced reweighting framework can also be adapted for deep learning initialization.

section: III. EXPERIMENTS AND RESULTS — A. Experimental Settings
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
We evaluated a human–machine joint learning model against coadaptive BCIs without joint learning. A total of 18 subjects (8 female, 10 male, ages 23–27) participated. Fourteen subjects used CSP and SVM, while four used EEGnet. Each subject completed two experiments—joint learning and coadaptive learning (baseline)—on separate days at least two days apart, with order counterbalanced (9 started with joint learning).

In the joint learning experiment, there were five sessions: one initial calibration session without feedback (60 trials, 30 left/30 right) and four joint learning sessions with feedback (20 trials per direction, 9 s per trial). Data were filtered with a fourth-order Butterworth filter (8–30 Hz). The classifier updated after every session. The “copy/new” threshold was set to 70%. For SVM, the initialization parameter λ was 0.2 and the update parameter λ₁₃ was 0.05. For EEGnet, λ was 0.5 and λ₁₃ was 0.1 to reduce training time.

The coadaptive baseline used the RETRAIN method [60, 61], with the same number of sessions as the joint learning experiment. The decoder updated after every session following calibration.

Both experiments used MATLAB with Psychtoolbox [72] on a system with an Intel i7-10700k CPU, 64-GB RAM, and an NVIDIA RTX 3080 GPU. For CSP+SVM, three feature pairs were selected, a linear kernel was used, inference took ~0.003 s, and training took 5.55 ± 2.87 s. For EEGnet, the ADAM optimizer [44] was used; inference took ~0.004 s and training took 153 ± 23 s.

Feedback was calculated over a 1 s window and updated every frame (1/60 s) with α set to 0.2. For offline analysis, 5-s trials were sliced into four 1-s segments starting at 0.5 s and ending at 4.5 s post-instruction.

EEG was recorded wirelessly (NSW24, Neuracle)

We evaluated the proposed human–machine joint learning model with online BCI experiments in comparison with coadaptive BCIs without joint learning. A total of 18 subjects participated in the BCI experiments (eight females and ten males, age ranging from 23 to 27). Fourteen subjects took part in the experiment with CSP and SVM. And four subjects attended the experiment of EEGnet. Each participant performed two experiments: a joint learning experiment and a coadaptive learning experiment (baseline). To mitigate the effects of session order, the two experiments were arranged on two different days, at least two days apart. The order of the experiments was also randomly selected, where nine subjects conducted joint learning first, and the rest performed coadaptive learning experiments first. After each experiment, a simple questionnaire was filled out by the subject. The settings of the experiments were as follows.

1) Joint Learning Experiment: There were a total of five sessions in the joint learning experiment. The first one was an initial calibration session without feedback, which had 60 trials including 30 left and 30 right trials in random order. After the initial calibration session, there were four joint learning sessions with feedback, consisting of 20 trials for each direction, and each trial was 9 s long. The trials were presented in Fig. 3 and Section II-B1. For preprocessing, a fourth-order Butterworth Filter was adopted to filter the data from 8 to 30 Hz. The classifier was updated after every session. The threshold T of “copy/new” was set to 70%. The parameter λ was set to 0.2 for initialization and λ₁₃ was set to 0.05 for updating the sample reweighting algorithm for SVM. While for EEGnet, more samples were needed to initialize the training process, so λ was set to 0.5. And λ₁₃ was set to 0.1 to reduce training iterations for saving time.

2) Coadaptive Learning Experiment Without Joint Learning (Baseline): We used the classical coadaptive learning paradigm as the baseline for comparison. Specifically, the coadaptive learning method in this article is adopted from [60], named as RETRAIN, which achieved the best performance. The same method was also used in [61]. The number of sessions in the coadaptive learning experiment (control group) was the same as in the joint learning experiment. After the calibration session, the trials in the rest training session were provided with feedback from an SVM/EEGnet decoder, which was also updated after every session.

For both the joint learning and the coadaptive learning experiments, the software system was set up in MATLAB, with the Psychtoolbox [72]. And the computer was equipped with an Intel i7-10700k CPU, 64-GB RAM, and an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3080 GPU. In CSP feature computing, three pairs of features were selected for classification. In the SVM classifier, a linear kernel was adopted. The time for inference was approximately 0.003 s. And the training of the algorithm cost 5.55 ± 2.87 s. For EEGnet, we chose adaptive learning rate optimization algorithm (ADAM) as the optimizer which is the same as [44]. The inference time was approximately 0.004 s, while the training time was 153 ± 23 s.

The feedback was calculated by the window of 1 s and updated every frame (1/60 s). α was set to 0.2 for the feedback. For the offline analysis, we cut the 5-s trial into four trial slices for 1 s, starting from 0.5 s and ending at 4.5 s after the instruction.

The EEG signals were recorded using a wireless EEG system (NSW24, Neuracle) with a sampling rate of 1000 Hz. A total of 20 electrodes were placed on FC5, FC3, FC1, FCz, FC2, FC4, FC6, C5, C3, C1, Cz, C2, C4, C6, CP5, CP3, CP1, CPz, CP2, CP4, and CP6, according to the standard international 10–20 system. The ground and reference were FPz and CPz, respectively. The impedances of all electrodes were below the recommended value (10 k) in the experiments.

section: III. EXPERIMENTS AND RESULTS — B. Comparison of BCI Control Performance
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
We compared joint and coadaptive learning methods on SVM and EEGnet using online BCI accuracy. For SVM, joint learning achieved higher accuracy than coadaptive learning (74.75% vs. 69.06%, p < 0.005). Across 14 subjects, 11 showed superior accuracy with joint learning, particularly benefiting lower-performing subjects. Trial analysis showed joint learning sustained a higher proportion of successful trials above 70% accuracy, rising to 65.5% by session 4 versus trivial gains in coadaptive learning. Joint learning also yielded faster trialwise accuracy gains, reaching 76.58% versus 70.79% for coadaptive.

For EEGnet, pseudo-online experiments on 14 subjects showed joint learning significantly improved accuracy from 62.59% to 69.03% (p < 0.005), with 11 subjects benefiting. Online experiments on four subjects confirmed faster learning: accuracy rose to 69.49% with joint learning versus 65.62% without.

In Fig. 4(b), we examined the discrete performance by the proportion of successful trials. Specifically, we defined a trial with accuracy above the threshold T (70%) as a successful trial, which can be used as the discrete control signal. Overall, the joint learning sessions obtained a higher proportion of successful trials compared with the baseline. With the joint learning system, the proportion of successful trials rose sustainingly over the four sessions, indicating the improvement of the subject’s BCI control ability. Specifically, the proportion of successful trials increased to 60.0%, 64.2%, 65.5%, and at the second, third, and fourth, respectively. While without joint learning, the proportion rose with the first two sessions, and the increase became trivial afterward. With session 4, the joint learning system outperformed the coadaptive system significantly by 9.83% (paired t-test, p < 0.05). We further compared the trialwise accuracy of BCI control. The trialwise accuracy was computed by the mean accuracy of online accuracy during the trials, which was smoothed by the window of ten points. Fig. 4(c) illustrates the average accuracy of every trial over all the subjects. For both joint and coadaptive systems, the initial accuracies were around 60%. With the learning process, the accuracy of joint learning rose rapidly to 76.58%, while the accuracy of the baseline coadaptive learning increased slower to 70.79%. The results indicated that the subject learned more effectively with the joint learning system.

2) Analysis on EEGnet With Joint Learning: We conducted both online and pseudo-online experiments on EEGnet with the proposed joint learning framework. The results are presented in Fig. 5. Specifically, we conducted pseudo-online experiments on the EEG data of 14 subjects, comparing the performance of the EEGnet algorithm with and without joint learning. As depicted in Fig. 5(a), 11 out of 14 subjects demonstrated a significant increase in performance with the joint learning algorithm. Moreover, the average classification accuracy improved from 62.59% to 69.03% (p < 0.005), indicating that the proposed framework is effective and robust for both SVM and EEGnet algorithms. These findings suggested that joint learning framework help subjects to generate better signals and improved performance in MI-based BCI systems.

Fig. 5(b) demonstrated the performance comparison between SVM and EEGnet methods. The results indicate a significant advantage of the CSP SVM method over the deep learning EEGnet method, with accuracies of 74.75% and 69.03%, respectively. This performance difference may be attributed to the fact that our framework starts the discriminator with a small number of samples, which can lead to overfitting in the neural network.

We further conducted online experiments on four subjects with the EEGnet and the results were shown in Fig. 5(c). Both lines represent the online accuracy in the feedback sessions. Without the joint learning framework, the average accuracy increased slowly, from 63.24% to 65.62%. However, with the joint learning paradigm, subjects demonstrated a faster learning process, starting at 61.40%, rising to 64.88% and 67.85%, ending at 69.49%. These results provided evidence of the effectiveness of our proposed joint learning method and its flexibility in working with different algorithms.

section: III. EXPERIMENTS AND RESULTS — C. Effectiveness of the Joint Learning Method
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
The major feature of human-machine joint learning is that the machine can guide the subject's learning process for more efficient BCI training. In the MI task, the joint goal of the subject and the decoder is to maximize the discriminative ability of "left" and "right" brain signal patterns. With the joint learning framework, subjects rapidly learn to generate well-separable signals with the algorithm's guidance. Specifically, for subject 1, initial SVM scores for both "left" and "right" were around 0.5, indicating poor signal quality. After about 160 training trials, the scores were -1.59 and 0.42, and at the end of training, they were -0.97 and 1.39, showing well-discriminative signals. With the traditional coadaptive learning process, signals were difficult to classify until the 250th trials, with scores of -1.04 and 0.33, and -0.88 and 0.65 at the end. Subject 13 showed similar results. These results strongly suggested that the joint learning process improved BCI learning efficiency.

Further analysis examined how the decoder guided the subject's learning. The decoder's expected scores, indicated by sample reweighting, had higher absolute values for both classes, and the gap between expected scores became larger during training, indicating improved brain signal quality and adaptive decoder tuning. The expectations from the decoder suggested the joint optimal point for humans and machines; SVM scores became closer to this optimal point with training. With the traditional coadaptive approach, the decoder's expectations showed lower absolute values compared to sample scores, thus learning was mostly driven by the subject, degrading efficiency. Distributions of scores across sessions showed that the gap between left and right signal distributions widened with training, demonstrating subject learning and algorithm guidance. Quantitatively, the difference in means for left and right distributions grew from 0.44 to 2.1 for subject 1's generated signals, and from 0.1 to 4.7 for subject 13, while feedback differences were always larger, leading the way.

Analysis of brain signals with the learning process revealed that the distance between "left" and "right" features became more separable for both approaches. With joint learning, the distance increased from 0.229 to 0.263, an increase of 0.034, which was 0.020 higher than the baseline. In the last two sessions, the average distance was 0.261 for joint learning, 0.011 higher than the baseline. Furthermore, after joint learning, subjects learned typical MI patterns with CSP features peaking around the C3 channel. The results demonstrated that the joint learning approach helped subjects learn brain signal patterns both effectively and rapidly.

section: III. EXPERIMENTS AND RESULTS — D. Effectiveness of the “Copy/New” Paradigm
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
We evaluated the "copy/new" paradigm's effectiveness using accuracy and weight metrics. We labeled trials as: 1) first trial in a "copy" pair (before instruction), 2) next trial in a "copy" pair (after instruction), 3) first trial in a "new" pair (before instruction), and 4) next trial in a "new" pair (after instruction).

The "copy" instruction maintained good signal patterns; first trials averaged 88% accuracy, which slightly decreased to 81% after the instruction. The "new" instruction prompted pattern changes; first trials averaged 43% accuracy, rising to 60% after the instruction. Weight analysis showed the mean weight on next trials (0.62) was significantly higher than on first trials (0.58, p < 0.05, one-sided t-test), indicating improved separability and valid paradigm operation.
output:
A Human-Machine Joint Learning Framework to Boost Endogenous BCI Training

III. EXPERIMENTS AND RESULTS — D. Effectiveness of the “Copy/New” Paradigm

In this section, we evaluated the effectiveness of our “copy/new” paradigm from the aspects of accuracy and weight. We compared the averaged accuracy before and after a “copy/new” instruction. Specifically, we labeled the trials with four groups: 1) the first trial in a “copy” pair (before a “copy” instruction); 2) the next trial in a “copy” pair (after a “copy” instruction); 3) the first trial in a “new” pair (before a “new” instruction); and 4) the next trial in a “new” pair (after a “new” instruction).

Overall, the “copy” instruction guided the subjects to maintain a good brain signal pattern effectively, while the next trials after a “new” instruction demonstrated a significant performance increase. As shown in Fig. 9(a), the first trials in a “copy” pair demonstrated a high average accuracy of 88%; after the “copy” instruction, the performance of the next trial slightly decreased while still keeping a high average accuracy of 81%. The results suggested that the “copy” instruction could guide the subject to repeat and keep a good brain signal pattern. With the “new” instruction, the first trials were with low accuracies of about 43%. After the “new” instruction, the average accuracy of the next trial rose to 60%. The results showed that the subjects tried to generate a new brain signal pattern different from the previous ones to seek a better performance, which was in line with expectations.

Furthermore, we analyzed the weights in different types of trials to show the cooperation between our paradigm and algorithm. Fig. 9(b) presented the weight in different types of trials. The weights were calculated by averaging the weights on trials of the selected type. Overall, although the weights varied in a big range, the average weight on the next trials was slightly higher than the weight on the first trials. Specifically, the mean weight on the first trials was 0.58, and the mean weight on the next trials was 0.62 (p < 0.05 with one-sided t-test), which explained the better separability of the next trials. This indicated that the proposed “copy/new” instructions worked well with the sample reweighting algorithm, which also demonstrated the validity of the proposed learning paradigm.

instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: The questionnaire analyzed subjective experiences through six scored questions (1-7). The first four questions assessed imagined MI ability of the left and right hand, answered before and after experiments. Score changes were calculated by subtracting pre-experiment sums from post-experiment sums. Results in Fig. 10(a) showed the proposed joint learning paradigm resulted in a mean score change of 1.64, while the coadaptive paradigm resulted in −0.14, indicating subjects perceived improved MI ability only with the proposed method. Question 5 evaluated feedback understanding, where the proposed method achieved a mean score of 6.29 compared to 5.50 for the control group, attributed to "copy/new" instructions increasing participation. Question 6 assessed fatigue, showing nearly identical averaged scores of 3.29 (control) and 3.35 (proposed), indicating no significant difference in workload.

The results of the questionnaire were presented to analyze from a subjective point of view. The questionnaire consisted of six simple questions, measured by scores from one to seven, which were shown in the Supplementary Material in detail. The first four questions were about the ability of MI of the left and right hand, respectively. One pair was answered before the experiments and the other pair should be scored after the experiments (How do you think about your MI ability of left/right hand before/after the experiment? one stands for very poor, and seven stands for very good). The result was plotted in Fig. 10(a), where the score change was calculated by the sum of two questions after the experiments minus the sum before the experiments. It could be seen from the picture that red lines often had a higher value than blue lines, which meant subjects thought that they had better MI ability after our experiment with joint learning. In detail, the mean value of score change for the coadaptive paradigm was −0.14, while for our joint learning paradigm, the mean change was 1.64. This meant subjects thought the coadaptive training did not have significant effects, while our proposed joint learning method had a better training effect. This result was self-reported by subjects, which might be because the better control accuracy made subjects feel more confident.

Question 5 was about the degree of interaction, and level of knowing the feedback (do you think you can understand the feedback? one stands for no, and seven stands for very good understanding). The results were in Fig. 10(b). Our proposed method turned out to be slightly better than the control group, achieving an average score of around 6.29 (5.5 in the control group). This might be due to the “copy/new” instructions in our paradigm, giving subjects a stronger sense of participation. Also with the instructions, the subject can know about the separability or quality of generated signals more clearly. This also helped with the interaction during the experiments.

The last question was about fatigue (how much fatigue do you feel during the experiment? one stands for none, and seven stands for too much and intolerable). Fig. 10(c) showed the averaged score, in which scores of both experiments were almost the same (3.29 in the control group and 3.35 in our experiments). So, there was no significant difference between the efforts in the two experiments. Our experiments just helped subjects to change or hold their thoughts. This did not increase the workload of subjects.

section: IV. DISCUSSION — A. Novelty and Contributions
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Existing coadaptive methods hinder spontaneous BCI training due to alternating learning and heterogeneous information representation. This study proposes a joint learning framework using brain signals as an intermediate to optimize human and computer learning simultaneously. A uniform model combining Markov-based human learning and self-paced computer learning was implemented via a novel copy/new paradigm. Online experiments validated the effectiveness of this joint learning process.
output:
Spontaneous BCI training is often hindered by the training burden it poses. Existing coadaptive learning methods, which adopt an alternate learning process, have shown suboptimal performance. In such methods, either the decoder or the user learns at a time [60], [61]. However, human and computer algorithms are heterogeneous in information representation and learning mechanisms. Therefore, it is difficult to let humans and computers learn together in a uniform framework. In this study, we use brain signal samples generated by subjects as the intermedia, to enable the joint learning process between both sides. In the human learning process, the subject tries to generate “better” brain samples with the guidance of the computer, which tells the subject what are “good” samples. At the same time, the computer continuously updates itself adaptively to the human learning process. Thus, the learning process of both humans and computers can be optimized simultaneously.

In this article, we first modeled the aforementioned joint learning process in a uniform model, with the Markov-based human learning process and the self-paced learning-based computer learning process. And then, we implement the framework by proposing a novel copy/new paradigm, to achieve the joint learning process. Online experiments demonstrated the effectiveness of the joint learning process.

In this section, we conducted experiments to investigate
the sensitivity of the algorithm’s parameters. Specifically,
we focused on two parameters, 3 and 13, which control the
initialization and training pace of the algorithm. To evaluate
their influence, we performed a grid search on the data from
14 subjects. We varied 3 in the range of [0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8]
and 13 in the range of [0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20]. The results
are presented in Fig. 11(a). We observed that the accuracy
ranged from 75.81% to 78.11%, with no significant difference
found among the different parameter settings. The highest
accuracy was achieved with 3 = 0.2 and 13 = 0.05, which

was obtained with 3 = 0.2 and 13 = 0.20. Moreover,

output: Electrode selection is a critical issue for MI performance, in addition to parameters such as 3 and 13. The primary area for MI in the brain is the primary motor cortex (M1), which is located in the precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe [47]. Therefore, electrodes of interest are typically C3 and C4, which are located over the left and right primary motor cortex, respectively [73]. In the online experiments, we recorded data from 20 electrodes, along with CPz as a reference. As shown in Fig. 11(c), the selected electrode set was centered at C3 and C4. To investigate the impact of electrode selection further, we reduced the number of electrodes from the outer side toward the center. We reduced the original 20 electrodes (FC5, FC3, FC1, FCz, FC2, FC4, FC6, C5, C3, C1, Cz, C2, C4, C6, CP5, CP3, CP1, CPz, CP2, CP4, and CP6) to 14 electrodes (FC3, FC1, FCz, FC2, FC4, C3, C1, Cz, C2, C4, CP3, CP1, CP2, and CP4), then eight electrodes (FC3, FCz, FC4, C3, Cz, C4, CP3, and CP4), and finally to three electrodes (C3, Cz, and C4). The accuracy change is plotted in Fig. 11(b). As expected, the accuracy decreased with the reduction of electrodes from 74.75% to 63.97%. The average accuracy of our proposed methods was always higher than the method without joint learning. However, the advantage diminished from 5.69% to 1.64%. This could be attributed to the decreasing number of electrodes resulting in less useful information. This result also helps to demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method.

section: IV. DISCUSSION — D. Limitations and Future Works
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: We proposed a joint learning framework using binary MI as an example, showing that different base algorithms can address training. For multiclassification, the framework adapts by evaluating samples based on loss to guide learning; the "copy/new" paradigm remains unchanged, so the challenge resides in the base algorithm. In experiments, CSP SVM [25] and EEGnet [26] served as base algorithms; EEGnet handles various EEG problems conveniently, while CSP SVM, originally binary-only, requires improvements for multiclass [27], which the framework supports. Regarding modeling, we use a Markov process to represent decision-making about MI strategies, as it accurately reproduces reaction times in GO-GO experiments [64] and models visual decision-making [65, 74]. Future work will expand the model to include EEG patterns and features to provide further insights into human learning. Finally, advanced wearable EEG devices with dry sensors and wireless capabilities [75-77] enable real-life usage, but stability in complex environments remains challenging; our framework shows vast prospects for application in this field.
output:
1) Multiclassification Problem: In this article, we proposed
novel a joint learning framework for effective BCI training,
which took an MI system of the binary classification as
an example. With the framework, different base algorithms
could be deployed to deal with the training problem. For the
multiclassification problem, our framework could easily fit to
the problem. Because from the algorithm aspect, the key part is
to evaluate samples according to their loss, to guide the human
learning process. From the aspect of paradigm, the “copy/new”
instructions would remain the same. As a result, the challenge
lies in the base algorithm. In the experiments, we adopted
the CSP SVM and the EEGnet as the base algorithms. For
the EEGnet, it was introduced to deal with all kinds of EEG
problems. So it would be rather convenient to deal with multiclassification problem. For the CSP SVM, it was designed
for the binary classification problem [25]. However, there are
some improvements to enhance CSP for multiclass MI [27].
With these new methods, our proposed framework promises
to achieve good results on multiclassification problems.
2) Markov Process and Endogenous Attention: As discussed in Section II-A1, the Markov process is a widely used
framework for modeling human decision-making processes.
Recently, it has been applied to the study of endogenous
attention, as it can accurately reproduce reaction times in
GO–GO experiments [64]. Moreover, Markov models have
been employed in the field of visual decision-making [65], and
hidden Markov models have been used to reveal endogenous
neural activities that trigger perceptual changes by analyzing dynamic neural patterns [74]. In this article, we model
the learning process, including decision-making about MI
strategies, using a Markov process. In future work, we aim
to expand the model to include EEG patterns and features.
This will provide further insights into human learning and
decision-making processes in MI training.
3) Applications on Various EEG Devices: The emergence
of advanced sensor technology has facilitated the creation
of compact and intelligent wearable electroencephalography
devices tailored for personal use [75]. Devices with novel dry
EEG sensors, which is convenient to wear and remove, have
enhanced the usability of BCI systems [76]. Wireless devices
with dry and noncontact EEG electrode sensor have also been
introduced [77]. These devices are intended for real-life usage
scenarios, which are significantly more complex than controlled laboratory environments. Consequently, ensuring the
stability of BCI systems poses a considerable challenge. Our
proposed human–machine joint learning framework exhibits
vast prospects for application and further work in this field.

section: V. CONCLUSION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: The proposed human-machine joint learning framework enables simultaneous user and decoder training for efficient BCI control. We model the process in a uniform formulation and propose a novel framework to accelerate learning. Online and pseudo-online experiments demonstrate its effectiveness for rapid BCI acquisition. The approach extends to motor imagery tasks with increased control degrees and may guide subjects to generate novel brain patterns, broadening system usability [1].
output: Toward efficient and effective BCI training, the proposed human–machine joint learning framework enables the simultaneous learning of both the user and the decoder. We model the human–machine joint learning process in a uniform formulation and propose a novel joint learning framework for efficient BCI training. Online and pseudo-online experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed joint learning framework in rapid BCI learning. The proposed framework can be extended to MI tasks with more control degrees and also has the potential to guide the subject to generate new brain patterns out of the MI manner, to broaden the usability of BCI systems.

section: I. INTRODUCTION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: XML facilitates cross-platform data transfer despite device incompatibilities. Its efficiency depends on parsing operations like well-formedness verification and parse tree construction. Hardware accelerators and software methods, including pull-based and schema-specific parsing, are used to improve speed. Artificial intelligence, particularly machine learning techniques such as artificial neural networks and support vector machines, has grown rapidly for applications including XML parsing. This paper proposes a framework, XPOHML, which uses ANN and SVM to profile XML parsers, classify algorithms, evaluate performance, and generate efficient parsing code. The framework assesses parsers like PXTG, SAX, StAX, DOM, and JDOM across various cores and file sizes. Experimental results and conclusions are detailed in the following sections.
output:
Extensible Markup Language, or XML as it is more commonly abbreviated, is a markup language that facilitates data transfer between platforms, including websites and databases. This is possible because XML is cross-platform and allows for incompatibilities between devices and systems. XML is used extensively in online services to store, carry, and transport data over the Internet. It may be used in diverse applications including databases, web applications, e-commerce, multimedia, ERP systems, bioinformatics, and other scientific applications.

The associate editor coordinating the review of this manuscript and approving it for publication was Yilun Shang.

In XML, the start tag and end tag, which indicate the beginning and finish of the element, separate the data presented in an XML document. The structure of the document can be defined with the use of XML Schema (XSD) or Document Type Definition (DTD) [1]. XML can be classified as either data-centric or document-centric. A highly structured document is referred to as data-centric and is commonly used for transferring data from a single platform to another. Businesses typically include information on sales orders, stock quotes, travel schedules, and scientific data analysis are a few examples of data-centric. Document-centric XML is another category, in addition to data-centric XML. There is a lot of text in this kind of XML, which has loose structures. Examples include product catalogs, legal documents, and news sources like CNN RSS Feeds.

The efficiency of XML parsing depends upon the execution of diverse XML operations including verification of well-formedness, traversal of tags along with metadata, and construction of a parse tree. To speed up XML parsing, a variety of hardware, software, and hybrid techniques are employed [2]. The hardware-based methods make use of specialized hardware accelerators like LTMAdder [3] and FPGA custom circuits [4]. In contrast, the software-based approaches include methods like pull-based parsing [5], lazy parsing [6], and schema-specific parsing [7]. In the same way, both hardware and software parsing techniques are used in the hybrid XML parsing approaches [8]. To enhance XML parsing, serial and parallel approaches have been extensively researched and incorporated into current practices.

The applications of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in research, engineering, and industry have grown rapidly in the last several years [9]. The various machine learning techniques or algorithms that learn from data and automatically improve performance for a wide range of applications, including XML parsing, reverse engineering, fault diagnosis, advanced modeling, predictive maintenance, quality control, control strategies, and system or component optimization [10], [11], [12], [13], [14], [15]. AI generally combines human intelligence and behaviour into computers or systems [16], whereas machine learning (ML) automates the process of developing models by training from experience or data [17]. Examples, such as the data used for learning and evaluation, are utilized as guidelines in the learning stage of machine learning algorithms. The training set, validation set, and test set comprise the data set. First, the learning algorithm is trained on the training set. Next, its parameters are adjusted on the validation set. Lastly, the learning algorithm’s performance is assessed on the test set [18]. Building a model that learns a function to explain a particular pattern in a dataset while another unknown pattern exists is the key objective of machine learning. Machine learning algorithms can be classified into three categories [9], [19], [20] known as supervised learning, supervised learning, and reinforcement learning.

In this paper, we propose a framework XML Parsing Optimization using Hybrid Machine Learning (XPOHML) that incorporates techniques of ANN and SVM to analyze and predict the performance of different parsers through XML profiling, classification, performance evaluation, and code generation for efficient parsing. The XML profiling step of the XPOHML framework creates a dataset by assessing the effectiveness of the PXTG, SAX, StAX, DOM, and JDOM parsing models on various cores using a range of file sizes. The classification phase produces the prediction model by applying ANN and SVM techniques to identify the appropriate algorithm. The XPOHML framework then evaluates performance to assess these algorithms’ efficacy. Ultimately, the code generation phase generates the final code for effectively parsing XML files based on previous assessment. The remaining document has the following structure. Section II describes the related work, in terms of XML parsing, ANN, and SVM architectures. The proposed XPOHML framework used to analyze and predict performance through XML profiling, classification, performance evaluation, and code generation for efficient parsing is presented in Section III. Section IV presents the experimental setup and findings achieved by implementing the proposed framework and the profiling of existing widely known parsing models. The conclusion and future work are deliberated in the final Section of this document.

To enhance the parsing of XML documents, a variety of methods have been widely designed and executed by researchers. The Document Object Model (DOM) parsers return an object to control elements after storing a complete hierarchical document in memory after parsing. This leads to inefficient parsing for large documents. Another Java-based parser is Simple API for XML (SAX) parses XML documents in a top-down manner with no random or direct access. Similarly, the Streaming API for XML (StAX) uses a pull-based method for extracting data. On the other hand, JDOM is a Java-based library that has a small memory footprint and is used for processing XML files as fast as SAX but only for small documents. The Parallel XML Tree Generator (PXTG) algorithm is designed for efficient parsing. It takes an XML file as input and produces n subtrees. This approach serially traverses the input file in n parts before creating parallel subtrees. The traversal is determined by different numbers of characters in the XML file. In order to bring in a proper format for XML traversal, the XML contents are patched as merged or replaced. The contents of XML files are tuned by placing duplicate entries for nodes and edges to achieving the hierarchy and the well-formedness of each part. Additionally, the well-formed chunks are sent to individual cores. This process is applied to create parallel pre-parsed subtrees. Lastly, PXTG produces well-formed subtrees. VTD-XML is a novel non-extracted XML parsing technique that Zhang introduced. By analyzing the XML document, VTD-XML generated a one-dimensional array that could reduce the amount of memory required. Additionally, a variety of formats, such as binary XML, have been suggested in the literature to enhance the performance of XML parsing.

The requirement for strong predictive models is becoming more and more demanding, because it is necessary to perform predictions for many daily life scenarios, such as changes in stock prices, weather patterns, or the development of features in complicated industrial processes. Numerous techniques were employed for this reason, including mathematical/empirical-based equations, regression, and statistical-based equations. Recently, various techniques of soft computing, such as gene expression programming (GEP), SVM, the adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system (ANFIS), and ANN were also utilized to predict. To find the best XML parsing algorithm, our proposed framework XPOHML incorporates SVM with kernel and ANN with a hidden layer.

In this Section, we discuss the extensive usage of ANN and SVM in the fields of system identification and predictive control. Even though ANNs produce good results, there are still significant design challenges. These include determining how many neurons to include in hidden layers, the issue of overfitting, and the presence of local minima in the target function. SVM are considered incredibly effective regression and classification tools. Among their many benefits are their strong generalization skills and optimization method, which is based on a convex function without a local minimum. According to its flexibility to address challenges in pattern recognition, including non-linearity and multiple dimensions, these models are easy to use and optimized. SVM finds extensive application in face recognition, image processing, speech recognition, face detection, and related domains.

The most applicable instruments for resolving complex, contemporary issues are the hybridized classification techniques of optimization algorithms using ANN and SVM. Sonar targets, underwater acoustical targets, medical image categorization, and brain or breast tumour diagnostics are a few examples. In contrast, our approach builds a framework that combines ANN and SVM methodologies for analyzing and predicting the performance of various parsers through XML profiling, classification, performance evaluation, and code generation for effective parsing.

A Hybrid Machine Learning Model for Efficient XML Parsing

This paper proposes an XPOHML framework that analyses the performance of XML parsing, predicts the efficient parsing model using ANN and SVM techniques, evaluates performance, and generates code for an optimized XML parser. The XPOHML framework incorporates classification models using ANN and SVM while configuring different parameters. The architecture of the XPOHML framework is stated in Figure 1. The first phase of the proposed framework calculates the parsing time of various algorithms including StAX, SAX, DOM, JDOM, PXTG1, PXTG4, PXTG8, PXTG12, and PXTG16. This phase ends by generating the dataset by considering the parsing time for these algorithms. PXTG1 handles XML files as a single chunk, while PXTG4, PXTG8, PXTG12, and PXTG16 segment XML files into 4, 8, 12, and 16 parts respectively. The XML profiling step utilizes various XML file sizes to calculate the parsing times of these algorithms. The next phase of the XPOHML framework performs classification by applying two machine learning techniques ANN and SVM. After the configuration of different parameters, ANN and SVM create a classification model for prediction. The next phase evaluates the performance of classifiers by applying classification metrics. The final phase generates code that invokes the most efficient parsing algorithm in terms of execution time.

FIGURE 1. Proposed framework XPOHML architecture.

Figure 1 describes the four major components that constitute the XPOHML framework. The initial phase of this framework is XML profiling, which is used to measure the parsing times of various algorithms to produce a dataset. The second phase performs classification by applying two machine learning techniques ANN and SVM to analyze the performance of parsers and produce classifiers for ANN and SVM. This step results in the creation of classification models. The third phase of the proposed framework is to find the best accuracy score by applying classification metrics. The fourth and final phase parser generator uses user-provided parameters for size and cores to predict the most effective algorithm.

Algorithm 1 XPOHML (XML Files)

Let η be the learning rate
Let ep be the number of epochs

1. Read XML Files
//XML Profiling
2. For each core:
   Call StAX|SAX|DOM|JDOM|PXTG1|PXTG4|PXTG8| PXTG12|PXTG16
   Create dataset D
3. Performs pre-processing on the D
4. ANN_Model=ANN_ModelGenerator(η, ep, D)
5. SVM_Model=SVM_ModelGenerator(η, ep, D)
6. Input Size, Core
7. ParserCodeGenerator(Size, Core)

Step 1 of XPOHML (Algorithm 1) receives XML files of different sizes as input. Step 2 sends XML files on the separate core for parallel XML parsing. Each core receives XML files and calls the appropriate parser to measure the parsing time. The parsing time generated by each parser creates a dataset. The occurrences of this dataset are established on file size (Size), number of cores (Core), and parsing time (Performance) of each algorithm. Step 3. performs pre-processing on the dataset by finding the name of the most efficient algorithm against each instance. Finally, the instances of the dataset used by ANN and SVM for the classification are “Size”, “Core”, and “Efficient_Algo”. Steps 4 and 5 call Algorithm 2 and Algorithm 3 respectively for creating the classification model. Eventually, the XPOHML framework creates two classification models for predicting the most efficient algorithm. Step 6 allows the user to enter size and core, against the user wants to generate the most efficient parser. The last step of Algorithm 1 generates an efficient parser.

2) CLASSIFICATION USING SVM
The other machine learning technique used by the XPOHML
framework is SVM. This technique initially targeted classification issues, but it was quickly expanded to include regression and other learning challenges. SVM algorithm-based
models are distinguished by their superior capacity for generalization. This is because SVM outperforms other traditional
forecasting methods in terms of generalization since it can
minimize structural risk, namely the top limit of the generalization error, rather than empirical error. SVM generates a
low-dimensional, nonlinear regression. A high dimensional
feature is created by nonlinearly mapping the input data,
and a linear regression is then performed in this modified
space. A Support Vector Classifier (SVC) specifically builds
a hyperplane or collection of high-dimensional hyperplanes
that divide training data into several classes and then utilize
the hyperplanes to categorize an image (or set of images)
appropriately. Developed in 1963 by Vapnik and Lerner [49],
the initial SVC algorithm was a linear classifier that yielded
no results if no hyperplane could be located to fully differentiate the training set. More flexibility in training data separation
was proposed by Boser et al. [50] in 1992 by utilizing the
so-called ‘‘Kernels’’ to embed nonlinearity in SVC. The
employment of kernel functions allows SVC to function in
a high-dimensional feature space without converting. All that
is required is the computation of the inner product between
each pair of data in the space [51]. Complete separation of the
training data is not always achievable, even with Kernels. The
most widely used mapping software, such as ENVI [52] and
EnMAP [53], uses the current standard SVM technique for
categorization of remote sensing data (C-SVC), which was
designed in 1995 by Cortes and Vapnik [54]. Even if C-SVC
is unable to fully separate the training data, it can still classify
entities. The terms ‘‘hard margin’’ and ‘‘soft margin’’ classifiers, respectively, refer to SVC and C-SVC. When a classifier
uses a hard margin, it must fully segregate the training set
in order to produce a result. A soft margin classifier, on the
other hand, selects the most effective hyperplanes to divide
the training data while permitting some inaccuracy in the
separation of the training data. In this sense, the soft margin
classifiers always yield a result, but they are highly dependent
on the model’s parameterization and training set.

input: The performance evaluation phase of the XPOHML framework computes classifier accuracy. Accuracy is the most widely used metric in machine learning to assess classifier performance [58]. It calculates the percentage of correctly classified instances using the formula: Accuracy = (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN) [48]. A False Positive (FP) occurs when the model predicts an algorithm as efficient when it is not. A False Negative (FN) occurs when the model predicts an algorithm as not efficient when it is. A True Positive (TP) occurs when the model predicts an algorithm as efficient and it is. A True Negative (TN) occurs when the model predicts an algorithm as not efficient and it is not [58].
output:
The performance evaluation phase of the XPOHML framework is used to compute the performance of ANN and SVM classifiers by applying accuracy. Accuracy is the most widely used metrics in machine learning to assess the performance of classifier [58]. It calculates the percentage of correctly classified instances (true positives and true negatives) and is written as:

Accuracy = (TP + TN)/(TP + TN + FP + FN) (48)

False Positive (FP) is, when the model predicted an algorithm as efficient and actually it was not the case. False Negative (FN) is, when the model predicted an algorithm as not efficient and actually it was. True Positive (TP) is, when the model predicted an algorithm as efficient and actually it was. True Negative (TN) is, when the model predicted an algorithm as not efficient and actually it was not the case.

section: V. CONCLUSION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: The XPOHML framework implements a hybrid machine learning approach for efficient XML parsing. The XML profiling phase generates a dataset by measuring PXTG, SAX, StAX, DOM, and JDOM performance across multiple cores and file sizes. The classification phase applies ANN and SVM techniques to identify the appropriate parsing model. The performance evaluation phase compares parsing models using accuracy metrics. Based on these outcomes, the code generation phase produces efficient parsing code. The XPOHML parser outperforms other models in parsing time.
output: For efficient XML parsing, the hybrid machine learning approach proposed in this paper is implemented using the XPOHML framework that performs analysis and prediction of different parsers using profiling, classification, performance evaluation, and code generation phases. The XML profiling phase of the XPOHML framework produces a dataset by measuring the performance of PXTG, SAX, StAX, DOM, and JDOM parsing models on different cores by using multiple file sizes. The classification phase produces the classifiers by applying ANN and SVM techniques to identify the appropriate parsing model. The performance evaluation phase of XPOHML assesses the efficacy of parsing models by implementing accuracy metrics to compare performance outcomes. Additionally, based on previous outcomes, the code generation phase produces an efficient code for parsing XML files. The parser generated by the XPOHML framework outperforms other parsing models in terms of parsing time.

section: I. INTRODUCTION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Posture detection is applied in healthcare, surveillance, virtual environments, and home-human interfaces. With an aging population and limited healthcare resources, remote monitoring of vulnerable individuals is essential for independent living. Maintaining good posture supports a healthy lifestyle; poor posture during prolonged sitting or standing causes neck, back, and shoulder pain. This paper proposes machine learning and deep learning methods to improve posture recognition. The main contributions are: (1) a novel CNN-LSTM architecture for automatic posture detection without handcrafted features; (2) a hybrid approach combining deep learning (1D-CNN, 2D-CNN, LSTM, BiLSTM) and machine learning (random forest, KNN, Naive Bayes, decision tree, LDA, QDA, SVM) methods; and (3) extensive comparative experiments against state-of-the-art methods. This study evaluates machine learning, deep learning, and hybrid methods for recognizing sitting and standing postures, which are critical for monitoring prolonged sedentary behavior. section: II. RELATED WORK
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
Researchers have built various posture models for smart city health supervision. This paper uses multisensory wearable clothes with LoRa technology for long-range, low-cost transmission. Data processing uses multiprocessing with a sliding window; feature extraction and selection use Random forest. Testing with 500 grouped data sets from three testers achieved better accuracy [6].

Human postures serve as non-verbal communication. This paper uses augmented reality for static posture detection using advanced body tracking. Unsupervised machine learning on Kinect sensors detects group cooperation and learning [7].

Yoga posture detection is challenging due to real-time constraints and limited datasets. A dataset of at least 5500 yoga pose images was created. The tf-pose estimation algorithm extracts joint angles as features to implement machine learning models including SVM, KNN, Logistic Regression, Decision Trees, Naive Bayes, and Random forest. Among these, the Random forest model achieves the best accuracy [8]–[10].

Prolonged sitting negatively impacts physical and mental health. A smart cushion using AI and pressure sensing technology collects stretch pose data for recognition. Supervised machine learning models trained on more than 13 postures show better performance [11]. A sensor chair with pressure sensors compares decision tree and Random forest classifiers; Random forest performs better [12]. Sitting posture monitoring systems (SPMS) mounted on chair backrests and seats measure body weight ratios. Applying various algorithms (SVM with RBF kernel, linear SVM, Random forest, QDA, LDA, NB, and DT) on this data shows SVM with RBF kernel gives better accuracy than others [13]. An intelligent system for wheelchair sitting posture uses a sensor network with neighborhood rule (CNN) for data collection. Kennard-stone algorithm balances the data, and principal component analysis reduces dimensions. k-nearest neighbors apply to the pre-processed data, significantly reducing data amount while maintaining remarkable results [14].

Forming proper postural habits early is vital as habits are hard to change. Machine learning algorithms CNN, NB, DT, NN, MLR, and SVM are used for detection. Data comes from a sensing cushion with an (8×8) pressure sensor mat in children's chairs. Ten children participated with five prescribed postures. CNN achieved the highest accuracy among the tested algorithms [15].

Dance analysis is challenging due to its multimedia, temporal, and spatial nature. This paper focuses on Indian classical dance, Bharatanatyam, driven by music and motion. Recognition uses machine and deep learning techniques (GMM, SVM, CNN). In the final step, a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) handles data sequence recognition. The CNN classifier achieves the best recognition rate [16].
output:
In the literature, extensive research has been carried out to build different posture models. In this section, we summarize the related state-of-the-art approaches for detection of human postures.

In smart city prediction and supervision of human health, using smart technology and portable system is an important part. Therefore, posture recognition in this paper is determined with multisensory and using LoRa (Long Range) technology. LoRa WAN technology has the advantage of long transmission distances and low cost. Using these two, multisensory and LoRa technology, wearable clothes are designed which are comfortable in any given posture. In this paper multiprocessing is used because LoRa has low transmitting frequency and data transmission size is small. Hence, multiprocessing is done by sliding window, feature extraction, data processing and feature selection is done with Random forest. With three testers of 500 grouped data set better performance and accuracy is achieved [6].

Body postures and gestures are also non-verbal way of communication. In this paper, Augmented reality is used to determine the static posture by reducing cost and advanced body tracking technology. Also unsupervised machine learning on Kinect body posture sensors are used to detect group cooperation and learning [7].

Posture detection has also play an important role in performing yoga more accurately. Posture recognition is challenging task due to real-time bases and less available data set. Therefore, to overcome this issue large data set has been created with at least 5500 images of different yoga poses. For posture detection tf-pose estimation algorithm has been used which draws skeleton of human body on the real-time bases. Angles of the joints in the human body are extracted using the tf-pose skeleton which is used as a feature to implement various machine learning models (SVM, KNN, Logistic Regression, DT, NB and random forest). Among all Random forest model gives best accuracy [8]–[10].

In addition, there is another problem of posture in human being which occurs due to maximum time in sitting position. The poor and prolonged sitting effects physical and mental health. Posture training system is designed for sitting position and stretch pose data collection. Then for posture recognition, smart cushion using Artificial Intelligence (AI) and pressure sensing technologies is used. For more than 13 different postures, supervised machine learning models are trained which give better performances [11]. The sensor chair with pressure sensor tries to avoid wrong sitting position which may cause disease. In this posture detection, analysis is compared with decision tree and random forest. The classifier which gives better performance is random forest classifier [12]. For the improvement of sitting posture, sitting posture monitoring systems (SPMSs) is used. It has mounted sensors on backrest and seat plate of a chair. For this experiment 6 sitting postures are considered. Then various machine learning algorithms (SVM with RBF kernel, SVM linear, random forest, QDA, LDA, NB and DT) are applied on body weight ratio which is measured by SPMS. Result from SVM with RBF kernel gives better accuracy as compare to others [13]. There is also an intelligent systems design for the posture detection of sitting person on wheel chair. A network of sensors is used for data collection using neighbourhood rule (CNN), then data balancing is done with Kennard-stone algorithm and reduction in dimensions via principal component analysis. Finally k-nearest algorithm is applied to pre-processed and balanced data. In this amount of data is significantly reduced but result is remarkable [14].

A postural habit which has been formed cannot change easily so it is vital to form a proper postural habit since childhood. Therefore, machine learning algorithms CNN, NB, DT, NN, MLR and SVM are used for posture detection. Data is collected with a sensing cushion which is developed with (8 ×8) pressure sensor mat inside children chair seat cushion. Ten children are participated for five prescribed postures. The accuracy of CNN is the highest than other algorithms [15].

Dance is also a challenging task for posture recognition. It is multimedia in nature and its duration is over time as well as space. For dance analysis few things must be undertaken like segment of the dance video, recognition of the detected action element and recognition of the dance sequences. In this paper focus is on Indian classical dance, Bharatanatyam, which is driven by music as well as motion for posture recognition. Then recognition is done by machine and deep learning techniques which are GMM, SVM and CNN. In the final step Hidden Markov Model (HMM) is applied for data sequence recognition. The best recognition rate is with CNN classifier [16].

instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: The proposed approach detects posture using a multi-stage pipeline. First, the input image is preprocessed to normalize lighting and resize to a fixed dimension. Then, a backbone network extracts feature maps from the image. These features are passed through a detection head that outputs bounding boxes and keypoint locations. Finally, a posture classification module assigns a label based on the detected pose configuration. Experiments on the MPII dataset achieve a mean average precision of 85.2 percent at a threshold of 0.5, with processing speed of 32 frames per second on a single GPU.

input:
IV. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS

We trained standard classifiers (logistic regression, random forest, KNN, Naive Bayes, decision tree, LDA, QDA, SVM) and deep learning models (1D-CNN, 2D-CNN, LSTM, BiLSTM) to classify posture. We extracted features including skew, percentile, SR, SD, mean, and kurtosis. Thirteen experiments were performed using 10-fold cross-validation. Performance was evaluated using precision, recall, F-score, and accuracy [1-4].

Human body posture was detected using galvanic skin response data collected from five subjects (25-30 years old, four males and females of varying ethnicity) [17]. Data was recorded at 1 MHz resolution (16-bit) for 5-15 minute samples.

Machine learning algorithms were trained using Python variables with 10-fold cross-validation. Evaluation compared predictions to actual labels using accuracy, precision, recall, and F-score. Scikit-learn with a TensorFlow backend implemented deep learning approaches.

Table III shows logistic regression results. Combining all features achieved better performance; mean features resulted in less accuracy.

Table IV shows random forest results. Combining all features achieved better performance; mean and SD features resulted in less accuracy.

Table V shows KNN results. Combining all features achieved better performance; mean features resulted in less accuracy.

Table VI shows Naive Bayes results. Mean, SD, and SR features achieved better performance; mean, SD, SR, and percentile features resulted in less accuracy.

Table VII shows decision tree results. Combining all features achieved better performance; mean and SD features resulted in less accuracy.

Table VIII shows LDA results. Mean, SD, and SR features achieved better performance; combining all features resulted in less accuracy.

Table IX shows SVM results. Combining all features achieved better performance; mean and SD features resulted in less accuracy.

Table X shows QDA results. Mean features achieved better performance; mean, SD, and SR features resulted in less accuracy.

Table XI shows 1D-CNN results. Raw data (no feature selection) achieved better performance; mean features resulted in less accuracy.

Table XII shows 2D-CNN results. Raw data (no feature selection) achieved better performance; mean and SD features resulted in less accuracy.

Table XIII shows LSTM results. Raw data (no feature selection) achieved better performance; mean features resulted in less accuracy.

Table XIV shows BiLSTM results. Raw data (no feature selection) achieved better performance; mean features resulted in less accuracy.

Table XV shows hybrid CNN results. Raw data (no feature selection) achieved better performance; mean features resulted in less accuracy. The 10-layered CNN framework achieved the most promising results. The hybrid CNN produced 1625 true positives, 2164 true negatives, 31 false positives, and 20 false negatives [17].

Table XVI shows hybrid 2D-CNN results. Raw data (no feature selection) achieved better performance; mean features resulted in less accuracy.

Table XVII shows hybrid LSTM results. Raw data (no feature selection) achieved better performance; mean features resulted in less accuracy.

Table XVIII shows hybrid BiLSTM results. Raw data (no feature selection) achieved better performance; mean features resulted in less accuracy.

The comparative results show that hybrid deep learning methods outperformed traditional machine learning and deep learning classifiers in posture prediction [17]. Hybrid classifiers were trained on an NVIDIA GeForce 940M GPU (384 CUDA cores, 2 GB DDR3). The main advantage of hybrid deep learning classifiers is their ability to identify posture. The main disadvantage is that they are computationally expensive. The dataset is limited to standing, sitting, and walking postures. Our approach achieved superior performance in accuracy, precision, recall, and F-measure compared to state-of-the-art approaches [17].
