V. CONCLUSION

Remote health monitoring enables independent living for elderly and vulnerable populations. This paper proposes a novel deep learning architecture for posture classification, including standing, sitting, and walking. A hybrid approach combining machine learning and deep learning methods is developed for posture prediction via meta-learning. Experimental results show the proposed hybrid approach achieves better performance than deep learning or machine learning methods alone.

input: We developed a machine learning algorithm to predict clozapine response in treatment-resistant schizophrenia using pre-treatment EEG data from 57 patients. The algorithm used linearly constrained minimum variance beamforming to localize source waveforms from 30 brain regions, applied symbolic transfer entropy to these waveforms, and classified patients as most- or least-responders based on the resulting effective connectivity matrix. The model achieved 95.83% accuracy in discrimination, indicating that pre-treatment EEG source symbolic transfer entropy may serve as a promising predictive tool for clozapine treatment outcome.

A Machine Learning Approach Using Effective
Connectivity to Predict Response
to Clozapine Treatment
Claudio Ciprian, Student Member, IEEE, Kirill Masychev
, Member, IEEE,
Maryam Ravan
, Senior Member, IEEE, James P. Reilly
, Life Member, IEEE,
and Duncan MacCrimmon
Abstract— Clozapine is an anti-psychotic drug that is
known to be effective in the treatment of patients with
chronic treatment-resistant schizophrenia (TRS-SCZ), commonly estimated to be around one third of all cases. However, clinicians sometimes delay the initiation of this drug
because of its adverse side-effects. Therefore, identiﬁcation
of predictive biological markers of clozapine response are
extremely valuable to aid on-time initiation of treatment.
In this study, we develop a machine learning (ML) algorithm
based on pre-treatment electroencephalogram (EEG) data
sets to predict response to clozapine treatment in 57 TRS-
SCZs, where the treatment outcome, after at least one-year
follow-up is determined using the positive and negative
syndrome scale (PANSS). The ML algorithm has three steps:
1) a brain source localization (BSL) procedure using the
linearly constrained minimum variance (LCMV) beamforming approach is employed on the EEG signals to extract
source waveforms from 30 speciﬁed brain regions. 2) An
effective connectivity measure named symbolic transfer
entropy (STE) is applied to the source waveforms. 3) A
ML algorithm is applied to the STE matrix to determine
whether a set of features can be found to discriminate
most-responder (MR) SCZ patients from least-responder
(LR) ones. The ﬁndings of this study reveal that STE features
can achieve an accuracy of 95.83%. This ﬁnding implies that
analysis of pre-treatment EEG could contribute to our ability
to distinguish MR from LR SCZs, and that the source STE
matrix may prove to be a promising tool for the prediction
of the clinical response to clozapine.
Index Terms— Clozapine treatment, effective connectivity, electroencephalography (EEG), EEG beamforming,
machine learning, odd-ball\paradigm, schizophrenia, symbolic transfer entropy.

section: I. INTRODUCTION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Approximately 30% of schizophrenia patients are treatment-resistant and do not benefit from conventional antipsychotics [1]. Clozapine effectively reduces symptoms in these patients [2]–[5], but carries risks of serious side effects like seizures and neutropenia, requiring regular blood monitoring. Furthermore, 40% to 70% of treatment-resistant patients fail to respond to clozapine [2]–[5]. Currently, response can only be determined through a treatment trial, causing delays. Howes et al. (2012) [6] showed a delay of around 4 years between diagnosis and clozapine initiation. Predicting clozapine response beforehand could reduce this delay and allow selective use in likely effective cases [8]. Emerging studies report biological differences between treatment-resistant and responsive cases, suggesting treatment-resistant schizophrenia is a distinct subtype [7], and clozapine-resistant cases may reveal additional subtypes [8]. This implies biological markers can predict symptom improvement prior to treatment initiation [8]. Neuroimaging markers, including EEG, structural imaging, SPECT, PET, MRI, CT, and EEG, have been explored. EEG is inexpensive and non-invasive, available even in small clinics, making predictive algorithms based on EEG signals more practical [9]. The goal of this study is to develop a machine learning algorithm based on pre-treatment EEG data to automatically predict clozapine response [10]. We employ modern state-of-the-art EEG signal processing methods that demonstrate significantly improved performance over previous approaches for this purpose.

Several neuroimaging studies have investigated predicting clozapine response. Konicki et al. (2001) [9] used CT to examine sulcal widening in 26 most responders (MR) and 10 least responders (LR), finding MR patients had significantly lower prefrontal sulcal widening, suggesting poorer response associates with greater frontal atrophy. Friedman et al. (1991) [10] evaluated 34 patients (12 non-responders, 13 moderate, 9 good responders), reporting prefrontal sulcal prominence is inversely related to clozapine response.

Using MRI, Honer et al. (1995) [11] evaluated 42 patients (15 MR, 27 LR), finding large posterior frontal and lateral temporal sulci predict poorer response. Lauriello et al. (1998) [12] tested 21 male veterans (10 MR, 11 LR), finding larger anterior superior temporal lobe CSF volumes predict greater improvement. Arango et al. (2003) [13] compared clozapine to haloperidol (22 vs 23 patients), finding larger right prefrontal gray matter volumes associated with greater negative symptom reduction, but no association with positive symptoms or hippocampal/caudate volumes. Molina et al. (2003) [14] investigated 25 treatment-resistant schizophrenia patients (12 responders), showing temporal cortex volume is directly associated with positive symptom improvement, while dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) content is inversely related. DLPFC volume was directly related to negative symptom improvement, and intracranial volume was negatively linked to disorganization syndrome improvement.

Moyett et al. (2020) [15] checked striatal connectivity using resting fMRI in 23 patients (13 MR, 10 LR), finding no significant difference between groups, suggesting striatal connectivity does not predict response. Using SPECT, Rodriguez et al. (1997) [16] investigated 39 patients (19 MR, 20 LR), finding MR groups had higher baseline perfusion in the right DLPFC, left and right basal ganglia, and thalamus. They discriminated MR and LR groups with 78.9% accuracy using thalamic and right DLPFC perfusion. Ertugrul et al. (2009) [17] reported increased perfusion in the right frontal cortex and thalamus links to better PANSS improvement in 22 patients (11 MR, 11 LR).

EEG has been a focus for predicting clozapine response due to its ability to capture brain abnormalities. Pillay et al. (1996) [18] investigated minor EEG abnormalities in 86 patients, finding greater functioning improvement in females with normal pre-treatment EEG. Knott et al. (2000) [19] reported clozapine-induced improvements in positive/negative syndrome scale (PANSS) and global psychopathology were related to greater pre-treatment quantitative EEG (QEEG) spectral power asymmetry in 13 patients (11 MR, 2 LR). II. RELATED WORKS

Several neuroimaging studies have been proposed in the literature for predicting response to clozapine therapy based on neuroimaging techniques [8]. Using CT, Konicki et al. (2001) [9] examined sulcal widening as a predictor of response to clozapine treatment using 26 most responder (MR) and 10 least responder (LR) patients. They found that the MR patients have significantly lower widening scores in the prefrontal sulci compared to LR ones, which suggest that poor response may be associated with a higher degree of frontal atrophy. Furthermore, Friedman et al. (1991) [10] evaluated 34 patients, 12 of which were classified as non-responders, 13 as moderate responders and 9 as good responders. They reported that prefrontal sulcal prominence is inversely related to clozapine response.

Using MRI, Honer et al. (1995) [11] evaluated 42 patients (15 MR and 27 LR). They found that large sulci in the posterior frontal and lateral temporal lobes predict poorer response. In another study, Lauriello et al. (1998) [12] tested 21 male veterans of the United States armed forces (10 MR and 11 LR). They found that patients with larger anterior superior temporal lobe cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) volumes showed greater improvement. Arango et al. (2003) [13] compared clozapine with Haloperidol, where 22 patients were assigned to clozapine and 23 patients were assigned to Haloperidol. They found that larger right prefrontal cortical gray matter volumes were associated with greater reduction in scale for the assessment of negative symptoms (SANS) scores after clozapine treatment. However, they did not find any associations with positive symptoms and hippocampal, caudate, or total intracranial volumes. Molina et al. (2003) [14] investigated associations between different brain region volumes and response to clozapine treatment using 25 TRS-SCZ patients, where 12 of them were responders to clozapine treatment. They showed that temporal cortex volume was directly associated with improvement in positive symptoms, whereas dorsolateral prefrontal cortical (DLPFC) CSF content was inversely related to the improvement in positive symptoms. Furthermore, DLPFC volume was directly related to improvement in negative symptom severity, and the intracranial volume was negatively linked to improvement in disorganization syndrome.

From these studies, greater brain region volumes, mainly in the frontal regions, are associated with a better response to clozapine treatment. Moyett et al. (2020) [15] checked the role of striatal connectivity to predict response using resting functional MRI (fMRI) of 23 patients (13 MR and 10 LR). They did not find any significant difference between striatal connectivity index (SCI) values of the two groups, which (as they mentioned) means striatal connectivity may not predict response to clozapine.

Using brain perfusion, Rodriguez et al. (1997) [16] used SPECT to investigate whether regional brain perfusion can be used as a predictor of response to clozapine treatment for 39 patients (19 MR and 20 LR). MR groups had higher baseline perfusion in the lower right and upper left DLPFC, left and right basal ganglia, and thalamus compared to LR groups. They also could discriminate MR and LR groups with 78.9% accuracy using perfusion in the thalamus and right DLPFC. Similarly, Ertugrul et al. (2009) [17] reported a link between increase in the levels of perfusion in the right frontal cortex and thalamus and better improvement in PANSS score using clozapine treatment in 22 patients (11 MR and 11 LR).

EEG is one of the most commonly used biological measurements that can effectively capture the abnormalities of different brain areas due to schizophrenia and the changes due to clozapine treatment, and thus has been the focus of a number of clinical studies (e.g. [18]–[23], [25]). Pillay et al. (1996) [18] investigated whether clozapine response can be predicted by minor EEG abnormalities such as generalized slowing or sharp waves, spikes, spike-wave patterns, and focal dysrhythmias using 86 patients. They found greater improvement in global assessment of functioning score in female participants with a normal EEG before clozapine treatment. Knott et al. (2000) [19] reported that clozapine-induced improvements in positive and negative syndrome scale (PANSS) and global psychopathology were related to greater pre-treatment quantitative EEG (QEEG) inter and intra-hemispheric spectral power asymmetry using 13 patients (11 MR and 2 LR). Kang et al. (2001) [20] used mutual cross-prediction analysis to determine if activity in one region was driving the dynamics of another region. Ten TRS chronic SCZ patients (4 MR and 6 LR) were involved in this study. They observed that the patients without a frontal lobe driving system and occipital response system had a higher chance of responding to clozapine. Gross et al. (2004) [21] examined the changes of theta frequency activity in the QEEG in 16 SCZ patients (13 MR and 3 LR) during clozapine treatment. They found changes in QEEG signals with clozapine treatment, mainly in the midline fronto-central area, were a more sensitive indicator of evaluating clozapine efficacy than the serum clozapine level. Khodayari-Rostamabad et al. (2010) [22] for the first time applied a machine-learning algorithm to predict clozapine responders based on their pre-treatment resting EEG measures, using first a leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO-CV) procedure on a group of 23 SCZ patients (12 MR and 11 LR), and then an independent test dataset with 14 SCZ patients (7 MR and 7 LR) to test the classifiers. Using statistical features such as coherence, cross-correlation coefficients, and mutual information between EEG electrodes, and the left-to-right hemisphere and anterior/posterior power ratio at various frequencies, they could successfully discriminate MR from LR with more than 85% accuracy. The authors reported a list of 20 features with highest predictive value, which mainly were selected from the left temporal and parietal areas. Ravan et al. (2015) [23] applied a machine-learning algorithm to Oddball EEG data of 47 SCZ patients before and after a year of clozapine treatment and 66 healthy controls (HCs). They first applied a source montage approach [24] to EEG data using BESA software (Megis Software GmbH, Munich, Germany) with a conventional three-shell spherical volume conductor head model. The source montage estimates cortex source activity from 15 predefined regions of the scalp, without considering deep brain activities, from the recorded scalp EEG. Then they used the cross-power spectral density (CPSD) function between these 15 areas as a measure of connectivity. They found five discriminating features that could simultaneously 1) discriminate all pre-treatment SCZ patients from HCs with the accuracy of 81.4%, 2) discriminate the pre- vs. post-treatment condition in the MR group with an accuracy of 85% and 3) discriminate LR-SCZ group from HCs even after treatment, with an accuracy of 79.6% all using a LOO-CV procedure, and 4) found no discrimination between post-treatment MR patients and HCs. The selected features were mainly from the joint activity between the prefrontal and right anterior temporal or right parietal areas at beta frequency band. Gica et al. (2019) [25] measured the absolute power change in EEG data after one month post-treatment for 23 patients to predict long term response. They found a significant correlation between the percentage of change observed in both the PANSS positive subscale and the general psychopathology subscale, and the percentage of change in the theta wave absolute power values in the frontal region in the first month. They also found significant correlation between the percentage of change observed in the global assessment of functioning (GAF) score, and the change in the theta wave absolute power values in the central region, and alpha wave absolute power values in parietal region.

Although there are several such studies identifying and characterizing deficits of schizophrenia and the efficacy of clozapine treatment, all these studies employed standard statistical parameters and conventional functional connectivity as features that are mostly measured based on scalp electrodes, which may cause false connectivity patterns due to volume conduction effect [26]. This is partially due to the fact that EEG data mostly reflects the electrical activity of the cortical areas. The brain activities of deep areas are attenuated and thus contribute considerably less to the scalp EEG signals. To address this issue, a number of brain source localization (BSL) techniques have been proposed as an alternative to channel-related connectivity (e.g. [27]–[29]). BSL techniques can isolate the signal originating from a particular brain region, and thereby suppress interference from other nearby regions, thus increasing the signal to noise ratio (SNR) of the desired signal. BSL methods can also suppress the volume conduction effect. Also, because several EEG electrodes can collect the activity of the same brain source, false connectivity indications between brain regions may arise.

Non-parametric BSL techniques include minimum norm estimates (MNE) [30] and their generalizations such as low-resolution electromagnetic tomography (LORETA) [31], standard LORETA (sLORETA) [32], exact LORETA (eLORETA) [33], and the focal underdetermined system solution (FOCUSS) method [34]. However, these approaches are proven to have poor spatial resolution. In contrast, parametric approaches such as the linearly constrained minimum variance (LCMV) beamformer [35], the fast fully adaptive approach [36], the robust minimum variance beamformer technique [37], and subspace approaches (e.g., MUSIC [38], RAP-MUSIC [39], and FINES [40] approaches) have been shown to exhibit better spatial resolution and less localization error. Among parametric approaches, the LCMV beamformer is popular because it uses all the adaptive weights or degrees of freedom (DoFs) and achieves superior spatial resolution with no localization bias [35].

Effective connectivity across brain regions [41] reveals the directed information flow through neurons, as opposed to functional connectivity, which is undirected and only reflects the statistical covariation of signals, as usually shown by coherency, cross-correlation, or phase lag index measures. Measures of effective connectivity must meet four requirements, in addition to being directed, to be a useful addition to already established methods [42]. These include: 1) there can be no a priori requirement for a definition or model of the type of interaction, 2) the method must be able to detect non-linear interactions, since strong non-linearities are detected across brain function, 3) must be able to detect effective connectivity even if there is a wide distribution of interaction delays between the two signals, as the signals may move between brain areas through multiple pathways with different conduction delays, 4) must be robust against linear cross-talk between signals. Transfer entropy as a non-parametric statistic measuring the degree of directed transfer of information between two random processes, does indeed fulfill the above requirements, and is therefore a useful approach for the quantification of effective connectivity [42].

Consider two random processes X = (x1, x2, . . . , xN) and Y = (y1, y2, . . . , yN), where xi and yi are the ith samples (in this case, originating from two different brain regions). Transfer entropy, which is related to Granger causality [43], is defined as the Kullback-Leibler distance between the distributions p(xi+1|xi) and p(xi+1|xi, yi). It is therefore a measure of the information that yi contributes towards the prediction of the future sample xi+1. If this quantity is non-zero, then yi influences, or causes, xi and there is information flow from the brain region corresponding to the process Y to that corresponding to X; i.e. the sources are "connected". Note that directionality implies that information flow from Y to X is not necessarily equivalent to that from X to Y.

Since transfer entropy is based on transition probability distributions rather than solely on second-order statistics (such as e.g., Granger causality [43]) the method includes dynamical information and is capable of dealing with nonlinear interactions. Thus, transfer entropy has gained growing popularity in several areas, particularly the neurological sciences.

There are several techniques to estimate transfer entropy from observed data (e.g. [44]–[46]). However, most of the techniques require large quantities of data, tuning of parameters, and are highly sensitive to noise, therefore limiting the use of transfer entropy in many applications. Symbolic transfer entropy (STE) [47] (which involves estimation of transfer entropy by adopting a technique referred to as symbolization) has been introduced as a robust, convenient, and computationally fast measure to quantify information flow in multidimensional dynamic systems and can be used to infer the direction of linear and non-linear information exchange between brain regions over a range of time delays within EEG data. Therefore, STE has potential for discriminating MR vs. LR brain activity.

The contribution of this paper is threefold. First, the high resolution LCMV BSL approach is used for the first time to extract the activities of different brain regions for schizophrenic patients. Second, the fast and robust STE approach is used, again for the first time, to measure the effective connectivity between brain regions. Third, an ML method is developed based on the features extracted from these effective connectivity measures to predict response to clozapine treatment.

The novelty of the present study therefore lies in applying the combination of advanced signal processing methods, i.e. LCMV BSL, STE, and ML to predict response. The combination of these more advanced techniques results in a significant improvement in the ability to predict responsiveness, relative to previous approaches which have not used our proposed combination of advanced signal processing methods.

A. Subjects
Auditory oddball evoked potentials were collected from 57 SCZ subjects (age [years]: mean = 36.95, std = 9.22, min = 17, max = 55, 37 male subjects (64.9%) and 20 female subjects (35.1%)). All subjects were unpaid volunteer SCZ subjects for this study. They were recruited from Hamilton Psychiatric Hospital, Hamilton, Ontario for developing, on an ongoing basis, analytic methodologies that might reveal QEEG features differentiating schizophrenia from recruited healthy volunteers. The study was reviewed and approved by the Research Ethics Board of the Hospital. All EEG data were collected with the informed consent of the subjects. All SCZ subjects met both the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, fourth edition (DSM-IV) criteria for schizophrenia and the Kane criteria for treatment resistance [2]. Patients meet these two criteria typically have chronic schizophrenia and suffer from severe symptoms. Post treatment EEG data were collected after a mean treatment duration of 1.4 years (min = 0.4 years, max = 4.6 years). The mean daily dose of clozapine employed was 347 mg (range 50–800 mg).

To measure the PANNS severity rating scale, first all available clinical information about the symptoms revealed by the SCZ patients were reviewed by an experienced clinician prior to starting clozapine treatment. Then the symptoms were rated by one of the three PANSS rating scales of “present”, “moderate” or “severe” on a one to six-point scale. The clinician was instructed to only score the explicitly described symptoms and avoid scoring the potential symptoms. The same rating procedure was repeated after clozapine treatment, at the time when a decision would be made regarding further on-going long-term maintenance of treatment. Since most studies report that, on average, only one third of TRS-SCZ patients respond to clozapine treatment [2], we rank-ordered all patients by percentage of reduction in severity score from baseline PANSS and then chose a threshold value of 40% such that the 57 patients were divided into 33.3% MR and 66.7% LR patients (19 MR and 38 LR).

The EEG data were recorded using a QSI-9500 system. Electrodes were referenced to linked ears and were placed in standardized locations according to the International 10/20 system. The impedances of the electrodes were below 5 k. The system contains 20 EEG electrodes (Fp1, Fp2, F7, F3, Fz, F4, F8, T7, C3, Cz, C4, T8, P7, P3, Pz, P4, P8, O1, Oz, O2), as well as 4 additional muscle and eye movement artifact electrodes. The subjects listened to the auditory odd-ball paradigm over stereo headphones, where two different 50 ms, 91.5 dB tone beep stimuli were delivered in random order. The standard stimulus was a 1000 Hz tone that presented 80% of the time, while the deviant (also referred to as an “oddball”) stimulus was a 2000 Hz tone presented 20% of the time. The inter-stimulus interval was randomly varied between 1.25 and 3 sec. The subjects were seated comfortably with eyes opened and instructed to show by finger lift when they hear a deviant stimulus. The patient’s performance was monitored continuously for accuracy and were given a break whenever it was required to maintain the accuracy in identifying the deviant tones at or beyond the 90% level. The duration of each epoch was 1024 msec and the epochs were sampled with a sampling frequency of 250 Hz. The recording system separately recorded the average of the standard and deviant epochs at each electrode until the total of 120 successful deviant epochs were recorded. The signals were band pass filtered between 0.5 and 80 Hz and notch filtered at 60 Hz during the recording. The signals were then digitally band pass filtered between 0.5 Hz and 50 Hz using the EEGLAB MATLAB toolbox to partially mitigate the effects of muscle artifacts and eye movements. Only the averages of the deviant epochs measured by each of the electrodes were used in subsequent analysis.

C. De-Artifacting

The recording system automatically rejected epochs with a peak to peak signal amplitude of more than 100 uV on any electrode. The subjects were given frequent “blink holidays” to decrease eye blinking during recording. To alleviate muscle artifacts, the subjects were seated on a comfortable chair. A trained technician observed the subject continuously during recording to identify epochs with muscle and eye artifacts. All such epochs were removed from the recordings. The recorded signals were then visually inspected off-line to detect and remove any residual muscle or eye artifacts verified by detection of a strong signal on any of the 4 artifact electrodes.

III. METHODS — D. EEG Source Connectivity Analysis

This stage used the LCMV beamforming approach with three steps: 1) selecting regions of interest (ROIs) to identify intracerebral sources, 2) applying LCMV beamforming to scalp EEG data to extract activity in selected ROIs, and 3) applying a spectral transfer entropy (STE) algorithm to compute effective connections between sources. An ML algorithm then selected the most relevant connectivity values for a classifier determining late/mild cognitive impairment (LR/MR) status.

1) ROIs for LCMV Beamformer: A head model was constructed using the OpenMEEG boundary element method (BEM) implemented in BrainStorm® software [48, 49]. This symmetric BEM model used three realistic layers (scalp, skull, brain) with conductivities of 1, 1/80, and 1 S/m, respectively, offering better precision than a 3-shell sphere model [50]. The head volume was partitioned into 12,058 voxels at 5mm spatial resolution. Anatomical labels corresponding to Brodmann areas were mapped from MNI to Talairach space [51]. To reduce estimation count, 30 ROIs were selected (15 per hemisphere; see Table I). The centroid of each ROI was defined as the voxel closest to the ROI mass center, justified by high internal voxel correlation [52].

The LCMV beamformer output y(k) at location q0 was computed as:

y(k) = W^T(q0)x(k)  (3)

where the N×3 weighting matrix W(q0) was computed to minimize output variance subject to a unit-norm constraint:

W(q0) = R_x^{-1}H

section: III. METHODS — E. Machine Learning

input:
The dataset contains EEG responses to odd-ball stimuli for 57 subjects, labeled as 19 MR patients and 38 LR controls. The machine learning procedure consists of four steps: feature extraction, feature selection, classification, and evaluation, aiming to classify unseen test subjects into MR or LR groups.

The first step extracts 4350 candidate STE connectivity features from all SCZ subjects' EEG data.

After extraction, a feature selection step reduces the number of features to avoid overfitting. This study uses the minimum redundancy maximum relevance (mRMR) filter method to select the most discriminating features. The mRMR algorithm selects features with maximum statistical dependence on the outcome variable while minimizing redundancy among selected features.

To prevent selecting features dominant in only a few subjects, the study employs a consensus nested cross-validation (CN-CV) procedure. This iterative process splits the dataset into stratified outer folds; in each iteration, one fold is held out for testing while the remaining data are split into inner folds for feature selection. The algorithm repeats until all outer folds have served as the test set.

In this study the data set consists of the EEG responses to the odd-ball (or deviant) responses for each of the Mt = 57 subjects, and their corresponding labels, 1 for the 19 MR patients and 2 for the 38 LR. The ML procedure contains four steps: feature extraction, feature selection, classification, and evaluation. The objective of the ML procedure is to determine whether a previously unseen test subject belongs to the MR or LR class.

The first step consists of extracting the candidate features in the form of Nc = 4350 STE connectivity values from the EEG data of all SCZ subjects.

After extracting candidate features, the second step is feature selection to reduce the number of features. This step is critical to avoid overﬁtting, which affects the performance of the classiﬁer. In this step we identify a set of Nr ≪ Nc most discriminating features to distinguish between the MR and LR classes. Various feature selection methods are available that can be separated into three categories: ﬁlter methods, wrapper methods, and embedded methods [54], [55]. Two main advantages of the ﬁlter method are computation efﬁciency and generalizability over different classiﬁers. In this study, we used the minimum redundancy maximum relevance (mRMR) feature selection algorithm, which is a ﬁlter method, to select the most distinguishable features [56]. The rationale for choosing the mRMR method is its ability to effectively reduce the number of selected redundant features while maintaining the most relevant features for the model. It is known that selecting the N best features individually does not necessarily lead to the best set of combined features because of their potential correlation and redundancy [57]. The mRMR method solves this problem by selecting features that have maximum statistical dependence (relevance) with the outcome variable (here the treatment response) and minimum statistical dependence (redundancy) within the selected features.

In order to avoid choosing features that are dominant in only a few subjects, we used the newly developed consensus nested cross validation (CN-CV) procedure [58]. The CN-CV procedure is an iterative process, where ﬁrst the dataset is split into k outer folds (here we use stratiﬁed K folds, where each fold has the same proportion of data for each class). Then at each iteration, one fold is held out for testing and is omitted from the training set while the remaining K − 1 folds are merged and split into L inner folds for feature selection. The iterations repeat until all outer folds have been considered as a test set once. The CN-CV algorithm structure is similar to nested CV (N-CV) [59], but unlike N-CV it does not train the classiﬁers in the inner folds. In contrast, CN-CV only performs feature selection in the inner folds. The steps of the CN-CV algorithm are as follows:

4. For Nr = 1, 2, . . . , NSF (total number of selected features)
4.1 Select the first Nr consensus features at each outer fold k, k = 1, 2, …, K.
4.2 Train the classifier based on the Nr selected features on the kth outer fold training dataset and evaluate its performance on the corresponding test dataset and save the accuracy metrics for outer fold k.
4.3 Calculate the average of any accuracy metric over all K outer folds and report it as the generalization accuracy metric using Nr features.
5. Select the first Nr features with the highest classification performance as the final set of selected features, and the corresponding generalization accuracy metrics as the final performance metrics.

Here we consider k = l = 5 in order to have 80% of the data for training and 20% for testing in each inner and outer iteration. At each inner fold, features with mRMR scores above 10−3 are considered as selected features for that fold. We use the conservative threshold value of 10−3, because features with smaller scores are likely irrelevant for classification.

TABLE II
THE 8 DISCRIMINATING FEATURES BETWEEN MR AND LR GROUPS

The CN-CV algorithm helps us to select most discriminating features that are in common across inner training folds, while the use of the inner folds prevents information leakage between outer folds. Furthermore, selecting features without training classifiers makes CN-CV method more computationally efficient than N-CV and selects fewer irrelevant features than N-CV [58]. In this study, the lowest number of features that gave adequate performance was Nr = 8, which is much lower than the 57 data samples and thus reduces the tendency for overfitting (the feature to sample ratio is 8/57 × 100 = 14.03%).

The third step is selecting the classifier for classification. In this step, the selected features are employed to the classifier. The classifier’s function is to provide a class label for a selected feature set corresponding to a given data sample. In our study, we compare the performance of three widely used classifiers: support vector machine (SVM), random forest (RF), and linear discriminant analysis (LDA) algorithms. A Gaussian radial basis kernel function, which was determined using the sequential minimal optimization technique [60], is considered for the SVM algorithm, and 30 trees are considered for the RF algorithm. These methods were implemented using the Statistics and Machine Learning Toolbox in MATLAB R2019b.

The final step is performance evaluation. Since the size of our available training set is small, to obtain an effective estimate of the ML performance, the CN-CV algorithm were used in this step to evaluate the performance.

section: IV. RESULTS
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
A set of 8 features discriminating MR from LR was identified using mRMR feature selection (Table II). Table III reports sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, precision, F1 score, and Kappa for SVM, RF, and LDA using 5-fold CN-CV. mRMR and RF were used for feature selection; RF ranks features by classifier importance.

From Table III, SVM achieved the highest averaged total accuracy of 95.83% (5 folds) with mRMR, followed by RF (93.37%) and LDA (91.48%). SVM and LDA had the highest sensitivity (93.75%), while RF had 85.42%. SVM and RF shared the highest specificity (96.87%), with LDA at 90.18%. RF had the highest precision (95%), followed by SVM (93.75%) and LDA (85%). SVM had the highest F1 score (93.75), followed by LDA (88.89%) and RF (88.65%). SVM also had the highest Kappa (0.91), followed by RF (0.84) and LDA (0.82). Fig. 2 shows SVM had the highest AUC (0.96), followed by RF (0.95) and LDA (0.94). These results prove the selected features are highly discriminating, with SVM showing the highest and most consistent accuracy. This is attributed to SVM’s effectiveness with imbalanced datasets and its non-linear radial basis kernel, unlike RF’s decision trees and LDA’s linear boundary. Furthermore, the minimum number of features for optimal RF performance is N_r = 12.

Comparing classifiers using RF-selected features showed reduced performance for SVM and LDA, suggesting less generalizability, while mRMR-selected features improved performance across all classifiers and provide better interpretability by reducing redundancy.

Fig. 3 shows a KPCA scatter plot (polynomial kernel) of 57 subjects (19 MR, 38 LR), clearly separating MR and LR clusters, though performance is better using all 8 selected features.

Previous studies correlated pre-treatment neuroimaging features with clozapine outcomes but did not develop predictive algorithms. ML was first used in [22], though it used scalp functional connectivity features prone to volume conduction artifacts. BSL mitigates this issue. Selected features overlap with prior studies identifying frontal areas [9]–[21] (features 1, 3, 4, 5, 8 in Table II) as predictive. Increased perfusion in thalamic and basal ganglia areas [16], [17] links to clozapine response; though not ROIs here, Yakovlev et al. [65] showed thalamic projections overlap the cingulate gyrus (features 3, 4, 5, 6, 8). Frontal, premotor, supplementary motor, orbital frontal, dorsal lateral prefrontal, and anterior cingulate areas connect to the basal ganglia [66]. Selected features also include left LTL (feature 2), left FG (features 6, 7), and left SPL (feature 1), linked to clozapine prediction in [22].

A set of 8 features which can discriminate between MR and LR have been identified in Table II using the mRMR feature selection approach. Table III shows the sensitivity, specificity, total accuracy, precision, F1 score, and the Kappa statistic for the widely used SVM, RF, and LDA classification approaches, using the outer 5 folds of the CN-CV method for performance evaluation. mRMR and the widely-used random forest (RF) approaches were used for feature selection. With the RF classifier, the feature selection process is embedded in the algorithm. The RF feature selection approach is used for comparison against the mRMR method. For the RF feature selection method, the features are ranked by the RF classifier and the best features are selected according to their RF rank.

TABLE III
CLASSIFICATION PERFORMANCE OF DIFFERENT CLASSIFIERS
DISCRIMINATING 19 MR FROM 38 LR SUBJECTS
USING SKF-CV WITH K=5

Fig. 2.
Comparison of ROC curve between SVM, RF, and LDA approaches.

In this study, sensitivity is the MR prediction rate, which refers to how well the MR subjects are predicted without being missed. Specificity is the LR prediction rate, and total accuracy is the total test prediction rate considering both the MR and LR groups. Precision is the fraction of truly predicted MR cases among all cases that are predicted MR. The F1 score is a measure of a test’s accuracy that considers both the precision and the sensitivity of the test data to compute the score, which is considered to be a better indication of overall classification accuracy. The Kappa statistic [61] corrects the degree of agreement between the classifier’s predictions and reality by considering the proportion of predictions that might occur by chance, and is recommended as an indicator of the consistency of the accuracy estimate [62].

Furthermore, Fig. 2 compares the performances of all three classifiers in terms of the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve [63] and the area under the ROC curve (AUC) value. ROC is a widely used tool that provides an indication of the tradeoff between classification sensitivity and specificity as the classifier confidence threshold increases or decreases. The AUC provides an aggregate measure of performance across all possible classification thresholds.

From Table III, the SVM classifier can discriminate MR from LR with the highest averaged total classification accuracy of 95.83% (averaged over the 5 folds) using the mRMR feature selection method, followed by the RF and LDA classifiers with total accuracies of 93.37% and 91.48%, respectively. The other five calculated accuracy metrics are sensitivity, specificity, Precision, F1-score, and the kappa statistic. SVM and LDA have the highest sensitivity of 93.75%, followed by RF with a sensitivity of 85.42%, while the highest specificity of 96.87% belongs to SVM and RF, followed by the LDA with a specificity of 90.18%. In terms of precision, RF has the highest value of 95%, followed by SVM and LDA with precision values of 93.75% and 85%. Furthermore, SVM has the highest F1-score (F1=93.75), followed by LDA (F1=88.89%) and RF (F1=88.65%) and the highest Kappa statistic (κ = 0.91), followed by RF (κ =0.84) and LDA (κ = 0.82). Finally, from Fig. 2, SVM has the highest AUC (AUC=0.96) followed by RF (AUC=0.95) and LDA (AUC=0.94). These high classification accuracies across different classification algorithms proves the selected features are highly discriminating between the two classes. In addition, these results show that SVM has the highest and most consistent overall classification accuracy. We believe this is due to the fact that SVM can deal with imbalanced datasets more effectively than RF, since RF is built on decision trees, which are sensitive to class imbalance. Also, the radial basis kernel function used by SVM potentially improves performance by imposing a non-linear decision boundary that can be adapted to best suit the data, while LDA can only choose the best linear transformation that maximizes separability.

In addition, from Table III, the minimum number of features for the RF algorithm for best performance is N_r = 12.

Comparing the performance of the three classifiers using the features selected inherently by the RF algorithm, we see a considerable reduction in classification performance for the SVM and LDA methods, suggesting less generalizability for the RF feature set. Alternatively, the effect of reducing feature redundancy afforded by mRMR method leads to a significantly better classification performance for all three classifiers. Such distinctive features would also provide better interpretability, since the model is not overwhelmed with redundant information.

To demonstrate the clustering behavior of the selected features, Fig. 3 shows a scatter plot containing 57 points corresponding to the 19 MR and 38 LR subjects. This figure is generated using the kernelized principle component analysis (KPCA) method with a polynomial kernel [64]. Although the MR and LR clusters are clearly separated in this figure, better performance is obtained using all 8 selected features.

Although previous studies (e.g. [9]–[21], [25]) found that pre-treatment changes in neuroimaging features are correlated with clozapine treatment outcomes, their findings did not lead to the development of a quantitative prediction algorithm. ML was used as a predictive algorithm in [22] for the first time. However, the authors used conventional functional connectivity that applied to scalp electrodes as features, which may cause false connectivity patterns due to volume conduction effects in scalp EEG data. BSL is an alternative to channel-related connectivity to mitigate this issue.

It is worth noting that some of the selected features using the proposed feature selection algorithm were from the regions that are also identified in previous studies. Most of these studies showed measures of frontal area as a predictive value to clozapine treatment [9]–[11], [13], [14], [16], [17], [20], [21] (features 1, 3, 4, 5, and 8 in Table II). Furthermore, it is shown there is a link between increase in the levels of perfusion in thalamus [16], [17] and basal ganglia [16] areas and response to clozapine treatment. While the thalamus and basal ganglia areas are not among the ROIs in this study, Yakovlev et al. (1966) [65] showed the high degree of overlap of the thalamic projections on the cingulate gyrus, which is selected in features 3, 4, 5, 6, and 8. Also, the frontal, premotor and supplementary motor areas, the orbital frontal cortex, the dorsal lateral prefrontal cortex, and the anterior cingulate all connect into the basal ganglia [66]. Three more areas that are included in the selected features are left LTL (feature 2), left FG (features 6 and 7), and left SPL (feature 1), where left LTL and left FG are a part of the left temporal lobe and left SPL is a part of left parietal lobe, where their measures are shown to be linked to the prediction of clozapine treatment [22].

section: V. CONCLUSION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: We developed the first ML algorithm using LCMV, BSL, and STE effective connectivity techniques to predict clozapine response using pre-treatment odd-ball EEG from 19 MR and 38 LR SCZ patients. We identified 8 discriminating features distinguishing MRs from LRs, with SVM achieving the highest accuracy: sensitivity 93.75%, specificity 96.87%, total accuracy 95.83%, precision 93.75%, F1-score 93.75%, and κ = 0.91. The LCMV BSL method is critical for increasing desired signal SNR from a specific ROI and suppressing volume conduction effects that may cause false connectivity estimates. This study showed that advanced signal processing and ML models improve prediction accuracy of clozapine responsiveness compared to other studies. The sample of 57 subjects is larger than most previous studies and benefits from a lengthy follow-up, increasing the probability of detecting clozapine effectiveness [67]. Combining BSL, STE, and ML analytic techniques may create a useful psychiatric tool to predict clozapine responsiveness, with potential extension to other treatments or mental disorders. Further improvement may be possible by combining clinical and laboratory features such as demographics, personality scores, blood tests, and treatment history with EEG measurements. Accuracy values in Table III are significantly improved over any other similar study in the literature, which we attribute to the use of more sophisticated signal processing techniques.
output: In this study, for the first time, we developed an ML algorithm based on LCMV, BSL and STE effective connectivity techniques to investigate the possibility of predicting response to clozapine treatment using pre-treatment odd-ball EEG measurements over 19 MR and 38 LR SCZ patients. We identified a set of 8 discriminating features that distinguish MRs from LRs, with the highest and most consistent accuracy being obtained using the SVM classifier (Sensitivity=93.75%, specificity=96.87%, total accuracy=95.83%, precision=93.75%, F1-score=93.75%, and κ = 0.91). This high classification accuracy supports the potential usefulness of ML methods in clinical psychiatry. The use of the LCMV BSL method is critical in this study to increase the SNR of the desired signal from a particular ROI and suppress the volume conduction effect, which may cause false connectivity estimates between regions. This study showed that the use of advanced signal processing and ML models improves the prediction accuracy of responsiveness to clozapine treatment compared to other studies. Furthermore, the sample of 57 subjects in this study is larger than most of the previous studies and has the advantage of a lengthy follow-up, which can increase the probability of detecting clozapine effectiveness [67]. Our finding suggests that combining BSL, STE, and ML analytic techniques may be employed to create a useful psychiatric tool to predict responsiveness to clozapine treatment. This methodology also has the potential to be extended to a model that can predict the response to different treatments available for SCZ patients or even for other mental disorders. It may be possible to combine a range of other clinical and laboratory features such as personal and demographic information, personality inventory scores, blood tests, and treatment history to EEG measurements to improve prediction performance even further. Finally, we note that accuracy values shown in Table III are significantly improved over those of any other similar study we have seen from the literature. We attribute this improved performance to the use of the more sophisticated signal processing techniques adopted in the present study. A major contribution of this paper is therefore the demonstration that the use of such advanced signal processing methods results in significantly improved performances over what has been previously obtained.

section: I. INTRODUCTION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: In competitive electricity markets, producers cannot influence the market price and must optimize output at the intersection of marginal cost and price. Market liberalization has shifted systems toward oligopoly, where producers can raise prices through economic or physical withholding, creating "market power" [1], [2]. Post-liberalization, price manipulation arises from implicit or explicit collusion among producers [3]-[7]. A long-term alliance to inflate prices above competitive levels constitutes collusion [10]. Such coalitions alter competitor bids and are chosen based on projected profit maximization [8], [9]. Modern wholesale markets, characterized by few firms, non-storable electricity, inelastic demand, and transmission congestion, enable collusion [10]. This behavior violates consumer rights and reduces efficiency, prompting regulators to prohibit coalitions [11], [12]. This paper focuses on explicit collusion and proposes methods to reveal and detect such behaviors.

fect the market price. They can only determine the
amount of their own production according to the market
price. Therefore, the optimum production level will be calcu‐
lated by the intersection of the marginal cost curve with mar‐
ket price. The limitations of power systems have pushed the
electricity markets from competitive environment toward oli‐
gopoly market. In an oligopoly market, there is a possibility
for producers to affect the market price. The producers who
are interested in raising the market price may increase their
bids (economic withholding) or reduce the production (physi‐
cal withholding) to influence the market price in their favor‐
able direction. The producers, who can affect the market
with any of the above mentioned methods, have the so
called “market power” [1], [2]. In addition to raising prices
higher than the competitive level, the ability of maintaining
the market price for a long period is important.
After the liberalization of the electricity market, price ma‐
nipulation and market power of individual producers [3]-[5]
can result from the joint decision and the alliance of two or
several producers. In such cases, the collusion is done in the
form of implicit and explicit [6], [7]. A long-term alliance
between several firms to inflate the market price out of its
competitive range is called collusion. Generation firms,
which cannot obtain their desired profit through fair competi‐
tion in oligopoly market, may collude and set their bid and
market prices to a value abnormally higher than what oligop‐
oly competition commands. Explicit collusion is a hidden
agreement for the interaction among electricity power pro‐
ducers who share confidential information in order to control
the market price. The goal of a coalition is to adopt or en‐
force unified strategies to increase the profit of its members.
However, the influence of a coalition does not remain limit‐
ed to the bids of its members and will alter the bids of its
competitors. Stakeholder’s choice of coalition is based on
the projected profit after the formation of the coalition. In
other words, each agent selects the coalition that provides
the maximum profit. Members of an explicit coalition share

[8], [9].
With the advent of modern wholesale electricity markets
in developed countries, these markets have become the sub‐
ject of many discussions. These discussions often originate
from the nature of the electricity markets, e.g., they are of‐
ten controlled by a few number of firms, the traded electrici‐
ty cannot be stored, the demand has an inelastic nature, and
technical limitations such as the congestion of transmission
line can lead to the isolation of sub-markets. These character‐
istics provide an enabling environment for coalitions, which
can be regarded as the collusion [10]. The absence of the
competition in a market where prices are set by the collu‐
sion leads to the violation of the consumers’ rights and the
reduction of producer’s efficiency. In light of these adverse
effects, regulatory organizations often prohibit such coali‐

I. INTRODUCTION

M. Esmalifalak is with the Predictive Modeling Department of Fiix Software, Toronto, Canada (e-mail: esmalifalak.mohammad@gmail.com). DOI: 10.35833/MPCE.2018.000566

Collusive behaviors in electricity markets are difficult to detect due to the unavailability of labeled collusion data. This paper proposes using supervised learning to address this gap. The approach first computes market equilibrium for varying loads and collusion scenarios, then trains detection models using equilibrium data and neighboring operation points. Support vector machines and decision trees are evaluated against other supervised and statistical methods.

Section II models Nash equilibrium and computes market equilibrium. Section III overviews the machine learning approach for collusion detection. Section IV describes finding quasi-actual system operation points. Section V applies the detection method to a typical electricity market and discusses results. Section VI concludes the paper.

The basic approach is to use supervised learning, but the
major problem of this approach is the unavailability of data
specifically referring to collusion. The alternative is to use
unsupervised learning techniques for this purpose [13], [14].
The detection mechanism introduced in [13] focuses on cir‐
cular trading, in which a ring of colluder trades a certain
share repeatedly to raise their price. The proposed method is
based on the interpretation of stock flow graph with Markov
clustering algorithm. Reference [14] focuses on the detection
of cross trading and investigates the aptitude of different
clustering algorithms for collusion detection in electricity
markets. Reference [15] detects the collusion using a twostep process in an energy market. Firstly, the behavioral pat‐
tern of the collusion is investigated. Then, by using a
change-point analysis, the behavior of each agent is studied
to reveal the possible structural breakpoints. The existence
of such breakpoints could be a sign for the collusion and has
to be analyzed more in a verification phase. In the verifica‐
tion phase, behavioral similarities of candidates are checked
using statistical methods. The execution of market power
and the inefficiencies of restructured electricity market in Al‐
berta, Canada, are studied in [16]. The hourly wholesale mar‐
ket data set from 2008 to 2014 is used to find that firms con‐
duct considerable power in the highest demand hours with
bounded excess generation capacity. A game-theoretic model
is used in [17] to analyze the behaviours of independent sys‐
tem operator (ISO) and the generator leading to collusive
transactions. Reference [18] demonstrates the relationship be‐
tween market concentration and collusion sustainability and
their dependence to the strength of the network externalities.
In [19], from the regulatory body’s viewpoint, a model pow‐
ered by game theory and agent-based systems is used to in‐
vestigate the behaviours of each market player. The pro‐
posed method looks at the tacit collusive behaviour of gener‐
ation firms as well as the possibility of explicit collusion.
Reference [20] intends to detect the possibility of collusive
behavior in the liberalized retail electricity market by testing
the validity of the Cournot model of imperfect competition.
The monthly data on the Japanese electric power industry
are applied from 2005 to 2010. It indicates that the possibili‐
ty of collusive behavior among the incumbents cannot be ex‐
cluded. Moreover, the test results imply that larger market
size and firm size might reduce the possibility of collusion
among incumbent retail electricity suppliers. Reference [21]
provides an approach to analyze the development of tacit col‐
lusion between a generator company (Genco) and a distribut‐
ed company (Disco) in a simulated electricity market. Behav‐
iors of Gencos and Discos are modeled using state-action-re‐
ward-state-action (SARSA) learning algorithm, and the mod‐
el is used to tune continual exploration and make the tradeoff between the exploration and exploitation. A typical mar‐
ket with three Gencos and two Discos to prove the possibili‐
ty of tacit collusion between a Genco and a Disco is ana‐
lyzed, which shows that the development of this type of col‐
lusion increases their utilities. Reference [22] studies the col‐
lusion during bilateral agreement in the direct electricity pur‐
chase market. Firstly, a multiple-to-multiple (MTM) model
of bilateral negotiation in direct electricity purchase market
is provided based on the traditional Rubinstein negotiation
model. Then, the collusion is divided into two categories.
Specifically, the collusion can be divided into two catego‐
ries. One is based on the pre-specified information and the
other is based on process communication. Then, the bidding
strategies under the above two collusions are studied in de‐
tail. Finally, the impact of the collusion on the market is ana‐
lyzed through simulations, and regulatory proposals are pro‐
posed. Reference [23] investigates the competition on local
electricity markets to avoid the effects of market power and
analyze the impact of tacit collusion on the possibility of ex‐
ercising market power. It shows that more competitions
would diminish the effects of market power, especially when
a high-level competition with market shares of no more than
20%, because each competitor is needed for peak produc‐
tion. They also indicate that the overall effect of tacit collu‐
sion seems to be small in order to manipulate the market
price by the colluder. Furthermore, tacit collusion in the
form of signaling has no impact on base agent markups.
This paper uses supervised learning methods to detect the
collusion in electricity markets. Market equilibrium is firstly
computed for different loads and collusions. Market equilibri‐
um data and their neighboring operation points are used to
train the collusion detection machine by applying support
vector machine (SVM) and decision tree algorithms. The ef‐
ficiencies of these algorithms are compared with other super‐
vised learning and statistical method.
The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section Ⅱ
describes the process through which Nash equilibrium is
modeled and market equilibrium is computed. Section Ⅲ
overviews the machine learning approach used to detect the
collusion. In Section Ⅳ, the method of finding quasi-actual
system operation points is described. In Section Ⅴ, the devel‐
oped collusion detection method is applied to the model of a
typical electricity market, and then the results are discussed
and analyzed in Section Ⅵ.

input: Machine learning originates from pattern recognition and computation learning theory in AI [26]. Algorithms developed with these concepts are expected to perform tasks on unspecified data [27]. The most important task is supervised learning [28]. In supervised learning, an algorithm is provided with input, output, and labeled training data. It then uses machine inference to develop a function that maps new data.

The concept of machine learning originates from pattern
recognition and computation learning theory in artificial in‐
telligence [26]. The algorithms developed with machine
learning concepts are expected to do their tasks for unspeci‐
fied data [27]. Machine learning has a multitude of tasks,
the most important of which may be the supervised learning
[28]. In the supervised learning, the algorithm with a certain
input, a certain output, and a group of labeled training data
is provided. The algorithm then uses machine inference to
develop a function capable of emulating the process and

section: III. MACHINE LEARNING — A. SVM Algorithm
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: SVM is a supervised algorithm used for data classification [29], [30]. It defines an optimal boundary between classes using a linear hyper-plane that maximizes the distance from each class [30]. The algorithm identifies support vectors as data samples bordering each class and searches for a hyper-plane maximizing the minimum distance to these vectors [30]. For multi-class classification involving more than two classes, specific methods such as one-against-one or one-against-all are required [31], [32]. If data are inseparable by a linear hyper-plane, they are mapped to a higher-dimensional feature space using a kernel function, enabling the fitting of a maximum-margin hyper-plane in the transformed space [33]. Factors affecting performance include the kernel function, its parameters, and the soft margin parameter C [34]. A Gaussian kernel with a single gamma parameter is a typical choice, and optimal values for C and gamma are typically determined via grid search and cross-validation [35].
output:
SVM algorithm [29], [30] is one of the most widely used
supervised algorithms in data classification. In fact, SVM al‐
gorithm is a binary classifier that defines the optimal bound‐
ary between two (or more) classes. Mathematically, SVM us‐
es a linear hyper-plane to separate two classes by maximiz‐
ing the distance of each class from this plan. The algorithm
uses a quadratic programming to find data samples that are
in the border of each class, and these samples are known to
support vectors. Then, the algorithm searches for the hyperplane which firstly has the maximum distance from each sup‐
port vector. Secondly, the distances between the hyper-plane
and each support vector are equal. As mentioned above, the
support vector algorithm is used only to separate the two
classes from each other. But for collusion detection and diag‐
nosis of the firms involved in the collusion, the number of
different classes may depend on the type of the collusion,
and the number of firms is more than those of the two class‐
es. Hence, for the category and classification of different
types of the collusion, specific methods of multi-class SVMs
must be used, which include one against one and one
against all methods [31], [32]. If the data are inseparable by
a linear hyper-plane, the data are mapped to a higher dimen‐
sional space which is called feature space by kernel func‐
tion. Through this procedure, the algorithm becomes capable
of fitting the maximum-margin hyper-plane in a transformed
feature space. This transformation could be linear or nonlin‐
ear and the transformed feature space could be of a higher
dimension. Note that in the transformed feature space, the
classifier is a hyper-plane, but in the original input space, it
could be nonlinear [33]. Factors deciding the SVM perfor‐
mance are the chosen kernel function and its parameters as
well as the soft margin parameter C. Gaussian kernel, which
has a single γ, is a typical choice for SVM [34]. The com‐
mon practice for finding the best values of C and γ is to con‐
duct a grid search, i.e., to repeat the calculations with differ‐
ent C and γ combinations and determine the values yielding
the best accuracy through cross-validation [35].

section: III. MACHINE LEARNING — B. Classification and Regression Tree (CART) Algorithm
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Decision tree is a supervised, non-parametric method using a hierarchical structure to classify data via flowchart-like trees. Based on the dependent variable type, the algorithm splits into classification trees for discrete variables and regression trees for continuous variables. The algorithm selects features at each stage to divide the dataset into class groupings until all data in a category has a single label. The CART algorithm, introduced in [37], uses binary division to create trees. At each stage, the Gini index selects the best attribute. One application is modeling customer behavior in financial markets, such as credit card fraud detection, where finding mathematical rules for individual behaviors is complex. This research models market participant behavior without detailed incentive knowledge. Synthetic data assumes known safe or fraudulent behaviors, but the machine learning approach distinguishes these behaviors without access to the creation rules.
output:
As a predictive model, decision tree is one of the super‐
vised learning and non-parametric methods with the hierar‐
chical structure which is used to classify different types of
data, and its results are delivered in a flowchart-like tree
structure. According to the dependent variable type, this algo‐
rithm is divided into two categories: classification trees for
discrete variables and regression trees for continuous vari‐
ables. In this algorithm, the fragmentation of the data is im‐
plemented by using the features as a tree. For better under‐
standing, it is written by using as if-then rules [36]. In each
stage of this method, a feature for the data is selected based
on the training data and the data set is divided into a class
grouping based on the chosen features. This continues until
all the data in a category has a single label. One of the most
famous decision tree algorithms is CART algorithm, which
leads to the creation of a tree with binary division intro‐
duced in [37]. CART algorithm is a non-parametric decision
tree learning technique, which is used to classify any type of
the data. In other words, the CART algorithm produces ei‐
ther the classification or regression trees, depending on
whether the dependent variable is categorical or numerical,
respectively. At each stage, the Gini index is used to select
the best attribute for the data used. One important applica‐
tion of machine learning is to model costumer behaviors in
financial markets, which comes from the fact that finding
mathematical rules to model the behaviors of individual cos‐
tumers is a very complex process, e.g., in credit card fraud
detection. It would be extremely hard to find reasons and
rules for justifying safe versus fraudulent behaviors without
the help of machine learning approaches. This research is an‐
other attempt to model the behavior of market participants
without the detailed knowledge about their incentives. In cre‐
ating synthetic data, it is assumed that we know safe or
fraudulent behaviors, but we let machine learning approach
distinguish those behaviors without access to any of rules
used to create synthetic data.

section: IV. COLLUSION DETECTION AND CLASSIFICATION — A. Data Generation
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: The objective is to provide a tool for ISO to detect and identify colluding firms using day-ahead data via machine learning. A major obstacle is the lack of knowledge about data associated with different collusion scenarios. Equilibrium points are obtained for various load demands and collusion types per Section II. Proper detection requires modeling beyond a single period or load class. An exact match between the market operation point and computed equilibrium is rare, but mature markets are close enough to equilibrium to assume peripheral points as quasi-actual operation points [25], [38]. Due to daily changes in power systems and producer ignorance of these changes, markets are not static. However, since daily changes are small relative to the whole environment and producers are rational, it is reasonable to assume markets operate close to Nash equilibrium. Thus, peripheral equilibrium points are used for synthetic data generation. The Nash equilibrium lies in a ball centered at the equilibrium point with a specified radius. To implement this, the intercept of each generation unit's supply curve is altered around its equilibrium value, and the resulting points are treated as quasi-actual operation points. Quasi-actual data are selected randomly within these balls. To create quasi-actual operation points for collusion states, the electricity market and collusion must be modeled. Colluding firms are treated as a single entity optimizing the sum of their profits rather than individual profits. In markets, collusion means two or more producers collaborate to raise electricity prices long-term, maximizing the sum of colluding firms' profits. To generate collusion-reflecting data, equilibrium points for all possible collusion scenarios are computed. In each scenario, all colluding producers are treated as one firm maximizing coalition profit. Equilibrium points and their peripheries for different collusion scenarios at various load levels serve as synthetic machine learning data.
output: The objective of this paper is to provide a tool that would allow ISO to detect collusion and identify the colluding firms using the day-ahead data, which is pursued via a machine learning paradigm. One problem that obstructs the use of trainable machines in collusion detection and classification is the lack of adequate knowledge about the data associated with different collusion among participants. According to Section II, equilibrium points are obtained for different load demands and different kinds of collusion scenarios. To achieve a proper collusion detection technique, the modeling should go beyond the limits of a single period or a certain class of load demand. An exact match between the market operation point and computed market equilibrium is rare. But mature electricity markets are often close enough to the equilibrium to allow the peripheral points of the equilibrium to be assumed as quasi-actual operation points [25], [38]. Moreover, due to different changes that occur every day in power systems, and the fact that power producers do not know these changes, market players are not faced with a static environment. Hence, electricity markets may not work exactly on their Nash equilibrium. However, since daily changes in the game environment are small in comparison to the whole environment, and all producers are rational and smart, it is reasonable to assume that electricity markets work at a point close to their Nash equilibrium. Thus we consider peripheral equilibrium points for creating synthetic data. The Nash equilibrium point is located in a ball with the center of the Nash equilibrium and a specified radius. To implement this assumption, the intercept of the supply curve of each generation unit is altered around its value at the equilibrium point. And the resulting points are considered as quasi-actual operation points. To determine quasi-actual data, suppose αp is the set that contains the intercept of the bid of all generation units at the pth equilibrium point. Balls B(αp, hαp) are defined for equilibrium points p=1, 2, ..., P, where αp and hαp are the center and radius of the ball p, respectively; P is the number of equilibrium points computed for different load levels and collusion scenarios; and h is the deviation percentage that represents the extent of deviation of quasi-actual data from the considered equilibrium points. Quasi-actual data are selected randomly within these balls. To create the quasi-actual operation points for collusion states, we need to model the electricity market and collusion. To model the collusion, the firms participating in the collusion are considered as a single entity, which means that generation firms that participate in the collusion seek to optimize the sum of profits of all firms participating in the collusion, instead of optimizing their profits separately and independently. In other words, in electricity markets, the collusion means that two or more power producers collaborate to increase the electricity price for a long time. The producers' bid is colluded so that the sum of profits of all colluding firms is maximized. To generate the data that reflect collusion behavior, equilibrium points for all possible collusion scenarios are computed. To simulate the collusion, in each scenario, all colluding power producers are considered as one firm that maximizes the profit of the coalition. Equilibrium points and their peripherals for different collusion scenarios at different load levels are considered as synthetic data for machine learning.

Section IV-B. Collusion Detection Training

The equilibrium and quasi-actual operation points train the detection machines. Attributes distinguishing colluding from non-colluding points are used for training. After training, real operation point data are input to detect collusion and participating firms.

The training attributes are: marginal cost of generators (MC), bid price of generators (BP), Lerner index (LER), market share (MS), and Herfindahl-Hirschman index (HHI). ISO estimates generator marginal costs using model [39], [40] since firms refuse to report them. The Lerner index measures the extent to which bid price exceeds real marginal cost, indicating firm market power. The Herfindahl-Hirschman index (HHI) measures market concentration [41], [42]. This paper uses k-fold cross-validation (estimator [43]) for classifier assessment and error estimation. Algorithm 1 outlines the collusion detection procedure under scenario SC.

According to Section Ⅳ-A, the equilibrium points and
quasi-actual operation points are used for training the ma‐
chines. In order to detect the collusion and the firms partici‐
pating in it, some attributes or criteria are required to distin‐
guish the operation points related to the collusion from those
without the collusion, which are used to train the trainable
machines. After training, the data of a real operation point
are given to the trained machine, and the machine detects
the occurrence of the collusion and firms participating in
JOURNAL OF MODERN POWER SYSTEMS AND CLEAN ENERGY, VOL. 9, NO. 1, January 2021
this violation. The attributes or criteria used for training the
collusion detection machine are as follows.
1) Marginal cost of generators (MC).
2) Bid price of generators (BP).
3) Lerner index for different generators (LER).
4) Market share of each producer with load demand (MS).
5) Herfindahl Hirschman index of the market with each
load demand (HHI).
Privately-owned generators naturally refuse to publicly re‐
port their marginal cost functions. It is assumed that ISO es‐
timates marginal cost functions of all generators using the
available model in [39], [40]. The Lerner index measures the
extent to which the bid price of a given firm exceeds its real
marginal costs. In other words, the Lerner index measures a
firm’s level of electricity power and describes the relation‐
ship between the elasticity and price margins. The Herfind‐
ahl Hirschman index is accepted as an indicator of market
competition that measures the level of the concentration in a
given market [41], [42]. The market simulation performed in
this paper aims to calculate the above-mentioned criteria at
the quasi-actual operation points under different collusive
conditions. In this paper, for model assessment and error esti‐
mation of classifier, k-fold cross-validation estimator is used
as a randomized method for error estimation [43]. Algorithm
1 shows the procedure of the collusion detection method,
where SC is the collusion scenario.

input: This study uses 41 load levels and 11 collusion scenarios to generate 451 training data samples, each containing 10 sub-samples. Equilibrium points serve as training data, while randomly selected peripheral equilibrium points are used for testing. Using SVM and CART algorithms on 4510 total sub-samples, the models correctly classified 3817 and 3238 instances, respectively. Error analysis indicates that class 11 has the highest misclassification rate. Optimal Gaussian kernel parameters (C=100, γ=5) were selected via k-fold cross-validation. Results show that training with equilibrium points alone yields poor performance, and peripheral points must be included in training to enable effective collusion detection.
