input: We divide data into normal and anomaly groups. The collusion detection algorithm is examined for 0£ h£±18. For each deviation, we calculate F1 score as a precision criterion. F1 = 2PrRe / (Pr + Re). Re = Tr / Ac. Pr = Tr / Po. F1 score evaluates predictive models on skewed data sets [50]. Lower precision or recall leads to lower F1 score. Higher F1 value represents a more accurate classifier. Fig. 7 shows that for h < 15, the statistical method has better performance than supervised methods in detecting anomaly data in electricity market. The main issues of collusion detection are detecting collusion occurrence and identifying colluding firms. Fig. 7 shows statistical methods outperform supervised methods in collusion detection. However, statistical methods cannot identify colluding firms, so supervised learning algorithms are more suitable. To determine the importance of criteria in collusion detection, we eliminate one criterion from the set and analyze all data sets. Table Ⅸ shows the decrease in accuracy of algorithms after eliminating different criteria. According to Table Ⅸ, the importance of HHI index in collusion classification is greater than other criteria. Also, the elimination of MC and LER at the same time strongly reduces the accuracy of the algorithms, which indicates that MC or LER is important and necessary as a major criterion in collusion detection and classification. Table Ⅸ shows a downward trend in the performance of the algorithms after eliminating different criteria. These results will be true until the designed algorithms could be used for categorizing 11 classes. If the number of scenarios in a new case study is less than 11, it is possible that the accuracy of algorithms is less after removing the indexes due to the sensitivity of SVM and CART algorithms to a large number of classes. Consider the bilateral collusion states as a class and multi-lateral collusion states defined in Table Ⅲ as the other class, Fig. 8 shows the classification of generated data set into two classes, if h= ±2, and only bid and market share are used as detection attributes. As shown in Fig. 8, considering γ = 0.2 and C = 100, after eliminating several criteria such as MC and LER, SVM has appropriate accuracy and discriminates the training and test samples related to the two classes with the accuracy of 93% and 92%, respectively. The red and blue samples (training and test samples of the bilateral class) among multi-lateral collusion samples are related to the bilateral collusion samples created at the high load levels. Thus, bid price in these samples is higher than that in other same samples. The bid price in multi-lateral collusion is much higher than that in bilateral collusion at lower load levels close to 3000 MW. The collusion detection framework is also examined under unconstrained condition, i.e., if generation constraints are ignored. The results of this part are not discussed in this paper. In the unconstrained case, the accuracy and performance of the collusion detection algorithm based on the mentioned approach are slightly better than that under the constrained condition. In the constrained model, the obtained data have some bias and have been distributed erratically. It means that all of the learning algorithms have a relative relevance to the data analyzed and evaluated. Despite a few problems with the generated data in the constrained model, e.g., its non-regularity distribution, SVM and CART algorithms outperform other algorithms and have an appropriate performance in the constrained model. Generally, the existing electricity markets are oligopoly markets, which means that the number of generation firms is limited although each generation firm may have several generation units in practice. A test system with 10 generation units classified in 4 generation firms is considered in this paper. The total running time of the computer is used as a criterion for computation complexity. section: VI. CONCLUSION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: A machine learning approach for electricity market collusion detection is proposed. Collusion scenarios among generation firms are identified, and market equilibrium is computed for various load levels and scenarios. Peripheral points of the equilibrium are determined, and collusion detection criteria are computed for these points. Support vector machines and decision trees are trained using these criteria. Simulation results indicate acceptable detection accuracy. A downward trend in accuracy is observed as selected peripheral points deviate from equilibrium points. SVM and decision tree algorithms outperform other machine learning techniques. The MC and LER indices have a more significant impact on collusion classification performance than other criteria. The detection program runs hourly; sustained collusion detected over a long period is valid, while hourly detection alone is insufficient for classification.
output:
In this paper, an approach for collusion detection in elec‐
tricity market is proposed based on machine learning. First‐
ly, the possible scenarios of collusion among generation
firms are identified. Then, for each load level and possible
collusion scenario, the market equilibrium is computed and
peripheral points of the equilibrium are determined. Collu‐
sion detection criteria are computed for the equilibrium and
their peripheral points. The computed criteria are used to
train the learning machines using SVM and decision tree al‐
gorithms. Simulation results show that the accuracy of the
used machines is acceptable in collusion detection. As the se‐
lected peripheral points deviate from the equilibrium points,
a downward trend in the accuracy of the collusion detection
algorithm is observed. SVM and decision tree algorithms are
compared with other machine learning approaches, and it is
observed that SVM and decision tree algorithms are the
most appropriate techniques to detect the collusion. Finally,
the impact of each criterion on the collusion detection accu‐
racy is evaluated and the MC and LER indices play more
important roles in collusion classification performance than
other criteria. ISO runs the collusion detection program at
any hour. If the results show the collusion of two or more
firms for a long time period, the collusion is valid. However,
if the results show the collusion occurs only in an hour, it
cannot be considered as a collusion.

section: I. INTRODUCTION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: The rapid growth of location-based services has made accurate positioning essential. While GPS dominates when line-of-sight signals are strong, it fails in dense urban or indoor areas. Fingerprint-based localization maps signal features to locations stored in a database. Received signal strength (RSS) is the most widely used feature due to simple hardware. Representative RSS-based methods include Radar and Horus.
output:
With the remarkable development of intelligent terminals in the recent years, location-based service (LBS) grows rapidly, which has dramatically changed our life. Consequently, accurate positioning has become an essential technology and caught more and more attention. At present, the global positioning satellite (GPS) is a dominant positioning technique and can satisfy the localization requirements in the most scenarios when user equipment (UE) receives strong enough line-of-sight (LOS) signals from satellites [1], [2]. However, GPS signals may suffer from serious attenuation in some cases, such as dense urban area or indoor environment. To address these limitations, various localization technologies are emerging recently. Among these technologies, fingerprint-based localization is a promising and popular technology and has drawn wide attention in both academia and industry [3].

The essence of fingerprint-based localization is to establish the mapping relationship between a location and its corresponding signal features. The mapping relationship is stored in a database as the fingerprint for positioning. In general, the exploited signal features mainly include the receive signal strength (RSS), the angle of arrival (AOA), the angle of departure (AOD), the amplitude in channel state information (CSI), the phase in CSI, or their combination [4]. Among these features, the RSS is the most widely used one due to its simple hardware and easy implementation. Radar [5] and Horus [6] are two representative RSS-based localization methods.

In this model, we assume that the transmitter and receiver are respectively equipped with uniform linear arrays of $M_t$ and $M_r$ antennas and there exists $L-1$ distinguished scattered paths. The discrete-time equivalent baseband channel at the $n$-th tap corresponding to the $m_t$-th transmit antenna and the $m_r$-th received antenna can be expressed as

$$h_{m_r m_t}(n) = \sqrt{\rho} \frac{1}{L-1} \sum_{l=0}^{L-1} \beta_l e^{j2\pi \frac{d}{\lambda}(m_r-1) \sin \theta_{a_l}} e^{j2\pi \frac{d}{\lambda}(m_t-1) \sin \theta_{d_l}} \times g(nT_s - \tau_l), \quad 0 \leq n \leq N-1,$$

III. FINGERPRINT-BASED POSITIONING METHOD — A. Network Architecture

Similar to supervised machine learning approaches, the fingerprint-based positioning method includes offline training and online positioning. In the offline stage, multipath MIMO CSI data is obtained and preprocessed into the required input form. Two fingerprint databases are then established by training two deep neural networks (DNN) for coarse and fine positioning. Using coarse positioning reduces training time when the targeted area is large. In both training stages, a three-layer back-propagation neural network (BPNN) is adopted, consisting of an input layer, a hidden layer, and an output layer. After the output layer, a softmax regression classifier follows and generates soft information on the classified output data. Therefore, the final output is a probability distribution. In the online stage, the CSI of the user equipment (UE) at an unknown location is collected and preprocessed. The estimated location is determined through a coarse-to-fine positioning algorithm based on the two fingerprint databases. Finally, the K-weighted nearest neighbor (KWNN) method is used to further improve positioning accuracy.

B. Preprocessing

We utilize time-domain multipath MIMO CSI for positioning rather than frequency-domain CSI. Based on the channel estimation result, the equivalent time-domain channel vector is obtained. Since the CSI includes phase information related to orientation and time delay, and amplitude related to propagation loss, the input channel vector for localization is expressed as h = [|h(0)|, ..., |h(N-1)|, ∠h(0), ..., ∠h(N-1)]^T for accurate localization, where |h(n)| and ∠h(n) are MrMt × 1 amplitude and phase vectors of the n-th time-domain channel sample, respectively. From this, the input vector dimension is 2NMrMt×1. This results in high computation complexity if the antenna scale is large. Therefore, the input channel vector is simplified to reduce localization complexity.

The testing points are generated randomly over the entire areas of interest and the localization performance metric is the mean-squared error distance (MSED) as following

ε = 1/S Σ_{i=1}^S (ˆx_i − x_i)^2 + (ˆy_i − y_i)^2, (9)

where S is the number of testing points and (x_i, y_i) and (ˆx_i, ˆy_i) is the true and estimated coordinates of the i-th testing points, respectively. In addition, we also adopt median error as another performance metric for evaluating localization performance.

Fig. 3 and Table I compare both the existing representative localization methods, FIFS [7] and Horus [6], with five different schemes corresponding to different combinations if amplitudes or/and phases of CSI are averages or not. The first one is named as amplitude-MIMO and phase-MIMO (AM-MIMO&Ph-MIMO), which simultaneously retains the phases of CSI and the amplitudes of CSI on different antennas. The second one is the method adopted in this article, called amplitude averaged with phase-MIMO (AM-ave&Ph-MIMO), where the amplitudes of CSI corresponding to all antennas are averaged while the phases are retained at different antennas. The third one is phase-average with amplitude-MIMO (Ph-ave&AM-MIMO), where the phases are averaged on different antennas but the amplitudes are retained. The fourth one is phase-MIMO with no-amplitude (Ph-MIMO&No-AM), which only retains the phases. The last one is amplitude and phase averaged (AM-ave&Ph-ave), where the amplitude and the phase both are averaged. In both representative methods, the FIFI one utilizes the CSI amplitudes in different subcarriers as fingerprints while the Horus one is based on the RSS. From Fig. 3 and Table I, we have the following observations.

• The AM-ave&Ph-MIMO has almost the same performance as AM-MIMO&Ph-MIMO and has only small performance difference over AM-MIMO&ph-MIMO. Therefore the CSI phases are more important than the CSI amplitudes for accurate localization.

• The AM-ave&Ph-ave in the last method has similar performance with the Ph-ave&AM-MIMO, hence the effect of the amplitude of CSI is small on the localization accuracy.

• The AM-ave&Ph-MIMO outperforms the Ph-ave&AM-MIMO and achieves 0.8349m MSED, so the phases of CSI are more important than the amplitudes of CSI.

• The five proposed positioning schemes based on the time-domain multi-path MIMO fingerprint are better than the other existing schemes based on frequency-domain CSI or RSS.

In summary, using the phases data of the time-domain CSI can achieve a better localization accuracy than using amplitudes of the time-domain CSI. Our AM-ave&Ph-MIMO scheme can effectively balance complexity and positioning accuracy. Furthermore, from Fig. 3 and Table I, our positioning method can obtain over 75% MSED below 1m while the other two schemes are only 41% and 29%, respectively. Meanwhile, the averaged amplitude information in the AM-ave&Ph-MIMO scheme can decrease the dimension of the input data so that the complexity of localization processes is reduced.

section: II. RELATED WORK — A. MOTIVATION IN EDUCATION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Researchers have explored why some students succeed while others struggle, noting that motivation is a key differentiator [14, 15, 16, 17]. Personal factors like age, gender, and culture interact to influence motivated behaviors [14]. Several theories explain these drives, with Self-Determination Theory (SDT) being the most widely recognized for its comprehensive explanation of motivation in learning [3, 18, 19]. SDT is particularly valuable in educational settings as it explains how different motivation types support or hinder learning behaviors [3]. SDT predicts student performance, persistence, and course satisfaction [18]. As illustrated in Figure 2, SDT identifies three primary motivation types: intrinsic, extrinsic, and amotivation [20]. Intrinsic motivation involves engaging in tasks for their own sake [20]. Extrinsic motivation arises from external factors and includes three subtypes: identified regulation, introjected regulation, and external regulation [20]. Amotivation describes a lack of reason to engage, resulting in failed engagement due to perceived incompetence, autonomy loss, and relatedness deficits [21].
output:
Many studies have been developed to understand why some students are more successful in their learning than others who appear to struggle and fail to reach their learning goals. Many authors, such as Pintrich [14], confirmed that motivation plays a key role in this difference; some students are driven by their belief in their own self-efficacy, giving them confidence in their abilities, while others find motivation through persistence and hard work to reach their goals. Furthermore, various personal characteristics and contextual factors, including age, gender, culture, and personal interests, are considered to interact to influence people’s motivated behaviors. Consequently, several theories have been advanced as explanations for what drives individuals to perform specific tasks, and several of these theories have been applied to the field of education. One of the most prominent theories is Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs [15]. Others include Self-Determination Theory (SDT) [2], Expectancy-Value Theory [16], and Achievement Goal Theory [17].

In this study, SDT is adopted as a foundation for exploring student motivation because it is the most widely recognized theory offering a comprehensive explanation of the role played by motivation in effective learning [3]. SDT is especially valuable in educational settings, as it explains how different types of motivation can either support or hinder learning behaviors. The appropriateness of SDT in educational contexts has been confirmed by many empirical studies, for example [18], applied SDT to explore student behavior in digital and blended learning environments. Furthermore, the research in [19] highlighted how Self-Determination Theory explains the reasons behind individuals’ decision-making. In educational contexts, this perspective helps students understand their own choices and take responsibility for the outcomes. Additionally, SDT can predict students’ performance, persistence, and course satisfaction. Chen and Jang [18] argued that SDT holds significant potential for addressing major learning challenges, such as student attrition, persistence, and academic achievement.

As illustrated in figure 2, SDT identifies three primary types of motivation: intrinsic, extrinsic, and amotivation.

Intrinsically motivated behaviors are those people engage in for their own sake [20]. For example, intrinsically motivated people tend to perform their tasks willingly and freely without needing external rewards. In contrast, extrinsically motivated behavior arises from external factors, such as rewards, recognition, or social expectations. There are three subtypes of extrinsic motivation. The identified regulation is the first subtype [20], which refers to behavior demonstrably influenced by external sources. For instance, a student may engage in a task for a personal interest, reflecting internalized motivation. Alternatively, the same task might be approached purely as a requirement for completing their degree, indicating motivation driven by external factors. The second subtype is introjected regulation, in which individuals engage in behaviors due to internal pressures, such as guilt, shame, or the need for self-worth and validation [20]. The last subtype of extrinsic motivation is external regulation. This type of behavior refers to a situation in which the student attaches no personal value to a project or course but engages with it in a perfunctory manner as they perceive that they have no choice but to respond [20]. In other words, a student who is motivated by introjected regulation engages with their learning, not because they want to learn, but simply because it is a requirement for being awarded their qualification.

The last type of motivation is called amotivation. Amotivation describes a situation in which a student perceives no reason to engage with their learning [21], lacks any motivation to act (competence, autonomy, and relatedness), and consequently fails to engage with their studies.

section: II. RELATED WORK — B. MACHINE LEARNING AND MOTIVATION IN EDUCATION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Traditional motivation measurement relies on self-reported surveys and interviews, which have been criticized for introducing biases that affect accuracy [22]. This study proposes machine learning (ML) as a promising alternative for analyzing learning management system (LMS) data to predict motivation [23]. Recent research has applied ML techniques for this purpose. For instance, [25] used a Random Forest model in multimedia contexts, reporting 99.9% accuracy after 100 runs, demonstrating ML's potential for motivation analysis [25]. Similarly, [26] utilized a decision tree model with five log variables (user ID, test accuracy, time spent on pages, number of accessed pages, and test time), finding that time spent and test performance are strong predictors [26]. Another study, [27], applied clustering based on self-determination theory [2] to seven LMS variables, finding engagement linked to time spent and session duration, while extrinsic motivation correlated with self-exam tests and intrinsic motivation with game usage; however, findings were limited by an invalidated motivational framework [27]. Furthermore, [28] used decision trees with 19 LMS features to identify motivational factors, and [6] classified motivation using neural networks, decision trees, and SVMs with LMS data, though the neural network model achieved only 76.92% accuracy due to a small sample size (129 students) and limited variables [6]. Overall, few studies have focused on ML for motivation prediction, and existing research is often limited by small datasets (e.g., 24 records in [26]) and lack of diverse sources [26]. This study addresses these gaps by combining LMS records and survey responses to enhance prediction reliability and accuracy [26]. Grounded in self-determination theory, it utilizes a larger dataset to provide stronger insights into behavioral drivers within an educational setting.
output:
Traditional methods for measuring motivation include self-reported surveys and subjective interviews. Still, these have faced criticism for their potential to introduce biases that could impact the accuracy and reliability of the findings [22]. This study uses ML as a promising approach to analyze students’ learning management systems (LMS) data, interactions, and performance to accurately predict student motivation. ML is a subset of artificial intelligence (AI) that focuses on training computers to learn from data and make predictions or decisions without explicit programming [23]. It relies on techniques that detect patterns within data and improve performance progressively over time [24].

Recently, researchers have utilized the benefits of ML techniques to better understand and predict student motivation. For example, the research in [25] investigates college students’ learning motivation using the Random Forest model in multimedia-based educational contexts. The paper employs advanced Random Forest models to predict student learning motivation based on their engagement and performance. The accuracy of predicting student motivation reached 99.9% after the model completed 100 runs. The study demonstrates that ML models can improve motivation analysis and prediction. Another study by [26] aimed to predict student motivation using five key log data variables: user identifier, test accuracy percentage, time spent on pages, number of accessed pages, and time spent on tests. To achieve this, a decision tree model was employed. Their findings reveal that time spent and test performance strongly predict student motivation. In a related study, [27] explored motivation prediction using seven variables extracted from an LMS. FIGURE 2. Self-determination theory based on [2]. The clustering technique was used to analyze motivation across three dimensions: engagement, energization, and motivation sources (internal or external). The results showed that engagement was primarily linked to variables such as time spent on tasks and average session duration, while extrinsic motivation was associated with self-exam tests. Additionally, intrinsic motivation was reflected in the game usage variable. However, the study faced limitations due to the invalidated motivational framework, which may have impacted the reliability and generalizability of the findings.

Additionally, the research in [28] explored 19 features extracted from LMS, utilizing decision tree models to derive association rules and identify key motivational factors. Likewise, [6] used LMS data such as assignment views and forum participation to classify students’ academic motivation through neural networks, decision trees, and support vector machines (SVM). Although the neural network model achieved the highest accuracy (76.92%), the study faced constraints due to a small sample size (129 students) and a limited selection of only four LMS variables. Furthermore, the model lacked alignment with established motivational theories, diminishing its theoretical significance.

Few studies have focused on using ML to explore and predict student motivation. Additionally, most existing research on student motivation prediction, such as [26], has been limited by small dataset sizes, often consisting of just 24 records, and the lack of diverse data sources. This study addresses these gaps by combining multiple data sources, including records from a Learning Management System (LMS) and survey responses, as mentioned earlier. This approach could enhance the reliability and accuracy of motivation predictions and create a more comprehensive dataset that captures various aspects of student behavior and motivation. Unlike previous studies, this research utilizes a more extensive dataset to provide stronger insights. Furthermore, the study is grounded in self-determination theory, a well-established framework in motivation research. This theoretical foundation fosters a deeper understanding of student motivation by examining key behavioral drivers within an educational setting.

input:
IV. METHODOLOGY — B. DATA PRE-PROCESSING

Survey data preprocessing removed administrative columns ("Date submitted," "Last update date") and identifiers ("First and Last Name") to protect privacy. The "Consent Statement" column was excluded as unnecessary for analysis. Likert scale responses were converted to numerical values ranging from 1 (lowest agreement) to 5 (highest agreement).

LMS data preprocessing used SAS Studio. Redundant items (AcademicYear, FirstDateAccess, LastDateAccess, FirstLoginDate, LastAccessDate, Comment) were removed. Key features were extracted: Lateness was categorized (positive = early, zero = on-time, negative = late) using average lateness; Click Count was calculated by summing real visits; Video engagement was computed by summing watched minutes; Assignment status was coded as -1 (late), 0 (on-time), or 1 (early). Normalization scaled features to a 0–1 range using min-max normalization. A log transformation addressed outliers in click and practical task features. Missing values were handled using predictive imputation via the Expectation-Maximization algorithm due to the infeasibility of deletion and bias issues with simple imputation.

A semi-supervised labeling approach combined self-reported motivation survey data (Intrinsic, Identified, Introjected) with LMS behavioral profiles. Aggregated metrics (time spent, access frequency, attendance duration, assignment interactions) were calculated for survey participants. Matching records were aligned by unique identifiers. Behavioral profiles were averaged by motivation type to create centroids, which served as initial points for K-means++ clustering with k=3, generating fully labeled LMS records.
output:
IV. METHODOLOGY — B. DATA PRE-PROCESSING

During this process, both the collected survey data and the LMS data were preprocessed to be ready for further analysis. First, several columns were removed from the survey dataset, specifically administrative columns such as “Date submitted” and “Last update date.” These columns did not directly contribute to the analytical objectives. Additionally, “First and Last Name” were excluded to protect respondents’ privacy. Although the “Consent Statement” column was essential for ethical compliance, it was considered unnecessary for the current analysis and was therefore removed. Removing these additional columns made the dataset more appropriate for analysis while also helping to protect participant confidentiality. Another data preprocessing action carried out involved converting the survey Likert scale responses from textual descriptions (e.g., “Does not Correspond at all” to “Corresponds exactly”) to numerical values to facilitate analysis. This was accomplished by assigning a numerical Likert scale ranging from 1 to 5, where 1 represented the lowest level of agreement or satisfaction, and 5 represented the highest.

Second, the preprocessing of LMS data was conducted using the Statistical Analysis System (SAS). SAS Studio is a web-based integrated development environment (IDE) developed by the SAS Institute, designed for data analysis, statistical modeling, and programming using the SAS language [33]. The data were aggregated based on the six common modules in the computer science department, as shown in figure 4. Additionally, two more groups (G1 and G2) were included to incorporate modules that shared common characteristics. This addition aims to test the validity of the developed model on both individual and grouped datasets. To further refine the dataset and enhance the model’s effectiveness, items found redundant in the context of this study were removed. These included AcademicYear, FirstDateAccess, LastDateAccess, FirstLoginDate, LastAccessDate, and Comment. The removal of these items made the dataset more suited to data analysis.

To enhance the quality of the LMS dataset, several key features were extracted, created, and processed for each student as follows:

• The Lateness feature was extracted for each student’s arrival time. For the purpose of providing more meaningful insights, this feature was categorized. Positive values indicate early arrival, zero values indicate on-time arrival, and negative values indicate lateness. This feature depends on the AverageLatenessToDate and has been transformed using equation 2, where Ls represents the lateness score for a student s, and $\bar{L}_s$ denotes the student’s average lateness score up to the given date.

$L_s = \begin{cases} 0, & \text{if the student arrives on time} \\ -\bar{L}_s, & \text{if } \bar{L}_s > 0 \\ |\bar{L}_s|, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$ (2)

• Click Count: The number of clicks per student in each module was calculated. This was done by counting the visits to online learning resources to track student engagement (see using Equation 3).

$C_s = \sum_{i} V_i$ (3)

where $C_s$ represents the total number of clicks for a student $s$, and $V_i$ denotes the number of real visits, which is derived from the NumRealVisits feature in the LMS.

• The video engagement feature was computed within each module for each student using equation 4. This feature, which tracks the degree of student interaction with video-based learning materials, is a key element in understanding student engagement.

$V_s = \sum_{j} M_j$ (4)

$V_s$ represents the total video minutes watched by a student $s$. The variable $M_j$ denotes the number of minutes which is dependent on the MinutesDelivered feature in the LMS dataset.

• Assignment Submission Status: Assignment submissions were assigned distinct values: -1 for late submissions, 0 for on-time submissions, and 1 for early submissions. With this categorization, it became easier to identify student submission patterns. This feature depended on two variables, DueDate ($D$) and DateSubmitted ($S$), and has been determined using equation 5.

$A_s = \begin{cases} 0, & \text{if } S = D \\ 1, & \text{if } S < D \\ -1, & \text{if } S > D \end{cases}$ (5)

The data were then transformed to be more suitable for certain analyses, visualizations, or applications [34]. This transformation could include operations such as normalization, scaling, filtering, encoding, or combining data from multiple sources [35]. In this study, normalization was applied to the LMS dataset to render all the feature values to lie in the range of 0 to 1. As observed in figure 6a, the LMS features show varying distributions. Certain features like Total Clicks and Total of Video Minutes have high variances due to the presence of extreme outliers. In contrast, most of the other features, such as TotalTime (Total Duration), TotalActivitiesAttendedToDate (Total Activities), TotalHoursAttendedToDate (Attendance), and Agreed Mark, show less variance due to having smaller ranges. Thus, the absence of normalization could lead to wide discrepancies in scale between the features, which could affect the performance of the final model. Therefore, normalization was an essential transformation to locate each feature on a similar scale to ensure that they were appropriate for analysis. Equation 6 was used to normalize the dataset values. In this equation, $x_i$ represents the individual value of a feature. The term $\min(x)$ refers to the smallest value observed in the dataset for that feature, while $\max(x)$ denotes the largest value within the dataset for the same feature.

$\text{Normalization} = \frac{x_i - \min(x)}{\max(x) - \min(x)}$ (6)

Figure 6b illustrates the spread of each feature, demonstrating that normalization has affected the initial high values, including attendance, agreed mark, lateness, and total activities, which are concentrated around the midrange.

Another issue observed in the normalized dataset was the presence of outliers, such as those in the number of clicks and practical task features. Outliers are data points that significantly deviate from the central tendency of the rest of the data points and can exert an undue influence, leading to inaccurate results [36]. Outliers can occur due to errors in data collection or measurement inconsistencies. Several techniques, such as log and square root transformations, can be adopted to address the issue of outliers in the data [37]. Either technique tends to provide similar results; however, in this study, a log transformation (see equation 7) was applied. In equation 7, $X'$ is the transformed value while $X$ represents the original feature value.

$X' = \log X$ (7)

FIGURE 5. Distribution of dataset features before and after normalization.

Another important challenge in data analysis is dealing with missing values. To preserve the quality and integrity of the dataset, a comprehensive scan was performed to identify missing values across all six modules. Notably, features such as Total Clicks and Total Video Minutes showed a significant amount of missing data. This is likely due to the design of the university’s LMS, which permits students to download course content and engage with it offline, leading to no interaction logs being recorded in those instances.

Additionally, features like Attendance and Lateness also had missing values, largely due to the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic. These features depend on students swiping their ID cards for classroom access; however, during lockdown periods, when physical attendance was suspended, no swipe-in data was captured. This absence of data would have significantly distorted these features, requiring special consideration during preprocessing.

There are several established techniques for handling missing data, including deletion, simple imputation, and predictive imputation such as Expectation-Maximization (EM) [38]. In this study, deletion was not considered feasible, as it would have resulted in the loss of a significant number of records, thereby compromising the integrity and representativeness of the dataset [39]. Simple imputation methods, such as replacing missing values with the mean, median, or mode [40], were also tested. However, mean imputation led to a large number of duplicate values and reduced variability, which could have introduced bias into the analysis. In contrast, predictive imputation using the Expectation-Maximization algorithm provided a more robust solution by estimating missing values iteratively while preserving the distribution and variability of the data. This method has been applied successfully in similar educational contexts [41], [42], and was therefore selected as the most appropriate technique for this study.

A semi-supervised data labeling approach was used to assign motivation-based labels to the LMS dataset by combining self-reported motivation data from the survey dataset with student behavioral data extracted from the LMS. The process started by aggregating each student’s LMS activity logs to create a comprehensive behavioral profile for those who participated in the survey. This aggregation was done by calculating the average values of key learning analytics metrics across all modules, including indicators such as time spent on activities, frequency of access, duration of attendance, and interactions with assignments.

Motivation labels were concurrently collected using a standardized academic motivation survey, in which students were categorized into one of three types: Intrinsic, Identified, or Introjected. Unique student identifiers were then used to align the survey responses with the corresponding behavioral data. Only students with matching records in both datasets were included in the labeling process. Each behavioral profile was paired with its respective motivation label to form a labeled subset of the LMS data.

The labeled data were then grouped by motivation type. Within each group, the behavioral vectors were averaged to compute a representative behavioral centroid. These centroids served as reference points for subsequent analysis and were used as initial points in the K-means++ clustering algorithm. Specifically, they provided the foundation for labeling additional, previously unlabeled LMS records based on their similarity to the established motivational profiles.

As previously mentioned, after calculating the centroids, these representative behavioral profiles were used as initial inputs for the K-means++ clustering algorithm. In this case, the number of clusters ($k$) was set to three to represent the three recognized motivation types, intrinsic, identified, and introjected. Algorithm 2 illustrates the entire clustering procedure. This step generated a fully labeled LMS dataset, which was one of the primary objectives of the data labeling phase. With each student’s behavioral profile now linked to a motivation type, the dataset became ready for subsequent analysis steps, including model training, evaluation, and additional prediction tasks.

After preprocessing the dataset, it was now ready for visualization to examine the diversity of instances within it. One of the key insights we aimed to uncover was whether the LMS dataset representing the three types of motivation was balanced. This variation is addressed, and it was observed that the number of motivation types was imbalanced as shown in Figure 6a. This highlights the need to tackle the issue of imbalanced data.

To address this issue, data balancing is a crucial step, especially in classification problems. When the class distribution is unbalanced, machine learning models may have difficulty performing well in minority classes since the majority classes outperform them. Fortunately, a technique called Synthetic Minority Oversampling (SMOTE) is available which corrects imbalances for minority classes by randomly increasing their representation and has proven to be a successful solution to this problem [43]. SMOTE creates synthetic samples by interpolating between minority class instances [44]. As a result of this technique, the model is not only generalized but also reduced from overfitting. As illustrated in figure 6, after applying SMOTE, the dataset was balanced and ready for further modeling.

input: The dataset was split 80/20 for training and testing. Three machine learning methods were used: Multinomial Logistic Regression (MLR), Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost). MLR is suitable for categorical dependent variables and calculates probability outcomes for each class [45, 46]. The prediction equation is defined in [8]. SVM is robust for classification and regression, particularly with non-linear boundaries using the Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernel [47, 48]. The classifier finds a hyperplane maximizing the margin between classes, defined in [9, 10, 11]. If f(X) > 0, Class 1 is assigned; otherwise Class −1. Slack variables allow misclassification in non-separable data [11]. The RBF kernel maps data into higher-dimensional space to enhance separability [13]. XGBoost is a high-performing predictor that improves generalization and reduces overfitting [49]. It models non-linear relationships among features such as TotalDuration, Attendance, and Grade [49]. XGBoost incorporates L1 (alpha) and L2 (lambda) regularization for refined model control [49]. The objective function consists of a loss function and a regularization term [14]. Multi-class classification is achieved via the Softmax function [15]. Each added tree minimizes the loss function by computing the gradient and Hessian [16, 17, 18].

section: V. FINDINGS AND DISCUSSION — A. ML ANALYSIS FINDINGS
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
A 10-fold cross-validation split data 80% for training and 20% for testing per fold. Hyperparameters were tuned experimentally. MLR used multinomial loss, lbfgs solver, and max_iter=200. SVM used an RBF kernel with C=1 and gamma=0.1. XGBoost used objective=multi:softmax, num_class=3, max_depth=3, eta=0.1, subsample=0.8, colsample_bytree=0.8, and n_estimators=150.

XGBoost achieved the highest accuracy, scoring 100% in most modules (CS 1-3, Individual, G1, G2). SVM ranged 94-98%. MLR was competitive with SVM in CS Modules 1 and 3 but lower in CS Module 2.

XGBoost obtained perfect precision, recall, and F1-scores in CS Module 3, Individual Module, and G1. SVM showed slight recall variations, particularly in Identified Regulations (CS Module 2, Optional Module). MLR exhibited the most performance variation and lower recall than SVM and XGBoost.

XGBoost generalizes well to unseen data. Its ability to weigh classes and manage data nuances [50] contributes to this performance. Regularization (alpha for L1, lambda for L2) controls model complexity, preventing feature domination and enhancing generalizability [50]. The boosting algorithm builds trees sequentially, correcting previous errors [51]. MLR and SVM lack this iterative improvement mechanism, which may limit accuracy in complex datasets [51].
output:
To evaluate the performance of the proposed machine learning (ML) models, a 10-fold cross-validation approach was used. In this process, 80% of the data was allocated for training and 20% for testing in each fold, ensuring a thorough and reliable assessment of the model's ability to generalize. The hyperparameters for each model were carefully chosen through experimental tuning to optimize performance. The summaries of the final configurations used in the experiments are:

• MLR was configured for a multi-class classification problem using multi_class='multinomial', with the solver set to lbfgs and a maximum iteration limit of 200 (max_iter=200) to ensure convergence.

• SVM used the Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernel (kernel='rbf') with C=1 to balance margin maximization and misclassification, and gamma=0.1 to control the influence of individual training examples.

• XGBoost was set with objective='multi:softmax' for multi-class classification, num_class=3, max_depth=3, eta=0.1, subsample=0.8, colsample_bytree=0.8, and n_estimators=150 to build 150 boosting trees with regularization to reduce overfitting.

These hyperparameter choices were determined through iterative experimentation and reflect a balance between model complexity and generalization.

Figure 7 illustrates the accuracy results of the three proposed ML. Among the three models, XGBoost consistently achieves the highest accuracy, scoring 100% in most cases, particularly for CS Module 1, CS Module 2, CS Module 3, Individual Module, G1, and G2. On the other hand, SVM follows closely behind with accuracy values ranging between 94% and 98%, showing strong performance but slightly lower than XGBoost in some modules. Multinomial Regression shows competitive accuracy, especially in CS Modules 1 and 3, where it performs equally to SVM, but slightly lower in CS Module 2.

Table 10 presents a comprehensive comparison of the performance metrics for the evaluated machine learning techniques. As shown by the findings, XGBoost consistently achieved the highest performance across all modules and motivation types, often obtaining perfect precision, recall, and F1-score (e.g., CS Module 3, Individual Module, and G1). SVM also performed well but displayed slight variations in recall for certain motivation types, particularly in Identified Regulations (e.g., CS Module 2 and Optional Module). In contrast, MLR exhibited the most variations in performance and achieved lower recall scores compared to SVM and XGBoost.

These findings demonstrate that XGBoost generalizes well to unseen data in most cases. This can be attributed to several factors; first, XGBoost has the ability to weigh different classes and manage the nuances of the data [50]. In addition, the regularization techniques used by XGBoost help control model overfitting, thereby increasing the model's accuracy. In our research, the regularization parameters (alpha for L1 and lambda for L2) were utilized to manage the complexity of the model. This prevents any single feature from playing a dominating role due to excessively large weights. In this way, regularization not only ensures the accuracy of the model but also enhances its generalizability across different datasets. Furthermore, the boosting algorithm in XGBoost builds trees sequentially, with each tree correcting the errors of the previous ones [51]. This iterative correction process leads to a more accurate model. In contrast, MLR and SVM inherently lack this iterative improvement mechanism, which may limit their accuracy in complex datasets.

V. FINDINGS AND DISCUSSION — B. LA FEATURES EXTRACTION

After evaluating model performance using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score, the XGBoost model was selected for feature analysis due to its superior accuracy. Table 11 highlights the most influential Learning Analytics (LA) features for each motivation type based on LMS data.

For intrinsic motivation, the key features were practical work, attendance, total duration, total activities, and video usage. Lam et al. [52] previously identified practical work as a key contributor to intrinsic motivation, aligning with these results. Maranan [54] found regular attendance enhances engagement and intrinsic motivation. Total activities were identified as a key indicator of active engagement [55]. Video usage was identified as a new factor; Ryan and Deci [56] note autonomy, which video usage supports, is fundamental to intrinsic motivation.

For identified regulation, the model identified four features: practical work and attendance (shared with intrinsic motivation), and grades and assignments (unique to this type). Practical work bridges the gap between theory and practice, aligning with [57]. Regular attendance is critical for achieving broader goals [58]. Grades function as external motivators instrumental for career opportunities [56, 57]. Assignments serve as structured goals linking present efforts to long-term ambitions [59].

For introjected regulation, the model identified practical tasks, total duration, and grades. Practical tasks may reflect engagement to avoid lower grades, particularly in Computer Science modules [60]. Total duration may be influenced by feelings of obligation rather than genuine interest [61]. Grades can drive motivation through guilt avoidance and self-esteem validation [60, 62]. Total clicks were also identified as a measure of superficial engagement driven by indirect regulation. Video usage was highlighted as students participate to gain approval or avoid judgment, aligning with the core of introjected regulation [56].

Some LA features influence multiple motivation types, which is expected as Self-Determination Theory (SDT) explains motivation types are closely connected [16]. For example, practical work may encourage intrinsic motivation or support identified regulation. However, LMS data captures behavior but not internal reasoning, making interpretability difficult; a student engaging in practical work may be driven by personal interest, future goals, or avoiding negative evaluation. Table 12, 13, and 14 provide comparative overviews of factors influencing identified regulation and introjected regulation between this study and previous research.

Integrating machine learning with LMS data offers a data-driven approach to determining key factors influencing student motivation. This insight is valuable for course planners and educators to tailor instruction and support individual needs. It can guide strategies to support student progress and foster intrinsic motivation. Additionally, identifying these factors enables the design of adaptive learning experiences, enhancing learning outcomes [56]. Beyond individual success, a motivation-aware framework can contribute to institutional goals by reducing dropout rates and promoting long-term academic achievement [16].

V. FINDINGS AND DISCUSSION — B. LA FEATURES EXTRACTION

After evaluating the model’s performance using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score metrics, it was essential to explore the impact of different LA features on the model’s decisions. This analysis enabled the identification and prioritization of the most significant features influencing the model’s predictions. Given its superior accuracy, the XGBoost model was chosen for this evaluation. The table in 11 presents the results of this analysis, highlighting which Learning Analytics (LA) features were most influential in determining each type of motivation.

As shown in Table 11, the most influential LA features associated with intrinsic motivation, based on LMS data, included practical work, attendance, total duration, total activities, and video usage. While previous studies have not directly examined the influence of these specific LMS derived features on motivational types, comparable insights have been reported using alternative research approaches. For instance, Lam et al. [52] identified practical work as a key contributor to intrinsic motivation, a finding that aligns with the current study and highlights the central role of this feature in enhancing student motivation. Similarly, Apiola et al. [53] emphasized the importance of practical work in computer science modules, demonstrating its direct relevance to fostering intrinsic motivation. Although their analysis did not utilize LMS data, the convergence of their findings with ours supports the reliability of this study and underscores the broader pedagogical value of incorporating practical activities to promote intrinsic motivation. Other key factors identified in our analysis are attendance and total duration, which are closely related. Attendance is measured by physical presence, while total duration reflects students’ online engagement in the LMS. Maranan [54] found that students who attended classes regularly were more engaged in practical and active learning sessions, which in turn enhanced their intrinsic motivation. This finding is consistent with our results, further supporting the link between attendance and motivation. Total activities were found to have a direct impact on intrinsic motivation, aligning with the findings of [55]. Their study emphasized the importance of student participation in learning activities, specifically highlighting total activities as a key indicator of active engagement. Their findings support the notion that students who engage in a higher number of learning activities are more likely to develop intrinsic motivation. Our study also introduces a new factor influencing intrinsic motivation that has not yet been previously explored: video usage. We believe that videos play a crucial role in enhancing learning experiences by providing both visual and auditory stimuli, making content more engaging than traditional text-based resources. Video tutorials allow students to control their learning pace and sequence, aligning with the concept of autonomy in SDT. According to Ryan and Deci [56], autonomy is a fundamental component of intrinsic motivation, as it fosters a sense of ownership and control over the learning process. The inclusion of video usage as a key predictor of intrinsic motivation in our study enhances the current understanding of how digital learning resources contribute to student engagement. A comparative overview of factors associated with intrinsic motivation, drawn from both this study and previous research, is provided in Table 12.

For the second type of motivation, identified regulation behaviors, the model identifies four different LA features, two of which (practical work and attendance) are shared with the first type (intrinsic motivation). The other two features (grades and assignments) are unique to this type. Practical work tasks are designed to test the application of theoretical learning to real-life situations, prompting students to bridge the experiential gap between theory and practice, which is important for their future career development. This aligns with findings by [57], who noted that tasks linked to future goals enhance identified regulation by fostering a sense of purpose. Nevertheless, regular attendance is demonstrably a critical factor, highlighting the importance of consistently participating in the learning process to facilitate students’ achievement of their broader goals, a claim also supported by [58].

The model also highlights that grade is one of the key factor influencing this type of motivation. This aligns with students’ long-term commitments to achieving high academic performance to reach their broader goals. As noted by [56], grades can function as external motivators that students adopt, particularly when they are seen as instrumental in advancing future career opportunities. Similarly, [57] emphasized that grades served as motivators when students perceived them as milestones toward their future objectives.

Interestingly, assignments, which were not identified as a significant factor in other studies, are found to play a crucial role here. We believe that this type of factor is about recognizing the value of an activity in relation to personal goals. With deadlines and specific expectations, assignments serve as indicators of progress and commitment to those goals, suggesting that they can indeed influence motivation. Assignments represent a tangible link between students’ present efforts and their long-term ambitions, such as achieving high grades or mastering a subject. From an educational perspective, assignments often function as structured goals that help students stay on track with their learning [59]. Students who prioritize timely submission tend to be motivated by a sense of responsibility, viewing the assignment not merely as a task, but as a meaningful step toward fulfilling their aspirations.

As can be observed from the above findings, some features like practical tasks and attendance, appear across different motivation types. This shows that these features can support more than one type of motivation, depending on how students see them. For example, practical tasks might encourage intrinsic motivation because they are fun and challenging. At the same time, they can support identified regulation by helping students understand how these tasks relate to their future goals. This kind of overlap is normal and shows how different types of motivation can be connected. The fact that these findings are similar to previous research supports their accuracy. At the same time, new features like assignments provide fresh insights gained from using LMS data. Table 13 presents a comparison of factors influencing identified regulation motivation between the current study and previous research.

Practical tasks, a key factor in the influence of introjected regulation, play a significant role in student motivation. This aligns with [60], who noted that students may engage in practical tasks, not out of personal interest, but to avoid lower grades. This is particularly true for Computer Science modules. Students’ engagement with these tasks may reflect introjected regulation, as they often participate due to internal feelings of responsibility to avoid disappointing their teachers or peers.

Total duration, another LA feature associated with introjected regulation, may be more influenced by internal pressure than by genuine engagement. Hayamizu [61] explained that the time spent on a module could be influenced by feelings of obligation rather than real interest. These findings underscore the psychological aspect of introjected regulation, where students’ actions are shaped by internal pressures, adding a layer of curiosity to the study of learning behaviors for researchers.

Grades, the third highlighted feature of introjected regulation, are shown as wielding a significant influence on student motivation. Introjected motivation can be seen in scenarios where the obtaining of grades is driven by guilt avoidance [60]. This tendency of students to validate their self-esteem through earning high grades has been seen by [62] as a form of introjected regulation. Students should be acutely aware of this influence on their motivation, as it can significantly shape their learning experience.

The machine Learning (ML) model has also identified the total clicks feature as having an impact on this type of motivation. In the context of this study, total clicks refers to the number of times a student interacts with online learning materials, such as clicking on a video, reading a text, or completing an exercise. In many cases, this feature can be seen as a measure of engagement that is motivated by the desire to be seen as a student rather than by a genuine commitment to learning. Total clicks can, for example, indicate a superficial engagement with modules rather than a more in-depth engagement and are therefore driven by indirect regulation.

The video feature was also identified by the machine learning models as important for this type of motivation. In the case of introjected regulation, as mentioned earlier, students take part in activities because of external pressure or a need to gain approval or avoid guilt. For example, students might watch video tutorials not just to learn, but to show that they are involved—hoping to get recognition or avoid being judged negatively. In other words, the desire to show off their commitment or to seek validation from teachers aligns with the core of introjected regulation. Table 14 presents a comparison of findings between the current study and previous research in relation to factors influencing introjected regulation motivation.

As shown in the findings above, some learning analytics (LA) features influence more than one type of motivation. This is expected, as Self-Determination Theory (SDT), a well-known theory in educational psychology, explains that motivation types are closely connected. Features like attendance, total activities, and practical work affect different motivation types because they represent essential parts of the learning process, no matter what kind of motivation a student has. These features reflect fundamental elements of student engagement and learning behavior, supporting intrinsic and extrinsic motivation forms. However, this also introduces a challenge in interpretability: even if the machine learning model identifies these features as significant across various types of motivation, understanding the reasons behind the behavior remains difficult. For instance, a student engaging in practical work may do so out of personal interest (intrinsic motivation), alignment with future goals (identified regulation), or to avoid negative evaluation (introjected regulation). Since LMS data captures behavior but not internal reasoning, interpreting the motivational role of overlapping features requires caution. Recognizing this complexity can provide deeper insight into the complex interplay between observable learning behaviors and the psychological drivers of motivation.

In conclusion, integrating ML with LMS data offers a powerful, data-driven approach to determining the key factors that influence different types of student motivation. This insight is valuable for course planners, administrators, and educators, as it enables them to tailor instruction and support to meet individual student needs. It can also guide lecturers and tutors in developing effective strategies to support student progress and foster intrinsic motivation. Additionally, identifying these motivational factors enables instructors to design adaptive learning experiences, creating an inclusive and supportive environment that enhances students’ self-esteem and learning outcomes [56]. Beyond individual success, a motivation-aware learning framework can also contribute to institutional goals by reducing dropout rates and promoting long-term academic achievement [16]. The integration of ML and LMS data, therefore, represents a transformative step in modern education, offering a scalable and data-driven method for enhancing student motivation and optimizing learning experiences.

V. FINDINGS AND DISCUSSION — C. MODEL DEPLOYMENT

The XGBoost model was trained using LMS data collected from 2018 to 2020, a period that encompassed both pre-pandemic and COVID-19 online learning phases. During this period, there was a major shift to online learning, leading students to spend more time engaged in online learning activities. The next step involved applying the trained model to classify student motivation using unseen data from students who enrolled in 2021, 2022, and 2023. This period was characterized by blended learning approaches. This leads to the hypothesis that the model will maintain its predictive accuracy despite the shift in learning environments. Additionally, it is expected that Learning Analytics (LA) features identified during the pandemic may exhibit variations when analyzed in a traditional educational setting. This evaluation will help determine whether the engagement patterns observed during the pandemic remain relevant or if new factors, influencing student motivation, emerge in the blended learning context.

After comprehensive preprocessing of the newly collected dataset, the model successfully classified students into the three motivation types (see Table 15). While most LA features remained consistent, some variations were observed, particularly in the case of introjected regulation for Computer Science Module (3). For the training data, the model identified total duration as a key factor, whereas for the unseen dataset, total activities emerged as more relevant. The shift from total duration to total activities as a key factor in introjected regulation for Computer Science Module (3) can be understood due to the following reasons:

1) Learning Environment Dependence
• In a fully online learning environment, students relied more on self-paced study, making total duration a key factor in motivation.
• In a blended learning environment, structured activities and face-to-face components encouraged task completion, making total activities a stronger indicator of motivation.

2) Course Nature Matters
• If a course requires more hands-on activities (like coding, problem-solving, and lab work in Computer Science), total activities will be a stronger predictor of engagement.
• If a course is more theoretical or self-paced, total duration may be more relevant in assessing motivation.

Therefore, introjected regulation is not a fixed measure; its impact varies depending on the instructional design and course structure. In highly structured, activity-based courses (especially in blended learning), the emphasis is on task completion (total activities), while in self-paced, theory-heavy environments (like online learning), the emphasis is on time investment (total duration).

This variability is also evidenced in the case of CS(1), where a shift in intrinsic motivation was observed from total duration in the training phase to grades in the unseen dataset. It is clear that this change reflects the influence of the learning environment and course nature, as CS(1) is a mathematics-based course that emphasizes problem-solving accuracy. In online learning, time spent on materials was key, whereas in a blended setting, grades became a stronger motivation indicator, highlighting the context-dependent nature of motivation factors.

For the Individual Project, the model identified attendance as the key factor for intrinsic motivation in the training dataset, whereas in the unseen dataset, total activities became the primary factor, with attendance remaining the second most influential. From an educational perspective, this suggests that both factors play a crucial role in student motivation, with engagement in activities complementing attendance in a blended learning environment.

According to the results of this study, most LA features remained consistent across different learning environments, with only a few changes. There is no doubt that these variations can be attributed to both the nature of the course and the method by which it is taught. These findings emphasize the importance of adapting learning environments and course designs in order to align with the factors that motivate students. An educator can better support student engagement and motivation by taking into account the nature of the course as well as the context of the learning environment.

Institutions can practically apply the suggested framework by utilizing the model’s flexibility across various learning environments through integration into their current Learning Management Systems (LMS), thus serving as a decision-support tool. This framework enables institutions to create real-time motivation profiles, allowing faculty members to customize their teaching plans based on course type and delivery method. In structured, activity-based courses like Computer Science, where task completion is a major indicator in mixed environments, teachers may emphasize participation through practical assignments and track attendance records. In theoretical courses, on the other hand, time spent on materials could still serve as a more significant indicator. Aggregate analytics also assists academic advisers and curriculum designers by highlighting changing motivation trends that inform course redesign and individualized learning programs. Ultimately, the framework offers a scalable, context-sensitive approach to enhancing student motivation and engagement through well-informed, AI-driven pedagogical interventions.

section: VI. CONCLUSION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
VI. CONCLUSION

This study proposes an integrated framework to predict Computer Science students' motivation using machine learning techniques based on Self-Determination Theory. The framework combines survey data with LMS records to transform unsupervised data into a supervised format. Three techniques—SVM, XGBoost, and MLR—were tested and compared to identify relevant LA features and predict motivation types. XGBoost demonstrated the best performance across datasets. The findings bridge AI-driven analytics and educational psychology, though results are limited to a single institution and Computer Science modules. The framework's implementation highlights potential for enhancing student engagement and academic success. Further validation in diverse learning environments is necessary. Future research could expand the framework to other fields and teaching strategies.

By classifying motivation types based on real-time LMS data, the framework can assist educators in customizing learning experiences. VI. CONCLUSION

This study proposes an integrated framework to explore and predict Computer Science students’ motivation using machine learning (ML) techniques. The framework is based on Self-Determination Theory (SDT) to classify types of student motivation. It also combines survey data with LMS records to transform unsupervised data into a supervised learning format, enabling more effective analysis. By integrating multiple data sources, the study provides a deeper understanding of the relationship between learning analytics (LA) features and student motivation.

Three machine learning techniques SVM, XGBoost, and MLR were proposed, tested, and compared to identify relevant LA features and predict types of student motivation, with the goal of selecting the most effective and generalizable model. Among these, the XGBoost model demonstrated significant performance in classifying students according to their motivational behaviors across different datasets. While the findings contribute to bridging the gap between AI-driven analytics and educational psychology, it is important to note that the study was conducted within a single institution and focused on Computer Science modules. As such, the generalizability of the results to other contexts or disciplines may be limited and should be interpreted with caution. The effective implementation of this framework in the field of computer science highlights its potential significance for enhancing student engagement and thereby supporting academic success. However, to verify its broader relevance, further validation in various learning environments is necessary. Future research could involve expanding the framework to include additional elements, adapting it to suit other academic fields, and evaluating its effectiveness in universities employing different teaching strategies.

By identifying and classifying motivation types based on real-time LMS data, the framework can assist educators in customizing learning experiences and providing targeted support. In practice, the model can be integrated into existing LMS systems as an analytics layer that tracks students’ learning behavior, including video usage, activity completion, and attendance patterns. A Machine Learning Based Framework for a Stage-Wise Classification of Date Palm White Scale Disease

Hessane et al. propose a feature extraction and machine learning framework to classify date palm white scale disease infestation stages. Eighty gray level co-occurrence matrix (GLCM) texture features and 9 hue, saturation, and value (HSV) color moments features are extracted from grayscale and color leaf images. Two machine learning algorithm types are tested: classical methods (support vector machine, k-nearest neighbors) and ensemble methods (random forest, light gradient boosting machine). Models are trained and evaluated on two dataset configurations: GLCM features only, and a combination of GLCM and HSV descriptors. The support vector machine classifier achieves the highest accuracy of 98.29% using combined GLCM and HSV features. This framework aids the oasis agricultural community in early detection of date palm white scale disease and the adoption of preventive measures to protect trees and crop yield.

Abstract: Date palm production is critical to oasis agriculture, owing to its economic importance and nutritional
advantages. Numerous diseases endanger this precious tree, putting a strain on the economy and environment.
White scale Parlatoria blanchardi is a damaging bug that degrades the quality of dates. When an infestation reaches
a specific degree, it might result in the tree’s death. To counter this threat, precise detection of infected leaves and
its infestation degree is important to decide if chemical treatment is necessary. This decision is crucial for farmers
who wish to minimize yield losses while preserving production quality. For this purpose, we propose a feature
extraction and machine learning (ML) technique based framework for classifying the stages of infestation by white
scale disease (WSD) in date palm trees by investigating their leaﬂets images. 80 gray level co-occurrence matrix
(GLCM) texture features and 9 hue, saturation, and value (HSV) color moments features are extracted from both
grayscale and color images of the used dataset. To classify the WSD into its four classes (healthy, low infestation
degree, medium infestation degree, and high infestation degree), two types of ML algorithms were tested; classical
machine learning methods, namely, support vector machine (SVM) and k-nearest neighbors (KNN), and ensemble
learning methods such as random forest (RF) and light gradient boosting machine (LightGBM). The ML models were
trained and evaluated using two datasets: the first is composed of the extracted GLCM features only, and the second
combines GLCM and HSV descriptors. The results indicate that SVM classifier outperformed on combined GLCM
and HSV features with an accuracy of 98.29%. The proposed framework could be beneﬁcial to the oasis agricultural
community in terms of early detection of date palm white scale disease (DPWSD) and assisting in the adoption of
preventive measures to protect both date palm trees and crop yield.

input: Date palms are a crop with significant socioeconomic and ecological importance in Morocco, accounting for around 60% of agricultural revenue in oases and employing over two million people [1, 2]. Palm date scale is a sap-sucking pest that, while considered a minor pest at low infestation levels, can cause tissue necrosis and tree death at high levels, negatively affecting fruit quality [3, 4]. The choice to use chemical treatment is determined by the degree of infestation, but visual control is a time and labor-expensive task [5]. This study evaluates the effectiveness of machine learning methods in identifying and staging white scale disease (WSD) within date palms. Feature extraction techniques were performed on a multiclass image dataset to produce gray level co-occurrence matrix (GLCM) and hue, saturation, and value (HSV) color moment descriptors. These characteristics were used to train classical and ensemble-based machine learning models, including multiclass support vector machine (SVM), k-nearest neighbors (KNN), random forest (RF), and light gradient boosting machine (LightGBM). Model performance was measured using Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1-score. The main contributions of this work are: (1) examining the potential for WSD detection and infestation degree classification using classical and ensemble-based machine learning methods; (2) exploring GLCM-based features and HSV Color Moments to find the most effective for WSD stage-wise classification; (3) conducting experiments to analyze the effect of using only texture features versus combined color and texture patterns in recognizing and classifying WSD; and (4) measuring the classification performance of each model using various stage-wise metrics.
