section: I. INTRODUCTION — B. Semi-Supervised Learning
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
In image and audio processing, supervised deep neural networks (DNN) trained on large annotated datasets achieve outstanding results [16]–[18]. However, acquiring labeled data is expensive and labor-intensive, especially in medical tasks where labels require expert inspection and costly technology. Private or sensitive information may also be present in labels. Gathering unlabeled data is significantly simpler and less expensive for many tasks.

Semi-supervised learning (SSL) reduces dependency on labeled data by incorporating unlabeled input throughout training [19]–[23]. Many SSL algorithms use datasets with a high proportion of unlabeled samples and few labeled ones. These strategies add a loss component computed on unlabeled data to achieve entropy minimization and/or consistency regularization, improving generalization [24]. Entropy minimization encourages accurate predictions on unlabeled input [21]. Consistency regularization enforces invariant predictions to input perturbations like noise, shifting, or flipping [20], [22], [23]. The consistency loss minimizes the difference between predictions on original and augmented unlabeled data $x_u$:

$||P(y|x_u; \theta) −P(y|\hat{x}_u; \theta)||_2$ (1)

where $\hat{x}_u = Aug(x_u)$.

This work applies SSL algorithms to ECG classification to enhance accuracy using widely available unlabeled datasets. To the best of our knowledge, these SSL algorithms are deployed for the first time in combination with split-learning [25], [26].

The fundamental principle of split-learning (SL) is to partition the model between clients and a server on a per-layer basis [25], [26]. In the simplest setup, each client computes the forward pass up to a cut layer using its own input. Cut layer weights are sent to the server, which performs the remaining calculations, completing the first forward propagation without exposing raw data. Gradients are then propagated backward from the final layer to the cut layer; only gradients at the cut layer are sent back to clients to complete backpropagation. This repeats until convergence, preventing clients from accessing each other's raw data directly.

Split-learning enables cooperating companies to train models collaboratively without sharing raw data or specific model details, preserving data privacy and security. It is frequently more efficient than competing privacy-aware methods like federated learning regarding computation, communication, and convergence speed, particularly when the number of clients is high and the model is large [25], [26].

This article uses split-learning alongside other techniques to maintain privacy between clients (hospitals or mobile devices) for cooperative ECG classification training and to reduce client-side training complexity.
output:
I. INTRODUCTION — B. Semi-Supervised Learning

In several areas, including image and audio processing, supervised learning and deep neural networks (DNN) powered by large and annotated datasets have achieved outstanding results [16], [17], [18]. On the other hand, getting annotated and labeled datasets are relatively expensive and typically involves a lot of labor. This is probably best shown by medical tasks, where labels are the product of a time-consuming inspection requiring numerous human experts and measurements that need the use of expensive technology. Data labels may also include private and sensitive information. It is significantly simpler or less expensive to gather unlabeled data for many tasks.

In order to reduce the dependency of machine learning models on only labeled data, semi-supervised learning (SSL) is a branch of machine learning that tries to incorporate unlabeled input more extensively throughout the training process. In fact, a number of SSL algorithms have been reported in the literature that makes use of datasets with a greater proportion of unlabeled samples and a smaller number of labeled ones [19], [20], [21], [22], [23]. By adding a new loss component that is computed on the unlabeled data itself and attempts to achieve entropy minimization and/or consistency regularization, these strategies aid the model's ability to generalize more effectively [24]. Regularization based on entropy minimization aims at helping the model generate accurate predictions based on unlabeled input. In general, the loss term in [21] reduces the entropy of P(y|xu; θ), which represents the probability distribution across class labels y given an unlabeled input xu with model parameter θ. Furthermore, by creating one-hot labels from high-confidence predictions on unlabeled data xu and presenting them to a typical cross-entropy loss. The authors in [19] indirectly utilize the entropy minimization. Furthermore, by applying a so-called sharpening function to P(y|xu; θ), the method in [22] implicitly achieves entropy minimization.

On the other hand, consistency regularization encourages the model to make consistent predictions for perturbed variations of the same input and, as a result, the same output distribution [20], [22], [23]. In other words, the model should be invariant to various input data augmentations. Adding noise to the input sample, shifting, or flipping, are all examples of data augmentation. These augmentations are intended to change the sample content without affecting its label.

Generally, consistency loss tries to minimize the loss term:

||P(y|xu; θ) −P(y|ˆxu; θ)||2 (1)

where ˆxu represents an augmented version of the unlabeled data xu, i.e., ˆxu = Aug(xu).

In this work, we used SSL algorithms in the problem of ECG classification as one method to enhance the system's accuracy using the widely available unlabeled ECG datasets. Moreover, these SSL algorithms were deployed, to the best of our knowledge, for the first time in combination with Split-learning, as will be explained in the next sections.

C. Split-Learning

The fundamental principle of split-learning (SL) is to partition the model in the training phase between the clients and the server on a per-layer basis. In the simplest split-learning setup, each client uses its own input to compute the forward pass through a deep network up to the cut layer. The cut layer weights are sent from the clients to the server, which then does the remaining calculations. By doing so, the first round of forward propagation is finished without exposing the raw data. The same method can then be used to propagate gradients backward from the final layer to the cut layer. The gradients at the cut layer of the server are the only ones sent back to the clients, where the remaining backpropagation is completed. This process is repeated until convergence occurs, without allowing clients to access each other's raw data directly. This process can be seen in Fig. 1.

Split-learning has benefits such as enabling different cooperating companies to train their models collaboratively without sharing any raw data or specific model details, preserving the security and privacy of sensitive data. Additionally, split-learning is frequently more efficient than competing privacy-aware distributed machine learning methods like federated learning in terms of computation, communication, and convergence speed, particularly in our case where the number of clients can be high and the model size is relatively large [25], [26].

In this article, we used split-learning alongside other techniques to maintain privacy between different clients (hospitals, or mobile devices in this scenario) for the purpose of cooperative ECG classification training as well as reducing the complexity of training on the client side.

section: I. INTRODUCTION — E. Our Contribution
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: We analyzed recent deep learning ECG classification models for performance and computational cost. We proposed a new temporal convolutional network (TCN) model that achieved comparable classification performance with minimal processing effort. We evaluated our approach using the PTB-XL dataset with data distributions reflecting real-life scenarios. We introduced a modified split-learning scheme featuring an autoencoder and adaptive threshold mechanism to ensure data privacy for cooperating entities while significantly reducing communication and computation overhead. We integrated two semi-supervised learning algorithms to utilize unlabeled ECG samples at edge entities. We proposed a complete, efficient, and private ECG classification pipeline combining the TCN model, modified split-learning, and semi-supervised learning. Our methodology defined the problem, compared deep learning algorithms based on computational complexity to select the best model, compared semi-supervised algorithms for integration, proposed split-learning with modifications for efficiency, and tested the pipeline across various scenarios.
output:
The contributions of our work are as follows:
r We analyzed the performance and computational cost of various recent deep learning-based ECG classification models that have been described in the literature.
r We proposed a new deep learning model based on temporal convolutional networks (TCN) that demonstrated a comparable classification performance to existing models while requiring very little processing effort.
r We used the public dataset (PTB-XL) in the classification tasks of this work with different data distributions that reflect real-life scenarios.
r We introduced a modified split-learning scheme that includes an autoencoder neural network and an adaptive threshold mechanism to ensure data privacy for all the cooperating entities while reducing communication and computation overhead with the server during the learning phase considerably.
r We employed two semi-supervised algorithms to utilize all of the ECG samples located in the edge entities, the majority of which are unlabeled.
r We proposed a complete, efficient, and private ECG classification pipeline system that utilizes a well-designed TCN model in combination with a modified split-learning scheme and a semi-supervised learning approach.

Our work utilized the following research methodology: First, the problem is defined and our proposed solution is conceptualized. Second, we compare a variety of deep learning-based algorithms used for ECG classification based on their computational complexity and choose the model that performed the best. Third, we compare a variety of SSL algorithms based on their computational complexity and chose two methods to integrate into our pipeline. Fourth, we propose using SL for ECG classification using the best performing model from the first step and then integrating our modifications to the architecture to increase the computational and computation efficiency. Finally, we test the whole ECG classification pipeline in a variety of scenarios.

The remainder of this article is organized as follows. In Section II, we provide an overview of our proposed system. This includes comparisons between different ECG classification models and detailed information about the proposed modified split and semi-supervised learning mechanisms. In Section III, we cover the experimental setup and discuss the overall system results and performance. Finally, we conclude our work and provide the code availability in Sections IV and V.

section: II. SYSTEM OVERVIEW — A. ECG Classiﬁcation Models
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
We evaluated seven ECG classification architectures for embedded deployment. Three architectures—WangFCN, WangResNet, and LSTM/GRU—were previously assessed on PTB-XL by [5], providing a baseline for comparison.

WangFCN [47], adapted by [5] for PTB-XL, uses 1D-convolution kernels with batch normalization and ReLU. The original uses kernel sizes of 5, 5, and 128, 256, 128 filters; [5] changed these to 8, 5, and 3 with 128 filters each, replacing global pooling with a classification head of two fully connected layers and sigmoid activation.

WangResNet [47], also adjusted by [5], uses three residual blocks with two convolutions each. It uses 128 filters with kernel sizes of 5 and 3, differing from the original [47] which uses 64 and 128 filters. [5] adds a second convolutional layer with kernel size 7 and 128 filters before the network. The classification head uses pooling and two fully connected layers, similar to WangFCN.

LSTM/GRU architectures were implemented as unidirectional variants following [5]. Two LSTM layers with hidden size 256 or two GRU layers with hidden size 256 are used, followed by a dropout layer (p=0.4) and the same classification head as the other models.

Three Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) were investigated for energy efficiency. Adopted from [15], [52], these use dilated causal 1D-convolutions with batch normalization and dropout. TCNs have fewer connections than CNNs, making them efficient for low-power settings [15]. The receptive field (RF) is calculated as RF = 1 + 2(KT - 1)(2M - 1). TCN3, adopted directly from [15], has M=3 layers and kernel size KT=11 with dilations [1,2,4], yielding RF=141. This is insufficient for 250 timestamps. To increase RF, two proposed architectures were designed: TCN4 with M=4 layers, kernel size KT=9, and dilations 1,2,4,8 yielding RF=241; and TCN5 with M=5 layers, kernel size KT=5, and dilations 1,2,4,8,16 yielding RF=249.
output:
We analyzed the performance and computational costs of many contemporary ECG classification models given in the literature in order to choose the model that is most appropriate and effective for embedded devices. We compared seven various architectures and looked at the computational work required for inference as part of our evaluation. Based only on their classification performance, three of these architectures have already been assessed on PTB-XL by [5]. This provides a solid starting point from which to compare our work. These are the seven architectures:

r WangFCN: was introduced in [47]. The authors suggested an architecture that applies three 1D-convolution kernels to time series data that has been sampled. The kernel size is set to 5. The authors did not include pooling layers between convolutions in their network since they are prone to overfitting and were forced to train their network on relatively short datasets. Given the size of PTB-XL, [5] implemented WangFCN on PTB-XL with the possibility of layer pooling. 128 filters are used in the first layer, 256 filters in the second layer, and 128 filters in the final layer in the original architecture of [47]. A batch normalization layer and a ReLU layer serve as the activation function after each layer. The output is then produced using global pooling and a softmax layer. The model was adapted by [5], to a kernel size of 8 in the first layer, 5 in the second layer, and 3 in the last layer. Further, instead of global pooling, [5] used a classification head with two fully connected layers and a sigmoid activation function.

r WangResNet: As gradients tend to vanish in the initial iterations, CNN layers cannot be stacked indefinitely, whereas deeper networks may be advantageous for challenging applications. Skip connections around convolutional layer blocks can be used to get around this problem [48]. Residual blocks are what these are known as. This method just requires each residual block to produce a shift on the input. Additionally, as residual networks have many potential gradients flows throughout the network, they can be thought of as ensemble classifiers. For object recognition and classification, residual networks exhibit excellent results [47]. One drawback is a propensity to overfit on tiny data sets, as demonstrated by [47]. WangResNet architecture also originates from [47] and was adjusted for the use on PTB-XL by [5]. It consists of three residual blocks with two convolutions each. 128 filters are used with convolution kernel sizes of 5 and 3. This stands in contrast to the original architecture by [47], which uses three convolutional layers and a filter size of 64 in the first block and 128 in the second and third. A second convolutional layer with a kernel size of 7 and 128 filters is added before the network in the version of [5]. The classification head, which consists of pooling and two fully dense layers, is the same as that used for WangFCN.

r LSTM/GRU: The classification of time series is another task for which Long Short-term Memory (LSTM) architectures are widely used [49]. They are Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN), in which the layer receives input from the output. A memory function has been created as a result. The underlying problem with transmitting information from one iteration to the next is that when the gradients grow close to zero, these networks have a propensity to forget the states from prior iterations [49]. By including a second recurrent connection that controls how relevant the stored information is, LSTMs try to get around this problem. It is frequently referred to as a forget connection as a result. Because this creates multiple operations, Gated Recurrent Units (GRU) were developed. These units only employ one hidden state and decide whether to use the information and how much to propagate to the next iteration based on two gates [49]. As a result, it has fewer operations than LSTMs. Furthermore, RNNs can be uni-directional or bi-directional. The difference is that uni-directional networks only propagate input in one direction, whereas bidirectional networks propagate input in both directions. The bidirectional RNN can therefore process future timestamps. Additionally, we concentrated on the implementation of [5] for the RNN evaluation, which modified the RNN designs offered by [50] for PTB-XL. In this study, we investigate the use of LSTMs and GRUs in their unidirectional variants. We created two unique architectures, one for LSTM and the other for GRU. Two GRU layers with a hidden size of 256 are present in the second design, while two LSTM layers with a hidden size of 256 are present in the first. Both of which follow the architectures in [5]. Following the LSTM/GRU layer, both architectures use a dropout layer with a probability of 0.4. Additionally, the same pooling classification head with two fully connected layers as in WangFCN and WangResNet is used.

r TCN3/TCN4/TCN5: We also aim to investigate the category of Temporal Convolutional Networks while exploring energy-efficient ECG classification (TCNs). TCNs, a novel type of convolutional network for time series, have the potential to perform better on time series data than CNNs and recurrent techniques [51]. Further, TCNs have the advantage of a low number of connections compared to CNNs. This makes them more efficient [15]. The use of hardware acceleration, such as FPGAs, can increase efficiency even further [4]. This demonstrates how TCN usage might be advantageous in our low-power setting. Additionally, it has already been proven by [15] that TCNs may outperform CNNs and ResNet in the field of ECG classification. The TCNs in this work were adopted from the encoder part in [15], [52]. The dilated convolution method is used by the encoder component to expand the receptive field. TCN blocks, made up of dilated causal 1D-convolutions, make up its constituent parts. According to [51], these TCN blocks are stacked with skip connections like residual blocks. The dilation indicates that certain stages bypass input values. By doing so, the model's receptive field is enhanced without adding to the computational load. Multiple dilated causal 1D-convolutions, batch normalization, and dropout layers may be found in every TCN block. Three TCNs are used here where they differ in the receptive field (RF) either by changing the kernel size (KT) or the number of layers (M):

RF = 1 + 2(KT - 1)(2M - 1). (2)

The first TCN is called TCN3 which was adopted directly from [15]; it consists of M = 3 layers and kernel size of KT = 11 with dilations of [1,2,4]. This architecture has a receptive field of 141 timestamps. In our case, this is not enough, since we are using samples of 2500 ms, consisting of T = 250 timestamps (141 << 250). To increase the receptive field from 141 to 250, we can either increase the number of layers M, the kernel size KT, or both. However, increasing the number of layers is preferable in our case since we need to split the architecture later in the split-learning scheme, and having one or two layers on the client side with a lower kernel size decreases its overhead calculation compared to the case of having a larger kernel size. Therefore, we propose two TCN architecture with more layers. The first proposed TCN architecture is called TCN4 and has of M = 4 layers with corresponding dilations of 1, 2, 4, 8 and a kernel size of KT = 9. From (2), TCN4 has a receptive field of 241, which is close to the full 250 timestamps. The second proposed architecture is called TCN5 with M = 5 layers, dilations of 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, and a kernel size of KT = 5 are proposed, yielding a receptive field of 249. Fig. 3 depicts the TCN5 architecture.

input: A modified split-learning mechanism was proposed to improve communication and computational efficiency on resource-constrained devices [53][40]. An autoencoder placed between the server and client compresses the client's split-layer output into a latent vector during the forward pass, reducing communication volume [53]. Additionally, an adaptive threshold mechanism limits client gradient updates during backward propagation, further decreasing computation [40]. Applied to ECG classification using a TCN model, the modifications reduced communication overhead by 74% and client computations by 28%, with only a 3% AUC drop [40]. The client contains two TCN blocks and a convolutional encoder that produces a latent vector 95% smaller than the original TCN output [this work]. Experiments determined that two client-side layers provide the best balance of classification performance and efficiency [this work].
output:
An Efficient and Private ECG Classification System Using Split and Semi-Supervised Learning

II. SYSTEM OVERVIEW — B. Modified Split-Learning

One of the best private-aware distributed machine learning algorithms that are suitable for devices with limited resources and is more environmentally friendly than its rivals is split-learning. For instance, the client model size can be changed to accommodate the required application's computational and communication needs. Additionally, when the client model size is large or there are a lot of clients, SL converges more quickly than FL and is more communication efficient [25]. Nevertheless, we suggested in [53] a modified split-learning mechanism that has two key modifications added to the original SL in order to handle the situations when SL is less communication efficient than FL and to make SL more efficient in general. An autoencoder (AE) neural network was first added between the server and the client. During the forward pass, it learns to recreate the client's split layer output, as seen in Fig. 4. The client-side encoder part learns from its input to create a significantly smaller latent vector. The server receives only this latent vector, which results in considerably less communication during training. The decoder element, which is located on the server, approximates the original encoder's input using the latent vector. The AE can also be trained on other datasets that are comparable and used as non-trainable layers in the model, or it can be trained on those same datasets for the first few epochs before being utilized as non-trainable layers.

Fig. 4.
Modified split-learning mechanism introduced in [53].

Second, the number of gradient updates given to the client during the backward propagation operation was constrained by an adaptive threshold mechanism (ATM). The mechanism is shown in Fig. 4 for static thresholds. At the conclusion of the forward pass, the loss will be computed at the server and compared to the static threshold or to the adaptive threshold (ATM), which is a function that depends on the epoch number [40]. Whether to propagate the gradients via the layers on the server only or through the server and the client will be decided by the algorithm. These two changes were demonstrated through experiments to significantly minimize data transfer between the server and client as well as computations on the client side while experiencing very little performance loss.

The modified split-learning was applied successfully on ECG data in our previous work [40] using a CNN-based model. The modifications help to decrease the communications overhead between the client and the server by 74% as well as the client computations by 28% while dropping the AUC by only 3%. In this work, we replaced the CNN model with the TCN model, which consists of 5 blocks (the same one as in Fig. 3) as well as changed the autoencoder architecture to accommodate the model changes. The model we used in our experiments is shown in Fig. 5. The client has two TCN blocks and a convolutional encoder, which encodes the output of the second TCN block during forward pass to a much smaller latent vector. The latent vector that will be sent to the server in our case is 95% smaller in size than the original output of the second TCN block.

In the split-learning scheme, it is better for the client to have a smaller part of the model in comparison to the server (fewer layers), because the server is considered to have higher computational power compared to the client. We tested the performance of our system with one and two client-side layers and found that two client-side layers provided better classification performance as well as better computation and communication efficiency, thus we decided to keep only two TCN layers on the client side.

Section II.C: Semi-Supervised Algorithms

In a prior study [54], nine SSL algorithms were evaluated for resource-constrained edge devices based on FLOPS, latency, accuracy, and memory. Results indicate that more complex algorithms achieve slightly better accuracy at the cost of higher calculations, memory, and latency, making them unsuitable for edge deployment. Simpler algorithms are preferred as they provide adequate accuracy with lower resource demands and faster convergence [54].

We incorporated MeanTeacher and FixMatch into our pipeline. MeanTeacher is suitable for resource-constrained devices as it achieves adequate accuracy with low latency, memory, and FLOPS [54]. FixMatch was included for comparison; it achieves higher accuracy but requires greater latency, FLOPS, and memory [54].

MeanTeacher working principle:
The algorithm averages prior model weights using exponential moving average (EMA) after each epoch or batch. It minimizes the predicted distance between the updated mean teacher model (weights $\hat{\theta}$) and the student model (weights $\theta$):
$\hat{\theta}(t) = \alpha\hat{\theta}(t -1) + (1 -\alpha)\theta(t)$
(3)
where $\alpha \in[0, 1]$ is a smoothing hyperparameter. Averaging weights during training generally improves accuracy and enhances intermediate representations, making it suitable for large datasets and online learning [54].

FixMatch working principle:
The model first checks if the prediction on weakly augmented unlabeled samples $P(A_w(x_u))$ exceeds a fixed threshold $\tau$; if so, it generates hard pseudo-labels. The prediction for a strong augmentation $P(A_s(x_u))$ is then calculated. Total loss $L_{tot}$ combines a supervised loss $L_s$ for labeled data and a scaled cross-entropy loss $L_u$ for unlabeled data:
$L_{tot} = L_s + \lambda_u L_u$
(4)
$L_s = \frac{1}{B} \sum_{b=1}^{B} H(q_l, P(y|A_w(x_l)))$
(5)
$L_u = \frac{1}{B} \sum_{b=1}^{B} 1(\max(q_u) \geq \tau)H(\hat{q}_u, P(y|A_s(x_u)))$
(6)
Where $H$ is cross-entropy, $b$ indexes batch elements, $B$ is batch size, $q_u$ is the predicted class distribution, $\hat{q}_u$ is the pseudo-label, and $1$(condition) is an indicator function [54, 55, 56].

Unlike the original FixMatch using image augmentations

In our earlier study [54], we analyzed nine distinct new SSL algorithms in terms of metrics essential to resource-constrained edge devices. Among these limitations are the typical FLOPS (floating-point operations per second), latency, accuracy, and memory usage. The findings show that more complex algorithms result in slightly better accuracy at the expense of additional calculations, memory use, and latency; hence, they might not be employed in edge devices with limited resources. On the other hand, simpler algorithms might be desirable for implementation on these devices because they deliver adequate accuracy performance while requiring less processing power and memory and converging more quickly. Fig. 6 depicts the performance of these SSL algorithms when they are trained on the CIFAR-10 dataset and reach 80% accuracy given that 8% of the data is labeled [54].

MeanTeacher and FixMatch are two SSL techniques that we tested and incorporated into our system pipeline. Mean-Teacher is an excellent candidate technique for implementation on resource-constrained devices since, according to our previous work [54], it achieves adequate accuracy with little latency, memory usage, and the number of floating-point operations per second (FLOPS). For comparison, research, and analysis reasons, FixMatch, a cutting-edge SSL algorithm that achieves greater accuracy at the expense of higher latency, FLOPS, and memory usage, was also introduced.

These two algorithms' working principles are as follows:

1) Mean-Teacher: After each epoch or batch, the Mean-Teacher algorithm employs exponential mean average (EMA) to average prior model weights (consecutive student models). More accurately, the Mean-Teacher method seeks to minimize the cost of the predicted distance between the updated mean teacher model's prediction (with weights $\hat{\theta}$) and the student model's prediction (with weights $\theta$):
$\hat{\theta}(t) = \alpha\hat{\theta}(t -1) + (1 -\alpha)\theta(t)$
(3)
where $\alpha \in[0, 1]$ is a smoothing coefficient hyperparameter. Instead of utilizing the final weights directly, a model's accuracy is generally improved by averaging model weights throughout training phases. Additionally, the target model has stronger intermediate representations because the weight averages enhance not just the top output but other layer outputs as well. These features make it salable for huge datasets and online learning and speed up the feedback loop between the student and teacher models.

2) FixMatch: On the other hand, this technique first checks to see if the prediction made by the model on weakly augmented unlabeled samples $P(A_w(x_u))$ exceeds a specified and fixed threshold $\tau$ for all classes (not to be confused with the static threshold used in the modified split-learning scheme), and if it does, it transforms the prediction to hard pseudo-labels. Then, $P(A_s(x_u))$, the model's prediction for a strong augmentation of the same samples, is calculated. A fixed scalar hyperparameter $\lambda_u$ that represents the proportional weight of the unlabeled loss is then used to scale two-component loss functions. The first loss function for the labeled and weakly augmented input $L_s$ with label $q_l$ is evaluated using a normal supervised classification loss, and the second cross-entropy loss function is calculated between the weakly and strongly augmented data predictions $L_u$:
$L_{tot} = L_s + \lambda_u L_u$,
(4)
$L_s = \frac{1}{B} \sum_{b=1}^{B} H(q_l, P(y|A_w(x_l)))$,
(5)
$L_u = \frac{1}{B} \sum_{b=1}^{B} 1(\max(q_u) \geq \tau)H(\hat{q}_u, P(y|A_s(x_u)))$.
(6)
Where $H$ represents the cross entropy function, $b \in\{1, \dots, B\}$, $B$ is the batch size, $q_u = P(y|A_w(x_u))$ is the model's predicted class distribution, $\hat{q}_u$ is the one-hot pseudo-label of $q_u$, and $1$(condition) is an indicator function that returns 1 if the condition was met and 0 otherwise.

In contrast to the original FixMatch article, which utilized augmentation techniques suited for images, we have employed alternative augmentation methods more appropriate for one-dimensional time-series data like ECG signals. Specifically, we have adapted augmentation strategies proposed in [55], [56], which include jittering, scaling, rotation, magnitude warping, and time warping. For weak augmentation, we used one of the aforementioned methods chosen randomly. On the other hand, for strong augmentation, we found that using three random combinations of the aforementioned methods gave the best results.

instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.

We trained seven model architectures on an 11th-generation Intel Core i9 CPU with 64 GB RAM using PyTorch [61]. The Adam optimizer [62] used parameters (α = 0.001, β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.99). We estimated FLOPS for the forward pass using the THOP library [64], assuming backward propagation FLOPS are double the forward pass [63].

Table I compares the architectures trained and tested using single-shot and sliding-window approaches, reporting trainable parameters, FLOPS, and relative FLOPS utilization normalized to LSTM. TCN architectures use significantly less computational power while maintaining comparable or better classification performance. For example, TCN5 uses 2.17% of the FLOPS of the LSTM model and 31.96% less than the closest non-TCN model (WangFCN). This lower cost originates from the parallelization properties of convolutions compared to recurrent networks and the reduced number of learned parameters achieved through dilated convolution. Therefore, TCN is more favorable for low-performance hardware and energy efficiency. We favor TCN5 over TCN3 and TCN4 despite its higher FLOPS because it achieves better classification performance by learning from the full 2500 ms sample. Using the sliding-window approach reproduced results from [5]; the single-shot approach performed worse as it uses only one randomly chosen window, potentially missing the target anomaly, resulting in significant performance loss despite lower computational cost. Consequently, we selected the sliding-window approach for training.

section: III. EXPERIMENTS AND RESULTS — D. Modiﬁed Split-Learning Mechanism
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
We tested the modified split-learning system on the PTB-XL dataset using the IoT setup from our previous work [40]. Hardware specifications and the neural network architecture are detailed in our GitHub repository [65].

We defined three data distribution scenarios: Original Data Distribution Case (ODD) with uniform class distribution; Modified Data Distribution Case 1 (MDD1), where each client holds data for one class; and Modified Data Distribution Case 2 (MDD2), where each client holds half the data for two classes. The testing dataset was fixed at 2163 samples across all classes. In MDD1, clients have full class data; in MDD2, data is split between clients. To mitigate non-IID effects, we added pretraining on a heterogeneous subset (5% and 10% of the full dataset) [66].

Table III reports average accuracy and AUC across clients for basic configurations (ODD, MDD1, MDD2), pretraining variants (+5%, +10% ODD), and systems incorporating an autoencoder (AE) and adaptive threshold mechanism (ATM). Performance deteriorates under extreme imbalance (MDD1, MDD2) [25]. Pretraining improves results by reducing data bias. The AE causes slight accuracy and AUC drops, but the ATM restores performance near original levels due to its regularization effect, similar to dropout [67]. If the base network lacks overfitting, the modified system may slightly reduce performance, as noted in previous work [40].

For the first three ODD cases, Table IV shows data transfer and FLOPS. Adding the AE and ATM reduced communications overhead by 71.7% and client FLOPS by 46.5% while maintaining classification performance. This makes the system suitable for mobile ECG classification on the edge and a green AI option for hospitals, offering lower energy use and faster processing while preserving data privacy. Finally, the system supports learning from unlabeled data via semi-supervised learning techniques.

We tested the modified split-learning system in Fig. 5 on the PTB-XL dataset using the test IoT setup in Fig. 9, which is the same setup used in our previous work [40]. The hardware specifications of the test system as well as the full neural network architecture that is hyper-parameter tuned are mentioned in our GitHub repository [65]. We defined multiple training and testing scenarios that include the following:

1) Original Data Distribution Case (ODD): The samples of each class in the PTB-XL dataset are uniformly distributed amongst all clients.

2) Modified Data Distribution Case 1 (MDD1): Each of the clients in this scenario has data representing only one class. This is an extreme case that causes the classification performance to be at its lowest.

3) Modified Data Distribution Case 2 (MDD2): Each of the clients in this scenario has data representing two classes. This is a more realistic case regarding our application, where we have local patients’ data representing some diseases. However, the performance is still expected to drop significantly compared to the ODD case.

In Table II, the training and validation sample count per client as well as the class distribution for each scenario are shown. The testing dataset is set to be the same for all cases (2163 samples) representing all classes. Moreover, in MDD1, each client has the full data of their assigned class. However, in MDD2, the client has half the data of the two classes assigned to it. For example, client 1 has half the data representing the class "NORM", while client 5 has the other half. Additionally, to reduce the impact of non-IID data on the classification performance, we added the option of using pretraining of the client models on a heterogeneous subset that contains all the classes, as other authors suggested in the literature [66]. We tested pretraining using 5% of the full dataset as well as 10% added to the different modified data distributions.

In Table III, the average accuracy and AUC score across clients are reported for the different split-learning system configurations. The results include the basic configurations (ODD, MDD1, and MDD2), the ones with pretraining (+5%, +10% ODD), and the ones including the modifications to the split-learning system; the autoencoder (AE), and the adaptive threshold mechanism (ATM). Taking a deeper look into the results, we notice the following: First, split-learning performance deteriorates under an extremely unbalanced data distribution, as in the cases of MDD1 and MDD2. This is an inherited problem in both FL and SL [25]. Second, we can see that pretraining has improved the classification results since it gave the model some examples from other classes, reducing the data bias effect. Third, the addition of the AE has caused both the accuracy and the AUC to drop slightly. However, the inclusion of the ATM has caused an increase in the classification performance back to almost the same as before. This is because the ATM has a similar regularization effect to adding a dropout layer in a neural network [67]. This helps reduce overfitting in the model and increases testing results. It is worth mentioning that if the network is not facing any overfitting before adding the modified SL, we expect the performance to drop slightly after applying our system similar to our previous work in [40]. Finally, to assess the advantage of the modified SL system on the system's overall efficiency, we show the data transfer and FLOPS for the first three ODD cases in Table IV. We can see that adding the AE and the ATM to the SL system built on the TCN network helped reduce the communications overhead between the client and the server by 71.7% and the FLOPS at the client by 46.5% while having almost the same classification performance. This makes our system a suitable option for mobile ECG classification on the edge as well as a green AI option for ECG classification in hospitals that require less energy and is much faster while preserving the privacy of data. Now the last point to discuss in our modified SL is the ability to learn from unlabeled data using semi-supervised learning techniques.

section: III. EXPERIMENTS AND RESULTS — E. SSL Performance
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: We integrated mean teacher and fix match into our system configurations. We trained using 10% labeled and 90% unlabeled data with a batch size of 64 (32 labeled, 32 unlabeled). Classification accuracy dropped 16–22% with only 10% labeled data. SSL techniques boosted accuracy by 9.1–15.7%. SL-Fix outperformed SL-MT in all configurations, with accuracy gains of 0.41–2.34%, but incurred a 367% FLOPS and 248% memory increase compared to SL-MT [54]. The Split-Fix threshold τ was set to 0.9 for PTB-XL, yielding 82.9% ODD accuracy; increasing to 0.95 or 0.99 dropped accuracy to 82.8% and 82.7%, while decreasing to 0.85 dropped it to 81.7% [23]. Higher τ improves pseudo-label quality at the cost of quantity [23]. Most FixMatch works use thresholds between 0.9–0.95 with little performance impact [23], [54], [68]. SL-MT is more efficient for edge ECG classification. All modified SL systems outperformed basic configurations with improved computation and communication efficiency.
output:
We analyzed integrating two SSL techniques (mean teacher and fix match) into our different system configurations discussed earlier. We trained the system using 10% labeled data and 90% unlabeled data. Both labeled and unlabeled data followed the distribution of their respective configurations. We used a batch size of 64 where 32 samples were randomly sampled from the labeled data and 32 were randomly sampled from the unlabeled data. The average accuracies of the supervised cases and the semi-supervised ones are shown in Table V. First, we see that training the system on only 10% of the data has caused the classification accuracy to drop significantly (between 16% - 22%). This is expected as deep learning algorithms' performance depends on having access to a huge amount of data, and having less data means fewer examples to learn from. Second, using SSL techniques helped boost the classification accuracy between 9.1% - 15.7%. This is a very good performance increase gained by utilizing unlabeled data that would not have been used otherwise, especially in the medical field where there is a scarcity of human-labeled data. Third, SL-Fix has a better increase in classification accuracy than SL-MT in all configurations. The difference, however, is small (between 0.41% and 2.34%). The performance increase of SL-Fix over SL-MT comes with around a 367% increase in FLOPS and a 248% increase in memory usage, as shown in our previous work [54].

Moreover, the Split-Fix threshold τ was fine-tuned specifically for the PTB-XL dataset and set to the value of 0.9 which yields the highest accuracy (82.9% in the ODD case), but increasing it slightly to 0.95 or 0.99 has a negligible impact where accuracy dropped to 82.8%, 82.7% respectively. Conversely, using a smaller threshold value results in a decrease in accuracy by more than 1.2%. For example, when τ = 0.85, the accuracy drops to 81.7%. It is important to note that the threshold value determines the balance between the quality and quantity of pseudo-labels as explained in [23]. Higher threshold values result in improved accuracy of pseudo-labels for unlabeled data but at the cost of a smaller contribution of unlabeled data to unsupervised loss. This suggests that achieving high accuracy depends more on the quality than the number of pseudo-labels [23]. The need to fine-tune the fixed threshold τ in Split-Fix for every new dataset is considered another disadvantage of this method in comparison to the Split-MT. However, most of the works that use the FixMatch algorithm for different datasets use threshold values between 0.9 −0.95 with not much effect on the overall system performance [23], [54], [68]. Overall, this makes SL-MT a more efficient option in the ECG classification task, especially if we run the system on the edge to achieve a green AI that saves resources. Finally, we notice that in all cases, our modified SL system achieved better results with SSL algorithms than the basic configurations, with the added advantage of increased communication and computation efficiency.

section: IV. CONCLUSION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
IV. CONCLUSION

We proposed a privacy-preserving deep learning approach for ECG classification designed for distributed, real-life scenarios. We selected the TCN model as the baseline for its efficiency and implemented a modified split-learning mechanism. Testing across multiple data distribution scenarios showed performance comparable to original split-learning while reducing client computations by 46.5% and communication overhead by 71%. Furthermore, we integrated semi-supervised learning to leverage unlabeled medical data, demonstrating a significant performance improvement over systems using only labeled data.

An Empirical Analysis of Machine Learning Algorithms for Crime Prediction Using Stacked Generalization: An Ensemble Approach

Sapna Singh Kshatri, Deepak Singh, Bhavana Narain, Surbhi Bhatia, Mohammad Tabrez Quasim, and G. R. Sinha

Received March 5, 2021, accepted April 16, 2021, date of publication April 22, 2021, date of current version May 12, 2021.

Ensemble learning method is a collaborative decision-making mechanism that implements to aggregate the predictions of learned classifiers in order to produce new instances. Early analysis has shown that the ensemble classifiers are more reliable than any single part classifier, both empirically and logically. While several ensemble methods are presented, it is still not an easy task to find an appropriate configuration for a particular dataset. Several prediction-based theories have been proposed to handle machine learning crime prediction problem in India. It becomes a challenging problem to identify the dynamic nature of crimes. Crime prediction is an attempt to reduce crime rate and deter criminal activities. This work proposes an efficient authentic method called assemble-stacking based crime prediction method (SBCPM) based on SVM algorithms for identifying the appropriate predictions of crime by implementing learning-based methods, using MATLAB. The SVM algorithm is applied to achieve domain-specific configurations compared with another machine learning model J48, SMO Naïve Bayes bagging and, the Random Forest. The result implies that a model of a performer does not generally work well. In certain cases, the ensemble model outperforms the others with the highest coefficient of correlation, which has the lowest average and absolute errors. The proposed method achieved 99.5% classification accuracy on the testing data. The model is found to produce more predictive effect than the previous researches taken as baselines, focusing solely on crime dataset based on violence. The results also proved that any empirical data on crime, is compatible with criminological theories. The proposed approach also found to be useful for predicting possible crime predictions. And suggest that the prediction accuracy of the stacking ensemble model is higher than that of the individual classifier.

section: I. INTRODUCTION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Researchers have attempted to curb crime using various modeling tools, but the rising crime rate necessitates new methods to assist policymakers. Human skillsets fail to manually track criminal records, necessitating novel analysis of crime-related information. Crime prediction currently focuses on risk fields and hotspot forecasts. Recent data processing techniques utilize expanded computer accessibility and data innovations to incorporate detailed felony databases. Violence, defined as threats or force, ranges from murder to harassment and is highly prevalent in specific districts of Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan, India, as well as across states concerning crimes against women. Notably, 17 districts among Maharashtra's poorest counties reported high murder rates, and defying public order occurred in districts of Rajasthan, Bihar, and Tamil Nadu. Machine learning techniques are generally suggested for predicting future violence percentages, though limited algorithms and small datasets have been used previously. This research claims novelty through empirical analysis of machine learning contributions. While machine learning models are widely used, new artificial intelligence procedures remain underexplored in many regions. Common classifiers achieving accuracy include Random Tree, K-Nearest Neighbor, Bayesian, Support Vector Machine, and Neural Network. This work proposes an ensemble-based classification model, the Stack-Based Crime Prediction Method (SBCPM), combining multiple algorithms via bagging and stacking to improve predictive efficiency. Key contributions include a multi-level crime stack tested on real-time databases, combining machine and ensemble learning, using stack generalization to minimize error, and improving accuracy by estimating violent crime through principle piling.

Recently, a lot of research and predictions have been attempted on how to curb crimes by various criminologists and researchers using different modeling and statistical tools. As the rate of crime is still on the hike, therefore, there is a potential need of some important research that can help the policy makers and the concerned department about challenges and issues in the area of crime prediction and control mechanisms. Skillset of human fails to keep track of criminal records, if handled manually. So, there is need for identifying in a novel way, which will help in analyzing crime related information. Analysis on crime prediction is currently based on two significant aspects, prediction of crime risk field [1], [2] and crime hotspot forecast [3]. Data processing techniques are applied to facilitate this task. The expanded accessibility of computers and data innovations have empowered law authorization offices to incorporate broad databases with detailed information about major felonies, such as murder, rape, arson etc. In recent years, huge number of crimes is being reported in the world. Violence is a major crime in which a criminal threatens to use force on the victim. It refers to both crimes in which a violent act is the motive, such as murder or rape, robbery, as well as crimes in which violence is used as coercion. Crime may not necessarily, be initiated using weapons, depending on the jurisdiction, and violence crimes can range from murder to harassment. Typically, violence crimes include murders, robberies, rapes, attempt to murder, kidnapping, thefts, riots, dowry death, dowry atrocity etc. The rate of violent crimes is very high in 22 districts of Madhya Pradesh state and 23 districts of Rajasthan state in India; whereas the number of states is 34 and 25 respectively for the above-mentioned states concerning the crimes against women. Commenting on the factual data in terms of the number of murders, it is reported that 17 districts listed among the poorest counties were in Maharashtra, with Andhra Pradesh and Rajasthan (having the next largest concentrations of violence crime districts). The crimes generally fall in the areas of violence criminal activities mostly against women. Similarly, defying public order as a crime was reported in 13, 12 and 11 districts of Rajasthan, Bihar and Tamil Nadu, respectively, out of total 100 districts [4].

The crime predictions are generally suggested by using machine learning techniques with respect to what percentage of future violence is possible in crimes. This research has been done for many years, but with some limited algorithms and small dataset. This research claims its novelty with the help of empirical analysis of machine learning and other contributions listed in this section. Though, machine learning models are widely used in crime prediction, but still despite of its expanding application and its gigantic potential, there are numerous regions, where the new procedures created in the zone of artificial intelligence have not been completely explored and has major drawbacks. The most common approaches which have reported achievable accuracy in machine learning classifiers are Random Tree Algorithm, K-Nearest Neighbor(KNN), Bayesian model, Support Vector Machine (SVM), Neural Network [5].

Among these algorithms, crime prediction technique is proposed by integrating a number of algorithms named as a crime prediction ensemble model using bagging and stacked ensemble techniques, reflecting the beauty of this research work. Ensemble model is a method for constructing a predictive model by combining multiple models to solve a single problem in order to improve predictive efficiency. Ensemble learning techniques have been shown to be important in many applications [6]. Introduction of prediction ensembles in ensemble learning based models is used to combine the output capability of more than one classifier to generate the final result. Ensembles can be compared to the efficiency that are generated with the previous single learning classifiers. This work proposes an approach for constructing an ensemble based classification model called ensemble-approach crime prediction method (SBCPM) for predicting crime, representing a supervised based technique, also known as tree-based or classification approach. The contributions of the research work are explained below:

• Multi-level method as crime stack is presented and tested for crime prediction tested on real-time database.
• Crime stack is developed as the combination of machine learning, and ensemble learning -based techniques.
• Stack generalization is used to minimize error rate.
• The accuracy is improved by applying the principle of piling in order to estimate violent crime.

The organization of the paper is as follows: Literature Review is presented and discussed in section 2. Section 3 describes the Crime Stack methodology and the data set information that is used for experimentation and evaluation. In section 4, descriptions of the evaluation criterion are detailed with the results obtained. Finally, the paper concludes with the future scope in Section 5.

The confusion matrix summarizes classification performance via four quadrants: True Positives (TP), True Negatives (TN), False Positives (FP), and False Negatives (FN).

In crime prediction, FP occurs when the model predicts crime but none occurs, while FN occurs when crime happens but is missed. TP correctly predicts crime; TN correctly predicts no crime.

Performance metrics derive from these quadrants. Accuracy equals (TP + TN) divided by total instances. Precision is TP divided by all predicted positives. Recall is TP divided by all actual positives. The F1-score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall.

The matrix also enables Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve and Area Under the Curve (AUC) analysis. Analyzing FP and TN rates helps determine the optimal classification threshold to minimize misclassification costs, which is critical in high-stakes domains like crime prediction where error consequences are significant.

The specific costs of FP and FN must guide interpretation. High FN rates may miss critical events, while high FP rates may waste resources on non-events. Therefore, analyzing FP and TN values is indispensable for robust model evaluation in crime prediction.

2. FP = TN

The confusion matrix is a fundamental tool in evaluating the performance of classification models. It provides a tabular summary of the predictions made by a model against the actual outcomes. The matrix is typically structured into four quadrants: True Positives (TP), True Negatives (TN), False Positives (FP), and False Negatives (FN). Each quadrant represents a specific type of prediction outcome, allowing for a comprehensive analysis of the model's strengths and weaknesses.

In the context of crime prediction, the confusion matrix plays a critical role in understanding the trade-offs between different types of errors. For instance, a False Positive (FP) occurs when the model predicts a crime will occur, but it does not. Conversely, a False Negative (FN) occurs when the model fails to predict a crime that actually happens. The True Positive (TP) represents a correct prediction of a crime, while the True Negative (TN) represents a correct prediction of no crime.

The relationship between these metrics is essential for calculating various performance measures such as accuracy, precision, recall, and the F1-score. Accuracy is defined as the ratio of correctly predicted instances (both TP and TN) to the total number of instances. Precision focuses on the proportion of true positives among all predicted positives, while recall (or sensitivity) measures the proportion of true positives among all actual positives. The F1-score provides a harmonic mean of precision and recall, offering a single metric that balances both concerns.

Furthermore, the confusion matrix is instrumental in deriving the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve and the Area Under the Curve (AUC). These tools visualize the model's ability to distinguish between classes across different classification thresholds. By analyzing the FP and TN rates, researchers can determine the optimal threshold that minimizes the cost of misclassification, which is particularly important in high-stakes domains like crime prediction where the consequences of errors can be significant.

The interpretation of the confusion matrix must consider the specific context and the relative costs of FP and FN. In some scenarios, a high FN rate might be unacceptable due to the potential for missing critical crime events, while in others, a high FP rate might be more problematic due to the allocation of resources to non-existent events. Therefore, a thorough analysis of the confusion matrix, including the specific values of FP and TN, is indispensable for the robust evaluation of machine learning models in the field of crime prediction.

Corresponding author: Vijayakumar Ponnusamy (vijayakp@srmist.edu.in)

ABSTRACT Blockchain networks serve as a transparent and secure ledger storage solution, yet they remain vulnerable to attacks. There must be some mechanism to protect the blockchain network from attacks. Among various attacks, the Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack is considered severe, which is challenging to detect accurately and reliably. Machine learning techniques are used to detect the attack, which requires exploring all global attack data in a single system, which is difficult in practice. This article proposes a distributed machine learning mechanism called Federated Machine Learning for detecting the presence of DDoS attacks. But in federated machine learning the model itself can be poisoned by the malicious collaborating node which is another problem that this article solves by storing the model in blockchain and by introducing a new reputation-based miner selection procedure. The proposed framework integrates the federation of machine learning within the blockchain network framework for detecting DDoS attacks. Under the integrated framework, miners are used to train the blocks and they also participate in the machine learning training. A dynamic reputation-based miner selection mechanism that can balance exploration and exploitation is proposed for optimal miner selection, which can ensure the high accuracy of the machine learning model and improve the security of blockchain from attacks like DDoS attacks and 51% attacks. The proposed framework is tested with Random Forest, Multilayer Perceptron, and Logistic Regression machine learning algorithms. The proposed mechanism achieved maximum accuracy of 99.1% using random forest model which is superior to the existing mechanism of detection of DDoS attacks.

section: I. INTRODUCTION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
A new blockchain-based technology has gained global popularity due to its unique properties, including security, immutability, decentralization, and transparency. Each block contains a list of transactions linked chronologically via cryptographic hashes, creating an immutable, tamper-proof record. Since the network is decentralized with no central authority and data are encrypted, it is resistant to attacks. However, various attacks exist, including 51% attacks, Sybil attacks, Eclipse attacks, and DDoS attacks. A 51% attack occurs when an entity controls over 50% of the network's mining power in a Proof of Work (PoW) network, allowing double-spending or transaction blocking. A Sybil attack involves creating fake identities to influence consensus, while an Eclipse attack isolates a target node with rogue nodes. Blockchain networks are susceptible to DDoS attacks, which can slow transaction processing or shut down the network by flooding it with traffic.

Traditional attack detection methods are ineffective due to the blockchain's growing size and new contract deployments. Many attacks are generated daily. Machine learning can analyze vast data volumes to identify patterns and irregularities in real-time, examining data flow, network packets, and communication patterns to detect suspicious activities. These techniques can identify persistent attacks like DDoS, DoS, and 51% attacks, as well as support anomaly detection and behavioral analysis. However, collecting attack data from various sources and training models is practically tricky. This challenge is solved by using distributed federated machine learning. In federated learning, distributed nodes train local models on local attack data, which are then aggregated at a central server to create a robust global model. Employing many distributed nodes for training is costly, so the proposed system integrates attack detection into the blockchain network, utilizing blockchain miners to train local models. This article focuses on DDoS attack detection using federated machine learning.

The proposed model utilizes available miner resources to detect DDoS attacks by integrating a federated learning mechanism. Federated learning is added to the data layer of the blockchain, replacing the block creation and request handling module. After developing a machine learning model with miner help to protect the global model from security attacks, the model is stored on the blockchain to secure it from tampering or alterations that could cause model failure. This integration supports DDoS attack detection, which is the uniqueness of the proposed method.

The article's contributions are as follows:

* The proposed mechanism uses federated learning to protect the blockchain attack scenario where the federated machine learning model is attacked by an attacker; this is eliminated by using blockchain to protect federated learning, increasing DDoS attack detection reliability.
* To improve security and reliability, miners are utilized for federated machine learning model training, block mining, and attack detection.
* The proposed federated machine learning model protects against blockchain attacks, including the possibility of mining nodes becoming attackers. A miner selection mechanism based on reputation value is proposed to select the optimal miner set for training the attack detection model, ensuring more secure model development and avoiding malicious users in the process. This enhances blockchain security, saves energy, and reduces computational power.
* To balance exploration and exploitation in utilizing data for training, a reputation-based incentive mechanism of blockchain is proposed to provide incentives to all miner nodes for training the local model. This enables new attack data to be exposed to the model, increasing reliability.
* The proposed miner selection and incentive calculation method balances exploitation and exploration to avoid a 51% attack and bring diversity to data training.

The remaining article is organized as follows: Section II presents related work; Section III presents the proposed framework for DDoS attack detection using federated machine learning; Section IV presents the dataset; Section V discusses the experimental setup and performance measures; VI concludes the article; and VII presents future work.

The spread of new technologies in recent years, like Software Defined Networking (SDN), has increased the plethora of platforms for Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack generation and it created new potential sources for more advanced DDoS attacks on the intended targets. A study [10] and classifies cutting-edge blockchain-based DDoS mitigation systems. The DDoS mitigation strategies are divided into four categories: near-attacker, network-based, near-victim, and hybrid solutions in the network architecture for SDN and IoT. The study’s findings explore the difficulties in conducting research and the potential paths for implementing blockchain-based DDoS mitigation solutions.

A thorough analysis of the DDoS detection and mitigation techniques currently used in SDN is reported [11]. Before proposing potential areas for future research, the work also covers current issues with SDN security and the applications of various security solutions.

Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) systems are used to supervise and monitor critical infrastructure and industrial operations [12]. Combining current SCADA systems with SDN has resulted in the creation of numerous SCADA systems based on SDN. A SCADA system faces various attacks because of their wrong deployments. SDN-based SCADA systems using Recurrent Neural Network (RNN), which includes Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Gated Recurrent Units (GRU), are recommended for detecting DDoS attacks in the study. The experimental work produced a DDoS attack detection accuracy of 97.62.

DDoS attacks can be detected using CMCNN [13] to improve generalizability and to lower the model’s incidence of reporting errors. Abstract properties of attack traffic are extracted using a stacked sparse auto encoder based on the Kullback-Leibler divergence parameter encoding. The model’s sparsity is altered by reducing the redundant data and coupling the abstract features. Encoded feature outputs are then successfully classified. An improved random gradient-descent technique is used for global parameter optimization, preventing fluctuation of the training parameters and speeding the convergence of the model.

CoChain-SC is used to mitigate intra-domain and inter-domain DDoS attacks utilizing SDN, blockchain, and smart contracts. It can efficiently reduce DDoS attacks within the target’s domain while sharing attack information, making it an effective solution across multiple domains to mitigate DDoS attacks and to combine an intra-domain approach based on SDN with an inter-domain scheme. CoChain-SC has 100% detection rate at 500 Mbps and a False Positive Rate of 23%.

Co-IoT is a collaborative DDoS attack mitigation technique employing smart contracts to promote attack collaboration among SDN-based domains [23] and to transfer attack data securely and efficiently. The attackers try to gain control over many compromised IoT devices and launch DDoS attacks against the victim. Co-IoT enables efficient DDoS mitigation along the path of current attacks and also provides mitigation near the source of the DDoS attack.

ChainSecure is used to protect blockchain nodes from DNS amplification attacks, which are a sort of DDoS attack. It is a scalable and proactive solution in Software Defined Networks. It comprises of three schemes [24], namely StateMap, which performs a one-to-one mapping between DNS request and response. Then, an Entropy calculation scheme that uses sFlow that is used to measure the disorder in data which can detect illegitimate flows and DNS DDoS Mitigation that effectively mitigates unlawful DNS requests. The results of the experiments reveal that ChainSecure protects blockchain nodes and can detect/mitigate the attacks fast, with high accuracy making it a promising solution to protect blockchain nodes against DNS amplification attacks.

Designing the blockchain layers is challenging, especially since the consensus layer is crucial. Identifying Long-Range Attacks (LRA) on Proof-of-Stake (PoS) is a tedious task. Previous research has revealed difficulties in spotting far-reaching attacks and keeping track of validator node operations on the blockchain network. To prevent long-range attacks, a study [8] suggested the classification of nodes on Proof-of-Stake using Deep Learning algorithms.

section: 4. Reliable DDoS detection: Reliability of the detection
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
The proposed framework ensures reliable DDoS detection by integrating blockchain and federated machine learning, where miners act as trainers. Blockchain securely stores the developed ML model to prevent attacks and ensure detection reliability. A reputation-based miner selection mechanism guarantees only legitimate miners participate in model development, thereby ensuring the developed model's reliability.

The system utilizes blockchain miners for federated local model training to prevent attackers from compromising the local model. Miners are selected based on a dynamically updated reputation value as a second layer of secure training. The primary novelty is a reputation function calculated from data quality, consisting of accuracy, stake, and winning frequency. Miners demonstrating high accuracy, significant stake, and frequent wins receive higher reputation scores and are selected as optimal. Possessing correct, quality data enables a miner to win more often and produce more accurate values.

Reputation updating occurs periodically whenever a new block generation request is created in the blockchain environment. Specifically, reputation is updated after each training round concludes and the server aggregates the model, meaning the reputation value for every node updates every time the server model upgrades to generate a global model.

A key novelty of the training mechanism is balancing exploitation and exploration while avoiding 51% attacks. Existing mechanisms fail to incentivize all blockchain participants; however, the proposed work allocates incentives to every participant based on reputation value. This inclusivity encourages more participants to engage in quality data training, preventing the exploitation of only a few selected miners. By ensuring all participants receive incentives, the system balances exploitation and exploration in the optimization process. This framework prevents monopolies in mining and local model training and effectively avoids 51% attacks, thereby securing local federated machine learning training.

The system flow proceeds as follows: clients send data for block creation, which is stored as a request record. A miner selection procedure based on reputation selects an optimal miner set for the block. The reputation score for miner M at time t+1 is calculated as the previous reputation plus changes in accuracy and stake, plus a function of winning frequency. Optimally selected miners mine the block based on stake, solve the puzzle, and train the local model using local attack data. All miners perform local training and transfer models to a parameter server for averaging into a global model. This global model is transmitted to the blockchain to create a block, ensuring the model's integrity and preventing attacks. Reputation updates and incentive allocation follow, where all participating nodes create local models and receive incentives calculated via a weighted combination of accuracy change and reputation. The winning miner mines the block at the queue's top. Once the global model is stored on the blockchain, all client nodes and miners read and utilize it for DDoS attack detection on their premises. The framework ensures no possibility of attacking local or global models, and the secured global model protects the blockchain from DDoS attacks.

VI. CONCLUSION

Detecting DDoS attacks in blockchain is challenging and can be addressed with federated machine learning. However, federated learning is vulnerable to model poisoning during transfer to an aggregating server. This article proposes a Blockchain-Integrated Federated Machine Learning Algorithm to secure the blockchain from DDoS attacks and protect the machine learning model from poisoning. The framework ensures the security of both the blockchain and the machine learning model while providing a robust detection mechanism. Three models—Logistic Regression, Multilayer Perceptron, and Random Forest—were compared for simple, medium, and complex problems. Random Forest achieved 99.1% accuracy in complex environments, outperforming Logistic Regression (88.5%) and Multilayer Perceptron (95.1%). output: Detecting DDoS attacks in the blockchain is a challenging task, which can be done with a federated machine learning algorithm. Still, the federated machine learning algorithm is prone to attack while transferring the locally trained model to an aggregating server. So, this article proposed a Blockchain-Integrated Federated Machine Learning Algorithm to secure blockchain from DDoS attacks and a machine learning model from poisoning attackers. This proposed framework ensures the security of both the blockchain and the machine learning model and provides a robust mechanism to detect DDoS attacks in the blockchain. Three machine learning models are compared to solve simple, medium, and complex problems and it is discovered that Random Forest can detect DDoS attacks in a complex environment with high accuracy. Logistic regression achieved an accuracy of 88.5%, and Multilayer Perceptron had an accuracy of 95.1%. The proposed model using Random Forest achieved 99.1% accuracy in detecting DDoS attacks, which is superior to the existing literature. The simulated attack performance of the random forest algorithm is compared with similar literature work. It is observed that for all the performance metrics, the proposed mechanism provides high-performance values. This article addressed only one type of attack called DDoS attack. In future, the same mechanism can be fine-tuned to detect other attacks. Detecting attacks alone will not be a solution for security mechanisms; future mitigation strategies will be developed in a typical practical SDN network environment.

Received March 11, 2022, accepted April 8, 2022, date of publication May 2, 2022, date of current version May 5, 2022.

An Online Transfer Learning Framework With Extreme Learning Machine for Automated Credit Scoring

RANA ALASBAHI
AND XIAOLIN ZHENG
, (Senior Member, IEEE)
Computer Science and Technology, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou 310027, China
Corresponding author: Rana Alasbahi (alssallamy16@hotmail.com)

ABSTRACT Automated Credit Scoring (ACS) is the process of predicting user credit based on historical data. It involves analyzing and predicting the association between the data and particular credit values based on similar data. Recently, ACS has been handled as a machine learning problem, and numerous models were developed to address it. In this paper, we address ACS issues concerning credit scoring in a batch of machine learning problems, namely, feature irregularities due to empty features in many records, class imbalance due to non-uniform statistical distributions of the records between classes, and concept drift due to changing statistical characteristics concerning certain classes and features with time. Considering the limited credit scoring data volume, we propose to address the challenge using the Transfer Learning with Lag (TLL) algorithm based on embedded shallow neural networks that enable knowledge transfer when the number of active features changes. Knowledge transfer is based on lags having an adaptive length that is changed based on performance change feedback. Furthermore, the framework proposes classifier aggregation and the chunk balancing mechanism for handling class imbalance. An evaluation was conducted using the Lending club, German, Default, and PPDai datasets. The results show the superiority of the proposed algorithm over the benchmarks in terms of the majority of classification metrics concerning both time series and overall results.

INDEX TERMS Credit scoring, machine learning, extreme learning machine, probability of default, missing features, data irregularities, class imbalance.
