NER identifies and classifies proper nouns into categories like persons, locations, and organizations [20]. It serves as a preprocessing component for applications such as Machine Translation [7], Search Results clustering [8], and Question Answering [21].

NER resources for Arabic are either outdated or costly [20]. Consequently, researchers must build their own resources, a process requiring significant human effort for annotation and validation [20]. This makes available Arabic NER resources time-consuming to use, as they are typically annotated manually [20]. Furthermore, existing Arabic NER studies usually consider only a few entity types—such as persons, locations, and organizations—while ignoring others from the source corpora [20]. The reasons for this limitation have not been investigated [20].
output:
Named entity recognition (NER) refers to the identification and classification of specific proper nouns into predefined target entity categories such as persons, locations, and organizations. NER is usually integrated as a useful preprocessing component of various ANLP applications [20], including Machine Translation [7], Search Results clustering [8], and Question Answering [21].

Contrary to English language, NER resources based Arabic language are either not up to date or costly. Thus, researchers have to build their own resources for research which require human effort for annotation and validation. Consequently, most of the available NER resources based Arabic language are annotated manually rendering their use time consuming. Moreover, the research studies in NER systems based Arabic language have usually considered few entities (e.g. person, location, and organization) from source corpora while other entity types are being ignored. The reasons have not been mentioned or investigated [20].

Readability is defined as the ease of understanding text due to writing style [22]. It is used to match appropriate texts to reader groups, widely applied in education, healthcare, and industry [22]. ANLP tools retrieve features representing readability levels, including lexical, morphological, and semantic features [23], [24].

Arabic readability research has drawn community attention, but most studies focus on shallow features like word and character counts after segmentation [23], [24]. Important attributes reflecting vocabulary difficulty, unfamiliarity, and cohesion/coherence between text elements are often overlooked. Current focus is mainly on Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) and pedagogical text, with less attention to informal text like Twitter tweets. Additionally, methods may need adaptation for text from other domains. Providing online tools with friendly interfaces is important for users such as teachers.

The ANLP applications we have described earlier use machine learning approaches (mainly supervised) and have recently attracted the focus of researchers. The development of these applications often includes many phases, as shown in Figure 2 and presented in detail in the following subsections.

FIGURE 2. The typical phases of ANLP applications-based machine learning.

A. CORPORA

The first step in ANLP-based machine learning studies is data collection. These data are text samples that are suitable for the concerned subject area. Few freely available collected and classified Arabic corpora exist, such as Al-Nahar, Al-Jazeera, Al-Ahram, Al-hayat, and Al-Dostor newspapers [3], Hadith corpus [13], Akhbar-Alkhaleej corpus [8], Arabic NEWSWIRE [33], Quranic Arabic Corpus [13], corpus Watan-2004 [35], KACST Arabic corpus [42], BBC Corpus [43], CCN Corpus [44] and Open Source Arabic Corpora (OSAC) [45], NADA corpus [59]. These corpora have been used in Arabic processing studies, especially in text categorization. For named entity recognition studies, benchmark data exist such as ACE 2003 [46] and ANERcorp [41]. On the other hand, for the other applications like spam detection, sentiment analysis, readability, and web document classification, benchmark corpora are still missing.

B. PREPROCESSING

Text preprocessing is a core natural language processing task. It applies operations to create another form from the inputted text. In ANLP, MADAMIRA and RapidMiner offer natural language processing operations. MADAMIRA provides the study of the structure of words and part of words (root words, prefixes, and suffixes) in the Arabic language [47]. It includes the critical characteristics of the well-known Arabic processing systems MADA [48]–[50] and AMIRA [51]. RapidMiner consists of many preprocessing operations including stemming, cleaning, and visualization. It is implemented using Java and can be operated with any operating system [52]. Data Cleaning, normalization, tokenization, and stemming are common text preprocessing operations in most ANLP applications. Table 1 summarizes these preprocessing operations.

• Data Cleaning: comprises the removal and/or correction of incorrect records from a data set [24], [31], [32], [34], [35].

• Normalization: focused on the removal of inconsistent variations of Arabic text [31]–[33].

• Tokenization: aims to detect and separate individual words by eliminating additional components such as punctuation marks, white space, and unique characters [21], [30], [31], [53].

• Stemming: is used to reduce multiple forms of the word to one form producing root or stem [30], [31], [33].

TABLE 1. Summary of the preprocessing operations.

Benajiba et al. [21] presented an Arabic NER method. In the preprocessing stage, they used AMIRA toolkit for tokenization. They stressed that, contrary to English language, Arabic tokenization is significant and challenging because of the Arabic’s morphological structure. So, it is primordial to avoid any error in this stage in order to obtain accurate results. They also prevented the removal of the suffixes to decrease ambiguity of the text. Duwairi et al. [31] handled the sentiment analysis of tweets. They started by splitting the tokens using colon, semicolon, comma, space. Then, they applied the normalization on the tweets. After that, they removed the Arabic stop words using a new dictionary integrated to RapidMiner. This is done to overcome the deletion of the negation that is considered as stop words in RapidMiner while it is capital in the analysis of sentiments. Finally, they used light stemming and stemming. The authors stressed that the integration of the dictionary increased the performance of their approach. Zahran and Kanaan [34] proposed a new approach for Arabic text categorization. In the preprocessing phase, they started by removing the non-Arabic letters. Then, the normalization is applied. After that, the stop words are deleted. The authors did not apply the stemming to avoid any conflation with the same form of root.

Supervised learning approaches are related to a labeled training data. Several types of supervised classifiers exist. In the following section, we will present a review of the most frequently used classifiers in ANLP applications.

1) SUPPORT VECTOR MACHINES (SVMs)
are well-known supervised machine learning techniques [53]. SVMs have been effectively employed in many problems related to pattern recognition in fields such as bioinformatics and biometrics. Regarding text processing, SVMs have achieved the best results in text categorization and are used extensively in NLP-related problems in different languages such as Arabic for methods like readability prediction and sentiment analysis [17], [24], [30]–[32].

2) NAIVE BAYES CLASSIFICATION (NB)
is the most straightforward and the second-most-used classifier. The Naive Bayes classifier is a prevalent technique for text categorization that assigns documents to associated categories such as spam or legitimate [28], [31], [32], [36] and positive, negative, or neutral [30]–[32], [60].

3) DECISION TREES
have been used in many NLP-related classification problems [61]. In addition to the Naive Bayes classifier, Decision Tree classifiers provide excellent results for spam detection [18], [25], [27], [28]. The decision tree classifier is a favored machine learning technique because the model is easy to understand. Abdallah et al. [62] showed that their hybrid approach with the rule-based approach using decision tree performed better than the existing classifiers for Arabic Named Entity Recognition applications.

4) k-NEAREST NEIGHBOR (k-NN) ALGORITHM
has been successfully applied to several problems related to ANLP due to its simplicity (e.g., Extraction of Semantic Relations between Concepts, [16]). The k-NN consists of instance-based learning, or lazy learning, where the learning is delayed until classification is conducted. k-NN is well-known in sentiment analysis applications [30]–[32]. It is also utilized in other ANLP applications for classification tasks such as spam detection [28] and web document classification [5], [40].

Wahsheh and Al-Kabi [28] applied three different classification algorithms to detect Arabic spammed Web pages using content based analysis. The obtained results using KNIME software showed that the k-NN (k = 1) achieved better accuracy than the Naive Bayes and decision tree. The main problem faced in this study is the lack of large number of Arabic Web pages with valuable information.

Duwairi and Qarqaz [30] presented an approach for Arabic sentiment analysis. They first generated an in-house dataset by collecting and labeling tweets and Facebook comments from the Internet using crowdsourcing. RapidMiner is then used for the preprocessing purpose. Finally, Naïve Bayes, SVM, and k-NN have been used for the classification task. Results showed that SVM gives the highest Precision while k-NN (k = 10) gives the highest Recall. The reason for these results is the fact that the dataset is not balanced as the number of negative reviews is larger than the positive reviews.

Several other classifiers have been used in different ANLP applications such as Conditional Random Fields (CRF) classifier [15], Neural Network ANN [33], Association rules [37], LogitBoost [27]. However, these classifiers are not commonly used in ANLP literature as the classifiers discussed earlier in this section, as shown in Figure 4.

section: IX. CONCLUSION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
High-quality corpora must be representative and balanced for their target genre or language. A major challenge in ANLP is the lack of standard gold corpora with correct tagging per recent guidelines [64], which is critical for accurate machine learning classification. Arabic data, including corpora and gazetteers, lacks specialized collection tools.

The number of text categorization classes and the accuracy of features representing Arabic characteristics directly affect performance. Researchers can utilize language-independent features that correlate across languages despite dissimilarities [17]. In sentiment analysis, identifying the direction of Arabic sentiment terms in tweets is difficult due to the language's complexity and Twitter's informal nature. Arabic readability measurement is still improving, and features affecting readability at word, sentence, or document levels are hard to identify [25]. Spam detection struggles to keep pace with the yearly increase in new spam types; however, incorporating web page language features can improve effectiveness [25].

There is a need for Arabic-tailored data collection tools combined with formal specifications to annotate application text and create gold-standard corpora. Expert consultation is required for these specifications. An initial attempt is MADAD [65], a general-purpose Arabic text annotation tool focusing on readability. Arabic language processing is inherently challenging due to high inflection and the absence of capitalization and punctuation rules. Basic ANLP tools like sentence splitters, tokenizers, and light stemmers exist to prepare data for higher processing stages, but heterogeneity and interoperability issues force researchers to develop them from scratch [66]. There is an urgent need for interoperable tools usable within a single project.

Named Entity Recognition (NER) at the word level can indicate text readability and assist in identifying sentiment terms [67]. NER also aids text categorization by removing non-influential entities like names and locations. Since NER is essential across fields, it requires language-appropriate features and models for superior performance. Readability measurements are also applicable to spam detection, as most spam is unreadable; an agent measuring text readability can determine if text is spam.

This survey provides a comprehensive review of ANLP and machine learning-based systems, addressing the gap in literature where previous works focused only on English or specific techniques. It serves as a theoretical foundation for researchers and presents various ANLP applications, methodologies, challenges, and solutions. Future work will cover ANLP systems using semi-supervised and unsupervised approaches, as well as Deep Learning, a new and interesting research direction.
output:
IX. CONCLUSION

High-quality corpora are representative and balanced considering the genre or language that they represent. However, one of the leading challenges in most ANLP applications is having standard gold corpora where all text is tagged correctly according to the most recent guidelines [64]. This challenge is critical for machine learning that relies on data to have the more accurate classification process. There is a lack of specialized tools to aid in the process of data collection and specifically in the Arabic language, considering all its types. Data include corpora, gazetteers, etc.

One of the most important aspects that affects the performance of text categorization is the existence of an adequate number of classes. Furthermore, there is a need to have representational and more accurate features from the text that indicate the text representational class and capture as many Arabic characteristics as possible. However, researchers can take advantage of language-independent features, the features that correlate across languages even though there is dissimilarity between each language [17]. In sentiment analysis applications, it is difficult to identify the direction of Arabic sentiment terms in tweets. This difficulty may be due to the complexity of the Arabic language itself and to the use of Twitter as an informal channel of communication. The readability measurement of Arabic text is still in the improvement stage. It is difficult to identify features that affect the readability of a given text. Choosing representative features affects classification performance. Spam detection researchers are still trying to identify the highest number of spam types. However, as the number of new spam types increases every year, this field should be up to date to eliminate the negative impacts of these new types of spam. By considering the features of a web page language, spam detection tools would be highly effective at capturing spam content [25].

There is a need for tools and data collection that are tailored to the Arabic language. These tools can be combined with a standard and formal specification to annotate an application representative text to create a gold-standard corpus. These specifications can be consulted with experts in the field. An initial attempt to create such a tool is MADAD [65], which is a general-purpose annotation tool for Arabic text with a focus on readability annotation. The same is also applied to ANLP preprocessing tools. Arabic language characteristics are intrinsically challenging for Arabic language processing developers and researchers. The most notable characteristics are the high inflection and the absence of capitalization and punctuation rules. A few basic tools have been established by ANLP researchers to process Arabic text such as sentence splitters, tokenizers, and light stemmers. These tools are used to prepare data for high-level processing stages. As a consequence of heterogeneity and interoperability issues, researchers are continuously developing these basic tools from scratch to be used in their projects. There is an urgent need to have such tools that contain similar and interoperable entities that can be used in one single project [66].

Moreover, we need to identify features that have an effect on text readability either on the word level, sentence level, or document level. An example of word level text readability is the NER application, which can help tag common entities in text and provide an indication of its readability. NER applications are also useful in other applications such as the process of identifying sentiment terms. This application will have a high impact on the sentiment analysis field. NER also has an impact on text categorization, where it helps remove named entities that do not have an impact on classification processes, such as people's names and locations. Since NER applications are essential in many fields, they must use features and models appropriate to the nature of the language used to have superior performance [67]. Readability measurements are also used in applications like spam detection. As almost all spam types represented as text are unreadable, the use of an agent that measures the readability of dubious text will be able to determine whether the text is spam.

This survey provided a comprehensive review of the available literature on ANLP and machine learning-based systems. Although some papers only reviewed the English language while others only reviewed ANLP machine learning techniques, this paper provided a comprehensive view on ANLP, covering this gap in the literature. This survey can serve as an important theoretical foundation for researchers who are interested in this topic. Additionally, we show different ANLP applications and their significance in such machine learning-based systems. Also, we present several systems that utilize ANLP-based machine learning techniques, their methodologies, challenges, and solutions. As this would lay a foundation for researchers and technology practitioners in the field providing them essentials about this topic. In the future work, we will cover more systems that utilize ANLP-based machine learning with semi-supervised and unsupervised approaches. We will also focus on the Deep Learning which is a new and interesting research direction.

ABSTRACT The use of computer-based and online education systems has made new data available that
can describe the temporal and process-level progression of learning. To date, machine learning research
has not considered the impacts of these properties on the machine learning prediction task in educational
settings. Machine learning algorithms may have applications in supporting targeted intervention approaches.
The goals of this paper are to: 1) determine the impact of process-level information on machine learning
prediction results and 2) establish the effect of type of machine learning algorithm used on prediction results.
Data were collected from a university level course in human factors engineering (n = 35), which included
both traditional classroom assessment and computer-based assessment methods. A set of common regression
and classiﬁcation algorithms were applied to the data to predict ﬁnal course score. The overall prediction
accuracy as well as the chronological progression of prediction accuracy was analyzed for each algorithm.
Simple machine learning algorithms (linear regression, logistic regression) had comparable performance
with more complex methods (support vector machines, artiﬁcial neural networks). Process-level information
was not useful in post-hoc predictions, but contributed signiﬁcantly to allowing for accurate predictions to
be made earlier in the course. Process level information provides useful prediction features for development
of targeted intervention techniques, as it allows more accurate predictions to be made earlier in the course.
For small course data sets, the prediction accuracy and simplicity of linear regression and logistic regression
make these methods preferable to more complex algorithms.

input: The modern ubiquity of computer use and internet access has dramatically impacted engineering education [1]. There has been a rapid rise over the last decade in the use of computer-based or online formats to facilitate or conduct higher-education courses, with enrollment in at least one online course now at 32% [2]. Many universities now include online programs, and online publisher resources have grown correspondingly. This movement is matched in training, with more than 60% of the 5.7 million hours of Boeing training in 2007 being partially or totally online [3]. The use of these technologies has created opportunities for greater student access and novel engagement methods. Online learning has equally great impacts on learning assessment. In traditional classroom settings, recording student progress is often a combination of subjective reviews and paper records [4]. The resultant data are typically "summative assessments," measuring cumulative knowledge (e.g., examinations), often only available at discrete points [5]. By contrast, online and computer-based learning creates an electronic log of a wide array of student-system interactions, such as individual question responses over a prolific set of homework, quizzes, and examinations. Data collection, both in depth and quantity impractical in traditional settings, is easily recorded electronically. From a practical perspective, these settings provide greater access to data at a finer temporal scale, as logs are recorded at every student interaction.

input: The system generates detailed logs that allow interpretation of process-level data, providing insights into learning progression beyond just end results. A primary objective of assessment is predicting future student performance, known as formative assessment, which evaluates learning during the process to adapt instruction for maximal effectiveness. For online courses, this feedback can modify content or presentation. In technology-supplemented courses, similar predictive feedback informs the timing and content of targeted interventions for struggling students, which may include instructor meetings, extra instruction, or study technique recommendations. For such interventions to be impactful, predictions must be both high-accuracy and obtained as early as possible in the course. Traditionally, instructors use statistical techniques like linear regression to analyze formative metrics in relation to final performance (summative assessment). These techniques fall under the burgeoning field of machine learning, a branch of artificial intelligence that identifies relationships between data using unsupervised or supervised algorithms. The rise in popularity of these techniques stems from their flexibility in processing large, high-dimensional datasets. Application of these techniques to educational datasets has risen dramatically, designated as Educational Data Mining (EDM). Much focus has been on online education, which generates large datasets well-suited for machine learning. However, there has not been an in-depth analysis of the nature of educational data and its impact on machine learning applicability. Specifically, the contribution of finer temporal resolution and process-level data from computer-based environments to machine learning models remains uninvestigated. Furthermore, the utility of varying machine learning techniques on these datasets is unclear. This research has two primary goals: first, to determine the usefulness of temporal and process-level information, in addition to traditional metrics, as features in machine learning prediction models; and second, to determine whether the type of machine learning technique used impacts prediction performance in classroom settings utilizing computer-based data.

This way, machine learning prediction models can be constructed both with and without the additional features. Second, the chronological progression of prediction accuracy is examined, to determine whether the finer temporal scale in the computer-based features allows for accurate predictions of final performance to be made earlier in the course.

The timing of the problem sets, projects, and tests are labeled on Fig. 2, and it can be seen that for the traditional model (without quiz data), model performance stays constant until new information from one of these sources is available.

Several observations can be made based on these results. First, the process-level models (that include quiz data) exhibit a lower SSE than the traditional model, which is expected since the feature sets of the process-level models are a superset of that of the traditional model. Second, it is apparent that the improvement in performance varies over time (as measured by the vertical distance between the traditional and process-level SSE), which is indicative that not all quizzes contribute equally to prediction performance. Consider the change in model performances for the all-quiz model between classes 2 and 3. At class 2, the performance is nearly identical to the other two models, and thus the quiz data available at that time (quiz 1) does not make a major contribution to reducing prediction error. By contrast, at class 3 this model improves considerably in performance, indicating that the new set of quiz information (quizzes 1 and 2) allows the model to achieve a much more accurate prediction of final grade. Interestingly, this effect is not solely the result of quiz 2, as the model of high-error quizzes does not see similar improvement at the availability of quiz 2 data. This indicates that it is not merely quiz 2, but the combination of the information from quizzes 1 and 2 that allow the all-quiz model to outperorm the others.

There are several interesting conclusions arising from the comparison of the two models that include quiz data in Fig. 2. As expected, the model with all quizzes is able to achieve a better fit of the data than the model that includes only the “high error” quizzes. For some time periods of the class (e.g., classes 4-6) the two models have very similar prediction performance. However, there are other time periods (e.g., class 11) where the model that includes all quizzes has a much lower SSE than the “high-error” model.

Based on the results in Fig. 2, we can also begin to answer the question of when accurate predictions of grade can be made with each of these models. The figure demonstrates that the quiz information improves the prediction over the traditional model, but does this allow for accurate predictions to be made earlier? The determination of how much accuracy is necessary to make a prediction is a complex topic. As has been stated earlier, prediction information has greater value the earlier it is available, but predictions become more accurate with time. Therefore the concepts of model accuracy and time are highly intertwined. Early, accurate predictions have great value for informing targeted intervention approaches. However, the nature of the intervention, cost, and efficacy over time will also play a role in choosing the appropriate model accuracy.

Therefore, the exact performance level necessary to inform intervention is domain dependent. However, we can still draw useful conclusions about the results of the specific temporal analysis in Fig. 2. A horizontal line on the graph in Fig. 2 indicates the time at which each model reaches any particular performance threshold. Consider the performance level represented by an SSE of 800. The all-quiz model achieves this level of performance by class 11, while the other two models do not reach this performance level until class 13, just after the first test. There are important implications of this timing difference. The prediction accuracy level that can be achieved after the first test with the traditional and “high-error” models can be achieved prior to the first test with the all-quiz model. This is very valuable from a targeted intervention approach, as an intervention prior to the first test could improve test performance for struggling students (such as through an extra study session, etc.). In the consideration of both the accuracy and temporal advantages provided by the process-level information, it is clear that this information provides considerable benefits to educators and students.

The study evaluated classification techniques using 10 data splits to minimize random assignment effects. Classification error was used as the performance metric, where lower values indicate better performance. A naive baseline error rate of approximately 54% was established, based on assigning all students to the most frequent class (misclassifying 19 of 35 students).

Results show no single method is consistently superior. Logistic regression and artificial neural networks (ANNs) generally outperformed support vector machines (SVMs), likely due to SVMs using a linear kernel that struggles with data non-linearities. ANNs have higher complexity than logistic regression models, making them less interpretable for targeted intervention. Given similar performance and greater interpretability, logistic regression was selected for subsequent temporal analysis.

section: IV. DISCUSSION/CONCLUSION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
The first objective was to assess the utility of process-level information (daily quiz scores) in machine learning prediction models. Results indicate that quiz data does not significantly improve post-hoc prediction performance, as models using agglomerative average or individual scores (Tables 3 and 5) achieved poor fits; other features, such as tests, are more useful. However, quiz information benefits predictions made partway through the course, as shown in Figures 2 and 3, since summative assessments have better direct correlation to final grades. This suggests process-level data is informative when other metrics are unavailable, allowing educators to inform targeted interventions earlier in the term. Using "high-error" quizzes to reduce the feature space improved performance over traditional models but not as much as including all quiz information over time, particularly before the first test.

The analysis compared regression and classification approaches. Post-hoc models require summative information (e.g., tests) for strong performance, with little difference between approaches when all course data is available. In temporal analysis, error decreases over time for both approaches, but progression differs. Classification error dropped from 17.14 (misclassifying 6 students) to 0 just before and after the first test, indicating a large accuracy change. Regression SSE dropped from 751 to 483, yielding an average error per student change from 4.63 to 3.71, which seems less impactful for intervention planning. This indicates classification experiences greater accuracy changes over time and rapidly approaches perfect prediction, while regression offers generally useful prediction earlier in the course. Thus, classification may have advantages later in the course, while regression is more consistent earlier.

Important caveats exist: required model accuracy and intervention timing depend on the domain, requiring subject-matter expert interpretation. For this dataset, if intervention costs are high relative to failed student costs, waiting for perfect classification is appropriate; this yields earliest intervention at class 13 with the all-quiz model, class 17 with the "high-error" model, and class 21 with the traditional model. Under different cost/benefit assumptions, intervention timing varies, but process-level quiz data allowed greater certainty in earlier intervention regardless of circumstances.

The second objective was to determine the impact of machine learning algorithm type on prediction.

For both regression and classification on this dataset, simpler models (linear and logistic regression) achieved similar prediction performance to more complex models (ANNs and SVMs). This suggests simpler, likely linear, relationships between features and targets. For more complex datasets, it remains unproven whether non-linear models like ANNs will perform stronger. Given the primary goal of preserving parsimony, the results recommend linear regression for regression analysis and logistic regression for classification.

In summary, process-level information in an educational course setting does not improve summative prediction when all other metrics are available, but provides greater accuracy earlier, especially without summative assessments. For these datasets, simpler machine learning algorithms achieve similar generalization to more complex models. Future research should investigate whether these properties hold for larger datasets and how to transform prediction results into targeted interventions via expert interpretation.

ABSTRACT Assessment of code smell for predicting software change proneness is essential to ensure
its signiﬁcance in the area of software quality. While multiple studies have been conducted in this regard,
the number of systems studied and the methods used in this paper are quite different, thus, causing confusion
for understanding the best methodology. The objective of this paper is to approve the effect of code smell
on the change inclination of a speciﬁc class in a product framework. This is the novelty and surplus of this
work against the others. Furthermore, this paper aims to validate code smell for predicting class change
proneness to ﬁnd an error in the prediction of change proneness using code smell. Six typical machine
learning algorithms (Naive Bayes Classiﬁer, Multilayer Perceptron, LogitBoost, Bagging, Random Forest,
and Decision Tree) have been used to predict change proneness using code smell from a set of 8200 Java
classes spanning 14 software systems. The experimental results suggest that code smell is indeed a powerful
predictor of class change proneness with multilayer perceptron being the most effective technique. The
sensitivity and speciﬁcity values for all the models are well over 70% with a few exceptions.

Change in software is unpredictable and tied to design theories rather than exact specifications [2], [3]. Researchers have used patterns and metrics to quantify software attributes and predict changes [5], [14]. Recent studies indicate code smell predicts change proneness more accurately than static metrics [6]. Code smell represents bad implementation choices, while good choices are design patterns [15]. Fowler [1] defined 22 code smells and suggested refactoring areas; thresholds like NOM, LOC, and variable counts are needed for detection [10]. Kaur and Jain [7] found random under-sampling before feature selection with Gene Expression Programming is the most effective strategy for predicting change proneness, with cascade correlation and Tree-Boost among top algorithms [7].

Vidal et al. [16] developed a code smell ranking tool based on segment alterations and modifiability. Saboury et al. [15] detected 12 code smell types in 537 JavaScript releases to analyze fault-proneness. Hecht et al. [4] examined individual and combined effects of three Android performance smells on open-source apps. Ma et al. [9] researched fault detection enhancement using code smell and Cohen’s Kappa. Hadj-Kacem and Bouassida [17] proposed a deep learning hybrid approach for smell detection, evaluating precision, recall, and F-measure, though validity issues existed. Fontana et al. [18] used machine learning with six classifiers evaluated on accuracy, ROC curves, and F-measure. Azadi et al. [19] suggested WekaNose for ML-based detection, though technicalities were lacking. Nucci et al. [20] evaluated machine learning performances on accuracy, F-measure, and AUC-ROC, though threats to validity existed. Other research is available in [11], [12], [13], [21], and [22].

This paper validates code smell for predicting class change proneness to identify prediction errors. First, two versions of 14 software systems were compared to identify change-prone classes. Datasets were formed by dividing software data into class relations and metrics, including previously used projects and checking for multiple versions. Ten-fold cross-validation divided data into nine training and one test subset. Six algorithms (Naive Bayes, Multilayer Perceptron, LogitBoost, Bagging, Random Forest, and Decision Tree) predicted change proneness using code smell. Predicted values were compared against actual change-prone classes using ROC analysis for true and false positives. Most past research does not use large datasets; some lack experimental analysis, and parameter changes alter results. Evaluation metrics are often limited in prior work. This paper evaluates code smell using ROC curves, sensitivity, specificity, cut-off points, and AUC for improved assessment.

Previous studies, such as Khomh et al. [8] and Gatrell and Counsell [3], showed significant smell-change relations but did not target large datasets, leaving issues like detected vs. manually validated smells, limited sizes, specific smell type analysis, and optimal effect values unresolved. Large datasets are needed as machine learning may be futile without them. No prior work empirically evaluated code smells versus code fault proneness. Most prior works explored only one or two projects. This research uses large support systems like SAP and ERP to guarantee high accuracy. It also provides intrinsic precision effects with high probability, relying on experimentally conducted data from various open-source systems.

This work’s advantages include analyzing the percentage of code components and their effect on change- and fault-proneness across a large set of software projects.

III. MATERIALS AND METHODS

A. DATASETS

The entire process can be divided into three parts:
1) Data acquisition and processing;
2) Change and smell estimation;
3) Analysis using Machine Learning Methods.

1) DATA ACQUISITION AND PROCESSING

The datasets for this study were collected as follows. Firstly, we downloaded two stable releases of each system as listed in Table 1. Pre-processing of datasets included removing all Java files in the versions that were not compatible with the current one. All 14 systems combined had approximately 10000 classes in two versions of each system out of which more than 8200 were left after pre-processing. This essentially means that we are left with around 4100 unique classes spanning over 14 software systems.

2) CHANGE AND SMELL ESTIMATION

In this step, the actual change of a class undergoes in two versions is calculated to obtain the metric values for each class in each system. They are then used to analyze each class for code smell. To calculate the exact change of a class that has gone through in the two stated versions, we used an open-source tool named CLOC to examine two versions of the same file and give as outputs below:

a) Number of Lines that are unchanged.
b) Number of Lines added to the prior version.
c) Number of Lines deleted from the prior version.
d) Number of Lines modified over the two versions.

These outputs are then used to calculate the amount of change as:

Total Change = No. of lines added + No. of lines deleted + 2 ∗ No. of lines modified.

After calculating the exact changes for each class, they are examined for odors of code smell using a commercial tool called Understand (http://www.scitools.com). It is mandatory to estimate metric values for each system and export the results in a comma-separated-value list. Threshold values selected for metrics are then applied and marked for the truth value of each smell in each class. The thresholds used for all metrics are along with the corresponding smell.

IV. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

The effectiveness of code smell metrics in predicting class changes across 14 software versions was evaluated using six machine learning algorithms. Performance was measured using sensitivity, specificity, and AUC. Sensitivity represents the percentage of correctly predicted error classes, while specificity reflects accurately anticipated no-error classes across various cutoff points. AUC quantifies the probability that a randomly selected changing class ranks higher than a non-changing class. Results for each algorithm are presented below.

input: A dataset of 4120 classes from 14 software versions was analyzed to predict class-level change proneness using code smells. Ten-fold cross-validation was used to train and test six machine learning algorithms: Naive Bayes, Multilayer Perceptron, LogitBoost, Bagging, Random Forest, and Decision Tree. Hybrid approaches combine static and dynamic features for Android malware detection.

Kouliaridis et al. [4] introduced Androtomist, an open-source tool with novice and expert modes. Testing on Drebin, Virusshare, and Androzoo datasets showed 100% accuracy on the first two and 91.8% on Androzoo using an ensemble of machine learning classifiers.

Alzaylaee et al. [28] proposed DL-Droid, a deep learning system using dynamic analysis and stateful input generation. Experiments on a dataset of 30,000 apps demonstrated 97.8% accuracy with dynamic features and 99.6% with both dynamic and static features, outperforming state-of-the-the-art approaches.

Lindorfer et al. [33] proposed MARVIN, a hybrid system using features including class structure, certificates, network activity, and permissions. Tested on 135,000 apps and 15,000 malware samples, MARVIN claimed 98.24% accuracy.

Chen et al. [35] proposed StormDroid, a hybrid model using permissions, API calls, sequences, and dynamic behaviors. Tested on approximately 8,000 apps from Google Play and Contagio, StormDroid claimed 93.8% accuracy and improved efficiency by approximately three times compared to single-threaded analysis.

Saracino et al. [34] proposed MADAM, a cross-layer model using static and dynamic features such as system calls, SMS, and app metadata. Tested on datasets from Genome, Contagio, and VirusShare, MADAM claimed 96.6% accuracy with limited battery consumption and low performance overhead.

input: To compute the optimized weights vector βv, a novel best-effort algorithm entitled "Optweights" (see Algorithm 1) is designed to iteratively create βv while satisfying conditions in (14). The algorithm initializes variables using Optweights.Initialization (Algorithm 2). A temporary vector βt is iteratively modified to reach the best possible βv. The vector of actual ratios to be maximized in (14) is denoted by diagonal to maximum ratio (DMR), computed using ComputeRatios(βt, CM). The algorithm works by requesting a specific requested diagonal to maximum ratio (RDMR), initially set to 1 and increased iteratively by RDMRStep. MNcc denotes the maximum obtained number of correct classes (classes satisfying constraints in 14). If the classifier cannot initially detect a specific class or differentiate between two classes, satisfying all conditions in (14) becomes impossible. Therefore, Optweights.Phase1 (Algorithm 3) first requests RDMR set to 1 and computes the number of classes expected to be detected correctly (Ncc). The value of MNcc is assigned to the maximum possible number of correct classes before performing any ratio maximization. At each step, the algorithm updates the obtained weights vector βv and increments RDMR by RDMRStep. For each class ci, the necessary βt(i) is computed to make the ratio for class ci reach RDMR. After finishing the trial to reach RDMR for all classes, the requested ratio for the first class is doubled as it plays the most important role in this classification (differentiating between malicious and normal behaviors). In fact, detecting whether a node is an intruder is considered more important than the type of attack itself. Assuming the system is under attack of class i and the ML model is trying to identify this attack without using any weighting scheme, around aij times the ML model will predict the attack as of class j. When using the weighted scores in (14), the ML model will predict that the attack is of type j* when βj*aij*> βjaij ∀j = 1...n, j≠j*. Therefore, for class i to be detected correctly, the designed weight should satisfy βiaii > βjaij ∀j = 1...n, j≠i. Or, equivalently, βiaii > maxj≠i(βjaij) ⇔ DMR(i) > 1. Thus, the number of correct classes (classes that have a DMR bigger than 1) is given by Ncc = Σi=1N (DMR(i) ≥ 1) (16). However, this is correct only if an attack of type i is predicted aij times (or a linearly proportional number) as of class j. That is, the actual and estimated confusion matrices are very close to each other, which generally happens after a large number of trials. After a relatively large number of trials, the number of correct classes is given by the number of elements of the DMR vector that are bigger than 1. The global maximum number of correct classes is updated. The algorithm stops the search if the new RDMR reduced the actual number of correct classes or if the requested RDMR did not affect much the new DMR. In this case, the algorithm exits the search loop and returns the vector βv that provides the higher DMR without affecting Ncc. In the first phase, the objective was to get a weight vector for which most of the classes satisfy one requested ratio RDMR to guarantee convergence for as many classes as possible. In contrast, in the second phase of the algorithm performed in the function Optweights.Phase2 (Algorithm 4), the objective is to reduce as much as possible the nondiagonal elements for each class ci so that the DMR is maximized for class ci and is not affected by any other class. This is done first by sorting the classes according to the number of times they appeared in TS1 and updating CM and βt accordingly. section: V. EXPERIMENTS — E. Discussion About Stopping Condition
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
We discuss the stopping condition to clarify the optimal threshold μ. We incrementally increased μ from 0.1 to 1.0 in steps of 0.1 on three representative data sets (seed2, cardiotocographyC1, Box H/ACA snoRNA) and measured the distinction between each stopping point and the overall best performance (Fig. 8).

Across all three data sets, the distinction initially decreased sharply and then stabilized as μ increased. This occurs because μ represents the maximum confidence level; as μ rises, more uncertain instances are labeled, forcing the model closer to optimal performance. Although the trend is consistent, the optimal μ at the inflection point varies by data set. For the easy data set (seed2), μ = 0.3 achieves good performance. For the medium data set (cardiotocographyC1), the best threshold is 0.4. For the difficult data set (Box H/ACA snoRNA), μ = 0.6 provides the best tradeoff between classification performance and labeling cost. A small μ exhausts instances near the classification boundary, while a large μ enlarges the margin and includes more instances. Easy data sets, characterized by low imbalance and low overlap, require small thresholds. Difficult data sets, with high imbalance, high overlap, and noise, necessitate larger thresholds to construct effective models. Practitioners should examine the initially labeled instance distribution to allocate an appropriate threshold.

Finally, we wish to discuss the stopping condition to make clear the optimal setting for the threshold μ. We randomly select three representative data sets that reflect the concepts of easy, medium, and difficult. We let μ increase from 0.1 to 1.0 with an increment of 0.1, and then the distinction between the performance of each stopping point and the overall best performance was presented in Fig. 8.

In Fig. 8, we observe an approximately uniform trend on the three different data sets. That is, at the beginning, the distinction always decreased sharply in synchronization with the increase of the threshold μ, and it then gradually became stable. It is easy to understand this phenomenon: the threshold denotes the maximum confidence level. As the threshold increases, more uncertain instances have been labeled, so the classification model must be closer to the optimal performance. Although the trends are similar on the three different data sets, their best thresholds corresponding to the inflection points are totally different. On the easy data set seed2, μ = 0.3 could guarantee to acquire a good enough performance, while on the medium data set cardiotocographyC1, the best threshold is 0.4. For the difficult data set Box H/ACA snoRNA, when the threshold μ equals 0.6, it provides the best tradeoff between the classification performance and labeling expenses. Revisiting Fig. 5, it is not difficult to understand the phenomenon earlier. In Fig. 5, a small threshold means exhausting the instances in a narrow margin surrounding the classification boundary, while a large threshold means enlarging the margin and exhausting more instances. Considering the easy data sets, which have low imbalance ratio and small classification overlapping, a small threshold is enough to guarantee precisely describing the classification boundary. However, for those difficult data sets with a high imbalance ratio, large class overlapping, high noise, and even small disjunctions, we have to assign a large threshold for them to construct excellent enough classification models. In practical applications, the readers are suggested to examine the instance distribution on the initially labeled set, and then allocate an appropriate threshold.

Using the big data platform described in [12], dataset-wide queries were launched to quantify the instances of bad data subtypes BD 1, BD 2.1, BD 2.2, and BD 2.3, as defined in Table 2.

Among the 1.61 × 10¹¹ rows of data in Interconnect A, the first section of Table 3 shows that 21.39% of the rows contain BD 1, which means more than 1/5 of total PMU rows have non-zero status (i.e., the PMU has self-detected issues or specialized settings). Regarding the zero-status (i.e., no self-detected PMU issues or specialized settings) PMU rows, while BD 2.2 issues (rows with non-numerical non-empty values, as defined previously) are negligible (0.07%/(1-21.39%) = 0.09%), roughly 1/3 (24.97%/(1-21.39%) = 31.8%) of zero-status PMU rows have at least 1 unreasonable numerical value; similarly, about 1/3 (24.81%/(1-21.39%) = 31.6%) of zero-status PMU rows present missing value issues. Therefore, bad data accounts for a significant fraction of the data in Interconnect A. Table 3 indicates how at least one instance of BD 1 occurs in all 212 PMUs in the Interconnect A dataset. For this interconnect, Figure 1 shows how the percentage of rows affected by BD1 in each PMU can reach as high as 100%. For 25 of the 212 PMUs – A183, A196, A227, A283, A288, A291, A332, A348, A359, A387, A417, A451, A469, A579, A598, A608, A612, A687, A697, A717, A730, A858, A876, A883, A971 – almost 100% of the rows present zero status, and there is very limited amount of data eligible for event analysis at all. BD 2.1 and BD 2.3 issues occur to 193 out of 212 (91%) PMUs in Interconnect A. Row counts for BD 2.1 and BD 2.3 are very similar; in general, the percentage of rows affected in each PMU vary from 0-85%, and a few PMUs that contain a significant BD 2.1 or 2.3 issues are A189, A268, A412, A441, A639, A842, and A937. BD 2.2 issue occurs to 8 PMUs (<5%) in Interconnect A, and for those 8 PMU affected, the percentage of rows with BD 2.2 are insignificant.

As shown in Table 3, among the 9.3 × 10¹⁰ rows of data in the Interconnect B dataset, only 2.53% of PMU rows have non-zero status values; and with regards to data rows with zero status (97.47%), only a negligible amount of data presents as BD 2.1, 2.2, or BD 2.3 issues. Although overall BD issues are insignificant for Interconnect B as detailed previously, there are 15 PMUs (35% of total PMUs) that present BD 1 issues, and all 45 PMUs present BD 2.1 and BD 2.3 issues to certain extent. In particular, a few PMUs draw our attention. For example, in B635, roughly 100% of the rows present BD 2.1 and BD 2.3 issues, and therefore, there is negligible amount of data can be used for further analysis. In another instance, the BD 1 issue is significant for B209, B850, and B864, more than 40% of rows need be properly filtered out prior to application of machine learning or data analytics algorithms.

Table 3 also indicates that for Interconnect C, a majority (97.99%) of the 2.4 × 10¹¹ PMU rows have zero-value status, among which BD 2.1 and BD 2.3 issues are dominating and the total percentage of affected rows falls between (10.5% and 21.0%). As shown in the last four rows of Table 3, it is observed that of all 188 PMUs in Interconnect C, 177 (94%) present a BD 1 issue, more than 50% presents BD 2.1 or BD 2.3 issues, and 10% present a BD 2.2 issue. Figure 3 shows that a few PMUs merit special attention: for instance, certain PMUs, such as C123, C141, C232, C294, C320, C484, and C733, have very significant quantities of BD 2.1 or BD 2.3, with almost 100% rows affected, and for those PMUs there is very limited data left for meaningful application of machine learning or data analytics. In addition, about 50% of data rows in C620 have a BD 1 issue (non-zero status).

Comparing the bad data statistics for all three datasets, it can be concluded that the overall quantity of bad data ranges widely among three FOA 1861 interconnects, and is the most severe for the Interconnect A dataset, followed by Interconnect C dataset, and then Interconnect B dataset. Comparing different bad data categories across all three interconnects, it is noticed that BD 1 (non-zero status issue), BD 2.1 (unreasonable numerical value issue), and BD 2.3 (missing value issues) are the major bad data issues reported in the training dataset, while BD 2.2 (non-numerical non-empty value issue) is negligible in the given training dataset. The results of this section provide some insight into the types of bad data issues observed through the United States PMU network and underscore the strong need for bad data filtering prior to application data analytics and machine learning algorithms.

It should be noted that the BD 1 definition introduced in Subsection II.A may be unfairly broad, and that there may be instances in which the measurements could still be considered to be ‘good data’ even if one or more flags in the status variable are set high. It is therefore worth considering a narrower definition of BD 1 defined only by bits 13, 14 and 15 of the status variable. As stated in [16], bit 13 indicates a loss-of-synchronism with the time reference, bit 14 indicates a PMU error or test mode, and bit 15 indicates a PMU error with no information about the integrity of the measurement—these may be considered flags associated with the ‘most egregious’ self-reported data quality conditions. If BD 1 were to be redefined to denote status variable entries in which only these bit 13, 14 and/or 15 is set to 1 (with all other ‘less egregious’ flags ignored), the BD 1 percentages would be only 1.0%, 2.1%, and 0.19% for Interconnects A, B, and C, respectively, instead of the 21.39%, 2.53%, and 2.0% reported in Table 3: an order of magnitude reduction in BD 1 for Interconnects A and C, but only a small reduction for Interconnect B.

Note that any redefinition of BD 1 may also modify the BD 2.1 to 2.3 counts, since BD 2.1 to 2.3 were defined to be mutually exclusive from BD 1. However, the BD 1 bad data counts calculated using the original, broader version of the BD 1 definition (i.e., the definition in Section II.A and in Table 2, which is used to generate the figures of this section) only account for 21.39% of the measurements from Interconnect A, and far less for Interconnects B and C. Therefore, if the narrower definition of BD 1 were used, and BD 2.1 to 2.3 were subsequently applied to the expanded number of potentially ‘good’ measurements that were no longer pre-emptively excluded as BD 1, it is not anticipated that the quantities of BD 2.1 to 2.3 bad data entry counts would change very much.

Due to the unique circumstances surrounding the assembly and provision of the synchrophasor datasets, the FOA 1861 project teams were only provided a limited understanding of the origin of the raw synchrophasor datasets prior to their distribution by the DOE. Consequently, FOA 1861 project teams were not provided detailed information regarding the practices of the data providers that may provide valuable insight into the data quality variation among the three interconnects. This variation may be attributed to factors such as PMU hardware procurement and commissioning practices, equipment management or maintenance practices, PMU data archival practices, and/or regulatory factors. While there were opportunities to discuss some of these details with several of the individual data providers during the FOA 1861 program, the identity and geographic location of the data providers was deliberately obfuscated in order to protect their privacy, and it was not possible to associate information obtained from any of the data providers with any specific interconnect. Consequently, at this time, it is not easy to speculate on the root cause of the variation of data quality between the three interconnects.

ABSTRACT This project presents an intelligent Alpha Factor Research System for stock market trading
that combines machine learning, deep learning, and explainable AI to discover and evaluate profitable
trading signals. Conventional approaches based on static technical indicators such as RSI, MACD, and
Bollinger Bands often lack adaptability and transparency when market conditions evolve. The proposed
system collects S&P 500 stock data, generates multiple technical indicators, and applies machine learning
models—specifically Random Forest and XGBoost—to rank alpha factors according to their predictive
importance. Deep learning techniques, including Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Autoencoders,
are used to uncover latent and orthogonal alpha signals that may not be directly visible through traditional
indicators. In addition to integrating established ML and XAI components, this work introduces a Dynamic
Latent Alpha Composition (DLAC) algorithm that systematically constructs composite alpha factors by
combining raw technical indicators with latent representations derived from PCA and Autoencoders. The
DLAC framework iteratively generates candidate factors through nonlinear transformations and interaction
terms, then filters them using SHAP-based importance scores and out-of-sample backtesting metrics such
as the Sharpe ratio and drawdown stability. This process produces a compact library of composite alpha
signals that capture higher-order market relationships beyond traditional feature-ranking pipelines. Model

III. METHODOLOGY — D. MODEL DEVELOPMENT

The model development phase established the computational foundation of the proposed Alpha Factor Research System. The design combined supervised and unsupervised learning paradigms to identify, rank, and interpret predictive alpha factors derived from the S&P 500 dataset. The implementation was performed using Python 3.10 and key analytical libraries such as scikit-learn 1.3, XGBoost 2.0, TensorFlow 2.13, and SHAP 0.42. All experiments were executed on a workstation with an Intel i7 CPU, 16 GB RAM, and an NVIDIA GTX GPU to support deep learning operations.

1) DATA PREPARATION AND TARGET CONSTRUCTION

Following feature engineering, data were structured into a supervised learning format. Each observation contained engineered technical indicators and derived features, while the target variable represented the next-day price movement direction. The label assignment was based on the difference between consecutive closing prices: y_t = 1 if (Close_{t+1} − Close_t) > 0, else 0 (Eq. 8). This binary formulation enabled classification models to predict upward or downward stock movements. The dataset was partitioned chronologically into 70% training, 20% validation, and 10% testing subsets to preserve temporal integrity. To prevent look-ahead bias, all preprocessing steps, including feature scaling, were fitted exclusively on the training dataset and subsequently applied to the validation and test sets without refitting. Standardization and normalization were applied to all input variables to guarantee balanced model convergence. A rolling-window time-series validation procedure was adopted. In this setup, the model was trained on an initial historical window and evaluated on the subsequent period, after which the training window was advanced forward in time, and the model was retrained for the entire dataset to allow for realistic chronological evaluation with predictions based solely on past information.

Next-day price direction was chosen as the target variable since short-horizon directional forecasting is extensively applied in high-frequency trading systems to provide frequent trading signals and to investigate model response in market dynamics. Although next-day returns are inherently noisy, this target formulation is intentionally selected to stress-test the model’s ability to extract meaningful signals under low signal-to-noise conditions, which is a more conservative and realistic evaluation setting. Even though short-term returns may be noisy, this work aims to assess whether machine learning models can capture immediate market momentum and micro-patterns that influence daily trading decisions. The study of longer-horizon targets, such as multi-day forward returns, is also a promising direction for future work.

The input to this module comprises the high-importance alpha factors identified by the ensemble models. To capture latent market structures beyond linear correlations, unsupervised feature extraction approaches were applied. where X represents the standardized feature matrix, W is the eigenvector matrix of the covariance of X, and Z is the transformed principal component space. Components explaining up to 95% of total variance were retained to ensure dimensional efficiency. Similarly, the PCA transformation and Autoencoder training were performed only on the training window, and the learned transformations were applied to subsequent validation and testing periods to preserve temporal causality and avoid information leakage.

In parallel, a deep learning-based Autoencoder network was trained to reveal nonlinear hidden representations of alpha signals. An encoder that compresses the input into a latent vector and a decoder that reconstructs the original input make up the autoencoder. The training objective minimizes reconstruction error:

L_{AE} = (1/n) Σ_{i=1}^{n} (x_i − x̂_i)^2, (12)

where x_i and x̂_i denote the input and reconstructed outputs, respectively. The Autoencoder structure was developed as a symmetric feedforward neural network design to learn latent representations of the input feature space. The encoder was a 3-layer fully connected network with 64, 32, and 16 neurons, respectively, followed by a latent representation layer of size 8, while the decoder was symmetric to this configuration to reconstruct the input features. In the hidden layers, the activation functions were Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) with the output layer having a linear activation. Then trained the model with the Adam optimizer (learning rate = 0.001) and mean squared error (MSE) reconstruction loss. The Autoencoder was trained until the validation reconstruction loss stabilized, with early stopping applied using a patience of 10 epochs to prevent overfitting. The quality of latent representations was validated by measuring reconstruction error on the held-out test set and confirming that the latent embeddings retained sufficient variance, with the top latent dimensions collectively explaining over 85% of the input feature variance. Training was done for 50 epochs with a batch size of 32 to gain stable convergence of latent factor representations. The latent embeddings generated by the encoder were subsequently integrated with the original features, allowing the downstream models to leverage both explicit and implicit trading signals.

4) DYNAMIC LATENT ALPHA COMPOSITION (DLAC) ALGORITHM

While traditional alpha-factor frameworks mainly rely on predefined technical indicators, this study introduces a Dynamic Latent Alpha Composition (DLAC) algorithm to systematically construct composite alpha factors by combining observable indicators with latent market representations. The goal of DLAC is to move beyond simple feature ranking and instead generate new signals that capture higher-order relationships within financial data. The novelty of DLAC lies not in its individual components but in their systematic integration — combining latent signal extraction, nonlinear feature composition, SHAP-based importance filtering, and backtesting validation into a single unified and iterative alpha discovery pipeline, which has not been previously formalized in quantitative trading literature.

Let X_t ∈ R^d represent the vector of engineered technical indicators at time t, and let Z_t ∈ R^k denote latent representations obtained from PCA and Autoencoder models. These are combined to form an extended feature space:

X̃_t = [X_t, Z_t] (13)

The DLAC framework then performs structured factor discovery through four sequential stages:

• Candidate Factor Generation: The extended feature set X̃_t is transformed into a pool of candidate alpha factors using nonlinear transformations, indicator interactions, ratios, rolling aggregates, and volatility-conditioned weighting schemes. This step allows the system to explore complex relationships between market variables.

• Composite Factor Construction: Each candidate factor is represented as a transformation function φ_j(X̃_t) = g_j(X̃_t) (14) where g_j(·) denotes transformation operators such as multiplication, normalization, smoothing, or interaction between indicators and latent features.

• Importance-Driven Selection: Random Forest and XGBoost models are trained on the candidate factor library. SHAP values are then computed to estimate the global contribution of each composite factor to prediction outcomes. Factors with low importance scores are discarded to retain only the most informative signals.

• Backtesting-Based Validation: The remaining candidate factors are evaluated using rolling-window backtesting. Only factors that demonstrate improved out-of-sample Sharpe ratio and stable drawdown behaviour are retained for the final model training stage.

The resulting DLAC-derived factors are integrated with the original feature set and supplied to the ensemble learning models for prediction. Figure 2 presents the proposed DLAC Alpha Factor Research Framework, illustrating the end-to-end workflow of the DLAC methodology. As summarized in Algorithm 1, the DLAC procedure combines latent representations, nonlinear feature interactions, and performance-based selection to identify informative composite alpha signals that are not directly observable through traditional indicator-based methods.

5) HYPERPARAMETER OPTIMIZATION AND TRAINING STRATEGY

This stage takes the enriched feature set generated by PCA, Autoencoder-based latent extraction, and the DLAC-generated composite factors as input. All models received rigorous hyperparameter adjustment to achieve a trade-off between bias and variance. Five-fold time-series cross-validation was used to tune hyperparameters for ensemble models using grid and randomized search approaches. To avoid overfitting, early halting and dropout regularization (rate = 0.2) were applied to deep learning models. The training technique uses adaptive learning rate scheduling to accelerate convergence. The final configuration of each model was selected based on validation performance and interpretability, assuring robustness and reproducibility across several experimental runs.

6) EXPLAINABILITY AND MODEL TRANSPARENCY

The final trained predictive models and selected features are provided as input to this stage, which produces global and local interpretability quantification measures of the contribution of each feature to the trading decisions. Model interpretability was achieved by the integration of Explainable AI (XAI) frameworks, notably SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) and LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations). SHAP values quantify the marginal contribution of each feature to the model’s prediction by computing Shapley values from cooperative game theory:

This approach provides both global and local interpretability, enabling analysts to trace how various factors influence buy/sell choices. LIME complements this approach by approximating the complicated model locally with a linear surrogate, providing intuitive presentation of factor effects for specific cases. These XAI technologies bridged the gap between interpretability and prediction performance in quantitative finance by ensuring that the produced models remained clear and explainable.

To evaluate the contribution of the proposed Dynamic Latent Alpha Composition (DLAC) algorithm, an ablation study was conducted comparing two configurations of the system. The first configuration used only traditional technical indicators and price–volume features, while the second configuration incorporated the DLAC-generated composite alpha factors derived from latent representations and nonlinear feature interactions.

Both configurations were trained using the same ensemble learning framework to ensure a fair comparison. The experimental results indicate that incorporating DLAC-derived factors improves predictive performance and enhances risk-adjusted trading outcomes. In particular, the inclusion of DLAC factors increases classification accuracy and improves the Sharpe ratio while maintaining stable drawdown characteristics.

Table 6 presents the ablation results comparing the baseline model with and without the DLAC-generated composite alpha factors. The results indicate that incorporating DLAC-derived features leads to improvements in both predictive accuracy and risk-adjusted trading performance. The findings further suggest that the DLAC algorithm captures higher-order market relationships that are not directly observable through traditional indicator-based approaches, thereby providing additional predictive signals that enhance the overall trading strategy.

The study introduced an intelligent, data-driven Alpha Factor Research System combining explainable AI, deep learning, and machine learning to automate factor discovery and assessment in quantitative trading. It aimed to overcome limitations of traditional rule-based systems using adaptable, interpretable, and performance-optimized models. The architecture combined Random Forest and XGBoost for factor ranking, Autoencoder and PCA for latent signal extraction, and SHAP and LIME for interpretability. The major purpose was to solve the constraints of traditional rule-based trading systems by employing adaptable, interpretable, and performance-optimized models capable of detecting hidden market patterns. The proposed architecture featured a combination of Random Forest and XGBoost for factor ranking, Autoencoder and PCA for latent signal extraction, and SHAP and LIME for interpretability. Experimental evaluation on S&P 500 financial sector data proved the usefulness of the approach in both prediction accuracy and risk-adjusted profitability. In comparison to baseline models, the Ensemble model improved the Sharpe ratio by 0.24 and attained a classification accuracy of 87%, demonstrating its higher predictive abilities. Future work will focus on extending the system to real-time factor updates using streaming data and reinforcement learning frameworks. Additionally, including macroeconomic and sentiment-based variables could further extend the alpha signal library. Exercises are used in rehabilitation programs, with difficulty ranging from easy to hard [12], [13]. Balance exercises vary stance, visual inputs, standing surface, and head motion [12]. In clinics, physical therapists (PTs) select and customize exercises for each individual [12]. Individuals typically refer to prior clinic instructions or paper-based instructions when exercising at home [14]. However, unsupervised in-home training is less effective than in-clinic training and does not lead to the same functional outcome improvements [15]–[17].

To improve in-home training effectiveness, researchers have introduced remote supervision, sensory augmentation, and semi-supervision [18], [19]. Telerehabilitation delivers rehabilitation via telecommunication networks [18]. Cikajlo et al. [20] showed that telerehabilitation with virtual reality tasks led to balance improvements similar to conventional in-clinic training for people with stroke. However, telerehabilitation generally requires video conference interactions for the duration of training, resulting in longer PT consultation times [21]. Video game–based in-home balance training improved clinical measures after a minimum of five weeks [22]–[25]. Kinetic or kinematic data are collected using balance platforms (e.g., Wii Fit) or video cameras with depth sensors (e.g., Kinect) and a display screen to provide visual cues. However, visual cues are ineffective for exercises performed with eyes closed or head movements. Additionally, platforms like the Wii Fit constrain stance positions. Bao et al. [13] demonstrated improvements in clinical balance outcomes using a semi-supervised home training protocol with vibrotactile sensory augmentation; both the experimental group receiving augmentation and the unaided control group showed significant improvements. PTs remotely determined exercise progression by reviewing participant data weekly and prescribing exercises based on step-outs and self-assessments on a 1-5 scale. However, participant self-assessments may not align with PT assessments [26], [27]. This misalignment can affect exercise appropriateness and limit program effectiveness.

Appropriate exercise progression is critical for achieving balance improvements in both clinic- and home-based settings [12]. The extent to which the expert is “in the loop” diminishes as the paradigm shifts from telerehabilitation to semi-supervised training [28]. Machine learning (ML) techniques could further support home-based balance rehabilitation. Researchers have demonstrated the utility of ML in supporting clinical gait assessments based on body motion [29]–[35]. Using motion data from wearable sensors, ML techniques have been leveraged to identify activity [29], mine gait patterns [30], and classify gait disorders [31]–[34]. For example, Begg et al. [
