section: II. LITERATURE REVIEW — C. GA and ML Integration for Trafﬁc Optimisation
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Previous research has focused on improving genetic algorithms (GAs) or machine learning (ML) frameworks separately for traffic control. Some integrated approaches exist, but mostly emphasize one paradigm. Authors in [33] used GAs for feature selection and SVMs for traffic network anomaly detection, though SVMs are limited across varying data streams. Authors in [34] used GA for feature selection and parameter optimization in regression models for software effort estimation, focusing on improving ML rather than the reverse. Authors in [35] explored how inductive machine learning can guide evolutionary algorithm breeding using decision trees to identify good and bad individuals; this study is similar but uses predefined populations, whereas this work generates populations from traffic simulation modeling to learn phase duration patterns. Authors in [36] used ML to replace simulation in engine design to reduce computation time; however, the complexity of this traffic problem stems from high stochastic behavior and infinite signal control plan combinations, requiring extensive training data. To the best of the authors' knowledge, no current work combines traffic simulation modeling, GA optimization, and ML tuning for traffic congestion management. The major contribution lies at the border of cross-disciplinary fields by combining data science approaches with traffic modeling and optimization. The primary benefit is speeding up computational times of traffic simulation modeling and reducing the search space of individuals, preventing the waste of significant resources analyzing simulation outputs.
output:

improving the GA or the ML frameworks for various trafﬁc
control approaches, some have proposed integrated approaches

Support Vector Machines to detect trafﬁc network anomalies.

a probabilistic model building GA (PMBGA), an estimation

algorithms (UMDA), a compact genetic algorithm (cGA) and

none of the current works have proposed so far a combination

major contribution lies at the border of cross disciplinary ﬁelds

section: II. LITERATURE REVIEW — D. Contribution Summary
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Our research addresses three perspectives. From a genetic algorithm (GA) viewpoint, the integrated approach achieves significant computational time savings and high acceleration in the breeding process by predicting fitness values from prior traffic simulation runs, thereby avoiding unnecessary model executions and pre-filtering high-performing individuals based on phase duration. From a machine learning (ML) perspective, a key literature gap exists as most models train agents to control signals under normal conditions; this work instead optimizes signal coordination to reroute vehicles around incident locations, accurately predicting near-future network performance using time-series data that includes signal changes and capacity drops. Finally, from a GA and ML integration perspective, this framework—combining these methods with microscopic simulation—has not been previously applied to traffic signal optimization. We believe learning from prior incident conditions allows efficient optimization and adjustment without the need to extensively test infinite phase durations.
output:
Our research contribution in this paper follows three main
perspectives:
From a GA perspective, the beneﬁt of using our integrated
approach is achieved in the signiﬁcant computational time
saving and in the high acceleration which is recorded in
the breeding process by predicting the ﬁtness value for each
individual from previous trafﬁc simulation runs. This avoids
not only running unnecessary trafﬁc simulation models which
would prove to be not efﬁcient enough, but also ﬁltering in
advance the best performing individuals (in our case phase
duration) that have previously given better results.
From an ML perspective, the major research gap in the
current literature is that most ML models are aiming at training
agents to control the trafﬁc signals based on the vehicles
of each approach of the intersection under normal trafﬁc
conditions. There is currently no research for trafﬁc signal
control optimization using ML approaches applied under traf-
ﬁc incident conditions. Our models consider the coordination
of the trafﬁc signals to reroute the vehicles around the incident
location. To summarize, previous trafﬁc signal control methods
using ML barely discussed the capability of solving the sudden
capacity drop problem caused by trafﬁc incidents. In all cases,
ML models are used for making real-time decisions which may
be hard to judge in terms of their reliability and applicability.
In this paper, ML modelling is used for performance (ﬁtness
value) predicting instead of making decisions directly. We use
various ML models to process the time series data of the trafﬁc
status under all known trafﬁc conditions including the changes
in the trafﬁc signal and the capacity drop at the time of the
reported accident. Finally, we accurately predict the network
performance in the near future.
From a GA and ML integration perspective, to the best
of our knowledge, there is no research using this framework
for trafﬁc signal optimization in the literature so far, and
even more together with trafﬁc simulation modelling at a
microscopic level. The dynamic nature of trafﬁc can be hard
to optimize especially under disruption conditions. Our belief
is that learning from previous incident conditions, we can
optimize and adjust trafﬁc more efﬁciently without the need
to expansively test inﬁnite phase durations of simply use a
restricted subset of possibilities.

input: The proposed model focuses on the response and clearance phases of traffic incidents, assuming prior detection and verification. The problem is formulated on a pre-determined affected road network to minimize total vehicle travel time. The network is defined by a set of links (A) and origin-destination pairs (W). Route flows (f_{w,r}) and link flows (v_a) are modeled as variables. Travel time on each link (t_a) is a function of link flow (v_a) and the link green split (λ_a). The objective function minimizes the integral of travel time with respect to link flow. Flow conservation is enforced such that the sum of route flows equals the origin-destination demand (D_w), and route flows link to link flows via a usage indicator (σ_{w,a,r}). A capacity constraint links link flow to capacity and green split (v_a ≤ λ_a S_a). Flows are non-negative. The total travel time is the objective to be minimized.

This paper is basically focused on the modeling of traffic management and control after an incident has been confirmed and reported by TMC. To simplify the case study, we assume that the incident was previously detected, verified and the duration of the incident clearance was predicted. In addition, the severity of the incident is also reported as an indication of the number of lanes affected. Last but not least, the incident affected area is determined using previous studies. Recently, Pan et al. [37] studied the spatial-temporal impact of traffic incidents based on archived data using advanced sensors and came up with the incident impacted area and the delay occurrence prediction in a road network. The affected area normally contains all the surrounding network which experiences the congestion caused by the incident and it is generally time-dependent to the reported location of the incident.

The problem we are trying to solve is how to optimize the traffic control plan around the incident location, in order to minimize the impact of the incident in terms of vehicle total travel time. III. METHODOLOGY — B. The Definition of Link Green Split

In this paper, the definition of “link green split” (λa) is the same as the one in the study of Yang and Yagar [38], which is the amount of green time granted for a link (link a) in a signalized intersection. As for Smith and Van Vuren [39], green time is divided into: phase green time and link green time. A phase is defined as a maximal set of compatible approaches in an intersection. Therefore, the phase green time is the green time of certain phase in a cycle in a signalized intersection. The link green time is the green time granted for a link by all the corresponding phases in a cycle of a signalized intersection.

Let jk be the proportion of green time for which the kth phase at junction j, therefore we can call jk a “phase green split”. The allocation of green time to all phases at a junction determines the green time of each link entering that junction, therefore for each link a, the “link green split” (λa) is the summation of all those phase green splits (jk) for which phase k at junction j contains the movement of link a, or:

λa = Σ jk

phases S jk contain link a

(6)

To be clear, for each junction j, the sum (over k) of “phase green split” jk will be 1:

Σ jk = 1.

(7)

C. Assumptions

In this paper, we assume that the O-D demands are predefined and fixed for the duration of our analysis. We use the traffic assignment model to get the link traffic flows which depend on link cost functions and O-D demands. Therefore, we can get deterministic link flows.

In Equation 7, we assume that the cycle loss time is included in each green time of an intersection, so we didn’t use a symbol to represent the cycle loss time. In addition, we assume that the amber (yellow) time for each phase is considered as the green time. In conclusion, the λa in this paper is the “link green split” other than the “phase green split”. In addition, the link travel time function (or cost function) is fixed for all links in the investigated road network which only depends on the link flow and the “link green split”. Therefore, the only parameter we try to optimize for each link is the “link green split” λa.

For traffic signals in the network, we assume that each phase of a cycle grants green to fixed movements. The cycle length and the order of phases in a cycle are fixed. Only the duration of each phase is tunable. The duration of all phases in all signalized intersections are actually the decision variables for the optimization problem.

In the first toy network, all the roads have two lanes and we simulate an incident affecting one of the two lanes at one location. We assume that all similar accidents have the same impact on any two-lane road sections in our network. The second network respects real world lane configuration and will be provided in Section VII.

The introduction of "link green split" creates an optimization problem for traffic signal timing due to its direct relationship with "phase green split" in Equations 6 and 7. The problem is transformed into optimizing traffic signal timing within a road network.

Data input requires: O-D configuration, O-D demand table, network configuration, link detail table (free-flow travel time, speed limit, capacity, lanes), and traffic signal configuration (signalized nodes, phases, cycle time, timings, phase green splits, and links per phase).

Optimization steps:
1. Import O-D configuration, demand, network configuration, link details, and signal configuration into a traffic simulation model.
2. Generate all possible fixed-time signal plans for all network nodes. Only phase duration varies; phase sequence and cycle length are fixed. A plan with n intersections is represented as [[p_{11}...p_{14}], [p_{21}...p_{24}], ..., [p_{n1}...p_{n4}]].
3. For each plan, update "link green split" using Equation 6: total green time per link divided by cycle length.
4. For each plan, run the Aimsun micro-simulation model to obtain total travel time (defined in Equation 1).
5. Identify the minimal total travel time and corresponding optimal signal plan across all evaluated plans.
6. Output the optimal signal plan.

3. Fitness Function Calculation: For each individual, the fitness function is calculated by decoding chromosomes to phase durations, updating signal timing, and running a microsimulation model to obtain total network travel time. The fitness value is the reciprocal of this travel time. Simulation was performed using Aimsun.

4. Reach Maximum Iterations?: Check if the maximum number of generations has been reached; if not, proceed to subsequent steps.

5. Tournament: Select two parents from the last generation. Randomly pick two chromosomes from the population and compare their fitness values; the higher-valued chromosome wins and is kept as a parent.

6. Crossover: Two parents are selected via the tournament module. Crossover occurs at a preset probability. For each child, a random inherent index $x_{inherent} \in (0,1)$ is selected. The child chromosome is calculated using Equation 9: Child = Father $\times$ $x_{inherent}$ + Mother $\times$ (1 − $x_{inherent}$).

7. Mutation: The mutation function alters children chromosomes at a preset probability. Only phases within a single intersection are mutated to maintain cycle time. For a child with chromosome [p11, p12, ..., pn4], randomly select intersection $u$, two phases $v$ and $w$ from $u$, and variation $Var \in (0, p_{uv})$. New durations are $p'_{uv} = p_{uv} - Var$ and $p_{uw} = p_{uw} + Var$. Other phase durations remain unchanged.

8. GA Optimization: Proceed to the next generation by repeating step 2 until the stopping criteria (maximal generations) is reached.

F. BGA-ML: The proposed boosted genetic algorithm integrates a machine learning component to reduce state space search and predict likely phase durations. The ML model is trained offline and the BGA-ML process launches online upon an accident report. The ML component predicts total network travel time to replace traffic simulation, reducing computational time. The framework was tested on a limited dataset involving a specific capacity drop incident. Data was formatted into a Python data frame; important features were selected for model training. Four regression models were tested: GBDT, XGBT, Random Forest, and Linear Regression. Model performance was evaluated using MAE, RMSE, R², and MAPE. Hyper-parameters were tuned using five-fold cross-validation.

3. Fitness Function Calculation: for each individual we calculate the fitness function by decoding the chromosomes to phase durations, updating the traffic signal timing according to the chromosome and running a micro-simulation model of the network for static user equilibrium. We used Aimsun as our simulation tool to generate the fitness function. Within this function, we first call the Aimsun traffic simulation model to assign the preset OD demand to the network and then run a microscopic stochastic route choice model to obtain the total travel time recorded in the network. At last we use the reverse of the total travel time as the fitness value.

4. ‘Reach the Maximum Number of Iterations?’: this module checks if the maximum number of generations has been reached; if not, it proceeds to the following steps.

5. “Tournament”: This module is used in order to obtain two parents from the last generation as a preparation for the next generation. In this module, we randomly select two chromosomes from the population, followed by a tournament between these two chromosomes and comparing their fitness function values. Higher valued chromosome will win this tournament and we keep the winner as one of the parents.

6. “Crossover”: Two chromosomes are selected using the “tournament” module, and the crossover happens under a preset probability (called probability of crossover. For each child, an inherent index x_inherent is randomly selected as a float which is in the range of (0, 1). Then the child’s chromosome is calculated as per Equation 9.

Child = Father × x_inherent + Mother × (1 − x_inherent) (9)

7. “Mutation”: the Mutation function changes the chromosome in children in a preset probability (called probability of mutation). In this application, the mutation function only mutates between phases within one intersection. The reason is to maintain the cycle time in each intersection. For example, one child has a chromosome of:

[p11, p12, p13, p14, p21, p22, p23, p24, …, pn1, pn2, pn3, pn4]

We then randomly select: a) an intersection u b) two phases v and w from this intersection and c) the variation (Var) within the range of (0, p_uv). The new duration of phases v and w are calculated as: p'_uv = p_uv − Var, p_uw = p_uw + Var. The rest of the phase durations of this child remain the same.

8. “GA Optimization”: we continue to the next generation by going to step 2 until the stopping criteria has been reached (in our case the hyper tuned maximal number of generations has been reached).

F. BGA-ML

The new proposed boosted genetic algorithm in this paper makes use of the GA structure presented in the previous section and adds the machine learning component in parallel, as presented in Figure 2. The machine learning part is trained offline and the BGA-ML process will be launched online whenever there is a reported accident. The following steps describe how the machine learning parts are interconnecting with the GA parts with the purpose of reducing the state space search and predicting the most likely phase duration to be chosen based on previous trained data sets. The biggest advantage of this approach is reducing the time that genetic algorithms spend in creating the initial and subsequent populations, and to learn from previous iterations in the past which were the best choices that met the optimization criteria, instead of always starting from random and new combinations which need intensive simulations to be run multiple times.

1) Optimization Process: Compared to the previous optimization approach in the GA algorithm, here the ML model will replace the traffic simulation; therefore it will have the same role as the traffic simulation which is to produce (more specifically to predict) the total travel time for different scenarios. This helps to reduce the computational time taken by running the traffic simulation for each new phase combination that the GA generates.

2) BGA-ML Framework: In this paper, we focus on the proof of concept of the BGA-ML framework applied on a limited data set of a possible traffic accident in our two traffic networks (one synthetic and one real). More specifically, we use the data generated by various simulation runs in the GA experiments in which only the selected incident is introduced and the ML model is trained with the specific capacity drop caused by this incident. The details of the incident will be described in the Section IV.

Note that the framework can be further extended and trained with a larger data set and random traffic disruptions. One possibility is to divide the big network into small sub-networks with similar characteristics. Other solutions can be clustering the road sections with similar macroscopic fundamental diagram (MFD). Therefore, further research will need to consider clustering of regions/road sections/sub-networks that have similar characteristics (this is an extension which we aim for in the future).

After the collection of the output data from previous simulation runs, we process and format it into a new data frame in Python, in order to build the features needed to train the machine learning models. Furthermore, we select the most important features that will be used for ML training and testing as detailed in the next sub-section “Feature Generation”.

Lastly, we apply different regression models to the training data set and validate them using a set of various performance metrics as detailed in Section III-F.5. By doing multiple tests over the performance of each ML model under different parameter variations, we will determine the best regression model for our problem with its best hyper-tuned parameters.

3) Feature Generation: As previously indicated, we record the output data while running the original GA using the traffic simulation with a traffic incident in one of the links of the network and use it as the training data set of our ML models. It’s very important to keep the training data set consistent with the GA mechanism to ensure the compatibility between the ML and the GA integrated optimization framework.

The ML models are trained to predict the total network travel time by using the following features:

• the traffic state of the network: in this paper, we simulate the incident for one hour simulation and output the total travel time for the one-hour period, therefore, we recorded profiled traffic status at each 10-minute time interval. Key features recorded are: the section capacity (considering the capacity drop after the incident), the section flow and the section speed.

Similarly, we record these features for each link at each ten minute period in the synthetic network. For the real network we recorded the feature every 5 minute to have a higher data granularity. To summarize, we collect a total of 72 links × 3 feature/link = 216 features.

• the traffic signal plan of the signalized intersections: this is the same as the decision variable in GA which is a vector of all phase durations for all signalized intersections. In this network, there are 4 signalized intersections, and each intersection has 4 phases, therefore we record 16 features which represent the signal plans.

Overall, after creating the feature matrix we have obtained a total of 232 columns, and 9743 data records to be used for the model training, validation and testing.

4) The Regression Models: Choosing the best fitted regression model that can be used for the double-layer optimization framework is not a trivial task and before making any decision, we used four different regression models including: Gradient Boosting Decision Tree (GBDT), Extreme-Gradient Boosted Decision Tree (XGBT), Random Forest (RF) and Linear Regression (LR). GBDT is an refined machine learning technique based on Decision Trees (DT) [41]–[44]. Boosting can be interpreted as an optimization algorithm on a suitable cost function [45] while the DT is a decision support tool which contains a tree-like structure and have been used extensively for various prediction approaches in either classification or regression problems. In a typical DT, each node that is inside the tree represents a decision making procedure, each branch represents the outcome of the decision making, and each leaf node represents a class label. The paths from root to the leafs represent the classification rules or the prediction path.

XGBT is a enhanced version of GBDT [46] by introducing a regularization parameter in the learning objective function (to control over-fitting); it also introduces a sparsity awareness algorithm for parallel tree learning and has a better support for multi-core processing (this makes it very appealing for real-time applications. Only recently they have started to gain more popularity and be applied successfully, for example, for incident duration classification or regression (see [47]).

RF is an ensemble learning method which constructs a multitude of DTs at training time and outputs the class that appears most often in classification or the mean prediction of the individual trees in regression [48], [49].

LR is a linear approach to modelling the relationship between a dependent variable and one or more independent variables; it is taken here as a baseline of the prediction outcome validation for more advanced machine learning models cited earlier.

The above mentioned ML models have been tested under various conditions to compare and evaluate the best performing model. The comparison and results are further discussed in Section IV-D with an emphasis on GBDT and XGBT, as these were the best performing models.

5) Performance Metrics: In order to compare the performance of each regression model and evaluate their accuracy and performance, we considered several performance metrics such as: the Mean Absolute Error (MAE), the Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), R Squared (R2), Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE). MAE is a measure of difference between two continuous variables calculated as:

MAE = 
∑_{i=1}^{n} |y_i − x_i|

∑_{i=1}^{n} |e_i|

where x_i is the prediction and y_i is the true value, therefore the absolute errors is |e_i| = |y_i − x_i|.

RMSE is an estimator which measures the average of squares of the errors and it’s calculated as:

RMSE = 
√( 1/n ∑_{i=1}^{n} (x_i − y_i)^2 )

where the squared errors is (x_i − y_i)^2.

R2 is the proportion of variance in the dependent variable that is predictable from the independent variable(s). The R2 provides a measure of how well observed outcomes are replicated by the model based on the proportion of total variation of outcomes.

MAPE is a measure of prediction accuracy of a forecasting method which usually expresses accuracy as a percentage as indicated below:

MAPE = 100%

6) Hyper-Parameter Tuning: The chosen machine learning algorithms have a set of hyper-parameters, which are parameters related to the internal design of the algorithm that cannot be fit from the training data. In order to fine tune the dozens of parameters for each regression model that we have been using in our optimization framework, we perform a five-fold cross-validation (5CV) method when deciding the training and testing data sets. First, we randomly divide our whole data set into five folds which have the same size. Then we choose 4 folds as the training data set and use the remaining 1 fold as the testing data set. We will shuffle the folds five times and each fold serves as a test data set once. For each regression, we tune the hyperparameters on each training data set, at each learning fold using various random combinations, evaluated using the 5CV. A detailed discussion on all settings is further provided in Section IV-C of the Case Study analysis.

When training the regression models, the average values of all performance metrics are recorded for further comparison.

section: IV. CASE STUDY — C. GA Parameter Tuning
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
The genetic algorithm requires four parameters: population size, maximum generations, crossover probability, and mutation probability. These were tuned with computational time in mind.

For the pilot experiment, four population size and generation combinations were tested. Results show that population sizes of 75 and 100 individuals converge simultaneously after the 20th generation, while a size of 50 converges slower initially. A size of 25 is the slowest, converging at the 40th generation, and is excluded from the optimal setup. Phase durations for intersections 1 and 3 are recorded; those for other intersections are in Appendix A. Population size 25 fails to converge phase durations optimally by the 20th generation.

The crossover probability is set to 0.8 across all experiments. A high crossover probability ensures fast convergence and does not affect mutation, which is applied independently after crossover. An elitism ratio of 0.4, half the crossover probability, removes worse performing individuals.

The mutation probability is set to 0.1. Mutation enriches the gene library and helps the algorithm escape local optima, but creates convergence noise; the set probability avoids this noise.

Computational time scales linearly with population size and generation ID. The first 10 generations consume more time, after which each generation takes consistent time. Computational time does not increase exponentially with population size.

The optimal parameters are: maximum iterations of 20, population size of 75, crossover probability of 0.8, mutation probability of 0.1, and an elitism parameter of 0.4. This configuration guarantees an average computational time of about 7 minutes per complete generation run.
output:
IV. CASE STUDY — C. GA Parameter Tuning

There are several parameters that need to be set up for the initial genetic algorithm creation, which are: the population size, the maximum number of generations, the crossover probability, and the mutation probability. These have been tuned with the computational time in mind and are detailed as follows:

1) Population Size and Maximum Number of Generations: the population size is the number of individuals in one population, in one generation. In our experiment by individual we refer to a traffic signal plan which is represented by a chromosome denoted as [p11, p12, p13, p14, p21, p22, p23, p24, ..., pn1, pn2, pn3, pn4]. The maximum number of generations is the maximum number of how many evolutionary generations we will run in one optimization cycle. It is determined by the performance of the fitness function and it is set up when the fitness function doesn't improve anymore.

In order to set these two parameters, we choose four possible combinations for our pilot experiment, which are shown in Table III.

As shown in Figure 5, the fitness values of the final optimal traffic signal solutions are plotted for each generation and for four different population sizes (25, 50, 75 or 100 individuals). We have also tested larger population sizes and the results indicate that the algorithm converges very fast and after 75 - 100 individuals, in a population there is no further improvement; therefore, we only show these 4 difference convergence rates for the above four population sizes in this subsection. The unit of the fitness value is (vehicle·hour). As we can see, the cases when the "population size = 100" and "population size = 75" present the same evolving trends and they both converge simultaneously after the 20th generation. The case when "Population size = 50" also converges at the 20th generation, but shows a different converging trend when compared to the "100" and the "75" cases, it is also slower in the initial stages of less than 10 generations. The case of "population size = 25" converges at the 40th generation, which is the slowest case to converge, therefore we exclude it as a possibility for the best optimization setup.

As a plus, the optimal traffic signal settings are recorded and the phase durations in intersection 1 and intersection 3 are shown in Figure 6 and 7 respectively. The phase durations for other intersections can be found in Appendix A. Once again, the fitness value converges at the 20th generation for all population sizes except for the "population size = 25" case, where the phase durations still do not converge towards the optimal values; reiterating this once again would be a unwise setting.

2) Probability of Crossover: this parameter enables to inherit a good fitness from the last generation to a new generation; a higher value guarantees a fast convergence, so the probability of crossover is set to 0.8 in all experiments in this paper. Because mutation is applied to all individuals independently after the crossover for each generation, setting up a high crossover probability would not affect the mutations. We also apply an elitism selection criteria after the crossover evaluation in order to remove the worse performing individuals. The elitism ratio is half of the crossover probability which is 0.4.

3) Probability of Mutation: the mutation generates new chromosomes which enrich the gene library and is a double-edged sword. On one hand, the mutation may happen to a chromosome with bad fitness values and transform it into a chromosome with better fitness values. On the other hand, mutation creates noise in the convergence of the GA and its diversity so the algorithm can jump out of local optima. In order to avoid noise in the convergence, the mutation probability is set to 0.1 in all experiments of this paper.

4) Computational Time: computational times are recorded at the beginning and at the end of a generation. Figure 8 shows the accumulative computational time of each generation with different population sizes. It shows the linear relationship between accumulative computational time and generation ID. Figure 9 shows that the first 10 generations always consume more time than the rest of generations and after 10 generations, each generation takes the same time to be finalized. Besides, we notice a linear relationship between the computation time and the population size for the same generation ID which indicates that the computational times of GA do not increase exponentially with the size of the population.

5) Optimal Parameter Choice: from previous combinations of GA parameters and observations mentioned above, we determine a set of parameters with fast and stable convergence and relatively short computational time. For our study, the maximum number of iterations is set to 20, the population size is set to 75, the crossover probability is set to 0.8, the mutation probability is set to be 0.1, the elitism parameter selection is set to 0.4, which guarantees an average computational time of about 7 minutes per complete generation run.

input: We used randomized search with 5-fold cross-validation to tune hyper-parameters across all regression models. The training data consisted of speed, flow, and density recorded over ten-minute intervals across 72 network sections, plus 16 signal phase features from 4 intersections, totaling 232 features. We ran 10,000 simulations with randomized traffic signal control plans and saved the resulting features to an external database. IV. CASE STUDY — D. BGA-ML Parameter Tuning

As previously mentioned, because we use different kinds of regression models, there are a lot of hyper-parameters within the models. The data used to train the ML models are the “initial state of the network” and the “traffic signal setting of the signalized intersections”. In our network, there are 72 sections and for each section we record the speed, the flow and the density over each of the ten-minute period of the simulation. In addition, we have 4 intersections which contain 4 phases, therefore, in total we have 3*72 + 16 = 232 features considered in the ML training. We ran 10,000 simulations using randomized traffic signal control plans and saved the 232 features in a database external to the traffic simulation model. After cleaning the runs with repeated traffic signal control plans, we have 9,743 good runs in our database.

For example, the “accuracy” scoring means that higher accuracy values are better than lower ones. At last, n_jobs is the number of processors used for parallel computing.

VI. DISCUSSION

In scenario 1, we simulated the daily normal traffic under normal traffic control plan. The GA model was applied to get the optimal traffic control plan. Then in scenario 2, a traffic incident was created in the network, and no more action was taken to respond to the traffic incident. The total travel time in scenario 2 increased by 111.38% when compared to the total travel time in scenario 1. We then simulated the case when we took instant response to the traffic incident and applied the GA model to re-estimate the optimal traffic control plan. The total travel time in scenario 3 only increased by 26.02% when compared to the total travel time in scenario 1. By comparing scenario 2 and 3, the proposed GA model is able to adjust the signal timings and to minimize the total travel time. In our case study, a 40.76% of total travel time saving is achieved in the network. Lastly we evaluated the BGA-ML model in scenario 4 and revealed that travel time is lower by 43% than in the regular GA with a further 25% improvement when compared to the no accident conditions; this reveals the power of BGA-ML to optimize the phase durations under any type of conditions. After a series of hyper-parameter tuning, we were able to shorten the computational time from 8 hours to 11 minutes, which proved to be a significant time saving procedure.

We also observe that the behavior of BGA-ML is different from the original GA. First, the BGA-ML model converges much faster than the GA. Although this might be caused by the training process and the range of training data which is limited; therefore the prediction of the ML may not cover the whole space of possible fitness values. It is safe to infer that ML boosted the BGA-ML's converging process considerably as it converges at about the 10th generation while the GA needs at least 15-20 generations to converge.

Secondly, also as a reason of the fast convergence, the prediction of the ML on the input data is very robust and fuzzy. In other words, a lot of chromosomes have the same fitness values in our trial. Although this is highly dependent on the training of the ML model, we believe it is unavoidable due to the lack of real-life training data.

Thirdly, some ML predictions are out of the feasible range. In our case, the prediction is the total travel time, but we observe some negative values predicted by the ML as shown in Figure 14. It is unrealistic to have the travel time to be negative, so we treat this as an over-fitting and we replace the prediction with a very large travel time by applying a heuristic rule. Lastly, the determination of the final output in BGA-ML is different than in the GA. Because of the nature of the ML model we discovered, it is more difficult to determine the optimal chromosome. After we observed all the chromosomes from the BGA-ML (in Figure 20), most of the chromosomes contains similar values except some noise which means we can use some statistical skills such as averaging all the chromosomes to determine the optimum. We calculate the average and the standard deviation of the phase duration for each phase which are shown in Table V with a relatively small standard deviation. We use the mean value as our optimum and we make a final adjustment by making all the phase duration into integers.

VII. REAL-WORLD APPLICATION OF THE PROPOSED FRAMEWORK

In order to showcase the strong capability of our approach, we have applied the previous findings and methodology to a real network of four traffic intersections situated in the Northern part of the city of Sydney, Australia. The main reasons for choosing this area are due to its close proximity to the northern distributor connecting the CBD with the northern part of the city, therefore a major interconnection hub. Fig. 21 showcases a snapshot of both the network selection as captioned from Google (b), together with the Aimsun representation of our network (a). We make the observation that the intersection numbering as well as the phase numbering are the same as in the initial toy network (see Fig. 4); the only difference is that intersection 4 of the real-world network has two dedicated left-turn lanes which are not associated to any phases according to Australian driving policy.

In this model we used the real traffic demand truncated from the large Sydney model containing the calibrated journey-to-work traffic demand. The simulated time is from 7AM to 8AM in the morning peak hour. The detailed number of trips are presented in Table VI where the ID of origins and destinations are numbered in Fig. 21 (a).

The incident location is on the Falcon Street eastbound which is near the intersection of Falcon St. at Miller St. in North Sydney, Australia (Fig. 22). The incident lasted one hour and affected one out of two lanes in Falcon Street.

Our results show that: under normal conditions, the investigated network has a total travel time of 57.29 vehicle·hour with normal traffic signal plan for the four signalized intersections (by normal we mainly refer to the signal control plan currently in use by the traffic management center). The signal plan is then generated using the regular GA algorithm, which is: {37, 9, 6, 38, 26, 17, 7, 40, 31, 17, 4, 38, 23, 17, 10, 40}. Then we introduce the incident without changing any of the traffic signals and the total travel time increased to 234.79 vehicle·hour which is almost 4 times higher than in regular traffic conditions.

At last, we applied the BGA-ML algorithm proposed in this paper to the traffic signals under incident conditions, and we obtain the new optimum traffic signal plan {25, 4, 31, 30, 9, 11, 24, 46, 32, 19, 4, 35, 26, 24, 5, 35}, with a predicted total travel time of 106.37 vehicle·hour (which is almost half than if the traffic signal would have been kept the same). This is a significant improvement and once again the results showcase the high efficiency of the proposed method. Also the phase durations are balanced better to achieve the optimal traffic signal control by reducing the initial phase for example from 37 to 25 seconds, while extending the third phase from 9 seconds to 31 seconds.

section: VIII. CONCLUSION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: This paper proposes a boosted genetic algorithm using machine learning (BGA-ML) to mitigate non-recurrent traffic incidents. The BGA-ML model adapts standard genetic algorithm components—initialization, fitness function, crossover, and mutation—for traffic signal timing optimization. Key parameters, including population size and maximum generations, are sampled prior to simulation, with optimal settings selected based on performance and computational time. The machine learning component is trained to replace the simulation model, predicting total travel time. Two experiments, one synthetic and one using a real-urban network in Northern Sydney, demonstrate that the BGA-ML model significantly reduces total travel time by approximately 50% compared to taking no action when traffic control plans are revised after an incident occurs.
output:
In this paper, a boosted GA method using ML is developed to mitigate the impact of non-recurrent traffic incidents in two traffic networks. The proposed BGA-ML model is transformed from a standard GA model by adapting the key components for traffic signal timing optimization. These components consist of: initialization, fitness function calculation, crossover, mutation and so on. Prior to the traffic simulation with traffic incidents, the key parameters of the GA such as the population size and the maximum number of generations are sampled; the best setting of these key parameters are worked out by choosing the best performance with relatively short computational time. Then we boost the original GA by embedding the ML to make a new BGA-ML model. The ML model is specially trained to replace the Aimsun simulation model in order to predict the total travel time.

section: VIII. CONCLUSION — C. Future Directions
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: The ML model predicts fuzzy outcomes due to all-at-once feature selection and network-aggregated travel time. Training individual models per road section is a potential solution, though it would require parallel models that scale poorly computationally. Future work should explore reinforcement learning and deeper models like Deep Learning for faster, more accurate predictions, acknowledging their need for large time-series datasets. A multi-objective optimization approach using travel time, queue lengths, and vehicle counts was considered; however, defining a loss function for contradictory objectives (e.g., minimization vs. maximization) remains a challenge, requiring hyper-tuning of weights or separate model architectures. The GA-ML model minimizes total network travel time (including waiting time outside the network) to avoid gridlock, as queueing outside increases exponentially during congestion. GBDT and XGBT emerged as the top regression models compared to LR and RF.
output:
Due to a all-at-once feature selection, the ML model in this paper predicts very fuzzy outcome. Travel time is network aggregated, which might aggregate slight fluctuations that appear on specific sections. One way to address this could be to train ML models for each individual road section. This would imply using section-based historical travel time data and make individual predictions. However, this would require parallel ML models to be launched for each individual section of a traffic network, which could easily scale up in terms of computational resources needed. Future work can be further developed to improve the way the best ML regression model learns from the traffic network and the incident response. This will mean exploring more reinforcement learning techniques online as new traffic data becomes available; we could train even faster models such as Deep Learning models for travel time prediction; they provide very promising results and have established new benchmarks in terms of accuracy. Deep learning models do need however large amounts of time-series data sets to be used and are generally applied to solve big-data problems. This indeed represents a very interesting research direction worth exploring with new data availability.

We have also considered applying a multi-objective optimization approach for our problem by using not only travel time but also queue lengths and/or number of vehicles in the intersection. While the multi-objective optimization does not pose any problem to us as we have previously proposed in one of our previous papers for traffic signal control optimization (see paper published in [12]), the great challenge in this framework would be in the machine learning loss function definition. Currently in the literature, there are no ML models which can optimize two contradictory loss function (a minimization of travel time and a maximization of flow for example); instead, there is rather a weighted loss function definition (see [53]) integrating multiple objectives together. While this can be achieved easily, the complexity comes from further hyper tuning and choosing the correct weights of each parts of the loss function, especially when the objectives are different (minimization versus maximization). This represents a future direction which would be later explored in an extended version of the current paper. It might need different ML models to be constructed and used with a different architecture behind.

APPENDIX D
The reason why we chose travel time as a minimization function of our GA-ML model is the fact that travel time is directly related to queue length and the number of stops of vehicles in the network. To prove this, we have extracted the following graph(s) to show the relation between travel time, queue length and number of stops.

We recorded all the related traffic parameters during the simulation every 10 minutes. Fig. 31 shows the relationship between the number of stops and the total travel time in one section (id=1190) of our simulation network. From the graph, we can see that when total travel time decreases, the number of stops decreases to less than 3. In this way, we can observe that when minimizing the total travel time, we also keep the number of stops in a small range. The trend is even clearer when we only analysed the first 10 minute of the simulation when the section is not fully congested.

Fig. 32 presents the relationship between the mean queue length and the total travel time in the same section. According to the graph, we can see two triangles, which are similar to the Macroscopic Fundamental Diagram (MFD) of flow vs. density. We observe that, when the mean queue length is small (from 0 to 12), the total travel time is linearly increasing since the congestion is building up. When the queue length reaches to a larger value (from 12 to 15), the vehicles are mostly stopped, therefore the number of vehicles decreases which leads to a small total travel time. The second triangle is formed when both lanes have queue building up. In summary, we can say that minimizing the total travel time cannot guarantee a minimized mean queue length and it can fall into any value of mean queue length from zero to 35 vehicles/km.

In our case, to avoid the gridlock, we use the sum of total travel time (inside the network) and the total waiting time (out of the network) as the total network travel time to avoid the gridlock. Because when the gridlock happens, the total waiting time (out of the network) will increase exponentially as all of the vehicles are waiting to enter the network.

In our case, the total travel time for all vehicles is a typical target for optimization which considers the vehicle delays inside the investigated network as well as the vehicle queueing time outside of the network (in Aimsun this is called the “waiting time outside network”). Therefore, it is the best optimization target.

This appendix shows the full rank of all the tested parameters for all ML models according to different performance metrics. Fig. 33 shows the full rank of regression models achieving the lowest MAE. Fig. 34 shows the full rank of regression models achieving the lowest MAPE. Fig. 35 shows the full rank of regression models achieving the lowest RMSE. Fig. 36 shows the full rank of regression models achieving the lowest R2. The results overall reveal GBDT and XGBT as best regression models when compared to LR and RF.

CapMatch: A semi-supervised contrastive capsule transformer with feature-based knowledge distillation for wearable human activity recognition.

This article proposes CapMatch, a semi-supervised method that hybridizes supervised and unsupervised learning to extract rich representations from wearable sensor data. In the unsupervised branch, CapMatch constructs similarity learning via pseudolabeling and contrastive learning on augmented "weak" and "timecut" data views. Feature-based knowledge distillation transfers intermediate layer representations from the weak-augmented model to the timecut-augmented model. A capsule transformer network, comprising four capsule-based transformer blocks and a routing layer, captures local and global activity patterns. With only 10% labeled data, CapMatch achieves F1 scores above 85.00% on the HAPT, WISDM, and UCI_HAR datasets, outperforming 14 semi-supervised algorithms. At 30% labeled data, CapMatch achieves F1 scores no lower than 88.00%, surpassing classical supervised algorithms like decision trees and k-nearest neighbor.

Index Terms— Capsule network, contrastive learning, human activity recognition, knowledge distillation, semi-supervised learning, similarity learning, wearable sensors.

input:
Human activity recognition (HAR) identifies people’s actions based on observations and environmental surroundings [1]. HAR has been widely used in various real-world domains, such as electroencephalography (EEG) analysis [2], gesture detection [3], and healthcare systems [4]. With the prevalence of mobile devices, e.g., smartphones and watches, wearable HAR data collection has become accessible and convenient. Thus, wearable sensor-based HAR has grown into one of the mainstream research topics in HAR [5]. Wearable HAR data are a series of time-ordered data points collected by wearable sensor(s), e.g., a triaxial accelerometer owns three sensors producing X-, Y-, and Z-axis data simultaneously. Such a series is associated with a single or multiple time-dependent variables, i.e., univariate and multivariate [6]. An HAR algorithm captures the local and global patterns from a given time series, e.g., those associated with one variable and those across multiple variables [7], [8]. Over the years, a large number of algorithms have been developed to address wearable sensor-based HAR problems, mainly through traditional and deep learning techniques [5], [6], [7]. Traditional algorithms are usually statistical or machine-learning-based methods, which focus on capturing shallow features from HAR data. For example, Zhu and Sheng [9] introduced a hierarchical hidden Markov model for context-based recognition. Chen et al. [10] proposed an HAR system with coordinate transformation and principal component analysis (PCA) and online support vector machine (SVM). In contrast, deep learning ones are able to extract the intrinsic connections among representations by constructing the internal representation hierarchy of data [11], e.g., Al-Qaness et al. [12] designed a multilevel residual network with attention for HAR feature extraction. Xia et al. [13] put forward a multiple-level domain adaptive learning model that used a single inertial measurement unit sensor to obtain accurate activity recognition. Shu et al. [14] presented a graph long short-term memory (LSTM)-in-LSTM method for group activity recognition, where person-level actions and group-level activity were modeled simultaneously. Unfortunately, all the algorithms above heavily relied on labeled data that usually consumed an incredible amount of human resource cost for raw data annotation.

Semi-supervised learning (SSL) leverages a small amount of labeled data to capture features from a dataset with a large amount of unlabeled data [15]. To mitigate the dependency on labeled data, SSL-based HAR has attracted increasingly more research interests. The SSL algorithms for HAR can be roughly classified into three categories: graph-based, self-labeled, and self-supervised. The graph-based algorithms use graph techniques to learn the similarity between the feature maps obtained from the HAR data, e.g., the multigraph-based SSL [16], shared structure discovery SSL [17], and dynamic graph-based SSL [18]. The self-labeled ones usually adopt a supervised classifier to label instances with the unknown class without any specific input data suppositions, mainly relying on two methods: cotraining [19], [20] and self-training [21], [22], [23]. The self-supervised algorithms consider a model’s class prediction as a pseudolabel of the training object, e.g., SelfHAR [24], CSSHAR [25], and ColloSSL [26]. In summary, the algorithms above usually use one or two of the four main SSL techniques, namely, entropy minimization, consistency regularization, pseudolabeling, and generic regularization. Unfortunately, most SSL algorithms for HAR ignore integration of these techniques and thus have limited ability to capture rich representations from the data.

Recently, algorithms hybridizing multiple SSL techniques have become prevalent in the semi-supervised image classification community. For example, MixMatch used a single loss to integrate entropy minimization, consistency regularization, and generic regularization [27]. ReMixMatch was an improved version of MixMatch, with distribution alignment and augmentation anchoring as two additional techniques [28]. FixMatch took the advantages of ReMixMatch and pseudolabeling to capture sufficient representations from input data [29]. Zhang et al. [30] integrated curriculum pseudolabeling into FixMatch to form FlexMatch for semi-supervised image classification.

The ensemble algorithms above, e.g., FixMatch and its variants (e.g., FlexMatch), usually consist of supervised learning based on a small amount of labeled data and unsupervised learning based on a large amount of unlabeled data. Their performance heavily depends on representation learning on the unlabeled data, where lower and higher level semantic information is of significant importance [31]. However, most of the ensemble algorithms only emphasize similarity learning on higher level semantic information, ignoring the importance of lower level semantic information on representation learning, which limits their ability of extracting abundant representations from unlabeled data. output:
II. RELATED WORK

Wearable human activity recognition (HAR) has been extensively studied using various sensor modalities and deep learning architectures. Early approaches relied on traditional machine learning methods applied to time-frequency features extracted from accelerometer and gyroscope data. However, the emergence of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) significantly improved classification performance by automatically learning spatial and temporal patterns from raw sensor signals.

Capsule networks (CapNets) have been proposed as an alternative to CNNs to address the limitation of max-pooling in preserving pose and spatial hierarchies. In the context of HAR, capsule architectures aim to better model the relationship between different body parts and activity dynamics. Some works have integrated capsule layers with attention mechanisms to focus on relevant sensor segments during activity classification.

Contrastive learning (CL) has gained traction as a self-supervised paradigm to learn robust feature representations without relying heavily on labeled data. By optimizing an objective that pulls together embeddings of augmented views of the same instance while pushing apart dissimilar instances, CL enables the learning of generic features that can be fine-tuned for specific HAR tasks. Recent studies have explored CL within transformer architectures to capture long-range dependencies in sensor sequences.

Knowledge distillation (KD) is a model compression technique where a smaller "student" network is trained to mimic the behavior of a larger "teacher" network. Feature-based KD, in particular, matches intermediate feature maps or embeddings between the student and teacher, allowing the student to retain the representational capacity of the teacher while operating under resource constraints. This approach has been effectively applied to reduce the computational cost of HAR models deployed on edge devices with limited battery and processing power.

Semi-supervised learning frameworks combine labeled and unlabeled data to improve model generalization. By leveraging the abundant unlabeled sensor data available in real-world scenarios, these frameworks can enhance the robustness of activity classifiers, especially in scenarios where labeling is expensive or time-consuming. The integration of contrastive objectives with distillation mechanisms has shown promise in creating efficient yet accurate HAR systems.

input: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers knowledge from a cumbersome teacher network to a lightweight student. Existing KD algorithms are divided into three categories: response-based, feature-based, and relationship-based [32]. Response-based methods transfer output logits; for instance, Feng et al. [63] used resolution-aware KD, and [64] used expert embedding KD to enhance capacity [65]. Feature-based methods share intermediate layer knowledge since FitNet [66]; Zhang et al. [67] applied layer-calibration for remote sensing, and Hao et al. [68] presented a data-free multilevel framework. Relationship-based methods capture inter-layer relationships; Yu et al. [69] used metric learning for feature embedding, Guo et al. [70] introduced multilevel attention, and [71] enabled cross-layer mutual distillation to improve student feature extraction.
output:
KD, one of the most popular regularization techniques, encourages knowledge transfer from a cumbersome network (i.e., teacher) to a lightweight one (i.e., student). According to the knowledge form, researchers roughly divide the existing KD algorithms into three categories: response-based, feature-based, and relationship-based [32]. The response-based method transfers the knowledge from the output (i.e., logits) of a teacher to that of a student [62]. For example, Feng et al. [63] introduced a resolution-aware KD method to transfer high-level semantic information to low-level one. In [64], an expert embedding KD method was used to enhance the knowledge capacity during the knowledge transfer process. In [65], a collaborative KD algorithm was used to improve the accuracy of image classification.

The feature-based method enables knowledge sharing between intermediate layers of a teacher and its student instead of output-to-output. Since the pioneering work FitNet [66], a considerable amount of feature-based studies have been conducted to solve various application tasks. For instance, Zhang et al. [67] designed an effective KD method based on layer-calibration and task-disentangle distillation for remote sensing. Hao et al. [68] presented a collaborative data-free framework with multilevel feature sharing for multiscale feature extraction. Different from the response- and feature-based methods, the relationship-based method pays more attention to capturing the relationships among layers in the student and teacher models. Yu et al. [69] devised a relationship-based metric learning model to improve the quality of image feature embedding. Guo et al. [70] introduced a multilevel attention-based KD approach to capture potential correlations between the teacher and student models. In [71], a cross-layer mutual distillation method enabled sufficient knowledge from the teacher to the student, improving the feature extraction ability of the student model.

section: III. CAPMATCH
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: CapMatch combines supervised and unsupervised learning processes (Fig. 1). Its feature extractor uses a capsule transformer network with four blocks and one routing layer. In supervised learning, CapMatch guides prediction vectors toward ground labels using a margin loss on labeled data. In unsupervised learning, CapMatch uses weak and timecut augmentation to generate views of unlabeled data. It establishes similarity learning on lower and higher-level semantic information from these views to enhance instance-level representation. Specifically, CapMatch supervises timecut-augmented prediction vectors with weak-augmented labels via a margin loss and forms similarity learning via a contrastive loss. Additionally, CapMatch promotes knowledge flow from intermediate layers of the weak-augmented model to the timecut-augmented model through feature-based knowledge distillation.
output:
III. CAPMATCH

This section first overviews the CapMatch’s structure. Then it describes the problem formulation, capsule-based transformer, routing, data augmentation, CL, feature-based KD, and loss function one by one.

A. Overview

CapMatch contains supervised and unsupervised learning processes, as shown in Fig. 1. The capsule transformer network, composed of four capsule-based transformer blocks and one routing layer, is the model’s feature extractor. CapMatch guides the prediction vectors toward the corresponding ground labels by a margin loss function on the labeled data in the supervised learning process. On the other hand, CapMatch leverages data augmentation, pseudolabeling, CL, and feature-based KD techniques to recognize the relationships among the features of classes obtained from the unlabeled data in the unsupervised learning process. Two data augmentation methods, namely, “weak” and “timecut,” are used to generate different views of the same sample. CapMatch establishes similarity learning on the lower and higher level semantic information extracted from the weak and timecut versions of the data to enhance the instance-level representation learning in unsupervised learning. To be specific, CapMatch not only allows the weak-augmented artificial labels to supervise the timecut-augmented prediction vectors by a margin loss function but also combines the outputs of the weak- and timecut-augmented models to form similarity learning by a CL loss function. Meanwhile, CapMatch promotes the knowledge flow from the intermediate layers of weak-augmented model to those of the timecut-augmented model via feature-based KD.

section: III. CAPMATCH — C. Capsule-Based Transformer
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: The capsule transformer network uses four capsule-based transformer blocks to capture local and global patterns in HAR data, providing rich representations via routing. Within the capsule community, existing transformer-based studies primarily use vanilla transformers or embed dynamic routing to form embedding transformers, but they ignore capsule interaction rules, such as treating capsule vector length as entity probability, resulting in missing information. To address this, this article designs a transformer-based capsule block following capsule interaction rules to relate input data representations and extract intrinsic connections and regularizations, as shown in Fig. 2. The core of each transformer is the multihead capsule attention, containing $n_{att}$ capsule-based attention modules. Each module, e.g., Attention$_i$, transfers a query, Query$_i$, and its key-value pairs, Key$_i$-Value$_i$, to an output, $V^{att}_i$. Different from vanilla attention, capsule-based attention considers capsule interaction rules, e.g., vector length represents entity probability. $V^{att}_i$ is defined as $V^{att}_i = \frac{Query_i \cdot Key^T_i}{\sqrt{d_i}} \cdot Value_i$, where $Key^T_i$ denotes the transpose of Key$_i$, $d_i$ is the dimension of Key$_i$, and $||.||$ outputs the vector length. Let $V_{mul}$ be the output of multihead capsule attention; $V_{mul}$ fuses $n_{att}$ capsule-based attention modules through the CONCAT function, $f_{concat}$, to provide sufficient global features. $V_{mul}$ is defined as $V_{mul} = f_{concat}(V^{att}_1, V^{att}_2, \dots, V^{att}_{n_{att}})$. Following prior work, a routing layer promotes capsule interaction to mine relationships. Given capsule j, its input $s_j$ is defined as $s_j = \sum_i k_{ij} \hat{v}_{j|i}$, where $\hat{v}_{j|i}$ is the prediction vector obtained by multiplying capsule i's output $v_i$ by weight matrix $W_{ij}$.

section: III. CAPMATCH — E. Data Augmentation
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Data augmentation is a widely used regularization method to improve model robustness in deep learning [27]-[29]. CapMatch uses two augmentation methods, "weak" and "timecut," to produce views from the same sample in unsupervised learning. Weak augmentation uses a jitter-and-scale strategy, such as adding a Gaussian function to raw data. Timecut is a modified Cutout [75] that transforms a small piece of raw unlabeled data without changing its overall trend. Fig. 3 shows raw data and its weak- and timecut-augmented versions on the WISDM dataset.

The loss function, L, includes a supervised loss, Lsup, and an unsupervised loss, Luns. As the studies in [34], [35], [36], and [37] suggest, Lsup uses the margin loss function to measure the average differences between the ground labels and their prediction vectors on labeled HAR data. Lsup is written as

Lsup = 1/nlab ∑_{i=1}^{nlab} yi max(0, m+ − V_lab_i) + λ(1 − yi) max(0, V_lab_i − m−)

where V_lab_i is the output of the proposed capsule transformer network associated with the labeled data, x_lab_i, and m+, m−, and λ are three coefficients for Lsup. As the previous studies suggest [34], [35], [37], we set m+ = 0.9, m− = 0.1, and λ = 0.5.

Luns consists of a KD loss function, LKD, a CL loss function, LCL, and a confidential marginal loss function, LCM. Similar to FixMatch [29], CapMatch leverages V_wea_j to generate an artificial label associated with V_tim_j when max(V_wea_j) ≥ t_CM, where t_CM is a coefficient for LCM. LCM is calculated by the following equation:

LCM = 1/nunl ∑_{j=1}^{nunl} yone_j max(0, m+ − V_tim_j) + λ(1 − yone_j) max(0, V_tim_j − m−)

where yone_j = 1 if max(V_wea_j) ≥ t_CM, and argmax(V_wea_j) produces a valid one-hot probability distribution of V_wea_j. Following [29], we set t_CM = 0.95.

The unsupervised loss of CapMatch, Luns, is defined in the following equation:

Luns = LCM + LKD + τLCL

where τ is a coefficient of LCL. Following the previous work in [76], we set τ = 0.1.

Thus, the loss function of CapMatch, L, is calculated as

L = Lsup + Luns + ϵ||θ||2^2 = Lsup + LCM + LKD + τLCL + ϵ||θ||2^2

where θ represents the model parameters of CapMatch, and ϵ is a coefficient of ||θ||2^2 (i.e., L2 regularization). Following [37], we set ϵ = 0.0005 in our experiments. Besides, the CapMatch’s pseudocode is given in Algorithm 2.

input: To evaluate CapMatch, three HAR datasets were used: HAPT [77], WISDM [78], and UCI_HAR [79]. HAPT data were collected from 30 volunteers (age 19–48) using smartphone accelerometer and gyroscope signals sampled at fixed 2.56 s windows (128 readings), resulting in 561-feature vectors with six activities and six static postures. WISDM [78] collected accelerometer data at 20 Hz from 1,098,207 examples across six activities. UCI_HAR [79] used 30 volunteers (age 19–48) wearing a Samsung Galaxy S II at the waist; three-axial linear acceleration and angular velocity were sampled at 50 Hz (20 Hz sample rate), covering six activities. Data were preprocessed using fixed time windows and filtering (low-pass, Kalman, wavelet) as suggested by [5]–[10]. Each dataset was split 7:3 into training/validation and testing sets; supervised methods used the 8:2 train-validation split, while semi-supervised methods further split training labels with ratios r ∈ {0.1, 0.2, 0.3} as in [80]–[82]. Experiments used an Ubuntu 18.04 system with an Nvidia GTX 1080Ti (11 GB) GPU and AMD R5 1400 CPU (16 GB RAM), with RMSProp optimizer (momentum 0.9, learning rate 0.001, decay 0.9).

1) CapMatch With Different tKD Values: tKD is a temperature coefficient to scale the features of the intermediate layers, which facilitates the knowledge flow in the intermediate layers. As shown in Fig. 4, 1.0 is the best setting for tKD because it helps CapMatch to obtain the highest F1 value on each HAR dataset.

2) CapMatch With Different tCL Values: tCL is a threshold value for CapMatch to learn the similarity between different views from the same sample. When tCL = 1.0, CapMatch achieves the highest F1 result on each dataset. That means tCL = 1.0 helps CapMatch mine rich connections and regularizations from the HAR data.

3) CapMatch With Different KD Losses: It is crucial to choose an appropriate KD loss function to measure the knowledge difference between a teacher and its student. Table III shows the F1 results obtained by CapMatch with different KD losses on three HAR datasets when r = 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3. L2 performs better than the other three losses. We investigate the effects of different components on CapMatch across three HAR datasets.

1) **Effectiveness of Routing**: CapMatch with routing significantly outperforms CapMatch without the routing mechanism (CapMatch w/o Routing) on all three datasets (Table IV, r=0.1, 0.2, 0.3).

2) **Effectiveness of CL**: CapMatch with contrastive learning (CL) achieves higher F1 scores than CapMatch without CL (CapMatch w/o CL) on each dataset, as CL enhances representation quality by quantifying view differences.

3) **Effectiveness of Feature-Based KD**: CapMatch outperforms both CapMatch w/o FKD and CapMatch w RKD (response-based KD [32]) in F1 measure, demonstrating that feature-based KD improves knowledge transfer between intermediate layers.

4) **Effectiveness of Capsule-Based Transformer**: CapMatch outperforms VanMatch (vanilla transformer blocks [72], [73]) and EmbMatch (embedding transformer blocks [74]) on all datasets. The capsule-based transformer relates capsules at different locations to mine rich connections in HAR data.

In summary, routing, CL, feature-based KD, and the capsule-based transformer are essential components for CapMatch.

We compare CapMatch against 14 SSL algorithms using F1 score. DTW-D, Self-Labeled SVM, Self-Labeled Clustering, SSSL, SelfHAR, SSRCA, UDA, En-Co-Training, Sparse-Coding, SSCLHAR, ActSemiCNN, MixMatch, FixMatch, and FlexMatch serve as baselines. CapMatch achieves the highest F1 value on each dataset. For example, CapMatch obtains 86.32% F1 on WISDM at r=0.1, while FlexMatch ranks second and DTW-D ranks last. CapMatch's F1 is at least 1.3% higher than FlexMatch's average across three datasets.

The performance gain stems from CapMatch's hybrid design combining pseudolabeling, contrastive learning, and feature-based knowledge distillation within a capsule transformer structure. FlexMatch also performs decently via consistency regularization and curriculum pseudolabeling, but DTW-D underperforms by relying solely on DTW without exploring rich features or regularizations.

Increasing the labeled ratio r from 0.1 to 0.3 improves CapMatch's F1, as more prior knowledge enables richer relationship mining. At r=0.3, CapMatch is compared against 16 supervised algorithms. It underperforms deep learning baselines but exceeds traditional methods like KNN, random forest, and decision tree on specific datasets; for instance, CapMatch achieves 89.14% F1 on WISDM versus KNN's 82.29%. Visualization via confusion matrices shows CapMatch achieves >80% per-class accuracy on UCI_HAR, but performs worst on HAPT due to short event data with few labels.

IV. EXPERIMENTS — E. Experimental Analysis

To evaluate the performance of CapMatch, we compare it with 14 SSL algorithms against F1 value, as follows.

1) DTW-D: A modified dynamic time warping algorithm for HAR [82].
2) Self-Labeled SVM: a modified self-labeled algorithm with SVM for HAR [83].
3) Self-Labeled Clustering: A modified self-labeled algorithm with clustering for HAR [83].
4) SSSL: A combination of the shapelet method and pseudolabeling for HAR [81].
5) SelfHAR: A self-supervised learning algorithm for HAR [24].
6) SSRCA: A semi-supervised recurrent convolutional attention algorithm for HAR [19].
7) UDA: Based on data augmentation and consistency regularization with the proposed capsule transformer network (see Fig. 1) as its feature extractor [84].
8) En-Co-Training: An SSL algorithm with cotraining for HAR [20].
9) Sparse-Coding: A sparse-coding SSL framework for HAR [85].
10) SSCLHAR: A contrastive SSL algorithm for HAR [25].
Fig. 6. F1 results obtained by CapMatch with r = 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3 on three datasets.
11) ActSemiCNN: An active semi-supervised CNN for HAR [22].
12) MixMatch: A modified MixMatch [27] adapted to HAR, with the proposed capsule transformer network (see Fig. 1) as its feature extractor.
13) FixMatch: A modified FixMatch [29] adapted to HAR, with the proposed capsule transformer network (see Fig. 1) as its feature extractor.
14) FlexMatch: A modified FlexMatch [30] adapted to HAR, with the proposed capsule transformer network (see Fig. 1) as its feature extractor.

Table V shows the F1 results with various SSL algorithms with different r values on three HAR datasets. One can easily observe that CapMatch performs the best among all the compared SSL algorithms on each dataset, e.g., CapMatch obtains the highest F1 value on the WISDM dataset when r = 0.1, namely, 86.32%. FlexMatch takes the second position while DTW-D leads to the worst performance. F1 value of CapMatch is at least 1.3% higher than that of FlexMatch in average with three datasets considered.

The following explains our observations above. Based on the capsule transformer structure, CapMatch gracefully hybridizes pseudolabeling, CL, and feature-based KD, being able to capture as many intrinsic connections among the obtained representations of classes in the unlabeled data as possible. Thanks to the consistency regularization and curriculum pseudolabeling techniques, FlexMatch can mine valuable information from the unlabeled data and achieves decent performance regarding F1 value on three HAR datasets. On the other hand, DTW-D cannot explore rich features and regularizations from the unlabeled data via the DTW technique only.

Second, to study the impact of r on the performance of CapMatch, this article shows the F1 results obtained by CapMatch with r = 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3 on three HAR datasets in Fig. 6. With more labeled data, more additional prior knowledge is brought to CapMatch, helping it mine richer relationships and regularizations from the data. That is why the CapMatch’s performance is gradually enhanced as the amount of labeled data increases.

Finally, we compare CapMatch with r = 0.3 with 16 supervised algorithms on three HAR datasets and collect the F1 results in Table VI. These supervised algorithms can be classified into traditional and deep learning algorithms, listed below.

TABLE V
F1 RESULTS OBTAINED BY VARIOUS SSL ALGORITHMS WITH DIFFERENT r VALUES ON THREE HAR DATASETS

1) Traditional Algorithm:
a) Primary Machine Learning Algorithms: SVM, KNN, GradientBoosting, random forest, and decision tree [5].
b) J48: A machine learning algorithm based on decision tree using iterative Dichotomiser [7].

2) Deep Learning Algorithm:
a) Stacked Denoising Autoencoder: A stacked denoising autoencoder method based fully connected neural networks for HAR [44].
b) 1DCNN: A 1-D CNN model for HAR [43].
c) 2DCNN: A 2-D CNN model for HAR [43].
d) Multihead Convolutional Attention: A multihead feature network integrating multihead CNN and attention for HAR [43].
e) CNNLSTM: A cascading model based on CNN and LSTM for HAR [49].
f) CNNBiLSTM: A cascading model based on CNN and BiLSTM for HAR [49].
g) LegoCNN: A lightweight CNN model based on Lego filters for HAR [46].
h) Perceptive Extraction Network: A perceptive extraction network integrating a feature network and a relationship network in parallel for HAR [6].
i) Deformable CNN: A learning model based on deformable CNN for HAR [47].
j) Selective Kernel Convolution: A multibranch CNN model based on selective kernel convolution for HAR [48].

All the semi-supervised and supervised algorithms are verified by the same testing datasets. One can easily see that CapMatch performs worse than all the deep-learning-based supervised algorithms but it performs better than several traditional supervised algorithms. To be specific, CapMatch outperforms KNN, random forest, and decision tree on HAPT, performs the best on WISDM, and performs better than decision tree on UCR_HAR. For example, the F1 value of CapMatch is 89.14% while that of KNN is 82.29% on the WISDM dataset. Therefore, CapMatch has the potential to address various SSL tasks in the HAR domain. Besides, to visualize the performance of CapMatch with r = 0.3 for each class of activity on each dataset, we show its confusion matrices on three datasets in Fig. 7. One can see that CapMatch with r = 0.3 performs the best on the UCI_HAR dataset, as the accuracy of each class activity exceeds 80%. On the HAPT dataset, CapMatch with r = 0.3 performs the worst because it cannot mine rich features from the short event data with few labels, resulting in poor performance in short events, e.g., lie-to-stand (Ltd) and sit-to-lie (StL). Overall, CapMatch with r = 0.3 performs well in most of the activity categories on three datasets, demonstrating its excellent feature extraction ability.
