29 November 2023. Date of publication 7 December 2023; date of current
version 23 May 2024. Paper no. TEC-01307-2022. (Corresponding author:
J. Kolb.)
The authors are with the Institute of Electrical Machines (IEM), RWTH
Aachen University, 52062 Aachen, Germany (e-mail: johann.kolb@iem.
rwth-aachen.de; kay.hameyer@iem.rwth-aachen.de).
Color versions of one or more ﬁgures in this article are available at
https://doi.org/10.1109/TEC.2023.3340337.
Digital Object Identiﬁer 10.1109/TEC.2023.3340337
Recent studies of tolerances and uncertainties in permanent
magnet synchronous machines (PMSMs) focus on eccentricity, magnetization faults and remanence ﬂux deviations of the
permanent magnets. At this, different output values such as
current, torque and back electromotive force (back-EMF) are
evaluated [3], [4], [5], [6], [7]. The tolerances are assessed with
One-factor-At-a-Time (OAT) analyses, which only comprise
individual inﬂuences. During operation, parasitic effects of the
tolerances can inﬂuence currents, torque and noise, which can
only be estimated in detail by analyzing various frequency
orders [8], [9]. To detect magnetic deviations Hall-effect sensors
have been installed in the air gap [10]. Of course, the machine
cannot be equipped with Hall-effect sensors for an EoL test, nor
is it opened. With superposed effects on the machine’s output
values the classiﬁcation of tolerance sizes as goodness of the
machine’s quality and condition becomes difﬁcult. Therefore,
for this purpose machine learning is utilized as evaluation technique.
Supervised Machine Learning (ML) has been employed for
different applications such as fault diagnosis for inverters and
open-circuit faults [11], [12], [13]. ML is also applied for Condition Monitoring (CM) of machine rolling bearings and eccentricity [14], [15], [16]. For an EoL test scenario, an autoencoder
is also applied as an unsupervised ML technique for vibration
analysis [17].
The presented studies focus on the evaluation of speciﬁc
tolerances and faults, but lack a holistic approach for the classiﬁ-
cationoftolerancesinelectricalmachinestoincreasetheproduct
quality. Furthermore, the combined inﬂuences of the tolerances
on the output values of the machine are not known precisely
enough, so that the underlying data are not suitable for tolerance
classiﬁcation. The studies on the effects of eccentricity and
magnetization deviations also indicate that a frequency spectrum
analysis is more suitable for evaluation than the analysis of
absolute data.
Additionally, the correlation between spatial magnetization
tolerances and faults leads to a surface acceleration that is also
position-dependent [18]. Consequently, asymmetrical arranged
vibration sensors are not suitable for classifying tolerance deviations and in various cases the vibration sensors are difﬁcult to
place, e.g. if the machine has cooling ribs or is highly integrated
into a drive train.
Thus, this study proposes a tolerance classiﬁcation based on
motor current signature analysis (MCSA) and torque analysis.
In contrast to the studies presented, a transient drive simulation comprising a PMSM, control, inverter and drive train

instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: A recent study on PMSM manufacturing tolerances presents a sensitivity analysis showing that housing radius, rotor radius, and static eccentricity majorly influence quality objectives [8]. Quality objectives are mean torque, torque ripple, and radial force variance [8]. Increasing housing radius expands the air gap, negatively affecting all objectives. Increasing rotor radius positively affects objectives. Static eccentricity positively influences mean torque and radial forces but negatively affects torque ripple [8]. The most important tolerances are housing radius, rotor radius, static eccentricity with its angle, and remanence [5]. Tolerances are normally distributed with limits defined as 3σ [8], [25], [26].
output:
The rotor of the PMSM consists of the lamination stack and permanent magnets. The stator is built up from segments with single tooth windings, that are pressed into the housing. The machine is then assembled together from the stator, rotor, end shields, bearings and electrical connections. Apparent winding faults such as divergent number of turns and phase resistances are checked with the winding machine and at the EoL test, respectively.

In a recent study examining the overall effects of manufacturing tolerances on the performance of the PMSM presented, the KOLB AND HAMEYER: CLASSIFICATION OF TOLERANCES IN PERMANENT MAGNET SYNCHRONOUS MACHINES WITH MACHINE LEARNING results of a sensitivity analysis show, that the housing radius, the rotor radius and the static eccentricity have the major influence on the quality objectives [8]. As quality objectives the mean torque, torque ripple and the variance of the radial forces are utilized.

With an increasing radius of the housing the main air gap expands so that the radius has a negative effect on all quality objectives. If, on the other hand, the rotor radius increases, this has a positive effect on the quality objectives. The static eccentricity has the highest positive influence on the mean torque and on the radial forces while it has a negative effect on the torque ripple.

Therefore, the most important tolerances considered in this study are the housing radius, the rotor radius, the static eccentricity with the associated eccentricity angle and the remanence, which can also affect the product quality [5]. The tolerances are normally distributed and the tolerance limits empirically determined as 3σ limits [8], [25], [26].

The test bench setup consists of the DUT, rotational speed and torque sensor and a load machine, which is equal to the simulationsetup (see Fig. 2). Machine 3 in contrast has a similar distribution to machine 1, but with the mean at 1.25%. The rotor and stator radius but also the eccentricity can have a major influence, as the simulation results indicate.

Subsequently, the amplitudes for each identified order in Section II-C are computed to classify the measured machine. Fig. 8 shows the harmonic orders ν of the d-current and Fig. 9 of the q-current.

The amplitudes of the d-current orders have a mostly clear tendency: machine 2 has the highest amplitudes for all orders, machine 1 the lowest and the amplitudes of machine 3 fluctuate near the mean. Compared to the simulation this could denote, that machine 2 has a higher eccentricity than machine 3 while machine 1 has the lowest eccentricity. A more differentiated picture emerges for the harmonic q-current orders. For order 3, machine 2 has the highest and machine 3 the lowest amplitude, while the amplitude of machine 1 is close to the mean. In contrast, the 6th order shows a significant difference between machine 2 and 3. While machine 1 is close to the mean value, machine 3 has a higher and machine 2 a lower amplitude. IV. CLASSIFICATION

For classification, three supervised ML methods (CART, SVM, KNN) and one unsupervised method (autoencoder) are compared based on accuracy. Ten percent of samples are excluded from the training dataset. Input features include harmonic orders (3, 6, 12, 15, 18, 36), current ripples (d-q), and torque ripple. These features are derived from simulation and measurement data.

CART is a non-parametric algorithm that splits training data using decision rules to reach target accuracy [31]. SVM extends data to additional dimensions to linearize nonlinear correlations, defining classes via hyperplanes maximized from support vectors [32]. KNN classifies data points by majority vote based on distance to neighbor points [33].

Sensitivity analysis ranks input variable influence by setting variables to their mean and subtracting prediction accuracy from one; higher resulting values indicate greater influence [34].

The autoencoder is an unsupervised method that encodes input data to a compressed representation and decodes it to reproduce the original input. Reconstruction quality is measured by mean squared error (MSE), calculated as 1/n Σ(O_i − I_i)^2 [35]. Higher MSE indicates larger deviations from the original input, enabling abnormality detection via threshold comparison.

IV. CLASSIFICATION

For classification different ML methods are utilized and compared belonging their accuracy. Three well-known methods for supervised learning that are applied on the data are CART (Classification And Regression Tree), SVM (Support Vector Machines) and KNN (K-Nearest-Neighbor). Also as unsupervised learning the possibility of applying an autoencoder on the data is discussed. For examining the accuracy of the classification 10% of the samples are excluded from the training data set.

The utilized output values are the discussed and already determined harmonic orders 3, 6, 12, 15, 18 and 36 as well as the ripple of the d- and q-currents. Furthermore, the orders 3, 6 and the ripple of the torque are used. These values are calculated from both simulation and measurement data and serve as input for the supervised and unsupervised ML methods.

CART is a non-parametric algorithm where the training data is split with the help of decision rules until a certain accuracy is reached [31]. The SVM algorithm works with additional dimensions such that the training data points are extended to vectors. Thus, nonlinear correlations are linearized, so that the classes of the data are defined with hyperplanes with a maximized distance to the support vectors [32]. The KNN algorithm is based on rules, where the distance to the neighbor data points is calculated. Data points are classified with a majority voting whereby the class is chosen which contains the most neighbors [33].

Furthermore, the sensitivity of the input variables is important for the analysis in order to understand and conceive the influences of the individual variables. The sensitivity analysis is performed here by setting the input variable to be analyzed to its mean value. Subsequently, the prediction accuracy is calculated. A low value means that the variable has a high influence on the result. To better represent the change, this value is subtracted from one, so that the variable with the highest influence has the highest value.

The autoencoder is an unsupervised learning method, which learns the features of the training data. The input data is encoded to a compressed representation and then decoded to its original input size, so that the learned behavior is reproduced [34]. The deviation between original input and decoded data is expressed as

MSE = 1/n Σ_{i=1}^n (O_i − I_i)^2 (4)

where I is the input data and O the output data of the autoencoder for all samples n [35]. The MSE thus increases, the larger the deviations between the input data and the reproduced data of the autoencoder become. Therefore, abnormalities can be detected by comparing the MSE values or defining a threshold value.

IV. CLASSIFICATION — A. End of Line Test

The first application scenario represents an end-of-life (EoL) test. Machines are classified as Good, Warning, or Fault. A reference machine is classified as Warning if one tolerance parameter exceeds 80% of the 3σ limits, and as Fault if the tolerance exceeds 100%. The autoencoder training data corresponds to the Good category; Fault data is composed of Warning and Fault categories.

Fig. 10 shows classification results as confusion matrices. For the CART method, the prediction for Good is reasonable, but the result for Warning has higher deviation and is inaccurate for Fault. The confusion matrices for SVM and KNN reveal a high correlation between reference and prediction, though SVM has the highest correlation. Overall prediction accuracy is depicted in Table II as correct categorized samples divided by all samples.

Fig. 11 shows sensitivity of inputs for the EoL scenario with SVM. The 36th order in both q- and d-currents has the highest influence. In the middle range are the 15th order in q- and d-current, the 3rd order of the d-current, and the 18th order of the q-current. Less relevant are the 6th order of d- and q-current, the 3rd order of q-current, the 12th order of d-current, and the 6th order of torque. A subtle influence has the torque ripple, q-current ripple, the 12th order of q-current, the 18th order of d-current, and the 3rd order of torque.

If the ML model is applied on measurement data (see Fig. 12), machine 3 is correctly classified as Good, in contrast to machine 1, which is incorrectly classified as Warning, and machine 2 with Fault.

The classification results of the autoencoder are presented in Fig. 13 and show that the mean mean squared error (MSE) for samples classified as Fault is higher than those belonging to test samples. The plotted standard error of the MSE is higher for Fault than for test samples. When the trained autoencoder is applied on measurement data, the result indicates a visible gradation between the three machines. Machine 1 shows the lowest MSE, machine 3 a slightly higher one, while machine 2 generates the highest MSE value with a gap of more than 30%.

B. Eccentricity

As a second application scenario, machines are classified by eccentricity eEcc,S with classes: > 0%, > 10%, > 20%, > 30% and > 40%. Confusion matrices are shown in Fig. 14; results coincide with the EoL classification. With the SVM method a reasonable correlation is obtained; the KNN method has slightly higher deviation, while the CART method indicates inaccurate prediction with overall performance shown in Table II.

The sensitivity analysis in Fig. 15 of the eccentricity classification entails a similar gradation as for the EoL classification. The 36th harmonic order of the d- and q-current has significant influence, as does the 15th order of the d-current and the 18th order of the q-current. A medium influence results from the 3rd and 6th orders of the d-current and the 15th order of the q-current. A lower influence is given by the 12th and 18th order of the d-current, the 3rd, 6th and 12th order of the q-current, the 3rd and 6th order of the torque and the ripples of the q-current and torque.

The ML model applied on measured machines in Fig. 16 shows that machine 1 is incorrectly classified with eEcc,S > 20%. Machine 2 with eEcc,S > 40% is also slightly misclassified, while machine 3 is correctly classified with eEcc,S > 0%.

C. Discussion

The classification based on the used variables works well for the two presented application scenarios. It turns out, that not all ML methods are suitable to the same extent. As a result, the CART method shows an inaccurate correlation between reference and prediction. The SVM method achieves the best results, while the KNN method exhibits a slightly lower recognition rate. There is no significant difference between the EoL and the eccentricity classification. In general, a larger number of samples can improve the detection and classification.

The sensitivity analyses reveal that not all variables have the same influence on the classification. Some variables are dominant, others have almost no influence. A training with all harmonic orders, which a preliminary evaluation has shown, produces partly worse results than if the orders are selected on the basis of the theory and simulations in advance. As a result, the single and twofold cogging torque orders have a major influence on the tolerance classification. Other harmonic orders also have an influence, but they are less important, while the ripples have almost no contribution to the classification.

The measured machines are consistently classified slightly too high in their deviations from the classification. In this respect, the variables that have a higher influence on the classification are somewhat different than in the simulation. This can be seen in the orders 36 of the d- and q-current, which have a high influence on the recognition, but are not as visible in the measurements as in the simulation. Possible reasons for the measured amplitudes not being present could be material influences and degradation. In the simulation, no iron losses and no cutting edge effects are considered, but these could have an influence on the amplitudes. Furthermore, the inverter as well as the cables could affect the amplitudes.

The autoencoder works for both simulation and measurement data. The samples classified as faults can be clearly distinguished from the test samples. The MSE values of the measurement data are significantly higher, but the deviations match those of the confusion matrices. Since the autoencoder is trained exclusively with data without faulty condition, it offers the potential to detect the deviations even without a corresponding number of faulty machines.

The more training data available, the better the machine learning algorithms are suited for classification, as it can train the detailed characteristics of the evaluated machine. Furthermore, the method can be generalized in principle, but since the operating principle of other types of machines is different, it must be shown that it can be applied to all types of electrical machines. If the computational time for the evaluation and ML is small enough, the method shown can be integrated into an EoL cycle for fault detection.

section: V. CONCLUSION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: A PMSM tolerance classification uses transient drive simulation with DOE and FOC control. Torque and current ripples, along with their frequency spectra, are analyzed from time-domain data. The relevant harmonic orders are multiples of the pole pair number and the cogging torque order, indicating that existing end-of-life and cogging torque evaluation methods require revision. Support vector machines achieve the highest classification accuracy for end-of-life testing and eccentricity ranking. Sensitivity analysis shows single and double cogging torque orders have the strongest influence, while current ripples are nearly irrelevant. When trained models are applied to measured machines, classification is slightly overestimated due to unmodeled material degradation and losses. An autoencoder applied to harmonic orders produces clearly distinguishable mean squared errors between test and fault states, maintaining the same machine gradation as the supervised approach. Future work will focus on dynamic operation classification, specifically during ramp-up conditions.
output: In this article the tolerance classification with a transient drive simulation of a PMSM is studied. First, various tolerance combinations are built with DOE and the associated machine designs are simulated in combination with a load machine, an inverter and a speed controller with a subordinate field-oriented current controller. The resulting torque and currents are analyzed as required for the classification. From the time data, the torque and current ripples as well as the frequency spectra are calculated. In the literature different equations are given which describe the orders that are influenced by the tolerances. In contrast, for this machine, the deduced relevant orders are multiples of the pole pair number and the order of the cogging torque which indicates that the state-of-the-art EoL and CM evaluation have to be revised for a conclusive statement of the machine’s quality. The performed classification reveals that SVM as supervised ML model is most suitable for the two application scenarios EoL test and eccentricity ranking with an adequate classification rate. The sensitivity analyses indicate a major influence of the single and twofold cogging torque order in contrast to the ripples which are nearly irrelevant for the classification. If the trained ML models are applied on the measured machines then the machines are classified slightly too high. An evident reason can be material degradation and losses that are not considered in simulation. As unsupervised algorithm the autoencoder is applied on the harmonic orders. The obtained result shows that the MSE between test and fault are clearly distinguishable. The measured machines are also classified too high, but the gradation of the machines is the same as computed with SVM. In further research, the analysis of the harmonic orders and the classification in dynamic operation, e.g. in ramp-up, is intensified.

The CMMLPM enhances ML system evaluation by consolidating multiple, often conflicting, metrics into a single value for hyperparameter optimization. In the context of ML classifications, five key performance measures are typically considered: accuracy (w1); precision (w2); recall (w3); F1-score (w4); and training time (w5). Notably, the training time (w5) demonstrates an SIB trend, whereas the other measures exhibit a BIB trend. These performance measures have been used in various research studies [27], [28], [29]. The CBPM considers a single performance measure by combining two conflicted performance measures in ML training [18]. This single combined measure can be represented through the CMMLPM by assigning the special weight value set which is as follows:

W := {w1, w2, w3, w4, w1, w5} = {1, 0, 0, 0, 1} (24)

where w1 is the weight value of accuracy and w5 is the weight value of the training time. It also indicates that only accuracy and training time are considered to construct CBPM and the rest of them are not considered. From (9) and (24), the standardized EWs are determined as follows:

bw1 = bw5 = 1/2, bw2 = bw3 = bw4 = 0.

The choice depends on the context and relative importance of metrics, ensuring flexibility in evaluating ML systems.

Although several techniques for MCDA have been introduced, the weight values in the set W may be chosen arbitrarily, depending on the purpose of an ML-based system.

III. CASE STUDIES

This section applies the CMMLPM to three real-world systems to select optimal ML algorithms. The first case selects the best algorithm for a credit card fraud detection system [27]. The second case develops a ML-based biometric authentication system and links CMMLPM to CBPM [18, 28]. The third case selects optimal models for a malware detection system [29]. All cases use actual datasets to demonstrate CMMLPM's adaptability across different applications. While effective, the methodology faces challenges including subjective weight allocation and the need for dynamic adaptability [18].

III. CASE STUDIES

This section demonstrates the practical cases of the CMMLPM which are targeted for selecting the best ML algorithms of systems. As mentioned before, this newly proposed performance measure is flexible because it is capable of being adapted to any kind of measurable multiple performance measures. The first study case is an example for choosing the best ML algorithm for the credit card fraud detection system [27]. Another study case is targeted to develop a new ML-based biometric authentication system and illustrates how CMMLPM could be applied for selecting the best ML model for the security system [28]. This study case additionally demonstrates the connection between CMMLPM and CBPM [18]. The third study is about selecting the best ML models for a malware detection system [29]. Notably, all the study cases bring the actual datasets from the real-world cases and demonstrate how CMMLPM could be adapted for evaluating the ML models in various systems. The CMMLPM is one of the best and effective methods for selecting the best ML model within the candidates although the methodology faces challenges such as the subjective nature of weight allocation and the need for dynamic adaptability across varying applications.

instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.

The research has been conducted into this innovative type of
performance measure. The CMMLPM signifies a significant
advancement in the systematic evaluation of ML systems.
CMMLPM addresses the complexities of conflicting performance metrics, providing users with an integrated evaluation
tool that enhances decision-making. This novel approach differs from the existing metrics which only accommodates one
or two measurements at once, thereby filling a critical gap
in the literature. Despite its advancements, the methodology
encounters challenges such as the subjective nature of weight
allocation and the need for dynamic adaptability across varying applications. The framework for determining appropriate
weight allocations warrants extensive investigation, as there
is currently no definitive method for selecting suitable performance measures or assessing the significance of these
chosen metrics. One of the future research could focus on
refining the framework to enhance the objectivity of weight
assignments while ensuring broader applicability across various fields. CMMLPM offers significant contributions to ML
performance evaluation, paving the way for more comprehensive assessments and informed model selection. Its innovative
contributions and flexibility establish it as an essential tool in
both research and industry practices, promoting a more holistic
view of ML system performance.

section: ABSTRACT
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Websites are rich resources for public health information access, and readability determines comprehension. Beyond linguistic features in traditional formulas, individual reading ability is influenced by age, morbidities, and cultural background. This paper presents a reader-oriented assessment combining readability formula scores with machine learning, incorporating reader background. Machine learning algorithms were trained on a dataset of 7 readability formula scores from 160 health articles on official websites. Results show the proposed tool provides a more effective reader-oriented assessment proxy for health information readability. The study’s key significance is its reader-centeredness, incorporating diverse reader backgrounds, and its clarification of the relative effectiveness and compatibility of different medical readability tools via machine learning.
output:
Websites are rich resources for the public to access health information, and readability ensures whether the information can be comprehended. Apart from the linguistic features originated in traditional readability formulas, the reading ability of an individual is also influenced by other factors such as age, morbidities, cultural and linguistic background. This paper presents a reader-oriented readability assessment by combining readability formula scores with machine learning techniques, while considering reader background. Machine learning algorithms are trained by a dataset of 7 readability formula scores for 160 health articles in official health websites. Results show that the proposed assessment tool can provide a reader-oriented assessment to be more effective in proxy the health information readability. The key significance of the study includes its reader centeredness, which incorporates the diverse backgrounds of readers, and its clarification of the relative effectiveness and compatibility of different medical readability tools via machine learning.

section: II. RESEARCH GAPS
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: The assessment of health information understandability has relied on formula-based readability tools, which were originally developed and clinically tested for native English speakers. As English becomes the dominant language in global health education, evaluating English materials for non-native readers requires evidence to inform policy. This study addresses a research gap by evaluating the suitability of existing readability tools for non-native speaker groups. Human raters from similar cultural backgrounds evaluated online health materials published by international health authorities, achieving interrater reliability over 0.7. The study then tested the validity of readability tools and machine learning algorithms to predict understandability for international students in Australian universities, aiming to support rapid, user-adaptive evaluation of health education materials.

section: III. READABILITY MEASUREMENT
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
Measuring readability is a key step to make health information understandable to the public. Several formulas exist, including Flesch Reading Ease [20], Gunning Fog Index [21], Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level [20], Coleman-Liau Index [22], SMOG Index [23], Automated Readability Index [24], and Lensear Write Formula [25]. These formulas are easy to calculate and provide quantitative evidence based on linguistic features like word and sentence length [1]. They have supported research on assessing and improving readability across various materials [26], [27].

Readability is defined as "the level of ease or difficulty with which text material can be understood by a particular reader" [28], making it a relative concept dependent on the reader. Formula calculations rarely consider diverse reader features. The "one score fits all" approach has obvious limitations.

output:
Measuring the readability is one important step toward making the health information understandable by the public. Thanks to continuous efforts by pioneering scholars in the field, several readability formulas were developed and widely used, including Flesch Reading Ease Score [20], Gunning Fog Index [21], Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level [20], Coleman-Liau Index [22], Simple Measure of Gobbledygook (SMOG) Index [23], Automated Readability Index [24], Lensear Write Formula [25], etc. Readability formulas are easy to calculate and provide quantitative evidence to support the research, as the formulas are built based on linguistic features, like word length, sentence length, etc. shown in Table 1. These formulas have been supporting researchers' studies for assessing and subsequently improving readability of assorted types of reading materials [26], [27].

As its definition goes "...the level of ease or difficulty with which text material can be understood by a particular reader who is reading that text..." [28], readability is a relative concept which largely depends on the readers of the text. While in the calculation of readability scores by mentioned formulas, diverse features of readers are hardly considered. The idea of "one score fits all" underlying mentioned readability formulas obviously have large space for improvement on this point.

Meanwhile, several scholars employ human assessors to rate the readability difficulty of medical materials [29]. Manual practice is both time-consuming and costly [30]. And for the massive health information on the internet, human rating is far from practical [31]. Another concern of human rating is the individual bias. Inconsistency of assessment is unable to provide a reliable reference for readability estimation and suggestions for easy-to-read improvement. But it cannot be denied that human assessment takes readers' characteristics into consideration in a satisfying way, as assessors make the judgement out of their backgrounds, which represents a group of people sharing similar social and cultural features. Therefore, when using human assessment results as criteria for readability estimation, inter-rater and intra-rater consistency is very important to ensure the positive use of human assessment.

section: IV. MACHINE LEARNING FOR READABILITY ESTIMATION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Machine learning (ML) offers an alternative to traditional readability estimation. While prior research established that ML methods improve accuracy over formula-based approaches, existing studies often group readability by author grade or age, which does not reflect reader capability. Some studies use human labelling to address this, yet they frequently ignore labeler demographics, which can introduce bias due to varying reading perceptions across groups. Additionally, prior work often dismisses the value of traditional formulas, focusing instead on 'superficial' lexical and syntactic features. This study argues these formulas retain value and proposes a hybrid model. Using 160 infectious disease articles from Australian websites, the research combines traditional readability statistics with ML to create reader-oriented assessment models. This is the first empirical study to combine these methods for English health information readability, examining how specific reader characteristics affect perceived difficulty.
output:
Machine learning (ML) provides an alternative way to estimate readability of written texts. Applying ML method into
readability assessment is not new, and numerous scholars
have come to the consensus that ML methods can help to
improve current readability estimation. In ML, readability
estimation is treated as a process of classiﬁcation, and ML
techniques work as a classiﬁer to predict which readability
level the text belongs to, with the guidance of multiple statistical features. This approach enjoys the advantage that the
whole process is data-driven, and the data are obtained automatically, with less manual labor and human bias involved.
Several studies introduce ML methods into readability
estimation, in a hope to include more linguistic features in
the evaluation process than traditional readability formulas
do. Variables processed by ML methods in previous studies were enlarged from grammatical features to semantic

extent [31]–[33]. Si and Callan conducted preliminary work
of using unigram language model to predict the difﬁculty of
reading science web pages [32]. They argued that readability
formulas ignore the content information in the evaluation,
so they used unigram to represent the content in their experiment. The result showed that the proposed method achieved
more accurate assessment for readability of science web
pages. With the help of a variation of the multinomial naïve
Bayes classiﬁer, Collins-Thompson and Callan captured
semantic difﬁculty across grade levels [31]. It concluded
that reasonably accurate readability measures can be built
by using simple statistical language modelling techniques.
Similarly, another study deployed Support Vector Machine
to classify queries from different grade categories [33]. Both
syntactic and semantic features were derived from queries,
and the model worked better than readability formulas.
However, when applying the ML techniques, researchers
grouped readability levels according to the grade or the
age of the author in advance. Then, they tested the model
accuracy through comparing the prediction results with the
grouping. Unfortunately, the grade or the age of authors
cannot represent the readability level because the readability
is assessed from the perspective of readers rather than the
authors. In other words, the grade or age of the author does
not necessarily equal to the grade or age of readers who can
understand the writing of the very author. This would directly
inﬂuence the statistical modelling and prediction accuracy.
Some other researchers also apply ML into readability
evaluation. They labelled the readability levels of texts by
human, rather than grade or years of education. Of course,
human labelling results is more reader oriented. What’s more,
it gives the ML techniques a full play as this approach is
more sophisticated at learning the regularities at training
phase, so as to be more accurate at approximating the human
results at testing phase [34]. In many studies, when employing human to label, researchers would disregard features
of human labelers in ML approach [33]–[36]. Even though
they have described the demographic features or education
background of the human labelers in their studies, these
features were not taken into consideration in the analysis
or discussion. This also supports the studies concluding that
human labelers do less well in some studies, because different
groups may have different understandings of reading level for
the same text [37]. These features are worthy being studied,
because the human labelers share similar backgrounds, and
the use of ML can be a means of tuning the readability models
to the needs of a particular group of readers.
Another neglect in previous ML approach in readability assessment studies is the value of traditional readability formulas. Literatures mostly extract linguistic features
at lexical, syntactical and textual level as ML features to
study [38]–[43]. Undoubtedly, these features inﬂuence the
readability level of texts, but the studies tend to deny the
value of traditional formulas as they were developed based
on ‘superﬁcial’ features of word and sentence length. This
study argues that the traditional readability formulas may
have their values in judging readability levels, therefore,
the study deploys statistics by traditional readability formulas
as features of texts to train and test ML models, so as to
combine traditional readability formulas together with ML
approach to better serve the readability studies.
Given
this
context,
this
study
presents
automatic
readability assessment models based on a case of 160 infectious diseases articles on websites in Australia. The models are developed based on mentioned readability formulas
and human evaluation for the purpose of supporting the
readability evaluation with concrete statistical evidence and
considering reader characteristics in the evaluation. And
ML methods are adopted to approximate human readability
assessment results, and the proposed reader-oriented readability models can adjust themselves according to speciﬁc
reader features. To our best of knowledge, this study is the
ﬁrst co-designed empirical study that examines the reading
difﬁculties of infectious disease health information online
in English language and uses a mix methodology to build
up the readability assessment models, combining existing

section: V. METHODOLOGY — A. STUDY DESIGN
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: This study evaluated medical readability through a three-step process. First, human assessors rated infectious disease materials, and these results served as the golden standard for labeling data. Second, seven traditional readability formulas scored the same materials to provide statistical features for model training. Third, nine machine learning tools were trained and tested against the human ratings to validate the proposed models. The study design prioritized a reader-centered perspective, requiring adaptive models to reflect diverse reader competencies across cultural, social, and educational backgrounds. Ultimately, the machine learning approach approximated human judgment, producing readability assessments similar to manual human ratings.
output:
This study of medical readability evaluation consisted of three steps. First, the materials on the topic of infectious diseases were rated manually by human assessors, and human rating results are treated as a golden standard for readability assessment. This was also the labelling procedure for ML training and testing later. Second, seven popular readability formulas were deployed to get readability scores of infectious diseases in a traditional manner. Multiple rating scores provided statistics for ML to build up models for readability evaluation. Third, nine ML tools were trained with mentioned data and tested with reference to human rating result to verify the proposed models.

The design of this study emphasized that readability is assessed from the perspective of readers, which requires that the assessment model must be adaptive enough to reflect different groups of readers’ competences to understand the medical materials, because in reality, readers are so diverse in cultural, social and educational backgrounds. In other words, a reader-oriented readability evaluation model is realized by ML method, which is actually approximating itself to a human rating process, ending up with similar human judgement of readability.

section: V. METHODOLOGY — B. DATA COLLECTION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: We investigated methods to estimate the readability of online infectious diseases education texts. Materials were sourced from credible international health websites, including Health on the Net [44], Australian Government Department of Health [45], and State Ministry of Health [46], [47]. A total of 1,200 articles were collected, and 160 were randomly selected as samples. Human assessors, screened for advanced bilingual skills but limited medical knowledge, rated the 160 samples on a 10-point Likert scale based on instant understanding. Their ratings were standardized using z-scores as the final human readability scores. Seven readability formulas were applied to each sample: Flesch Reading Ease Score [20], Gunning Fog Index [21], Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level [20], Coleman-Liau Index [22], SMOG Index [23], Automated Readability Index [24], and Lensear Write Formula [25]. These seven scores served as statistical features to train and test machine learning models.

In this study, we investigated methods to estimate the
readability level of online medical information, speciﬁ-
cally, infectious diseases education texts for the public. The
source of materials is credible international health websites,
i.e., Health on the Net [44], Australian Government Department of Health [45], State Ministry of Health [46], [47].
A total of 1,200 individual articles of varying length were
collected, and 160 of them were selected randomly as samples
to study in the present study, covering different readability

Human assessors were asked to read and rate all the sample

from non-English speaking families, with advanced bilingual skills and high education level, yet limited medical
knowledge about infectious diseases. Each assessor was
presented with 1,200 materials individually. They were
requested to rate the readability of the materials on a 10-point
Likert scale with their subjectively instant understanding of a
text. The one-point indicated no effort would require from
the readers to understand the text, and the text appeared to be
extremely easy to understand. The ﬁve-point would require
some effort in reading to understand with the overall reasonable understandability, whereas the 10-point indicated the
highest level of understandability despite the enormous effort
from the readers, they could still feel confused or lost after

inﬂuence of individual bias. The rating results of assessors
are standardized with z score as the ﬁnal readability score by
human.

section: V. METHODOLOGY — C. DEVELOPING ML MODELS
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Using seven medical resource readability formulas, we constructed and compared nine ML models: XGBoost Tree, Random Trees, Bayes Net, Random Forest, C&R Tree, C5.0, CHAID, Quest, and Neural Net. We converted standardized human evaluation scores into binary data: scores between 5.180 and 6.379 were classified as Band 1 (higher readability), and scores between 6.379 and 7.577 as Band 2 (lower readability). The ML models predicted group affiliation (high versus low readability) based on automatic evaluation results from seven instruments: Flesch Reading Ease, Gunning-Fog Index, Flesch-Kincaid US Grade Level, Coleman-Liau Index, SMOG Index, Automated readability index, and Lensear Write Formula.

Using the seven medical resource readability evaluation formulas, we constructed and compared the performance of nine ML models: XGBoost Tree, Random Trees, Bayes Net, Random Forest, C&R Tree, C5.0, CHAID, Quest, and Neural Net. Figure 1 (data presented in Tables 3, 4) shows the gains of the different ML models at the model training and testing stages. In ML, information gain is often exchangeable with Kullback–Leibler divergence, or the amount of information gained about a random variable or signal from observing another random variable. In our study, we used the seven well-established medical resource readability evaluation tools to predict the likely outcomes of the target variable under investigation, i.e., the human judgement of medical material readability.

The development of ML models is known as decision tree training, which identifies predictor variables and their associated value ranges in the classification process of the categorical target variable values. Specifically, in our study, the ML modelling explores the value ranges of the formula-based readability tools which can be used as effective variables to explain the variations in the readability scores by independent human assessors. The symbol $ indicates the estimated value/state of the target variable. In order to train the ML models, we first converted the standardized scores of the human evaluation into binary data (Table 2). Human evaluation scores between 5.180 and 6.379 were classified as Band 1 (TILEN – higher readability or lower difficulty group of texts); and human evaluation scores between 6.379 and 7.577 were classified as Band 2 (TILEN-lower readability or higher difficulty group of texts). The ML models predicted the probability of the group affiliation (high readability 1 versus low readability 2) of each text based on the automatic evaluation results of the seven medical readability instruments (Flesch Reading Ease, Gunning-Fog Index; Flesch-Kincaid US Grade Level; Coleman-Liau Index; SMOG Index; Automated readability index; Lensear Write Formula).

Tables 3 and 4 show incremental gains of ML models. The BEST-Scores refers to the ensembled model based on optimization of 9 discrete ML models. At the initial 10% training stage, BEST scores_TILEN explained 20.339% of total variation in binarized target variable scores (readability based on human assessment). Model gains increased steadily by an average 20% in the next four stages, completing after analyzing 50% of training corpus texts. In testing, BEST scores_TILEN first explained 19.047% of total variation in testing corpus texts, completing after evaluating 60% of testing corpus. Tables 3 and 4 show the incremental gains of the ML models. The BEST-Scores refers to the ensembled model based on the optimization of the 9 discrete ML models. In the model training stage, at the initial 10% level, the ensembled model ($BEST scores_ TILEN$) explained as much as one fifth (20.339%) of the total variation of the binarized scores of the target variable, i.e. the readability of infectious disease educational resources based on the human assessment. By contrast, C&R Tree, C5.0, CHAID and Quest had better performance at the model testing stage, but less effective performance at the model training stage. The three best ML models were XGBoost Tree ($XGT-Scores$), Random Trees ($R-Scores$) and Bayes Net ($B-Scores$) which completed the classification after analyzing 60% of the infectious disease corpus texts in both the model training and testing stages.

Figures 2 shows the classification of the target variable (human evaluation of the readability of infectious disease educational resources) using Flesch Reading Ease and Lensear Write Formula scores as the two large predictor variables (predicator importance: 25, 18, respectively). Medical texts about infectious diseases were classified into two contrastive groups: Y-axis shows the predicted group affiliation of medical: Band 1 included texts of higher readability (human-based evaluation of difficulty scores ranging between 5.18-6.38); Band 2 clustered texts of lower readability (human evaluation of difficulty scores ranging 6.38 and 7.58). X-axis shows the Flesch Reading Ease (FRE) scores generated automatically by the formula. XGBoost Tree identified two value ranges of Flesch Reading Ease Scores: 0-50 and 50-100. In Figure 2, a large number of medical texts of higher readability (Band 1 on Y-axis: $XGT-Scores_Bin$) have FRE values between 38-85; by contrast, the majority of medical texts of lower readability (Band 2 on Y-axis) have FRE scores between 0-38. These value ranges were identified by XGBoost as key grammatical and lexical features (averaged sentence lengths in words and averaged word lengths in syllables) of medical texts on infectious diseases. Lensear Write Formula was used as another important predicator variable in the XGBoost Tree modelling process. In Figure 2, within the cluster of medical texts of higher readability ($XGT: Band 1$), the majority of texts had Lensear Write Formula scores between 0-15; whereas within medical texts of lower readability ($XGT: Band 2$), a large number of texts had Lensear Write Formula scores between 15-20. Findings in Figure 2 suggest that higher readability (5.18-6.38 on 1-10 difficulty scale) tends to be associated with higher Flesch Reading Ease scores (38-85) and lower Lensear Write Formula scores (0-15); by contrast, lower readability of medical texts on infectious diseases (6.38 and 7.58 on 1-10 difficulty scale) tends to be associated with lower Flesch Reading Ease Scores (0-38) and higher Lensear Write Formula scores (15-20). The effectiveness of the other predictor variables (the other 5 automatic medical readability formula) was largely reduced compared with the FRE scores and Lensear Write Formula. For example, in Figure 3, most texts of both higher and lower readability clustered within the value range of 0 and 20 of Coleman-Liau Index scores, reflecting the limited effectiveness of this predictor variable in separating medical resources of varying reading difficulties.

With the Random Tree Model, the predictor importance of Flesch Reading Ease (FRE) scores remains the largest predicator (0.35). This was followed by Lensear Write Formula (0.17) and Coleman-Liau Index (0.11). Figures 4 and 5 show the decision tree modelling outcomes of the Random Tree Model. Similar to the findings presented in Figures 2 and 3 of the XGBoost Tree Model, Flesch Reading Ease (FRE) scores and Lensear Write Formula scores facilitated the automatic classification process. The value range between 40 and 85 on the Flesch Reading Ease scale characterized the higher readability of medical resources on infectious diseases (data points marked by their group affiliation of 1 along the Y-axis of $R-Scores$). By contrast, the lower value range of 0 to 40 of the FRE scores proved to be indicative of medical texts of lower readability (illustrated by their affiliation to $R-scores 2$ along the Y-axis). On the other hand, medical resources of higher readability (clustered at the bottom of the graph) tended to be marked by cold colors (dark to bright blue and bright green), indicating lower Lensear Write Formula scores between 0 to 15. Medical resources of higher difficulty (clustered at the top of the graph) were distinguished by relatively warmer colors in Figure 4 (bright green to orange), linked with relatively higher Lensear Write Formula scores of between 15 and 25. Figure 5 shows the classification result of the Random Tree Model using Gunning Fog Index and Coleman-Liau Index as the predicator variables. Echoing the findings presented in Figure 3, neither of these two readability tools proved effective in separating medical texts of lower versus higher readability scores based on the human evaluation.

output: Health information readability assessment represents an increasingly complex issue in health education research and health resource development, given the use of English as the dominant language in global health education and promotion. Our study explored the effectiveness of using machine learning to predict the readability of health materials for non-English speaking people, with a particular focus on international students enrolled in tertiary institutes of English-speaking countries (Australia, in this case). The selection of human raters from very similar language and cultural backgrounds, the same age group (18-25), and educational levels (university graduates) has ensured the consistency of the evaluation results, and subsequently, the precision, effectiveness of the machine learning algorithms developed to predict the readability of health materials for this reader group. In future research, more experiments are needed to develop models to predict health information suitability for different people, as it is suspected that for diverse readerships, the accuracy of the models may well vary. Further, readability tools rely on a very small number of linguistic and textual features such as average word length and average sentence length. This has largely simplified the complex research topic of health information accessibility. More linguistically rich health information analysis is required to allow the discovery of new linguistic interventions and methods to improve the readability of health information for diverse readers. This can be achieved through introducing more linguistically rich text annotation, analysis using natural language processing technologies.

Received 2 April 2025, accepted 30 April 2025, date of publication 5 May 2025, date of current version 23 May 2025.

Comparative Study of Machine Learning and Deep Learning Models for Early Prediction of Ovarian Cancer

HARDIK DHINGRA AND ROOPASHRI SHETTY
Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Manipal Institute of Technology, Manipal Academy of Higher Education, Manipal, Karnataka 576104, India
Corresponding author: Roopashri Shetty (roopashri.shetty@manipal.edu)

ABSTRACT Ovarian cancer remains one of the most difficult gynecological cancers to detect early, often resulting in poor survival rates. This study presents a comparative analysis of machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) models for the early prediction of ovarian cancer using clinical and biomarker data. The dataset undergoes comprehensive preprocessing, including handling missing values, outlier removal, normalization, and dimensionality reduction via PCA. Feature selection methods such as Feature Importance, Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE), and autoencoder-based techniques are employed to enhance model performance. Various classifiers, including KNN, SVM, Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and deep networks like ANN, FNN, CNN, and RNN, are evaluated. Ensemble models such as Bagging, AdaBoost, Stacking, and XGBoost are also implemented. Our results show that the Feedforward Neural Network (FNN), combined with autoencoder-based feature selection, achieved the highest accuracy (85.71%), indicating its potential as a reliable predictive model for ovarian cancer. This comparative study highlights the significance of integrating optimized preprocessing, feature engineering, and model selection for effective early diagnosis.

INDEX TERMS Autoencoders, data preprocessing, deep learning, ensemble learning, feature selection, machine learning, medical diagnosis, ovarian cancer.

section: I. INTRODUCTION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
Ovarian cancer is a fatal gynecological malignancy with low survival rates due to asymptomatic early progression and lack of reliable diagnostic methods [1, 2]. Traditional screening has limited sensitivity, often detecting disease only in advanced stages [2]. Developing accurate, non-invasive, and cost-effective early detection mechanisms is critical for improving patient outcomes [3].

Machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) are influential tools in medical diagnostics capable of analyzing complex data and uncovering hidden patterns [4]. This study aims to develop accurate ML and DL-based models for ovarian cancer detection by optimizing feature selection and evaluating classification strategies using clinical and biomarker data [5]. The contribution is determining the optimal pipeline for robust prediction.

The ovarian dataset from a secondary source was preprocessed to ensure data quality, involving outlier removal, missing value handling, Principal Component Analysis (PCA) for dimensionality reduction, and normalization [6, 7]. Four baseline ML classifiers—K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Logistic Regression (LR), and Random Forest (RF)—were employed to assess predictive performance [5]. Feature selection techniques, including Feature Importance Graph, Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE), Univariate Selection, and Correlation Analysis, were applied to refine the dataset [8]. Baseline classifiers were reassessed using the refined feature set to quantify accuracy improvements.

Ensemble learning techniques, including Stacking, Bagging, XGBoost, and AdaBoost, were incorporated to improve generalization and boost classification accuracy [9]. Additionally, the effectiveness of deep learning models—Artificial Neural Networks (ANN), Feedforward Neural Networks (FNN), Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN), and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN)—in detecting intricate data patterns was explored [10]. An autoencoder-based feature selection approach was also employed to assess its impact on classification performance [6].

This study systematically examines these techniques to determine the optimal combination of preprocessing, feature selection, and classification methods for ovarian cancer prediction. Successful outcomes could aid in developing more accurate, scalable, and accessible diagnostic tools, helping healthcare professionals detect ovarian cancer earlier and enhance patient survival rates.

Ovarian cancer is among the most aggressive and fatal gynecological malignancies, primarily due to its asymptomatic progression in the early stages and the absence of reliable diagnostic methods for timely detection [1]. Traditional screening approaches, such as imaging techniques and biomarker-based blood tests, have limited sensitivity and specificity, often detecting the disease only in its advanced stages when treatment options are less effective [2]. Consequently, one of the main reasons behind cancer-related mortality among women is Ovarian Cancer. The critical challenge in combating this disease lies in developing early detection mechanisms that are accurate, non-invasive, and cost-effective, which could significantly improve survival rates and patient outcomes [3].

The associate editor coordinating the review of this manuscript and approving it for publication was Harikrishnan Ramiah.

With the advent of data-driven methodologies, Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) have become influential tools in medical diagnostics [4]. These methods can analyze large volumes of complex data, uncovering hidden patterns and correlations that may elude traditional statistical methods. By leveraging ML and DL models, researchers aim to develop predictive models which are capable of distinguishing between benign and malignant cases with high accuracy [5]. The integration of these advanced computational techniques in ovarian cancer diagnosis presents an opportunity to enhance early detection, optimize clinical decision-making, and ultimately improve patient prognosis [3].

This study aims to develop accurate ML and DL-based models for ovarian cancer detection by optimizing feature selection, evaluating classification strategies, and identifying the most effective combination of preprocessing and modeling techniques. Establishing a baseline, four widely used ML classifiers—K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Logistic Regression (LR), and Random Forest (RF) are employed to assess their predictive performance [5]. Recognizing the importance of feature selection in enhancing model accuracy, four distinct techniques such as Feature Importance Graph, Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE), Univariate Selection, and Correlation Analysis are applied to select the most important features while removing redundant or irrelevant ones [8]. To complement traditional feature selection, an autoencoder-based feature selection, a deep learning approach that learns efficient representations of input data is also employed [6], allowing to assess its impact on classification performance.

section: II. LITERATURE REVIEW

input: Literature review reveals that machine learning and deep learning models significantly improve ovarian cancer prediction. Wang and Zhang compared ResNet, DenseNet, Vision Transformer, and Swin Transformer against expert assessments using transvaginal ultrasound; the Swin Transformer achieved an AUC of 0.92 with 87.2% sensitivity and 94.3% specificity [11]. Chen and Zhou found ensemble learning algorithms outperformed individual classifiers, improving AUC and accuracy by 19% and 16% respectively across 49 risk factors in 349 patients [12]. Li and Wang utilized ML models on SEER data; Random Forest achieved 88.72% accuracy and 82.38% AUC, while XGBoost regressor attained an RMSE of 20.61% and R2 of 0.4667, using SHAP to identify key features like histologic type and tumor stage [13]. Zhang and Huang developed a LightGBM model for early diagnosis, achieving 88% accuracy and detecting disease ~17 days before clinical confirmation, with CA125 levels as a significant indicator [14]. Huang and Liu employed XGBoost on whole-exome sequencing data from 47 patients to predict driver genes, achieving 94.6% accuracy and identifying candidates including LAMA3 and COL6A1 [15]. Liu and Zhao proposed an integrated diagnostic framework combining clinical, imaging, and genetic biomarkers using ensemble learning, achieving 91.2% accuracy and enhanced early detection [16]. Sun and Wu applied Random Forest, KNN, and XGBoost to classify ovarian cysts via transvaginal ultrasound; XGBoost performed best with 94.3% accuracy, surpassing traditional radiological evaluations [17]. Yang and Chen introduced an interpretable AI framework using SHAP to identify key diagnostic features in premenopausal and postmenopausal women; the model achieved 90.1% accuracy, highlighting age, CA125 levels, and genetic mutations as significant predictors [18]. Zhao and Lin integrated genomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic data to predict chemotherapy response; their deep learning-based multi-omics model achieved an AUC of 0.85, outperforming single-modality approaches [19]. Feng and Wang employed CNNs to analyze histopathology slides, stratifying high-risk and low-risk patients with a concordance index of 0.78 [20]. Srinivasu et al. conducted a comprehensive review of machine learning applications in healthcare, focusing on supervised and unsupervised algorithms to improve time-series metrics and heart rate data transmission accuracy [21]. Khalifa and Albadawy introduced ClinicalBench to compare clinical prediction capacities of large language models against traditional ML models across various clinical scenarios [22]. Zhang et al. offered a comprehensive review of multimodal learning techniques in healthcare, discussing how integrating multiple data sources improves diagnostic accuracy while addressing integration challenges [23]. Ali et al. concentrated on Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods in healthcare, emphasizing the importance of interpretability for transparency and trustworthiness in clinical decision-making [24]. Wang et al. conducted a systematic review on enhancing clinical trial outcome prediction with artificial intelligence, exploring how AI improves prediction accuracy to aid therapeutic intervention development [25].

input:
The research pipeline integrates machine learning and deep learning to build an ovarian cancer prediction model.

Data preprocessing includes handling missing values, removing outliers, applying Principal Component Analysis (PCA), and normalization. Four feature selection methods—Feature Importance, Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE), Correlation Analysis, and Univariate Selection—identify relevant predictors.

Four machine learning classifiers—Support Vector Machine (SVM), k-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Logistic Regression (LR), and Random Forest (RF)—are trained on the refined dataset. Comparative Study of Machine Learning and Deep Learning Models for Early Prediction of Ovarian Cancer

The dataset considered in this study [26] comprises patient records with multiple clinical and biochemical features relevant to ovarian cancer diagnosis. It includes blood test parameters such as mean platelet volume (MPV), red blood cell count (RBC), hemoglobin (HGB), and white blood cell count (WBC), which provide insights into hematological conditions. Additionally, tumor markers like human epididymis protein 4 (HE4), alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and cancer antigen 125 (CA125) are included, aiding in identifying malignancies. Metabolic indicators such as glucose, creatinine, calcium levels, and liver function enzymes further contribute to understanding patient health profiles. The dataset encompasses both pre- and post-menopausal cases, allowing for a comprehensive analysis of ovarian cancer risk factors. Given the critical nature of early detection, feature selection and model optimization play a significant role in improving predictive accuracy.

III. METHODOLOGY — B. DATA PREPROCESSING

A preprocessing pipeline was implemented to ensure model reliability. The pipeline transformed raw data into a structured format for classification (Fig 2).

1) HANDLING MISSING VALUES
Medical datasets often contain incomplete records due to data entry errors or unavailable results [27]. Ignoring missing values introduces bias or reduces sample size, negatively impacting performance [28]. Various strategies exist depending on the missing data proportion. Missing Completely at Random (MCAR), Missing at Random (MAR), and Missing Not at Random (MNAR) describe different missingness mechanisms [29]. Deletion removes rows or columns with missing data. Imputation replaces missing values; mean or median substitution is used for numerical data, with median preferred for skewed distributions [32]. Mode imputation replaces missing categorical values [31]. Advanced methods like K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) or regression impute based on data patterns [33]. An indicator variable can denote missingness if significant [30]. In this study, median imputation was chosen because it is robust to outliers and efficient for medical datasets with skewed feature distributions [34]. Deleting data was avoided as it reduces sample size [35], and while advanced imputation offers precision, it adds unnecessary complexity [36].

2) REMOVING OUTLIERS
Outliers are data points deviating considerably from the majority of the dataset [37]. They can deform models, affect performance, and lead to misleading interpretations. Causes include measurement errors, natural variations, and experimental errors [38]. Detection methods include the Z-Score method, which flags values beyond ±3 standard deviations from the mean [39]. The Interquartile Range (IQR) method uses the 25th and 75th percentiles to identify outliers [40]. Visualization techniques like boxplots and histograms also reveal outliers [41]. Machine learning methods such as Isolation Forests and Local Outlier Factor (LOF) detect anomalies based on isolation or neighborhood density [42, 43]. Handling methods include removal if due to error, or transformations like log or power to reduce impact. Capping (Winsorization) replaces extremes with valid nearest values, and binning groups extremes into categories [44]. In this study, the Z-score method was selected as a simple and efficient detection technique [45]. Given that many medical features follow a normal distribution, standard deviations effectively flag extremes. Unlike machine learning methods requiring more computation, or IQR better suited for skewed data, Z-score is straightforward for this dataset.

3) NORMALIZING DATA
Normalization scales numerical features consistently to prevent model bias toward features with larger magnitudes [46]. This is critical because algorithms such as SVM, KNN, and Neural Networks are sensitive to feature magnitude variations [47]. Unnormalized features with larger ranges can overpower learning, causing inaccurate predictions. Normalization also improves gradient descent convergence and enhances data interpretability and visualization [48]. Common techniques include Min-Max Scaling, which maps data to a predefined range (usually [0,1]), though it is sensitive to outliers [49]. Z-Score Standardization transforms data to have a mean of 0 and standard deviation of 1, suiting normally distributed data [50]. Log Transformation reduces skewness, particularly in right-skewed distributions like financial data [51]. Robust Scaling uses median and interquartile range, making it resistant to outliers [52]. Technique choice depends on data nature and algorithms used [53]. Min-Max Scaling is useful when a known range exists and algorithms like KNN or Neural Networks are applied. Z-Score Standardization is appropriate for normally distributed data and algorithms like SVM or Linear Regression. Log Transformation is best for highly skewed data.

In this study, Z-Score Standardization was implemented because it scales features consistently without being affected by outliers [49]. It works well for magnitude-sensitive models like SVM and Neural Networks. Unlike Min-Max Scaling, it does not require a fixed range and is ideal for medical data often following a normal distribution, ensuring better performance.

4) FEATURE SCALING
High-dimensional datasets often contain redundant or highly correlated features, increasing computational complexity and negatively affecting performance [51]. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) reduces dimensionality while retaining essential information [52]. PCA transforms data into a lower-dimensional space, retaining maximum variability [53]. This improves computational efficiency and model performance via noise removal and feature prioritization [54]. PCA identifies features contributing most to data variance [55]. III. METHODOLOGY — B. DATA PREPROCESSING

To ensure the reliability and accuracy of the machine learning models in prediction of ovarian cancer, a robust data preprocessing pipeline was implemented. The preprocessing steps, as illustrated in Fig 2, transformed the raw dataset into a structured and refined form suitable for classification. The major steps involved in preprocessing are as follows:

1) HANDLING MISSING VALUES

Medical datasets often have incomplete records due to data entry errors or unavailable test results [27]. Ignoring these missing values can introduce bias or reduce the sample size, which can negatively impact model performance [28]. To handle missing values, various strategies are employed depending on the proportion of missing data. There are different types of missing data: Missing Completely at Random (MCAR), which refer to a scenario where missing values occur randomly with no identifiable patterns or relationships; Missing at Random (MAR), refers when the missing value probability relies on observed data but not on the missing data itself; and Missing Not at Random (MNAR), where the missing values are influenced by unobserved data, making imputation more challenging [29].

FIGURE 2. Data preprocessing pipeline.

Several methods are available for handling missing data [30]. Deletion methods involve removing rows with missing values, particularly when they are few, or removing entire columns if a significant proportion of values are missing, especially if the column is not essential for the analysis. On the other hand, imputation methods focuses on replacing all the missing values [31]. For numerical data, techniques such as mean or median imputation can be applied [32], where missing values are substituted with the mean or median of the corresponding column. Median imputation is preferred for skewed distributions. For categorical data, methods like mode imputation can be used, which uses the most frequent category to replace missing values. Methods like backward and forward fill are generally utilized in time-series data, where missing values are replaced by the last or next available value, respectively. More advanced imputation methods, like predictive imputation, models such as K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), regression, or deep learning to calculate and fill missing values based on patterns in the data are used [33]. If the missing values themselves are significant, an indicator variable can be created, where a binary column is added to denote the presence of missing data (1 for missing and 0 for not). This can help retain the informative nature of missingness in certain situations.

In this study, median imputation was chosen because it handles missing values efficiently without being influenced by extreme values. In contrast to mean imputation, which can be distorted by outliers, the median is more robust, making it a better choice for medical datasets where some features may have skewed distributions. Deleting data is not an option since it would reduce the sample size [34], and while advanced methods like KNN or regression-based imputation could provide more precise estimates, they add unnecessary complexity [35]. Median imputation offers an optimal blend of simplicity, efficiency, and accuracy for our dataset [36].
