IV. EXPERIMENTS

This section provides an overview of the experiments conducted based on the research methods discussed in Section III. The evaluation of the algorithms focuses on three main tasks: article generation, text paraphrasing, and code generation. For machine learning algorithms, we selected text classification models such as SVM, random forest (RF), logistic regression (LR), Gaussian naive Bayes (GNB), and k-nearest neighbor (KNN). In the context of deep learning algorithms, we utilized RNN and their variations including gated recurrent unit (GRU) [26], long short-term memory (LSTM) [27], bidirectional GRU (BiGRU), bidirectional LSTM (BiLSTM), text convolutional neural network (TextCNN) [28], as well as the pretrained bidirectional encoder representations from transformers (BERT) [29] model based on Transformer [30]. Generally speaking, machine learning algorithms are suitable for data with simple features that are easy to distinguish, while deep learning algorithms are suitable for big data processing. All selected models are commonly used in the field of text classification and training of all models are performed on a single GeForce RTX 3090 (24 GB) GPU. The dataset is divided into training set, validation set, and test set, with the ratio of 14:3:3, and all data partitions are randomly assigned. The models are first trained on the training set, and the best performing model on the validation set is selected and tested on the test set. PCA is used for dimension reduction in the machine learning models, resulting in a dimensionality of 512. For the models employed in these three tasks, machine learning models were trained using the scikit-learn framework with default parameters. For classical deep learning models, specific hyperparameters are listed in Table I. The parameter seq_length defines the fixed input length for the model; text longer than this length is truncated, while shorter text is padded with a value of 0. The dropout parameter represents the probability of deactivating neurons, helping to prevent overfitting. embed_dim indicates the dimension of the word embeddings, analogous to dimensionality reduction via PCA in machine learning. hidden_dim denotes the number of hidden layers, adjusted in the experiments based on changes in seq_length. Parameters num_filters and filter_size specify the size and number of convolutional kernels in the TextCNN model, which uses 1-D convolution for feature extraction. The patience parameter sets the threshold for the early stopping mechanism, where training halts if validation loss does not decrease after a set number of iterations. Finally, vocab_size defines the vocabulary size for the dataset. As a pretrained model, the BERT model was fine-tuned with different datasets, adjusting only the learning rate, which was set to 10−5 during training.

The results of the TPT are shown in Tables III and IV and in Fig. 4(a) and (e)–(h). In comparison to the article generation experiment, we categorized the dataset into interrogative and declarative. We first conducted combined training using all the data and recorded the performance results of the trained models on both the overall dataset and individual class data. Afterward, we retrained and evaluated all the models based on the individual class data.

Under the combined training scenario, in the overall evaluation models, the SVM model performed the best among the machine learning models, with accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score reaching 75.58%, 75.58%, 75.58%, and 75.58%, respectively. The remaining models performed poorly, with the GNB model even having an accuracy of less than 60%. Among the deep learning models, the BERT model performed the best, with evaluation metrics of 89.49%, 92.15%, 86.23%, and 88.76%.

Under the evaluation mode of individual class data, these two models still performed the best. In the interrogative sentence texts, the BERT model achieved an accuracy of 90.90%, while the SVM model achieved an accuracy of 82.32%.

In the declarative sentence texts, the BERT model achieved an accuracy of 88.04%, while the SVM model achieved an accuracy of 68.60%. In this task, compared to the overall evaluation, the performance slightly improved in the evaluation of interrogative sentence data, while the evaluation performance decreased for declarative sentence data. This applies to all machine learning and deep learning models. Furthermore, except for the BERT model, the other models showed significant fluctuations in performance across different datasets. The deep learning models exhibited about a 10% difference in performance between the evaluation of interrogative sentence texts and declarative sentence texts. The model with the largest fluctuation in the machine learning section (KNN) had a deviation of almost 25%.

In the case of single training, all machine learning models, except for KNN, have a slight improvement in evaluation metrics compared to combined training. Deep learning models (except BERT) have little difference compared to combined training when trained on question sentence texts, but they have a close to 3% improvement when trained on declarative sentence texts compared to combined training. As for the BERT model, its performance is worse than combined training when trained with single data, which is related to the amount of data used for fine-tuning the model.

In addition, in the case of single training, models trained on declarative sentence texts perform worse than models trained on question sentence texts, which is consistent with the conclusions obtained from combined training, further indicating the more prominent characteristics of generated data in question sentence generation.

Further analysis reveals that performance differences are closely tied to sentence type. Interrogative sentences usually follow fixed syntactic patterns and contain prominent markers (e.g., wh-words), making them easier for models to capture. Declarative sentences, by contrast, are more semantically diverse, resulting in decreased performance across models. Deep learning models, especially BERT, demonstrate strong advantages because paraphrase detection requires understanding semantic equivalence rather than surface features. However, when trained on a single class subset, BERT's performance drops due to reduced training data diversity, which limits its fine-tuning capacity. Traditional methods such as SVM, being less sensitive to data scale, sometimes maintain competitive performance in smaller data settings. These findings indicate that data complexity (syntactic structure and semantic diversity) directly affects model robustness, and deep semantic models are more adaptable to challenging cases than traditional methods.

The evaluation results of the CGT are shown in Tables V and VI and Fig. 4(c)–(d). Compared to the TPT experiment, the code generation dataset used includes five subcategories, representing different programming languages (Python, Java, C++, PHP, and JavaScript). Both combined training and single language training were conducted to obtain comprehensive results. Combined training was conducted on the overall dataset, while single training was performed on specific programming language data. Python has the largest amount of data with 13,204 samples. Java and JavaScript have a similar amount, with 10,798 and 10,267 samples, respectively. PHP has 8,256 samples, while C++ has relatively fewer samples with only 3,145.

In combined training results, SVM and BERT were the best among the machine learning and deep learning models. In terms of deep learning, the BERT model shows good overall performance with an accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score of 95.29%, 97.36%, 92.29%, and 94.61%, respectively. The accuracy of other traditional neural networks fluctuates around 93%. Both the BiGRU and BiLSTM networks show a performance improvement of nearly 1% compared to the GRU and LSTM networks, validating that bidirectional networks can enhance the model's understanding ability. Among the machine learning models, SVM performs the best with an overall performance of approximately 90%, reaching 89.85%, 90.01%, 89.85%, and 89.85% for accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score, respectively. This even surpasses the deep learning model BiLSTM. However, except for GNB, the accuracies of other models fluctuate around 80%. Regarding the evaluation results for individual programming languages, the Java language performs the best with the highest accuracy of 98.12%. The results for the other four programming languages are fairly close. For the best performing BERT model, the accuracies for C++, PHP, Python, and JavaScript are 95.52%, 95.65%, 94.69%, and 93.90%, respectively. Furthermore, these results are reflected in the designed models throughout the experiment.

In single training, overall performance was similar to combined training, with all models achieving their highest accuracy on the Java dataset. On Python, deep learning models generally improved in accuracy by 1–2%, with the exception of the TextCNN model, while machine learning models saw a decrease in performance, ranging from 1% to 4%. In Java, most models maintained similar performance to combined training, though the GNB model experienced a decrease of approximately 4%. On C++, BiGRU, BERT, SVM, and LR models showed accuracy declines of 2.32%, 1.98%, 2.41%, and 7.05%, respectively, while other models improved. Deep learning models gained between 2% and 5%, with machine learning models showing the largest improvement of 14.01% (KNN). Results on the PHP dataset were similar: most deep learning models improved slightly by around 1%, aside from the BiLSTM model, which dropped by 1.06%. Machine learning models generally decreased by 1–3%, except for a slight 0.34% gain in the GNB model.

Finally, deep learning models achieved consistent performance improvements in JavaScript, with BiGRU showing the highest increase of 2.28%, while all machine learning models saw declines. The largest decrease was observed in the GNB model, with a drop of 11.21%.

The performance variation across programming languages can be explained by differences in syntax and dataset size. Java achieves the highest accuracy because of its strict grammar and redundancy, which provide clearer statistical patterns for classification. In contrast, C++ has more flexible syntax, higher ambiguity, and the smallest dataset, leading to lower performance. Deep learning models, especially bidirectional RNNs and BERT, show advantages because they can capture long-range dependencies across tokens and code blocks, which is essential in programming language tasks. Interestingly, SVM remains competitive with some deep learning models since programming languages contain explicit keywords and operators that are easily captured by traditional feature-based methods. These results demonstrate that task type and data characteristics significantly influence model performance.

section: IV. EXPERIMENTS — D. LLM-Based Model Detection Test
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: We evaluated two zero-shot text detection methods, Fast-Detect-GPT [31] and Glimpse [32], on three tasks using different LLMs. Results on the AGT showed both frameworks outperformed machine learning models but lagged behind deep learning methods, with Fast-Detect-GPT exceeding Glimpse. Larger LLM parameter sizes improved Fast-Detect-GPT performance. In TPT and CGT, both methods yielded weaker results, characterized by high recall but low precision, indicating a tendency to overpredict machine-generated text. In text paraphrasing, short samples hindered probability distribution capture. In code generation, niche datasets limited evaluation effectiveness. Analytically, the high recall and low precision reveal poor discriminative balance, attributed to generic probability estimation without domain adaptation. Fine-tuned deep learning models, such as BERT, achieve more balanced performance by adapting to task-specific distributions. These findings confirm that while zero-shot methods offer flexibility, their reliability is limited by sensitivity to domain characteristics and data complexity.
output:
In order to verify the effectiveness of traditional machine learning and deep learning methods in text detection tasks, we introduced two latest zero-shot text detection methods: Fast-Detect-GPT [31] and Glimpse [32]. Fast-Detect-GPT is an optimized version of Detect-GPT [33]. This method introduces conditional probability curvature to capture word selection differences between LLMs and humans. Glimpse is an innovative probability distribution estimation method that can predict the complete probability distribution from partial observation data and is suitable for the detection of proprietary LLMs. Both are zero-shot detectors that do not rely on proprietary datasets for training, but require the use of LLMs for evaluation. We evaluated these two methods on three tasks based on different LLMs, and the results are shown in Table VII.

Results demonstrate that on the AGT, both frameworks exhibited superior performance, surpassing machine learning models under comparable conditions. However, they still lagged significantly behind models based on deep learning methods. Notably, Fast-Detect-GPT consistently outperformed Glimpse. The choice of LLM was a critical factor influencing the results, with Fast-Detect-GPT showing better performance when paired with models of larger parameter sizes compared to those with smaller parameters. In the TPT and CGT, both methods yielded relatively weaker results. Specifically, the recall value is high, which means that the model is easier to identify as human-written samples and has a higher false positive rate. In text paraphrasing, the predominance of short text samples posed challenges for both methods in accurately capturing probability distributions. In code generation, the samples consisted of computer science-related code, a relatively niche dataset, which proved difficult for zero-shot models to evaluate effectively. In the CGT, Glimpse generally performed better, a result closely tied to the expressive power of the selected LLMs.

Analytically, the high recall but low precision indicates that zero-shot detectors tend to overpredict machine-generated text as human-written, showing poor discriminative balance. This is largely due to their reliance on generic probability curvature estimation without adaptation to specific datasets or linguistic domains. In contrast, fine-tuned deep learning models, such as BERT, adapt to task-specific data distributions and, therefore, achieve more balanced performance. These observations confirm that while zero-shot methods are flexible, they are highly sensitive to domain characteristics and data complexity, limiting their reliability in practical detection scenarios.

IV. Experiments — E. Real-World Dataset Test

To evaluate detection methods on authentic classroom data beyond public benchmarks, we compiled a dataset of 100 samples: 50 from student submissions and 50 generated by LLMs Grok and GPT4o, focusing on computer science questions. We tested machine learning, deep learning, and LLM-based methods. Traditional machine learning and deep learning methods are well-suited for this data. The deep learning model BERT achieved an F1-score of 0.8515 on real-world data, confirming the generalizability and stability of its recognition performance. However, zero-shot methods relying on large-scale models performed poorly, often exhibiting high recall rates and misclassifying LLM-generated samples as human-written. We hypothesize this is related to the choice of evaluation models used in these methods. These findings confirm that supervised approaches perform well on real data, supporting AI-assisted detection tools. This contrast illustrates that fine-tuned models retain robustness and adaptability under noisy domain-specific data, while zero-shot detectors lack effective generalization beyond curated benchmarks. The findings highlight the importance of data-task alignment: general LLM-optimized models may fail in educational scenarios, whereas task-specific supervised approaches maintain stability.
output: Chinese higher education now tends to use process assessment, such as multiple assignments, rather than final exams. While this is positive, students may use LLMs to complete their assignments, posing a challenge for teachers and necessitating supportive detection tools. To confirm the effectiveness of machine learning and deep learning methods in real classroom cases, we compiled a test dataset from real classroom cases. The dataset contains 100 samples, 50 of which are from answers submitted by students in class, and 50 are generated by the latest LLMs Grok and GPT4o. The sample content mainly focuses on the field of computer science, including programming questions and short-answer questions. All questions are answered by students in class to ensure that they do not use external tools. This dataset reflects a realistic educational scenario in which students may use LLMs to complete formative assessments. Our goal is to evaluate how well detection models perform on authentic noisy classroom data—beyond standard public benchmarks. We tested the machine learning, deep learning, and LLM based methods mentioned earlier, and the test results are shown in Table VIII. Results show that both traditional machine learning and deep learning methods are well suited for this dataset. The classic deep learning model BERT achieved an F1-score of 0.8515 on real-world data, confirming the generalizability and stability of its recognition performance. However, zero-shot methods relying on large-scale models performed poorly, often exhibiting high recall rates. These methods tend to misclassify samples generated by LLMs as human-generated. We hypothesize that this is likely related to the choice of evaluation models used in these methods. These findings confirm that the aforementioned methods still perform well on real data, supporting the development of AI-assisted detection tools. This contrast illustrates that fine-tuned models retain robustness and adaptability even under noisy domain-specific classroom data, while zero-shot detectors lack the ability to generalize effectively beyond curated benchmark datasets. The findings highlight the importance of data-task alignment: models optimized for general LLM text may fail in realistic educational scenarios, whereas task-specific supervised approaches can maintain stability.

section: V. CONCLUSION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
V. CONCLUSION

This study evaluated traditional machine learning and deep learning models across text generation, paraphrasing, and code generation tasks, plus a real classroom dataset. Deep learning models, particularly pretrained Transformers like BERT, consistently outperform traditional methods in tasks requiring nuanced semantic understanding. Classical models like SVM remain competitive when feature structures are simple and data are limited, showing that model choice is task-dependent. Zero-shot detection methods relying on large language models show limited reliability in educational contexts, often yielding high recall but low precision. Despite these findings, the study has limitations: evaluation relies on specific datasets that may not capture the full heterogeneity of real educational assignments, deep learning models remain difficult to interpret, and traditional models struggle with cross-domain transferability. Future work will pursue three directions: 1) constructing large-scale real classroom datasets across disciplines to improve generalization; 2) co-designing educator-centered detection tools focusing on usability and integration; and 3) investigating interpretable and lightweight model designs, including attention-based visualization and domain adaptation strategies, to enhance transparency and efficiency in classroom environments. In summary, while AI-based text detection has strong technical feasibility, practical deployment in education requires balancing accuracy, interpretability, and scalability to support creativity and integrity in academic assessment. This study systematically evaluated traditional machine learning algorithms and deep learning models across three textrelated tasks, namely, article generation, text paraphrasing, and
code generation, as well as a real classroom dataset. The results highlight several key takeaways. First, while both machine learning and deep learning methods demonstrate strong
performance on controlled datasets, deep learning models, particularly pretrained Transformers such as BERT, consistently
outperform traditional methods in tasks requiring nuanced
semantic understanding. Second, classical models like SVM
remain competitive when feature structures are simple and data
are limited, underscoring that model choice is task dependent.
Finally, zero-shot detection methods relying on LLMs show
limited reliability in educational contexts, often yielding high
recall but low precision.
Despite these encouraging ﬁndings, our study has several limitations. The evaluation relies on speciﬁc datasets that may not
fully capture the heterogeneity of real educational assignments,
where writing styles, domain knowledge, and linguistic diversity
vary considerably. Deep learning models also remain difﬁcult to
interpret, which is problematic in educational contexts. In addition, traditional models, though lightweight and interpretable,
struggle with cross-domain transferability and demand repeated
ﬁne-tuning for new data distributions.
Building on these insights, future work will pursue three
directions.
1) Large-scale real classroom dataset construction: We plan
to collaborate with educators across disciplines to curate
a broader dataset covering free-response questions, essays, programming tasks, and paraphrasing exercises to
improve model generalization across contexts.
2) Educator-centered tool development: We aim to co-design
detection tools with teachers, focusing on usability, interpretability, and integration with existing platforms, enabling real-time support for formative assessments.
3) Interpretable and lightweight model design: We will investigate approaches such as attention-based visualization, attribution scoring, and class activation mapping
to enhance transparency, while exploring few-shot and
domain adaptation strategies to ensure that models remain
efﬁcient and portable in classroom environments.
In summary, while AI-based text detection shows strong technical feasibility, its practical deployment in education requires
balancing accuracy, interpretability, and scalability. Addressing
these challenges will be crucial for building reliable teacherfriendly tools that support creativity and integrity in modern
academic assessment.

Deepfake audio is synthetic AI-generated content that mimics real speech. Most prior work used the ASVSpoof or AVSpoof datasets; this study uses the Fake-or-Real dataset, created with a text-to-speech model and divided into four sub-datasets (for-rece, for-2-sec, for-norm, for-original) based on length and bit rate. section: I. INTRODUCTION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
Deepfake is a portmanteau of deep learning and fake, referring to digitally created content where original human faces or audio are swapped with computer-generated ones [1], [2]. It first surfaced on Reddit in 2017 and carries legal difficulties infringing on portraiture, reputation, and copyright, inflicting economic and reputational harm [3], [4]. Fabricated videos of politicians can cause media crises and social instability [5], [6], [7]. Audio deepfakes, AI-generated audio appearing real, have been used in criminal activities, making detection crucial [8]. Between 2018 and 2019, deepfake articles increased from 60 to 309 [8], with predictions of over 730 by 2020's end [9]. Most research focuses on video deepfakes [10].

Deepfake audio detection based purely on audio is less explored than video approaches, which utilize audio and spatio-temporal information [11]-[15]. This research aims to derive a methodology for identifying deepfake audio from real audio. Key contributions include proposing a transfer learning-based approach for deepfake detection and extending experiments on the Fake-or-Real dataset using machine and deep learning. A superior feature extraction approach using MFCC features from audio sources is employed. Results reveal that the SVM model outperforms other ML models compared to most dataset subsets, except the for-original dataset. The VGG-16 model produced highly encouraging results when applied to the for-original dataset.

Deepfake is a portmanteau of deep learning and fake. Deepfake is a type of digitally-created content in which the original human faces in a photo, video, or recording have been swapped out for computer-generated ones [1], [2]. Deepfake first surfaced on Reddit in 2017 when a user named “deepfakes” submitted a falsified video on this website with a different actor’s face. As a new technology, it unavoidably carries a slew of legal difficulties that infringe on personal interests like portraiture rights, reputation rights, and copyright and inflicts economic and reputational harm to businesses [3], [4]. Furthermore, a fabricated video of a politician or government being released will cause a media crisis, social instability, and national instability [5], [6], [7]. Audio deepfakes are AI-generated or modified audio that appears to be real. Since audio deepfakes have been employed in several criminal activities in recent years, the ability to detect them is crucial. Detecting deepfake in audio, video, and text is a broad and active research domain. Between 2018 and 2019, there was a significant increase in the number of articles about deepfake (from 60 to 309) [8]. Articles about deepfakes were expected to increase to over 730 by 2020’s end, according to predictions made on July 24 [9]. In [10] found that most focus is on video deepfakes, particularly in developing video deepfakes.

Deep Fakes are increasingly detrimental to privacy, social security, and Authenticity. However, recent works have focused on deepfake video detection, achieving greater accuracy. However, audio spoofing and calls from malicious sources are generated through deep fakes, which need a specially trained model for handling this. The deepfake audio detection based purely on audio is less explored than image and video-based approaches, as these works simultaneously utilize the audio and Spatio-temporal information in the video to train the deep learning model. However, only the audio-based classifier’s classification and detection are very significant. Hence, to this end, we proposed an approach based on multiple machine learning algorithms to improve the accuracy of the classification models using Random Forest, Decision Tree, and SVM algorithms. We provide comparative results and analysis of the baseline models. We conducted our experiments on Fake-or-Real Dataset, and there were four sub-detests.

The ASVspoof2015 [11] is the first automatic speaker verification spoofing and countermeasures dataset that stimulates research in this field. It decreases the equal error rate (EER) by less than 1.5%. Some attacks have even 50% EER. However, unknown attacks can have five times more EER. Further, in ASVspoof2017 [12], the limits of replay spoofing attack detection are worked upon. The EER of 6.73% and the Instantaneous frequency cosine coefficients (EFCC) drastically improve countermeasures performance. Then ASVspoof2019 [13] put more emphasis on countermeasures concerning automatic speaker verification and spoofed audio detection. Other than that, computer vision algorithms such as convolutional neural networks (CNN) is used low-quality audio spectrograms for synthetic speech detection [14]. The time information can be lost in CNN-based models. Hence, probabilistic forecasting with a temporal convolutional neural network is used for improving automatic speaker verification and spoofed audio detection [15].

This research aims to derive a methodology for identifying deepfake audio from non-synthetic or real audio. It provides the following contributions to identify deepfake audios effectively by resolving the restrictions discussed above:

• Propose a transfer learning-based approach to detect deepfake.
• Extend work on deepfake audio detection on the Fake-or-Real dataset by conducting detailed experiments on Fake-or-Real datasets and sub-datasets using machine and deep learning-based approaches.
• Use a superior feature extraction approach to obtain MFCC features from audio sources.
• Results reveal that the SVM model outperforms other ML models compared to other dataset sub-sets except for the for-original dataset. The VGG-16 model produced highly encouraging results when applied to the for-original dataset.

The paper will proceed as described below. Section II explains the literature review methods. The suggested approach and algorithms are described in III. The analysis and results of the experiments are provided in Section IV. Section V presents the discussion on the proposed approach. Finally, Section VI presents the overall conclusion.

To detect audio deepfakes, one must first understand the procedures of generation. As the name suggests, audio deepfake algorithms are classified into three types: Replay attack, speech synthesis, and voice conversion are all possible. This section gives the reader each subcategory’s most recent and relevant frameworks.

Audio forensics is a branch of forensics used to authenticate, enhance, and analyze audio information to aid in investigating various crimes. Audio as forensic evidence must be modified and analyzed before criminal prosecution. However, more significantly, it must be validated to demonstrate that it is genuine and has not been tampered with. To reduce the audio signal complexity and ease of reconstruction encode, the frequencies higher than the Nyquist frequency [18] are used, and the authors [19] utilized non-uniform sampling for audio subsampling.

Replay attacks consist of repeatedly playing back a recording of the voice of the intended victim. Replay attacks come in two forms, the first is far field detection, and the second is copy-and-paste detection [20], [21]. As of now, deep convolutional networks are used as a method for detecting complete replay attacks [22]. Several methods have been developed for identifying replay attacks, and they center on the characteristics that are provided in the network. The method of using deep convolutional networks to detect replay attacks was found to have an Equal Error Rate (EER) of zero percent on the ASVspoof2017 training and test dataset [12].

Speech synthesis (SS) is recreating human speech digitally, typically using computer software or hardware. TTS is a component of SS that takes in written material and outputs spoken language based on that text according to predetermined linguistic rules. Text reading and AI personal assistants are just two applications of speech synthesis. Another perk of speech synthesis is that it can mimic various voices and dialects without relying on canned recordings. Lyrebird, a powerful speech synthesis company, employs deep learning models to synthesize 1,000 sentences in a second. TTS largely relies on the quality of the speech corpus to build the system, and regrettably, creating speech corpora is expensive [23].

Speech synthesis is the artificial reproduction of human speech using software or hardware system programs. To synthesize 1,000 sentences per second, Lyrebird uses deep learning models. Therefore, WaveGlow is concerned with modifying specific time-aligned data. Incorporating information into sound files by using encoding techniques like a mel-spectrogram. A modified WaveNet vocoder is the second component. For audio data, [26], [27] used GAN-based generative models. It operates on Mel spectrograms and employs a fully convolutional feed-forward network as the generator. The authors give a summary of their recently created data set. It comprises 117,985 created audio segments of 16-bit Pulse Code Modulation(PCM) wav format and is available on zenodo.

The current study has poor performance validation and testing results detecting deep false audios. Feature-based techniques are required to improve the outputs of machine learning models. The deep learning approaches show better results but require greater training time and computational resources. Hence, the potential for machine learning approaches in deepfake detection is explored, while the limitation of handling higher feature sets and complexities can be solved through a transfer learning-based deep learning approach.

We improved upon previous feature-based algorithms by utilizing MFCC-based features, indicating considerable improvements in accuracy. Our approach outperforms the feature-based baseline by 10 to 20 percent on average across datasets. The For-norm dataset performs poorly with simple SVM algorithms, though windowing techniques combined with MFCC can perform better. We conducted experiments on machine learning algorithms categorized into statistical models (QDA, LDA, Gaussian Naive Bayes) for dimensionality reduction and noise reduction, tree-based models (Decision Tree, Extra Tree, Random Forest) that handle multidimensional data without domain knowledge, and boosting models (Ada Boost, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost) that combine weak learners to increase accuracy on feature-rich audio data. Additionally, we proposed a VGG-16-based deep learning model for the larger, superset dataset. Using transfer learning on MFCC image features, we obtained 93% accuracy using half of the original dataset, with larger data volumes correlating to higher accuracy.

section: VI. CONCLUSION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Deepfake audio detection is critical for security against scamming and spoofing. This study improves the Fake-or-Real (FoR) dataset, combining state-of-the-art audio datasets with custom deepfake audios compiled into four sub-datasets. Experiments using MFCC features and multiple machine learning algorithms achieved higher accuracy than state-of-the-art studies. Using the for-2sec dataset, SVM attained 97.57% accuracy. The Gradient Boosting classifier achieved 92.63% accuracy on the for-norm dataset. The SVM model achieved the highest accuracy of 98.83% on the for-rerec dataset. Future work will explore different MFCC window sizes and input sizes. Additional research will evaluate model robustness against audio fluctuations and distortion, and investigate few-shot learning and BERT-based models. Models will also be tested in ambient noise and reverberation conditions. Feature extraction methods such as i-vector, x-vector, combined MFCC and GFCC, and combined DWT and MFCC are planned for future investigation.

The detection of audio data is significant as an essential tool for enhancing security against scamming and spoofing. Deepfake audios have garnered significant public attention as society rapidly recognizes its possible security danger. However, deepfake audio is extensively studied in combination with Spatio-temporal data of video. This study improves upon the Fake-or-Real (FoR) dataset, which comprises state-of-the-art audio datasets and custom audios for deepfake audio classification. It is further compiled into four sub-datasets.

This study conducted experiments with multiple audio data features to detect deepfakes in audio data. This work extracts MFCC features from audio for feature engineering. Several machine learning algorithms are applied to the selected feature set to detect the deepfake audio. This approach gave higher accuracy and results in all cases than other state-of-the-art studies for audio data. This study obtained 97.57% accuracy with SVM using the for-2sec dataset compared to other ML models, while 92.63% was obtained by the Gradient Boosting classifier using the for-norm dataset. This study obtained 98.83% highest accuracy using the SVM model on the for-rerec dataset. We plan to explore the different window sizes for MFCC and various input sizes for models in the future. Future work can be done on evaluating these models against potential fluctuation and distortion in the audio signal, understanding which signal is greater. Moreover, studies on the state-of-the-art few-shot learning and Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) based models can be conducted. Furthermore, we plan to evaluate our models in ambient noise and reverberation circumstances. We intend to use feature extraction methods like i-vector, x-vector, a combination of MFCC and GFCC, and a combination of DWT and MFCC, which were not taken into account in the current scenario of experiments because it is the beginning of our journey to identify Deepfake audio.

section: ABSTRACT
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Software-Defined Networking (SDN) enables large-scale management but introduces security risks from Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks. Machine learning (ML) techniques are potent tools for anomaly detection and mitigation. This paper proposes a novel traffic classification approach for SDN environments to distinguish benign from malicious traffic using supervised ML. A unique dataset tailored for DDoS attack detection is introduced, overcoming limitations of existing datasets like unrealistic topologies and lack of public availability. Benchmarking against the CICDDoS2019 dataset validated the custom dataset's efficacy and relevance. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed random forest model, achieving 98.97% accuracy and a False Alarm Rate (FAR) of 0.023. These findings underscore the potential of ML-based approaches in enhancing network security and resilience against DDoS attacks in SDN environments.
output:
Software-Defined Networking (SDN) is a promising solution for large-scale network management that offers extensive opportunities for optimization. However, the centralized control inherent in SDN also exposes networks to security threats, notably Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks. To address these challenges, machine learning (ML) techniques have emerged as potent tools for anomaly detection and mitigation. This paper proposes a novel approach for traffic classification within SDN environments that distinguishes between benign and malicious traffic using supervised ML techniques. This study introduces a unique dataset tailored for DDoS attack detection, overcoming the limitations of existing datasets, such as unrealistic topologies and lack of public availability. Benchmarking against the CICDDoS2019 dataset validated the efficacy and relevance of the custom dataset. This research has significant implications for real-world applications, offering improved capabilities for detecting and mitigating DDoS attacks in SDN infrastructure. Experimental results demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed random forest model, achieving a remarkable accuracy of 98.97% and a minimal False Alarm Rate (FAR) of 0.023. These findings underscore the potential of ML-based approaches in enhancing network security and resilience against DDoS attacks in SDN environments, paving the way for future advancements in network-defense strategies.

section: I. INTRODUCTION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
Software-Defined Networking (SDN) offers a novel architecture for managing network infrastructure through centralized control and programmable features, enhancing flexibility and efficiency. The architecture decouples the data, control, and application planes, allowing administrators to define traffic rules at the application layer. Open-source platforms like OpenFlow and OpenDaylight foster vendor-agnostic innovation. However, the centralized controller introduces a single point of failure, making SDN environments susceptible to Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks, which can cause network-wide disruptions.

Traditional detection methods, such as IP-address-based filtering, are often inadequate due to tactics like IP spoofing. Machine Learning (ML) techniques have been integrated to enhance detection capabilities by analyzing traffic data in real time and identifying anomalous patterns from historical attack data. However, applying ML to SDN faces challenges, including the need for real-time classification in dynamic environments and the limitations of existing datasets, which often feature outdated topologies and unrealistic scenarios, leading to high false-positive rates.

This study proposes a novel approach to improve traffic classification in SDN using supervised ML techniques. By focusing on realistic network configurations and contemporary DDoS scenarios, the approach aims to overcome existing dataset limitations. The method has been validated against the CICDDoS2019 dataset, demonstrating potential for improving the security and reliability of SDN-based infrastructures.
output:
Software-Defined Networking (SDN) has emerged as a novel technology architecture that offers potential solutions to the ever-evolving challenges faced by industries in managing and optimizing the network infrastructure. Moreover, with its centralized control and programmable features, SDN has garnered significant attention because of its ability to enhance network flexibility, scalability, and efficiency. The SDN architecture comprises three distinct layers: application, control, and data. Figure 1 illustrates this layered approach, which facilitates the decoupling of the traditionally tightly integrated data, control, and application planes. In SDN, the data plane responsible for forwarding network traffic is decoupled from the control plane, which determines how traffic should be handled. This decoupling enables greater flexibility and agility in the network management. Furthermore, at the application layer, network administrators can exert control over the entire network by defining the rules and policies governing traffic behavior and resource allocation. This centralized control allows efficient network management and optimization. Open-source platforms, such as OpenFlow and OpenDaylight, have played crucial roles in SDN adoption by providing interoperable solutions that do not rely on any specific vendor. This fosters innovation and flexibility in network deployment.

However, the centralized nature of SDN introduces significant security challenges, particularly the risk of Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks. A single controller governing the entire network can become a single point of failure, thereby exposing the network to security threats. DDoS attacks, characterized by their distributed nature and orchestration from multiple sources, can overwhelm a target network or service, leading to severe disruptions in availability and performance. As illustrated in Figure 2, centralized control in SDN magnifies the impact of these attacks because a compromised controller can lead to network-wide failures. This makes DDoS attacks a critical threat to SDN environments.

Traditional methods of detecting and mitigating DDoS attacks in SDN are often inadequate owing to the unique characteristics of these networks. Techniques such as IP-address-based filtering struggle with tactics such as IP spoofing, making it difficult to distinguish between legitimate and malicious traffic. In SDN environments, DDoS attacks targeting the data plane can cause congestion and service degradation, whereas attacks targeting the control plane can have even more severe consequences, disrupting the entire network operation by compromising the centralized controller. Moreover, DDoS attacks can target network interfaces, exploit vulnerabilities in network devices, and disrupt the communication between different components of the network, leading to service outages and compromised network integrity.

The detection of DDoS attacks in SDN remains a critical challenge owing to the complexity and dynamic nature of the network traffic. Traditional detection methods often struggle to identify attacks in their early stages, leaving networks vulnerable to prolonged disruptions and potential data breaches. This has led to increased interest in the integration of Machine Learning (ML) techniques to enhance DDoS detection capabilities. ML algorithms can analyze vast amounts of network traffic data in real time, enabling the early detection of anomalous patterns indicative of DDoS attacks. By learning from historical attack data, ML models can recognize subtle deviations from normal network behavior and trigger alerts before an attack fully manifests itself.

However, applying ML techniques to SDN environments presents specific challenges that must be addressed to ensure their effectiveness. One of the primary challenges is the requirement for real-time traffic classification in highly dynamic network environments. SDNs generate a large volume of diverse traffic patterns, making it difficult to differentiate between benign and malicious traffic in real time. As a result, this complexity can lead to high false-positive rates, which degrade the network performance by misclassifying legitimate traffic as malicious. In addition, the effectiveness of ML-based DDoS detection depends on the availability of high-quality training data. Existing datasets often suffer from limitations, such as outdated network topologies, unrealistic attack scenarios, and a lack of public availability, which undermines the generalization capabilities of ML models trained on them.

To address these challenges, this study proposes a novel approach for improving traffic classification in SDN environments using supervised ML techniques. By focusing on realistic network configurations and contemporary DDoS attack scenarios, this study aims to overcome the limitations of existing datasets and enhance the detection capabilities of ML models for distinguishing between benign and malicious traffic. Furthermore, the approach has been validated against well-established datasets such as CICDDoS2019, demonstrating its potential for improving the security and reliability of SDN-based network infrastructures.

section: I. INTRODUCTION — A. LITERATURE CONTEXT AND RESEARCH
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: This section reviews existing literature on DDoS detection in SDN using ML. Previous studies have explored ML techniques but often overlook feature selection, dataset transparency, and benchmarking. Many generated datasets are unavailable or lack detailed characteristics, hindering reproducibility. Furthermore, reliance on single datasets like KDD99 or CICDDoS2019 limits generalizability. Our research addresses these gaps by introducing a novel, publicly available custom dataset generated via the Mininet emulator. We evaluate five supervised ML algorithms—logistic regression, SVM, random forest, KNN, and XGBoost—on this dataset and benchmark performance against the CICDDoS2019 dataset. This integrated approach of dataset creation, algorithm evaluation, and public benchmarking represents a significant contribution to the field.
output:
I. INTRODUCTION — A. LITERATURE CONTEXT AND RESEARCH

CONTRIBUTIONS

This section provides a critical review of the existing literature on DDoS attacks on SDN using ML techniques. Several studies have explored the application of ML to detect and mitigate DDoS attacks in SDN environments. However, a significant gap identified in these studies is the lack of attention paid to the selection of significant features within the dataset. Despite the proliferation of research in this area, existing studies have often overlooked the importance of feature selection, which is crucial for the effectiveness and efficiency of ML models for DDoS detection and mitigation. Furthermore, while numerous researchers have generated datasets for DDoS attack analysis in SDN, these datasets often lack detailed characteristics and are not publicly available. This lack of transparency and accessibility hinders the reproducibility and comparability of the research findings, thus limiting the advancement of knowledge in the field. Moreover, many studies failed to benchmark their datasets against existing public datasets or establish performance metrics, thereby limiting the evaluation and validation of their proposed methods. The absence of benchmarking not only undermines the credibility of research but also inhibits progress in the field by hindering meaningful comparisons and advancements. Overall, our research contributions stand out from previous studies in several respects.

Sahoo et al. [19] The dataset referred to as “Dataset-I” in this study, comprising 2,160,668 records with 27 features, is described as a modern DDoS dataset utilized for training and testing purposes. In contrast, Dataset-II, known as NSL-KDD, is explicitly mentioned as a refined version of the KDD’99 dataset. It is noteworthy that Dataset-I is not publicly available because its source or generation method is not explicitly stated in this study. This lack of accessibility to the dataset underscores the importance of transparency and reproducibility in research, highlighting the need for publicly available datasets to facilitate validation and comparison of results in the field of DDoS attack detection.

The study conducted by Kujur and Patel [20] was inadequate for providing detailed information regarding the characteristics and composition of the dataset. Without a thorough understanding of the properties of a dataset, it is difficult to determine its suitability and representativeness in assessing models for detecting DDoS attacks in SDN environments. Moreover, the study failed to mention any validation or verification processes for the Mendeley dataset. The absence of proper validation procedures raises concerns regarding the reliability and reproducibility of experimental findings.

Isyaku et al. [21] conducted a study comparing the effectiveness of eight ML classifiers in detecting and mitigating DDoS attacks in SDNs. They used a generated dataset, but the study lacked transparency regarding dataset sourcing and availability. This raises concerns regarding scalability and representativeness of the results. External validation of real-world datasets is crucial for enhancing the credibility and impact of the research. The study also evaluated ML classifiers based on the prediction time, learning time, and accuracy. However, it is important to consider the precision, recall, and F1-score, which offer a more comprehensive understanding of classifier performance, particularly for imbalanced datasets. Our study can improve this by incorporating additional evaluation metrics to provide a more comprehensive assessment of classifier performance, thus enhancing the overall quality of the research.

Rahman et al. [22] created an online dataset by generating normal and DDoS packets using the hping3 program in Python. They captured DDoS and normal traffic separately using Tshark to avoid confusion when labelling the dataset. DDoS traffic was flooded at a rate of 78 packets/s and captured for 30 min, whereas normal traffic was captured for 3 h to balance the dataset. Three supervised learning models, namely, Support SVM, Naive Bayes (NB), and nearest centroid (NC), were applied to classify network traffic based on applications in an SDN platform. This study lacks transparency regarding the dataset used for training and testing ML models, failing to specify its source, characteristics, and representativeness. In addition, while utilizing 24 packet-level features for DDoS detection, they do not provide a comprehensive list or description of these features, which hinders the evaluation of their effectiveness. Furthermore, the performance evaluation of the models lacks depth, as it only reports basic metrics without analyzing the model performance under different conditions or comparing it with existing approaches. Finally, the novelty of this work is diminished by the lack of comprehensive experimentation, benchmarking, or significant innovations in methodology, failing to advance state-of-the-art SDN security.

Raikar et al. [23] discussed accurate traffic classification in SDN using supervised learning techniques. This study highlights the limitations of traditional traffic classification techniques and the need for more accurate and scalable solutions. This manuscript lacks detailed information about the dataset used for training and testing supervised learning models. Without sufficient details regarding the dataset, including its size, diversity, and representativeness, it is challenging to assess the generalizability of the proposed models. Furthermore, analysis of evaluation metrics and comparisons with existing methods are lacking. The discussion of these challenges is incomplete, reducing the study’s practical relevance. Finally, the study could benefit from improved organization and clarity to enhance understanding and coherence and explore the model’s applicability in various network scenarios.

Ashodia and Makadiya [24] discussed the RF and DT algorithms to provide better accuracy and decision rates compared to other ML algorithms for detecting malicious traffic in SDN environments. This study does not discuss the validation strategies or techniques used to assess the quality, authenticity, and representativeness of the dataset. In addition, the dataset may lack diversity in terms of network topologies, traffic characteristics, and attack scenarios, potentially limiting its utility for a comprehensive performance evaluation and benchmarking of detection algorithms. Furthermore, the authors failed to disclose the provenance of the dataset employed, thereby compromising transparency and impeding their ability to replicate and validate their results. This lack of clarity regarding the origin of the dataset raises serious questions about its trustworthiness and appropriateness for the rigorous evaluation of DDoS detection methods.

Studies, such as those referenced in [25] and [26], which rely solely on individual datasets, such as CICDDoS2019 [25] and CIC DoS [26], run the risk of limiting the generalizability of their findings. By exclusively using a single dataset, these studies may overlook the broader landscape of cybersecurity threats and fail to capture the full spectrum of real-world scenarios, potentially affecting the applicability of their results. Without testing multiple datasets with varying characteristics, the robustness and applicability of the proposed system in different contexts remain uncertain. Although Sudar et al. [27] achieved notable progress in improving DDoS attack detection in network security through the utilization of ML models, their reliance on the KDD99 dataset raises concerns regarding the comprehensiveness and robustness of their methodology. The absence of benchmarking against other widely recognized datasets commonly employed in intrusion detection systems hinders the ability to conduct a comparative analysis and assess the relative strengths and weaknesses of the proposed ML models. Consequently, the conclusions drawn from this study may be compromised in terms of their credibility and applicability.

Our study introduces a novel dataset specifically designed for DDoS attack classification that is publicly available for research purposes. In section IV can be found detailed descriptions of the features of the dataset and the network topologies used in its generation. The novelty of our work lies in the integration of three distinct modules.

• The first module focuses on creating a dataset, ensuring its comprehensiveness and relevance to DDoS attack scenarios in SDN environments.

• In the second module, we employed five machine learning models for DDoS attack classification. This approach allows a comprehensive evaluation of the effectiveness of the dataset for training and testing various classification algorithms.

• The third module benchmarks our dataset against other publicly available datasets, with a particular focus on comparing its performance with that of the widely used CICDDoS2019 dataset. This comparative analysis provides valuable insights into the strengths and limitations of our dataset and its potential utility in real-world applications.

The novelty of this study can be summarized as follows:

• Novel Custom Dataset Creation: One of the primary contributions of this study was the development of a novel custom dataset using the Mininet emulator. By leveraging this emulator, we were able to simulate realistic network environments and generate data that closely reflected real-world scenarios. This custom dataset fills a crucial gap in the literature by providing researchers with a new resource for evaluating network security algorithms and methodologies.

• Evaluation of machine-learning algorithms: We conducted a comprehensive evaluation of five supervised ML algorithms; logistic regression, support vector machine, random forest, K-nearest neighbor (KNN), and XGBoost on our custom dataset. Through rigorous experimentation and analysis, we assessed the performance of these algorithms for detecting and classifying network intrusions and anomalies. Our findings shed light on the strengths and limitations of each algorithm in the context of our dataset, providing valuable insights for researchers and practitioners.

• Benchmarking Against Public Datasets: In addition to evaluating our custom dataset, we compared the performance of the machine learning algorithms on our dataset with that of CICDDoS2019, a widely used public dataset. This comparative analysis allowed us to contextualize the effectiveness of our custom dataset and algorithms relative to the established benchmarks. By identifying areas of improvement and potential research directions, our study contributes to the ongoing advancement of network security research and practices.

• Implications for Real-World Applications: Our research findings have practical implications for real-world network security applications. By identifying the most effective machine-learning algorithms for detecting network intrusions and anomalies, organizations can enhance their cybersecurity defence and mitigate potential threats more effectively. Moreover, the availability of our custom dataset enabled researchers and practitioners to conduct further studies and develop innovative solutions tailored to specific network environments and requirements.

To the best of our knowledge, previous studies have not comprehensively integrated feature selection, dataset transparency, and benchmarking against established datasets in a single study that focuses on DDoS attack classification. To address these objectives, The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related research. In Section III, we explore the machine learning models selected for SDN threat detection. Section IV outlines the dataset creation process using Mininet emulator. Section V presents the proposed framework for DDoS detection in SDN using machine learning classification. The experimental setup details are provided in Section VI, followed by the results and discussion in Section VII. Finally, Section VIII concludes the paper.
