Prior works have developed several analog antenna array BA techniques which can be broadly categorized into the three main algorithm types: hierarchical beam searches, compressive sensing (CS) algorithms, and machine-learning-based methods. All three types attempt to minimize the BA overhead by reducing the number of sounding beam measurements required. Each type can use a unique sounding beamformer design and directional beam selection method.

Hierarchical BA algorithms like [10], [11], and [12] utilize adaptive, sectorized codebooks to reduce the number of sounding beams used. While these methods may minimize the number measurements, they must complete some computation for beam selection between each beam measurement. In this work, we wish to avoid this additional overhead time by instead using a fixed codebook, or a set of beams that are designed and selected prior to deployment.

CS BA algorithms, such as [13] and [14], typically use measurements from pseudorandom noise (PN) quasiomnidirectional sounding beams with a matching pursuit (MP) algorithm to reconstruct the angles-of-arrival (AoAs) of significant paths. Phase retrieval CS algorithms, such as [15] and [16], work with only power measurements instead of raw I/Q samples but fail to overcome array impairments. Although not a CS algorithm, Agile-Link [17] similarly uses a compressive, fixed codebook design, a random set of beams with multiple directional fingers to segment the AoA space. This algorithm and codebook design are not robust to array impairments, however, as the voting-based AoA recovery relies entirely on prior knowledge of the true beam pattern.

In contrast to RSS-MP, our machine-learning-assisted CNN beam alignment algorithm [22] is designed to implicitly handle imperfect factory calibration using in-field measurements after UE deployment. Based on mmRAPID [9], this simple supervised CNN's architecture is shown in Fig. 2, with sounding RSS measurements as input features and the estimated best directional beam index as the output label. The CNN is deployed and trained using a two-stage method. During Stage I, each UE device collects its own training data by measuring the RSS from both Ws and Wd, finding the features and labels respectively. During Stage II, the CNN is then trained on the collected data (either on a cloud server or locally on the UE), the UE device weights are updated, and subsequent BA with only measures RSS from the smaller Ws, reducing BA overhead. We specifically use our CNN extension of mmRAPID for BA with CL, since the convolutional layers have been shown to better exploit spatial correlation of the compressive measurements [22]. As a modification of mmRAPID, the CNN BA algorithm scales the required number of BA measurements logarithmically with the array size [9]. Future mmW and sub-THz arrays may grow in size and number of elements, increasing the overhead advantage of our ML BA algorithms compared to exhaustive searches whose overhead grow linearly with Nr.

The main drawback of our CNN design is the longer training time required compared to non-ML methods. While the CNN is relatively shallow with a limited number of trainable parameters, specifically six trainable layers and 4096⌈⌈M/2⌉/2⌉+ 129K + 27456 parameters, this still requires training unlike the simple search in RSS-MP. Additionally, the CNN's inference runtime is slower than RSS-MP, requiring 32768⌈⌈M/2⌉/2⌉+12352⌈M/2⌉+224M+128K+ 8448 FLOPs compared to RSS-MP's M(K + 1) −1 FLOPs. Embedded processor optimizations like post-training NN quantization can bring single sample runtimes below 20 µs for the original mmRAPID.1 Further code and accelerator hardware optimization could further reduce this runtime. Modern cell phone processors often contain GPUs and neural processing units (NPUs) optimized for ML workloads. For example, the Apple A18 Pro mobile processor has a 2.289 TFLOPS GPU and a 35 TOPS NPU [48]. Since a 12 measurement CNN requires ∼200k FLOPs, the A18 Pro GPU could support inference in 87 µs without quantization, but the NPU could theoretically support inference in 5.7 ns with an int8 quantization.

input: To reduce training time, we propose a transfer learning version of the CNN. While the CNN improves beam alignment (BA) robustness by implicitly calibrating for the user equipment's array impairments, this requires retraining for every codebook update and coupling matrix. Since total codebook learning (CL) training time scales linearly with iterations and Monte Carlo (MC) trials, reducing BA algorithm training time is imperative for practical CL. Transfer learning reduces training time by reusing layers shared with a base model. We introduce transfer learning in CL by training a base CNN without impairments at the start of each iteration. An application-specific model trains only the last dense layer for each MC trial with a different coupling matrix. Regardless of the base model, other layers are fixed, reducing trainable parameters to 129K. In our experiments, transfer learning (CNN-TL) reduced the average CL training time per M by 42%. IV. CS BA ALGORITHMS FOR CODEBOOK LEARNING

C. CNN WITH TRANSFER LEARNING

To reduce training time, we propose a transfer learning version of the CNN. While the CNN improves BA robustness by implicitly calibrating BA for the UE's array impairments, this also requires the algorithm to be retrained for every codebook update and coupling matrix. Since the total CL training time scales linearly with both the number of iterations (which depends on the codebook size) and the number of MC trials, reducing the BA algorithm training time is imperative for practical CL, as we will discuss in Section V. Transfer learning is a common method to reduce the training time of related ML models. Each application-specific model trains only a subset of layers by reusing layers shared with a base model that is trained before any of the application-specific model instances.

We introduce transfer learning in CL by training a base CNN without impairments at the start of each iteration. An application-specific model is trained for each MC trial with a different coupling matrix, but only needs to design weights for the last dense layer. Regardless of the base model used, the other layers are fixed and non-trainable, reducing the number of trainable parameters in the application specific model to 129K. Fig. 3 depicts how each CL iteration trains the CNN with transfer learning (CNN-TL). In our experiments, we have found CNN-TL to reduce the average CL training time per M by 42%. Since the TL saves 50% of training time for the CNN alone, CNN training consumes the majority of CL training time. Without impairments, CNN-TL maintains the same or higher BA performance but decreases average training time for a given set of hyperparameters from 1 minute 15 seconds to 43 seconds. This time linearly increases with the number of impairment MC trials.

The canonical DL problem jointly estimates X and D, constrained by maximum sparsity and dictionary normalization; this problem is nonconvex and NP-hard. Most algorithms solve this using alternating optimization, alternating between sparse coding—commonly using orthogonal matching pursuit (OMP)—and dictionary update. The reconstruction loss is modeled as the Frobenius norm of the difference between Z and the dictionary multiplied by the sparse representation.

section: V. DICTIONARY LEARNING AND CODEBOOK DESIGN — D. CODEBOOK LEARNING SYSTEM DEPLOYMENT
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: The proposed system deploys the CL algorithm before UE deployment using factory and operator-collected channel statistics. If an ML algorithm is used for beam alignment (BA), CL acts as a meta-learning algorithm optimizing structured feature extraction beamformers. CL training uses simulated data based on known statistics, while BA training data is collected in the field after UE deployment. The deployment procedure involves five steps: (1) inputting prior statistics to simulate data for CL training; (2) alternating optimization of the BA sensing codebook using simulated data; (3) loading fixed, optimized codebooks onto all UE devices at the factory; (4) collecting CNN training data using both codebooks for BA measurements to capture field impairments; and (5) deploying a per-UE trained CNN that uses only the optimized codebook for BA. RSS-MP integrated with CL would skip steps (4) and (5), but RSS-MP is not well suited for compressive BA with unknown array impairments. To reduce BA overhead, the CL algorithm is run over a range of measurement counts (M), with the final codebook size determined by the smallest M meeting operator BA performance statistics, using a 3 dB maximum 90th percentile gain loss threshold. A key weakness of the CL formulation is the lack of convergence or stability guarantees due to the non-convex codebook design and ML BA algorithm optimization; hyperparameters and initializations must be designed empirically. Despite this, CL is suitable for creating factory codebooks for a given UE device line, requiring only a single run completed upfront at the factory on large-scale servers or cloud ML services. The total computation scales as O(C_cnn + C_grad)N_M C_I_tot.

Dictionary learning for phase-less beam alignment codebook design in multipath channels.

Previous dictionary learning works have found that the initial dictionary is critical to alternating optimization finding a high-performing result. Typical algorithms use random atom initialization, but some employ more sophisticated design [51]. This work selects pseudo-omnidirectional and directional beams as heuristic initial codebooks for dictionary learning, denoted as $W_{s,\text{init}}$. The first type, pseudo-omnidirectional beams, have low angular correlation between beams and contain random phases for each antenna element. For example, with 2-bit phase states, the weight of the $m$th code is $W_{\text{PN},s;n,m} = \exp(j\theta_n)$, where $\theta_n \in \{0, \pi/2, \pi, 3\pi/2\}$. These are included because they are the default beam type used with most compressive beam alignment algorithms, including the original mmRAPID design. They are also close to typical dictionary learning initialization, as they use randomized weights for randomized beam patterns.

The second heuristic initialization codebook is a centralized subset of directional beams selected from $W_d$ pointing near boresight. These provide strong initial structure before dictionary learning modification, essentially the opposite of pseudo-omnidirectional beams.

Dictionary Learning for Phase-Less Beam Alignment Codebook Design in Multipath Channels

V. DICTIONARY LEARNING AND CODEBOOK DESIGN — E. CL INITIALIZATION AND HEURISTIC CODEBOOKS

Previous DL works have found that the initial dictionary can be critical to the alternating optimization finding a high performing result. Typical DL algorithms will use one of a few forms of random atom initialization, but some works do more sophisticated initialization design [51]. In this work, we select PN beams and directional beams as heuristic sounding beam designs to test as the initial codebook for CL, denoted as Ws,init. The first type of sounding beams, PN beams, have random, pseudo-omnidirectional antenna patterns with low angular correlation between beams and contain random phases for each antenna element. For example, with 2-bit phase states, weight n of the mth code is WPN s;n,m = exp (jθn), where θn ∈ {0, π/2, π, 3π/2}. We include PN beams, in part, because they are the default beam type used with most compressive BA algorithms, including the original mmRAPID design. Additionally, PN beams are close to the typical DL initialization, as they use randomized weights for randomized beam patterns. Our second heuristic initialization codebook is a centralized subset of directional beams, selected codes from Wd pointing near boresight. We included directional beams to provide strong initial structure before CL modification, essentially an opposite to PN beams.

As baselines for our learned codebooks, we use the PN and directional initialization codebooks as well as a third heuristic beam design, multi-finger sub-array (SA) beams. SA beams concatenate multiple directional beams from mutually-exclusive sub-arrays within the array [22], creating multiple, wider and lower-gain main lobes. In this work, we split the array into three equally-sized sub-arrays with ±25◦ offsets for the side SAs pointing relative to that of the center SA. Formally, the weights for the ith SA of the mth code pointing toward θm,i is wi,n = exp (φi,n), φi,n = 2πn sin(θm,i)d/λ. The overall weight vector is thus WSA s;n,m = [w1, . . . , wNsa] where Nsa is the number of SAs. Examples of SA and PN beam designs are shown compared to CL beams in Fig. 7 in Section VII-B.

VII. CODEBOOK LEARNING SIMULATION RESULTS

We evaluated the performance of CL-designed codebooks through Python simulations with the ML components built in Tensorflow and Keras 2.8. Our system parameters are listed in Table 3, where the RSS measurements were modeled through geometric simulations with random AoAs. The array impairments, when added, were modeled with random phase and gain offsets to elements as listed in Table 3, where Bi,j = gi,j exp
−jωi,j. These results use two sets of impairments; both sets use the same distribution of diagonal gain and phase offsets, but set 1 has no coupling while set 2 uses random offsets listed on Table 3. Note that the antenna spacing was selected to match real 60 GHz phased arrays on the Facebook Terragraph radios used in [9]. Additionally, the impairment levels were empirically selected to mimic experimental antenna pattern distortion on the Terragraph arrays. These arrays have been factory-calibrated to meet directional beamforming requirements, but they maintain some uncalibrated impairments because the calibration is not thorough. Our simulation code is publicly available [53].

input: The three loss functions were compared using codebooks learned exclusively with each loss over 50 CL update iterations on 2-path channels without impairments [1]. Fig. 5(a), 5(b), and 5(c) show the stacked beampatterns for reconstruction loss (Reconst.), classification error (CCE), and coherence regularization (Reg.) respectively, while Fig. 5(d) shows initial codebook patterns. The reconstruction loss codebook exhibits a randomized, nearly omnidirectional pattern due to gradient quantization. CCE and Reg. both emphasize initial codebook directions, but CCE creates secondary lobes in new directions, while Reg. widens the main lobe and emphasizes different angular sections. Since each loss incorporates different features, a combination is intuitively expected to provide the best performance. Empirically, this claim was supported; the best combinations tested are listed in Table 4. These were determined by first testing many combinations without impairments to narrow hyperparameters, then testing 12 selected combinations with impairments to choose the final ones. Since codebook training time scales linearly with the number of MC coupling matrices, testing without impairments allows faster cycle optimization. However, random impairments change measurement dynamics, requiring simulations with impairments for final selection. CCE loss generally works best with lower impairment uncertainty, while Reg. helps more at higher uncertainty. Ultimately, the best loss function must be empirically selected as it depends on channel and impairment randomness [1].

We first demonstrate the differing impacts of the three loss functions described in Section VI through codebooks learned exclusively with each loss. Fig. 5(a), 5(b), and 5(c) show the stacked beampatterns of all codes within three codebooks generated by reconstruction loss (Reconst.), classification error (CCE), and coherence regularization (Reg.) respectively. These 5-code codebooks were learned using data from 2-path channels without impairments and the CNN-TL BA algorithm over 50 CL update iterations. For comparison, the initial codebook beampatterns are shown in Fig. 5(d).

These plots emphasize how each loss function spreads the gain of the maximally directional initial codebook across the AoAs. The reconstruction loss codebook shows a randomized, nearly omnidirectional pattern, due to the quantization of the gradient updates discussed earlier. The CCE and coherence regularization beams both emphasize the directions of the initial codebook, but each loss modifies these beams differently. The CCE loss creates secondary lobes in new directions, while the regularization widens the main lobe of each initial beam and emphasizes different angular sections.

Since each loss incorporates different features into the codebook, we intuitively believe that a combination of the losses will provide the best performance. Empirically, we found this claim to be true, with the next section showing the beampatterns of one of the best loss combinations we tested. For brevity, we do not provide an exhaustive performance comparison of all tested hyperparameters in this paper and instead show results from our best combinations, listed in Table 4. These loss combinations were determined by testing many combinations without impairments to quickly narrow down possible hyperparameters, then testing 12 selected combinations with impairments to choose the best ones.

Since the codebook training time linearly scales with the number of MC coupling matrices, testing loss combinations using data without impairments helps narrow down possible weights with faster training cycles. However, random impairments change the measurement dynamics, so simulations with impairments are needed to make the final selection.

We have found that CCE loss generally works best with lower impairment uncertainty, while coherence regularization helps more at higher impairment uncertainty. Ultimately, the best loss function must be empirically selected as it depends on the channel and impairment randomness. Our results in Section VII-D will show how multiple loss functions can perform well with different impairment distributions, and that the best loss function is typically a combination of multiple proposed loss components.

section: VII. CODEBOOK LEARNING SIMULATION RESULTS — C. CODEBOOK LEARNING DESIGN RESULTS: TRAINING,
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: We compare BA performance over four parameters: codebook initializations from Section V-E, ML-assisted BA algorithms from Section IV, CL codebooks, and heuristic baselines, with results measured using the CDF of gain loss. We provide three recommendations for CL training: train with channels having α ≥ αt (where αt is the strongest expected multipath); use high SNR training data (30 dB after transmit beamforming); and initialize CL codebooks with directional beams rather than randomized PN beams. Transfer learning reduces BA training time by approximately 50% and total CL training time by approximately 40% using 5 codes, though it shows less runtime benefit for CL due to additional gradient operations. We balanced BA performance and CL training complexity by training CL codebooks with transfer learning but switching to full training during testing.

VII. CODEBOOK LEARNING SIMULATION RESULTS — C. CODEBOOK LEARNING DESIGN RESULTS: TRAINING, INITIALIZATION, AND BA ALGORITHMS

In this section, we discuss our guidelines for CL training and demonstrate our best design for the CL sparse coding stage and initialization. Although much work has been done to optimize the CL process to produce better BA performance, we do not include many of these results in this paper. Instead, we provide guidelines for the training process and CL parameters from our extensive empirical test results and provide examples of these design considerations. In particular, we compare BA performance over four major parameters: codebook initializations from Section V-E, ML-assisted BA algorithms from Section IV, codebooks from CL or heuristic baselines, and transfer learning from Section IV-C. All of these results measure BA performance using the cumulative density function (CDF) of gain loss, with better CDFs showing higher probabilities of lower gain losses.

While developing CL, we uncovered three recommendations for training CL codebooks. First, we found that CL codebooks should train using channels with α ≥ αt, where αt is the strongest multipath channels that the algorithm is expected to support in realistic deployments. The strength of the multipath of the CL training data is a trade-off, since stronger multipath better trains the algorithm to handle the most difficult channels but also sacrifices the maximum accuracy with weaker multipath. In this work, we train with α = 1.5 although the expected supported multipath is stronger at αt = 0.25. The optimal training α must be found empirically with simulated validation data. Second, CL training data should use a high SNR. Although strong noise in training data is known to help some ML algorithms, CL tends to learn less effectively with noisy data. In this work, we train with 30 dB SNR after transmit beamforming. Finally, we empirically discovered that CL is best initialized with directional beams instead of randomized PN beams. Fig. 8 demonstrates directional (Dir.) beam initialization outperforming PN beams in terms of gain loss distribution for CL codebooks trained with the CNN. This is consistent with typical DL results, where bad initializations are known to severely limit learned-dictionary performance due to the highly non-convex nature of the DL optimization problems [49]. Further design of Ws,init is left for future work.

We also found that transfer learning significantly improved CL and BA training speed with limited impact on BA performance. With 5 codes, TL reduced training time by an average of approximately 50% for BA training and by approximately 40% for total CL training. Note that TL shows less runtime benefit for CL due to the additional codebook gradient operations required which are not affected by the weight transfer. Fig. 10 illustrates CNN BA performance with TL training, without impairments in Fig. 10a or with impairments set 2 in Fig. 10b. Although TL generally met or improved gain loss statistics over standard training gain loss statistics, randomized impairments degrade performance. TL was necessary to train CL codebooks with more impairment instances while maintaining a reasonable computational workload, even though the performance was degraded compared to standard training. We balanced BA performance and CL training complexity by training CL codebooks with TL, but switched to full training when testing the learned CL codebooks.

section: VII. CODEBOOK LEARNING SIMULATION RESULTS — E. REQUIRED MEASUREMENT OVERHEAD
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: We compare the measurement overhead of our selected codebook against baseline heuristics when using the CNN BA algorithm. The goal is to meet a maximum 3 dB gain loss in 90% or more of channels across varied multipath levels and two SNRs with two impairment sets. Results show that learned codebooks support stronger multipath channels (smaller α) with equal or fewer measurements than existing designs, particularly under simpler impairments. While heuristic codebooks sometimes require fewer measurements in weak multipath conditions, our design goal was a single robust codebook for strong multipath and unknown impairments, which our algorithm achieves. Notably, the best heuristic codebook changes by scenario; for example, a directional codebook nearly matches learned performance under high SNR with coupling but requires many more codes in other scenarios. This performance flip is attributed to antenna coupling distorting beam patterns and increasing sidelobe gain, which is more beneficial at higher SNRs. Unlike heuristic designs requiring manual tuning, our CL algorithm automatically produces appropriate codebooks from data. Critically, any codebook using the proposed CNN requires far fewer measurements than a traditional exhaustive search or RSS-MP. An exhaustive search would require 128 directional beam measurements, many times more than our CNN regardless of channel conditions. Furthermore, due to strong randomized impairments, RSS-MP shows no benefit over the exhaustive search.
output:
We now compare the overall BA overhead reduction of our selected CL codebook with the baseline heuristic codebooks, when all codebooks are used with the CNN BA algorithm. To capture the practical benefit of using learned codebooks, we compare the required number of measurements to meet a maximum of 3 dB gain loss in 90% or more channels for each codebook. Fig. 11 includes these codebook comparisons tested over varied multipath levels and with two SNRs and the two sets of impairments. Note that all of these results use the same CNN weights and learned codebooks, trained exclusively with 10 different instances of the coupling matrices and α = 0.25 multipath channels. These figures demonstrate that the learned codebooks are able to support stronger multipath channels (i.e. smaller α) with the same or fewer measurements than existing codebook designs, particularly with the simpler impairments in set 1. While the heuristic codebooks sometimes allow fewer measurements than the CL codebooks for weak multipath conditions, separate smaller codebooks could be designed to be competitive at weaker channels. Our design goal was to produce a single codebook that is robust to strong multipath channels and unknown impairments, and our CL algorithm produced beams that were more robust than existing designs.

One interesting observation is that the best heuristic codebook changes between the different scenarios. For Fig. 11d in particular, with high SNR and impairments with coupling, the directional codebook was best heuristic design and nearly matched the CL codebook performance. However, in most other scenarios, particularly the Fig. 11a with the opposite parameters, the directional codebook needed many more codes than the other heuristics. We expect that this flip in performance is caused by the impairments, since antenna coupling distorts the beam patterns. For the directional codebook, this increases the angular observation area by increasing the sidelobe gain. Stronger sidelobe response is more useful at higher SNRs, as measurements from the sidelobes emerge above the noise floor. While heuristic codebooks require these design choices to be made manually by the system designer, CL can automatically produce appropriate codebooks from provided data.

Importantly, the required number of measurements for any of these codebooks using the proposed CNN is much fewer than using a traditional exhaustive search or RSS-MP. An exhaustive search would require a full sequence of 128 directional beam measurements, many times more than our proposed CNN regardless of multipath or impairment strength. Due to the strong randomized impairments, RSS-MP shows no benefit over the exhaustive search, as in [22].

section: VIII. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: CL algorithm uses compressed sensing dictionary learning and alternating coordinate descent to design fixed codebooks from simulation data. CL incorporates compressive beam alignment performance by back-propagating gradients through the system model, making it suitable for machine learning-assisted beam alignment. CL-designed codebooks improve gain loss performance and reduce beam alignment overhead for strong multipath channels with unknown impairments. Future work includes optimizing CL for transfer learning and robust initializations, and extending the method to complex array geometries where intuitive beams are absent.

In this work, we presented a novel algorithm to design fixed
codebooks for phase-less beam alignment with unknown
impairments. The codebook learning (CL) algorithm, based
on compressed sensing dictionary learning, utilizes simulation data to design beams through an alternating coordinate
descent optimization. The performance of compressive beam
alignment algorithms is incorporated into the codebook
design explicitly by back-propagating gradients through the
system model, making CL particularly well-suited for use
with machine learning assisted beam alignment methods.
We provided guidelines for better training with CL and
presented results comparing potential design considerations.
In most cases, CL-designed codebooks improved gain loss
performance and reduced the required BA overhead for strong
multipath channels with unknown impairments.
For future work, the CL algorithm itself can be further
optimized for transfer learning and more robust codebook
initializations. This work also could be extended to alternate system configurations, such as with more complex
array geometries, where good sounding beams may be less
intuitive.

instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Machine teaching is an inverse problem of machine learning that aims to steer a student toward a target hypothesis, assuming the teacher knows the student's learning parameters. Prior work focused on balancing teaching risk and cost to find optimal examples from a student model, but this solver fails when the student does not reveal learning parameters. This article proposes a distribution matching-based strategy that iteratively shrinks teaching cost within a smooth surrogate, eliminating boundary perturbations from the version space. The method redefines teaching as a cost-controlled optimization process, requiring no further exploration of the student's parameter distribution. Given any limited teaching cost, training examples have a closed-form expression. Theoretical analysis and experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach.

Distribution Matching for Machine Teaching
Xiaofeng Cao
and Ivor W. Tsang , Fellow, IEEE
Abstract— Machine teaching is an inverse problem of machine
learning that aims at steering the student toward its target
hypothesis, in which the teacher has already known the student’s learning parameters. Previous studies on machine teaching
focused on balancing the teaching risk and cost to find the
best teaching examples deriving from the student model. This
optimization solver is in general ineffective when the student does
not disclose any cue of the learning parameters. To supervise
such a teaching scenario, this article presents a distribution
matching-based machine teaching strategy via iteratively shrinking the teaching cost in a smooth surrogate, which eliminates
boundary perturbations from the version space. Technically, our
strategy could be redefined as a cost-controlled optimization
process that finds the optimal teaching examples without further
exploring the parameter distribution of the student. Then, given
any limited teaching cost, the training examples would have
a closed-form expression. Theoretical analysis and experiment
results demonstrate the effectiveness of this strategy.
Index Terms— Learning parameters, machine teaching, surrogate, teaching cost, teaching risk.

section: I. INTRODUCTION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
Artificial intelligence (AI) refers to machines performing tasks considered intelligent [1]. Machine learning (ML) improves AI through experience using annotated training data to explore common patterns [2]. The core issue of ML is constructing effective models by inducing feasible parameters [3], where informative training examples accelerate model convergence [4]. ML progress occurred in two stages: model diversity (e.g., unsupervised, supervised, semisupervised paradigms [5]-[7]) and parameter optimization robustness (e.g., gradient descent, Bayesian optimization [8]-[10]). However, the optimal training subset lacks a closed-form expression [11].

The ML community addresses this via machine teaching [12], redefining model construction as a teacher-student interactive process where the teacher provides parameter information for the student [13]. Theoretical concepts like teaching complexity and teaching dimension were proposed based on typical ML contents [14]. The core issue of machine teaching is controlling the ML paradigm when a teacher knows the student's learning parameters and seeks better training examples to improve generalization [15]. This problem was studied by [16], which explores optimal training data to drive the student to its target hypothesis. Many paradigms adopt a teacher-student manner, e.g., curriculum learning in human education [17] and iterative query algorithms to annotators in active learning [18]. The key assumption is that the teacher knows the target parameters of the student model, such as a specified hyperplane in the support vector machine (SVM) classifier and geometric properties of clustering centers [19]. Typically, a machine teacher interacts with their student by exploring teaching examples that minimize parameter disagreement (difference) between the current training model and its desired one [20], [21].

In simple terms, machine teaching finds the best training data for students automatically. With machine teaching, teaching examples can be closed form to supervise the training model, e.g., teacher-student learning [22] and knowledge distillation [23]. Furthermore, one unsupervised teacher can find the best teaching examples as clustering prototypes depicting the inherent skeleton of clusters [24]; an annotation expert can minimize labeling cost by picking highly informative teaching examples that maximally update the classification hypothesis [25]; a transfer learning task establishing a source paradigm using teaching examples can be adopted in homeomorphic target domains [26]. Moreover, machine teaching can help automachine learning encapsulate an advanced pipeline used in consistent distributions and tasks [27], where automachine learning is considered a key step to achieve AI. As the most relevant ML study to machine teaching is active learning [28], its key assumption is that a student who frequently interacts with an annotator would perform better or no worse than passive learners who randomly solicit training examples. Generally, active learning forwardly updates the current training model toward its target, which is always agnostic. We next employ a threshold classifier to further explain active learning and machine teaching.

Considering an interval [−1, 1] with positive and negative labels over a uniform distribution P (see Fig. 1), the parameterized threshold classifier at θ∗= 0 stipulates the classification function f for any (x, y) ∼P: y = f (x) = +1, s.t. x ≥θ∗, y = f (x) = −1, s.t. x ≤θ∗, where y denotes the label of x, and P denotes its distribution. Drawing i.i.d. n samples from P, a passive (random) learner will make n times of querying from f (x) that yields a generalization error of ∥θ −θ∗∥= O(1/n) due to an average uniform spacing 1/n, where θ yields a passive learner. Given an error ϵ, a passive learner needs O(1/ϵ) data sent to the classifier. Specifically, the passive learner at least receives 10 000 samples from P to obtain the desired error of 0.0001. For an active learner who usually employs binary search, the learner halves the remaining interval and removes the data over it, and thereby, receives around O(log1/ϵ) samples to obtain an error ϵ because ∥θ −θ∗∥= O(1/2n). Specifically, the active learner at least receives 13 samples from P to obtain the desired error of 0.0001. However, a machine teacher who knows θ∗only needs two teaching examples to obtain ϵ:

RTIFICIAL intelligence (AI) [1] is a broad concept of
machines being able to perform science and engineering tasks in ways that we would consider to be intelligent.
To automatically improve AI through experience, machine
learning [2] studies the advanced computation algorithms,
which work on annotated training data, intending to explore
the common patterns inside the data. Therefore, machine
learning is one of the most important ways we expect to
achieve AI. The core issue of machine learning is to construct
effective models by inducing feasible parameters [3], where
those highly informative or representative training examples
accelerate the convergence of the learning model. In the
past decades, the progress of machine learning went through
about two stages: 1) the diversity of model construction,
e.g., unsupervised paradigm [4], supervised paradigm [5],
and semisupervised paradigm [6], and 2) the robustness of
parameter optimization, e.g., gird search [7], Bayesian optimization [8], gradient descent search [9], and evolutionary
optimization [10]. However, the optimal training subset still
has no closed-form expression.
The machine learning community, thus, begins to solve this
challenging problem. A novel concept termed machine teaching [11] was subsequently proposed. In such a scenario, the
model construction process is redefined as a teacher–student
interactive process, where the teacher provides necessary
parameter information for the model construction of the student. A set of theoretical concepts, such as teaching complexity and teaching dimension [12], was proposed and given
meaningful descriptions based on typical machine learning
contents. Meanwhile, the core issue of machine teaching also
was presented: how to control the machine learning paradigm,
if there is a teacher who has already known the learning
parameters of the student and wants better training examples
to improve its generalization?
This question was studied well by [13], which explores
the optimal training data via driving the student to its target
hypothesis. It has been shown that many promising paradigms
adopt such a teacher–student manner [14], e.g., a curriculum
to the human education system in curriculum learning [15],
an iterative query algorithm to an annotator in active learning [16]. The key assumption is that the teacher already knows
the target parameters of the student model, such as a specified
hyperplane in the support vector machine (SVM) classifier,
and the geometric properties of clustering centers. Typically,
a machine teacher interacts with their student by exploring
those teaching examples that minimize the parameter disagreement (difference) of the current training model and its
desired one [17], [18].
In simple terms, machine teaching can help to find the
best training data for students automatically. With machine
teaching, those teaching examples can be closed form to
supervise the training model of a student, e.g., teacher–student
learning [19] and knowledge distillation [20]. Furthermore,
one unsupervised teacher can find the best teaching examples
as the clustering prototypes to depict the inherent skeleton
of those clusters [21]; an annotation expert can minimize the
labeling cost by picking up those highly informative teaching examples, which can maximally update the classification
hypothesis [22]; a transfer learning task, which establishes a
source paradigm using the teaching examples, can be adopted
in homeomorphic target domains [23]. Moreover, machine
teaching can help automachine learning to encapsulate an
advanced pipeline used in a class of consistent distributions
and tasks [24], where automachine learning is considered
as one key step to achieve AI. As far as we know, the
most relevant machine learning study to machine teaching
is active learning [25]. Its key assumption is that a student
who frequently interacts with an annotator would do better or
no worse than other passive learners who randomly solicit
the training examples. Generally, active learning forwardly
updates the current training model into its target, while the
target is always agnostic. We next employ a threshold classifier
to further explain active learning and machine teaching.
Considering an interval [−1, 1] with positive and negative labels over a uniform distribution P (see Fig. 1), the
parameterized threshold classifier at θ∗= 0 stipulates the
classification function f for any (x, y) ∼P: y = f (x) =
+1, s.t. x ≥θ∗, y = f (x) = −1, s.t. x ≤θ∗, where y denotes
the label of x, and P denotes its distribution. Drawing i.i.d.
n samples from P, a passive (random) learner will make n
times of querying from f (x) that yields a generalization error
of ∥θ −θ∗∥= O(1/n) due to an average uniform spacing 1/n,
where θ yields a passive learner. Given an error ϵ, a passive
learner needs O(1/ϵ) data sent to the classifier. Specifically,
the passive learner at least receives 10 000 samples from P
to obtain the desired error of 0.0001. For an active learner
who usually employs binary search, the learner halves the
remaining interval and removes the data over it, and thereby,
receives around O(log1/ϵ) samples to obtain an error ϵ because ∥θ −θ∗∥= O(1/2n). Specifically, the active learner
at least receives 13 samples from P to obtain the desired error
of 0.0001. However, a machine teacher who knows θ∗only
needs two teaching examples to obtain ϵ: (θ∗−ϵ/2, −1) and
(θ∗+ϵ/2, +1). Then, for any student, they will easily achieve
better performance using those teaching examples.
The minimization on ∥θ −θ∗∥is adopted for a linear
learner. For a model-agnostic student in teaching, a general
strategy is to minimize the teaching risk L( ˆθ, θ∗) over the
student’s parameter disagreement. Its assumption is that the
teacher knows θ∗and the optimization on L( ˆθ, θ∗) is natural.
However, if the student does not disclose any cue (also
termed a black box) on θ∗, the estimation on L( ˆθ, θ∗) would
be difficult even infeasible, and the teaching optimization
would also explore in infinite parameter space. Theoretically,
shrinking the training set into an approximately minimal subset for any unknown family of hypothesis is inevitable
against a black box, yielding consistent properties as the full
training [16]. In this article, we consider this challenging
problem from a distribution perspective, which transforms the
estimation of L( ˆθ, θ∗) to distribution matching, i.e., finding an
alternative assumption for the transformation of the teaching risk. Motivated by this, we present a comprehensive theoretical
analysis and optimization scheme. Contributions of this work
are summarized as follows.
1) We introduce the idea of distribution matching for
machine teaching a student who does not disclose any
cue of the learning parameters, i.e., a black box.
2) We propose to teach a black box in a surrogate, which
eliminates boundary perturbations from the version
space, yielding consistent properties as with its original
hypothesis class. To guarantee this scheme, we prove
that teaching in surrogate has safety (w.r.t. Section V-A)
and convergence (w.r.r.t. Section V-B) protocols.

present

optimization

examples without further exploring the parameter distribution of the student.
4) We present a distribution matching-based machine
teaching strategy (w.r.t. Section VI-C) by iteratively
shrinking the teaching cost.

While active learning controls annotation effort via human experts or an oracle with label information, this often results in a suboptimal target model. From this perspective, machine teaching studies the optimal control of active learning. Related works on these two avenues are presented in this section.

When a model trains on abundant data from an underlying distribution, a teacher selects examples to supervise students [13]. Two factors are studied: teaching set size and whether the teacher knows the student's parameter distribution.

Early works addressed size by studying teaching complexity [27]. Introducing the teaching dimension, complexity is characterized by the minimum examples needed to identify the desired hypothesis. When the training set of a model consists of plenty of data from an underlying distribution, a teacher always desires to pick up some teaching examples from the original dataset to supervise its students [13]. In this teaching process, the teacher can be generalized as a human expert, a learning algorithm, or a system. Two factors are studied in the teaching process: how to fix the size of the teaching set, and whether the teacher knows the full knowledge of the parameter distribution of the student model?

Early works answered the first problem by studying the teaching complexity. Introducing a novel concept named teaching dimension [27], the complexity of teaching is usually characterized by the minimum number of teaching examples used to identify the desired hypothesis. If the teaching examples are selected independently of the original data pool, the student can cooperate with a teacher who supervises a teaching set. Recently, machine teaching [28] studied the teaching model when the student was a convex minimizer, such as the least square regression, and simple SVM. In [14], they presented a theoretical interpretation against multiple-teacher teaching, rather than a single teacher. Under the joint teaching for conjugate Bayesian learners, Zhu [29] proposed a new concept called class teaching dimension. In this definition, the teacher independently picks up some students as a representation of the whole class of learners. Indeed, it shrinks the original teaching dimension by the representation features of the learner class.

In real-world applications, a variety of learning tasks involving machine teaching were studied. For instance, in curriculum learning [15], [30], a human can intelligently annotate or recognize examples when the teaching examples are not randomly presented but organized in a meaningful order. Those orders help the teachers to optimize a group of teaching sets for the subsequent learning tasks, such as teacher–student training [19] and knowledge distillation [20], [31]. To improve the generalization of an active learner, Dasgupta et al. [16] proposed a black-box teaching scheme to shrink training sets for any family of the classifier by merely serving up the relevant examples beforehand and does not need to observe the feedback from the learner, where “shrink” can be deemed as a typical distribution matching-based machine teaching strategy.

section: II. RELATED WORK — B. Active Learning
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Active learning [32], [33] aims to find optimal training data like machine teaching but updates models forward. Learners query labels from unlabeled data to improve performance within a given annotation budget. Theoretically, learners maintain a version space [34] of candidate hypotheses, shrinking its size via minimal queries. However, version space theory is computationally intractable [25] for nonlinear classifiers, as guaranteeing returned hypotheses from this space is intractable. To address this, Balcan [35] and Hanneke [36] constructed algorithms that predict data affecting subsequent hypotheses, assigning weight coefficients. Their convergence guarantees, based on PAC-style theory [1], are rigorous and tighter than supervised learning bounds. Alternatively, importance-weighted active learning [37] provides unbiased sampling via loss weighting, allowing observation of generalization error and label complexity changes. In practice, pool-based active learning [38], [39] samples data to reduce error by repeatedly visiting the unlabeled pool. When supervising black-box learners, precise prior labels and classifier parameters are unavailable; only label queries are accessible. This limits traditional strategies that estimate error disagreements [40]. To reduce classifier dependence, query by committee [41] uses multiple classifiers to evaluate error changes and selects data maximizing member disagreement. However, estimating error changes incurs high time and space costs. Beyond fundamental active learning, related paradigms like linear discriminant analysis [42] and deep multimodal hashing [43], [44] can also be adopted to find teaching sets.
output:
Active learning [32], [33] adopts the same sampling goal as machine teaching to find the optimal training data, but forwardly updates the models. In this task, the learners are given access to interactively query the labels of a group of unlabeled data. The learning goal is that the queries can substantially improve the performance of a learning model within a given annotation budget. Theoretically, the learners always try to maintain a version space [34], which covers a series of candidate hypotheses and shrinks its size via querying as little as possible data. However, the version space-based learning theory, unfortunately, has drawbacks of computational intractability [25], i.e., guaranteeing that only hypotheses from this space are returned is intractable for nonlinear classifiers. To develop a new strategy that addresses the abovementioned limitations, Balcan [35] and Hanneke [36] constructed learning algorithms to predict which data may significantly affect the subsequent hypothesis, thereby giving different weight coefficients. The convergence guarantees, adopted from a PAC-style [1], are rigorous and tighter than the generalized bounds of any supervised learning algorithms. The other technique, termed importance-weighted active learning [37], provides an unbiased sampling approach with the loss weighting and has more practical use in observing the changes of generalization error and label complexity (the number of required samples to achieve the desired error).

In practical tasks, traditional active learning methods, such as pool-based active learning [38], [39], sample the data that reduces the error rate in the described change by repeatedly visiting the unlabeled data pool. Usually, the learner is given access to the hypothesis class easily, i.e., can favorably observe the hypothesis updates by estimating the error disagreements (differences). However, when supervising a black-box learner, obtaining precise details of the prior labels and a list of classifier parameters are not available, and only the queries on labels are accessible. This makes many of the traditional strategies, which estimate the error disagreements, not applicable, or at the least unable to work well [40]. To reduce the dependence on a single classifier, query by committee algorithm [41] uses a set of classifiers to evaluate the error rate changes and selects the data which maximizes the disagreement among the committee members. However, estimating the error rate changes in settings of single or multiple classifiers will cost expensively on time and space complexities. Besides the fundamental active learning, there are also some related supervised and unsupervised learning paradigms that also can be adopted into finding the teaching set, e.g., linear discriminant analysis [42] and deep multimodal hashing [43], [44].

section: III. MOTIVATIONS — B. Teaching a Black Box
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
When parameter information is limited, students degenerate into black boxes. To find the optimal teaching set for curriculum learning without class information [47], active learning with weak hypotheses [48], and Bayesian inference with poor priors [49], [50], a new teaching strategy is needed. Our main proposal for solving this black-box scenario is to optimize an approximate distribution for teaching.

Why teach in a surrogate? From the hypothesis class perspective, the teaching set must independently draw significant hypotheses presenting effective model generalizations. Perturbations around decision boundaries, including noise [51], out-of-distribution data [52], and adversarial examples [53], typically produce insignificant hypotheses. Smoothing these boundary perturbations can substantially eliminate such insignificant hypotheses. Consequently, teaching hypotheses generated from a surrogate with smooth boundaries are required to tightly cover significant hypotheses (see Definitions 1 and 2), resulting in safety protocols on generalization error and label complexity.

From a teaching optimization perspective, the learning parameter is decided by its associated hypothesis, and any model-agnostic hypothesis is generated from an associated distribution or training set. We assume that θ* is generalized from the optimal hypothesis h*, i.e., R(θ*, D) = R(h*, D), and θ̂ is generalized from the desired hypothesis ĥ, i.e., R(θ̂, D) = R(ĥ, D). Let D' ⊂ D be the optimal surrogate with respect to h*, and bD ⊂ D' be the desired training set with respect to ĥ. A distribution matching-based machine teaching algorithm, which transfers parameter disagreement estimation into hypotheses, thereby approximating the hypothesis to distribution in metric space H, is then established:

input: We compare clustering performance on the full dataset and its surrogate to explain theoretical results. Density estimation characterizes boundary perturbations as low-density observations within a fixed hypersphere $S$. We estimate density $f_S(u)$ using a distance metric $f_H(u,v)$, where $\psi(u,v)$ equals 1 if the hyperbolic distance is within radius $r$, else 0. For a more general formulation using Euclidean distance, we define $F_S(u)$. To implement iterative halving for distribution matching-based machine teaching, we employ the Poincaré distance $f_H(u,v)$ to nonlinearly rank the transformed teaching risk. Specifically, let $B_d$ be the open $d$-dimensional unit Poincaré sphere; for $u,v \in B_d$, the Poincaré distance is $f_H(u,v) := \text{arccosh}\left(1 + 2 \frac{\|u - v\|^2}{(1 - \|u\|^2)(1 - \|v\|^2)}\right)$. The case study uses three real-world datasets (digit, USPS, Fashion-MNIST), with all features scaled such that $\|x_i\|^2 < 1$. Datasets have sizes $3823 \times 65$, $9298 \times 257$, and $70,000 \times 784$. We evaluate clustering risk using 1-adjusted rand index (ARI) and 1-mutual information (MI) coefficients. The protocol minimizes risk $R(h,D)$ via k-means, hierarchical, and spectral clustering on $D$ and surrogate $D'$. The shrinking parameter $r$ is 0.4, and $|D| - |D'| = 0.05n$, eliminating perturbations from $0.05n$ boundary examples. Section VII. Experiments

We compare our distribution-based machine teaching algorithm against typical baselines that estimate parameter disagreement to generalize teaching risk. When teaching a black box, parameter estimation is inefficient due to improper disagreement or an inestimable space.

Section: VII. EXPERIMENTS

Typical machine teaching algorithms estimate the parameter disagreement of models to generalize the teaching risk, where the teacher knows the desired parameter. When teaching a black box, parameter estimations may be inefficient due to improper parameter disagreement or inestimable parameter space. We, thus, select a series of supervised and unsupervised machine learning baselines, which can be generalized as typical machine teaching, to compare our distribution-based machine teaching algorithm.

To solve (2) of general machine teaching, there exist three conditions which can simplify its optimization process: 1) control M(D) with (1)'s solver of active learning; 2) reduce the search space for limited risk minimization; and 3) fix M(D) with unsupervised machine learning. To realize these conditions, three groups of experiments are presented. 1) Regulate M(D) to minimize the risk disagreement of ∥R(θ, D) − R(θ∗, D)∥, i.e., supervised way. 2) Shrink the search space of D to observe the perturbations to typical machine learning and our machine teaching algorithms. 3) Minimize ∥R(θ, D) − R(θ∗, D)∥ with quantitative M(D), i.e., unsupervised way.

1) Datasets: The datasets used in the first two groups of experiments are the full training data of Adult, Phishing, Satimage, and MNIST datasets, where ∥R(θ, D) − R(θ∗, D)∥ is over those training data. The sizes of these datasets are 11 055 × 68, 1 605 × 14, 4435 × 36, and 60 000 × 780, respectively. The datasets used in the third group of the experiment are CIFAR10 and CIFAR100, where ∥R(θ, D) − R(θ∗, D)∥ is over their test data. The sizes of the two datasets are all 60 000 with 32 × 32 pixels.

2) Baselines: Four supervised learning algorithms that regulate M(D) to minimize ∥R(θ, D) − R(θ∗, D)∥ are selected, including expected error reduction (ERR) [65], preclustering [66], transductive experimental design (TED) [62], and self-paced active learning (SPAL) [67]. Specifically, they are active learning algorithms. Three typical unsupervised machine learning algorithms that minimize ∥R(θ, D) − R(θ∗, D)∥ with quantitative M(D) are selected: k-medoids, hierarchical, and spectral clustering. Those baselines are finally used in the experiment of teaching a deep neural network. A case study of teaching Gaussian data is first presented before the experiments. Note that distribution-based machine teaching is denoted as DM-based machine teaching in all experimental figures.

3) Specification of ∥R(θ, D) − R(θ∗, D)∥: Our main assumption is to transfer ∥R(θ, D) − R(θ∗, D)∥ into distribution matching. To verify the effectiveness of our machine teaching strategy, we specify ∥R(θ, D) − R(θ∗, D)∥ over the ground-truth error risk. Specifically, given a classification model, we set R(θ, D) = 1 − errD(θ) and R(θ∗, D) = 1 − errD(θ∗), where θ and θ∗ are generated from the teaching set and full training set, respectively. In short, R(θ∗, D) and R(θ, D) are specified as the optimal and current classification errors, respectively.

section: VIII. DISCUSSION ON OUR ASSUMPTION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: This study validates Assumption 3, which posits that the risk of the optimal hypothesis $R(\theta^*, D)$ approximates that of the generated hypothesis $R(h^*, D)$. To test this, diverse classifiers—k-nearest neighbors (KNR), random forest, multilayer perceptron (MLP), and support vector machine (SVM)—were used to generate teaching sets for subsequent supervised classification. Training parameters were set as follows: KNR with $k=10$, RandomForest with 600 trees, MLPClassifier with hidden layer size 100, 1000 max iterations, L2 penalty 0.0004, and learning rate 0.001, and SVM with penalty 1.0, RBF kernel, degree 3, and tolerance 0.003. Distribution matching-based machine teaching reduces expected learning risk as $M(D)$ increases. Reported perturbations of $\|R(\theta, D) - R(\theta^*, D)\|$ range from 0.06 to 0.14, where $M(D)/n$ ranges from 0.1 to 0.5. Notably, learning curves for MLPClassifier on digit and RandomForest on FashionMnist do not decrease consistently, suggesting iterative halving may delay risk reduction. SVM achieves the lowest perturbation value. Furthermore, increasing $M(D)$ tightens the approximation of $D$, driving $\|R(\theta, D) - R(\theta^*, D)\|$ toward zero, with the constraint that $M(D) < n$.

section: IX. CONCLUSION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: We proposed a distribution matching-based machine teaching algorithm to estimate teaching risk against a black box. Theoretical analysis confirmed that teaching in a surrogate maintains safety and convergence protocols equivalent to the original hypothesis space. A case study supported this perspective and demonstrated that the Poincaré distance in hyperbolic geometry yields smoother teaching boundaries than Euclidean distance, enabling subsequent iterative halving in this geometry. Experiments showed that distribution matching-based machine teaching outperformed supervised and unsupervised learning algorithms in minimizing expected learning risk disagreement. This work raises the open question of whether disagreement estimations on distribution and model parameters can be co-taught. Future work will study more practical teacher-student learning models in real-world tasks, such as computer vision.
output: In this work, we proposed a distribution matching-based machine teaching algorithm with regard to estimating the teaching risk on distributions against a black box. Theoretical analysis proved that teaching in a surrogate has safety and convergence protocols as the original hypothesis space. The case study further presented support for this theoretical perspective and demonstrated that the Poincaré distance of hyperbolic geometry could derive smoother boundaries for teaching in surrogate than that of the Euclidean distance. We, thus, projected the subsequent iterative halving in this geometry. Experiments demonstrated distribution matching-based machine teaching outperformed the supervised and unsupervised machine learning algorithms in minimizing expected learning risk disagreement. Finally, this work leads to an open question: can we co-teach the disagreement estimations on the distribution and model parameters? Furthermore, more practical teacher–student learning models in real-world tasks, such as computer vision, would be studied in the future.

ABSTRACT Machine learning methods have achieved good performance and been widely applied in various real-world applications. They can learn the model adaptively and be better fit for special requirements of different tasks. Generally, a good machine learning system is composed of plentiful training data, a good model training process, and an accurate inference. Many factors can affect the performance of the machine learning process, among which the diversity of the machine learning process is an important one. The diversity can help each procedure to guarantee a totally good machine learning: diversity of the training data ensures that the training data can provide more discriminative information for the model, diversity of the learned model (diversity in parameters of each model or diversity among different base models) makes each parameter/model capture unique or complement information and the diversity in inference can provide multiple choices each of which corresponds to a specific plausible local optimal result. Even though diversity plays an important role in the machine learning process, there is no systematic analysis of the diversification in the machine learning system. In this paper, we systematically summarize the methods to make data diversification, model diversification, and inference diversification in the machine learning process. In addition, the typical applications where the diversity technology improved the machine learning performance have been surveyed including the remote sensing imaging tasks, machine translation, camera relocalization, image segmentation, object detection, topic modeling, and others. Finally, we discuss some challenges of the diversity technology in machine learning and point out some directions in future work. Our analysis provides a deeper understanding of the diversity technology in machine learning tasks and hence can help design and learn more effective models for real-world applications.

section: I. INTRODUCTION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Machine learning can automatically learn model parameters from training data to satisfy application requirements, achieving success in areas like object detection and urban scene understanding [1]–[8]. However, real-world applications often suffer from limited labeled data and large model parameter counts, leading to overfitting and difficult accurate inference [1]. Diversity in machine learning addresses this by reducing redundancy in data or models and providing informative representations, thereby improving performance [1]. This survey systematically covers diversity-promoting methods across three categories: data diversification, model diversification, and inference diversification [1]. Data diversification maximizes information in training samples, including batch construction and active learning, to enable better model fitting with limited data [9]–[14]. Model diversification encourages parameter diversity (D-model) or diverse ensemble models (D-models) to model unique information and avoid convergence to similar local optima, improving performance in tasks like speech recognition and image segmentation [19]–[27]. Inference diversification, or multiple choice learning (MCL), promotes diverse choices with complementary information rather than similar one-pixel-shifted outputs, further improving discriminative power [28]–[32]. The work addresses three key questions: how to measure and enhance diversity; the difference and similarity between model and modelset diversification; and real-world application potential [1]. Enforcing diversity balances training data, encourages parameter diversification, and diversifies inference choices, leading to better overall model performance [1]. The paper is structured into general machine learning models (Section II), diversity methods (Sections III–V), and extensive applications (Section VI) [1].

systems presents similarity between each other where the
next choice will be one-pixel shifted versions of others [28].
Therefore, to overcome this problem, diversity-promoting
prior can be imposed over the obtained multiple choices from
the inference. Under the inference diversiﬁcation, the model
can provide choices/representations with more complement
information [29]–[32]. This could further improve the performance of the machine learning process and provide multiple
discriminative choices of the objects.
This
work
systematically
covers
the
literature
on
diversity-promoting methods over data diversiﬁcation, model
diversiﬁcation, and inference diversiﬁcation in machine
learning tasks. In particular, three main questions from the
analysis of diversity technology in machine learning have
arisen.
• How to measure the diversity of the training data,
the learned model/models, and the inference and
enhance these diversity in machine learning system,
respectively? How do these methods work on the diversiﬁcation of the machine learning system?
• Is there any difference between the diversiﬁcation of the
model and models? Furthermore, is there any similarity
between the diversity in the training data, the learned
model/models, and the inference?
• Which real-world applications can the diversity be
applied in to improve the performance of the machine
learning models? How do the diversiﬁcation methods
work on these applications?
Although all of the three problems are important, none of
them has been thoroughly answered. Diversity in machine
learning can balance the training data, encourage the learned
parameters to be diversiﬁed, and diversify the multiple
choices from the inference. Through enforcing diversity in
the machine learning system, the machine learning model
can present a better performance. Following the framework,
the three questions above have been answered with both the
theoretical analysis and the real-world applications.

We consider the task of general supervised machine learning models, which are commonly used in real-word machine learning tasks. All of the steps can affect the performance of the machine learning process.

Let $X = \{x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{N_1}\}$ denote the set of training samples and $y_i$ is the corresponding label of $x_i$, where $y_i \in \{c_{l_1}, c_{l_2}, \ldots, c_{l_n}\}$ ($C$ is the set of class labels, $n$ is the number of the classes, and $N_1$ is the number of the labelled training samples). $$\max_W L(W|X)$$
$$\text{s.t. } g(W) \geq 0$$

(1)

where $L(W|X)$ represents the loss function and $W$ is the parameters of the machine learning model. Besides, $g(W) \geq 0$ is the constraint of the parameters of the model. Then, the Lagrange multiplier of the optimization can be reformulated as follows.

(2)

where $\eta$ is a positive value. Therefore, the machine learning problem can be seen as the minimization of $L_0$.

Figs. 3 and 4 show the flowchart of two special forms of supervised learning models, which are generally used in real-world applications. Furthermore, we can diversify these base models directly to enforce each base model to provide more complement information for further analysis.

II. GENERAL MACHINE LEARNING MODELS — C. UNSUPERVISED LEARNING

As discussed in former subsection, limited number of the training samples will limit the performance of the machine learning process. Instead of the active learning, to solve the problem, unsupervised learning methods provide another way to train the machine learning model without the labelled training samples. This work will mainly discuss a special unsupervised learning process developed by [38], which is an end-to-end self-supervised method.

Denote ci(i = 1, 2, . . . , 3) as the center points which is used to formulate the pseudo classes in the training process where 3 represents the number of the pseudo classes. Just as subsection II-B, U = {u1, u2, . . . , uN2} represents the unlabelled training samples and N2 denotes the number of the unsupervised samples. Besides, denote ϕ(ui) as the features of ui extracted from the machine learning model. Then, the pseudo label zi of the data ui can be defined as

zi = min k∈{1,2,...,3} ∥ck −ϕ(ui)∥,

Since the center points play an important role in the construction of the pseudo classes, diversifying these center points and repulsing the points from each other can better discriminate these pseudo classes. This would show positive effects on improving the effectiveness of the unsupervised learning process.

D. ANALYSIS

As former subsections show, diversity can improve the performance of the machine learning process. In the following, this work will summarize the diversification in machine learning from three aspects: data diversification, model diversification, and inference diversification.

To be concluded, diversification can be used in supervised learning, active learning, and unsupervised learning to improve the model’s performance. According to the models in II-A and II-B, the diversification technology in machine learning model has been divided into three parts: data diversification (Section III), model diversification (Section IV), and inference diversification (Section V). Since the diversification in training batch (Fig. 3) and the diversification in active learning and unsupervised learning mainly consider the diversification in training data, we summarize the prior works in these diversification as data diversification in section III. Besides, the diversification of the model in Fig. 3 and the multiple base models in Fig. 4 mainly focus on the diversification in the machine learning model directly, and thus we summarize these works as model diversification in section IV. Finally, the inference diversification in Fig. 3 will be summarized in section V. In the following section, we’ll first introduce the data diversification in machine learning models.

instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
Supervised learning models typically use minibatches for accurate training estimation. Classical methods rely on uniform random sampling, which can create redundant minibatches and reduce effectiveness. Alternative approaches use non-uniform sampling to enforce diversity.

Determinantal point processes (DPP) define a distribution over data subsets that prefers diverse configurations over redundant ones [39]. A DPP uses a positive semi-definite kernel function φ, where the probability of selecting a subset X is proportional to the determinant of the kernel matrix φ(X) [6]. The kernel φ(xi, xj) decomposes into a correlation term R(xi, xj) and a prior term π(xi)π(xj) [8]. When data are uniformly distributed, the prior is constant, simplifying the kernel to the correlation term R(xi, xj) [9]. DPPs assign higher probabilities to subsets with dissimilar items, thereby reducing the selection of redundant data and generating stochastic gradients with lower variance [9]. To accelerate training, [10] regularizes the DPP with a fixed positive semi-definite matrix (R-DPP). Furthermore, [12] generalizes mini-batch diversification to arbitrary repulsive point processes, specifically Stationary Poisson Disk Sampling (PDS). PDS enforces a minimum distance r between sample points using a distance measurement D(xi, xj), such as Euclidean distance ||xi − xj||² or a heat kernel e^(−||xi−xj||²/σ) [10, 11]. The PDS algorithm iteratively selects random points, discarding those within distance r of existing points in the batch [12]. The computational complexity of PDS is significantly lower than that of DPP [12]. Under these diversification priors, each minibatch contains samples with greater diversity and information, enabling more effective model training and the extraction of more discriminative features from objects.

section: IV. MODEL DIVERSIFICATION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
In addition to data diversification, model diversification can improve representational ability. Due to limited and imbalanced training samples, general machine learning processes learn highly similar parameters, causing redundancy and reducing model representational ability. Therefore, parameters or multiple models can be diversified during training to improve representational ability (D-model and D-models).

A. D-MODEL

The first method diversifies model parameters during training to directly improve representational ability. Under a diversification prior, each parameter factor models unique information, and all factors model a larger proportion of information [22]. Traditionally, Bayesian methods and posterior regularization methods impose diversity over model parameters [138]. The optimization can be formulated as maximizing the log-likelihood plus a diversity prior: max_W log P(X|W) + log P(W) [19, 20]. Diversity-promoting priors measure similarity between learned factors to encourage diversification. Prior works have developed measurements from six aspects: distance, angular, eigenvalue, divergence, L2,1, and DPP [40-42, 45-51, 53-59].

1) BAYESIAN METHOD

Model parameters can be calculated using the Bayesian method: W ∝ P(W|X) = P(X|W) × P(W) [17]. Here, W = [w1, w2, ..., wK] denotes model parameters, K is the number of parameters, P(X|W) is the likelihood, and P(W) is the diversity-promoting prior. The optimization is formulated as: W* = arg max_W [log P(X|W) + log P(W)] [19]. The diversity prior log P(W) encourages learned factors to be diversified [19, 20].

2) POSTERIOR REGULARIZATION METHOD

Posterior regularization methods impose diversity by adding side information into parameter estimation [138]. The diversity-regularized optimization problem is: max_W [L0 + γ f(W)] [21]. Here, f(W) measures diversity of factors, L0 is the optimization term, and γ is the tradeoff parameter between optimization and diversification [21].

3) DIVERSITY REGULARIZATION

Diversity regularization encourages factors to repulse from each other or be uncorrelated [40-42]. The key problem is calculating factor diversification. Prior works impose diversity from six aspects:

a) DISTANCE-BASED MEASUREMENTS

The Euclidean distance between factors wi and wj encourages diversification: f(W) = Σ_{i≠j} ||wi - wj||² [22]. The heat kernel method uses a Gaussian function: f(wi, wj) = -e^(-||wi-wj||²/σ) [2, 3, 143].

b) ANGULAR-BASED MEASUREMENTS

Cosine similarity measures redundancy between latent factors: cij = <wi, wj> / (||wi|| ||wj||) [45, 46]. The diversity prior encourages factors to be orthogonal (cij → 0) [28]. Angular measurements are invariant to scale, translation, rotation, and orientation [19, 21, 47]. The angular between factors is formulated as 0ij = arccos(<wi, wj> / (||wi|| ||wj||)) [30]. A diversity function uses mean and variance of angular: f(W) = 9(W) - 5(W) [31], where 9(W) is mean angular and 5(W) is variance. This prior encourages angular between factors to approach π/2 [32]. Inner product measurement encourages orthogonality: P(W) ∝ e^(-γ Σ_{i≠j} <wi, wj>) [33]. Relaxed exclusivity uses L1 norm: P(W) ∝ e^(-γ Σ_{i≠j} ||wi ⊙ wj||₁) [36].

c) EIGENVALUE-BASED MEASUREMENTS

Eigenvalues of the kernel matrix κ(W) = WWᵀ encourage orthogonality. Submodular spectral diversity (SSD) regularizes eigenvalues to approach 1: P(W) = e^(-γ Σ_{i=1}^K (λi(κ(W)) - 1)²) [38]. Uncorrelation and evenness normalizes eigenvalues into a probability simplex and minimizes KL divergence with uniform distribution [40, 41]. Log-determinant divergence (LDD) combines orthogonality and sparsity: P(W) = e^(-γ (tr(κ(W)) - log det(κ(W)) + τ||W||₁)) [42].
