Data analytics extracts knowledge from collected data [52]. Unlike machine learning, which teaches computers tasks without explicit programming, analytics analyzes raw data to aid decision-making [6].

Algorithms have been applied in business, marketing, health care, transportation, and education [6], [87]–[89], helping individuals make informed decisions based on available data [6].

Data analytics is divided into three categories: exploratory, confirmatory, and qualitative [90].

Exploratory Data Analytics (EDA) discovers new features and underlying structures in data [90]. It is split into graphical and quantitative methods [90]. Graphical methods include histograms and probability plots [90]. Quantitative methods include confidence intervals for the mean and variance [90].

Confirmatory Data Analytics (CDA) tests hypotheses. Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) compares data from two or more processes, assuming equal variances, often using Bartlett's test [91], [92]. The Chi-Square test checks if dataset variance equals a specific value, important in manufacturing [91], [92].

Qualitative Data Analytics (QDA) interprets non-numeric data such as text, images, and interviews [93]. It is prevalent in social sciences and text analysis [93], [96]. Key terms include 'Theme' and 'Characteristic' [94]. The process involves iterative sorting and categorizing by theme [94], [95], [96].

Machine learning can serve as a data analysis method, automatically building analytical models to identify data patterns [97].
output:
Data analytics has become an increasingly important tool for users to extract knowledge and inferences from the abundant amount of collected data [52]. This analysis has become easier with the emergence of sophisticated computers and software that are able to perform exhaustive computations in lightning quick speeds. In contrast to machine learning which tries to 'teach' computers to perform certain tasks without explicitly programming them, data analytics try to analyze and make inferences based on the raw collected data in order to take better decisions [6].

To this end, different techniques and algorithms have been developed. These algorithms have been applied in various fields such as business, marketing, health care, transportation, and education [6], [87]–[89]. This has helped individuals make more informed decisions about the data available at their hands by making use of the results of such techniques.

Fig. 8 shows the different data analytics types and algorithms that will be discussed.

FIGURE 8. Different data analytics categories and algorithms.

1) TYPES

Data analytics algorithms and techniques can be divided into three main categories: exploratory, confirmatory, and qualitative. Each category represents a different goal and approach when it comes to dealing with the data.

(i) Exploratory Data Analytics (EDA): Exploratory Data Analytics (EDA) is a group of techniques that tries to determine/discover new features within the data [90]. These techniques often give insights into the available data and uncover the underlying structure found within the data. The difference between EDA techniques and machine learning techniques is that EDA techniques analyze the data and try to infer the adequate model. On the other hand, machine learning techniques first try to find the model and then analyze its parameters [90]. EDA techniques can be divided into two main groups: graphical and quantitative. Some of these techniques are discussed below [90]:

• Graphical:
– Histograms: Histograms give a graphical summary of the distribution of a univariate dataset. This can be done to one feature of the collected data.
– Probability Plot: Probability plots are another graphical technique that helps analysts assess whether the data follows a specific distribution or not. The data is plotted against a theoretical distribution. If the plot has a linear form, then this implies that theoretical distribution fits the data well. If the plot does not have a linear form, then the considered distribution is not representative of the data.

• Quantitative:
– Confidence intervals for the mean: These intervals provide a range of where the true mean may lie given the dataset available. Since the data contains only a sample of the actual possible instances of a specific feature, then the calculated mean of the data is not the true mean of the feature. Hence, confidence intervals are used to indicate the lower and upper limits of the true mean.
– Variance: Variance is a measure of how the data varies around the mean. It gives an idea of how wide or narrow the distribution is. This can help the analyst determine how sensitive the dataset is to a variation in a specific variable.

(ii) Confirmatory Data Analytics (CDA): Confirmatory Data Analytics (CDA) is a group of techniques that try to confirm whether a hypothesis is true or false. Such techniques assume that there is a specific hypothesis and perform tests that either confirm the validity or invalidity of the hypothesis. Two well known tests are discussed below [90].

• Analysis of Variance (ANOVA): ANOVA techniques are often used to compare data collected from two or more processes. The idea is to test whether the processes have equal variances. Bartlett's test performs ANOVA by testing for what is called homogeneity of variance. The hypothesis is assumed to be that all the variances are equal. Performing this analysis answers the question of whether the variances are truly equal or not with some specific confidence level. This type of tests is often used when the dataset seems to be normally distributed and is one of a set of statistical tests called 'parametric tests' which also include t-tests [91], [92].

• Chi-Square Test for variance: This test is used to see if the variance of a dataset is equal to a specific value. This is often very important in manufacturing processes because manufacturers desire that their production process's variability is greater or smaller than some threshold.

These tests output a value that allows the analyst to determine whether the original hypothesis is valid or not. Based on this, he/she can take action and change some aspects of the considered process. This type of tests is often used when the dataset does not seem to be normally distributed, but rather follows other distributions. It is one of a set of statistical tests called 'non-parametric tests' that include tests like Wilcoxon rank sum test and Spearman's rank correlation coefficient [91], [92].

(iii) Qualitative Data Analytics (QDA): Another type of data analytics is Qualitative Data Analytics (QDA). This type encompasses the set of processes and techniques that try to explain/interpret qualitative (non-numeric) data such as videos, interview transcripts, images, and documents [93]. These techniques are very prevalent in social sciences in which a lot of the data collected is non-numeric in nature. They are also prevalent in text analysis by searching for recurring words or topics.

There are some key terms that often pop up in QDA techniques. Words such as 'Theme' that provides a general idea of the topics apparent in the data and 'Characteristic' which represents a single item in a text often appear when performing QDA. The process of performing QDA involves having to iteratively and progressively notice, collect, and think about things [94]. This process is not linear since the cycle keeps on repeating and you do not go through it step by step, but rather do these steps simultaneously. This process is shown in Fig. 9.

To perform QDA, techniques like sorting and categorizing the collected data into groups based on theme can help simplify the analysis. After sorting the data, further analysis is performed by trying to interpret the significance of the sorting or by trying to explain the findings based on the sorted data.

These techniques have been used in different applications like text mining, marketing research, business, criminology, and sociology [95], [96].

It is worth mentioning that machine learning can be used as one method for data analysis. This is because in essence, machine learning can be thought of as a data analysis method that builds the analytical model automatically [97]. Hence, it can help identify and uncover patterns found within the data.

section: V. RESEARCH OPPORTUNITIES USING MACHINE

Online course platforms like Coursera, edX, and Udacity generate massive data streams, with over 78 million students and 10,000 courses across 600 universities [3]. Each student produces nearly 1,000 event log entries monthly, and courses see approximately 60,000 visits monthly [4], establishing e-learning as a primary contributor to Big Data.

Machine learning and data analytics are needed to extract useful information for more efficient, intelligent systems. The following research opportunities address specific e-learning challenges:

*   **Transmission/Delivery:** Comparing student performance between synchronous and asynchronous course formats using quantitative and qualitative analytics can determine the optimal delivery mode based on location, forum interaction, and grades. Text mining and supervised learning (e.g., SVM, ANN) can analyze forum sentiment to identify discouraged students and inform engagement strategies.
*   **Personalization:** Beyond existing clustering and classification works [23]–[25], [38], [39], opportunities include classifying students by learning style to recommend courses or formats; predicting final grades from early performance using logistic regression or ANN to identify at-risk students and struggling concepts; and analyzing the statistical significance of logins on performance to adapt content.
*   **Collaborative/Cooperative Learning:** Analyzing collaboration levels via forum engagement and unsupervised clustering (e.g., k-means) can assess group project effectiveness. Grouping students by learning style can improve cooperation and information sharing.
*   **Evaluation & Assessment:** Comparing student performance and feedback between traditional classroom and online formats using quantitative analytics can measure e-learning efficiency. Combining sentiment analysis of feedback with activity log data provides a comprehensive effectiveness measure.
*   **Enabling Technologies:** Regression algorithms can train systems for load forecasting using labeled traffic data, allowing infrastructure providers to predict resource needs. Machine learning can also identify high-bandwidth applications; for example, modifying course format from synchronous to asynchronous or providing less demanding content formats can distribute traffic load based on developed patterns and models.

section: VI. CONCLUSION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Data growth necessitates machine learning and analytics for information extraction. These algorithms are beneficial across fields like healthcare and energy. E-learning, despite providing information access, faces challenges in content delivery and personalization. This survey reviewed applicable algorithms and their use in e-learning, detailing the field's characteristics and challenges. It also discussed implementations and proposed research opportunities for further exploration. (Refs. [1]-[5])
output: The growth of data available from various devices has led to the need to analyze and extract useful information from it. Machine learning and data analytics techniques have been proposed as means to satisfy this need. From supervised learning and unsupervised learning to exploratory and confirmatory data analytics, these algorithms are proving to be beneficial and essential in various applications and fields such as healthcare, business, and energy. Among these applications is the field of e-learning. E-learning is a field that has gathered interest in recent times due to the proliferation of technology throughout the world. Despite its ability to provide access to information, e-learning is facing many challenges such as how to deliver content and how to personalize the e-learning experience. In this survey, we discussed the various machine learning and data analytics algorithms and glanced over some of the works in which they were used in different fields. Moreover, the field of e-learning was explored thoroughly by providing definitions and the characteristics describing it. Furthermore, some of the challenges faced within this field have been investigated. Also, some of the works that implemented machine learning and data analytics in e-learning were discussed. Finally, a few research opportunities have been proposed to give insights into the areas that need further exploration.

ABSTRACT Solar energy is a green energy source that can be used to generate electricity, making it one
of the oldest existing renewable energy sources. However, solar energy values are not always available
in many areas far from urban cities, due to the high cost of purchasing and maintaining measuring
instruments. In these areas, the only way to know the values of solar radiation from is to predict these
values. To address this problem, we have designed an efficient model capable of forecasting hourly solar
radiation a climate with a combination of arid and humid conditions using real-time data from meteorological
variables measured by a Meteorological Station located in a university area isolated from the central city.
For the development of our model, 11 meteorological variables were collected from January to December
2023. From this, dimensionality reduction was carried out using the Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
technique, obtaining the 8 most appropriate representative variables for the prediction of solar radiation
using different Machine Learning (ML) models. To ensure the reliability of our model, we compared the
performance metrics of several ML models. Finally, ensemble techniques were applied to enhance prediction
accuracy by combining various ML algorithms. The best results were obtained using the Stacking Regressor
(SR), achieving an R2 of 0.92, RMSE of 47.30 W/m2, and MAE of 18.27 W/m2, demonstrating high
predictive performance in the target climate region.
INDEX TERMS Machine learning, meteorology, prediction, solar radiation.

I. INTRODUCTION

The energy released by the Sun, transmitted through electromagnetic radiation, is known as solar radiation. This energy is a mixture of radiation with wavelengths between 200 and 4000 nm, which are called ultraviolet radiation, visible light, and infrared radiation. In turn, the magnitude that measures the solar radiation that reaches the Earth is the irradiance, also called global solar radiation, which is defined as the power per unit of area, and is measured in (W/m2).

Solar energy is known to be a renewable green energy source and this energy can be harnessed with the use of photovoltaic techniques to generate electricity. According to [1], it is mentioned that solar radiation data is necessary in various applications such as solar panel, agricultural crop models, air quality models, and hydrological models. On the other hand, in [2], it is mentioned that the continuous use of fossil energy has caused a serious environmental pollution problem; therefore, to solve this serious problem, the use of renewable energy is proposed. A source of renewable energy is solar energy that can generate the demand for electricity necessary for industries and the population in general. In [3] they mentioned that renewable energies, such as solar and wind, have been gaining popularity for more than a decade and could be used in rural, underdeveloped areas that desire energy independence.

However, changes in solar radiation over time are caused by meteorological conditions, meaning factors like cloud cover and air pollution can influence the intensity of solar radiation [2].

In the study by [4], it is stated that predicting global solar radiation in a particular area is crucial, as it offers investors valuable information on the solar resources of that region, which can be highly advantageous for the development of large-scale solar energy projects. According to [5], solar radiation is an essential parameter for the design and efficient operation of solar energy systems. In many locations, records of solar radiation are not accessible because of the high costs associated with acquiring and maintaining the necessary measurement instruments. As a result, it is important to predict solar radiation with a reasonable degree of accuracy for these areas using different solar radiation estimation models.

A classic form of prediction from historical data commonly used is the use of linear or polynomial regression models. However, in our work we implement a Solar Radiation prediction model using Machine Learning (ML) algorithms based on the most representative values of the meteorological data obtained during the year 2023. This is because ML based methods outperform classical regression methods for predictive modeling due to several reasons such as:
• They handle nonlinearities in the data more effectively than classical regression methods, which assume linear relationships.
• They identify patterns between variables that may not be evident with classical regression methods, leading to more accurate predictions.
• They adapt to the presence of outliers, missing values, or measurement errors.
• They perform an automatic selection of features, identifying the most relevant features for prediction.
• They are able to handle large amounts of data and complex problems, making them suitable for large-scale predictive modeling.

Our study area is the National University of Engineering (UNI) and is located in the northern area of the city of Lima, where it is known that it is an area where solar energy greatly affects. Having difficulties in obtaining these values of incident energy due to the lack of measuring devices, it is essential to know these monthly values of solar energy, so that it can be used for other purposes such as the use of photovoltaic cells.

This challenge is particularly relevant in the context of Sustainable Development Goal 13 (SDG 13) established by the United Nations, which calls for urgent action to combat climate change and its impacts. Accurate solar radiation prediction models contribute to this goal by facilitating the deployment of renewable energy systems, especially in arid and under-resourced areas, thereby supporting climate adaptation and mitigation strategies [6].

Lima, Peru, has a climate classified as subtropical desert (according to the Köppen climate classification) [7], [8], [9]. This type of climate is characterized by a unique combination of arid and humid conditions, mainly influenced by its proximity to the Pacific Ocean, the cold Humboldt Current, and the proximity to the Andes. The main characteristics of this climate include:
• Low Precipitation: Lima is one of the driest capitals in the world, with annual rainfall generally not exceeding 10 mm, which significantly limits the development of vegetation.
• High Humidity: Despite the scarcity of rainfall, the city experiences high levels of humidity due to the moderating effect of the ocean and the Humboldt Current.
• Mild Temperatures: Lima’s climate is moderate year-round, with cool winters (12–19 ◦C or 54–66 ◦F) and warm summers (12–29 ◦C or 64–84 ◦F).
• Frequent Presence of Fog: ‘‘Garúa,’’ a typical coastal fog, is common in the winter months and contributes to a cool, cloudy environment.

From a technical point of view, Lima’s climate combines three main elements of the Köppen classification:
1) Desert (B): Characterized by extremely low annual precipitation, insufficient to support significant vegetation.
2) Hot (W): Represents arid regions with consistently high temperatures, especially during the warmer months.
3) Subtropical (h): Indicates a warm climate with an annual mean temperature above 18 ◦C (64.4 ◦F).

Together, these features make Lima’s climate exceptional compared to other typical desert climates, lacking extreme heat variations and being marked by unique coastal conditions such as persistent fog.

To carry out our study, a medium-sized weather station was installed at the UNI facilities, with the aim of collecting various meteorological data. From this information, monthly predictions of solar radiation could be made. It should be noted that there are numerous studies worldwide that estimate solar radiation using different developed models. In our case, the model was specifically applied to a city characterized by an arid climate and low rainfall, which adds a particular context to the analysis.

As a result of this study, we developed two predictive models using the data collected throughout 2023. The first model utilized traditional Machine Learning methods, while the second employed advanced Ensemble techniques. These Ensemble methods combine the outputs of multiple base models to enhance overall performance, boost prediction accuracy, and create a more resilient model capable of handling the inherent variations and complexities present in meteorological data.

[23] Explored single neural networks (SNN) and bootstrapped aggregate neural networks (BANN) for hourly global solar radiation prediction using data from the Bouzareah-Algeria Renewable Energy Development Center; concluded BANN model is suitable for predicting solar radiation in locations without measurement equipment.

[24] Developed DeepSI, a Bayesian deep learning model combining bidirectional LSTM autoencoders and transformers with Monte Carlo dropout for long-term solar irradiance forecasting using downscaled climate data; applied deep learning techniques for real-time, short-term prediction based on observed meteorological data in a subtropical desert climate.

output:
The study in [10] highlights the need for more accurate daily irradiation forecasts in Singapore. To address this, they developed a climate research and prediction model using multivariate statistical learning techniques. This model provided hourly daily irradiation forecast data for three years. The results were compared with those from the Global Forecast System, a numerical weather prediction model used by the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

In [11], a daily forecasting model for hourly solar irradiation was proposed, which does not require historical irradiation data but uses some meteorological data. The model employed a recurrent neural network (LSTM-RNN) to manage long- and short-term memory and was compared with a forward neural network (FFNN). Experiments were conducted using meteorological data from stations in various countries representing different climates. The results showed that the LSTM-RNN approach was more accurate than the FFNN. Then in [12] they carried out an estimate of solar radiation east of the Mediterranean in Turkey, taking data from the Turkish State Meteorological Service. The authors used an ANN model to perform this estimation. In their work, the best estimation performance was obtained by optimizing the number of neurons used in the hidden layer of the network with the trial-and-error method.

Independently, in [13], compared different prediction models for solar radiation, focusing on multi-layer perceptron (MLP), boosted decision trees, and a new combination of these models with linear regression for predicting daily global solar irradiation (DGSR). The models were validated using real data from southern Algeria. Results showed that the MLP model outperformed the other models. In [14], both an ANN model and a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) model were developed for solar radiation prediction. The authors utilized meteorological data from a weather station in Alabama. Their results indicated that the RNN model achieved higher prediction accuracy compared to the ANN model. Then, in [15], the performance of various evolutionary neural network models was evaluated to address the solar radiation prediction problem in Toledo, Spain. The prediction relied on satellite measurements and variables, eliminating the need for data from ground stations or atmospheric soundings. The authors reported that the results obtained for solar radiation estimation at the Toledo radiometric station demonstrated excellent performance with the evolutionary neural networks tested.

Independently in [16] developed a model for monthly solar radiation prediction in Turkey using multi-gene genetic programming (MGGP), an evolutionary algorithm based on symbolic genetic programming. The study compared the performance of the MGGP approach against three classical empirical equations widely used in the literature. Using long-term meteorological data from 163 weather stations across seven climatic regions of the country, the authors demonstrated the superiority of the AI-based model in generating more accurate and practical equations.

In the work of [17], the importance of predicting global solar radiation for the development of solar energy conversion systems was emphasized. The objective was to predict solar radiation data for four provinces in Turkey using machine learning algorithms such as ANN, K-NN, SVM, and Deep Learning (DL). The models were trained with meteorological data collected by the Turkish State Meteorological Service for the years 2018-2019. The study concluded that the ANN algorithm was the most accurate. Then, in [18] mentioned that several types of ANN were developed to predict solar radiation in Makurdi, Nigeria. In their work they used: A Forward Backpropagation Neural Network (FFNN), a Radial Basis Function Network (RBFN) and Generalized Regression Neural Network (GRNN). The objective was to improve prediction accuracy by using an ANN ensemble for the average monthly global solar radiation.

Independently, in the work of [5], it was built an ANN model to reliably estimate solar radiation. In their work the authors investigate different ANN models with three different algorithms. These models were trained with meteorological data collected over one year from six hot-climate locations in Tamil Nadu, India. In the work of [4] the prediction of global solar radiation in 27 European cities was carried out. In their work they used 6 different Machine Learning algorithms such as: Linear model (LM), Decision Tree (DT), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Deep Learning (DL), Random Forest (RF) and Gradient Boosted Trees (GBT). The study concluded that the Support Vector Machine (SVM) algorithm provided the most accurate predictions.

Then, in [19], two ANN models were utilized for predicting daily solar radiation based on meteorological data. The first model was a multilayer perceptron neural network (MLP-NN), while the second was a nonlinear autoregressive network with exogenous inputs (NARX). Independently, in [20], a new hybrid approach for global solar radiation (GSR) prediction was introduced, leveraging Deep Learning techniques. These predictive models are particularly beneficial for optimizing the performance of photovoltaic power systems in the solar energy industry. The system proposed by the authors was tested in a GSR daily forecast system of six solar parks in Australia.

In the work of [21], they presented a study comparing 2 empirical models against 3 machine learning models such as: Artificial Neural Networks (ANN), Support Vector Machine (SVM) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM). Using monthly data from 6 stations in Turkey, they found that in terms of its metrics, the best model was the LSTM, followed by the ANN and SVM. In their work, the authors concluded that it is more appropriate to use machine learning models than empirical equations. Then, in [22], they indicated that the estimation of monthly Solar Radiation was carried out using five different approaches based on machine learning. The models used are Support Vector Machine Regression (SVMR), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Gaussian Process Regression (GPR), Extreme Learning Machines (ELM) and K Nearest Neighbors (KNN). In their work, the authors found that the LSTM and GPR algorithms are an alternative for forecasting Solar Radiation in Turkey, which has arid and semi-arid climatic regions.

In [23], the authors explored the use of single neural networks (SNN) and bootstrapped aggregate neural networks (BANN) to predict hourly global solar radiation. In their research, the authors acquire data from the Bouzareah-Algeria Renewable Energy Development Center. The authors concluded that the BANN model is particularly suitable for predicting solar radiation in locations without measurement equipment, such as solarimeters or pyrometers.

In [24] developed DeepSI, a Bayesian deep learning model combining bidirectional LSTM autoencoders and transformers with Monte Carlo dropout for long-term solar irradiance forecasting using downscaled climate data. Unlike their long-term focus, this study applies deep learning techniques for real-time, short-term prediction based on observed meteorological data in a subtropical desert climate. Finally, [25] conducted a comparative study using real data from a solar plant in Turkey, applying machine learning models and time series techniques to predict irradiance and temperature at 5-minute intervals. Their work highlights models such as Random Forest and MLP, focusing on improving the performance estimation of photovoltaic systems.

section: III. MATERIALS AND METHODS — B. DATA COLLECTION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
In this study, meteorological parameters were collected from a MKIII-RTI-LR RAINWISE station installed on the Docimasia Laboratory roof at the National University of Engineering (UNI) in Lima, Peru, throughout 2023. The collected parameters included Wind Speed, Wind Direction, Ambient Temperature, Relative Humidity, Barometric Pressure, and Precipitation.

The raw data underwent cleaning and preprocessing prior to dimensionality reduction. Missing values were detected and imputed using seasonal means or controlled normal noise. Outliers, identified via the interquartile range method (thresholds: 165.0–331.0 W/m²), were smoothed or excluded, representing 10.16% of the total dataset (189,644 observations). Seasonal data were then consolidated into an annual dataset for analysis.

Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was applied to reduce dimensionality. Three components were extracted, explaining 66.55% of the total variance: Component 1 (Thermal sensation: Outside Temperature, Wind Chill, Heat Index, Pressure), Component 2 (Humidity: Wind Chill, Dew Point, Relative Humidity), and Component 3 (Wind: Wind Direction, Peak Wind Speed). These components highlight the main patterns of variability in the dataset.

According to PCA criteria, the model relies on the following parameters: Outside Temperature, Wind Chill, Heat Index, Pressure, Dew Point, Relative Humidity, Wind Direction, and Peak Wind Speed.

Performance validation used regression metrics including Mean Squared Error (MSE), Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), Coefficient of Determination (R²), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE). The Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) was also used to evaluate predictive power relative to observed data means.

1) TREATMENT OF THE DATA OBTAINED

Nowadays, most scientific disciplines generate large volumes of data from their experiments. However, a significant portion of this data is highly redundant and can be effectively reduced to a smaller set of variables without losing critical information.

Before applying dimensionality reduction techniques, the raw meteorological data underwent a thorough cleaning and preprocessing phase to ensure accuracy and reliability. The initial dataset, collected monthly, was grouped by climatic seasons (summer, autumn, winter, and spring) to analyze trends and detect inconsistencies such as missing values or noisy data.

To address these issues, the following steps were implemented:

• Detection of Missing Values: The percentage of missing data for each variable was calculated across all seasons, revealing significant gaps in specific time periods that required correction.
• Noise and Outlier Treatment: Outliers were identified using the interquartile range (IQR) method, with thresholds set at a lower bound of 165.0 W/m2 and an upper bound of 331.0 W/m2. A total of 19,271 outliers were detected, representing 10.16% of the total dataset (189,644 observations). These extreme values were either smoothed through percentile-based techniques, specifically using the 90th percentile threshold, or excluded entirely when their influence on data trends was deemed significant.
• Imputation of Missing Values: For short-term gaps, missing values were imputed using the mean of surrounding observations within each season. For longer-term gaps, controlled noise was added based on a normal distribution, ensuring realistic and non-redundant patterns in the data.

Following this preprocessing, the seasonal data were consolidated into an annual dataset, preserving the integrity of seasonal trends while ensuring a consistent and high-quality foundation for the Principal Component Analysis (PCA) stage. These steps were essential to identify and retain the most representative variables for the subsequent machine learning models. The mathematical procedures that make this variable reduction possible are called dimensionality reduction techniques that are widely developed by Statistics and Machine Learning [26].

In [27] they mentioned that data preprocessing is the central stage in data mining, and dimensionality reduction is a technique used for data preprocessing. Dimensionality reduction involves applying various methods to eliminate excessive and irrelevant features from Machine Learning models. Moreover, it plays a crucial role in identifying and removing features that negatively impact the performance of the Machine Learning model.

Among dimensionality reduction methods, one of the most efficient consists of identifying and selecting a subset of features that are most relevant to the target variable. This approach is known as feature selection, and it is especially effective when dealing with tabular data in which each column represents a specific type of information.

In our case, to reduce and group our meteorological data we used the statistical technique called Principal Component Analysis (PCA). This technique simplifies the analysis, keeping as much relevant information as possible. In [28], it is stated that PCA is a mathematical tool designed to capture and represent the variation within a dataset using a reduced number of factors.

After applying PCA, three components (Component 1, Component 2, and Component 3) were obtained, grouping our variables as follows:

• Component 1 (Thermal sensation): Outside Temperature, Wind Chill, Heat Index, Pressure.
• Component 2 (Humidity): Wind Chill, Dew Point, Relative (Out) Humidity.
• Component 3 (Wind): Wind Dir, Peak Wind Speed.

These three components explain approximately 66.55% of the total variance in the data, with Thermal Sensation accounting for 35.78%, Humidity for 19.41%, and Wind for 11.36%. This highlights their importance in representing the main patterns of variability in the solar radiation dataset. They constitute the structural model of solar radiation in Lima. Figure 5 shows the structural model obtained from applying the PCA.

According to the PCA criteria, it is determined that our model relies exclusively on the following parameters: Outside Temperature, Wind Chill, Heat Index, Pressure, Dew Point, Relative Humidity, Wind Direction and Peak Wind Speed.

FIGURE 5. Structural model and results of applied analysis.

2) PERFORMANCE METRICS

To validate the performance of the machine learning models applied in this study, a set of commonly used regression metrics was considered: Mean Squared Error (MSE), Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), Coefficient of Determination (R2), and Mean Absolute Error (MAE). These metrics are widely used to evaluate machine learning models, especially in regression tasks.

In particular, for comparative analysis of models, R2 is used as it helps to evaluate the explanatory power and the comparison of models between data sets by means of variance. On the other hand, to assess the actual magnitude of the error, RMSE is used for interpretability, or MSE if it is desired to penalize larger errors.

Finally, to avoid sensitivity to outliers, the MAE metric is used, as it provides a balanced view of the mean error. Additionally, the Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) was used to assess the relative percentage error between predicted and actual values. MAPE is scale-independent and provides an intuitive interpretation of prediction accuracy. Lower values of MAPE indicate better model performance.

Furthermore, the Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) metric was included to evaluate the predictive power of the models compared to the mean of the observed data. NSE values closer to 1 indicate high predictive ability and better agreement between predictions and observations.

section: IV. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS — A. MACHINE LEARNING MODELS FOR SOLAR RADIATION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: The study evaluated six models for solar radiation prediction in the Rimac district, Lima-Peru during 2023. Random Forest (RF) performed best, achieving the lowest MSE and RMSE, an R² of 0.91, and a MAPE of 32.35%. Decision Tree (DT) followed with an R² of 0.87 and a MAPE of 31.95%, while K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) showed the highest MAPE at 72.64%. Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) and Gradient Boosting (GB) demonstrated moderate performance with R² values of 0.63 and 0.64, respectively. All models used a random_state of 42 for reproducibility.
output:
PREDICTION
It is desirable to develop an algorithm capable of predicting solar radiation values based on multiple input variables. The most appropriate models in our study are the following: Polynomial Regression, Decision Trees, Random Forest, Artificial Neural Networks, K Nearest Neighbors and Gradient Boosting.

1) POLYNOMIAL REGRESSION (PR)
This method extends linear regression by allowing the relationship between the dependent variable and the independent variables to be modeled using higher degree polynomials. It can fit more complex curves, but can become computationally expensive with very high polynomial degrees and can suffer from overfitting. The MSE and RMSE are relatively high, suggesting that the model may not fit the test data well. The R2 is moderate, indicating that the model explains approximately 57% of the variability of the data. The MAE is relatively low, suggesting that the model predictions are close to the true values on average, but there may still be discrepancies in some predictions.
Parameters used:
• degree=2. Specifies the degree of the polynomial to use. Figures 6 and 7 show the analysis of the plot and its validation.
FIGURE 6. Polynomial regression plot.
FIGURE 7. Polynomial regression validation.

2) DECISION TREES (DT)
Decision trees are a widely used algorithm for data classification and regression. They are predictive models that use a tree-like structure to make decisions based on characteristics or attributes of the input data. It performs noticeably better than polynomial regression with lower MSE and RMSE. An R2 of 0.87 indicates that the model can explain 87% of the variability in the test data. The MAE of 19.08 shows considerable precision. Decision trees are prone to overfitting, but provide good model interpretation. The execution time obtained is reasonable and fast.
Parameters used:
• random_state: 42. This parameter sets a seed for the model’s random number generator, ensuring that the results are reproducible. Figures 8 and 9 show the analysis of the plot and its validation.
FIGURE 8. Decision tress plot.
FIGURE 9. Decision tree validation.

3) RANDOM FOREST (RF)
It is a supervised learning algorithm that creates several decision trees using a training dataset. The outcomes from these trees are then combined to produce a single, more robust model than the individual results from each tree [29]. This model demonstrates excellent performance, characterized by very low MSE and RMSE values. An R2 of 0.91 means that the model can explain 91% of the variability in the test data. The MAE of 18.44 indicates a prediction accuracy similar to that of Decision Trees but with greater robustness against overfitting. The execution time is longer due to the complexity of training multiple trees, but it is still quite practical.
Parameters used:
• random_state: 42. Sets a seed for the random number generator, ensuring that the results are reproducible. Figures 10 and 11 show the analysis of the plot and its validation.
FIGURE 10. Random forest plot.
FIGURE 11. Random forest validation.

4) ARTIFICIAL NEURAL NETWORKS (ANN)
Artificial Neural Networks are computational models inspired by the human brain, composed of layers of interconnected neurons. These networks are trained using the error backpropagation algorithm, which adjusts the connection weights between neurons to reduce the error function. Capable of learning non-linear data representations, Artificial Neural Networks are highly effective for various classification and pattern recognition tasks [30]. This model shows moderate performance with relatively high MSE and RMSE values. An R2 of 0.63 means that the model can explain 63% of the variability in the test data. The MAE of 59.62 is also considerably high. Additionally, the 14-minute runtime is considerably longer compared to other models, which can be a limiting factor in applications where computing time is crucial.
Parameters used:
• layers. Dense: 64 neurons. Dense layers are the basic layers of neural networks.
• activation function: ReLU is a nonlinear activation function that helps the network learn complex nonlinear relationships.
• model.compile: Optimizer ‘adam’, loss ‘mse’, metrics ‘mae’. The build configures the model for training. Adam is an optimization algorithm that combines the advantages of other algorithms, such as AdaGrad and RMSProp, for efficient updating of model weights.
• model.fit: 100 epochs, batch_size 32, validation_split 0.2. Train the model with the training data. An epoch refers to a complete pass through the entire training dataset. More epochs can lead to better model fit, but also a higher risk of overfitting. Figures 12 and 13 show the analysis of the plot and its validation.
FIGURE 12. Artificial neural networks plot.
FIGURE 13. Artificial neural networks validation.

5) K NEAREST NEIGHBORS (KNN)
It is an algorithm within supervised learning that primarily functions to classify values by identifying the ''most similar'' (closest) data points learned during the training phase and making predictions for new points based on that classification. The KNN model performs well with higher MSE and RMSE than Random Forest and Decision Trees. An R2 of 0.75 means that the model can explain 75% of the variability in the test data. The MAE of 41.91 shows moderate accuracy. The KNN is quite fast to run, but its performance can decrease with large data sets.
Parameters used:
• n_neighbors: 5. Number of neighbors to use for prediction, 5 is the default value.
• weights: ‘uniform’. Weight function for prediction. ‘uniform’ means that all neighbors have the same influence.
• algorithm: ‘auto’. Algorithm used to calculate nearest neighbors. ‘auto’ selects the most efficient method based on the value of n_neighbors and the characteristics of the data set.
• leaf_size: 30. Size of the sheet passed to the BallTree or KDTree. Affects the speed of tree construction and query.
• p:2. Power of the Minkowski parameter. When p = 2, the Euclidean distance is used.
Figures 14 and 15 show the analysis of the plot and its validation.
FIGURE 14. K Nearest neighbors plot.
FIGURE 15. K-Nearest neighbors validation.

6) GRADIENT BOOSTING (GB)
It is a supervised learning algorithm that builds a more robust model from the combination of multiple simpler decision trees. In each iteration, the model is adjusted and the residual errors of the previous model decrease. The term gradients is related to the optimization technique used to minimize the loss function [31]. This model achieved moderate performance, with an R2 of 0.64, indicating it explains 64% of the variability in the test data. The MSE and RMSE are relatively high, indicating that the predictions are not very accurate. The execution time is reasonable, making Gradient Boosting a viable option when seeking a balance between accuracy and time efficiency.
Parameters used:
• random_state: 42. Fixes the seed to ensure reproducibility of results.
• loss: ‘ls’. Loss function to optimize ‘ls’ (least squares) for regression.
• learning_rate: 0.1. Learning rate that reduces the contribution of each tree. A lower value may lead to better results, but requires more iterations.
• n_estimators: 100. Number of decision trees to build. A higher value may improve accuracy but increases training time.
• subsample: 1.0. Fraction of samples used to train each tree. Subsampling can reduce variance and avoid overfitting.
• criterion: ‘friedman_mse’. Criterion to measure the quality of division in trees, ‘friedman_mse’ is the default.
• min_samples_split: 2. Minimum number of samples required to split a node.
• min_samples_leaf: 1. Minimum number of samples needed on one sheet.
• max_depth: 3. Maximum depth of trees. Limiting depth can help avoid overfitting.
Figures 16 and 17 show the analysis of the plot and its validation.
FIGURE 16. Gradient boosting plot.
All these results are presented in Table 3.
From Table 3, it can be observed that among all evaluated models, the Random Forest (RF) algorithm yielded the best performance for predicting meteorological variables during 2023 in the Rimac district, Lima-Peru. Its ability to model non-linear relationships and mitigate overfitting makes it particularly effective across various metrics, achieving the lowest MSE and RMSE, the highest values for R2 and NSE, and a MAPE of 32.35%, which is generally considered to represent reasonable prediction accuracy. Although RF has a higher execution time compared to simpler models, its precision and robustness justify its use in accuracy-critical applications.
Other models, such as Decision Tree (DT) and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), also showed good predictive performance. DT achieved competitive accuracy with a relatively low MAPE (31.95%) and the shortest computation time, making it suitable for scenarios where speed is essential. KNN, on the other hand, exhibited the highest MAPE (72.64%), indicating limited reliability despite a short execution time. Gradient Boosting (GB) and Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) demonstrated moderate performance. While capable of capturing complex patterns, their MAPE values were above 25%, and their higher computational cost did not yield significantly better predictive accuracy compared to RF. Each model presents specific strengths and limitations. Therefore, the choice of the most suitable model should consider the application’s particular needs, including required accuracy, interpretability, and computational constraints. For real-time or large-scale applications, faster models like KNN or GB may be preferable, while for tasks demanding higher accuracy and robustness, Random Forest stands out as the optimal choice.

section: V. DISCUSSION OF RESULTS
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Previous studies have addressed solar radiation prediction using machine learning, though many operate in tropical or high-cloud-cover regions [1]. This study focuses on a subtropical desert climate in Rímac, Lima, characterized by low rainfall, high humidity, and persistent cloudiness [1]. Despite limited locally available variables, the proposed Ensemble Learning (Stacking Regressor) model achieved an R² of 0.92, RMSE of 47.30 W/m², and MAE of 18.27 W/m², placing it at a competitive level compared to reference models [1]. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was fundamental for dimensionality reduction, selecting 8 representative variables from the original 11 and grouping them into thermal sensation, humidity, and wind components to optimize performance and interpretability [1]. However, the absence of cloud cover or sunshine duration variables reflects data availability limitations at the selected meteorological station [1]. Additionally, the proposed approach features a less complex computational architecture, making it suitable for low-resource environments such as rural communities lacking advanced meteorological infrastructure [1]. Despite these good results, the model was validated using data from only one year (2023), which may limit long-term generalization; longer time series are more effective at capturing seasonal variability and extreme events [1]. Therefore, future research should include multi-year datasets to better assess the model’s ability to generalize over time and across different conditions [1].

However, many of these studies were conducted in different climate contexts, such as tropical climates or regions with greater access to cloud cover and duration data of the sunshine.

In contrast, this study focuses on a subtropical desert climate, specifically in the district of Rímac, Lima, a region characterized by low rainfall, high humidity, and persistent cloudiness—conditions that are not widely represented in the solar radiation prediction literature. Despite working with a limited set of locally available variables, the proposed model, based on Ensemble Learning (Stacking Regressor), achieved an R2 of 0.92, RMSE of 47.30 W/m2, and MAE of 18.27 W/m2, placing it at a competitive level compared to the reference models in Table 5.

However, the absence of variables such as cloud cover or sunshine duration, which are relevant for estimating solar radiation, reflects the limitations of data availability at the selected meteorological station.

In addition, the proposed approach features a less complex computational architecture, making it suitable for implementation in low-resource environments, such as rural communities without access to advanced meteorological stations. This is a crucial aspect, as many ensemble models like LSTM and ANN require substantial computational resources, limiting their applicability in areas with less technological infrastructure.

Despite the good results obtained, it is important to note that the model was validated using data from only one year (2023), which may limit its long-term generalization. ABSTRACT The primary objective of this research is to determine whether a patient has glioma, a specific kind of brain tumour, by examining various diagnostic markers using a variety of machine learning as well as deep learning approaches, and involving XAI (explainable artificial intelligence) methods. Through the integration of patient data, including medical records, genetic profiles, algorithms using machine learning have the ability to predict how each individual will react to different medical interventions. To guarantee regulatory compliance and inspire confidence in AI-driven healthcare solutions, XAI is incorporated. Machine learning methods employed in this study include Random Forest, decision trees, logistic regression, KNN, Adaboost, SVM, Catboost, LGBM classifier, and Xgboost whereas the deep learning methods include ANN and CNN. Four alternative XAI strategies, including SHAP, Eli5, LIME, and QLattice algorithm, are employed to comprehend the predictions of the model. The Xgboost, a ML model achieved accuracy, precision, recall, f1 score, and AUC of 88%, 82%, 94%, 88%, and 92%, respectively. The best characteristics according to XAI techniques are IDH1, Age at diagnosis, PIK3CA, ATRX, PTEN, CIC, EGFR and TP53. By applying data analytic techniques, the objective is to provide healthcare professionals with a practical tool that enhances their capacity for decision-making, enhances resource management, and ultimately raises the bar for patient care. Medical experts can customise treatments and improve patient outcomes by taking into account patient's particular characteristics. XAI provides justifications to foster faith amongst patients and medical professionals who must rely on AI-assisted diagnosis and treatment recommendations.

The most typical kind of Central nervous system cancer which arises from glial cells is glioma [1]. One kind of brain cancer that penetrates the outer layer of the brain is glioma. Glioblastoma is the most malignant type of tumours [1]. Gliomas are growths of cells that start in the brain or spinal cord. Healthy brain cells called glial cells mimic the cells found in gliomas. By encircling nerve cells, glial cells facilitate their functionality. When a glioma grows, a clump of cells called a tumour forms [2]. The tumour can expand to the point that it presses against brain or the spinal cord, causing signs and symptoms. The symptoms depend on the precise region of the brain or the spinal cord that is impacted. Malignant gliomas can enter healthy brain tissue and grow swiftly. Treatment options for gliomas generally involve surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, and other treatments. Depending on where the glioma is, different symptoms could be present. The type of glioma, its size, and the rate of its growth can all affect the symptoms. Common symptoms and indications of glioma comprises headache, nausea, decreased brain activity, memory loss, alterations in personality or temperament, issues of vision, issues with speech [2], [3]. In Figure 1, the method of treating a glioma tumour is shown. In 2007, World Health Organization (WHO) categorized brain tumours according to the type of cell and grade (grades I–IV), adopting histopathological criteria of diffuse gliomas that relate to similarities with suspected cells of origin and anticipated levels of differentiation [4], [5]. Grade I tumours tend to occur in children and are typically benign tumours, indicating that they are usually treatable [6]. Three tumour types are classified as grade II: oligodendrogliomas, astrocytomas, and oligoastrocytomas, which are a combination of both. Adults commonly experience them. All low-grade gliomas have the potential to grow into high-grade tumours in later stages. Anaplastic Astrocytomas, Anaplastic Oligodendrogliomas, and Anaplastic Oligoastrocytomas are all examples of grade III tumours. Compared to grade II, they are more assertive and intrusive. According to the WHO classification, grade IV glioma, which is identified as Glioblastoma Multiforme (GBM), is one of the deadliest tumours [6].

Brain tumours classified as gliomas might differ from one another in terms of their genetic and Molecular makeup. Several factors are taken into account when predicting how glioma would behave and how it will progress. Each variable’s explanation and potential impact on glioma prediction are Gender, Age at diagnosis, Race, ATRX, PTEN, EGFR, CIC, MUC16, TP53, IDH1, GRIN2A, IDH2, FAT4, FUBP1, BCOR, RB1, CSMD3, NOTCH1, SMARCA4, PIK3CA, NF1, PIK3R1, and PDGFRA [7]. While gender may not have a direct impact on glioma prediction, it can be thought of as a demographic feature that may be associated with other factors. The age of the patient during the diagnosis is a crucial prognostic indicator. In general, younger patients typically experience greater results than older people. For instance, gliomas in paediatric patients could differ in their features and prognoses. The incidence and prognosis of gliomas can vary depending on race. ATRX, PTEN, EGFR, CIC, MUC16, TP53, IDH1, GRIN2A, IDH2, FAT4, FUBP1, BCOR, RB1, CSMD3, NOTCH1, SMARCA4, PIK3CA, NF1, PIK3R1, and PDGFRA are examples of genetic mutations that can occur. These particular genetic changes or mutations may manifest in glioma cells. Each of these changes alters the tumour’s Molecular make-up and, consequently, its behaviour. Patients with glioma may have different treatment options and a different prognosis depending on whether these mutations are present or absent. For instance, better prognoses are linked to IDH1 and IDH2 mutations [8], while poorer prognoses are linked to amplification of EGFR [9] and PTEN loss. TP53 mutations may influence the tumour’s virulence [10]. Genetic testing is essential for glioma Molecular profiling in order to identify the tumour subtype and customize treatment. All of these factors may be taken into consideration by glioma prediction models to evaluate the hazards, and possible treatments for specific patients. Machine learning algorithms, for example, can examine a mixture of these elements to forecast how the disease would most likely develop and the best course of treatment. It is imperative to consult with medical professionals who can provide tailored guidance based on these variables and the most recent discoveries about the diagnosis, management, and prognosis of gliomas [11].

Prediction of patient suffering from glioma tumour can be achieved with artificial intelligence and machine learning classifiers. Artificial intelligence (AI) refers to creation of computer systems and algorithms that are capable of performing activities that frequently need human intelligence, like learning from data, reasoning, solving problems, and understanding natural language. Robots and autonomous systems are included, along with the various additional techniques and purposes, including neural networks and machine learning [12]. Algorithms for artificial intelligence (AI) perform complex operations on enormous volumes of data. These activities consist of recognizing text and imaging, remote medical care, precise disease identification, and disease prediction [13]. A subfield of artificial intelligence called machine learning (ML) is concerned with developing algorithms and models that enable computers to process data, draw conclusions, and make predictions without being explicitly programmed [14], [16]. It involves using statistical techniques to help computers become more proficient at a particular task through iterative learning from experience. The healthcare industry can benefit greatly from machine learning since it can analyse vast amounts of patient data to find trends, predict disease outcomes, and help with early diagnosis. In addition, machine learning can be used to streamline administrative procedures, enhance medicine development, and improve treatment regimens, ultimately leading to better patient care and cheaper healthcare costs [17], [18]. As a result of the recognition that classifiers must be utilised appropriately in order to provide transparency, accountability, and ethics, Explainable AI (XAI) was created [15]. Black-box models have new potential because to the explainability element, which also enables healthcare stakeholders the assurance of interpreting deep learning (DL) [19], [20] and machine learning (ML) algorithms [19], [21]. Transparency in predictive analysis is essential for the healthcare sector, and XAI intends to work on improving it [15]. The idea of creating artificial intelligence systems and machine learning models in a way that allows people to understand and interpret its decisions and behaviours is known as explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). XAI aspires to render artificial intelligence accountable and transparent by outlining the justifications for the decisions that AI systems make [22].

Machine learning algorithms can forecast whether or not a patient has been diagnosed with a glioma tumour using genetic and Molecular makeup markers. By examining a wide range of genetic markers, the algorithms can determine the level of seriousness of the illness of a person and the possibility of complications. This will aid in early diagnosis and detection. It will assist in early treatment planning for patients and prevent subsequent issues, improving the health of the patient. Continuous observation and analysis can also enable early patient intervention for those who are at risk, enhancing overall healthcare and health outcomes. Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) is essential for fostering trust, addressing ethical concerns, ensuring regulatory compliance, debugging models, enhancing user understanding, and promoting collaboration. It provides transparency and interpretability in AI systems, making them more accountable and accessible.

section: II. RELATED WORK
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Researchers have used machine learning to forecast glioma diagnosis. Ouerghi et al. [23] used multi-modal MR image fusion with random forests on 80 MIC-CAI BraTS 2019 patients, achieving 96.5% accuracy using 21 features. Tian et al. [24] proposed a radiomics approach using 153 multi-parametric MRI patients, where SVM models achieved 96.8% accuracy separating LGGs from HGGs and 98.1% separating grade III from grade IV. Cho et al. [25] analyzed 285 cases from the BraTS 2017 Challenge, selecting five features via minimal redundancy maximum relevance; three classifiers obtained 94% mean training accuracy and 92.13% maximum test accuracy, with average test AUCs of 0.9030. Wu et al. [26] proposed a non-invasive framework using 161 glioma cases from Henan Provincial People’s Hospital (2012–2016), using an elastic net for feature selection and linear regression to obtain 93.57% sensitivity, 86.53% specificity, 0.9638 AUC, and 91.30% accuracy. Cao et al. [27] constructed a framework using LASSO regression and nine machine learning models on 229 TCGA LGG and GBM patients, reporting AUCs >0.900 and accuracies >0.790 for validation sets. Rathore et al. [28] retrieved 2D quantitative imaging features from 735 images, verifying texture features via SVM with 75.12% accuracy and 0.652 AUC via tenfold cross-validation.
output:
To forecast whether the patient is diagnosed with glioma or not, a number of research have already used machine learning approaches. The following research projects have significantly advanced knowledge:

Using multi-modal MR image fusion, Ouerghi et al. [23] examined the function of radiomic feature integration in conjunction with machine learning techniques in the distinction of low-grade gliomas from high-grade gliomas. 80 histologically verified glioma patients from the MIC-CAI BraTS 2019 dataset i.e., 40 high-grade gliomas and 40 low-grade gliomas were analyzed for this research [23]. Five machine learning algorithms were created and examined using the fused and the recovered data utilizing a tenfold cross-validation plan. As an outcome, the model of random forests, which used 21 characteristics chosen from the raw data, achieved the highest accuracy of 96.5%. Utilizing texture information based on 153 multi-parametric MRI patients, a radiomics approach has been proposed by Tian et al. [24]. For separating grades III from IV and LGGs from HGGs, respectively, SVM models were created utilizing 30 and 28 optimum characteristics. The accuracy of the SVM (support vector machine) algorithm was 96.8% for separating LGGs from the HGGs and 98.1% for separating grade III from grade IV, which was acceptable compared to utilizing single sequence MRI or histogram parameters [24]. A total of 285 cases collected for the Brain Tumour Segmentation 2017 Challenge were examined by Cho et al. [25]. Five prominent characteristics were chosen for the machine learning models using the minimal redundancy maximum relevance algorithm. The three different classifiers (support vector machines, logistic regression, and random forest) obtained 94% of mean accuracy for training class and 92.13% of maximum accuracy for test class [25]. For training cohorts, they displayed an average AUC of 0.94, whereas for test cohorts, it was 0.9030 (as for logistic regression it is 0.9010, for support vector machine it is 0.8866, and for random forest it is 0.9213). A non-invasive glioma prediction framework is proposed in by Wu et al. [26]. Between 2012 and 2016, experiments were carried out on about 161 cases of glioma from the Henan Provincial People’s Hospital. The outcomes showed that the de-redundancy algorithm was widespread and had an accurate grading impact. The 2D segmented tumour was used to calculate 346 radiomics characteristics. A candidate feature was built using mutual information. Then an elastic net was used to carry out the feature selection. The prediction model was developed using linear regression to obtain the necessary sensitivity of 93.57%, specificity of 86.53%, 0.9638 AUC, and 91.30% accuracy. Cao et al. [27] produced a quantitative framework according to the location of tumour and volume of tumour, characteristics employing data from the 229 The Cancer Genome Atlas LGG and GBM patients [27]. Two of the sample approaches were used in the construction and testing of the LASSO regression i.e., least absolute shrinkage and selection operator and nine machine learning models: institution-based and repeat random sampling (with 70% of training set and 30% of validation set) [27]. The best results were obtained via stack modelling and support vector machines (AUC > 0.900, accuracy > 0.790 for validation set derived from institution-based sampling; AUC > 0.930 for average validation set, accuracy > 0.850 for repeat random sampling). The regression model demonstrated the best performance for the LASSO approach (institution-based sample validation set, with AUC 0.909 and model accuracy of 0.830). From 735 photos, Rathore et al. [28] retrieved 2D quantitative imaging characteristics, including conventional, clinical, and textural characteristics. Tenfold cross-validation using the 735 glioma images resulted in a successful verification of the texture features (accuracy: 75.12%, AUC: 0.652) using the SVM algorithm. Table 1. summarizes the related work with a deep and wide review.

In an effort to make decision-making processes and models more understandable and comprehensible, this field conducts research on them.

output: We used a dataset that has been made available to the public for this study [39]. The UCI Machine Learning Repository has access to the Glioma Grading Clinical and Mutation Features Dataset. Given that gliomas are prevalent primary tumors of the brain and are classified as either GBM (Glioblastoma Multiforme) or LGG (Lower-Grade Glioma) based on imaging and histological criteria, the grading procedure heavily relies on the clinical and molecular/mutation aspects. Three clinical characteristics and the twenty most frequently altered genes from TCGA-LGG and TCGA-GBM brain gliomas are taken into consideration in this dataset. The dataset includes the clinical and molecular/mutation factors that are used in the prediction task to identify patients with specific clinical, molecular, and mutational characteristics as LGG or GBM. The molecular/mutation factors are described as 0 = NOT_MUTATED; 1 = MUTATED. There are 889 patients with 23 attributes in this set of patients. The target variable in this dataset is grade (binary classification problem) which stated a patient to have LGG or GBM. Out of 889 patients, 487 suffered with LGG while 352 suffered with GBM. Out of 23 attributes there was 1 numerical attribute and 22 categorical attributes. The attributes had no null values. Table 2 lists the dataset’s attributes.

input:
Raw datasets contain defects, unpredictable behavior, and missing values [40]. Preprocessing was required to address these issues and prepare data for deployment [40].

The dataset was already balanced; no undersampling or oversampling algorithms were implemented [41], [42].

Data normalization rescaled attributes to have zero mean and unit variance using a conventional scaler [43]. Standardization removed the impact of outliers on dataset variability [43].

Categorical data was transformed to numerical format via one-hot encoding for machine learning compatibility [43]. One-hot encoding was not performed for this study.
output:
The processing of dataset turns unprocessed data into forms that are comprehensible and useful. Raw datasets present several issues, including defects, unpredictable behaviour, absence of trends, and unpredictability [40]. Preprocessing is also required for the purpose to address missing values and discrepancies. The dataset was preprocessed, and a few further operations were required to be prepared for employing in deployment.

Balancing the dataset allows for training a model easily by avoiding it from getting biased toward one class. There are two approaches for balancing data: undersampling and oversampling. Despite being simple to construct as well as capable of enhancing model run-time, undersampling has some downsides. The elimination of data points from the original set of data can result in loss of important information. Oversampling in this manner results in false scores from the minority class. So, in this study, the dataset was already appropriately balanced, so there was no need to implement any extra balancing algorithms [41], [42].

Data normalization entails rescaling the attributes to ensure their means and variance are both equal to 0. Standardization aims to preserve the variations in value limitations while reducing every attribute to a comparable scale. We employed the conventional scaler technique for feature scaling. Following the standardization procedure, an outlier has no longer impact on dataset hence, standardization do not have variability restriction.

To allow algorithms to analyze and learn from nonnumerical aspects, categorical data must be transformed to numerical format for use in data analysis and machine learning. A key method for characterizing binary vectors of categorical data in machine learning and data analysis is one-hot coding. Every group or label in the dataset appears as a binary vector, with just a single component set to "hot" (set to 1) and all other elements set to "cold" (set to 0). The one-hot encoding method of feature engineering is critical for preparing data for tasks such as classification and regression [43]. For our study, one hot encoding was not performed.

III. MATERIALS AND METHODS — C. FEATURE SELECTION

In this study, Pearson’s Correlation, Principal Component analysis and Mutual information were used to select the best characteristics. These algorithms aided in the extraction of crucial attributes while also reducing the quantity of data.

1) PEARSON’S CORRELATION

Pearson’s correlation coefficient analysis was conducted after an initial assessment of the dataset to see how each attribute influenced the outcome. The coefficient value “r” as well as the output were perfectly associated if the value reached close to “1/1,” while “0” value indicated no association. Positive correlation coefficient value implies that component influenced the outcome positively. If it was unfavorable, the outcome was influenced in the opposite direction. The method for evaluating correlation coefficients is based on an idea that analyzing the degree to which specific variable’s attributes are associated can help to determine the value of attribute collection in a dataset [44], [45]. Few variables correlated positively, while others correlated negatively. Figure 2 depicts the correlation heatmap.

2) MUTUAL INFORMATION (MI)

The Mutual Information Method is one of an effective approach for selecting features [46]. This filtering method requires consideration of the numerical properties of the dataset. Mutual information depends on an entropy, which is the measure of how unpredictable the features are. The qualities were rated according to the relative contribution of each to the desired variable, as shown in Figure 3.

3) PRINCIPAL COMPONENT ANALYSIS (PCA)

Principal component analysis (PCA) is frequently employed in modern data analysis. The purpose of PCA is to find a highly meaningful foundation for reexpressing a particular set of data. Dimensionality reduction, compression of data, extraction of features, and data visualization are just a few examples of uses. Principal components, which are produced by linearly combining the original variables, are a set of new orthogonal variables produced by PCA [47]. Using Principal Component Analysis (PCA), one can make certain datasets less dimensional. enhances interpretability while retaining most of the information. It accomplishes this by introducing fresh, unrelated covariates. This new variable discovery, or what we refer to as the key components, will lessen the difficulty of solving the eigenvalue/eigenvectors problem [48].

The Principal Component Analysis (PCA) technique aids in determining which set of data most accurately captures the topic under study. People receive several components via the PCA technique, which reduces the dimensionality of a multivariate dataset by condensing the dimensions into a single variable [49] as shown in Figure 4.

4) IMPORTANT FEATURES

Some features that are constant include IDH1, Age at diagnosis, PIK3CA, ATRX, PTEN, CIC, EGFR and TP53. These characteristics were selected to be examined further. Table 3 depicts the list of key features from Pearson’s Correlation, Mutual Information and PCA.

input: Dataset selection and preparation, model training, deployment, and performance assessment are the core steps of the machine learning process. Iterative testing and model enhancements improve performance. The end goal is an algorithm that accurately synthesizes fresh data to address the query. Effective hyperparameter tuning is required to select the best model. Grid search optimization was used to acquire optimized parameter values by manually examining each value in the predefined hyperparameter space; many algorithm performances are influenced by hyperparameter configurations. Ensemble models were used via stacking; three stacks across two levels were built, combining random forest, KNN, logistic regression, and decision trees in the first level, and XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, and AdaBoost in the second level, with the ultimate stack created by further ensembling. XAI techniques (SHAP, LIME, ELI5, Qlattice) were applied to interpret model outputs, ensuring transparency and human-understandable explanations of inner workings. An automated ML pipeline, comprising connected data processing modules for data preparation, model selection, feature selection, hyperparameter tuning, and evaluation, was applied to maximize model efficacy.

Our AI models were evaluated using classification metrics including precision, recall, F1-score, accuracy, and AUC score. The classifiers aim to identify patients with gliomas, specifically Lower-Grade Glioma (LGG) and Glioblastoma Multiforme (GBM).

1. **Accuracy**: This metric measures the percentage of correctly classified cases, encompassing both true positives and true negatives, to distinguish between LGG and GBM patients.

2. **Precision**: This metric calculates the proportion of true glioma cases (LGG or GBM) among all patients predicted to have a glioma.

Major objective of deep learning (branch of machine learning) is to train the artificial neural networks for learning and prediction from data. Its capacity to automatically identify and depict intricate patterns in data has led to its enormous rise in popularity. This makes it ideal for a variety of applications, including natural language processing, autonomous systems, image and speech recognition, and more. The ability of deep learning models, especially deep neural networks with numerous hidden layers, to automatically extract hierarchical features from unprocessed data enables them to carry out tasks that were once believed to be beyond the scope of traditional machine learning techniques. Deep learning continues to expand our knowledge of artificial intelligence and has revolutionized a number of areas, including healthcare, banking, and self-driving automobiles [52].

Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) are computer processing devices which heavily borrow from how the human brain operates. An enormous number of interconnected computational nodes (neurons) form the fundamental building block of artificial neural networks (ANNs). These distributed neurons work together to optimize the outcome and learn from the input. [53]. The input layer receives the data, which is subsequently distributed to the hidden layers after it’s loaded as a multidimensional vector. The hidden layers perform the learning process, using the preceding layer’s decisions to assess whether a stochastic modification will eventually enhance or damage the output. The term “deep learning” refers to systems that have multiple hidden layers stacked on top of each other [53]. The fundamental component of innumerable artificial neural networks (ANNs) is still a single neuron that receives an input and then executes action (like scalar product following non-linear function) [53].

The class score that is generated as the ultimate output will still be represented by the network using single perceptual scoring function (weight) from the initial picture vectors that are input. CNN’s primary benefit over its predecessors is that it can identify important traits automatically without human oversight, making it the most widely used [54]. Convolutional neural networks are made up of several building pieces, including fully connected, pooling, and convolution layers. They use a backpropagation algorithm to autonomously and adaptively learn the spatial hierarchies of information [55]. Convolutional neural networks are a kind of feedforward neural network which are capable of extracting features from data that has convolution patterns. An artificial neuron is analogous to a biological neuron; CNN kernels are diverse sensors that can react to varied stimuli; activation functions mimic the process by which neural electric signals that surpass a specific threshold are passed on to the subsequent neuron. The creation of loss functions and optimizers allowed the CNN system as a whole to learn what is expected [56].
