section: VI. EVALUATION — B. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
VI. EVALUATION — B. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS

The testing phase results for all experiments are described below. Figures 4a, 4b, and 4c show the Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) for the best models on the Ballarat, Austin, and Sri Lankan datasets, respectively. Tables 6, 7, and 8 contain the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and MAPE values for the best model in each experiment on Ballarat, Austin, and Sri Lankan datasets, respectively.

For the Ballarat dataset (Figure 4a, Table 6), the Random Forest model and N-BEATS model show the best performance for single-model and multi-model training approaches, achieving 8.3% and 8.47% MAPE, respectively. The single-model Random Forest is the most successful model, predicting waste generation patterns with an average improvement of 3.85% over other machine learning models and 6.82% over deep learning models. Prophet also achieved 8.47% MAPE. Auto ARIMA and TCN showed a significant improvement of over 15% reduction in MAPE with the multi-model approach. Average performance across all model types was 15.85% for single-model and 10.67% for multi-model, indicating the multi-model approach worked better for Ballarat.

For the Austin dataset (Figure 4b, Table 7), Linear Regression obtained the best performance in all scenarios. Error rates are comparable to Ballarat. The best Linear Regression model outperforms other machine learning models by 4.37% and deep learning models by 2.46% in the single-model approach. In the multi-model approach, Linear Regression is 1.49% greater than machine learning models and 1.96% greater than deep learning models. Auto ARIMA results improved by over 12% with the multi-model approach. LSTM and N-BEATS showed decreased performance in the multi-model approach. The single-model approach averaged 11.07% MAPE, while the multi-model approach averaged 9.56%.

For the Sri Lankan datasets (Figure 4c, Table 8), the Random Forest model shows the best performance with an average of 32.86% MAPE, except for the Boralesgamuwa dataset where Light GBM showed the best single-model performance at 28.84% MAPE. Random Forest was most successful in capturing patterns in the Sri Lankan datasets, which lacked visible seasonal patterns. On average, deep learning models did not show significant improvement over machine learning models. Random forests achieved comparable results to the best deep learning models after grid search.

C. DISCUSSION

1) EFFECT OF SEASONALITY IN DATA
Overall, the average predictive error was 13.26% for Ballarat and 10.31% for Austin, and 25.64% for Sri Lankan datasets, irrespective of approach. This disparity is attributed to seasonal patterns in Austin and Ballarat. Figures 5 and 6 show actual vs. predictions; Figure 5 (Ballarat) shows models capture variations accurately with seasonality, while Figure 6 (Moratuwa-Sri Lanka) shows both machine learning and deep learning models struggle to learn temporal patterns in non-seasonal data.

2) SINGLE-MODEL OR MULTI-MODEL APPROACH
The multi-model approach specifically focuses on weekly seasonal patterns. While the multi-model approach reported slightly better performance than the single-model approach on average, the biggest difference comes with increased training effort and resources. Figure 7 shows average training time was 710.15 seconds for single-model and 301.5 seconds for multi-model. Average MAPE values were 26.7% and 24.59%, respectively. The multi-model approach takes significantly less time to train deep learning models, reducing computational cost. For situations with higher time constraints, the multi-model approach may be more suitable, obtaining similar performance with less training time, specifically for deep learning models.

3) MACHINE LEARNING OR DEEP LEARNING
Deep learning models show a marginal better reduction in error, accounting for less than a 5% decrease in MAPE, indicating less utility for this forecasting task. Deep learning models take significantly longer to train than machine learning models, averaging 54 times more training time. Machine learning models were trained on CPU with less computational cost, while deep learning models used a dedicated GPU. Datasets spanned different time periods (Austin: 14 years; Moratuwa: 3 years), but the best machine learning and deep learning model performance varied by less than 2% MAPE, concluding dataset length is not a significant factor for model selection. Exploring Molecular Descriptors and Fingerprints to Predict mTOR Kinase Inhibitors using Machine Learning Techniques

The mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) kinase is a serine/threonine kinase that forms two distinct multi-protein complexes, mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) and mTOR complex 2 (mTORC2), which play critical roles in regulating cell growth, proliferation, metabolism, and survival. Dysregulation of the mTOR signaling pathway is implicated in various diseases, including cancer, diabetes, and neurodegenerative disorders. Consequently, there is significant interest in developing mTOR kinase inhibitors as therapeutic agents. However, the discovery of novel inhibitors through traditional experimental high-throughput screening is often time-consuming, expensive, and limited by the chemical space explored. In silico approaches, particularly machine learning (ML) techniques, have emerged as powerful tools to accelerate the drug discovery process by predicting the biological activity of compounds based on their molecular features. These techniques rely on the representation of molecules through molecular descriptors and fingerprints, which encode structural, electronic, and steric properties. The selection and calculation of appropriate descriptors are crucial, as they directly influence the predictive performance of ML models. This paper explores a wide range of molecular descriptors and fingerprints to identify optimal representations for predicting mTOR kinase inhibitors. We evaluate the performance of various ML algorithms, including support vector machines, random forests, and neural networks, using different descriptor sets. The goal is to provide insights into the structure-activity relationships of mTOR inhibitors and to guide the design of more effective therapeutic candidates.

Second-generation ATP-competitive mTOR kinase inhibitors (mTOR KIs), such as AZD-8055, CC-223, and Torin 2, bind catalytic subunits of both mTOR complexes and are considered more efficient. The combination of rapamycin and AZD-8055 gives rise to the third-generation inhibitor RapaLink-1 [13]. Second-generation mTOR KIs have therapeutic advantages over first-generation inhibitors, and third-generation inhibitors have entered the drug development pipeline. Additionally, known mTOR KIs targeting cancer are in various stages of clinical trials [14]. This motivated the development of computational approaches to predict new clinical mTOR KIs. Pipeline steps: mTOR bioactivity data collection, train/validation split, molecular feature extraction and dimension reduction, classification model learning and evaluation, comparative analysis, best model selection, and kinase dataset screening.

Dataset: mTOR bioactivity data downloaded from ChEMBL [32]; 1804 unique human mTOR kinase inhibition compounds with IC50 0.07–50000 nM (target CHEMBL2842). 1590 active (IC50 < 10 µM), 214 inactive. 80% training (1444 compounds), 20% validation (360 compounds). Training set further split into 5 folds for model training and testing.

Feature extraction: 1D/2D descriptors and 166-bit MACCS fingerprints calculated via PaDEL [33]. 3D descriptors excluded due to sparsity. 1171 informative descriptors and 133-bit MACCS fingerprints retained.

Variable importance: Random forest (RF) used to rank descriptors via mean decrease accuracy (MDA) and mean decrease gini (MDG). Out-of-bag (OOB) error used for model validation and stopping criteria.

Deep neural network autoencoder: Three-layer autoencoder in R (h2o library) used for dimension reduction of MACCS fingerprints. Best descriptor set and reduced fingerprints integrated into hybrid feature set.

Classification: Four classifiers built on molecular descriptors/fingerprints: Random Forest (RF) [36], Support Vector Machine (SVM) [37], Decision Tree (DT) [42], and Neural Network (NN) [38]. RF implemented via randomForest library in R; SVM via e1071/LIBSVM with RBF kernel; DT via RPART/CART with 10-fold cross-validation; ANN via nnet/caret with hyper-parameter optimization (size, decay).

Best model selection: Models validated on held-out validation set; best model selected based on Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC). Selected model screened 40,922 compounds from kinase SARfari database to predict mTOR kinase inhibitor-like compounds.

2.1
Pipeline Implemented
The pipeline of our proposed approach mainly consists of
the following steps: (i) mTOR bioactivity data collection, (ii)
partition of data into training and validation sets, (iii)
molecular feature (descriptors and ﬁngerprints) extraction
and dimension reduction, (iv) classiﬁcation model learning
and evaluation, (v) comparative analysis, (vi) best classiﬁcation model selection, and (vii) Kinase dataset screening.
Fig. 3 presents the visualization of these steps.
2.2
Dataset
The
mTOR
bioactivity
dataset
is

from

total number of 1804 unique compounds with IC50 values
between 0.07 nM and 50000 nM (that is, 0:07 nM IC50
50000 nM) associated with target id CHEMBL2842 are
selected. The 2D structures of the compounds are converted
into 3D structures using CORINA v2.64 software, and molecules are saved in 3D-sdf format. Out of 1804 compounds,
1590 compounds with IC50 values less than 10 mM are considered as active and remaining 214 compounds with IC50
values 10 mM are considered as inactive. As reported in
[22], 10 mM cut-off value is considered as a reasonable starting point for hit-to-lead activity.
As shown in Table 2, out of the complete dataset of 1804
molecules, 80 percent (1444) molecules are considered as
the training set, whereas remaining 20 percent (360) molecules are considered as the validation set. The training dataset is again divided into ﬁve parts using random sampling
technique, such that four parts are used to train classiﬁcation model, while keeping aside one part to test the model.
The training and testing processes are repeated ﬁve times

such that test sets differ in each iteration, and every molecule gets its participation in training and testing at least
once. After validating the trained classiﬁcation models, the
best performing model on the basis of Mathews correlation

retrieved from the kinase SARfari database to predict
mTOR kinase inhibitor-like compounds.
2.3
Feature Extraction and Dimension Reduction
Prior to splitting the mTOR bioactivity dataset into training
and validation sets, 1D/2D/3D descriptors and 166-bits
MACCS ﬁngerprints (FPs) are calculated using PaDEL
descriptor software [33]. Since the calculated 3D descriptors
are sparse, they are excluded from the list of descriptors for
further study. A total number of 1444 1D/2D descriptor columns and 166-bits MACCS FPs are ﬁltered separately to
remove the redundant columns. As a result, 1171 informative descriptor columns and 133-bits MACCS FPs are
retained for further analysis.
2.3.1
Variable Importance Measures
Variable Importance Measures (VIMs) are calculated to
rank, select, and prioritize the molecular descriptors. Unlike
other algorithms, random forest (RF) is not prone to overﬁtting as the variable selection is randomized during each
tree-split. Therefore, VIMs are calculated based on prediction error and splitting criteria using RF classiﬁcation
model. By default, RF takes two-third of the dataset to train
the model and keeps one-third of the dataset for testing during regression task, and 70 percent of the data as training
set and 30 percent of the data to test the model during
classiﬁcation task. The dataset separated for testing is called
out-of-bag (OOB) sample, and it is used to calculate OOB
error. The OOB error calculated during model training represents the performance over test dataset, and it is equivalent to the error captured by n-fold cross-validation. Hence,
training can be terminated on stabilization of OOB error
[34]. Prediction error is calculated using the percentage of misclassiﬁcation in classiﬁcation task, and mean square error
(MSE) in case of regression task which assigns mean
decrease accuracy (MDA) values. The prediction error is
ﬁnally calculated as the difference between out-of-bag
(OOB) error calculated from newly generated dataset by
randomly changing the order of the selected predictors, and
the OOB error calculated from the original dataset. Shifting
an important predictor generally increases the OOB error,
which ultimately increases the MDA values. On the other
hand, decrease in gini index (DGI) is used as splitting criteria to assign mean decrease gini (MDG) values to multiple
descriptors present during the construction of the trees (the
lowest the Gini index, the purest the split). Hence, selection
of an important predictor for splitting is based on high
decrease in Gini index, resulting in high MDG. In this study,
each of the 1171 molecular descriptors of the training dataset are assigned MDA values based on the percentage of misclassiﬁcation and MDG values using RF classiﬁcation task.
2.3.2
Deep Neural Network-Based Autoencoder
Neural networks with more than one hidden layer are
known as deep neural network (DNN). DNN has achieved
great success in diverse areas of research, primarily in natural
language
processing,
computer
vision,
and
more
recently in bioactivity predictions [28]. The architecture of
autoencoders (aka autoassociative network) are derived
from DNN. Autoencoders have adjustable, multilayer
encoder network to generate low-dimensional code by
transforming the high-dimensional input data, and a similar
decoder network to retrieve the inputs from the code. Thus,
autoencoders receive self-supervised training to extract features with minimal information loss, and are non-linear
abstraction of principal component analysis [35]. In this study,
simple architecture of autoencoder with three hidden layers
and each having equal number of nodes are used for dimension reduction of MACCS ﬁngerprints (FPs) using h2o
library in R. Finally, best performing descriptors set and
dimensionally reduced MACCS FPs are integrated to generate hybrid feature set.
2.4
Machine Learning Techniques for Compound
Classiﬁcation
Supervised machine learning technique for compound classiﬁcation for predicting bioactivities needs a labeled training dataset which is designed using known annotated
compounds with speciﬁc activities. The training set is then
used to develop classiﬁers that assign class labels to unseen
samples. In this study, molecular descriptors and/or ﬁngerprints based models are built to predict mTOR kinase inhibitors using four popular classiﬁers—Random Forest (RF)
[36], Support Vector Machine (SVM) [37], Decision Tree
(DT), and Neural Network (NN) [38].
RF [36] is an ensemble learning algorithm in which predictions are made either by collecting majority votes or by
calculating average predictions of the ensembles. RF builds
and averages a large collection of mutually related trees.
One of the important features of RF is the use of OOB sample, which is used to calculate unbiased classiﬁcation error
during generation of large number of trees. RF is capable of
showing excellent performance in presence of large number
of predictors, much higher than the number of observations.
Moreover, RF is a well-established data analysis tool in bioinformatics [39], [40] which we have implemented using
randomForest library in R.
SVM [37] is a supervised learning algorithm, which performs both classiﬁcation and regression task for prediction.
SVM uses maximum-margin to perform the classiﬁcation
task. First, the data vectors are mapped into an d-dimensional
space, then the algorithm ﬁnds a hyperplane for the new
space with maximal margin between positive (active) and
negative (inactive) class samples in the training dataset. In
our implementation, d represents the number of molecular

function is used to choose the penalty parameter c and kernel

used e1071 package of R for implementing the LIBSVM [41],

DT [42] is a supervised learning algorithm, which incorporates both numeric and categorical variables, as well as missing values. DT uses tree-like structure, which consists of a
root node, decision nodes, and terminal or leaf nodes to support the decision. Removal of a decision node from the decision tree is called pruning. We have used the CART [42]
algorithm which is implemented through RPART library in R.
CART reduces the size of an overly large grown tree to minimize the estimated misclassiﬁcation error. The size of the decision tree is controlled by the complexity parameter (cp), and it
is used to select an optimal tree size. By default, 10-fold crossvalidation is employed in CART for model evaluation.
ANN [38] is conceptualized from the architecture of human
brain. The simplest unit of a neural network is called neuron.
The neurons are organised into layers, called input layers, hidden layers, or output layers depending on their position in the
network. ANN is categorized based on the arrangements of
neurons in certain topology and connections to each other. In
this study, we have used nnet function of caret library in R to
train neural network models. Two hyper-parameters – size
and decay are optimized using cross-validation to generate
optimal classiﬁcation models. The size parameter describes
the number of units in hidden layer, and decay parameter is
the standardized parameter which is used to avoid overﬁtting
of the classiﬁcation model.

3.1 Prioritization of Molecular Descriptors
MDA and MDG values were calculated for 1171 descriptors using a Random Forest model with 500 trees. OOB error was minimized by tuning mtry, selecting 23 as the optimal parameter. Molecular descriptors were selected based on MDA and MDG rankings, retaining only those with pairwise correlation coefficients below 0.75. This yielded eight feature sets with 5 to 20 selected descriptors (Table 4). Files with all descriptor values are available (GitHub: chetna-kumari/mTOR_Inhibitor). The Pearson correlation coefficient between descriptors x and y was calculated using the standard formula (Eq. 1).

3.2 Dimension Reduction of Molecular Fingerprints
A deep neural network autoencoder with three hidden layers of 100 nodes each was used to reduce 166-bit MACCS fingerprints. Model performance was evaluated using MSE, RMSE, MAE, SMAPE, and R². An architecture with 100 nodes per layer achieved the lowest MSE and RMSE (0.002 and 0.042, respectively) and a high R² value of 0.995. The encoded features from the middle layer were selected for downstream modeling.

3.3 Classification Model Learning and Evaluation
Classification models were trained on eight descriptor sets, one fingerprint set, and one hybrid feature set using four classifiers (RF, SVM, DT, NN). Five-fold cross-validation was used for evaluation. Models were assessed using accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, F1-score, ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, and MCC. The best performing model used 20 MDA-ranked descriptors with the NN classifier, achieving an MCC of 0.815 on the validation set.

3.4 Comparative Analysis
The proposed approach was compared against a state-of-the-art method by Wang et al. [22]. That study used Recursive Partitioning and Naive Bayes on 13 descriptors and two fingerprint types, achieving an MCC of 0.777. The proposed model using 20 descriptors and NN outperformed this, achieving an MCC of 0.815 on the validation set (Table 7).

3.5 Best Classification Model Selection
The final model was selected from three candidates: a set of 20 prioritized descriptors, autoencoder-reduced fingerprints, and a hybrid feature set. The 20-descriptor set with the NN classifier achieved the highest MCC (0.815). Table 8 lists the top descriptors, which span nine categories, with three from electrotopological state, five from autocorrelation, and two from molecular distance edge. The NN model was selected for kinase bioactivity screening.

3.6 In silico Screening of Kinase Bioactivity Datasets
A subset of 26,421 compounds was screened from the Kinase SARfari database (40,922 total compounds) using the best-performing model. The model successfully discriminated active and inactive mTOR molecules, demonstrating its utility for preliminary virtual screening of mTOR kinase inhibitors.

neurons in each layer, we have considered same number of
neurons (nodes) in each hidden layer of the DNN which limits
the number of adjustable parameter combinations. In this
study, the parameter settings for generating autoencoders are
as follows: no:ofhiddenlayersðhÞ ¼ 3, no:ofnodes ¼ 100, no:of
epochs ¼ 100, costfunctionðl1Þ ¼ 0:00001, activationfunction
¼ tanh. We executed several autoencoders with different sets
of neurons (assuming same in each layer), and evaluated their
performance using four primary metrics—mean squared error
(MSE), root-mean squared error (RMSE), mean absolute error
(MAE), symmetric mean absolute percentage error (SMAPE),
and one composite metric – R2 (coefﬁcient of determination)
[43]. The calculated values of MSE, RMSE, MAE, SMAPE, R2,
and number of nodes (#Nodes) using autoencoders are given
in Table 5 and visualized in Fig. 7. Comparatively lower values
of MSE, RMSE, MAE and SMAPE, higher value of R2, and
higher number of nodes are preferred for dimension reduction
using autoencoder. In this study, the ﬁnal architecture of
autoencoder is selected on the basis of MSE and RMSE values.
It can be observed from Table 5 that the MSE and RMSE values
decrease with increasing number of nodes. On analysis, we
found that autoencoder with 100 nodes in each of the three
layers achieves small MSE and RMSE values, and do not
change signiﬁcantly after further increasing the number of
nodes. At this point, the MAE and SMAPE values are also reasonably small, whereas R2 value is considerably high (that is,
0.995). Therefore, we have chosen three hidden layers with 100
nodes in each layer in autoencoder architecture and selected
the nodes from the middle layer.

The current release of ChEMBL (version 25) marks a rapidly

data to be screened, based on which the classiﬁcation models
are trained. Therefore, out of total 40,922 compounds
retrieved from the kinase SARfari database, only 26,421 compounds are considered for screening using the best classiﬁcation model, and the screening result is shown in Table 10. It

able to discriminate active and inactive mTOR molecules, and
this model can be used for predicting mTOR kinase inhibitorlike compounds in preliminary stages of the virtual screening.

section: DISCUSSION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: mTOR is a validated pharmacological target due to its druggability and role in human diseases like cancer. This study developed in silico classification models to predict mTOR kinase inhibitors and intervene in the autophagy pathway. Molecular descriptors and fingerprints were calculated from the mTOR bioactivity dataset in ChEMBL using paDEL software. The dataset was split into training (4) and validation (1) sets via random sampling. RF classifier was used for variable importance and classification. Descriptors were selected based on misclassification rate and Gini index, then filtered by correlation coefficients. Autoencoders with three hidden layers of 100 neurons reduced 166-bit MACCS fingerprints. Since no single feature sufficiently discriminates inhibitors from non-inhibitors, models were built using varying numbers of top-ranked descriptors, reduced fingerprints, and hybrid feature sets with four classifiers (RF, SVM, DT, NN). Performance was evaluated using accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, F-measure, ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, and MCC. Models based on descriptor sets generally outperformed reduced MACCS fingerprint models. On the validation set, the model using 20 prioritized descriptors (from top-40 MDA-ranked) with NN classifier achieved the highest MCC (0.815). This model was used to screen compounds from the kinase SARfari database, a repository of bioactivity data for conserved catalytic sites in protein kinases. The model is biased toward predicting active compounds, likely due to the disproportionate class distribution in ChEMBL and SARfari datasets, which favor active compounds. Inactive molecules are under-represented, skewing models toward the majority class. Handling class imbalance can be achieved via undersampling, oversampling (e.g., SMOTE), or using appropriate metrics like PR-AUC and MCC. Previous work [49] addressed this issue in the mTOR dataset using SMOTE. The main findings are: models with highest MCC values (validation MCC=0.815, training MCC=0.760) use MDA for descriptor selection; the best validation classifier is NN using 20 prioritized descriptors; the three most important descriptor categories are atom type electrotopological state, autocorrelation, and molecular distance edge; and the model can discriminate active and inactive mTOR compounds, making it useful for preliminary virtual screening of kinase inhibitor-like compounds.

mTOR is a well established pharmacological target due to
its druggability and intervention in many human diseases
including cancer. In this study, we have developed a series
of in silico classiﬁcation models to predict mTOR kinase
inhibitors-like compounds with intent to therapeutically
intervene autophagy pathway in cancer. The molecular
descriptors and molecular ﬁngerprints of mTOR bioactivity
dataset from ChEMBL database are calculated using paDEL
software. The complete dataset is divided into training set
and validation set (4:1) by applying random sampling. The
training dataset is used to build the classiﬁcation models,
which are internally validated using 5-fold cross validation.
Validation set is used for external validation of the trained
classiﬁcation models. We have used RF classiﬁer for two
purposes—to calculate variable importance measures, and

ABSTRACT Neurological disorders are among the leading causes of both physical and cognitive disabilities
worldwide, affecting approximately 15% of the global population. This study explores the use of machine
learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) techniques in processing Electroencephalography (EEG) signals
to detect various neurological disorders, including Epilepsy, Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), and
Alzheimer’s disease. We present a detailed workflow that begins with EEG data acquisition using a headset,
followed by data preprocessing with Finite Impulse Response (FIR) filters and Independent Component
Analysis (ICA) to eliminate noise and artifacts. Furthermore, the data is segmented, allowing the extraction
of key features such as Bandpower and Shannon entropy, which improve classification accuracy. These
features are stored in an offline database for easy access during analysis, to be then applied for both
ML and DL models, systematically testing their performance and comparing the results to prior studies.
Hence, our findings show impressive accuracy, with the random forest model achieving 99.85% accuracy
in classifying autism vs. healthy subjects and 100% accuracy in distinguishing healthy individuals from
those with dementia using Support Vector Machines (SVM). Moreover, deep learning models, including
Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) and ChronoNet, demonstrated accuracy rates ranging from 92.5%
to 100%. In conclusion, this research highlights the effectiveness of ML and DL techniques in EEG signal
processing, offering valuable contributions to the field of brain-computer interfaces and advancing the
potential for more accurate neurological disease classification and diagnosis.
INDEX TERMS Electroencephalography (EEG), neurological disorders, machine learning, deep learning.

instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
I. INTRODUCTION

EEG signals reflect brain activity related to cognitive and motor functions. This work provides an overview of EEG characteristics and their application in brain-computer interfaces for diagnosing pathological illnesses. Neuronal electrical activity, transmitted via axons and dendrites as action potentials, forms the basis of brain communication. EEG arises from pyramidal neuron activation in the cortical layer and is measured on the scalp. These signals are weak and require sophisticated capture techniques. They exhibit statistical variation across time, frequency, and space, organized into delta, theta, alpha, beta, and gamma bands associated with specific brain states. Electrode placement follows the 10-20 system (Fig. 1). Acquisition methods are invasive or non-invasive. Invasive methods offer precision via surgical insertion, while non-invasive methods are safer and more accessible. Despite diagnostic potential, challenges remain, including signal artifacts, limited spatial resolution, inter-subject variability, deep structure inaccessibility, data interpretation inconsistencies, and analysis complexity.

In subsequent sections, methodology for EEG analysis—including preprocessing, feature extraction, and machine learning and deep learning models—will be discussed. Results and implications for brain-machine interfaces and neurological classification will follow. This work concludes with findings significance and future research directions.

The detection and classification of neurological disorders using EEG data have advanced through machine learning and deep learning integration. Key contributions include: using the DASPS dataset with discrete wavelet transform and power spectral density features to achieve 87.5% accuracy with a random forest model [13]. Epileptic seizure detection using the TUH dataset with intrinsic mode functions and XGBoost yielded 88.21% average accuracy [14]. The CHB-MIT database identified three optimal EEG channels via NSGA-II; 1D-CNN and 2D-CNN models reached 86.36% accuracy [15]. Major depressive disorder early detection using the MODNA dataset with multi-head self-attention, a two-branch CNN, and a fully connected layer achieved 91.06% accuracy [16]. Classification of autism, epilepsy, Parkinson's disease, and schizophrenia using AlexNet and ResNet-50 achieved accuracies of 98.63% and 99.71% respectively [17]. Seizure subtype detection using the TUSZ dataset with combined 1D and 2D CNN models yielded an F1 score of 61.1% [18]. Traditional methods, such as SVM and multiwavelet analysis on EEG data, achieved 68.20% accuracy [19], highlighting the limitations of these techniques compared to advanced deep learning approaches.

The study of EEG signals plays a crucial role in understanding the complex functioning of the brain and its impact on cognitive and motor functions, as well as sensory processing. This article aims to provide a comprehensive overview of EEG signals and their characteristics in the context of brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) for the diagnosis of pathological illnesses. The structure and functioning of neurons, which form the fundamental units of the brain, are explored, highlighting the transmission of electrical signals through axons and dendrites. These signals, known as action potentials, form the basis of electrical activity in the brain and are responsible for communication and transfer between neurons.

EEG signals are the result of the activation of pyramidal neurons in the cortical layer of the brain. These signals are measured on the scalp's surface and provide valuable insights into brain activity. However, the electrical fields generated by these signals are relatively weak and require sophisticated techniques to capture and analyze them accurately. EEG signals exhibit statistical features that vary with time, frequency, and space. They are characterized by different frequency bands, including delta, theta, alpha, beta, and gamma, each associated with specific brain states and activities.

Acquiring EEG signals involves the placement of electrodes on the scalp according to standardized systems such as the 10-20 system as seen in figure 1. These electrodes detect the electrical activity generated by the brain and facilitate the recording of EEG data. The acquisition of EEG signals can be performed using invasive or non-invasive techniques. Invasive methods involve the insertion of electrodes directly into brain tissue, providing precise and detailed information but requiring surgical procedures. Noninvasive methods, on the other other, are safer, painless, and more accessible, making them suitable for research and clinical settings. Despite the potential of EEG-based diagnostic tools for identifying neurological disorders, there are several challenges that need to be addressed. These challenges include signal artifacts, limited spatial resolution, signal variability among individuals, limited information on deep brain structures, lack of standardization in data collection and interpretation, and the complexity of signal analysis. Overcoming these challenges is crucial for the development of reliable and effective diagnostic tools based on EEG signals.

FIGURE 1. The standard 10-20 system for electrode placement.

In the following sections of this work, we will discuss the methodology used for analyzing EEG signals, including data preprocessing, feature extraction, and the application of machine learning and deep learning models. The results obtained from these analyses, along with their implications for the field of brain-machine interfaces and neurological disease classification, will be presented. This work concludes with a discussion on the significance of the findings and future directions for research in this area.

The detection and classification of neurological disorders using EEG data have significantly advanced, thanks to the integration of machine learning and deep learning techniques. Researchers have explored various methods, datasets, and feature extraction approaches to improve accuracy and reliability. This section provides an overview of key contributions in the field.

Feature extraction methods and the choice of datasets are critical in EEG-based classification. In [13], the DASPS dataset was used, with states labeled based on the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAM-A) and the Self-Assessment Manikin (SAM). Features were derived using discrete wavelet transform (DWT) and power spectral density (PSD), leading to a random forest model achieving an accuracy of 87.5%. Another study [14] focused on epileptic seizure detection using the Temple University Hospital (TUH) dataset, combining intrinsic mode function (IMF) and extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) to achieve an average accuracy of 88.21%. Moreover, the CHB-MIT database was also used in a separate effort, where the authors [15] identified three optimal EEG channels using a non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II (NSGA-II). By applying 1D-CNN and 2D-CNN models, they reached an accuracy of 86.36%.

Further, deep learning models have shown great promise in classification tasks involving EEG data. In [16] addressed the early detection of major depressive disorder (MDD) using the MODNA dataset. A combination of multi-head self-attention mechanisms, a two-branch convolutional neural network (CNN), and a fully connected layer resulted in an accuracy of 91.06%. Another effort, in [17] targeted four common neurological disorders like autism, epilepsy, Parkinson's disease, and schizophrenia. Using datasets such as KAU-ASD, the Universidad Federal do Pará (Brazil), the IOWA USA Parkinson dataset, and IBIB PAN, they achieved accuracies as high as 98.63% for autism and 99.71% for epilepsy using AlexNet and ResNet-50. Additionally, research [18] on seizure subtype detection using the TUSZ dataset combined 1D and 2D CNN models, leading to an F1 score of 61.1%.

Despite these successes, some challenges remain present. For example, this study [19] decoding EEG data using support vector machines (SVM) and multiwavelet analysis achieved a relatively modest accuracy of 68.20%. This highlights the limitations of traditional machine learning techniques when compared to more advanced methods. Similarly, the study on seizure subtype classification using the TUSZ dataset faced difficulties in achieving high F1 scores, reflecting the complexities of capturing subtle differences between subtypes.

II. METHODOLOGY

A. DATASETS

This study investigates machine learning and deep learning techniques for classifying EEG signals associated with neurological disorders. Four datasets were acquired to include healthy controls and patient groups.

1) UNIVERSITY OF SHEFFIELD EEG DATASET [20]
Records from 28 individuals with autism spectrum condition and 28 neurotypical controls. 56 total recordings, each 150 seconds long, eyes closed. Recorded with Biosemi Active Two at 512 Hz.

2) CHB-MIT EEG DATASET [21]
916 hours of EEG from 22 pediatric patients with intractable seizures (age 3-22). 23-28 electrodes via 10-20 system. Sample rate 256 Hz. 198 seizures annotated with onset/offset times.

3) IBIB PAN EEG DATASET [22]
EEG from 14 paranoid schizophrenia patients and 14 healthy controls. 19 channels, 10-20 system. Sample rate 250 Hz. 28 recordings, 15-25 minutes each.

4) AHEPA GENERAL HOSPITAL OF THESSALONIKI EEG DATASET [24]
36 Alzheimer’s patients (~485.5 min), 23 Frontotemporal Dementia patients (276.5 min), and 29 healthy controls (402 min). 19 scalp + 2 reference electrodes, 10-20 system. Sample rate 500 Hz. Total >19 hours.

B. PREPROCESSING

Raw EEG signals were enhanced via filtering, artifact removal, and epoching.

1) FILTERING
FIR and IIR filters removed noise. Bandwidths of 0.5–45 Hz and 0.5–60 Hz captured Delta, Theta, Alpha, Beta, and Gamma bands. Frequencies above 60 Hz treated as artifacts.

2) ARTIFACT REMOVAL
Independent Component Analysis (ICA) identified and removed physiological and non-physiological artifacts. ICA decomposition: X = ÂS (1), source estimation Ŝ = WX (2). Assumes statistical independence of sources, at least one non-Gaussian source, and a linear mixing process.

The methodology employed in this study aims to comprehensively investigate the effectiveness of machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) techniques in classifying EEG signals associated with neurological disorders. It consists of several key components, including data acquisition, preprocessing, feature extraction, implementation of ML and DL models, and performance evaluation metrics.

A. DATASETS

These EEG abnormalities provide valuable clues about the underlying brain processes in individuals with these neurological conditions. By analyzing EEG signals, we can gain a deeper understanding of the behavioral and cognitive aspects of these pathologies. We describe the process of acquiring the EEG datasets used in our study. Our aim was to obtain a diverse set of EEG recordings that included healthy individuals as well as patients with different neurological conditions. We acquired the following datasets:

1) UNIVERSITY OF SHEFFIELD EEG DATASET [20]
Obtained from the University of Sheffield, consists of EEG recordings from 28 individuals with autism spectrum condition and 28 neurotypical individuals serving as controls. With 56 recordings total, each recording involved a 2.5-minute (150 seconds) session with eyes closed during rest. The EEG system used in this dataset was the Biosemi Active Two system, and the sampling frequency was set at 512 Hz.

2) CHB-MIT EEG DATASET [21]
Acquired from Children’s Hospital Boston. EEG is recorded for 916 hours from 22 pediatric participants with intractable seizures for a total of one hour or four hours. Five males and 17 females participated in this research, ranging in age from 3-22 years and 1.5-19 years, respectively. The EEG montage employed the international 10-20 system with the number of electrodes varied between 23 to 28 electrodes for different patients. The sampling rate for EEG was set to 256 samples per second, with 23 EEG signals per file, and 198 seizures were annotated with their beginning and end times.

3) IBIB PAN EEG DATASET [22]
IBIB PAN was sourced from the Department of Methods of Brain Imaging and Functional Research of Nervous System in Warsaw, Poland. It comprises EEG data from 14 individuals diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia and 14 healthy controls. The EEG montage uses the standard 10-20 system with 19 EEG channels, and the data was sampled at a frequency of 250 Hz. With 28 recordings, each recording lasts around 15 to 25 minutes each.

4) AHEPA GENERAL HOSPITAL OF THESSALONIKI EEG DATASET [24]
Includes EEG recordings from 36 individuals with Alzheimer’s disease (totaling approximately 485.5 minutes), 23 with Frontotemporal Dementia (276.5 minutes), and 29 healthy controls (402 minutes). The recordings were acquired using the 10-20 international system with 19 scalp electrodes and 2 reference electrodes, sampled at 500 Hz. Altogether, the dataset comprises over 19 hours of EEG data, making it a valuable resource for distinguishing EEG patterns between Alzheimer’s, Frontotemporal Dementia, and healthy individuals.

These datasets provide a wide range of EEG recordings encompassing various neurological disorders. The EEG signal may represent some of the common behaviors associated with these illnesses, and examination of this signal might give insights into the brain processes behind these behaviors; thus, we performed data cleaning on the acquired EEG datasets as shown in Table 1.

TABLE 1. Details of preprocessing steps applied to EEG datasets.

To gain a better understanding of the distribution of brain activity in different neurological pathologies, we used topographic maps in our study. Topomaps provided us with a visual representation of the activity patterns across the scalp based on EEG data. We used the MNE library integrated into Python to plot topomaps of these different datasets. By examining the spatial distributions of EEG activity for each pathology, as shown in Figure 2 Below and table 2, we were able to gather insights into the specific frequency bands and their power variations.

We can analyze that individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) may exhibit repetitive behaviors, such as higher power in theta and alpha frequency bands during repetitive or stereotyped activities and increased amplitude or variability of the EEG signal [4] in response to sensory stimulation, indicating sensory hypersensitivity. Whereas epilepsy is characterized by the detection of epileptic discharges or spikes in the EEG signal to locate seizures [5], [6] and classify epilepsy types, with altered brain activity during cognitive tasks, such as lower alpha power during concentration tests and increased theta power during memory tasks. Moreover, schizophrenia exhibits a reduction in the amplitude observed during attention and working memory tasks. We can also detect lower gamma band power [7], associated with abnormalities in sensory processing and perceptual organization. Dementia reveals decreased alpha band power during resting-state EEG recordings, distinguishing EEG patterns between Alzheimer’s, Frontotemporal Dementia, and healthy individuals, indicating cognitive impairment [25]. Similarly, Alzheimer’s disease [26] manifests shrinkage in alpha and beta power during resting-state EEG recordings, associated with cognitive impairment.

FIGURE 2. Topographic map(topomap) representation for various pathological illnesses.

The usage of topomaps allowed us to visualize and comprehend the distribution of brain activity associated with various cognitive processes and mood states in different neurological conditions. To probe deeper into the analysis of these neurological pathologies we will describe in the next section our preprocessing phase,

B. PREPROCESSING

To enhance the quality of the EEG data, we applied preprocessing techniques [27], [28], which involve preparing raw EEG signals by reducing noise, removing artifacts, and segmenting data to improve its usability for analysis and classification tasks. The steps we followed are detailed below:

1) FILTERING

We applied Finite Impulse Response (FIR) and Infinite Impulse Response (IIR) filters to clean the EEG signals by removing noise and unwanted frequency components. To capture the five brain wavebands mentioned earlier (Delta, Theta, Alpha, Beta, and Gamma), we alternated between bandwidths of 0.5–45 Hz and 0.5–60 Hz. Frequencies above 60 Hz were considered artifacts, as the EEG recordings were collected while patients were resting with their eyes closed, where such high frequencies typically represent external noise rather than brain activity.

2) ARTIFACT REMOVAL

The second step was artifact removal, which focuses on identifying and eliminating artifacts, unwanted signal components such as physiological artifacts (e.g., sweat, electrode movement) and non-physiological artifacts (e.g., electromagnetic interference). To ensure the effective identification and removal of these artifacts, we used Independent Component Analysis (ICA), a powerful technique that decomposes mixed signals into independent components. The general equation for Independent Component Analysis (ICA) can be expressed as (1):

• A is the mixing matrix.
• Ŝ is the matrix of source signals, representing the independent components to be estimated.

To estimate the independent components Ŝ, the ICA algorithm computes an unmixing matrix W such as shown in (2):

The following assumptions are made:

• The source signals (Ŝ) are statistically independent.
• At least one source signal is non-Gaussian.

This approach enabled us to isolate and eliminate artifacts while preserving meaningful signals. Figure 3 illustrates examples of ICA outputs, including extracted event-related potentials (ERPs), segmented images, and dropped segments.

FIGURE 3. The extraction of components using Independent Component Analysis (ICA).

3) DATA EPOCHING:

Finally, we performed data epoching, a process that segments continuous EEG data into smaller, more manageable pieces. This step is critical for preparing the data for further analysis. In our case, we divided the preprocessed EEG data into 10-second epochs. These segments were then stored in an offline database to be used during the training phase. By systematically applying these preprocessing techniques, we ensured that the EEG data was clean, free of artifacts, and well-prepared for subsequent stages of analysis and classification. as shown in figure 4.

Feature extraction identifies statistical features to enhance automated learning [29]. Standard deviation measures signal variability [30]; skewness highlights amplitude distribution asymmetry; kurtosis identifies signal outliers [30]. Power spectral density is estimated using Welch's method [30] to assess frequency content. Band power quantifies energy within specific frequency bands [31]. Shannon entropy captures signal randomness [32]. Wavelet decomposition uses the PyWavelets library with db4 wavelet for 5-level decomposition [34], [35].

Classification employs machine learning and deep learning models [36], [37]. Five machine learning models were used: SVM, KNN, Logistic Regression, LDA, and Random Forest [38]-[40]. Parameter optimization used grids; KNN neighbors ranged 3-15, Random Forest trees 100-500 and depth 0-20. GroupKFold cross-validation evaluated models using non-overlapping subject groups [36]. Deep learning models include CNN and ChronoNet [41], [42]. The CNN architecture has five convolutional layers with 5 filters, kernel size 3, and LeakyReLU activation; MaxPool1D and AveragePooling1D with pool size and stride 2; dropout rate 0.5; and a final dense sigmoid layer [41]. The ChronoNet model uses 1D convolutional layers with batch normalization and ELU activation, followed by stacked GRU layers. GRU update and reset gates are defined by equations (5) and candidate state by equation (6); hidden state update follows equation (7). The final dense layer uses softmax activation; loss is sparse categorical cross-entropy with Adam optimizer [42]. Models trained on 80% training, 20% testing data; ML used 10-fold cross-validation [36]. Classifiers ranked by accuracy, recall, F1-score, and sensitivity per Algorithm 1.

D. CLASSIFICATION
In this section, We employed machine learning (ML) [36]
and deep learning (DL) [37] models for the classification
of EEG signals related to different medical pathologies.
For ML models, we used well-established algorithms such
as Support Vector Machines (SVM) [38] and K-Nearest
Neighbors (KNN) [39], [40].
1) MACHINE LEARNING CLASSIFIERS
We employed five different machine learning (ML) models
for the classification of EEG signals: Support Vector
Machines (SVM), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Logistic
Regression, Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA), and
Random Forest. SVM is a supervised learning algorithm
that separates data into distinct classes by identifying a
hyperplane that maximizes the margin between them. KNN,
on the other hand, classifies data based on the majority vote
of its k nearest neighbors.
Each model underwent a parameter optimization process
using a parameter grid tailored to the respective model’s
hyperparameters. For instance, the number of neighbors in
KNN was varied from 3 to 15, while for Random Forest,
the number of trees ranged from 100 to 500, and the
maximum depth of the trees was adjusted from none to 20.
A consistent pipeline was applied to each model, beginning
with feature standardization using StandardScaler, followed
by classification using the selected model.
This approach ensured the parameters were fine-tuned
to improve classification performance and minimize overfitting. To evaluate the models, we used GroupKFold
cross-validation, ensuring non-overlapping groups based on
the subjects for efficient and reliable results.
2) DEEP LEARNING CLASSIFIERS
As for deep learning models, we implemented Convolutional
Neural Networks (CNNs) [41] and ChronoNet [42] in
our study. CNNs are particularly effective for analyzing
spatial patterns in EEG signals. These networks consist
of convolutional layers that extract meaningful features by
applying filters across the input data. ChronoNet, on the
other hand, is a specialized recurrent neural network (RNN)
[43] designed to capture temporal dependencies in sequential data. This capability makes ChronoNet particularly
well-suited for analyzing the time-series nature of EEG
signals.
• CNN Model

We compiled our model using the Adam optimizer

section: III. RESULTS
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: We evaluated three classifiers (SVM, KNN, Logistic Regression) on EEG data processed with two feature sets and epoch durations of 120s, 40s, and 10s. Results show that 10s epochs and the second feature combination achieved optimal performance. In multiclass classification using SVM, KNN, and linear regression, KNN achieved 99.88% accuracy on the Autism dataset. Incorporating wavelet decomposition (DWT) slightly affected Schizophrenia and Epilepsy metrics but significantly improved Autism classification, with Random Forest reaching 99.77% accuracy on Healthy vs. Epilepsy using 11 channels. Random Forest generally outperformed other classifiers due to its ensemble nature. Age-specific analysis revealed that older age groups (61-73 years) performed better for Alzheimer’s classification, while younger groups showed higher accuracy in Healthy vs. Dementia tasks. A comparison of CNN and ChronoNet architectures across five binary tasks showed CNN achieved 99.91% accuracy on Healthy vs. Autism, while ChronoNet achieved 99.62% accuracy on the same task. Both architectures struggled with Alzheimer’s classification, achieving 92.5% and 91.71% accuracy respectively. Our proposed method, using diverse feature extraction and preprocessing techniques, demonstrates higher efficiency than state-of-the-art works on the CHB-MIT database, indicating potential for wearable seizure prediction devices.
output:
In this section, we conducted multiple experiments and compiled a variety of results, which are showcased in the tables and graphs below. Each study followed the outlined framework depicted in Figure 9, beginning with data acquisition, followed by preprocessing, feature extraction, and concluding with classification.

For the initial evaluation, we focused on three well-known classifiers: Support Vector Machines (SVM), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), and Logistic Regression. These classifiers have been widely used in similar studies [18] and have demonstrated effectiveness in EEG signal classification.

To ensure accurate classification, feature extraction and segmentation of EEG signals into epochs were crucial steps. We selected 10 features based on their ability to capture the underlying characteristics of EEG signals. These features were chosen based on previous studies [13], [17], [22], [23], which demonstrated their effectiveness in EEG signal classification. We employed two feature combinations to achieve optimal results:

• The first combination included minimum, maximum, standard deviation, mean, mean square, skewness, and kurtosis.
• The second combination included features such as bandpower, Shannon entropy, kurtosis, mean, skewness, and Pwelch.

Additionally, the segmentation of EEG signals into epochs was performed with three different durations: 120s, 40s, and 10s. This allowed us to evaluate the performance of the ML models on segmented data. The results, as presented in Table 5, showed that the 10s epoch length provided the best classification performance. Hence shorter epochs are more effective in capturing the temporal dynamics of EEG signals. Moreover, the second combination of features demonstrated better accuracy compared to the first combination, indicating the effectiveness of the selected features in capturing the underlying characteristics of EEG signals.

Moreover, we conducted a multiclass EEG classification with three different classifiers SVM, KNN and linear regression. Results are represented in table 6 and bar chart in figure 11.

From Table 10, we observe that incorporating wavelet decomposition (DWT) slightly impacts the performance metrics for the Schizophrenia and Epilepsy datasets but significantly enhances classification accuracy for Autism dataset. For instance, in the Healthy vs. Epilepsy task, Random Forest achieves nearly perfect classification with an accuracy of 99.77% for 11 channels with DWT features. Similarly, for the Autism dataset, KNN achieves the highest performance with an accuracy of 99.88%, demonstrating its ability to effectively classify spatial-temporal EEG features.

TABLE 7. Metrics table for the accuracy of DWT for different types of classifiers.
TABLE 8. Impact of age groups in the accuracy of different classifiers.

FIGURE 10. The box plot indicates the classification performance of proposed method and five comparison methods.
FIGURE 11. Bar chart for multiclass EEG data classification with three classifiers accuracy evaluation.

Across the classifiers, Random Forest generally outperforms others due to its ensemble nature, which captures complex patterns in the data. These results were illustrated in the box plot in figure 10

In Table 11 analyzing the datasets with age-specific features reveals interesting trends. For Alzheimer’s classification, older age groups (61-73 years) demonstrate slightly better performance compared to younger groups (<28 years) across most classifiers. For instance, SVM and Random Forest achieve accuracies of 97.28% and 99.16%, respectively, for the older age group. Similarly, in the Healthy vs. Dementia task, the younger group yields slightly higher accuracies, with Random Forest attaining 99.858%. These findings suggest that age-based segmentation plays a critical role in EEG-based diagnosis, potentially indicating unique age-related signal patterns.

Overall, the results highlight the efficacy of combining tailored feature sets (e.g., DWT and age-based features) with efficient classifiers such as SVM and Random Forest. Furthermore, shorter EEG epochs (as used in these datasets) allow the models to capture nuanced temporal dynamics, resulting in high classification performance across all tasks.

The performance of two architectures CNN (Table 9) and ChronoNet (Table 10) was evaluated across five binary classification tasks: Healthy vs. Schizophrenia, Healthy vs. Autism, Healthy vs. Epilepsy, Healthy vs. Dementia, and Healthy vs. Alzheimer’s. Metrics such as loss, accuracy, F1 score, recall, and sensitivity were used to assess their effectiveness.

From Table 9 the CNN architecture demonstrated exceptional performance for most datasets. For example, in the Healthy vs. Autism task, the CNN achieved a near-perfect accuracy of 99.91% with a very low loss value of 0.0038, indicating its effectiveness in capturing the underlying patterns in the data. Similarly, in the Healthy vs. Schizophrenia task, an accuracy of 99.28% was observed, with an impressive F1 score of 0.9935, showcasing the architecture’s reliability in classifying EEG signals for neurological disorders. However, for the Healthy vs. Alzheimer’s dataset, the CNN showed a noticeable drop in performance, achieving an accuracy of 92.5% and a loss value of 0.2. This suggests that Alzheimer’s EEG signals might present unique challenges, requiring further optimization of the CNN model.

Table 10 highlights the performance of the ChronoNet architecture with similar tasks and metrics. ChronoNet consistently achieved high scores across most tasks, with the Healthy vs. Autism dataset yielding an accuracy of 99.62% and an F1 score of 0.9975. For the Healthy vs. Dementia task, the architecture also performed well, achieving an accuracy of 98.47% and sensitivity of 98.16%. However, in the Healthy vs. Alzheimer’s classification, ChronoNet struggled, achieving a relatively lower accuracy of 91.71%, indicating room for improvement when addressing Alzheimer’s-related EEG signals.

A comparison of our proposed method with state-of-the-art works is presented in Table 11. All the works listed in Table 11 used the same CHB-MIT database. It is evident that our proposed method is more efficient than the others when using different feature extraction methods and advanced preprocessing techniques. As a result, this method holds potential for implementation in wearable seizure prediction devices that are both computationally lightweight and energy-efficient.

section: IV. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUDING REMARKS
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: The study evaluated machine learning and deep learning models for EEG-based diagnosis of schizophrenia, autism, epilepsy, dementia, and Alzheimer's disease. Feature selection using Pwelch, Shannon entropy, and bandpower, combined with 10s epochs, yielded optimal performance. SVM and random forest algorithms achieved high accuracy, and the inclusion of Discrete Wavelet Transform improved results in certain tasks. A CNN model demonstrated strong accuracy, particularly for schizophrenia, autism, and epilepsy classification. The ChronoNet architecture captured temporal dependencies effectively. The proposed approach achieved higher accuracy than previous work [21], [22]. However, the relatively small dataset size limits generalizability. Integrating other modalities, such as fMRI or genetic data, could enhance robustness. Additionally, improving deep learning interpretability is necessary for clinical trust. The system shows potential to support early, precise diagnosis and personalized treatment strategies. Future work should address dataset limitations, multimodal integration, and model interpretability to facilitate clinical translation.
output:
The present study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of machine learning and deep learning models for the classification of EEG signals in diagnosing various brain disorders, including schizophrenia, autism, epilepsy, dementia, and Alzheimer's disease. The results obtained from both machine learning and deep learning models provide valuable insights into the potential of EEG-based diagnostic systems. The feature extraction process played a crucial role in accurately classifying EEG signals, as it involved selecting relevant features that capture the underlying characteristics of the signals. Two combinations of features were evaluated, and it was found that the second combination, involving Pwelch, shannon entropy and bandpower, outperformed the first one. The choice of epoch length for signal segmentation also had a significant impact on classification performance. The 10s epoch length yielded the best results, indicating that shorter epochs are better suited for capturing the temporal dynamics of EEG signals. These findings align with previous research suggesting the importance of appropriate segmentation techniques for accurate classification of EEG signals. The SVM and random forest algorithms consistently performed well across different datasets, achieving high accuracy rates. The inclusion of optimized features and Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) improved accuracy in some classification tasks, highlighting the potential of feature optimization techniques for enhancing classification performance.

The deep learning results showcased the effectiveness of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and the specialized ChronoNet architecture for EEG signal classification. The CNN model achieved impressive accuracy rates, particularly in the classification of healthy individuals from those with schizophrenia, autism, and epilepsy. The usage of sequential data analysis in ChronoNet, incorporating various neural network components, contributed to its ability to capture temporal dependencies and extract relevant information from EEG signals. The ChronoNet architecture demonstrated high accuracy rates for most classification tasks, further emphasizing the potential of deep learning approaches in EEG-based diagnostics.

The results of this study were compared to related work in the field. It was found that our approach achieved significantly higher accuracy rates compared to a previous study by [21], [22].

While the proposed system demonstrated high classification accuracy, there are several limitations to consider. The size of the datasets used in the experiments was relatively small, which may limit the generalizability of the findings. Future research should focus on acquiring larger and more diverse datasets to ensure the models' performance across different populations and clinical settings. Moreover, the current study primarily focused on EEG data for classification. The integration of other modalities, such as functional MRI or genetic data, could enhance the accuracy, robustness, and reliability of diagnostic models. This multimodal approach would provide a more holistic view of neurological disorders, enabling better clinical decision-making.

Additionally, the interpretability of deep learning models remains a significant challenge. Efforts should be made to develop techniques that provide insights into the decision-making processes of these models, making them more transparent and enabling clinicians to trust and use them effectively.

The findings also have important implications for clinical practice. By demonstrating high accuracy, our approach has the potential to support clinicians in early and precise diagnosis, enabling timely and personalized treatment strategies. The ability to classify multiple disorders simultaneously underscores its relevance as a decision-support tool in enhancing diagnostic workflows.

In conclusion, this study contributes to the growing body of knowledge in the field of neuroinformatics and paves the way for developing innovative diagnostic tools. Despite the limitations, the evidence suggests that both machine learning and deep learning approaches hold promise for advancing EEG-based diagnostic systems. Future research should address these limitations and challenges, focusing on expanding datasets, exploring multimodal data integration, and improving model interpretability to facilitate the translation of EEG-based diagnostic systems into clinical practice.

FSVM-CIL: Fuzzy Support Vector Machines for Class Imbalance Learning

Rukshan Batuwita and Vasile Palade

This work addresses the limitations of standard SVMs on imbalanced datasets. While SVMs perform well on balanced data, they produce suboptimal models when faced with class imbalance. Furthermore, the SVM algorithm is sensitive to outliers and noise. Existing Class Imbalance Learning (CIL) methods mitigate imbalance but do not adequately handle outliers. Fuzzy SVMs (FSVMs) assign membership values to training examples to improve robustness against noise and outliers. However, standard FSVMs still suffer from class imbalance. This paper presents FSVM-CIL, a method to improve FSVMs for CIL. Evaluated on ten real-world imbalanced datasets, FSVM-CIL was compared against five existing CIL methods designed for standard SVMs. Results demonstrate that FSVM-CIL is an effective CIL method, particularly in the presence of outliers and noise.

FSVM-CIL: Fuzzy Support Vector Machines
for Class Imbalance Learning

Rukshan Batuwita and Vasile Palade

Abstract—Support vector machines (SVMs) is a popular machine learning technique, which works effectively with balanced
datasets. However, when it comes to imbalanced datasets, SVMs
produce suboptimal classiﬁcation models. On the other hand, the
SVM algorithm is sensitive to outliers and noise present in the
datasets. Therefore, although the existing class imbalance learning
(CIL) methods can make SVMs less sensitive to class imbalance,
they can still suffer from the problem of outliers and noise. Fuzzy
SVMs (FSVMs) is a variant of the SVM algorithm, which has been
proposed to handle the problem of outliers and noise. In FSVMs,
training examples are assigned different fuzzy-membership values
based on their importance, and these membership values are incorporated into the SVM learning algorithm to make it less sensitive
to outliers and noise. However, like the normal SVM algorithm,
FSVMs can also suffer from the problem of class imbalance. In
this paper, we present a method to improve FSVMs for CIL (called
FSVM-CIL), which can be used to handle the class imbalance
problem in the presence of outliers and noise. We thoroughly evaluated the proposed FSVM-CIL method on ten real-world imbalanced datasets and compared its performance with ﬁve existing
CIL methods, which are available for normal SVM training. Based
on the overall results, we can conclude that the proposed FSVM-
CIL method is a very effective method for CIL, especially in the
presence of outliers and noise in datasets.
Index Terms—Class imbalance learning (CIL), fuzzy support
vector machines (FSVMs), outliers, support vector machines
(SVMs).

section: I. INTRODUCTION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Support Vector Machines (SVMs) [1]–[3] are a widely used machine learning technique successfully applied to real-world classification problems. Although SVMs work effectively with balanced datasets, they often produce suboptimal results with imbalanced datasets [4]–[14], creating models biased toward the majority class with low minority class performance. Furthermore, the standard SVM algorithm is sensitive to outliers and noise [15], [16], which are common in real-world data. Fuzzy Support Vector Machines (FSVMs) [17] handle outliers/noise by assigning fuzzy membership weights to training examples, but remain sensitive to class imbalance. This paper proposes FSVMs for Class Imbalance Learning (FSVM-CIL), which assigns fuzzy membership values under a cost-sensitive learning principle to address both class imbalance and outliers/noise. Evaluated on ten real-world imbalanced datasets, FSVM-CIL outperforms five existing internal and external imbalance-learning methods applied to normal SVMs, demonstrating effectiveness for CIL in the presence of noise [17].

input: SVM models developed with imbalanced data can have separating hyperplanes skewed toward the minority class [5], [6]. This skewness generally causes a high number of false-negative predictions, lowering positive-class performance compared to the negative class [4]–[14]. Available class imbalance learning (CIL) methods for SVM are divided into external and internal categories [14], [18], [19]. A comprehensive review of these methods is available in [14].
output:
SUPPORT VECTOR MACHINES
It has been well-studied that the SVM algorithm can be sensitive to class imbalance [4]–[14], i.e., the separating hyperplane of an SVM model, which was developed with an imbalanced dataset, can be skewed toward the minority (positive)
class [5], [6]. This skewness generally causes the generation of
a high number of false-negative predictions, which lower the
model’s performance on the positive class compared with the
performance on the negative (majority) class.
As mentioned earlier, there exist CIL methods that can be
applied to reduce the effect of data imbalance, when developing SVM classiﬁers with imbalanced datasets. Generally, these
methods can be divided into two categories: external methods
and internal methods [14], [18], [19]. A comprehensive review
of different CIL methods can be found in [14]. The following two
sections brieﬂy discuss the external- and internal-imbalancelearning methods that can be applied for SVM training.

section: III. CLASS IMBALANCE LEARNING METHODS AVAILABLE FOR — A. External Methods
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: External methods preprocess training data to balance classes before classifier training. Random undersampling removes majority examples randomly to meet a target ratio [18]. Random oversampling duplicates minority examples to meet a target ratio [14]. SMOTE generates synthetic minority examples in the neighborhood of existing examples rather than duplicating them [20]. Informed sampling methods were introduced in [21]. A clustering-based method was proposed in [22], and a genetic algorithm-based method was proposed in [10]. Ensemble learning addresses class imbalance [23]. SVM-based ensemble systems for imbalanced learning were developed in [11]–[13]. Boosting methods have been adopted for CIL in [24] and [25].
output: The external methods are independent from the learning algorithm being used, and they involve preprocessing of the training datasets to balance them before training the classifiers. Different resampling methods, such as random and focused oversampling and undersampling, fall into this category. In random undersampling, the majority-class examples are removed randomly, until a particular class ratio is met [18]. In random oversampling, the minority-class examples are randomly duplicated, until a particular class ratio is met [14]. Synthetic minority oversampling technique (SMOTE) [20] is an oversampling method, where new synthetic examples are generated in the neighborhood of the existing minority-class examples rather than directly duplicating them. In addition, several informed sampling methods have been introduced in [21]. A clustering-based sampling method has been proposed in [22], while a genetic algorithm-based sampling method has been proposed in [10]. Ensemble learning has also been applied to handle the problem of class imbalance [23]. SVM-based ensemble systems for imbalanced dataset learning have been developed in [11]–[13]. Moreover, different boosting methods have also been adopted for CIL in [24] and [25].

The combination of fuzzy logic and SVMs has been explored in various ways [17]-[40]. Lin and Wang [17] proposed a method using fuzzy-membership values for each training example based on class importance, reformulating the SVM algorithm to assign different contributions to input points. Wang et al. [30] extended this by introducing separate membership values for positive and negative classes. Another extension based on "vague sets" was proposed in [31]. A distinct approach using fuzzy-basis function kernels was proposed in [32], and a fuzzy support vector regression method was proposed in [33].

In contrast, other approaches assign fuzzy-membership values to SVM outputs combined with output classes. Xie et al. [34] use the SVM decision value to define output class membership, while [35] uses fuzzy-output decision values for multiclass classification. Mill and Inoue [36] propose using positive and negative support vector strengths to generate membership values. Methods for extracting fuzzy rules from trained SVMs have been proposed in [37]-[40].

This paper considers the Fuzzy-SVM method initially proposed in [17] as a solution for outliers and noise. Although it uses fuzzy-membership functions, this method differs from general fuzzy-classification methods involving fuzzification, defuzzification, and fuzzy reasoning [41]-[45]. Generally, general fuzzy-classification methods are based on fuzzy-rule-based systems, neurofuzzy systems, and fuzzy measures [41]-[45]. Other methods handle fuzzy attribute values and/or fuzzy targets [45]. Conversely, the FSVM method considered here uses fuzzy-membership functions to define different misclassification costs for each training pattern [17].

The normal SVM-learning algorithm considers all training points uniformly, making it sensitive to outliers and noise [15], [16]. The FSVM method proposed in [17] assigns different fuzzy-membership values $m_i$ (weights) for different examples to reflect their importance to their own class, where more important examples receive higher membership values and less important ones, such as outliers and noise, receive lower values. Then, the SVM soft-margin optimization problem is reformulated as:

Fuzzy Support Vector Machines

Fuzzy Support Vector Machines

There has been some significant research carried out towards the combination of fuzzy logic and SVMs in different ways, and the term "Fuzzy SVMs" has been used to refer to most of these different approaches. Lin and Wang [17] applies a fuzzy-membership value for each training example, which is based on the importance of that example of its class, and reformulates the SVM learning algorithm such that different input points can make different contributions when finding the separating hyperplane. Wang et al. [30] extended this approach by introducing two membership values for each training example, which define the memberships of both positive and negative classes. This approach has been further extended, which is based on the concept of "vague sets" in [31]. Another type of fuzzy SVM method, which uses a special type of kernel function constructed from fuzzy-basis functions, has been proposed in [32]. A method for fuzzy support vector regression has been proposed in [33].

In contrast, several other approaches have been developed to assign fuzzy-membership values for the outputs generated by SVMs together with the output class. Xie et al. [34] use the decision value, which is generated by the SVMs, to define a membership for the output class, while [35] uses the fuzzy-output decision values for multiclass classification. Mill and Inoue [36] propose a method that uses the strengths (αi) of positive- and negative-support vectors to generate the fuzzy-membership values for the output classes. On the other hand, several methods have been proposed in [37]–[40] to extract fuzzy rules from the trained SVM models.

In this paper, we consider the Fuzzy-SVM method, which was initially proposed in [17], as a solution for the problem of outliers and noise. Although, fuzzy-membership functions are used, this method is different from general fuzzy-classification methods that usually involve fuzziﬁcation, defuzziﬁcation, and fuzzy reasoning. Generally, fuzzy-classification methods are based on fuzzy-rule-based systems [41], neurofuzzy systems [42], [43], and fuzzy measures [44]. Other fuzzy-classification methods handle fuzzy attribute values and/or fuzzy targets [45]. On the other hand, the FSVM method considered in this paper uses fuzzy-membership functions to define a different misclassification cost for each training pattern, as discussed below.

The normal SVM-learning algorithm considers all the training points uniformly, and therefore, it can be sensitive to outliers and noise [15], [16]. As mentioned earlier, the FSVM method proposed in [17] assigns different fuzzy-membership values mi (or weights) for different examples to reflect their importance for their own class, where more important examples are assigned higher membership values, while the less-important ones, such as outliers and noise, are assigned lower membership values. Then, the SVM soft-margin optimization problem is reformulated as follows:

s.t. yi(w · Φ(xi) + b) ≥ 1 − εi

In this formulation, the membership mi of a data point xi is incorporated into the objective function in (13), and therefore, a smaller mi could reduce the effect of the parameter ξi in the objective function, where the corresponding xi is treated as less important. In another view, if we consider C as the cost assigned for a misclassification, then each example is assigned with a different misclassification cost value miC, such that more important examples are assigned higher costs, while less important ones are assigned lower costs. Therefore, the SVM algorithm can find a more robust hyperplane by maximizing the margin by letting some misclassification of less-important examples, such as outliers and noise.

In order to solve the FSVM optimization problem, (13) is transformed into the following dual Lagrangian [17]:

This FSVM algorithm has been successfully applied to reduce the effect of outliers and noise in different domains with different ways of assigning fuzzy-membership values (see [46]–[50]).
