Parenteral Nutrition (PN), first introduced in 1967 as a tool to support an infant with intestinal atresia and weight loss after surgery [1], is a form of nutrition delivered directly into the bloodstream through intravenous infusion. The primary objective of PN in preterm newborns is to provide nutrition mimicking what they would have received in utero, promoting optimal growth and development outside the womb [2].

Neonatologists and healthcare professionals carefully assess the nutritional needs of each infant based on clinical guidelines, personal expertise, and objective conditions of the newborn (e.g., temporal data, medical condition, and growth patterns). This decision process can be time-consuming and variable, requiring constant monitoring and adjustment as the infant’s condition evolves. The choice of basic nutrients (e.g., macronutrients: carbohydrates, proteins, and lipids), on the other side, is a simpler sub-problem, based on general standards and the actual growth pattern and blood tests of the baby.

Clinical Decision Support Systems (CDSS) have been offering for several years real-time advice and alerts to clinicians [3], leveraging patient-specific data and guidelines for medication management, diagnosis, and treatment planning. Predictive modeling uses statistical and machine learning algorithms to predict patient outcomes and risks, facilitating proactive interventions [4]. Although decision support tools and data-driven techniques have been successfully proposed in health care, to the best of our knowledge, there are no tools to suggest the composition of parenteral nutrition bags. Existing tools and techniques include a variety of approaches to improve clinical decision-making [5].

Our study aims to assist healthcare professionals in making evidence-based decisions regarding parenteral nutrition management while reducing the time and effort required for manual calculations. The idea is to analyze the patient’s basic information to estimate individualized macronutrient requirements per day for each hospitalized newborn, which will support the medical specialist’s decision.

To achieve our aims, we collected daily nutrition data on 1,210 infants admitted to the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) of the public hospital “S.Maria della Misericordia” in Perugia, Italy. This data includes all information about the nutrition received on the days of hospitalization, and general information about the infant, such as age or daily weight. With this study, we aim to answer at least the following research questions:

• Can machine learning serve as an effective and efficient framework for developing a specialist decision support system for the macronutrient composition of parenteral bags?
• Which machine learning models and techniques are preferable for this purpose?
• Which features of the dataset are most significant and most useful for decision-making?

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. After an introduction to parenteral nutrition in infants and a presentation of related work in Section I-B, we will outline the methodology and the techniques implemented in Section II, describe the settings in Section III, illustrate the results of the experimental phase in section IV, and close the paper with some final considerations and insights for future work and studies in Section V.

section: I. INTRODUCTION — A. PARENTERAL NUTRITION OF NICU INFANTS
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
Parenteral nutrition (PN) provides critical substrates for optimal growth in NICU infants [6], [7]. Beyond vitamins and electrolytes, PN formulations include macronutrients: carbohydrates (dextrose/glucose as a major energy source), proteins (amino acids for tissue repair), and lipids (blends of soybean oil, medium-chain triglycerides, and fish oil for essential fatty acids and calories) [6]. Fluids (sterile water or electrolyte solutions) are added to maintain hydration and fluid balance.

Energy requirements are estimated based on the state of the art [8], [9]. For neonates in a thermoneutral environment, the resting metabolic rate ranges from 40 to 60 kcal/kg per day [9]. Weight gain requires approximately 3 to 4.5 kcal per gram, accounting for stored energy and synthesis [8]. To approximate fetal growth rates with a target daily weight gain of 12–15 g/kg, an additional 45 to 67 kcal/kg above the resting metabolic rate is necessary [8].

Managing PN for preterm newborns involves assessing nutritional needs considering gestational age, weight, and growth trends to prevent underfeeding or overfeeding [8]. Maintaining fluid and electrolyte balance is vital, especially in infants with renal or cardiac issues [8]. Ongoing research advances in PN formulations, delivery systems, and technology are required to optimize management [8].

Daily growth serves as a parameter to evaluate nutritional adequacy. The goal of PN is to match the weight gain of a fetus born at nine months gestation, used when preterm infants’ underdeveloped organs are not ready for enteral nutrition [8].
output:
The quality and timing of PN administration play a critical role in providing the optimal substrates for appropriate growth [6], [7]. Other than vitamins, minerals, and electrolytes, parenteral nutrition formulations, typically include macronutrients:

• Carbohydrates: e.g., dextrose or glucose, a major energy source included in PN to meet the body’s energy requirements.
• Proteins: amino acids or protein hydrolysates provide essential building blocks for tissue repair, growth, and other metabolic processes.
• Lipids: Usually containing a blend of soybean oil, medium-chain triglycerides, and fish oil, they are administered to provide essential fatty acids and a source of calories.

Fluids i.e., sterile water or electrolyte solutions, are added to maintain hydration and ensure adequate fluid balance.

When prescribing parenteral nutrition in the NICU, it’s crucial to estimate the appropriate energy needs of neonates. The state of the art provides basic ranges for such nutritional values [8], [9]. The exact requirement in the range will be stated based on the daily blood test. For neonates fed parenterally in a thermoneutral environment, the estimated resting metabolic rate ranges from 40 to 60 kcal/kg per day [9]. When considering growth, each gram of weight gain entails an energy requirement of approximately 3 to 4.5 kcal, accounting for stored energy and the energy expended in component synthesis. To achieve an ideal daily weight gain of 12-15 g/kg, approximating fetal growth rates, an additional caloric requirement of 45 to 67 kcal/kg above the estimated resting metabolic rate is necessary [8].

Current challenges for sanitary staff in managing PN for preterm newborns encompass accurate assessment of nutritional needs, considering factors like gestational age, weight, and growth trends, to prevent underfeeding or overfeeding. Maintaining a fluid and electrolyte balance is also vital, particularly in infants with fluid-sensitive conditions or renal and cardiac issues. To meet these challenges, ongoing research advances in PN formulations and delivery systems, adherence to guidelines, and the incorporation of new technologies are required to optimize the management of PN in infants [8].

To evaluate if the macronutrient composition of a nutritional bag is appropriate, doctors observe the growth trend of the baby. The goal of parenteral nutrition is to bring the baby up to the same weight that she/he would have if born after nine months of gestation: it is used when the underdeveloped little internal organs of the preterm newborn are not ready for enteral nutrition (i.e., nutrition by the mother’s milk or other food by mouth). The daily growth is still, thus, a properly generalizable parameter to evaluate the adequacy of nutrition.

The advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has profoundly impacted various medical fields, including therapeutics, diagnostics [10], drug discovery, and medical imaging [11], also including real-time clinical support in intensive care units [3]. Although AI-based clinical decision-support systems [10] offer apparent advantages over rule-based counterparts [12], they often face challenges such as the availability of extensive datasets and the issue of imbalanced data, particularly in the realm of healthcare, where privacy is paramount [13], more than ever when taking care of data regarding minors [14]. On the other hand, with proper data anonymization and security protocols, the risk/benefit ratio leans on the benefit that AI can provide to neonatology. While integrating these tools into routine clinical practice holds transformative potential, it’s imperative to recognize the limitations of AI [15] and ensure its judicious application [16], [17], in particular in terms of general AI ethics and results interpretability [18], [19]. AI applications in neonatology encompass a wide range of areas [20], including monitoring vital signs, predicting diseases like respiratory distress syndrome, stratifying risks for conditions like retinopathy of prematurity and intestinal perforation, and heart failure [21].

A conspicuous gap exists in the scientific literature on applying AI and machine learning methodologies for estimating parenteral nutritional outcomes within the context of NICU, and all the related challenges represent open problems. In fact, despite the burgeoning interest and successful deployment of AI/ML techniques in various medical domains, the specialized area of neonatology, particularly for the estimation of PN-related variables, remains an open research topic, which endeavors the pressing need for novel investigations and innovative methodologies in this domain. Works exist focused on predicting the nutritional status of neonates based on the mother’s data [22], where machine learning techniques such as Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, K-Nearest Neighbor, Linear Discriminant Analysis, Gaussian Naive Bayes, and Support Vector Machine have shown brilliant performance and achieved overall good accuracy. This approach applies only to neonates fed with the mother’s milk.

Another relevant recent application is using ML-based decision support systems to identify malnutrition in NICU patients [23], leading to malnutrition-related extrauterine growth restriction. The demographic and clinical parameters were used to develop the models using fivefold cross-validation with a neonatal nutritional screening tool on 512 patients: the length of hospital stay (LOS), parenteral nutrition treatment (PN), postnatal age (PNA), surgery, and sodium were the most important variables in predicting the presence of weight gain at discharge with a random forest classification. Growth is, in fact, the most relevant element on which to focus to understand if the nutrition is adequate. This focus on understanding the quality of nutrition highlights that an ML-based approach using random forest can be useful when focusing on growth, which is notable also for results interpretability [24].

section: I. INTRODUCTION — C. MACHINE LEARNING REGRESSION MODELS
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: This study evaluates supervised machine learning regression models for estimating unseen data from limited datasets. Four models were selected based on computational efficiency, model size, and performance with small data: Random Forest (RF), Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM), Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Multilayer Perceptron (MLP). RF is an ensemble method that averages multiple decision trees trained on random data and feature subsets to reduce overfitting, offering fast construction and handling of high-dimensional, non-linear data [19], [24]. GBM builds trees sequentially, with each tree correcting errors from prior ones, prioritizing high predictive accuracy while leveraging decision tree interpretability. SVM finds a hyperplane to fit data, minimizing error margins and using a kernel trick to manage non-linear relationships, though it offers lower interpretability. MLP is a basic Artificial Neural Network with input, hidden, and output layers using activation functions to model complex patterns, widely used for learning from large data volumes.
output:
Machine learning (ML) is a branch of artificial intelligence (AI) that focuses on developing algorithms that enable systems to learn patterns from data. ML can be categorized into supervised, unsupervised, semi-supervised, and reinforcement learning. This study focuses on supervised learning, which uses historical data to train a model capable of accurately estimating new, never-before-seen data. The following models have been chosen due to their computational time (both in training and inference), model size, and ability to deal with a limited-size dataset.

1) RANDOM FOREST
Random Forest (RF) is an ensemble learning technique that combines estimations from multiple decision trees to improve accuracy and reduce overfitting. In regression, RF outputs the average estimation of individual trees. Each tree is trained on a random subset of data and features, introducing randomness that helps mitigate overfitting. RFs are particularly effective with complex, high-dimensional data, capturing non-linear interactions between variables. Decision Trees, as a base component of RF, express possible outcomes through rules, providing simplicity in interpreting results [19], [24] and fast construction.

2) GRADIENT BOOSTING MACHINE
Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM) is an ensemble technique that builds decision trees sequentially, where each new tree corrects errors made by previous ones. This method is powerful for capturing complex relationships in data and is well-suited for tasks requiring high predictive accuracy. Like Random Forest, GBM leverages the interpretability and fast construction of Decision Trees while enhancing accuracy through sequential learning.

3) SUPPORT VECTOR MACHINE
Support Vector Machine (SVM) is a supervised learning algorithm for classification and regression. In regression tasks, SVM finds a hyperplane that best fits the data while minimizing error margins. SVM employs a kernel trick to handle non-linear relationships by transforming data into a higher-dimensional space. Despite its complexity and sometimes lower interpretability, SVM's predictive power makes it suitable for many problems.

4) MULTILAYER PERCEPTRON
A Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) is a basic Artificial Neural Network (ANN) type with multiple layers of interconnected neurons, including input, hidden, and output layers. Each neuron applies an activation function to the weighted sum of its inputs, introducing non-linearity and enabling the network to capture complex relationships. ANNs, e.g. MLPs, mimic the structure and learning ability of biological neural systems and have been widely used due to their ability to learn from large volumes of data and model intricate patterns.

input: We aim to build an evidence-based decision support system for infant nutrition in the NICU. The immediate problem is estimating macronutrients (carbohydrates, proteins, lipids) and volume for parenteral bags using historical and personal infant data. We evaluate machine learning as a viable framework for automatically estimating daily parenteral bag composition.

Dataset sourced from the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit at Hospital of Perugia, Italy, containing records of 1210 patients treated with parenteral nutrition (PN) between 2006 and 2023, comprising 18,333 daily data entries. Data were preprocessed for anonymization per European General Data Protection Regulation, resulting in 15 final variables including gestational age, infant age, hospitalization length, daily weight, and parenteral/enteral macronutrients and fluid volume.

To train machine learning models, the database was processed to extract significant features and a 3-day history of nutritional details and weights. This approach considers the prevailing role of prior nutrition to estimate daily requirements, as previously shown [24], and adds categorical variables identifying specific infant groups (described in Table 2).

Since growth trend is the core parameter for predicting nutrition values [23], particular attention was paid to features describing weight and physiological weight loss membership. Weight Category and Entrance Weight Category were chosen to maximize data fit. Physiologically, 1800 grams corresponds to approximately 32 weeks, representing the transition between moderately and very preterm. The additional variable Growth Category was introduced to differentiate growth from weight loss states, specifically distinguishing physiological loss typical of the first days after birth from non-physiological loss.

The dataset for this study was sourced and anonymized by the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit of the Hospital of Perugia, Italy. Patients' data are available on daily parenteral nutrition treatment assessments performed by NICU clinicians during each patient's hospital stay. This dataset encompassed records of 1210 patients treated with PN between 2006 and 2023, comprising 18,333 daily data entries. The dataset has been preprocessed, first of all, for anonymization of data based on the European General Data Protection Regulation, and contains in its final version 15 variables, including patient's anonymized data about gestational age, infant age, length of hospitalization, daily weight, and daily data about their parenteral and enteral macronutrients and injected fluid volume (see Table 1).

To train each machine learning model, this original database is processed to obtain a set of significant features about the infants, and a 3-day history of their nutritional details and weights. This decision was made considering both the prevailing role of nutrition in the previous days to estimate the correct nutrition for a day, and the results obtained in [24]. Moreover, to facilitate the work of the algorithms and obtain more accurate predictions, we added categorical variables, calculated from the original data, identifying specific groups characterizing the infant. Variables and groups are described in Table 2.

Since the growth trend is the core parameter of predicting good values for nutrition [23], we paid particular attention to additional features describing the membership in specific groups related to weight and physiological weight loss conditions. Weight Category and Entrance Weight Category were chosen to maximize the fit of the data. From a physiological point of view, 1800 grams corresponds to about 32 weeks, which roughly represents the transition between moderately preterm and very preterm. The additional variable Growth Category was introduced to differentiate states of growth from states of weight loss, differentiating those related to the physiological loss - typical of the first few days after birth - from non-physiological loss.

Figure 1 shows an infographic of feature and target variables.

Data analysis has been carried out using the open-source RStudio software (version 2022.07.2 +576). Data underwent standardization and scaling, as required by algorithms like SVM and MLP [25]. For the regression problem, traditional machine learning was implemented using the Caret package, and Keras library. Reproducibility is ensured by setting the seed number to 5000. Given the absence of missing values, no imputation was performed. Errors in date variables and out-of-range weight values were rectified through systematic data series checks in a preprocessing phase, together with the healthcare professionals in charge of the data, and by using the dplyr library to filter data with constraints.

We used standard regression model evaluation metrics to assess model performance and aid in model evaluation and selection. In particular, we used:

• Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE): Measures the square root of the average squared differences between estimation and actual observation. It gives a higher weight to large errors.

• R-squared (R2): Represents the proportion of the variance in the dependent variable that is predictable from the independent variables. It indicates how well the model fits the data, i.e. the predicted values are validated by matching the observed ones [26].

The choice of algorithm for healthcare decision support requires balancing precision, interpretability, explainability, and computational costs [1].

Random Forest (RF) and Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM) are the most interpretable and explainable models used in this study [1]. RF provides feature contribution rankings to show the hierarchy of influential patient characteristics or nutritional variables [1]. GBM highlights the gradual contribution of features throughout its ensemble to explain the estimation process [1].

Both RF and GBM are efficient, with execution times in fractions of a second, and scale well due to their ensemble-based nature and parallelization capabilities [1].

Estimation accuracy is inherently linked to input data quality; inaccurate or incomplete data may lead to suboptimal performance [1]. Ongoing validation and refinement are essential to maintain accuracy across diverse patient populations and healthcare settings [1].

COMPUTATIONAL COSTS
Although the precision of algorithms in prediction is generally the most widely used criterion, the choice of the algorithm to be used in a decision support system for healthcare applications should consider a balance between precision, interpretability, explainability, computational costs, and the specific needs of the clinical context.

In machine learning, interpretability and explainability refer to how well humans can understand and trust model decisions. Interpretability is the extent to which a model’s output can be understood based on its input. An interpretable model allows users to comprehend the factors leading to a decision. On the other hand, explainability goes a step further. It refers to the ability to provide understandable reasons able to explain a model’s predictions, and explanations for how and why a model arrived at a certain output. Even if the model explainability techniques have been developed for complex or opaque techniques (like deep neural networks), using inherently explainable methods is crucial for ensuring the trustworthiness, fairness, and accountability of machine learning systems, especially in critical applications like healthcare. For instance, models based on decision trees are inherently interpretable and explainable because their inner workings are transparent.

In this study, the most interpretable and explainable models are RF and GBM; they offer a transparent view of the factors influencing the estimation, which can be particularly advantageous for healthcare professionals. These models generate decision rules and feature contribution rankings that help elucidate how a particular estimation was made. For example, RF can provide insights into the hierarchy of features used to make decisions, allowing practitioners to understand which patient characteristics or nutritional variables are most influential in determining nutritional needs. Similarly, GBM can highlight the gradual contribution of various features throughout the model’s ensemble, offering a step-by-step explanation of the estimation process.

Regarding efficiency, both RF and GBM are renowned for their speed and scalability. Execution time is irrelevant for all the studied models (i.e., fractions of a second). Their ensemble-based nature allows for parallelization of computations, making them efficient even when dealing with large datasets.

Regarding the limitations of the models, it should be mentioned that the accuracy of estimations is inherently linked to the quality of the input data. Inaccurate or incomplete data may lead to suboptimal model performance. Ensuring data quality remains a challenge in real-world healthcare settings.

In particular, ongoing validation and refinement are essential to ensure that the tool remains accurate and relevant across different patient populations and healthcare settings.

instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
V. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK

This study aimed to establish the basis for an evidence-based decision support system to automatically estimate crucial nutritional values (macronutrients) and parenteral bag volume in neonatal clinical ICU. The primary objective was to determine if machine learning can serve as an effective and efficient framework for this aim, exploring and evaluating different techniques for estimating these values. To train models, a comprehensive dataset with patient records and dietary information was set up.

Results revealed promising estimation abilities across all models, with R-squared values consistently exceeding 0.7 for all target values. These findings prove the potential of machine learning as a valuable tool for nutritional outcome estimation in neonatal clinical practice.

Moreover, since the choice of the most suitable algorithm is a multifaceted decision, interpretable and explainable models, like Random Forest and Gradient Boosting Machines, were considered. These models offer transparent insights into prediction factors, aiding professionals in understanding the reasoning behind recommendations. Feature contribution rankings identified the history of nutritional details as among the most important features for estimating values.

While this study marks a significant step forward in the parenteral nutritional outcome estimation field, several avenues for future development deserve attention. Expanding the dataset to include a more diverse patient population, such as data on health conditions and known pathologies from different hospitals, could enhance model performance and generalizability and reduce possible biases introduced by doctor preferences.

A more interesting development might be to extend the models to understand which treatments favored the ideal growth of infants. This would require additional processing of the dataset.

Broadening the range of estimated data, e.g., including micronutrients, should also be among the next research steps.

ETHICAL IMPACT STATEMENT
Data are presented by type and classification results only, with no disclosure of personal data. The data treatment complies with EU General Data Protection Regulation. This study aimed to establish the basis for an evidencebased decision support system to automatically estimate
crucial nutritional values (macronutrients) and parenteral
bag volume in neonatal clinical ICU. The primary objective
was to establish whether machine learning can serve as an
effective and efficient framework for this aim, hence we
explored and evaluated different machine learning techniques
for the critical task of estimating such values. To train our
models, we set up a comprehensive data set with patient
records and dietary information.
The results revealed promising estimation abilities across
all models, with R-squared values consistently exceeding
0.7 for all target values. These findings prove the potential of
machine learning as a valuable tool for nutritional outcome
estimation in neonatal clinical practice.
Moreover, since the choice of the most suitable algorithm
is a multifaceted decision, balancing various factors, we had
to consider that interpretable and explainable models, like
Random Forest and Gradient Boosting Machines, can offer
transparent insights into prediction factors, aiding healthcare
professionals in understanding the reasoning behind recommendations. These models provide decision rules and feature
contribution rankings, making them advantageous for clinical
contexts.
Moreover, given the analysis of understanding the relevance of features, we were convinced that the history of
nutritional details is among the most important features and
should be considered in any study, identifying which other
computed features do not seem to be considered crucial for
estimating values.
While this study marks a significant step forward in
the parenteral nutritional outcome estimation field, several
avenues for future development and improvement deserve
attention. Expanding the dataset to include a more diverse
patient population, e.g., adding data on health conditions
and eventual known pathologies, and data from different
hospitals could further enhance the model performance and
generalizability and reduce possible biases of the dataset
introduced by the doctors’ preferences.
A more interesting development might be to extend the
models and their optimization rules to understand which
treatments favored the ideal growth of the infants. This would
require an internal revision of the learning algorithm and
probably additional processing of the dataset.
Broadening the range of estimated data (e.g., including
micronutrients), should also be among the next research steps.

input: The Hough transform is generally used for shape detection [15]. Circular or elliptical shape recognition can be done with the circular Hough transform [8]. Algorithms based on the Hough transform can only deal with gray scale images. In the implementation of this research, the image is first converted into binary data through edge detection. A pixel on an edge has a value of one and a pixel not on any edge has a value of zero. Then all pixels with positive values vote for possible circle parameters (center position and radius of a circle). instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Ref [9] proposed an ellipse recognition method using curvature analysis of perimeter segments. After edge detection, segment perimeters are calculated, and connection points between overlapped ellipses are identified as extrema of the curvature derivative. These points split the perimeter into segments, which are regrouped before final ellipse fitting; the number of successful fits corresponds to the bubble count. Prior to curvature or Hough transform analysis, noise reduction is performed. The region of interest is extracted by first rotating the detector horizontally via line detection, then isolating the area with the most clustered edge information using edge detection. A median filter is applied last to reduce high-frequency noise while preserving edges.
output:
Ref [9] reported a robust ellipse recognition method based on analysis of curvature information. This method uses perimeter information of an object. After edge detection, perimeters of segments are used for curvature calculation. As shown in Fig. 3, because the curvature usually changes rapidly in connection points of two overlapped ellipses, the algorithm attempts to detect the connection points through identifying the extrema of the derivative of surface curvature. The detected connection points will separate one perimeter into several perimeters. All these perimeters are then regrouped according to if they might belong to the same ellipse. The final stage is ellipse fitting. The number of successful ellipses fit is considered to be the number of bubbles in the image.

It should be mentioned that, before performing the circular Hough transform detection or curvature analysis, the image was processed to reduce noise. As shown in Fig. 4(a), only part of the original image is the SDD. Further bubble recognition algorithm should only be performed on the SDD area. To extract the SDD from the background, line detection is first performed to rotate detector to the horizontal. Then with an edge detection method, the algorithm can recognize the area with the most clustered edge information [as shown in Fig. 4(b)]. This area is extracted as the area of interest, which is the SDD. A median filter is applied for noise reduction at the final stage. The median filter is used because it can effectively reduce high frequency noise without losing too much edge information.

SVM [16] is a supervised learning model for pattern recognition and classification [17], originally introduced in [18] and [19] for its robustness on noisy and sparse data [20].

The method classifies binary labeled data by finding a separating hyperplane with maximum margin distance to both groups [21]. For bubble recognition, images are divided into 10x10x3 color patches via a sliding window with a 4-pixel stride [22]. Given a 2160x4096 image size, over 500,000 patches are generated per image, each treated as a 300-dimensional vector [23].

SVM operates in two phases: training and testing. During training, patches are manually labeled as positive (+1, bubble regions with ~30px average diameter) or negative (−1) [24]. The optimization minimizes ½w·w + C∑ξᵢ subject to yᵢ(w·xᵢ + b) ≥ (1−ξᵢ) and ξᵢ ≥ 0 [25]. After training, the model labels patches in 123 test images. Positive patch counts estimate bubble numbers per image [26].

SVM [16] is a supervised learning model that can recognize patterns and classify data [17]. It was originally introduced in [18] and [19]. The method became popular because of its remarkable robustness on noisy and sparse data [20].

The SVM method is generally used for the classification of binary labeled data sets. When learning on the training data set, it tries to separate the data with a hyperplane which has a maximum distance to both groups of data. Fig. 5 shows an example in two-dimensional space. There are infinite numbers of lines which can separate the two groups of the dots. The SVM method selects the line that maximizes the margin, which is the distance from the line to the closest dot. For dealing with data that are not linearly separable, the kernel technique can be used [21].

To use the SVM method for bubble recognition, the image is divided into 10 pixels × 10 pixels × 3 color patches (as shown in Fig. 6) through a sliding window. The moving pace of the sliding window is 4 pixels. Since the size of each image is 2160 × 4096, over a half million image patches were produced from one image. Each image patch can be treated as a vector with 300 dimensions.

The SVM method is a supervised machine learning method. There are usually two processes when using a supervised machine learning algorithm. One is the training process and the other one is the testing process. During the training process, the algorithm is learning through labeled examples. During the testing process, new image patches are given to the algorithm. The algorithm labels those image patches from the experience it has learned during the training process.

For the training process of the SVM method, image patches from two images were used. Each patch is manually labeled as positive (+1) or negative (−1). A positive label means that the image patch is part of a bubble (the average diameter of a bubble is about 30 pixels in the image) and a negative label means the opposite.

In the mathematical representation, each image patch is a vector (xi) with 300 dimensions. The SVM solves the following problem:

Earliest neural computing traces back to [22]. Ivakhnenko [23] performed the first deep-learning-like research with multiple nonlinear layers. Neural networks have since been applied across biology, medical science, and AI, showing remarkable performance [24]–[26].

A network with more than three hidden layers is classified as deep learning.

input: To compare algorithm performance, accuracy and precision of bubble counting were evaluated using manual counts as ground truth. Algorithms were tested on images with varying bubble counts. Accuracy was determined by the R value of linear fitting between algorithm output and manual counts. Precision was determined by the standard deviation error of that fitting. IV. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION — B. Algorithm Comparison

To compare the algorithms, the accuracy and precision of the bubble counting are two major properties. The accuracy refers to the closeness of a calculated bubble number to the ground truth. The precision refers to the closeness of two or more counting results (for the same ground truth) to each other. An algorithm is better than another when it has both better accuracy and better precision.

To compare the accuracy and precision of algorithms, we used manual counting results (N_m) as the ground truth. Assume bubble counts of algorithms is N_a, then the ground truth can be calculated with N_m = k × N_a + b where k and b are constants. The value of k and b are not important for the accuracy and precision. The reason is that they can be calculated in the calibration process and one can easily calibrate N_a with known k and b. The property that matters for accuracy and precision is the linearity between N_m and N_a. Only with good linearity, can accurate and precise results from N_a, k, and b be obtained.

In the experiment, images of detector with different number of bubbles were analyzed by algorithm. The algorithm output was compared with manual counting results. The accuracy is evaluated by the R value of the linear fitting between N_a and N_m. The precision was evaluated by the standard deviation error of the linear fitting.

Fig. 10. Performance of four different methods.

Fig. 10 shows the comparison result. The DNN demonstrated the best accuracy and precision according to the result (highest R value and lowest deviation error). As the actual number of bubbles decrease or increase, the DNN can maintain very good linearity and low standard deviation error. As a result, accurate bubble numbers of an image can be calculated with the output of DNN.

AKRAM GALAL AND XAVIER HESSELBACH, (Senior Member, IEEE)

ABSTRACT The number of nano-sensors connected to wireless electromagnetic nano-network generates different traffic volumes that have increased dramatically, enabling various applications of the Internet of nano-things. Nano-network traffic classification is more challenging nowadays to analyze different types of flows and study the overall performance of a nano-network that connects to the Internet through micro/nanogateways. There are traditional techniques to classify traffic, such as port-based technique and load-based technique, however the most promising technique used recently is machine learning. As machine learning models have a great impact on traffic classification and network performance evaluation in general, it is difficult to declare which is the best or the most suitable model to address the analysis of large volumes of traffic collected in operational nano-networks. In this paper, we study the classification problem of nano-network traffic captured by micro/nano-gateway, and then five supervised machine learning algorithms are used to analyze and classify the nano-network traffic from traditional traffic. Experimental analysis of the proposed models is evaluated and compared to show the most adequate classifier for nano-network traffic that gives very good accuracy and performance score to other classifiers.

input: Galal and Hesselbach investigate traffic classification in electromagnetic nano-networks using a synthetic dataset generated from background traffic received by a micro/nano-gateway. The dataset contains four classes: TCP packets, UDP packets, nano-to-nanocommunication packets (NN0), and nano-to-Internet communication packets (NN1). Five standard supervised machine learning algorithms—Decision Trees Classifier (DTC), Support Vector Machines (SVM), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Random Forest (RF), and Naïve Bayes (NB)—are evaluated on this dataset. input:
There are various standard ML algorithms applicable to data problems, each with distinct benefits and limitations. This paper investigates which model type is generally suitable for analyzing electromagnetic nano-network traffic crossing micro/nanogateways. We review the most common algorithms previously used for wireless network traffic analysis and classification: decision trees, support vector machines, K-nearest neighbors, random forest, and naïve Bayes. Each algorithm contains tunable hyper-parameters optimized experimentally to achieve optimal performance.

Decision trees are acyclic graphs composed of nodes and leaves, where inner nodes represent input features and leaves represent outcomes. Splitting follows a top-down greedy approach using information gain. While popular for their simplicity and rule-based conversion, they handle both categorical and continuous variables.

Support vector machines (SVM) are non-probabilistic binary classifiers representing feature vectors in multidimensional space to find linear class separation. When linear separation is impossible, the kernel trick increases dimensionality to enable easier separation.

K-nearest neighbors (K-NN) is a non-parametric approach for classification or regression. Output consists of the K-closest training examples in feature space; classification relies on majority vote among neighbors.

Random forest (RF) is an ensemble algorithm aggregating numerous decision trees trained on bootstrapped, randomly selected subsets of data. Outcome is determined by majority voting, providing variance reduction compared to single decision trees.

Naïve Bayes (NB) is a simple classifier based on Bayesian statistics, popular for efficiency in high-dimensional datasets. It assumes feature independence using maximum likelihood estimation for class-conditional probabilities, though this assumption is often violated in practice.

In general, there are various standard ML algorithms, which can be applied to almost any data problem. Each algorithm has its benefits and limitations. In this paper, we are trying to answer a simple question: which type of machine learning model should be generally used in the analysis of electromagnetic nano-network traffic that crosses the micro/nanogateway. So, we discuss the most common and the most popular algorithms that were previously used in the literature for the analysis and classification of wireless network traffic. They are decision tree classifier, support vector machines, K-nearest neighbors, random forest and naïve bayes. Each learning algorithm has certain hyper-parameters or values, which can be tuned to get better results by experimentally finding the best combination of values per hyper-parameter.

1) DECISION TREES
A decision tree is an acyclic graph used to make decisions. These graphs are composed of leaves/branches and nodes, where inner nodes correspond to a specific feature of the input vector and leaves are the outcome. If the value of the feature is below a certain threshold, the left branch is followed; otherwise, the right branch is followed. At the end of a leaf node, the class to which the example belongs is made. Classification trees are very popular classification algorithms due to their simplicity, as they can be easily converted to a rule-based classification system. Moreover, they can be graphically represented. The training follows a top-down greedy algorithm that works by iteratively splitting the nodes, using normally an information gain-based metric as an optimization criterion. DTC is mostly used for classification problems. Surprisingly, it works for both categorical and continuous-dependent variables [16], [19].

2) SUPPORT VECTOR MACHINES (SVM)
SVMs are non-probabilistic binary classifiers. They are considered one of the most powerful supervised classification algorithms, as they work by representing each feature vector in a multidimensional space and trying to find a linear separation for the classes. In some cases, a linear separation of the space is not possible and cannot provide a solution, hence the kernel trick is used by increasing the dimensionality of space, making an easier separation in a much higher dimensional space [16], [19].

3) K-NEAREST NEIGHBORS (K-NN)
The K-NN algorithm is a non-parametric approach used for either classification or regression. In both scenarios, the output consists of the K-closest training examples in the feature space. In the K-NN classification, the output is a class membership. An object is classified by a majority vote of its neighbors, with the object being assigned to the class most common among its K-nearest neighbors [16], [19].

4) RANDOM FOREST (RF)
RF is an ensemble learning algorithm that consists of the aggregation of a large number of decision trees, each one based on a different part of the training set. They are randomly selected. These instances are called bootstrapped samples, and the outcome is generally decided by majority voting among all the bootstrapped samples. RF is one of the most widely used ensemble learning algorithms, and it provides a reduction of variance compared to a single decision tree [16], [19].

5) NAÏVE BAYES (NB)
NB is a simple classifier algorithm based on Bayesian statistics. It is popularly used because of its efficiency in multiple scenarios, especially in high-dimensional datasets. Its functionality uses maximum likelihood estimation by assuming that data features are mutually independent, which is not true in most cases. This assumption provides an easy calculation for the class-conditional probabilities [16], [19].

Classification predictions generate four outcomes that form a confusion matrix: true positives (correctly predicted class), true negatives (correctly predicted non-class), false positives (incorrectly predicted class), and false negatives (incorrectly predicted non-class). Higher diagonal values in the matrix indicate more correct predictions. The three main evaluation metrics are accuracy, precision, and recall. Accuracy is the percentage of correct predictions. Precision is the fraction of true positives among all predicted positives. Recall is the fraction of true positives among all actual positives.

When performing classification predictions, there are four types of outcomes that could occur. These outcomes control the performance metrics and form a matrix called the confusion matrix, which is used to evaluate the quality of the output of a classifier. The higher the diagonal values of the confusion matrix, the better the indicator for many correct predictions. Traffic classification in telecommunication networks supports monitoring, management, and QoS [19]. In nanonetworks, it enables performance monitoring, resource provisioning, and anomaly detection [19]. Traditional techniques based on port numbers, payloads, or host behavior are limited; port-based methods fail due to dynamic assignment and tunneling, while payload-based methods are computationally intensive due to encryption [19]. Machine learning is the prevailing modern approach, with supervised and unsupervised methods applied to large datasets [19].

[20] proposed a semi-supervised method to discover traffic characteristics and assign service classes, addressing unbalanced distributions [20]. [21] used SVM for campus backbone classification, achieving accurate results with biased and unbiased samples, though only one algorithm was analyzed [21]. [22] compared six supervised algorithms using ISP data and PCA feature extraction [22]. [23] compared six algorithms using two feature selection methods across five traffic classes [23]. [24] proposed a smart city classification technique using four algorithms on campus data to improve QoS [24].

In electromagnetic nano-networks, traffic prediction and classification are active research fields [25]. Exploring traffic features enables intelligent resource management. Nano-device heterogeneity creates diverse traffic types, increasing randomness and making accurate prediction and classification difficult [25]. High-accuracy wireless traffic prediction is important for automatic resource allocation to meet real-time demands [25].
output:
Traffic classification is an important process for telecommunication networks to observe a wide range of operations, measurements and management activities [19]. In nanonetworks, traffic classification can be useful for performance monitoring, resource provisioning, traffic prioritization, selfconfiguration devices, network management, QoS and security by identifying unknown traffic or detecting anomaly behavior to maintain adequate nano-communication.

Generally, traffic classification techniques can be categorized based on port number, payload, or host behavior, but these techniques are considered traditional approaches, and they are not widely applicable. As port-based techniques are unreliable due to the use of dynamic port assignment, tunneling and port number changes to avoid firewalls. While payload-based techniques are computationally intensive and complicated due to encryption. Similarly, host-based traffic classification techniques are highly susceptible to routing asymmetries. In contrast to these legacy approaches, machine learning is the most widespread technique used for traffic classification recently. As supervised and unsupervised, ML has been successfully employed for traffic classification, showing high accuracy and applicability to large datasets [19].

Different studies in the literature provide analysis of traffic classification based on machine learning and investigate QoS support using different datasets. The authors in [20] proposed a classification method to discover traffic characteristics and dynamically assign service classes to IP packets. They applied semi-supervised machine learning techniques, considering packet characteristics such as the unbalanced traffic distribution between classes. While the authors in [21] used SVM to classify the network traffic in campus backbone networks. In their study, SVM achieved reliable and accurate results using biased and unbiased test samples. However, they only analyzed one ML algorithm, neglecting other algorithms.

The authors in [22] compared six supervised machine learning algorithms for traffic classification in the backbone network. Their datasets contain Internet Service Provider (ISP) data traffic, and they used principal component analysis for feature extraction and analyzed its influence on the classification results. While the authors in [23] compared six supervised learning algorithms for traffic classification. Their experiments were conducted using two feature selection methods and five traffic classes. While the authors in [24] proposed a traffic classification technique for smart cities using four supervised machine learning algorithms on datasets containing campus data traffic aiming to improve the QoS in smart city networks.

In electromagnetic nano-networks, traffic prediction and classification are active research fields. Exploring the traffic features enables intelligent resource management and provisioning. Different applications of nano-networks and the heterogeneity of their nano-devices provide a high-level diversity in the generated traffic types. This diversity results in growing randomness in traffic and makes it increasingly difficult to be accurately predicted and classified. Therefore, the high-accuracy prediction of wireless traffic is important to allow automatic network resource allocation with real-time demands [25].

section: III. TRAFFIC GENERATION AND DATASET FEATURES — A. THE PROPOSED TRAFFIC GENERATOR
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: We developed a packet generator to simulate nano-network traffic combining TCP, UDP, and nano-network packets for a micro/nano-gateway. Real-world nano-network data is costly to collect; therefore, we generated a synthetic dataset based on the NanoSim simulator [38]. This simulator models electromagnetic communication using an event-based NS3 framework. In NanoSim, the message processing unit generates random packets periodically; the network layer adds a header independent of routing, and the MAC layer uses transparent-MAC for direct transmission. The generated nano-device message has a fixed five-field header: flag, source Dev-ID, destination Dev-ID, packet-ID, and Time To Live (TTL). The flag indicates forwarding to a gateway or nano-router. Dev-IDs are unique identifiers assigned to nano-devices. The network header structure and field lengths are modifiable. The packet-ID is assigned sequentially by the message processing unit, and the TTL ranges from 100 to 1000, decrementing by one per hop [38], [39]. Our proposed traffic generator creates data flows of four packet types: TCP, UDP, and two nano-packet categories. NN0 represents nano-to-nano communication (router to router), while NN1 represents nano-to-Internet or cloud communication (router to Internet/cloud). Figure 2 illustrates the algorithm flowchart generating the synthetic dataset used in the analysis.
output:
We developed a packet generator to generate nano-network traffic combining TCP and UDP traditional network traffic to simulate the traffic received by a micro/nano-gateway. The gateway receives both types of traffic from the nano-scale communication side and the traditional network side. It is worth noting that in AI/ML there is a heavy reliance on a real dataset, as it has more certainty when compared to synthetic data. However, the main reason why synthetic data is used through a generation model is that synthetic data may be more cost-effective and efficient than collecting real-world data in some cases. At present, real-world nano-network traffic is costly to collect due to the lack of availability and the difficulty of having fully operational nano-sensors work in functional nano-network. Accordingly, at the time of simulating this model, there was no access to certain datasets representing the real nano-network traffic and its packet format. So, to overcome this challenge, and as the quality of synthetic data is highly dependent on the quality of the model that creates it, the design of the proposed nano-network traffic generator has been motivated by an existing network simulator, i.e., NanoSim that is discussed in [38]. Hence, a synthetic dataset has been created and used in the simulation. This synthetic data can mimic many properties of authentic data from the NanoSim simulator, especially the packet header format of the nano-sensor payload.

NanoSim simulator is an event-based NS3 simulator used for modeling electromagnetic nano-network communication and its protocol stack. In this simulator, the message processing unit creates random packets generated periodically with a packet size adjusted by the end-user. The network layer adds a network header independent of the routing technique, while the MAC layer follows a certain strategy that has no kind of control, hence the packet is transmitted from the network layer to the physical interface of the nano-router directly based on a technique called transparent-MAC. In this simulator, the generated message from the nano-device has a fixed header structure consisting of five fields. They are the flag field, the source Dev-ID, the destination Dev-ID, the packet-ID and the Time To Live (TTL). Figure 1 illustrates the nano-network header packet blueprint, where the flag field has been added to indicate if the packet is forwarded to the micro/nano-gateway or a nano-router. Source and destination Dev-IDs are set to the Dev-ID of the local nano-machine and the receiver, respectively. Dev-ID is a unique identifier, and it is assigned to nano-devices, e.g., nano-gateway, nano-router and nano-machine. The structure of the header added by the network layer, as well as the value and the length of each field, can be modified depending on the use case. The packet ID is assigned by the message process unit sequentially, whereas the TTL is set to a value between 100-1000, and it is decreased by one after each hop. The high value of TTL is considered under the assumption that a message on a wireless nano-network can reach its destination after traversing hundreds of nano-devices [38], [39]. Accordingly, the generated bytes stream from a nano-router includes the nano-network packet header associated with the encapsulated payload, then this stream is transmitted through the physical interface of the nano-router towards the micro/nano-gateway.

Our proposed traffic generator generates data flow, which consists of multiple random packets composed of four types. They are TCP packets, UDP packets and nano-network packets, which can be classified into two types, nano-to-nano-communication packets (NN0) and nano-to-Internet-communication packets (NN1). The first type of nano-packet represents the communication scenario between nano-routers, i.e., when a nano-router transmits a packet to another nano-router, while the second type of nano-packets represents the communication scenario with the Internet, i.e., when a nano-router transmits a packet to the Internet or the cloud. Figure 2 illustrates the flowchart of the methodology used by the proposed traffic generator algorithm, which provides the synthetic dataset used in our analysis.

IV. PERFORMANCE EVALUATION OF LEARNING MODELS

In this section, we develop the tools and techniques necessary for a model to make the micro/nano-gateway able to classify the nano-network traffic properly. The model will classify traditional traffic from nano-network traffic, where traditional traffic can be classified into TCP or UDP packets, while nano-network traffic can be classified into nano-to-nano-communication domain packets or nano-to-Internet communication domain packets. We investigate five different algorithms, all of which are supervised learners and determine which is best at modeling the data. These models are decision tree classifier, support vector machines, the K-nearest neighbors, random forest and naïve Bayes.

We start by evaluating the performance achieved by the five learning models and then present an optimization technique for all approaches by tuning their corresponding hyper-parameters. After that, a full comparison between all approaches has been presented. For the sake of training and testing, we consider 10-fold cross-validation in all the results presented in this section. Parameters on each optimized algorithm are calibrated based on the best-performance grid search test.

In this simulation, we answer the question of which type of machine learning model is optimal for the analysis and classification of micro/nano-gateways traffic. This is achieved by calculating the accuracy, Fscore and confusion matrix for each model to quantify its performance. These metrics are very useful in the analysis, as they describe how good the model is at making predictions and classifications. Moreover, we draw the learning curves for both training and cross-validation sets to diagnose and visualize the performance during the learning phase, i.e., to figure out how much a machine learning model benefits from adding more training data or samples, and whether the estimator suffers from a high bias (underfitting) or high variance (overfitting).

We achieve these objectives by implementing the following steps for each classifier:

• Calculate the accuracy and Fscore for the unoptimized model and check its learning curves.
• Tune the corresponding hyper-parameters of the model.
• Calculate the accuracy and Fscore for the optimized model and check its learning curves.
• Calculate the normalized confusion matrix for the optimized model.

section: V. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: AI/ML integration in telecommunication networks enables operators to predict information, adapt to network changes, and manage resources for high performance. Empowering nano-networks with AI/ML improves their operational techniques, as ML shapes electromagnetic nano-network functionalities in resource management, monitoring, and prediction. This paper develops a nano-network traffic generator combined with traditional background traffic, then employs five supervised ML algorithms to model and classify micro/nano-gateway traffic using a synthetic dataset. The main objective is to construct an accurate classification model for nano-network traffic received by micro/nano-gateways. The dataset originates from the packet generator, which creates nano-packets representing nano-network traffic alongside background TCP and UDP traffic. We demonstrate the outstanding performance of DTC, SVM, KNN, RF, and NB algorithms for analyzing traffic from macro and nano wireless domains. Models are evaluated by classification accuracy, F-score, learning curves, and normalized confusion matrices. NB and KNN generally outperform DTC, SVM, and RF; however, NB is nominated the best model due to its higher diagonal confusion matrix. Therefore, NB represents an appealing ML model for electromagnetic nano-network traffic analytics, as it is the most accurate for this problem. Future work will explore ensemble learning methods to obtain better predictive performance than individual algorithms, expanding ML studies to improve detection and prediction accuracy with enhanced performance metrics.

ABSTRACT Encouraged by growing computing power and algorithmic development, machine learning
technologies have become powerful tools for a wide variety of application areas, spanning from agriculture
to chemistry and natural language processing. The use of quantum systems to process classical data using
machine learning algorithms has given rise to an emerging research area, i.e. quantum machine learning.
Despite its origins in the processing of classical data, quantum machine learning also explores the use of
quantum phenomena for learning systems, the use of quantum computers for learning on quantum data and
how machine learning algorithms and software can be formulated and implemented on quantum computers.
Quantum machine learning can have a transformational effect on computer science. It may speed up the
processing of information well beyond the existing classical speeds. Recent work has seen the development
of quantum algorithms that could serve as foundations for machine learning applications. Despite its great
promise, there are still signiﬁcant hardware and software challenges that need to be resolved before quantum
machine learning becomes practical. In this paper, we present an overview of quantum machine learning in
the light of classical approaches. Departing from foundational concepts of machine learning and quantum
computing, we discuss various technical contributions, strengths and similarities of the research work in this
domain. We also elaborate upon the recent progress of different quantum machine learning approaches, their
complexity, and applications in various ﬁelds such as physics, chemistry and natural language processing.

section: I. INTRODUCTION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Daily data generation reaches 2.5 exabytes, equivalent to 250,000 Congress Libraries. This volume reflects over 3.2 billion internet users contributing 347,222 tweets and 4.2 million Facebook likes per minute. With these datasets, researchers can investigate financial strategies, climate change, biological processes, and economic phenomena. This data growth outpaces traditional computational power despite Moore’s Law, which predicts transistor density doubling every two years since 1965. Transistor miniaturization will likely end soon, making quantum computing attractive. Quantum computers use quantum phenomena to efficiently solve complex mathematical problems traditional computers find hard or unfeasible. Furthermore, quantum operations are expected to enable a new family of quantum-enhanced machine learning algorithms. This is possible because quantum calculations rely on subatomic particles existing in multiple states simultaneously, contrasting with the binary 0 or 1 nature of traditional computers. The GPU development for parallel processing has addressed some big data issues in traditional computation, benefiting from Moore’s Law. However, increasing problem complexity has led AI stacks to include diverse hardware back-ends, including CPUs, TPUs, and neuromorphic chips. However, a comprehensive theory of QML is currently absent, and existing algorithms often require significant modification for quantum hardware due to fundamental differences between qubits and bits. FIGURE 1. Mix of heterogeneous back-end hardware currently used by AI. In the future, this will also incorporate quantum technologies to enable certain learning algorithms [1] and deep learning models in the same way that GPU's have done in the past. Figure 1 describes the role of quantum computing in machine learning.

Quantum machine learning (QML) is the intersection of machine learning and quantum computing. QML attempts to use the capacity of quantum computers to process data at much faster speeds than traditional computers. QML refers to the use of quantum systems to incarnate algorithms that allow computer programs to improve through experience. Thus, in QML, quantum computers are used to tackle machine learning problems making use of the natural efficiency of quantum computers. Recall that quantum states in superposition can lead to important speedups as a result of the ability to evaluate multiple states simultaneously. As noted in [2], there is no comprehensive theory of QML yet. Sasaki and Carlini [3] have delved into the notion of semi-classical and universal strategies whereby, in the former, classical methods are adapted to work on quantum systems whereas in the latter the methods are purely quantum in nature. In [4], the authors explain how learning algorithms may be accelerated via quantisation, i.e. the partial or total translation of the algorithm to its quantum counterpart. Both [3] and [4] argue for the use of quantum primitives.

Moreover, note that quantum computers may not be a complete replacement for traditional computers. That said, they will allow us to extend the categories of computer-tractable problems. First of all, certain conventional tasks are ideally suited for quantum computers. Further, quantum computers can perform computations and solve problems conventional computers can not do. For example, no conventional hardware can generate a truly random number. That's why the generators in conventional computers are referred to as spontaneous pseudo generators. This is, however, a straightforward task for a quantum computer. Likewise, when trying to imitate natural processes with conventional bits (e.g. subatomic component behaviour), it is not only computationally complex but also costly. It is very easy to do such calculations on a quantum computer as underlying physical objects representing Qubits match and arise from quantum phenomena.

Despite its promise, existing code and algorithms do not often apply to a quantum processor. This is due to the natural difference between Qubits and bits. This is a problem at the core of QML work, whereby quantum or quantum-inspired algorithms may be quite different in nature as compared to their counterparts executed on conventional computers or GPUs.

The RBMs are generative models that, because of their strong connections with the Ising model, are particularly suitable to be studied from a quantum perspective. The computation of the log-likelihood and the sampling operations from an RBM has been shown to be computationally hard [20]. that, according to the authors, makes it possible to model a rich class of problems (i.e. problems that would otherwise be classically difficult to model, such as quantum states). It is not known whether these models can give any advantage to classical tasks. Kieferova and Wiebe [29] suggest that quantum Boltzmann machines could provide advantages for tasks such as rebuilding a quantum state density matrix from a set of measurements (this operation is known as quantum state tomography in the quantum information literature). The Review by Schuld et al. In fact, Schuld et al. [2] did not reproduce the fundamental characteristics of the ANN (for example, Hopfield’s attractive dynamics). On the other hand, it can be argued that the single biggest challenge for a quantum ANN is that quantum mechanics are linear, but artificial neural networks require nonlinearity [30].

Further, the optimization of quantum neural networks in the NISQ (Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum) era is currently facing two major challenges. The first is local optimization. This is, the stochastic nature of the objective function, combined with readout complexity considerations, has made the direct translation of classical local optimization algorithms challenging. Gradient-based optimisers either rely on quantum back-spreading of errors [19] requiring additional gate depth and quantum memory or use finite-difference gradients [31] that typically require multiple quantum circuit evaluations for each gradient descent iteration. Recent work has proposed sampling analytical gradients [32] to reduce this cost. However, these approaches also require a large number of measurement runs and therefore remain expensive.

The second major challenge for optimization of quantum neural networks regards the initialization of their parameter space. Although some proposals have been made for the QNN parameter initialization heuristics [33], there is still a need for more efficient and flexible versions of such heuristics. By initializing cost landscape parameters in the neighbourhood of a local minimum, one can ensure more consistent local optimization convergence in fewer iterations and a better overall response to the global landscape. Good initialization is therefore crucial in order to improve the convergence of local optimisers to local extremes with reasonably good local minima.

III. BACKGROUND

Quantum is the smallest unit possible of any physical entity, for instance energy or mass. In 1900, Max Planck suggested that the energy at the atomic and subatomic levels be composed of a discrete packet called quanta [34]. Recall that wave-particle duality is characteristic of how, depending on the environment, matter and light sometimes behave like a wave and sometimes as a particle. In this setting, quantum theory is characterised by the determination of the probability of a particle being at a given point x in space, not its exact location. This notion is at the center of quantum mechanics and will be important in the following sections.

In quantum mechanics, vectors are expressed in the braket notation, i.e. ⟨a| and |a⟩, whereby the former is a row vector and the latter is a column vector. In this notation, for convenience, the inner product is expressed as ⟨b|a⟩, where ⟨b| and |a⟩ are bra-ket vectors. Similarly, let H be a Hermitian matrix, its eigenvector equation is given by H⟨a| = λa|a⟩, where ⟨a| is the eigenvector and λa is the corresponding eigenvalue. Our choice of a Hermitian matrix here stems from the importance of this sort of matrix in quantum mechanics. Recall a Hermitian matrix is defined as that which is equal to its transposed complex conjugate.

For each Hermitian matrix, there are two separate eigenvectors each of which will give rise to an eigenvalue. In the physical world, Hermitian matrices represent a measurable observable. Eigenvectors represent the possible state of the system. Eigenvalues then represent the actual results we get when we undertake the measurements. One thing that is notable here is that, in many cases, the Hermitian operator cannot be directly measured. This also applies to the eigenvector. The eigenvalue in contrast is measurable, whereby the result of the measurement can determine the eigenvector and, therefore, indicates the state of the system.

A. QuBit

The QuBit is a complex vector pair that points to a point on a unit sphere. We have illustrated this in Figure 4. A QuBit can also be viewed as zeros and ones in a fuzzy combination. Quantum bits could in theory consist of anything acting like an electron or atom in a quantum manner. Thus, QuBits can be represented by:

• An electron orbiting a nucleus: where |0⟩ and |1⟩ are the ground state and excited state, respectively
• A photon: where |0⟩ and |1⟩ are its polarization states.

In practice, QuBits in the computing industry are tiny superconductive circuits that are made from nano-technology that can run in two directions. The nature of QuBits makes them ideal for multi-tasking, this is one of the reasons why computing power could explode exponentially if computations are based upon QuBits rather than just bits. Figure 3 compares classical to quantum data.

QuBits are the basic unit of quantum information. They are, in effect, the quantum incarnation of the classic binary bit with a two-state device. A QuBit is a quantum mechanical device of two different levels. The key distinctions between a bit and a QuBit are shown in Figure 3. Moreover, the mathematical model for QuBits is related to the representation, by a two-dimensional vector, of the state of a quantum object over two states, which always has a norm of unit length.

In quantum computing, a quantum register is a system comprising multiple Qubits. A quantum computer stores its quantum data in one or more quantum registers. Note that quantum and classical registers are conceptually different. A classical register of n bits is comprised of an array of n flip-flops. A quantum register of size n is simply a n Qubits array. A detailed overview of the n Qubits register compared to a n bits register is given in Figure 5.

Logical logical gates are used in quantum computing, but, again, logical gates have different purposes to those used in quantum computing. Quantum logic gates are essentially a transformation of one or more Qubits. We have given a description of the quantum gate types in [20] in Figure 6.

Further, in quantum computing, a quantum algorithm is based on a practical model of quantum computation. A classical algorithm, i.e. non-quantum, is a finite sequence of instructions or a step-by-step problem-solving procedure, where a classic computer will execute any step or instruction that can be defined using binary operations. In the same way, a quantum algorithm is a step-by-step procedure where each step can be performed on a quantum computer. Although it is also possible to do all classic algorithms on a quantum computer [35], the term quantum algorithm is usually used for those algorithms that are inherently based on quantum object properties. These are expected to use some of the key features of quantum computation, such as quantum superposition or quantum entanglement.

Figure 7 shows the four big classes of quantum algorithms that are commonly used in quantum computing. These algorithms are primarily based upon quantum annealing, simulation, or the versatility and properties for universal computers. This is since quantum annealing and simulation often employ the notion that the quantum system should evolve naturally in time, whereby quantum universal computers are expected to be able to control the evolution process itself. Each category also varies by the amount of processing power (Qubits) needed and the number of potential applications, as well as the time necessary to become commercially viable. The lowest energy state provides the optimal solution, corresponding to the most likely outcome in quantum annealing. Physics solves optimization problems because minimum energy states correspond to local minima; quantum annealing finds these states. Sampling problems differ from optimization by aiming to characterize the energy landscape rather than recover the minimum state, which is useful for machine learning to learn and predict system states. The main types are quantum-applied and quantum-enhanced learning [1]. Quantum-inspired ML runs on classical hardware using quantum concepts like tensor networks [46] and fast linear algebra [47], while quantum-generalized ML extends fundamental concepts like density matrices to quantum data [1]. IV. QUANTUM MACHINE LEARNING

A. CONTEXT
Quantum Machine Learning (Quantum ML) is an interdisciplinary field incorporating Quantum Physics and Machine Learning (ML). This is a symbiotic association using the power of Quantum Computing to generate quantum versions of ML algorithms and applying classical ML algorithms to analyse quantum systems. More comprehensively, quantum machine learning is a field where the power of quantum computing and the properties of quantum physics are used for machine learning tasks and applied accordingly to related fields. The two main types of quantum machine learning are quantum-applied machine learning and quantum-enhanced machine learning. Further, quantum-inspired machine learning and quantum-generalized learning ideas stand out as two very promising lines of research in line with the QML philosophy. In Table 1 we provide a brief survey of books and review articles for the benefit of the interested reader.

Note that the speed-ups that can be achieved using quantum computers are not achievable by quantum-inspired machine learning [45] since these methods are often designed to run on conventional machines. Quantum-inspired machine learning is, for example, focused on quantum processing to generate new classical learning models and new ways to train and evaluate them. Examples here are ideas involving tensor networks as learning models [46], the approaches of Tang for fast stochastic linear-algebraic manipulations [47], and inspirations behind the projective simulation of Briegel [48].

Quantum-generalized machine learning generalizes the fundamental concepts like density matrices generalize classical notions of information. Quantum machine learning questions what machine learning can look like if data or environments really are quantum objects. Quantum systems are popular for creating odd and counter-intuitive patterns that cannot be generated by any classical computer. The two most important complexity classes are P and NP. P contains problems with efficient polynomial-time deterministic algorithms. NP contains problems where solution verification is efficient, regardless of difficulty. NP-Complete problems are those where every NP problem reduces to a canonical polynomial-time solvable form; solving this form efficiently solves all NP problems of that family.

The class of problems solvable by quantum computers is BQP, or "bound error, quantum, polynomial time." BQP is the quantum equivalent of BPP on classical computers, defined as problems resolvable by polynomial-time algorithms with correctness probability limited to half overall instances. A problem is BQP if a quantum computer answers correctly with high probability in polynomial time.
