Abstract—Visualization of biological mechanisms by means of pathway graphs is necessary to better understand the often complex
underlying system. Manual layout of such pathways or maps of knowledge is a difﬁcult and time consuming process. Node duplication
is a technique that makes layouts with improved readability possible by reducing edge crossings and shortening edge lengths in drawn
diagrams. In this article, we propose an approach using Machine Learning (ML) to facilitate parts of this task by training a Support
Vector Machine (SVM) with actions taken during manual biocuration. Our training input is a series of incremental snapshots of a
diagram describing mechanisms of a disease, progressively curated by a human expert employing node duplication in the process. As
a test of the trained SVM models, they are applied to a single large instance and 25 medium-sized instances of hand-curated biological
pathways. Finally, in a user validation study, we compare the model predictions to the outcome of a node duplication questionnaire
answered by users of biological pathways with varying experience. We successfully predicted nodes for duplication and emulated
human choices, demonstrating that our approach can effectively learn human-like node duplication preferences to support curation of
pathway diagrams in various contexts.

section: INTRODUCTION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
Creating a diagram representation of a large, complex network depends on graph characteristics and appropriate layout for the use-case [1]. Network visualizations represent complex biological process models, such as pathways, allowing better understanding of embedded knowledge [2]-[4]. While many automatic layout approaches exist from graph visualization [5], [6], the gold standard for biological pathway layout remains human-curated layout, as seen in resources like Reactome and KEGG [7], [8] and projects like PD Map and ReconMap [9]-[12]. This curation is time-intensive yet important [13]. Curators typically spend days or months manually updating and laying out large networks when a new pathway is created or updated to reflect new knowledge [14]. Many research communities, such as disease-maps.org, need solutions to reduce or simplify graph curation aspects [14].

Because of molecular promiscuity and cross-talk between biological processes, pathway models contain nodes participating in multiple interactions. A fundamental curation task involves choosing to duplicate (clone) some nodes to reduce crossing edges. This phenomenon is handled in most resources [7], [8] and supported by a dedicated marker in the SBGN graph notation language [15]. Duplicating the right nodes produces a more readable layout with fewer edge crossings and less routing. However, many duplicated nodes hinder understanding of linked processes, and some cloned nodes may need merging (de-duplication), especially when a diagram is newly constructed, extended, or if duplication progresses too far [16]. Node duplication choice currently relies on expert curator intuition and preference. An intelligent method to suggest duplication is needed.

participate in multiple interactions. Therefore, one fundamental task of the curation process consists of choosing to
duplicate (i.e., clone) some nodes and, as a result, reduce
the number of connections crossing larger parts of the pathway. The phenomenon of duplicated elements or nodes is
handled in most commonly available resources [7], [8] and
is supported with a dedicated marker in the SBGN graph
notation language [15]. By duplicating the right nodes, the
graph can be transformed by the curator to produce a more
readable layout with less edge crossings, and less edge routing. On the other hand, if a pathway contains many duplicated nodes it also hampers the understanding of linked
processes and some cloned nodes may need to be merged
(de-duplicated). This could be the case when the diagram is
newly constructed, extended with new sub-graphs, or if
duplication has progressed too far. Fig. 2 shows two simple
equivalent pathway examples where (a) contains two candidate nodes for duplication and where (b) has both of them
duplicated. The node duplication choice is currently up to
the expert curator, who is relying on intuition, experience
and preference. An intelligent method that can suggest a

input: The primary contribution of this work is a solution that suggests to the curator a set of nodes for duplication in a manner similar to how an expert human would. By using the prediction on the inverse case, the method may likewise be converted to suggest nodes for de-duplication. Our solution is provided as a plugin for an existing biological pathway visualization platform, MINERVA [2], as a tool to support the work of the platform’s curators. This plugin scores by predicted probability of (de-)duplication and highlights candidate nodes selected by the user. Another contribution lies in proving the effectiveness of ML techniques for learning to replicate one task of expert graph curation and layout, i.e., human-like node duplication. We believe that our approach can be used to address other aspects of the curation and layout process in the future. The approach is described in detail so that it may be adopted by other researchers in graph and network visualization, for instance as part of an automatic layout algorithm or as a way to automatically merge multiple pathways. The plugin and instructions loading on Minerva are available at https://git-r3lab.uni.lu/minerva/plugins/nodup. The remainder of this article is organized as follows: related work is presented in Section 2, the proposed approach in Section 3, with results and validation in Sections 4 and 5. Finally, discussions and conclusions are presented in Sections 6 and 7.

In this article, we focus on learning to predict human-like
node duplication choices to support the biological pathway
curation and layout process. We use common graph structure and vertex metrics to train ML models to propose
nodes for duplication. Because of this, our approach is also
applicable in cases, where the layout is not available in

we compare node duplication preferences of a group of

method.

2
BACKGROUND AND RELATED WORK
2.1
Biological Pathway Layout
There is a wide range of available biological visualization
tools [16], [17] and online platforms that visualize biological
pathway data, e.g., [2], [7], [8]. Biological pathway models
support relationships between more than two elements at
once. For example, reactants (input), products (output) and
process modiﬁers may all be connected by a single interaction. Graphs with such a property are called hypergraphs,
where elements are connected by hyperedges. Hypergraph
models play an important role in representing state of
human knowledge about multi-element processes like gene
expression and signalling in living cells. When visualizing
pathway diagrams stored in well-accepted formats, such as
SBGN [15] and SBML [18], these hyperedges are represented visually as a small square with links to the elements
inﬂuencing, or inﬂuenced by, the reaction, see Fig. 1. A
more in-depth outline of requirements in terms of humanlike layout and representation of pathway graphs can be
found in [19].
Human curated layouts are generally preferred for visual
interpretation over those automatically generated, especially for complex diagrams [6]. In addition, humans have a
preference for grid layouts [20], with strongly related clusters positioned close to each other [21]. Another key aesthetic factor is edge crossings, and the handling thereof in
manual graph drawings [22].
Node duplication (often referred to as node cloning or
vertex splitting) is a technique by which edge crossings,
established as a key aesthetic, can be removed [23]. It has
been speciﬁcally examined as a technique for social network
visualization [24], and is often used within biological pathway curation. In biology, many molecules can take multiple
roles in different pathways, depending on e.g., cellular
localization or substrate availability. Therefore, node duplication may be used not only to optimize a given aesthetic,
but also to represent the same pathway element in different
contexts.
2.2
Machine Learning and the SVM Model
In this work we apply Supervised Learning (SL), a common
Machine Learning (ML) methodology. SL can be thought of
Fig. 1. An example of a biological pathway, visualized using CellDesigner [4].
Reactions, that can also be interpreted as hyperedges, are displayed as
small squares that link, among others, reactants, inhibitors, activators, and
products of the process. The style of the edge determines the implication of
the biological element, and the shape of the elements themselves designate
their type: proteins, molecules, complexes, phenotypes, etc. (see details
about the diagram legend on celldesigner.org).
Fig. 2. A simple example showing the impact of node duplication.
as teaching a system the desired output corresponding to
given input. After successful training of such a model, new
output values can be predicted based on yet unseen input
values. Typical SL tasks include classiﬁcation and regression, with the most wide-spread models being Support Vector Machines (SVM) [25] and variants of Artiﬁcial Neural
Networks (ANN).
Classiﬁcation is deﬁned as the task of assigning labels to
data points, and in our case it will mean a binary decision,
whether a node should be duplicated or not. This decision
is originally made by a human curator, and an SVM will be
trained through actual samples to emulate such human
decisions. The SVM maps the pre-designed feature datapoints into a higher dimensional space, using kernel functions, then ﬁnds linear hyperplanes that separate the datapoints efﬁciently into classes. We employ here three commonly used kernel functions: Laplace, Polynomial and the
Radial Basis Function. Intuitively the stronger exponential
Radial kernel allows for a sharper separation of close datapoints than the Laplace kernel. The Polynomial kernel can
be seen as a smoother global function allowing for extrapolation into feature space regions where no training samples
were given. The parameter settings available along with reasonable tuning ranges can be seen in Table 3.
2.3
Machine Learning for Graph Layout
While machine learning has been considered for graph visualization [26], to our knowledge no prior work exists that
employs machine learning to predict node duplication in
pathways. The closest contribution we found is the use of
ANN by New et al. [27] to dynamically predict which nodes
the user wants to be shown. In turn, Kwon et al. [28] use an
SVM-based approach for the layout of large graphs based
on their topological similarity measured using graph kernels. Their work focuses on large graphs, which may otherwise take hours to layout, and provides a fast method for
showing what the graph would look like using various
layouts and a fast estimation of aesthetic metrics, using a
training data set of existing layouts. This approach could
potentially be adapted to predict node duplication.
In other works, Meyer [29] proposes a Self-Organizing
Map (SOM) layout approach organizing the graph on an
input grid lattice in 2D/3D space. Intuitively, the objectives
of the proposed approach resemble those of basic forcedirected layout. Cimikowski presents an ANN based algorithm to solve the minimum crossing number by adapting a
linear graph embedding in [30]. This work, and later variants [31], [32], [33], [34] allow efﬁcient veriﬁcation of layout
planarity and estimation of the number of crossings in the
non-planar case.
3
APPROACH
This Section describes how we train an ML algorithm to predict which elements of a diagram can be duplicated to
improve pathway layout. The input for learning is a series
of incremental snapshots describing the transformation of a
large diagram to a layout that favours node duplications
over edge crossings. From these graphs we derive a matrix,
where, per-vertex and per progression number, a classiﬁcation labelling (duplicated: Y/N) is generated along with a
number of per-vertex graph metrics. This matrix and labelling is suited for classiﬁcation by the SVM model and once
trained and tuned, it can be applied to any pathway.
3.1
Pathway Graph Datasets
The learning input is a series of 18 incremental snapshots
the AlzPathway [10] diagram, a map of pathways and
mechanisms implicated in Alzheimer’s disease. This map
has been rearranged into a modular layout, which reduced
edge crossings, decreased its mean network distance and,
due to node duplication, increased the number of elements
(see [11] for more details). For validation and tuning we use
another diagram that combines pathways and mechanisms
of Parkinson’s disease, the PD map [9], and has a format
similar to AlzPathway. As the test set we use the ReconMap
[12], a large diagram of the human metabolic pathway, and
25 selected Reactome pathways. For the user study we
selected four of the smaller Reactome pathways, Table 1
summarizes the datasets used in this work.
3.2
Node Duplication
In this work, node duplication is understood as cloning a
node in its entirety, where the duplicates are exact copies of
the original. A consideration to make is the assignment of
the edges to the generated clones. If the node has two edges
it is trivial to assign one edge to each copy. With more edges
multiple combinations may be possible, both concerning
how many duplicates to create and how to distribute the
edges among them. Our focus is on identifying which nodes
should be duplicated, based only on graph structure, hence
we are agnostic to the position of duplicate nodes, but also
to how many clones should be made and how to distribute
the edges. At this stage of the work, these considerations
will still be the responsibility of the curator.
A simple example of a graph in which two nodes are
duplicated can be seen in Fig. 2. It can be determined
whether or not nodes in an edited graph are the result of a
cloning operation by comparing the nodes and their neighborhood to that of the previous graph snapshot. Let’s
assume that the graph in Fig. 2b is the result of cloning
nodes in Fig. 2a essentially representing two consecutive
states in a curation process. First, if the node was added and
represents a copy, it becomes a possible candidate. Next an
actual duplicate node can be determined by inspecting the
set of edges of its immediate neighbors, while also considering the direction and type of the edges. In this example, the
nodes 2 and 4 can be classiﬁed as the nodes duplicated to
produce 2 þ 20 and 4 þ 40.

3.3
Graph Transformation and Feature Space
A pathway can be regarded as a hypergraph, see Figs. 3a
and 3b, where the two hyperedges connect multiple nodes.
Therefore it can be converted to a generalized graph representation G ¼ ðV; EÞ of vertices V and edges E. This is done
by replacing each reaction hyperedge by a vertex, and a set
of edges, making the resulting graph bipartite, with all reactions in one set and biological elements in the other, see
Fig. 3c. The hypergraph can also be converted to a bi-partite
mapping representation where all elements linked by a
hyperedge are connected completely by edges, see Fig. 3d.
With the hypergraph transformed into these simple
graph representations, indicative per-vertex feature values
can be deﬁned based on common graph metrics (See
Table 2). The ﬁnal set of features used has been established
in experiments, however the optimal sub-set is a topic for
future work. Some take only a reduced neighborhood
around the vertex in question into account, such as the distance sets and sub-graph metrics, with the intention to produce stable features that do not vary with the size of the
graph. To produce input for the SVM model, all these features are normalized to the interval [0,1] and organized in a
matrix with one column per feature and one row per vertex.
The ﬁve distance sets are normalized differently: to ensure
that the graph size and other global speciﬁcities do not
impact the generalizability of the approach, the node counts
associated with the distance sets are ﬁrst scaled by a constant value.
This constant value is deduced from the number of nodes
found in a grid shaped graph at 1 to 5 hops away from any
given node and amounts to 4; 8; 12; 16 and 20 respectively,
see Fig. 4. The choice of a grid graph is not arbitrary, but is
due to the fact that most pathway graphs to a large part
have a structure that resembles that of a grid and hence we
can estimate the expected number of nodes based on this
hypothesis. To guarantee a value in [0,1] the scaled node
counts are limited with a tanh function which leads to
higher sensitivity around the expected value, while still
allowing some variation for outliers.
3.4
Training Data and Processing
The training data is based on a curation of the AlzPathway
graph, see Table 1. The curation progress is described by a
set of 18 incremental snapshots, which are then preceded by
one generated collapsed graph. This collapsed graph is in
essence equivalent to the ﬁrst graph, except that all duplicate nodes are eliminated by contraction, to serve as a
completely non-curated initial state for which the layout is

Following the method described in Section 3.2 the 19
pathway graphs are compared one by one in a sequence,
in order to determine and classify all the nodes that undergo
a duplication operation by the human pathway curator.
Next, the graph transformation and processing described in
Section 3.3 is applied to each of the graphs producing a single training data set. The duplication classiﬁcation is added
to this dataset to be used as ground truth for training.
The data is cleaned of contradictory entries that have
similar features to a duplicated node (within 1 percent of
feature space extent), but are not labelled as duplicated.
Nodes with a degree < 2 and of Complex type do inﬂuence the feature calculations, but are excluded from the
dataset as they cannot be duplicated and are hence not
regarded as candidates. The dataset constructed as
described above is suitable as a training set for an ML classiﬁer such as the SVM model, that can also provide prediction probabilities. This allows to adjust the acceptance
threshold and hence bias the prediction towards labelling more or less nodes for duplication. The standard
acceptance-threshold is p 0:5, but by setting a higher
acceptance-threshold only the nodes with higher probability will be labelled. This means producing less correctly
labelled actual duplicates (i.e., true positives) while simultaneously minimizing the number of wrongly labelled
duplicates (i.e., false positives). A trade-off that we will
examine further in the following sections.
All data processing steps as well as the SVM-based classiﬁcation are implemented in the R scripting language [35].
The SVM implementation is available as a part of the mlr
library [36].
4
EVALUATION OF PERFORMANCE
Here we describe the different techniques and experiments
conducted to train, validate and test our ML approach. The
sequence of Alzheimer disease maps (AlzPathway) is used
to train the SVM, the Parkinsons Disease Map (PD Map)
instance is used as validation set for tuning of the SVM
parameters. Finally, the previously trained and tuned SVM
is tested on the large ReconMap of the human metabolism
and numerous smaller Reactome pathway instances, see
Table 1 and Section 3.1.
Standard metrics for classiﬁcation performance evaluation are used based on True (T) and False (F), Positive (P)
and Negative (N) prediction counts with P referring to the
nodes that are duplicated. Emphasis is on the True Positive
Rate (TPR) = TP/P, sometimes referred to as ‘sensitivity’,
‘recall’ or ‘hit rate’ and the False Positive Rate (FPR) = FP/
N, see [37]. We are mostly interested in the performance in
terms of reported TPs with low FPs. This is due to the usecase scenario of suggesting a human digestible amount of
nodes that should be duplicated.

4.1
Tuning with the Parkinson’s Disease Map
The AlzPathway dataset processed as described in Section 3.4
is used for training. Performance at various tuning settings
is determined by predicting duplicates in the collapsed
PD Map (see Section 3.4) and evaluating the ability to
identify the nodes that were actual duplicates in the original
PD Map. Through repeated sampling of the parameter space
1,000 times (see Table 3), the performance of a wide range of
parameter settings is determined.
The full resampling of the algorithm parameter space
is shown in Fig. 5. It is encouraging to see that more than
10 percent correct predictions are achieved before any False
Positives are reported, and a TPR around 25 and 50 percent
can be reached while maintaining a FPR as low as 2.5 and
12 percent respectively. We use these tuning results to select
the best parameter sets for each kernel that produce a TPR
of at least 50 percent and use these in the remaining tests.
Table 4 shows these in detail, and they are also labelled
among the other sets in Fig. 5.
4.2
Application to the Human Metabolism Map
The previously determined best tuning settings, achieving a
TPR above 50 percent for the PD Map, are applied to the the
larger ReconMap [12] graph for testing. This is equivalent to
a real situation where a curator starts with a new map and
uses the trained SVM model to generate helpful duplication
predictions for it. Biasing with the acceptance threshold we
can achieve any wanted level of TPR (with a corresponding
FPR). The highest TPR achieved while still maintaining a FP
and hence also a FPR of zero, is 13.5, 16.4 and 15 percent for
the three kernels respectively, corresponding to 80, 97 and
89 TPs of the actual 592 Positives. Likewise half (296) of the
duplicated nodes are identiﬁed with as few as 90 FPs of
1141 Negatives, meaning a FPR of 7.9 percent. The full
results are seen in Fig. 6 and summarized at speciﬁc TPR

4.3
Application to 25 Reactome Pathway Graphs
To validate the approach on a broader set of graphs, the
method is applied to a selected set of Reactome pathways.
The Reactome database contains a wide range of small and
large pathway graphs. We select the 25 largest samples
respecting certain criteria: human pathway graphs with
reactions, proteins and molecules representing more than
5 percent and more than 20 elements with degree > 1.
The experiment is repeated for the 25 selected Reactome
pathway graphs with the same pre-tuned settings as
described in Section 4.2. The results can be seen in Fig. 7
with vertical bars representing min/max FPR-values and
grey transparent areas bounded by dotted lines representing 25 to 75 percent percentile intervals. All kernels provide
accurate average predictions with TPR of over 50 percent
with a FPR down to 10 percent. The Laplace kernel has a

ﬁgure and the top row in Table 6.
4.4
Plugin Implementation
The ﬁrst steps towards user exposure have already been
implemented in the form of a plugin for the MINERVA platform [2]. The plugin can be loaded into the sidebar and provides two sortable lists showing the duplication and the deduplication suggestions adding prediction probability and
selection functionality, see Fig. 9. The full processing chain
on the PD Map (5,664 nodes, 6,176 edges) from request to
presentation of results takes 118.6 (1.517 sd) seconds (in 5
repetitions). Consecutive calls are near-instant as the results
are buffered. The majority of the time can be attributed to
processing in R in a Virtual Machine with a single core
assigned on an Intel Xeon E5-2680 @ 2.40 GHz server.
5
USER VALIDATION STUDY
To further validate and evaluate our approach we compared the ML-based predictions for node duplication with
the responses of pathway users by means of Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) and Area Under Curve (AUC)
analysis [37], [38]. To this end, we have conducted a user
study on selected Reactome pathway graphs, for which a
subset of randomly selected nodes was collapsed.
5.1
Graph Samples and Permutations
Four Reactome pathways were selected for the study
(R-HSA-3229133, R-HSA-428157, R-HSA-2160456, R-HSA-
196071) for their small size and aesthetic appearance. For
each of these pathways, two modiﬁed versions where generated, producing a total of 8 graphs. The modiﬁcation consisted in selecting 3 to 5 nodes at random. For each selected
node, we merge (de-duplicate) them with all their duplicates, and place the merged node at the original position.
Ten nodes in total, with a maximum of 5 merged nodes and
5 or more nodes randomly selected, were labelled from one
to ten in each graph, see Fig. 8a. In each graph, these ten
labelled nodes were evaluated by users as candidates for
duplication. The survey graphs retained their element
names and original layout, except for edge routing and
edges added due to de-duplication. Color codes indicating
the type of the elements were deﬁned, see Fig. 8b.
5.2

section: DISCUSSION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Using machine learning, this work predicts duplicated nodes in biological pathway curation. Learning from AlzPathway and validating on the PD Map, the SVM model achieved a true positive rate (TPR) of 25 percent with a false positive rate (FPR) as low as 2.5 percent, proposing 105 nodes to the curator, of which 86 are valid duplication candidates. Final testing on the ReconMap and 25 Reactome pathway maps showed that the collapsed and filtered ReconMap, containing 592 duplicated nodes, achieved a TPR of 25 percent with the Laplace kernel, corresponding to 148 correct propositions and 26 false positives. The Polynomial kernel correctly suggested 97 of these 592 nodes without any false positives. Across the 25 Reactome maps, TPR ranged from 5 to 67 percent with zero false positives reported. On average across the three kernels, TPR was 28, 26, and 25 percent, identifying roughly a quarter of actual duplicates without error. Identifying nodes for duplication in large biological pathways is inherently difficult and ambiguous, influenced by individual curator preferences and rigor. A user survey comparing machine learning results to actual user responses underlines this difficulty; although user agreement with consensus was well above chance, human-like node duplication prediction is difficult to quantify. The trained SVM models placed slightly above average compared to human responses. The approach is pathway agnostic, relying on generic graph representations of the hypergraph, and confidently works on larger diagrams with similar structural characteristics. All machine learning features rely solely on graph structure without requiring a given layout, deliberately isolating structural metrics from aesthetic ones for broader applicability. Node positions and aesthetics are promising topics for future research, as is the elimination of redundant features. The best performing kernel cannot be definitively determined; the Laplace kernel shows better performance on the PD Map and ReconMap, which are visually and stylistically closer to the training data, while the Polynomial kernel performs slightly better on the divergent Reactome pathways, potentially due to its ability to extrapolate outside training data. The Radial kernel generally performs worse, though good settings were found in the false positive mid-range during tuning.

section: CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE WORK
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: To support the curation and layout of large biological pathways, this work focuses on node duplication, i.e., splitting or cloning nodes to reduce edge crossings. We present a Machine Learning approach using 66 structural graph features and a curation history to predict which nodes to duplicate, mimicking human curators. An SVM model, trained and validated on pathways of various sizes, achieves a True Positive Rate of at least 50 percent with a False Positive Rate of 10 percent. We also demonstrate that the inverse operation, de-duplication, is useful when merging pathways; a plugin for the Minerva platform uses the SVM to suggest duplicates, displayed in a double list view with probability scores. Given the subjectivity of manual curation, these findings are encouraging. Future work includes identifying the most efficient subset of the 66 features, exploring geometric or graphlet-based features, determining the optimal number and distribution of duplicates, and supporting general layout via sub-structure methods. Wider application requires more fine-grained training data, potentially obtained by integrating crowdsourcing into online pathway platforms.
output:
To support the curation and layout of large biological pathways we focus on the technique of node duplication, i.e., splitting or cloning a node to bring a graph closer to a planar structure, with the goal of producing a layout with less edge-crossings. The technique is widely used by pathway curators on highly connected elements and most state-of-the-art graph visualization approaches in bioinformatics recognize and address this issue. Here, we present an approach using Machine Learning (ML) relying on a set of 66 features developed from structural graph metrics (i.e., no existing layout or position information is used) and a graph curation history. By modelling the duplication question as a classification problem we are able to successfully predict which nodes to duplicate in a manner mimicking a human curator. The general applicability of the approach is demonstrated by validating the trained and tuned SVM using pathways of various size and structure, achieving or exceeding a performance TPR of 50 percent with a FPR of only 10 percent (see Sections 4 and 6).

We demonstrate that a relationship exists between the designed structural graph metrics and human layout choices across multiple pathway graphs from different sources. It is further shown that an ML model like the Support Vector Machine (SVM) is able to learn and predict such relationships. At the current state, the approach may be used as a first step to duplicate nodes in a sophisticated layout algorithm.

Another example is when building biological pathways by merging several graphs together. In this use case, the inverse de-duplication operation, may be very useful to a curator or even applied in an automatic pathway merging procedure. In fact, it can be tested in such scenarios, using the plugin we have developed for the Minerva [2] platform that queries our SVM model to suggest duplicates for the displayed pathway. The result is shown in a double list view of duplication and de-duplication suggestions. The predicted probability score can be used to sort the lists by the most likely candidates for duplication and de-duplication and a click will center the view on the nodes in question, see Fig. 9.

Considering that manual curation is subjective and depends on individual expertise, the findings of this work are encouraging. Now that this proof of concept implementation has demonstrated the feasibility of using ML on layout aspects of graphs, the door is open to perform further investigations. A first direction is to determine which subset of the 66 features is the most efficient or if better features can be designed, for instance based on geometric distance, or on graphlets as in the work of Kwon et al. [28]. Further extensions of our approach could be used to determine the number of duplicates to create for each node and how to distribute edges among these clones. The future approach may also offer support in the placement of created nodes or even help to perform layout in general, for instance by selecting sub-structure layout methods as in the work of Archambault et al. [41] and parametrizing these. To support development of a wider range of applications more fine-grained training data is required. This could possibly be obtained by integrating crowdsourcing functionality into an existing online pathway platform, as suggested by Borgo et al. [42]. The crowdsourced graph transformations and layouts could be used to create larger training data sets, across a range of pathways and purposes.

ABSTRACT Estimating and analyzing traffic patterns become essential in managing Quality of Service (QoS) metrics while assessing internet data traffic in cellular networks. Cellular network planners frequently apply various approaches to predict network traffic. However, most existing studies focus on using the available local data to jointly build prediction models, facing data security challenges and time complexity, especially with multi-dimensional datasets. Therefore, this paper proposes a framework to handle traffic prediction with the considerable potential of Machine Learning (ML) algorithms. An Adaptive Machine Learning-based Cellular Traffic Prediction (AML-CTP) framework is presented to select a suitable ML algorithm for multi-dimensional datasets. Its objective is to streamline and speed up the selection of an appropriate model for predicting network traffic load. The framework employs two density-based clustering algorithms to categorize similar nearby traffic into various clusters, considering data similarity and convergence. Additionally, it assesses data quality and homogeneity by training models with data samples from each cluster to accurately determine the most suitable machine learning model. The optimal model is selected from four supervised predicting algorithms, reducing training time and hardware complexity. Two case studies from a popular telecommunication equipment corporation in Egypt are implemented using real-life cellular traffic with multi-dimensional features. The case studies show that the framework can help reduce the computational cost of training the model and reduce the risk of overfitting. The experimental results show that selecting the best prediction model training could save up to 85% of computational time compared to two state-of-the-art techniques while achieving an accuracy of 98.8%.

section: I. INTRODUCTION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
A rapid increase in smartphone subscriptions and streaming services has led to a growth in traffic data, influencing Quality of Service (QoS) for users. Optimizing network resources, specifically transmission power and traffic steering, is necessary to maintain QoS. Accurate prediction of 4G and 5G LTE-A traffic is essential to enhance QoS and detect congestion. However, Machine Learning (ML) model training is often hindered by long computation times and data characteristics like distribution and homogeneity. Therefore, analyzing data similarity and homogeneity is crucial for selecting an accurate prediction algorithm and reducing computational costs.

This paper introduces the Adaptive Machine Learning-based Cellular Traffic Prediction (AML-CTP) framework to facilitate and speed up suitable model selection for network traffic load prediction. The framework applies two density-based clustering algorithms, DBSCAN and Kernel Density Clustering (KDC), to categorize similar traffic into clusters. It then evaluates data quality and homogeneity within these clusters to train models and select the most accurate predictor from four supervised algorithms: Linear Regression (LR), Support Vector Regression (SVR), Decision Tree (DT), and Light Gradient Boosting Machine Model (LGBM). An overall view of the proposed AML-CTP framework is illustrated in Figure 1. It starts by preprocessing collected real-life Key Performance Indicators (KPIs), including feature selection and visualization. The framework then applies DBSCAN and KDC to split the data into clusters. Output clusters are fed into a co-association matrix to check data similarity. Subsequently, the AML-CTP extracts data samples with the same probability distribution as the original population to train the ML models and select the most suitable one. Two case studies using real-life KPIs from a major Egyptian telecommunication equipment corporation examine large, high-dimensional LTE-A datasets.
output:
Nowadays, a rash growth of traffic data exists due to the rise of smartphone subscriptions and streaming video services. As a result, this influences the Quality of Service (QoS) of network users. Therefore, many network-level optimizations should be performed to maintain the best QoS for users. However, an optimization problem is challenging for the best QoS that adjusts the transmission power [1], [2], [3]. Steering traffic from congested cells frees the physical resource blocks (PRBs) of congested cells and is considered a network that optimizes resource allocation [4], [5]. Hence, predicting 4G and 5G LTE-A traffic became essential to significantly enhance telecommunications QoS [6], [7]. Accurate monitoring and prediction of mobile traffic help improve optimizer goals; consequently, any overload or congestion in any band can be detected [3], [8].

Over the past decades, Machine Learning (ML) has become a crucial backbone of information technology. However, with the significant increase in data sizes, training time for models can range from hours to weeks. Hence, it poses intense pressures across computation, networking, 2024 The Authors. This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives 4.0 License. For more information, see https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/ and storage [5]. In turn, this affects the choice of the ML model. Also, the nature of the data, which includes correlation, distribution, and homogeneity, influences the selection process of the final model. Since ML deals with the data and behaves accordingly without being programmed, data analysis is required to evaluate and estimate the benefits of optimizer goals. Practical data analysis leads to the successful choice of the most accurate prediction algorithm and saves computational time and memory usage [9], [10], [11]. Therefore, analyzing the similarity, closeness, and homogeneity in traffic data is essential to selecting the appropriate ML model. Moreover, clustering techniques are applied to large datasets, so the data is partitioned into clusters containing similar elements. Then, an extraction rule is estimated based on the pattern of occurrence of data tokens [12], [13]. In addition, for unknown traffic, dividing data into classes requires more information on the nature of the traffic. Thus, clustering methods are used to gain some perception of the structure of the data. The optimal clustering algorithm collects data in one cluster when the data is homogeneous and similar. A smaller sample size may be present in the data when the clusters are more heterogeneous. This sample size can sufficiently capture the underlying patterns and relationships in the data [14].

Therefore, this paper introduces the Adaptive Machine Learning-based Cellular Traffic Prediction (AML-CTP) framework. The AML-CTP aims to facilitate and speed up the selection of a suitable model for network traffic load prediction. The framework considers the similarity and convergence of the data by applying two density-based clustering algorithms to categorize similar near traffic in various clusters. In addition, it considers the data quality and homogeneity by training these models with data samples from each cluster to get the exact indication of the best ML model. Finally, the best model is chosen from four supervised predicting algorithms, reducing the training time and hardware complexity.

An overall view of the proposed AML-CTP framework is illustrated in Figure 1. It starts by preprocessing the collected data from real-life key Performance Indicators (KPIs). The prepossessing process includes analyzing the data, selecting uncorrelated traffic features, and data visualization [15], [16]. Then, the framework applies the Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN) clustering algorithm [17], [18] and the Kernel Density Clustering (KDC) algorithm [19], [20] to split the data into clusters. Then, the output clusters are fed to the co-association matrix to check data similarity [21], [22], [23], [24]. After that, the AML-CTP extracts a data sample with the same probability distribution as the original population. Finally, these data samples are used to train the ML models and select the most suitable one.

Four ML prediction models are used to attain the best performance and aggregate predictions. These models are Linear Regression (LR), Support Vector Regression (SVR), Decision Tree (DT), and Light Gradient Boosting Machine Model (LGBM). Then, a separate validation dataset is evaluated to ensure the models can generalize well to new, unseen data to avoid the risk of overfitting and improve the overall accuracy and robustness of the model. Two case studies are examined using real-life KPIs collected through one of Egypt’s most popular telecommunication equipment corporations. Both case studies utilize large, high-dimensional LTE-A key performance indicators datasets.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows: Section II represents related work of cellular mobile traffic prediction models. Section III describes the proposed framework’s details. Section IV introduces two real case studies and discusses the experimental results. Finally, the main conclusion and future work are presented in Section V.

instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Existing work applies ML to optimize wireless networks and predict traffic. Operators gather cellular datasets for monitoring [25, 26]. Constructing predictive models faces challenges due to mobile traffic diversity and varying collection precision [27-31]. Recent solutions primarily depend on Deep Learning (DL) to handle high-dimensional datasets and achieve high accuracy for long-term prediction [32-37]. LSTM, CNN, GRU, DBN, and stacked Auto-Encoder models are commonly applied [32-37]. However, these systems involve substantial computational load and complex parameter setup [38-41]. Ensemble learning approaches utilizing LGBM have been incorporated, but ensuring prediction accuracy requires genuine training data from the target environment [36]. Further research is required to explore ML in innovative architectural systems, including preprocessing methodologies to eliminate data violations and model development.
output:
Machine learning can play a valuable role in various aspects of telecommunication technologies, including enhancing services for end-users on the network. With the ongoing rise in the number of users and the corresponding increase in data size, it becomes necessary to analyze data using statistical processing methods to reduce the expenses associated with manual analysis. These methods are also effective in identifying errors and data noise. Therefore, incorporating machine learning techniques can optimize network operations and contribute to the early prediction of network failures, preventing significant degradation of the network’s Quality of Service.

Initially, network operators gather available datasets from the cellular network operator for monitoring purposes [25]. A detailed examination of mobile datasets can be found in [26]. However, constructing predictive models with mobile datasets poses numerous challenges. The primary issue stems from the diversity of mobile traffic datasets. Additionally, varying data collection approaches can produce datasets of differing precision, adding complexity to the machine learning training process. Furthermore, the substantial growth in 5G and 6G introduces several challenges in handling big data and selecting the optimal prediction model. Consequently, identifying the most suitable prediction model is not always straightforward, particularly when dealing with extensive and high-dimensional datasets.

Existing research has explored the use of ML in optimizing the performance of wireless networks. For example, in [27], an experimental study assesses popular supervised and unsupervised learning methods. The experimental analysis in [27] identifies SVM, LR, and DT as the most accurate algorithms among the supervised learning approaches. Another study [28] examines existing techniques for traffic prediction that leverage machine learning, offering concise descriptions of traditional machine learning models and methods in this survey. This rationalizes utilizing these machine learning algorithms in the proposed framework for traffic prediction. Moreover, another study [29] utilized the Radio Environment Map as the data source, which depicts a coordinate plane with X and Y axes, representing the spatial distribution and intensity of a specific feature using a thermal strip. Then, the authors augmented the dataset with information on the mobile drive test unit’s speed to forecast the network performance. Chaudhary and Johari [30] introduced a novel ML-based algorithm for routing in wireless networks. They gathered a small and imbalanced dataset, employing random oversampling to augment sample numbers and balance the dataset. The proposed algorithm utilized supervised machine learning methods to predict the network type of the source and destination nodes. Also, Sliwa et al. [31] employed ML algorithms to predict data rates, focusing on the concept of utilizing cars as mobile sensors. The authors suggested a method that considers the current channel situation to determine the optimal time for the transaction.

In general, existing network traffic load prediction solutions [32], [33], [34], [35], [36], [37] mainly depend on Deep Learning (DL) [38] to build the prediction model. A deep learning model can handle high-dimensional traffic datasets. Also, they can usually obtain high accuracy for long-term prediction. During the last few years, different types of DL techniques have been applied to network traffic load prediction; those techniques mainly depend on deep learning, neural networks, or a combination of both techniques. Long short-term memory (LSTM) based solution is introduced in [32]. Also, LSTM and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) collaborative solutions are in [33]. In [34], Gated Recurrent Units (GRU) and CNN combined solutions are employed. Deep Belief Networks (DBN) based solutions in which estimation solutions based on DBN are introduced in [35] and [36]. A stacked Auto-Encoder (SAE) based solution that proposed a Downlink-based traffic prediction method that uses a Stacked Demising Auto-encoder (SDA) model to learn generic traffic features is in [37].

Moreover, the direct advantages of clustering to improve prediction accuracy through data quality enhancement are explored in [39]. However, these investigations focus on distinct, non-uniformly distributed data. The widely used K-means clustering algorithm is applied, generating multiple clusters for a finite dataset. There is no definitive optimal clustering of the data; specific clusters may be unnecessary, some might signify sampling noise, and specific information could be exclusive to a particular grouping. Nonetheless, the emergence of novel information from these clusters provides an opportunity to employ a different clustering algorithm in prediction tasks, mainly when dealing with homogeneous data.

However, the primary limitations of these systems involve substantial computational load and complex parameter setup. Ensemble learning approaches have also been incorporated, utilizing an integrated LGBM model through bagging and LGBM [41]. Nonetheless, ensuring the accuracy of predictions in ensemble learning-based solutions poses a challenge due to the requirement for genuine training data derived from the target environment [36]. Hence, further research is required to explore the significance of implementing machine learning in innovative architectural systems to gather performance data in wireless networks. It involves creating preprocessing methodologies to eliminate data with notable violations and developing machine learning models.

section: III. PROPOSED AML-CTP FRAMEWORK — A. PHASE 1: DATA PREPROCESSING
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Data collection initiates Phase 1. Missing values are replaced with the median. SelectKBest selects important features based on Sklearn [42], analyzing correlations as cited in [7] and [43]. Traffic load is normalized using Min-Max scaling. PCA [44] reduces dimensionality, retaining components based on cumulative explained variance ratio [45] to visualize patterns and remove noise.
output:
As in Figure 2, the phase starts with data collection. After collecting data, it contains various underlying properties and information saved in a local database. First, the AML-CTP framework starts the cleaning phase by dealing with missing values. In many analyses, missing values can be a problem. Therefore, all missing values are replaced with the median. As a result, different cells vary significantly in their traffic loads. Feature selection effectively solves the problem of high-dimensional data analysis by removing irrelevant and redundant data. Hence, this can reduce computation time, improve learning accuracy, and better understand the learning model or data. Sklearn’s SelectKBest chooses the most important features to include in the learning process [42]. It also analyzes the correlation between features as in [7] and [43]. The proposed AML-CTP framework normalizes the traffic load using Min-Max scaling to avoid significant data variance.

Finally, the proposed framework utilizes the Principal Component Analysis (PCA) [44] algorithm to reduce data dimensionality. PCA is a linear dimensionality reduction technique that extracts information from a high-dimensional space by projecting the data into a lower-dimensional subspace. It tries to keep the essential parts with more data variation and remove the non-essential parts with fewer variations. A vital part of using PCA is estimating how many components are needed to describe the data. Therefore, the cumulative explained variance ratio can exhibit the components needed [45]. PCA can help visualize the data in a 2D or 3D space. Thus, data can be plotted to understand the underlying pattern better. Also, it removes noise by condensing many features into a few principal components. So, PCA speeds up ML algorithms, especially with high-dimensional data.

By that, the most critical part of preparing data is finished. The next phase aims to decide which data sample can be used for training the ML models.

section: III. PROPOSED AML-CTP FRAMEWORK — B. PHASE 2: DATA REDUCTION BASED ON
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: The proposed AML-CTP framework groups similar data points using multiple clustering algorithms to reduce dataset size. It combines DBSCAN and Kernel Density Clustering (KDC) via a Co-Association matrix to identify dense regions and outliers. DBSCAN uses an Epsilon (eps) radius and minimum points (minPts ≥ D+1) to separate noise from clusters. KDC employs a bandwidth parameter, where Silverman’s method determines optimal softness to avoid overfitting or underfitting. The framework evaluates cluster quality using Homogeneity and Silhouette scores. Homogeneity, ranging from 0 to 1, measures if clusters contain a single class, with higher scores indicating better reduction. Silhouette scores, ranging from −1 to 1, assess cluster separation, where values near 1 indicate well-defined groups. Samples are extracted based on these metrics, ensuring representative training data with reduced volume.
output:
HOMOGENEITY

Recently, ML-based approaches have been investigated to detect the dataset pattern and organize similar data types. The concept of similarity is closely related in the context of clustering algorithms. Therefore, the proposed AML-CTP framework groups together data points that are similar based on some measure of similarity or distance. It also utilizes a Co-Association technique, like a voting mechanism used to combine the clustering results.

The main idea for using more than one clustering algorithm is that the more often two packets fall into the same cluster when several clustering algorithms are applied, the more similar they are. The considered clustering algorithms use density functions. The algorithms used are Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise and Kernel density clustering. The first algorithm, DBSCAN, is used to identify the outliers (noise) as the points in low-density regions. The AML-CTP framework applies this algorithm and configures the main parameters. The first one is the Epsilon Value (eps); Epsilon is the circle’s radius around a data point, and all other data points that fall inside the circle are considered neighborhood points. In other words, two points are neighbors if their distance is less than or equal to eps. Second, a minimum minPoints can be derived from several dimensions (D) in the dataset, as minPts ≥ D + 1. Larger values are usually better for noisy data sets and will form more significant clusters [7].

The second one, the KDC algorithm, uses a kernel density estimator to identify clusters in a dataset. KDC also requires the specification of a bandwidth parameter, which determines the amount of softness applied to the density estimate. A bandwidth that is too small can result in overfitting and the identification of small, noisy clusters, while a bandwidth that is too large can result in underfitting and merging distinct clusters. One of the ways to determine bandwidth is Silverman bandwidth.

After considering cluster algorithms, the framework handles datasets with irregularly shaped clusters and noise in the data. Considered clustering algorithms: The Co-Association matrix compares the results of two clustering algorithms (DBSCAN and KDC). A N×N matrix (Co) is created to construct the co-association matrix, where the (r,s) position is either one if observations r and s belong to the same cluster and 0 otherwise. The average of all these matrices constitutes the co-association matrix. All elements of matrix Co are initialized to 0; then iterate over all pairs of data points and increment the corresponding element if both algorithms assign data points r and s to the same cluster, Co(r, s) is updated.

After that, a sample selection criterion is applied to extract the training samples from each cluster. The selection criteria are dependent on the Silhouette Score and homogeneity measures. Those techniques are used in clustering analysis to evaluate the quality of extracted samples from clusters. Also, the Rand Index (RI) is measured to check similarity. The RI is calculated by comparing the number of pairs of data points that are either in the same cluster or different clusters. That can be done by selecting a random small sample of data points from each cluster with a high RI. Extracted samples with M number of sample rows of the training dataset (Z = {v1, v2, ..., vN}) with N rows of the dataset for ci clusters are presented as:

Z′ = {v1, v2, . . . , vM}, where M < N (1)

A sample is density maintained as follows:

X δ∈cj pr v ∈Z′ | v ∈cj = δj | cj) (2)

where δj is a constant for any cluster cj, j = {1, ...,k}s

A sample is uniform, as in the following equation:

pr v ∈Z′ | v ∈ci = pr v′ ∈Z | v′ ∈cj if any v ∈ci, v′ ∈cj where, i, j ∈{1, 2, . . .} (3)

Therefore, uniform sampling can be formulated as follows:

pr(v ∈Z′|v ∈Z) = M/N (4)

The proposed framework uses the homogeneity measure to assess the degree to which clusters contain only samples of a single class. That score can be calculated as:

Homogeneity score = 1−H(Z′, C)/H(C) (5)

where Z′ is the true labels of the samples, C is the cluster labels assigned by the clustering algorithm, and The homogeneity measure ranges from 0 to 1, where a higher score indicates better clustering. A score of 1 indicates perfect homogeneity, meaning each cluster contains only samples of a single class. In contrast, 0 indicates the opposite. A large homogeneous population typically requires a smaller sample size for accurate results, while a more heterogeneous population may require a larger sample size [46].

Likewise, the Silhouette score can measure how similar an object is to its cluster compared to others.

Silhouette score = (µ2 −µ1)/max(µ1, µ2) (6)

where µ1 is the mean distance between the sample and all other samples in the same cluster. µ2 is the mean distance between the sample and all other samples in the nearest neighboring cluster. It ranges from −1 to 1, where a higher score indicates better clustering. A score of 1 indicates that the object is well-matched to its cluster and poorly matched to neighboring clusters, while a score of −1 indicates the opposite [46].

After the homogeneity tests, the proposed AML-CTP framework understands the dataset and extracts the most suitable samples that can be used for training. Now, it is ready to apply different ML algorithms, further explained next.

input: The AML-CTP framework predicts network traffic load using regression models. It evaluates Linear Regression with polynomial features, Support Vector Regression, Decision Tree, and LGBM to handle high-dimensional data efficiently. III. PROPOSED AML-CTP FRAMEWORK — C. PHASE 3: TRAINING ML MODELS FOR TRAFFIC PREDICTION

The main goal of the AML-CTP framework is network traffic load prediction. Therefore, the problem is considered a regression situation. The considered regression algorithms can substantially reduce the computational complexity of searching when dealing with big data. However, good accuracy is maintained, and model overfitting is avoided. Hence, the proposed framework utilizes different ML models from which the best model is chosen. These models are selected since they can handle high-dimensional data while retaining fast training time and high efficiency [47], [48]. Consequently, the AML-CTP framework conducts experiments with several machine learning algorithms, including Linear Regression with polynomial features, Support Vector Regression, Decision Tree algorithm, and LGBM. A brief explanation of each ML algorithm is given as follows:

The first assessed algorithm is a linear regression with polynomial features. It finds the relationship between a given dataset and predicted network traffic load. Therefore, it captures nonlinear correlations between variables by fitting a nonlinear regression line. A standard regression model takes the form as follows:

L = θ0 + θ1v1 + θ2v2 + ... + θMvM (7)

where L is the predicted network traffic load value of the dependent variable, θ0 is the intercept, and θ1, θ2, ..., θM are the predicted regression coefficients representing the contribution of the independent predictor variables v1, v2, ..., vd, respectively.

The second algorithm (SVR) guarantees the flexibility to define the acceptable error in our model and find an appropriate line to fit the data. The objective function of SVR is to minimize the coefficients. Instead, the error term is handled in the constraints; the absolute error is assumed to be less than or equal to a specified margin, called the maximum error, ϵ (epsilon). Therefore, epsilon is tuned to gain the desired accuracy. The proposed framework's objective function and constraints for Minimize (Error) are as follows:

Min 1/2 ||θ||²

where |Li − θi vi| ≤ ε

for i = {1, 2, ..., M} (8)

where Li is the target network traffic load value, θi is the coefficient, and vi is the predictor (feature) [49].

The decision tree algorithm is also considered one of the embedded ML algorithms of the proposed framework. That algorithm is reasonably simple to understand and is effective. The primary goal of a decision tree is to split a data population into smaller segments. Then, binary trees are structured, where each node represents a test on a feature, and each leaf node holds an output. DT is induced in a top-down order to construct the tree. Building a decision tree is about locating the attribute that provides the maximum information gain. The information gain is calculated using the decrease in entropy after splitting a data set on an attribute and can be calculated as:

Max(Gain(v, L) ≡ Max(Entropy(v) − Σ (|vs|/|v| Entropy(vs)) (9)

where vs is the sum of every node value, v is the sum of the sample value, and Entropy(vs) is the entropy of the current node.

As formulated in Equation (9), the key hypothesis of the mathematical model of the DT model is entropy, which takes a lot of information to describe a sample adequately. Therefore, the DT algorithm can be considered a regression algorithm with less computational time and good accuracy [50].

The proposed framework also considers the LGBM as one of the embedded MLs in the system. LGBM is a high-performance gradient-boosting machine learning algorithm. It uses histogram-based algorithms to speed up training and reduce memory usage. LGBM is highly efficient and accurate, supports parallel learning, and is suitable for large datasets. Additionally, LGBM contains two techniques that work together: Gradient-based One Side Sampling (GOSS) and Exclusive Feature Bundling (EFB), which overcome the inadequacies of the histogram-based algorithm used in all GBDT (Gradient Boosting Decision Tree) frameworks [50], [51], [52]. Hence, these models are trained using the data samples output from Phase 2. Then, the obtained quality metrics are examined by the AML-CTP framework to choose the best model.

instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.

After training, models are evaluated using R², RMSE, and MAPE. R² measures fit quality, with 1 indicating a perfect fit; its formula is R² = 1 − Σ(vᵢ − Lᵢ)² / Σ(vᵢ − v̄ᵢ)² [50, 53]. RMSE measures average vertical distance from the fitted line; RMSE = √(Σ(vᵢ − Lᵢ)² / M) [50]. MAPE measures prediction accuracy as a percentage; smaller values indicate better accuracy [13].

Execution complexity is analyzed for LR, SVR, DT, and LGBM. LR complexity is O(mp² + p³). SVR complexity is O(m³ + m²p). DT complexity is O(m²p). LGBM complexity is O(mptd), where m is samples, p is features, t is trees, and d is tree depth.

Model selection uses a score combining accuracy and complexity. Score = ωₐ × Accuracy / (ω𝒸 × Complexity) [14]. Weights ωₐ and ω𝒸 adapt based on network load. During light load, accuracy weights are dominant; during peak load, complexity weights are foremost. The model with the highest score is selected for the complete dataset.
output:
III. PROPOSED AML-CTP FRAMEWORK — D. PHASE 4: MODEL SELECTION

After training ML models, the considered ML models are evaluated using the accuracy and execution time metrics. The first metric is R2, a common measure of how well the curve fits the data. A value of one indicates a perfect fit between actual and predicted values, which value has the same propensity. The mathematical formula for computing R2 is [50] and [53]:

R2 = 1 − PMi=1 (vi − Li)2 PMi=1 (vi − Lmean i)2 (10)

where vi is the actual value for data samples, Li is the predicted network traffic load. Lmean i is the mean of the observed data given by:

Lmean i = 1 M XM i=1 vi (11)

Also, RMSE is used to measure how well the model fits predicted variables. Which is the average distance of a data point from the fitted line measured along a vertical line. The RMSE is calculated through the following equation:

RMSE = s PMi=1 (vi − Li)2 M (12)

Finally, The MAPE is calculated as a percentage used to measure how close predictions are to the eventual outcomes. A smaller value of MAPE represents better prediction accuracy. The MAPE is determined by:

MAPE = 100 × M X i=1 vi − Li vi (13)

Another metric evaluated is execution, which is related to data preprocessing. Therefore, the complexity analysis for LR, SVR, DT, and LGBM is demonstrated.

Assume that there are a p number of features. So, the complexity of the LR algorithm is calculated as (O Mp2 + p3).

However, SVR computational time differs from that of LR. Hence, it has a complexity of (O M3 + M2p).

Furthermore, the overhead complexity for the Decision Tree algorithm is based on splitting the dataset. It can be formulated as (O M2p).

The LGBM has time complexity, like the gradient boosting method. It depends on the t number of trees, and the tree may have d as the depth. So, it can be calculated as (O mptd).

We introduce the criteria that adaptively accommodate the minimal computational delay and the maximum accuracy to select the best ML model. That can be a higher accuracy indication if both MAPE and RMSE must be close to 0, while R2 should be close to 1. A smaller time complicity value denotes a lower computational time. Based on insights from our industrial partner, a telecommunication carrier in Egypt, the framework outputs the model score with the following formulation:

ScoreModel = ωAc × AccuracyModel ωComp × ComplicityModel (14)

In Equation (14), the Model symbol presents the embedded ML models {LR, SVR, DT, LGBM}. The ωAc and ωComp are weights that depend on the relative value of the accuracy indicator and complicity value, respectively.

Also, the AML-CTP framework adaptively sets the weights based on the network load and required prediction time. The network load is quantified using the number of active users registered. For instance, in light-load times when the traffic is expected to be low, the AML-CTP framework sets the accuracy weight as dominant. Alternatively, the framework favors computational complexity over model accuracy during beak time and sets the complicity weight as foremost. Finally, the ML model with the highest score should be selected as the best model. Then, the AML-CTP framework is ready to apply the selected ML model to the complete dataset. A full, detailed description of the AML-CTP framework flow chart is illustrated in Figure 3.

instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
The first case study uses an LTE KPI dataset from an Egyptian telecom corporation, previously analyzed in [7]. Traditionally, Key Performance Indicators are divided into radio network and service categories. This analysis focuses on three KPI types—Integrity, Utilization, and Traffic—to observe cell edge user throughput and its correlation with traffic load across frequency bands. Integrity KPIs measure service quality (throughput and latency). Utilization KPIs measure resource distribution (uplink/downlink resource block usage). Traffic KPIs assess traffic volumes (radio bearers, downlink/uplink volume). The final dataset contains 77 features and 259,223 rows [7].

A second dataset was collected over four weeks from 6,000 cells across 200 network sites, containing 80 features and 443,136 rows. The framework is applied to different geographic locations and providers because data from these locations exhibits similar behavior [7]. Data is split into training and testing sets to prevent overfitting. Experiments use a double cross-validation process, where selected models are tested and evaluated using a validation set to assess overfitting to specific training

The first case study dataset is KPI from an LTE mobile network. It is collected from the traffic data from one of Egypt's most popular telecommunication equipment corporations.

Our previous work thoroughly analyzes the used dataset [7].

Traditionally, Key Performance Indicators are divided into radio network KPIs and service. In our analysis, we focus on three types of KPIs to observe the throughput of cell edge users and its correlation with traffic load across different frequency bands. These categories include Integrity KPIs, Utilization KPIs, and Traffic KPIs. Integrity KPIs measure the impact of eNBs on service quality, such as throughput for cells and users, as well as latency for served users. Utilization KPIs measure network utilization and resource distribution based on demands, encompassing uplink resource block utilization and downlink resource block usage rates. Traffic KPIs assess traffic volumes on LTE Radio Access Network, categorized by the type of traffic, including radio bearers, downlink traffic volume, and uplink traffic volume. The final dataset used in the first case study consists of 77 features and 259,223 rows [7].

Moreover, over four weeks, another dataset is collected for the second case study from 6,000 cells in 200 telecommunication network sites. It has 80 features and 443,136 rows.

Furthermore, we investigate applying the proposed framework to different geographic locations and telecommunication providers. That is because data collected from different geographic locations exhibit the same behavior, as discussed in [7]. Therefore, the provided data is considered a suitable representative sample. Moreover, the dataset is split into training and testing sets to prevent overfitting. Then, the experiments apply a double cross-validation process in which the selected models are tested and evaluated using a validation set to assess whether the model is overfitting to a particular set of training examples [7].

The first phase of the framework eliminates 24 non-numerical features used for eNB identification and handover descriptions [11], [45], [55]. Missing values are imputed with row medians. Feature selection uses Sklearn’s SelectKBest [7], [43] to extract a final set of 50 features for traffic load prediction. PCA reduces dataset dimensionality; the first ten components capture ~95% variance, while 50 components fully describe it [11]. A two- or three-dimensional PCA projection representing 87.17% variance is deemed acceptable for visualization [11].

The KDC algorithm, initialized with the Silverman bandwidth formula, performs clustering. In the first case study, DBSCAN identifies one cluster of 250,648 rows (96.7% data) and noise of 8,575 rows [Fig 6(a)]. In the second case study, DBSCAN identifies two clusters (198,565 and 244,423 rows) and noise of 1,148 rows [Fig 6(b)]. KDC identifies four clusters with main clusters of 205,136 and 237,401 rows representing 99.6% data [Fig 7(b)].

Co-assigned labels from DBSCAN and KDC show high agreement. In the first case study, the primary clusters overlap significantly with a Rand Index (RI) of 0.99 [Fig 8(a)]. The AML-CTP framework selects optimal samples for training. LR experiments with polynomial degrees 1–4 to maximize the quality metric [56]; the fourth degree achieves highest accuracy in both cases. Quality metrics (R2, MAPE, RMSE, comp) are evaluated for embedded ML models [Table 4]. In the second case study, LGBM achieves the most favorable accuracy in the first cluster (noise-free). The DT algorithm is the second-best performer there. In the second cluster (containing noise), DT yields the best quality metrics due to its robustness to outliers, while LGBM is sensitive to noise. SVR performs well in both clusters, slightly better in the first due to lower outlier sensitivity.
