FRAMEWORK
As a start, the first phase of the framework is applied to analyze the data. The analysis eliminates 24 features from the data since these columns are not numerical and are used to identify the frequencies and the ID of each eNB. Also, some of these columns describe information regarding user handover [11], [45], [55], which is outside of the scope of the analysis. A deeper investigation and further analyses of the collected dataset can be found in our previous work [7], [43]. Also, regarding missing values, all null values are compensated with the median value of the entire row. After calculating the feature score using Sklearn’s SelectKBest [7], [43], the high-scored features are utilized to choose the final feature set. Therefore, the method that extracts a final set of 50 features will have the highest score. This final set is then used as the network traffic load prediction target. Each feature is further explained in detail in [7] and [43]. Finally, normalization is applied to the selected dataset to avoid significant data variance. As for large-scale multi-dimensional datasets like the collected data, visualization is an essential task. Hence, PCA is applied to diminish the data into a lower dimension. PCA estimates how many components are needed to describe the data.

The curve in Figure 4 quantifies the number of dimension variances that can be contained within the first N components. The first ten components represent approximately 95% of the data variance. Also, to fully describe the variance, a total of 50 components are needed.

Consequently, the analysis considered a two- or three-dimensional projection (with two or three principal components), representing 87.17% of the data variance for two components, a more than acceptable percentage to represent the data [11].

Moreover, the plots in Figure 5 represent the complete datasets with two components using PCA. Figure 5(a), two-dimensional representations are sufficient to show that a hyperplane’s fit to the data points distribution is excellent. Figure 5(b) shows the distribution of classes on a two-dimensional vector space.

FIGURE 6. The output of the KDC algorithm for two case studies.
The considered clustering algorithms are applied to datasets. The detection method calculates the average distance between each point and its k nearest neighbors. Then, the average k-distances are plotted in ascending order on a k-distance graph. The optimal value for epsilon is the point with maximum curvature or bend (i.e., at the most significant slope). The calculated Epsilon value for our dataset in the first case study is 3596.999. Alternatively, the clustering minPoints is considered 15 since it represents a suitable value for the collected dataset.

In the first case study, the DBSCAN clustering algorithm’s output is one cluster of 250,648 data rows shown in Figure 6(a) with dark blue color and represents 96.7% of data and noise of 8,575 data rows with red color. According to data density in the second case, the output of the DBSCAN clustering algorithm is two clusters of 198,565 data rows and 244,423 data rows represented in Figure 6(b) with green and blue color and noise of 1148 data rows with brown color.

The KDC clustering algorithm is applied after applying the Silverman bandwidth formula in the first case study. The output of the KDC clustering algorithm in first case study is 12 clusters with one main of 249,346 data rows that are represented in Figure 7(a) with blue color a and represent 96.3% of data. The rest of the 11 clusters contain the rest of the data with different colors, each centered with an ‘o’ character and a limited number of data rows.

FIGURE 7. Output of DBSCAN clustering for two case studies.
After applying the Silverman bandwidth for the second case study, the Gaussian kernel is also used as a kernel function, and the output of the KDC clustering algorithm is 4 clusters with 205,136 data rows, 237,401, 1006, and 593 data rows. The main two clusters are represented in Figure 7(b), with blue and green colors representing 99.6% of data; the other two clusters contain the rest of the data with brown and yellow colors.

Figure 8 illustrates the density distribution of similarity measure scores for two case studies. The co-associated matrix of these scores is empirically determined using DBSCAN and KDC clustering algorithms for the respective case studies. Agreement and similarity between the labels assigned by the two clustering algorithms. Conversely, the remaining clusters exhibit significantly lower values of RI.

As anticipated, the co-associated matrix for the dataset in the first case study is generated for a single cluster and noise, as output by DBSCAN, and eleven clusters, the output of KDC. Notably, the data in the first cluster of both clustering algorithms predominantly overlap, as depicted in Figure 8 (a). The Rand Index is recorded at 0.99 in this first cluster, indicating a high level of agreement. In Figure 8 (b), nearly the entire dataset in the second case study can be categorized into two primary clusters, and the data within these clusters are identical. The DBSCAN algorithm divides the dataset into two clusters and identifies one noise cluster. Meanwhile, the KDC model reveals four clusters, with respective Rand Index values of 0.982 and 0.991 for the two main clusters. These high RI values indicate strong similarity results between the clusters.

In Table 1, Homogeneity and Silhouette Score measures for clusters with high RI in both case studies are computed, verifying the data similarity in each cluster with high scores near one value. The AML-CTP framework, as presented, selects optimal samples from a dataset for training purposes. These samples should be manageable to ensure efficient processing, enabling statistical measures of a selected subset to approximate a response from the entire dataset in instances where similar clusters exhibit a high RI, such as one cluster in the first case and two clusters in the second case, random samples of 1500 data rows are drawn from each cluster, maintaining the same distribution probability as the entire cluster.

LR with polynomial features, Support Vector Regression, DT algorithm, and LGBM models are trained using the data samples. The optimal parameters are obtained to maximize the performance of LR and LGBM. As for LR, the framework experimented with different degrees (first to fourth degrees) to determine the best quality metric degree [56]. The R2% values are calculated with each model and presented in Table 2. The LR with polynomial features of the fourth degree achieved the highest accuracy in both cases.

Regarding LGBM, the hyperparameter values are determined using Bayesian optimization hyperparameter tuning [57], [58]. Table 3 illustrates the final values of LGBM’s hyperparameters.

Next, the quality metrics are evaluated for the embedded ML models (LGBM, LR with fourth-degree polynomial features, SVR, and DT) to identify the most suitable model. As Table 4 illustrates, the quality metrics include R2, MAPE, RMSE, and time complexity (comp). In the results of the initial case study, it is evident that the LGBM algorithm exhibits higher accuracy, accompanied by an acceptable computational time, aligning with the expectations of our industrial partner. Since LGBM is efficient for large datasets, it achieved the best performance in the first scenario.

Analyzing a selected sample from the two clusters in the second case study reveals that the LGBM algorithm achieves the most favorable accuracy indication among all other algorithms in the first cluster. As the first cluster does not contain noise (as explained in Section IV-B), LGBM sustained its superior performance. The DT algorithm is the second-best performer. Also, as LR fundamentally assumes a linear relationship between features and the log odds of the target variable, the LR model performs the least favorably in both clusters since this assumption does not hold in the second scenario.

Interestingly, the DT algorithm yields the best quality metrics in the second cluster. Since the data in this cluster contains noise, and with LGBM being sensitive to noisy data and outliers, DT is considered the most suitable algorithm. Decision trees are relatively robust to outliers, making them more suitable for this cluster. Finally, SVR is an effective algorithm, especially with nonlinear data. Hence, it performed well in both clusters. It performs slightly better in the first cluster since it is less sensitive to outliers than other regression algorithms. In general, the results exhibit the strengths and weaknesses of each algorithm given the underlying data in each cluster and show that the suitability of each model may vary depending on various factors, such as the data’s linearity and the noise’s existence.

Hence, the discrepancy between actual and predicted traffic volumes is assessed for each ML model during peak hours. As illustrated in Figure 9, LGBM demonstrates superior prediction accuracy compared to other algorithms, with DT ranking as the second-best performer. Negative values indicate instances where the predicted value surpasses the original value, and the variance between the original and predicted values falls within 1 to −0.2 MB. This approach significantly reduces the time required to identify the most accurate prediction module by carefully selecting relevant data samples, resulting in a 53.3%-time reduction in the first case study. The framework highlights the efficacy of LGBM in traffic quality prediction.

Similarly, Figure 10 illustrates the disparities between the actual and predicted traffic within each pair of clusters. The variations range from −0.01 to 0.16 MB in the first cluster and from −0.1 to 0.5 MB in the second cluster. These findings empirically validate the effectiveness of the proposed AML-CTP framework in adapting to changes in network load. In both case studies, the framework demonstrated a time-saving of over 85% when utilizing a sample of 1,500 data rows from similar clusters in the first case study and over 90% time reduction in the second case study. It is anticipated that even more significant time savings can be achieved with a more representative sample size relative to the total number of rows in the utilized samples.

input: The paper addresses the challenge of predicting cellular network traffic loads using multi-dimensional datasets. It proposes the AML-CTP framework, which combines two-density clustering techniques (KDC and DBSCAN) with a co-associated matrix to categorize traffic into clusters. High-quality clusters are identified using RI, silhouette score, and homogeneity metrics. Four low-complexity algorithms are then fitted to these clusters for prediction. Case studies using real LTE-A KPI data show that model performance varies by cluster, with LGBM demonstrating superiority in one scenario. The framework reduces computational time in sample selection and suggests routing predicted traffic to underutilized cells or carriers during peak hours to improve edge-user Quality of Service. [1]

V. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK

The paper discusses the challenge of accurately predicting network traffic loads in cellular networks, especially when dealing with complex, multi-dimensional datasets. Therefore, it is advisable to explore multiple algorithms before selecting the most suitable one. Also, it introduces clustering methods to understand the data structure. So, applying a single algorithm with identical hyperparameter tuning across different datasets is challenging. This paper emphasizes the importance of understanding the data and its characteristics to select appropriate algorithms, with visualization aiding in this process. It presents a proposed AML-CTP framework to minimize runtime overhead by analyzing the data’s nature in traffic prediction. The AML-CTP framework proposed combines two-density clustering techniques (KDC and DBSCAN) with a co-associated matrix to categorize unknown traffic into clusters. High-quality clusters are identified using metrics like RI, silhouette score, and homogeneity. Four high-speed, low-complexity algorithms are then fitted to these clusters for prediction. Two case studies using real KPI data from LTE-A networks demonstrate the framework’s effectiveness, with one showing the superiority of the LGBM model. The framework saves significant computational time in selecting suitable data samples and demonstrates the effectiveness of different models for different clusters. It suggests steering predicted traffic to cells or carriers with low traffic during peak hours to enhance the Quality of Service for users at cell edges.

Machine Learning-Based Continuous Intracranial Pressure Prediction for Traumatic Injury Patients

Structured Abstract— Objective: Abnormal elevation of intracranial pressure (ICP) can cause dangerous or even fatal outcomes. The early detection of high intracranial pressure events can be crucial in saving lives in an intensive care unit (ICU). Despite many applications of machine learning (ML) techniques related to clinical diagnosis, ML applications for continuous ICP detection or short-term predictions have been rarely reported. This study proposes an efficient method of applying an artificial recurrent neural network on the early prediction of ICP evaluation continuously for TBI patients. Methods: After ICP data preprocessing, the learning model is generated for thirteen patients to continuously predict the ICP signal occurrence and classify events for the upcoming 10 minutes by inputting the previous 20-minutes of the ICP signal. Results: As the overall model performance, the average accuracy is 94.62%, the average sensitivity is 74.91%, the average specificity is 94.83%, and the average root mean square error is approximately 2.18 mmHg. Conclusion: This research addresses a significant clinical problem with the management of traumatic brain injury patients. The machine learning model data enables early prediction of ICP continuously in a real-time fashion, which is crucial for appropriate clinical interventions. The results show that our machine learning-based model has high adaptive performance, accuracy, and efficiency.

section: I. INTRODUCTION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Patients with traumatic brain injury require ICU monitoring, where hemorrhage increases intracranial pressure (ICP), potentially causing ischemia and fatal outcomes if untreated [1]–[3]. Continuous ICP monitoring improves survival rates [4]. Previous noninvasive methods, including transcranial Doppler and optic nerve sheath diameter measurements, have been explored [5]–[10], as have machine learning (ML) techniques applied to ICP waveform or image features [13]–[15]. Earlier studies reported classification accuracies of 74% and 91% for children, and an RMSE of 3.7 mmHg [13]–[15], but these rely on limited CT scans or high-quality signals unsuited for real-world noise [13]–[15]. Invasive monitoring carries risks of infection and hemorrhage [10], [16]. Scalzo et al. applied ML to invasive ICP data using decision trees [17]. This study proposes an ML pipeline for real-time ICP estimation that denoises data and predicts future signals. A Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model, a recurrent neural network, is used for prediction [18]. First, a statistical smoothing method processes the ICP data. Then, an LSTM model per patient predicts the ICP signal every 10 minutes post-initialization. The normal adult ICP ranges from 5 to 15 mmHg; mild hypertension is 20 to 30 mmHg [19], [20]. Thus, 20 mmHg serves as the ICP event classification threshold. Model performance is evaluated using accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and root-mean-square error (RMSE).
output:
Patients diagnosed with traumatic brain injury (TBI), a major cause of death and disability worldwide, require immediate treatments in an ICU with restless support from different medical specialists [1]. In prevalent cases of TBI, the occurrence of hemorrhage causes an increased ICP. The elevated ICP, along with impaired cerebrovascular autoregulation, can lead to brain ischemia and subsequent hypoxia [2]. Besides that, the brain tissue is sensitive to compression. During the high ICP, vital brainstem structures have an increased incidence of pressure exposures, shortly resulting in dangerous or even fatal outcomes [2], [3]. Referring to the guidelines for TBI management [4], continuous ICP monitoring is assigned to the patients to detect prolonged elevated ICP events, which is believed to improve the survival rate. Targeted treatments to maintain the ICP below a critical threshold for a sufficiently long term are considered to decrease the likelihood of unfavorable outcomes.

There have been previous efforts on developing noninvasive ICP monitoring methods, including the transcranial Doppler techniques [5], optic nerve sheath diameter measurements [6]–[9], and imaging-based methods (e.g., computed tomography (CT) [9], [10], magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)) [11]. Machine learning (ML) techniques have become a powerful tool to make predictions or perform classifications for medical diagnoses [12]. Three previous studies proposed a noninvasive methodology on early intracranial hypertension detections based on ML techniques using ICP waveform analysis or image features (including midline shift, intracranial cavities, and ventricle size) extracted from medical imaging modalities (e.g., CT or MRI) [13]–[15] with varying degrees of prediction accuracy. The classification accuracy in the first study [13] was about 74% in ICP levels predicted with multiple features sources. The second study [14] reported an accuracy of 91% for predicting increased ICP classification for children. Another study based on noninvasive ICP data with thirteen patients reported a root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 3.7 mmHg with their ICP estimation [15]. All these three studies [13]–[15] used noninvasive methods to achieve ICP estimates. The first two methods [13], [14] predicted the ICP based on CT scans. The CT scan can only be executed on the patients a limited number of times due to the risks of ionizing radiation exposure. Also, the CT scan requires a particular time to be performed, which causes the real-time ICP estimation to be unachievable. The ICP signal is a time series of physiological data. Thus, models to provide binarized classification may still be too simple to achieve ICP tracking and predictions in a real-time and continuous manner. The third study [15] highly relies on the excellent quality signal, which may not apply to real-world medical scenarios. The waveform-targeted method may be sensitive to the noise components of ICP signals that occur during TBI patients’ routine care (e.g., patient movements, bed adjustment, or simple connection problems), which may hinder the accuracy and unavoidably yield unreliable diagnosis predictions [10]. Compared to their methods, our machine learning pipeline provides continuous ICP estimation in real-time. Furthermore, our method is designed to compensate for the noise/artifact frequently evident in clinical data. Overall, our proposed method provided a better performance on ICP predictions, confirmed by the higher accuracy and the lower RMSE.

The accurate way to monitor ICP is using invasive techniques (including fluid-based systems and implantable micro-transducers) along with certain risks of intracranial infection and hemorrhage [10], [16]. ML applications on ICP data collected invasively are not commonly found. ML techniques were applied to the ICP data collected invasively by Scalzo et al. [17]. They suggested using extremely randomized decision trees to predict intracranial hypertension with ICP wave morphology-related features and obtain improved results compared to multiple linear regression models and the adaptive boosting algorithm. Time components intrinsically increase the complexity of a sequenced dependence among the ordered data. Thus, conventional regression models may not perform well with the time series forecasting problems. Our study is a step forward as it proposes an ML application for early detection of the upcoming intracranial hypertension in a real-time manner. In this work, a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model [18], as an artificial recurrent neural network (RNN), is used for predicting ICP events. First, a statistical-based method is applied for smoothing the ICP data and minimizing the negative effect caused by the noisy data. Second, with the processed ICP data, an LSTM model was generated for each patient and predicted the following ICP signal in every next 10-min period after the model initialization. The normal adult ICP is typically within a range of 5 to 15 mmHg; mild intracranial hypertension is described with an ICP readout from 20 to 30 mmHg [19], [20]. Thus, 20 mmHg on ICP readouts is selected conservatively as the criterion for the ICP event classification in this study. Lastly, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and RMSE were calculated to evaluate the models’ performance.

II. METHODS AND PROCEDURES

A. DATABASE

The CHARIS database [21] used in this study was obtained from the PhysioNet [22]. The studies were approved by the Rutgers Research Ethics Committee (IRB) and have been performed in accordance with the ethical standards as laid down in the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki and its later amendments or comparable ethical standards. The study was exempt from informed consent since no patient contact nor identity was involved, and no procedures were performed [21]. The ICP data (unit: mmHg) were monitored with either a subarachnoid bolt or ventriculostomy of thirteen patients diagnosed with traumatic brain injury (TBI). All the data acquisitions were initialized from patients arriving in surgical ICU rooms of Robert Wood Johnson Medical center of Rutgers University (NJ, USA). During the data acquisition, the sampling rate was 0.02 seconds per sample. The resolution of 1.41 mV at ±5 V analog input range was equivalent to a pressure resolution of 0.14 mmHg and a dynamic range of ±500 mmHg. The sampling duration was varied for different subjects. The data involved high-frequency noise and signal distortion. Additionally, patient demographic information was not originally included.

input: Data preprocessing was critical for improving neural network prediction outcomes. First, global thresholding kept ICP data within the range of -5 to 50 mmHg; values outside this range were set to null and forward-filled to maintain continuity. Second, a sliding smoothing window of 60,000 data points (20 minutes) was applied; data points outside +/-3 standard deviations were replaced with the window mean. The window advanced by 3,000 data points (5% step) until the end of the dataset. Finally, the ICP data was downsampled from 50 Hz (0.02 s/sample) to 0.017 Hz (60 s/sample), assigning one compressed data point per 3000 raw data points. Visual inspection was still required to remove meaningless continuous abnormal segments. One patient’s raw and processed ICP data are shown in the results for comparison.

section: II. METHODS AND PROCEDURES — C. MODEL TRAINING
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: The machine learning code was written using Python 3.6 [23]. The LSTM model was implemented using Keras [24], a popular open-source library for artificial neural networks. Processed ICP data was normalized using a scalar of 50 mmHg. For model compilation, the number of units was set to 100, the loss function was mean square error (MSE), and the optimizer was Adam with a learning rate of 0.001 [25]. Training used 15 epochs. The first 30 minutes of ICP data initiated the model. To predict one data point representing the following 1 minute, the model used 20 data points; the predicted value was appended to the previous input to predict the next point until 10 minutes (10 data points) of ICP data were generated. After model activation, every 1 minute of upcoming raw ICP data (3000 data points) was preserved for real-time preprocessing. All processed ICP data was stored historically by expanding the ICP record. With every last 20 minutes of ICP data on the record, the LSTM predicted a result representing the following 10 minutes, occurring 10 minutes after the previous prediction. This 10-minute prediction was classified as a high or low ICP incident compared to the ground-true label (generated from smoothed ICP data within the same time frame). A 10-minute ICP segment was labeled as a high event if more than 60% of data points (6 points) were above 20 mmHg; otherwise, it was labeled as low. Model validation calculated accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity. The model was trained recursively: after each prediction, ground-true data served as the next input to update the model. This process continued until the end of the ICP signal for each patient. Regression analysis evaluated the significance of the difference between actual and predicted ICP data. Pearson correlation assessed the linear relationship, while Spearman rank-order correlation quantified the monotonic relationship. RMSE, accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity further validated model accuracy. Defining a high ICP incident as a positive case, sensitivity was calculated as true-positive counts divided by the sum of true-positive and false-negative counts. Specificity was calculated as true-negative counts

section: III. RESULTS
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
Statistical analysis of raw and processed ICP data (Table 1) demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed preprocessing method. For the 6th patient, raw ICP data ranged from −395.51 to 400.66 mmHg with evident artifacts. Global thresholding removed significant abnormal readouts, and subsequent smoothing removed abnormal peaks and locally recognized outliers. Processed ICP data were downsampled, allowing the overall trend for the 6th patient to be clearly observed. Given that ICP waveform information is prone to distortion and false predictions, features related to the ICP trend were focused on instead. After preprocessing, the range of processed ICP data was 1.60 to 31.34 mmHg with lower standard deviation values. Similar results were observed for other patients (Table 1).

Regression analysis (Table 2) revealed a high degree of similarity between model predictions and actual ICP data, with Pearson R² values ranging from 0.58 to 0.97 and significant p-values. Linear relations varied among patients, but a strong linear correlation (R > 0.7) was found in all patients according to reference [26]. Spearman’s rank correlation showed minimal coefficients of 0.82, indicating strong monotonic relationships. p-values confirmed significant correlations. When actual ICP data increased, predicted data increased at a nonconstant rate. Conversely, when input data to the LSTM model was abnormally low or high, predictions decreased or increased in a nonlinear manner, suggesting LSTM predictions follow overall trends and are less affected by extreme values.

Predicted ICP data (red) accurately followed actual ICP data trends (black) for all patients with small errors, making subtle differences difficult to visually distinguish (Figure 3).

A total of 7127 ICP incidents (2452 high ICP incidents) were detected across all patients, ranging from 138 to 1920 incidents. Due to noise near the end of data collection, affected portions were truncated manually, breaking the linear relationship between incident number and hospital stay duration. High ICP incident percentages ranged from 0% to 69.69% (average 22.06%). The 9th patient had no high ICP events (sensitivity NaN). Excluding the 9th patient, average model performance was: accuracy 94.62%, sensitivity 74.91%, specificity 94.83%. Minimum accuracy was 93.70% (across nine patients) and 96.14% (across seven patients). The 2nd patient had the lowest accuracy at 88.91%. Minimum sensitivity was 87.50% (across six patients), with values below 70% found in five patients. Sensitivity was lower for the 3rd, 7th, 8th, 12th, and 13th patients, who had low high ICP incident percentages (1.72% to 6.88%), causing underfitting. Minimum specificity was 80.41% (2nd patient). Average RMSE was 2.18 mmHg (range: 0.89 to 4.31 mmHg), indicating predictions followed target trends without large errors.
output:
Statistical analysis of the raw ICP data and the processed ICP data are shown in Table 1 to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed data preprocessing method. Among the original ICP data from the 6th patient, the range of the raw ICP data was from −395.51 to 400.66 mmHg, and artifacts were evident (Fig. 2A). After global thresholding, nearly all the significant artifacts with abnormal high/low readouts were removed, as shown in Fig. 2B. By applying the described data smoothing methods, the ICP data were further smoothened, and abnormal peaks were removed, as shown in Fig. 2C. During this step, outliers were recognized and discarded locally. Lastly, the processed ICP data were downsampled (the outcome is shown in Fig. 2D). The overall trend of ICP data for the 6th patient can be clearly observed. Considering the fact that the ICP waveform information was prone to distortion and would yield false diagnosis predictions, it would not be much beneficial to maintain the physiological ICP waveforms during the data preprocessing. Instead, the features related to the ICP trend were focused on in this study. After the data preprocessing, statistical analysis results (Table 1) showed that the range of the processed ICP data was close to a physically reasonable range (from 1.60 to 31.34 mmHg) with lower SD values. For the other patients, similar statistical analysis results are obtained, as shown in Table 1; the effectiveness of the proposed data preprocessing method was observed among all the patients’ data.

Table 2 shows the regression analysis performed for each patient to reveal the high degree of similarity between the model predictions and the actual ICP data. The Pearson correlation coefficients of determination (R²) ranged from 0.58 to 0.97, and the p-values indicated significant correlations between the predictions and the actual ICP data. The linear relations between the predictions and the actual data varied among the patients. According to [26], a strong linear correlation (R > 0.7) was found in all patients. The strength of the relation between the actual data and the predicted ICP was shown during Spearman’s rank correlation. The minimal Spearman’s rank correlation coefficients were 0.82, which was considered a strong correlation (in a monotonic relationship), and the p-values indicated the significant correlations between the predictions and the actual ICP data. With a positive Spearman correlation coefficient, when the actual ICP data increase, the predicted ICP data increase with a nonconstant rate, whereas the rate of increase (or decrease) in a linear relationship is constant. When the input data to the LSTM model is abnormally lower (or higher), the prediction will decrease (or increase) but in a nonlinear manner. Thus, the LSTM predictions should show more stability following the overall trend and less likely to be affected by extreme input values. In this study, the LSTM models were able to follow the data trends during the entire period.

In Figure 3, the predicted ICP data (labeled in red) resulting from the proposed method were plotted against the actual ICP data (labeled in black) for all patients. Our models’ ICP predictions accurately followed the trend of the actual ICP data with small errors. It is difficult to visually distinguish subtle differences between the actual ICP data and the predicted ICP data, even if different colors are used.

In Table 3, a total of 7127 ICP incidents (2452 high ICP incidents) were detected among all the patients, and the number of ICP incidents ranged between 138 and 1920. Since the ICP signals included inconsistent amounts of noise close to the end of the data collection, these portions of noise were truncated manually. Thus, the incident number and the duration of hospital stays were not in a linear relationship after the proposed data processing steps. The percentage of high ICP incidents ranged from 0% to 69.69%, and the average was 22.06%. The 9th patient had an absence of a high ICP event. Thus, the sensitivity was shown with NaN (Not a Number). After excluding the 9th patient, the overall LSTM model performance was as follows: the average accuracy was 94.62%, the average sensitivity was 74.91%, and the average specificity was 94.83%. A minimum of 93.70% accuracy was found among nine patients, and a minimum of 96.14% accuracy was found among seven patients. The lowest accuracy (88.91%) was found for the 2nd patient. A minimal 87.50% sensitivity was found among six patients, and a sensitivity of less than 70% was found among 5 patients. The sensitivity values were lower for the 3rd, 7th, 8th, 12th, and 13th patients who had a low percentage of high ICP incidents (ranging from 1.72% to 6.88%). The relatively small number of high ICP events caused underfitting problems for predicting high ICP incidents. A minimal 92.75% specificity was found among 11 patients. Among all the patients, the minimal specificity was 80.41% and was found in the 2nd patient who had the highest ICP incidence rate. Since high ICP events were found more frequently and the low ICP events were rare with the 2nd patient, this unbalanced event ratio could cause a relatively higher sensitivity value with a lower specificity value. Among all the patients, the average RMSE was 2.18 mmHg and ranged from 0.89 to 4.31 mmHg, indicating that the model predictions followed the target data trend quite well without large errors. Besides the imbalanced data effect, the proposed ML method can achieve high accuracy, high specificity, and good sensitivity for all the patients for the continuous realtime ICP event predictions in the short-term period.

section: IV. DISCUSSION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
A smoothing method selectively suppressed native noise from raw ICP signals. After preprocessing, an LSTM model monitored the next ICP event within 10 minutes per patient. Despite noise and data imbalance, the model identified 'low' events with 95.62% precision and 'high' events with 90.21% precision. Low RMSE and strong correlation between actual and predicted data indicate the model follows trends well. The method efficiently compensates for noise/artifact during preprocessing, making it highly feasible for transfer learning to new patients. An experienced doctor may struggle to predict trends continuously, and visual ICP estimation is prone to subjective errors. The model predicts ICP trends 10 minutes ahead, assisting medical decision-making. Mannitol can lower ICP after intravenous administration, and predictions can integrate into infusion pumps for automated injections, enabling real-time personalized ICP therapy plans. ICP data were collected from clinical settings; sensor disturbances during surgery were not labeled. Despite noise, the method provides accurate continuous estimations with high applicability. This work represents a beneficial step forward for time-series ML modeling of ICP predictions, outperforming limited existing ML predictions.

Compared to prior studies, this model achieved 94.62% accuracy, 74.91% sensitivity, and 94.83% specificity, outperforming studies using CT scans [13, 14]. It also achieved an RMSE of 2.18 mmHg, improving upon a method estimating ICP from blood pressure and cerebral blood flow [15] (RMSE: 3.7 mmHg). Unlike previous models relying on arterial blood pressure (ABP) or linear slope relationships [17, 28], this model predicts future ICP events using only real-time ICP signals. It requires only a 30-minute ICP signal for initialization, providing fast deployment. Short-term (10-minute) prediction is more practical than long-term classification, reducing uncertainty in high-risk event monitoring. Due to individual patient differences, personalized models are needed; this work generates unique models for each patient to better fulfill personalized medicine needs. The LSTM model can provide continuous 10-minute estimations at a real-time pace after a 30-minute initialization. Future research could combine additional patient information, such as continuous blood pressure, for long-term prediction. Pre-trained LSTM models using simulated cerebral hemodynamics data [30] or patient-specific anatomical features from CT scans could improve efficiency and precision.
output:
In this study, an effective smoothing method was developed
which selectively suppressed the native noise from raw ICP
signals. After the ICP data were preprocessed, an LSTM
model was applied to monitor the next ICP event in the
upcoming 10-min period for each patient. Despite the varying
degrees of noise and data imbalance, the LSTM model can
correctly identify ‘low’ events (with 95.62% precision) and
‘high’ events (with 90.21% precision). The low RMSE and
the strong correlation coefﬁcients between the actual and the
predicted ICP data show that the model follows the trend quite
well. The signiﬁcant difference test results also verify that.
In a real-world scenario, varying degrees of noise/artifact will
always exist. These noise/artifact components are efﬁciently
compensated in the data preprocessing steps in our method.
Therefore, our method is highly feasible and practical in
performing transfer learning to new patients.
Although an experienced doctor may be able to predict the
trend when looking at the preprocessed data, this relies on
4901008
some well-trained doctors who may not always be available.
Also, continuous ICP assessment for days and nights during
the long duration of patient stays might be challenging. Additionally, the ICP estimation obtained via visual inspection is
prone to subjective errors, especially with the existence of
noise/artifact. Thus, the ICP assessment performed by continuously monitoring a screen may not be feasible or efﬁcient.
The proposed model in this study predicts the ICP trend in
the following 10 minutes, which can provide extra assistance for decision-making on arranging medical treatments.
Furthermore, continuous ICP evaluation shows that mannitol
can lower the ICP after intravenous administration [27]. The
ICP trends and predictions can be integrated into infusion
pumps for automatically controlled intravenous injections.
The availability of infusion treatments in real-time could be
useful in generating a personalized ICP monitoring/therapy
plan for future intracranial hypertension prediction tasks. The
ICP data applied in our study were collected from actual clinical settings. During signal collections, any artifact or sensor
disturbance caused in surgical procedures are not labeled in
the original data. Despite the noise involved with the ICP data,
our method provides accurate ICP estimations continuously
with high applicability. There are only limited ICP predictions using ML models, and this work would be a beneﬁcial
step forward for future time-series machine modeling of ICP
predictions.
There are some similar studies focusing on machine learning methods for ICP event prediction. In the ﬁrst study
[13], the dataset contains CT scans from 17 patients with
mild to severe TBI. The CT scan features were combined
with demographic information to predict a raised ICP event.
Their model achieved 73.7% accuracy, 76.6% speciﬁcity, and
68.6% sensitivity. In the second study [14], the dataset also
consists of CT scans collected from 475 children. Their model
predicted ICP increases based on CT scans and achieved an
accuracy of 91% for the testing data. Compared to these two
studies, our model performed better and achieved 94.62%
accuracy, 74.91% sensitivity, and 94.83% speciﬁcity. The
dataset in the third study [15] was collected from 13 patients.
The mean ICP value was estimated from measured blood
pressure and cerebral blood ﬂow volume. Nearly 7-hours
of data were analyzed (in comparison, we analyzed 1195
hours of data). Their method yielded ICP estimations with
an RMSE of 3.7 mmHg. Still, our model performed better,
and the RMSE in our work was 2.18 mmHg.
In the past, Scalzo et al. [17] used ML to improve the
temporal accuracy of ﬁnding changes in ICP values for ﬁnding intracranial hypertension events. Their method relies on
monitoring both the arterial blood pressure (ABP) and ICP
and changes in the slope of a linear relationship between the
two signals [21]. However, they cannot predict the spurious
ICP events in advance. Differently, our models uniquely provided a prediction of a future (10-minutes) ICP event with
good accuracy. Another recent outcome prediction model was
developed using statistical and frequency features of ICP,
ABP, and carotid perfusion pressure to predict neurological
outcomes in patients with TBI using Gaussian processes
[28]. They tried to predict an intracranial hypertension event
30 minutes in advance based on 4-hour continuous data from
TBI patients. Instead of focusing singularly on predicting
classiﬁcation, our model predicts ICP estimation and classi-
ﬁes the ICP events with real-time ICP pressure signals accurately alone without knowing other physiological parameters;
this capability distinguishes our work from previous studies.
Extra medical monitoring activity unavoidably increases the
cost of critical care medicine for the patients and introduces
task complexity for the medical staff. Even though ABP
data is available in the CHARIS database, the tremendous
amount of noise made the blood pressure data unbeneﬁcial
to be included in this study. Additionally, our model could
be initialized quickly with a half-hour ICP signal from the
beginning of ICP monitoring, which provides fast installation
and ﬂexibility. Furthermore, the short-term ICP data prediction will be more practical than knowing the ICP event
classiﬁcation in the long term. For the one-hour case, it may
turn out high-risk ICP events could have happened earlier or
later within an hour, but knowing the ICP events in the next
10 mins could largely reduce this uncertainty. Therefore, the
proposed method can help monitor patients’ ICP and efﬁ-
ciently forecast the occurrence of short-term ICP escalations.
Due to the individual differences between the patients, one
conventional model/method may not always perform well for
all the subjects. Personalized healthcare is currently receiving
more and more attention [29]. In this work, the ICP prediction
model is generated uniquely for each patient. The major
beneﬁt of creating a unique model for each new patient is
to better fulﬁll personalized medicine needs. Our machine
learning pipeline can provide continuous ICP estimation for
the following 10 min at a real-time pace. Additionally, the
LSTM model featured with fast installation/deployment only
required the ﬁrst 30 min of ICP data to be initiated. After the
activation, the predictions are generated accurately until the
release of the patients. Since the LSTM model is applicable to
high-dimensional data, for future research, combining additional patient information (e.g., simultaneous and continuous
blood pressure) with the current ICP readout might help
provide long-term ICP prediction (more than 10 min ahead
in time). Additionally, a pre-trained LSTM model capable
of being activated instantly without initialization could be
tested. This approach might ease the transfer learning of the
proposed method. As suggested by [30], cerebral hemodynamics models can generate simulated ICP data to develop
a pre-trained LSTM model. This approach might improve
the efﬁciency of the LSTM model development. Additionally, the patients’ demographic information (e.g., age, gender) and anatomical features (e.g., brain width) extracted
from CT scans would be valuable for designing a patientspeciﬁc cerebral hemodynamics model geared toward precision medicine. There is room for future improvement on
the proposed method; however, this research showed the
feasibility of using the LSTM model to predict ongoing ICP
for patients in a crucial short-term period.

section: V. CONCLUSION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: A recurrent neural network model was developed for real-time 10-minute prediction of intracranial pressure (ICP) changes over 1195 hours. The machine learning method achieved good accuracy in continuous ICP event prediction. The long short-term memory model demonstrated high adaptability across varying patient data. Continuous prediction and early detection of high ICP events may save lives by enabling timely treatment plans.
output:
This study introduces an efﬁcient artiﬁcial recurrent neural network model for the following 10-min prediction
of ICP changes and events in a real-time fashion for
1195 hours. The proposed ML method achieved good accuracy in terms of continuous predictions of the ICP event.
The high adaptive performance of the LSTM model has
been demonstrated among varying patients’ data. Continuous ICP prediction and detection of future incidents of high
ICP might help save the lives of TBI patients. This technology can help perform timely and appropriate treatment
plans.

Machine Learning-Based Detection Method for Wafer Test Induced Defects

Cheng et al. propose a machine learning method to detect test-induced defects in wafer testing. The method analyzes test path patterns and defines features for automatic defect classification. Using test data from six real products, various machine learning algorithms were applied. Experimental results show the method effectively distinguishes test-induced from fabrication-induced defects, achieving an average prediction accuracy of over 97%.

Abstract—Wafer test is carried out after integrated circuits (IC) fabrication to screen out bad dies. In addition, the
results can be used to identify problems in the fabrication process and improve manufacturing yield. However, the wafer test
itself may induce defects to otherwise good dies. Test-induced
defects not only hurt overall manufacturing yield but also create problems for yield learning, so the source problems in testing
should be identiﬁed quickly. In the wafer acceptance test process,
dies are probed in a predetermined order, so test-induced defects,
also known as site-dependent faults, exhibit speciﬁc patterns that
can be effectively captured in test paths. In this paper, we analyze
characteristics of test-induced defect patterns and deﬁne features
that can be used by machine learning algorithms for the automatic detection of test-induced defects. Therefore, defective dies
caused by the wafer test can be retested for yield improvement.
Test data from six real products are used to validate the proposed
method. Several machine learning algorithms have been applied,
and experimental results show that our method is effective to
distinguish between test-induced and fabrication-induced defects.
On average, the prediction accuracy is higher than 97%.
Index Terms—Wafer test, wafer map, test-induced defects, sitedependent fault, test yield, machine learning.

section: I. INTRODUCTION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: The fabrication of VLSI circuits involves many manufacturing steps on a single wafer. The wafer test, performed after the back end of line, ensures only good dies are packaged. Because the number of sites tested simultaneously can exceed 800, dies must be probed through a predetermined test path. Dies failing the test are discarded, preventing defective dies from packaging and providing manufacturing defect information for root-cause analysis. However, the test process itself can induce defects in good dies, reducing yield and complicating root-cause analysis. Wafer maps visualize these defects, and while image processing recognizes manufacturing defect patterns, test-induced defects have not been extensively explored. This paper proposes a machine learning based test-path recognition (TPR) method to automatically diagnose wafer test-induced defects. Experimental results show prediction accuracy exceeding 97% with proper algorithms. The contributions are: proposing a TPR method for automatic diagnosis of test-induced defects; enabling retest to improve test yield; and distinguishing defects from the foundry versus the test house.

The goal of this work is to determine whether the cause of a defective die is from the fabrication process or the test process. An efficient way to achieve this goal is to identify the site-dependent faults, which are the most significant test-induced defects in the wafer test. Examples of site-dependence are illustrated in Fig. 5. In each row, three graphs are given from left to right: a wafer map, the corresponding test path, and a histogram showing the number of fail dies vs. site number. In each wafer map, a red dot indicates a fail die and a green dot stands for a pass die. The first row in Fig. 5 provides an example of site-dependent faults under the test configuration given in Fig. 1. It is obvious that the contours of fail dies match the test path, and the number of fail dies in site 4 is significantly larger than the other sites.

In contrast, the wafer maps in the next two rows do not have site-dependent defect patterns. There are no obvious contours in the second row, while in the third row there is an obvious contour but it does not match the test path. In fact, the contour in the third row is due to a scratch in the fabrication process. Furthermore, defects are uniformly distributed among the four sites in these two cases.

If a set of defects are induced in the wafer test process, the corresponding fail dies satisfy the following two conditions.
• Condition 1: Contours of fail dies are consistent with the test path.
• Condition 2: Fail dies concentrate on specific sites.
Such defects will be referred to as wafer test induced site-dependent faults henceforth.

section: IV. TEST PATH RECOGNITION (TPR) METHODOLOGY
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
We propose a machine learning framework to automatically identify site-dependent faults with high accuracy. The approach consists of two steps.

A. Pre-Processing

The detection of site-dependent faults relies on two conditions; however, these are necessary but not sufficient, as fabrication defects may also produce failing dies satisfying the conditions. Such patterns must be removed to achieve high prediction accuracy.

1) Clusters Removal: Manufacturing problems can create defects concentrated in small areas, resulting in local defect patterns in wafer maps. Applying the DBSCAN algorithm [11] locates these clusters. Removing them reveals the site-dependent distribution; for example, after removal, the number of defects at site 1 becomes much larger than other sites, clearly indicating site-dependent faults [11]. Dies at the outer rim of a wafer are prone to fabrication errors and may be falsely classified as site-dependent if associated with a specific site. Removing these outer rim defects is necessary before fault identification.

2) Outer Rim Removal: Dies at the outer rim of a wafer are prone to fabrication errors and may be falsely classified as site-dependent if associated with a specific site. Removing these defects is necessary before fault identification.

We propose a machine learning based framework to automatically identify site-dependent faults with high accuracy. The proposed approach consists of two steps.

A. Pre-Processing

The detection of site-dependent faults is based on the aforementioned two conditions. However, it should be noted that the two conditions are necessary but not sufficient for site dependence. Other defects induced in the fabrication process may also produce fail dies that satisfy the conditions. Such defect patterns need to be removed first in order to achieve high prediction accuracy.

1) Clusters Removal: Some manufacturing problems create defects concentrated in a small area, and the results are various local defect patterns in wafer maps. Clustering defects will create continuous fail dies along a test path, and such defects may be falsely classified as site-dependent faults in some cases if the fail dies appear heavily in certain sites. On the other hand, local clusters tend to put fail dies evenly among all sites, so they are not likely to be classified as site-dependent faults. An example is shown in the second row of Fig. 5. However, the existence of clustering defects tends to obscure the site-dependent distribution and makes it difficult to correctly identify site-dependent faults. An example is shown in Fig. 6.

Fig. 6(a) gives the original wafer maps, in which the area with clustering defects is marked by red, and the corresponding fail die distribution is given in Fig. 6(b). There is no obvious site-dependence in Fig. 6(b). When we remove the local clusters in Fig. 6(a), the updated wafer map is illustrated in Fig. 6(c), and its fail die distribution is given in Fig. 6(d). In this case, the number of defects corresponding to site 1 is much larger than the other sites, a clear indication of site-dependent faults.

Fig. 7.

Wafer map colored by site

Since clustering defects are usually created in the fabrication process, they should be not be considered for site-dependence. In addition, they interfere with the site-dependent fault identification process and adversely affect the prediction accuracy. Therefore, we need to remove clustering defects in advance. An efficient way to locate clusters is achieved by applying the density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise (DBSCAN) [11] algorithm. DBSCAN is an unsupervised machine learning scheme that can be used to find clustering points in a given map. Once the clustering defects are located, they will be removed from the wafer map, as shown in Fig. 6(c).

2) Outer Rim Removal: Dies at the outer rim of a wafer are prone to err in the fabrication process. These defects will be classified as site-dependent if they happen to be associated with a specific site. Fig. 7 shows a wafer map colored by site; in other words, defect dies test by the same site are assigned the same color given at the bottom-right corner. Blue points at the outer rim are fail dies probed by site 8 but they are not test-induced defects. Therefore, they should be removed as well. In contrast, red points form several contours matching the test path, a clear indication of site-dependence.

section: IV. TEST PATH RECOGNITION (TPR) METHODOLOGY — B. Feature Extraction and Selection for Machine Learning

After pre-processing, wafer maps are classified using machine learning with three features: F1 (normalized fail-die count per site), F2 (TestDNA fail-die count per hardbin per site), and F3 (site continuity measure).

1) F1: Normalized fail-die count per site is calculated as the number of fail dies at a site divided by the total fail dies across all sites, identified by significant site-dependent clustering in histograms.

2) F2: TestDNA fail-die counts per hardbin per site are used, as site-dependent faults cluster in the same hardbin; for example, hardbin 144 defects are predominantly from site 4.

3) F3: The continuity measure $S_n$ for site $n$ is defined as the ratio of the variance $\sigma_n$ of time intervals between consecutive fail dies to the total fail die count $F_n$. Intervals are sorted by test order; 5% right-side outliers are removed prior to calculation to mitigate the impact of non-failure test gaps.

ADBT is sensitive to misclassified data and less susceptible to overfitting. Within NNs, we tested MLP [16], and two DNNs with 10 and 20 layers. Many machine learning (ML) methods can be used for classification. In order to achieve the best prediction, we have evaluated three popular categories of machine learning: linear model, ensemble method, and neural network.

For the linear model, we select logistic regression (LR) [13] and support vector machine (SVM) [14]. For the ensemble model, we use AdaBoost Decision Tree (ADBT) [15]. ADBT is sensitive to misclassified data and it is less susceptible to overfitting.

In the neural network (NN) category, we have tried three variations: multilayer perceptron (MLP) [16], and two deep neural networks (DNN) with 10 and 20 layers, respectively. Experimental results show that all methods can achieve good prediction accuracy. Overall, NN-based methods provide better performance than the other three algorithms (LR, SVM, and ADBT). Details of the NN models and associated parameters are given below.

1) MLP: We employ an MLP consists of three layers of perceptrons and two dropout layers, where each dropout layer sits between two fully connected layers of perceptrons. The number of nodes in the input layer is adjusted according to the numbers of hardbins and sites. The activation function used in the output layer is a sigmoid function, while a rectifier linear unit (ReLU) is used in the other layers. In the training process, a stochastic gradient descent (SGD) optimizer with learning rate = 0.01 is used and the number of epochs is 200.

2) DNN (10 Layers): This DNN consists of eight fully connected layers and two dropout layers. The dropout layers are added after the third and the sixth fully connected layers. As in the MLP, only the output layer uses a sigmoid function while other layers use a ReLU as the activation function. The other conditions are the same as the MLP.

3) DNN (20 Layers): The structure is similar to the 10-layer DNN, except that four dropout layers are used and each dropout layer follows three fully connected layers.

V. CASE STUDY

The proposed method is evaluated in this section. A real product P-0 is employed for analysis. In all, 1139 wafers are used, in which 911 (80%) wafers are used for training and 228 wafers are used for the test. The number of test sites is 8. MLP is used for classification.

The classification results fall into four cases: true positive, true negative, false positive, and false negative. Let the numbers of these cases be denoted as tp, tn, fp, and fn, respectively.

Four metrics are used to evaluate the classification results: accuracy, precision, recall, and F-score. The metrics are defined as follows:

Accuracy = (tp + tn) / (tp + tn + fp + fn)
Precision = tp / (tp + fp)
Recall = tp / (tp + fn)
F-score = 2 * (Precision * Recall) / (Precision + Recall)

A. Pre-Processing

First, we need to evaluate the effectiveness of applying preprocessing. Four conditions are evaluated: no pre-processing, only cluster removal (CR) is applied, only outer-rim removal (ORR) is applied, and both types of pre-processing are applied. The results are summarized in Table I.

The results show that both pre-processing steps are helpful but the combination achieves even better results. The main reason is that clusters and outer rims are noises for ML algorithms. The learning algorithm will create a more accurate model with cleaner training data.

B. Features

Next, we will study how the proposed features affect the classification results. In this experiment, a subset of {F1, F2, F3} is used for classification, and the results are given in Table II.

The results suggest that using either F1 or F2 achieves roughly the same level of performance. However, applying both F1 and F2 gives much worse results. The reason is that these two features have common components that cause interference. F3 alone does not give good results, but the feature is relatively independent of F1 or F2. As a result, we can get improved performance when coupling F3 with either F1 or F2. Finally, using all three features achieves the best results among all possible combinations.

section: VI. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
The proposed method uses 28,600 NXP wafers from six products with site counts of 4 to 32. Training uses 80% of wafers; the remaining 20% serve as test data. Table III summarizes the experiment setup, including wafer counts and feature numbers, where NN input nodes match the feature count.

Table IV summarizes linear and ensemble model results, while Table V covers NN models. All results use 5-fold cross-validation. Linear models (SVM, LR) perform comparably but are inferior to the ensemble method ADBT. NN models provide the best results, with average prediction accuracy and F-score exceeding 97% across all models.

Performance generally improves with increased NN layers, though the gain is limited. The 20-layer DNN achieves the best results except for product P-3, where MLP performs better due to its smaller input node count, which prevents overfitting.

Precision decreases while recall increases as NN layers grow, indicating more false positives and fewer false negatives. Since the goal is to identify test-induced defects for retest, recall takes precedence, making more complex DNNs preferable.

Prediction accuracy improves with more training data, as demonstrated using product P-6 with wafer counts ranging from 1,000 to 9,000. With 80% used for training and 5-fold cross-validation, results show that models can be improved throughout a product's life cycle as more data becomes available

VI. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND ANALYSIS

The proposed method is validated using 28,600 wafers from NXP. The wafers come from six products and the number of sites ranges from 4 to 32. The experiment setup is summarized in Table III. The number of wafers, the number of wafers used for training, and the number of test wafers are given in columns two to four. In each case, 80% of the wafers are used for training while the other 20% are used for the test. The number of test sites used for each product is given in column 5. The last column gives the number of features used in the ML model. For all the NN models, the number is equivalent to the number of nodes in the input layer.

The prediction results of the linear and ensemble models are summarized in Table IV, and the results of the NN models are given in Table V. All the results are obtained using 5-fold cross-validation.

The performance of the linear models (SVM and LR) are comparable, and both of them are inferior to the ensemble method ADBT. Overall, the NN method provides the best results. In all three NN models, the average prediction accuracy is better than 97%, so is the performance measured by F-score.

In general, the performance improves as the number of NN layers increases, although the difference is limited. The 20-layer DNN achieves the best performance in all cases except P-3, for which MLP provides the best results. The reason is attributed to the fact that the number of input nodes for P-3 is much smaller than the other products, so a smaller prediction model can achieve better results without overfitting.

Another interesting result is that precision deteriorates as the number of NN layers increases while recall improves. This implies that a more complicated NN model tends to produce more false positives and fewer false negatives. Since our goal is to identify as many test-induced defects as possible to enable retest, recall should take precedence over precision. In this case, a more complicated DNN is preferable.

The accuracy of a prediction model is affected by the amount of training data, as shown in Fig. 11. We use P-6 in this experiment, and the number of wafers ranges from 1000 to 9000. In each case, 80% of the wafers are used for training. The results are obtained with 5-fold cross-validation as well. This implies that one can keep on improving the prediction model during the life cycle of a product with more training data available.

ABSTRACT Predictive maintenance (PdM) has become a critical strategy for improving the efficiency and reliability of industrial machinery. Integrating machine learning methods into a PdM system provides a promising solution for optimizing maintenance strategies, preventing equipment failures on the production line, and reducing downtime. This research presents a data-driven approach for detecting faults in industrial machines using sensor data. The method aims to optimize system performance, resulting in economic savings including energy consumption, and maintenance costs. The approach outlined in this research includes the establishment of a PdM system designed for yarn production machines empowered by machine learning methods. The effectiveness of PdM applications depends on careful selection of machine learning methods. This study examines four machine learning algorithms and a deep learning algorithm for predictive modeling. The algorithms were trained on historical data to identify underlying patterns and correlations between operational parameters and failure events. The trained models were deployed in the PdM system to continuously monitor the health condition of industrial machines on ThingSpeakTM IoT interface platform in real-time. This research also presents a systematic process for developing a predictive maintenance framework. The process includes data acquisition from industrial machinery, preprocessing, feature selection, model training, and deployment. The effectiveness of the proposed system is validated through extensive experimentation and case studies conducted in an industrial setting. Evaluation metrics revealed that the deep learning algorithm outperformed the other approaches, achieving an accuracy score of 0.96 and a prediction validation score of 0.86. The results show significant improvements in predictive accuracy and enhanced operational efficiency compared to reactive maintenance approaches.

An unforeseen failure can result in a catastrophic accident or a failure in the system may cause a downtime resulting in financial losses [1]. Early diagnosis and prediction of fault can prevent the critical system failures and downtime. Efficient maintenance approaches, particularly PdM of machinery, manufacturing systems, production processes have emerging importance in predicting overall life cycle of machinery and machining tools [2], [3].

We can categorize maintenance systems as proactive maintenance, preventive maintenance (PvM), predictive maintenance (PdM), and Run-To-Failure (R2F) maintenance. R2F maintenance is the repair process when the machine breaks down. Preventive maintenance, on the other hand, is a scheduled maintenance where maintenance tasks are planned at a certain time of period recommended by the machine manufacturer and varies from limited maintenance schedules consisting of lubrication and minor tunings to a comprehensive plan involving repairs, major adjustments, and machine rebuilds for the critical plant machinery [4]. Reactive maintenance and preventive maintenance are extensively used by many companies today, but globally competitive companies use the PdM and proactive maintenance systems, aligning with the significance and sensitivity of their operations.

Proactive maintenance represents a maintenance approach that detects faults at the initial stages of the failure cycle, often characterized by their elusive nature. The effectiveness of proactive maintenance is ensured by the continuation of production with a standby machine [5]. The system must be continuously monitored in real time by intervening into the system with the slightest observed deviation. Predictive maintenance uses smart methods and tools to determine the possible failures in systems and to estimate their remaining useful life (RUL) [6]. The smart tools for the PdM systems are energy analyzers for energy management; ultrasound devices for leak detection in pneumatic systems and heat exchangers, detection of valve leaks, bearing and lubrication error detection in rotating equipment, cavitation, and wear detection in pumps; thermal cameras, oil analyzers, emission measurement and combustion efficiency measurement devices and vibration analyzers periodically check whether there is a fault in a system. PdM enables the manufacturer to plan proactive maintenance, maximize equipment operation and reduce downtime and costs. Effective PdM does not only involve smart computing techniques, but also means organizational culture changes including technology and information enhancements to a digital environment [7].

We aimed to determine where the specific production machines in the facility started to deteriorate and maintain the system in a planned stop within the scope of PdM activity in the third phase before the machines become completely inoperable. The problems identified in induction motors can be attributed to several factors: shaft/coupling problems account for 3%, rotor bar problems contribute to 7%, stator winding faults make up 21%, and the majority of faults, 69%, are associated with bearings [8].

The most common of industrial applications where computer aided PdM systems used is in predicting the bearing damage. The main tools are vibration and ultrasound listening analysis. In this context, three main factors contribute to determining the damage level in bearings that encompass are vibrations, surface or system temperatures, and the energy consumed by the system.

II. STATE OF THE ART — A. PREDICTIVE MAINTENANCE SYSTEMS

Predictive maintenance (PdM) systems represent a paradigm shift from reactive and preventive maintenance strategies, leveraging real-time data and advanced analytics to forecast equipment failures before they occur. Unlike preventive maintenance, which relies on fixed schedules, PdM utilizes condition-based monitoring to perform maintenance activities only when necessary, thereby reducing unnecessary downtime and operational costs. The core objective is to transition from time-based to condition-based maintenance, optimizing the maintenance window and extending the lifespan of critical components. This approach is particularly vital in high-speed industrial environments, such as artificial yarn machines, where unexpected breakdowns can lead to significant production losses and safety hazards. Recent advancements in sensor technology, wireless communication, and machine learning algorithms have enabled the deployment of sophisticated PdM solutions across various manufacturing sectors.

section: methods — B. IoT AND ML IN PdM APPLICATIONS
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
IoT networks connect smart devices to collect sensor data for predictive maintenance (PdM) [16]. Data flows from edge devices through gateways to the cloud for analysis [17]. IoT integration with AI and ML streamlines data acquisition and processing [17].

IoT enables data acquisition from machines to support PdM, improve shop floor management, and reduce downtime by predicting equipment failures [18, 19]. MQTT protocols with PLCs facilitate efficient data collection for ML-based PdM systems [20].

Li et al. conducted an Industry 4.0 experimental study using an intelligent PdM system to detect internal machine faults and accurately identify failure locations [1].

Sahasrabudhe et al. analyzed ML algorithms for PdM to detect abnormal conditions, locate faults, and predict remaining useful life (RUL) using RF regressors and MATLAB Diagnostic Feature Designer [21].

Es-sakali et al. reviewed PdM methods from knowledge-based to data-driven approaches, noting RUL prediction is challenging due to nonlinear characteristics and data scarcity. They found algorithm choice depends on developer expertise, with SVM and ANN being predominantly utilized [9].

Butte et al. framed PdM as both a classification problem (probability of failure) and a regression problem (time to failure). They concluded that supervised learning methods, including generalized linear models, tree-based ensembles (RF), and deep learning (DL) methods, best fit PdM problems [22].
output:
The concept of the IoT relates to the robust networking of smart devices over the wide area network [16]. In smart manufacturing systems, PdM utilizes Internet of Things (IoT) and Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) to collect data from the sensors, then the collected data is stored and evaluated according to historical data. An IoT system is composed of internet connected smart devices that use embedded controllers, communication hardware and sensors to collect and transfer data via an IoT gateway or an edge device. Data transferred to the cloud can be analyzed by built-in analysis programs on the IoT platforms and can be accessed and visualized online. Integration of AI and ML methods has empowered the collected data to be effectively processed, streamlining the data acquisition procedures.

Through data acquisition from machines and manufacturing systems, IoT platforms will support PdM [18], improve shop floor management, and decrease downtime by predicting occurrence of critical equipment failures [19]. Data was collected with IoT on industrial machines using Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) with PLC for the efficient operation of the PdM system based on ML, and this data was used in the development of a SCADA-based machine learning system in [20].

Li et al. performed an experimental study based on Industry 4.0 with the use of an intelligent PdM system in detection of faults occurring inside a machine and they collected necessary data [1]. By employing the devised experimental configuration, faults were introduced into the system and the precise location of these failures were accurately identified.

In the study on the experimental analysis of ML algorithms in PdM, Sahasrabudhe et al. aimed to detect abnormal conditions in the operation of the equipment, to determine the location of the fault in the system and to find the RUL of the machine based on the developed ML-based PdM models. For this purpose, they used RF regressor as an ML algorithm and MATLAB® Diagnostic Feature Designer application fault diagnosis and prognostics and presented the results [21].

In their systematic literature review, Es-sakali et al. studied on PdM using approaches from knowledge-based to data-driven based methods [9]. They stated that the task of RUL is challenging due to the complicated, uncertain, nonlinear characteristics, and operational circumstances as well as lack of data required for the ML approaches in data-driven models. Their findings indicated that the choice of algorithms hinges on the expertise of the developer. Though, it was observed that SVM and Artificial Neural Network (ANN) emerge as the predominantly utilized ML algorithms within the literature. These two algorithms have demonstrated considerable effectiveness in various PdM applications. Butte et al. [22] expressed the PdM problem in two ways as a classification problem to determine the probability of part failures before the expected number of products has been processed, and as a regression problem to predict the remaining time before subsequent failure is likely to arise. They concluded that the supervised learning methods as the generalized linear models and tree-based ensemble methods such as RF and gradient-boosted machine, and DL methods best fit to PdM problems.

APPLICATION
The integration of computer aided PdM systems into businesses has led to the modular availability of essential components for these systems, marketed as IoT technology components. These modular parts are now accessible for businesses, rendering the need for elaborate system installations, such as server systems and database servers for data storage. Cloud technology has enabled the establishment of plug-and-play as well as track-and-trace systems, significantly reducing both the financial investment and annual operating costs. Siemens, Eton, and Schneider are now offering energy monitoring and PdM modules for cloud applications, further reducing costs.

In this technological landscape, thousands of microcontroller units (MCUs) and sensors will communicate in the IoT network and considering the diversity and size of the data collected from these devices. Program software and big data storage, and visualization has now been reduced to a few commands by the cutting-edge computer technology. Artificial intelligence, machine learning, data mining and intelligent computing methods will become increasingly pivotal for data optimization, assessment of failure statuses, and prediction of failure probabilities. Machine learning will play a significant role in modeling of future systems and developing advanced systems through real data from the field.

Data optimization in ML involves improving the quality and efficiency of training data. Its main goal is to enhance the overall performance of ML algorithms by addressing issues such as data anomalies and outliers. Our data optimization steps include:
• The initial step involves selecting the date of all machine maintenance from the main database as the starting point. Subsequently, the next 200 data points are chosen as training data.

The IoT-based sensor system acquires data from eight points across five distinct sensors within an extruder group of an artificial yarn production machine (Fig. 2).

A decisive component is the MPU6050, a three-axis accelerometer SoC sensor capable of collecting samples at up to 1 kHz via the I2C protocol. It utilizes three 16-bit ADCs and features a configurable accelerometer range of ±2G to ±16G [23]. An on-chip 1024 Byte FIFO buffer reduces system energy consumption by allowing the processor to read burst data while remaining in low-power mode. However, inherent noise within the raw accelerometer data requires optimization for meaningful analysis.

The MLX90640 infrared (IR) 32 × 24-pixel temperature sensor measures object temperatures ranging from −40°C to 300°C in industrial environments with ±1°C accuracy [24]. I2C interface ports and thirty-four programmable I/O pins which are employed to connect the sensors to the cloud with the embedded programs. The ESP32-S3 is the Xtensa LX7 dual-core model which has a speed up to 240 MHz, 384 kB of RAM and 512 kB of programming memory. It can be programmed with Python and C++ programming languages.
