This approach ensured that all function blocks operated concurrently in real time. The coordination of transitions between these function blocks and the allocation of each function to the appropriate core of the microcontroller were facilitated by leveraging the capabilities of the FreeRTOS library. FreeRTOS commands streamlined the organization of the multitasking PdM program, contributing to optimized system performance.

Deep learning (DL) encompasses methods that learn multiple representation levels in deep architectures [22]. Unsupervised and semi-supervised feature extraction, along with hierarchical extraction, are superior aspects of DL algorithms [44]. Common neural network classes used in DL include feedforward NN, DBM, RNN, radial basis function NN, DBN, Kohonen self-organizing NN, and CNN [44]. DL models learn faster from large data volumes using dropout and convolutions, though they demand more data than other algorithms [45].

DNN is a multilayer perceptron class with more than three hidden layers, trained to learn from datasets without manual feature extraction [44]. Increased processing layers outperform shallower models. The core learning algorithm calculates derivatives layer-by-layer; vanishing gradients cause exponential decreases, potentially leading to longer training times or divergence if the cost function is not minimized [44]. Training time must be balanced against data volume, as excessive samples add time without value. Adding neurons to model complex problems risks overfitting outliers, delaying training and reducing prediction quality. The optimal hidden neuron count must be chosen empirically to fit the problem size and type [44].

We applied DL to collected PdM sensor data using Python. Pandas was employed for data cleaning, analysis, and manipulation [44]. NumPy provided numerical computing functions and array routines [44]. We used Keras, a high-level DL API running on TensorFlow, for its simple workflow and industrial performance [45]. The core Keras structures are layers and models; we used the Sequential model for linear layer stacking and Dense for fully connected layers. Dropout was applied to accelerate learning. Activation functions were chosen to optimize model performance.

Each layer can be customized to detect a defined feature from simple aspects to complex ones [44]. A failure state was synthesized by multiplying a subset of data by a coefficient; healthy data was labeled "0" and failure data labeled "1". A test set comprising 15% of the total data was reserved for validation. Experiments ran on an i7-7700HQ system (16GB RAM, 2.8GHz, GTX1050Ti GPU). VI. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS

Before applying ML and DL methods, a preliminary process was conducted. This involved retrieving a raw dataset with approximately 1400 data points. This dataset involved measurements from vibration along three axes, winding temperature, and energy consumption of the motor. The data was obtained from the healthy operational state of the extruder group within the BCF machine. The dataset was retrieved from the ThingSpeakTM platform and then transferred to MATLAB® for further analysis. Subsequently, the data was saved as a csv file in Excel format as a reference data, including timestamps. Then part of the data in this dataset was multiplied with a coefficient to generate data reflecting the conditions for failure state. The failure state was marked with a value of "1" and data from healthy operation was marked as "0" to signify the absence of failure. This generated data augmented with the original data (of about size 2800) was called from Python and reordered. Timestamps were excluded and the sequential data was randomly fragmented into a training set for developing the ML models. To ensure a more uniform distribution of "faulty" and "healthy" working status throughout the system and facilitate effective training of the dataset, we chose to randomize the distribution of the data.

A test set of 15% of the overall dataset was kept for validating the prediction performance of the models. The algorithms applied to our dataset ran on a seventh-generation computer, i7-7700HQ 64 bit, 4-core processor with 16 GB RAM, 2.8 GHz frequency, 6 MB cache memory, 8 GB GeForce GTX1050Ti GPU.

The dataset is trained, tested, and validated for 100 epochs for DL algorithm, and the results are given in Table 1 in comparison with the other ML models, namely, RF algorithm, SVM, SVR (Gaussian nonlinear), and DT. The model with five inputs in the dataset was evaluated with 16929 trainable parameters in DL, and the output is the failure probability from 0 to 1. Accuracy of DL algorithm is shown graphically in Fig. 11.

Data collection was performed using sensors connected to an IoT system. Collected data was stored in the cloud and analyzed retrospectively or instantly to predict system faults using ML-based methods.

Updating data on ThingSpeak™ every 20 seconds publishes active temperatures on the stator windings and cooling fin, X/Y/Z axis vibrations, and energy consumption histogram distributions online. This allows monitoring from any internet-connected device. MATLAB® commands created over ThingSpeak automatically send email alerts if the system exceeds determined working limits, enabling quick intervention by predicting malfunctions.

Six ML methods were evaluated for the PdM system of the BCF machine using Python 3.9.16. Deep Learning (DL) was superior to other methods in accuracy and validation. However, 239 seconds of training time for 100 epochs delays failure state prediction. For 10 epochs, training time reduces to 15 seconds, but accuracy drops to 0.757 and validation to 0.8185. Decision Tree (DT) was the second-best algorithm with an accuracy of 0.93 and validation of 0.9. Training times for other algorithms were under one second and not displayed in the interface's variable explorer. Support Vector Machine (SVM) had the highest validation accuracy for failure prediction.

Python was favored because selecting the right method, classifier/regressor, and suitable hyperparameters/optimizers yields the best results in the least training time with high accuracy.

MATLAB® Regression Learner app was first preferred to predict faults using Tree, Gaussian Process, Ensemble Tree, and SVM regression methods with optimized hyperparameters, as ThingSpeak™ allows writing and executing MATLAB® codes for data preprocessing and analysis. Built-in MATLAB® was used for data transfer, analysis, and visualization. Data was imported to MATLAB® on a computer, and the ML application was run to find the best-fit model. MATLAB® is preferable for those not skilled in writing codes.

Analyzing R2, MAE, and RMSE metrics from Table 2, SVM regression with a polynomial kernel of order 3 was deemed most appropriate. It provides the highest coefficient of determination (R2), indicating a good data fit to the regression model, and moderate prediction speed. SVMs are preferred for reduced overfitting susceptibility, faster training, and lower computational demand. Consequently, this algorithm is preferred as a resource-efficient model for constrained environments. Although DL achieved higher accuracy, SVM regression was deemed most suitable based on a balance between accuracy, interpretability, resource requirements, and robustness.

The second-best fit model was Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) with the ARD-Matern52 kernel and exact fit/predict method, which has shorter training time than SVM but is slightly less accurate. The Random Forest (RF) Ensemble Tree model combined with the least-squares boosting (LSBoost) algorithm and Bayesian hyperparameter tuning in MATLAB had the lowest prediction speed of ~3600 obs/s and the longest training time. Validation accuracy was 0.83, slightly lower than SVM.

The RMSE of the DNN learning algorithm (core of DL) is 0.074719, superior to the RMSE value of 0.097 in [17]. DT accuracy is slightly higher than that in [16], and the proposed model's RMSE is superior to [14]. Random Forest has lower accuracy compared to [17].

VII. DISCUSSION — T. Akyaz, D. Engin: Machine Learning-Based Predictive Maintenance System for Artificial Yarn Machines

Data collection can be performed. In this study, sensors connected to the designed and implemented IoT system were used to determine the working regimes of the machines. The collected data was stored in the cloud and analyzed retrospectively or instantly and was used to predict faults in the system using ML-based methods.

By updating the data on the ThingSpeak™ website every 20 seconds, the active temperatures on the stator windings and the stator cooling fin of the motor measured by IR temperature sensor and Pt-100 temperature sensor, vibrations in the X, Y and Z axes and the histogram distributions of the energy consumption at a certain time are publicized graphically online, and it is possible to monitor them from any internet-connected device. With the help of MATLAB® commands created over ThingSpeak, it automatically sends e-mail in case the system goes out of the determined working limits. In this way, it is foreseen that the changes in the system are noticed, and the necessary interventions are made quickly by predicting the malfunction situation.

In this paper, we evaluated six different ML methods for the PdM system of the BCF machine. Five ML methods including DL were applied to the dataset using Python programming language 3.9.16 Release. The evaluation metrics in Table 1, have revealed that DL algorithm is superior to the other four approaches in terms of accuracy and validation. However, 239 s training time for 100 epochs delays the prediction of failure state for the BCF machine in the PdM system. For 10 epochs, the training time reduces to 15 s, but the accuracy is also reduced to 0.757 and validation to 0.8185. The second-best algorithm is DT with an accuracy of 0.93 and a prediction validation of 0.9. The training time of the algorithms other than DL are not presented in Table 1 because the training lasted less than a second which was not displayed on the programming interface’s “variable explorer” pane. Validation of the prediction of failure in the PdM system is highest in SVM.

Python programming language is favored in this study because when you write the codes for the ML methods and select the right method, classifier/regressor and choose the suitable hyperparameters and optimizers, the model training gives the best results in the least training time with high accuracy.

We first preferred MATLAB® Regression Learner app to predict faults in the PdM system using Tree, Gaussian Process, Ensemble Tree and SVM regression methods with optimized hyperparameters using optimizable algorithms because ThingSpeak™ IoT platform allows to write MATLAB® codes and execute them for preprocessing of our raw data and analyzing the collected data with the integrated MATLAB® analytics. We easily used built-in MATLAB® for data transfer, analysis, visualization purposes. Furthermore, we imported the collected data to MATLAB® on our computer and run MATLAB® ML application and tried to find the best-fit model. If one is not skilled in writing codes, MATLAB® Regression Learner app is preferrable to train the collected data.

Analyzing the results of R2, MAE and RMSE performance evaluation metrics given in Table 2, we have decided that the most appropriate method is SVM regression method with polynomial kernel function of order 3, because it produces significant accuracy with its highest coefficient of determination (R2) which means that the data fit well to the regression model, and moderate prediction speed comparatively. SVMs are preferred for their reduced susceptibility to overfitting, faster training capabilities, and lower demand for computational resources. Consequently, this algorithm is preferred as a resource-efficient model in environments constrained by limited resources. Given these factors, even though the DL algorithm achieved a higher accuracy, the SVM regression have been deemed the most suitable model for the specific application based on a balance between accuracy, interpretability, resource requirements, and robustness.

The second-best fit model is the GPR with the ARD-Matern52 kernel function and the exact fit and predict method because it has a shorter training time compared to the SVM but is slightly less accurate. RF of Ensemble Tree ML model combined with least-squares boosting (LSBoost) algorithm and Bayesian hyperparameter tuning method applied in MATLAB gives the lowest prediction speed of ∼3600 obs/s, but it takes the longest training time. We expected optimal prediction performance with these settings and preferences, but the validation accuracy of 0.83 is slightly lower than SVM.

The obtained results can best be compared with the related work in [17] in literature where the number of layers and neurons and the selected activation functions and optimizers are the same with our DL model. The RMSE obtained in our DNN learning algorithm which is the core of DL is 0.074719 where it is superior compared to the RMSE value of 0.097 in [17]. The DT accuracy is slightly higher than the accuracy presented in [16], and the RMSE of our proposed model is superior compared to [14]. Random forest has lower accuracy compared to [17].

Additionally, when compared to a commercial IoT system with comparable sensors and microcontrollers, the cost of the implemented system is $53, which is one third of a commercial IoT system. Machine stops will lead to higher financial loss when R2F maintenance is performed in a shop floor. If R2F maintenance was chosen in our system at the shop floor, when an unplanned shutdown occurs possible repair process for the machine breakdown can be the bearing replacement of the attached fan which will lead to a total shutdown of 4 hours. Due to this fan failure, financial losses would have occurred from the following items:

1. The salary of 8 workers working in the machine will be paid in vain. When we assume each person is working with a minimum wage person then an average labor cost of 8 people in a 4-hour stop will be $173.

2. If the blades of the fan are damaged, the price of a new fan is around $2500.

Section: VIII. CONCLUSION

This research highlights the significance of using real-world sensor data from operational predictive maintenance systems, rather than relying on synthetic or simulated datasets, which is a common practice in many existing papers. This comprehensive approach in development of a PdM system for artificial yarn production machines uses the equipment data via a cost-effective IoT module without the need to invest in commercial IoT devices. The collected field data from this module is a valuable resource for AI and ML applications in predictive maintenance. Furthermore, our IoT-based system is adaptable to various machinery and can accommodate additional sensors as required. The importance of IoT technology suggests a promising future for research and development in this field, particularly when combined with AI methods such as deep learning, machine learning, and heuristic approaches.

Title: Magnetocardiography-Based Ischemic Heart Disease Detection and Localization Using Machine Learning Methods

Authors: Rong Tao, Shulin Zhang, Xiao Huang, Minfang Tao, Jian Ma, Shixin Ma, Chaoxiang Zhang, Tongxin Zhang, Fakuan Tang, Jianping Lu, Chenxing Shen, Xiaoming Xie

Objective: Develop a fast and accurate automatic ischemic heart disease detection and localization methodology.

Methods: T wave was segmented from averaged Magnetocardiography (MCG) recordings and 164 features were extracted. Features were categorized into time domain, frequency domain, and information theory groups. Machine learning classifiers compared included k-nearest neighbor, decision tree, support vector machine (SVM), and XGBoost. Three best-performing classifiers were ensemble-averaged using all 164 features for detection. For localization, XGBoost was used with 18 time domain features to classify ischemia by stenosis location (LAD, LCX, RCA).

Results: For ischemic heart disease (IHD) detection, the SVM-XGBoost model achieved accuracy = 94.03%, precision = 86.56%, recall = 97.78%, F-score = 92.79%, AUC = 0.98, and average precision = 0.98. For ischemia localization, XGBoost accuracy was 0.74 for LAD, 0.68 for LCX, and 0.65 for RCA.

Conclusion: An automatic IHD detection and localization system was developed. T wave repolarization synchronicity is an important factor to distinguish IHD from normal subjects. Magnetic field patterns are associated with stenosis

section: I. INTRODUCTION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
IHD causes about one third of deaths in people beyond age 35 in western countries [4] and is the leading cause of death in China during the same period [6]. It occurs when blood flow to the heart is limited due to coronary artery stenosis, causing myocardial damage that can lead to infarction, arrhythmia, or sudden cardiac death [7]. Early diagnosis and intervention are critical for reducing mortality [8].

Electrocardiography (ECG) is a routine clinical procedure for early IHD diagnosis, but its lower sensitivity and specificity [10] force most suspected patients to undergo cardiac CT or coronary angiography (CAG), which carry risks of excessive radiation and allergic reactions [12].

Magnetocardiography (MCG) is a promising non-invasive tool for early IHD detection [14]. Compared to ECG, MCG is less influenced by electrode-skin contact interference and more sensitive to tangential and vortex currents from ischemic tissue. However, MCG interpretation is labor-intensive and relies heavily on interpreter experience, limiting clinical acceptance. An automatic system for early ischemia detection and localization would be extremely beneficial to clinicians.

Recent machine learning advances show advantages for automatic cardiac disease detection. Table I summarizes previous MCG and ECG studies. Embrechts et al. [1] and Fenici et al. [2] proposed direct kernel-based methods to separate abnormal heartbeats, achieving the best results with direct kernel partial least squares (DK-LPS): sensitivity 92%, specificity 75%, accuracy 83%. Kangwanariyakul et al. [3] compared machine learning methods for IHD detection, achieving maximum sensitivity 96.65%, specificity 86.36%, and accuracy 78.43% with a Bayesian neural network (BNN). Steinisch et al. [7] extracted mean sample entropy and classified 4 CAD subjects from 6 controls using linear discrimination analysis. Studies using private datasets suffer from small database size and variation, particularly for MCG where large public datasets are unavailable. ECG studies based on public datasets may not achieve equal performance when transferred to clinical environments, as these datasets are biased toward representative and easy-to-identify abnormal cases. Feature selection significantly impacts model performance. Previous studies proposed features from time, frequency, and information theory categories, each effective for revealing aspects of electro-physiological signals. However, few studies evaluate feature importance. To address this, a relatively large feature group was designed containing time domain, frequency domain, and information theory features. Analysis found that features describing T wave repolarization synchronicity are the core features to identify IHD subjects, and features describing magnetic pole characteristics are associated with locations of coronary stenosis.

The goal of this study is to develop a reliable multi-channel MCG-based IHD early detection and localization system. The database came from a retrospective study of cardiovascular disease across multiple hospitals in China. Coronary angiography was applied to the IHD group as the gold standard, and detailed medical records, including the degree and location of stenosis, were well documented. Feature design integrated MCG features from time domain, frequency domain, and information theory. Apart from signal entropy, two novel information theory features were employed: Gini index and singular value decomposition entropy. Classifier performance was compared including KNN, DT, SVM, and extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) [22]. To detect IHD cases, three classifiers with best performance were selected and model ensemble was applied to average prediction results. All 164 features were used in this stage. To localize ischemia, IHD group was classified according to stenosis locations: left anterior descending (LAD), left circumflex artery (LCX), and right coronary artery (RCA). For this task, XGBoost classifier and 18 time domain features were used.

IHD occurs when the blood flow to the heart is limited due to coronary arteries stenosis. It causes myocardial damage, leading to severe consequences such as myocardial infarction, ventricular arrhythmia, and even sudden cardiac death. IHD is preventable, and early diagnosis and proper intervention are critical in reducing the rate of mortality [8].

Electrocardiography (ECG) has been recognized as a routine clinical procedure for the early diagnosis of pre-symptomatic IHD disease. However, due to its lower sensitivity and specificity [10], a majority of suspected IHD patients are forced to undergo cardiac computed tomography (CT) or coronary angiography (CAG) at the risk of excessive radiation exposure, allergic reaction to contrast agent etc. [12].

Compared to ECG, MCG is less influenced by electrode-skin contact interference, whereas more sensitive to the tangential and vortex current caused by ischemic cardiac tissue. Despite its superior signal quality, the interpretation of MCG is labor intensive and strongly relying on the experience of interpreter, limiting its acceptance in clinics. Therefore, an automatic system that can detect and localize ischemia from early stage would be extremely beneficial to clinicians.

Recent advances in machine learning show the advantages of discriminative classifiers to automatically detect cardiac diseases. Table I summarizes a list of previous related MCG and ECG studies. Past studies showed promising results in the automatic detection of cardiovascular diseases. However, a few problems still concern. First, studies using private datasets suffer from small database size and database variation, particularly for MCG studies where large public dataset is unavailable. On the other hand, ECG studies based on public datasets may not achieve equal performance when been transferred from benchwork to clinical environment, since public ECG datasets are composed by representative and easy-to-identify abnormal cases and they could be biased for the task of early diagnosis.

Feature selection also has a significant impact on model performance. Previous studies have proposed features from three categories: time domain features [17], frequency domain features [18], [19] and information theory features [20]. Each category is shown to be effective and be able to reveal certain aspects of the complicated electro-physiological cardiac signals. However, few studies are conducted on evaluating the importance of different features [21]. To solve this problem, we designed a relatively large feature group containing above three categories. By analyzing feature importance weights, we found that: 1. features describing T wave repolarization synchronicity are the core features to identify IHD subjects, and 2. features describing magnetic pole characteristics are associated with locations of coronary stenosis.

The goal of this study is to develop a reliable multi-channel MCG based IHD early detection and localization system. The database came from a retrospective study of cardiovascular disease including multiple hospitals in China. Coronary angiography was applied to IHD group as the gold standard, and the detailed medical records, including the degree and location of stenosis, were well documented. The feature design integrated MCG features from time domain, frequency domain and information theory. Apart from signal entropy, we employed two novel features from information theory i.e., Gini index and singular value decomposition entropy. We compared the performance of different machine learning classifiers including: KNN, DT, SVM and a recently proposed extreme gradient boosting method (XGBoost) [22]. To detect IHD cases, we selected three classifiers with best performance and applied model ensemble to average prediction results. All 164 features were used in this stage. To localize ischemia, we classified IHD group according to stenosis locations, including left anterior descending (LAD), left circumflex artery (LCX) and right coronary artery (RCA). For this task, we used XGBoost classifier and 18 time domain features.

section: III. METHODS — B. Feature Extraction
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.

We summarized 18 time domain features in Table II, describing maximum cardiac current, magnetic field map pattern, and positive/negative magnetic pole distribution during the TT interval. Ten features were defined in Lim et al. [17]; 6 additional magnetic pole features were proposed, describing positive/negative pole area and displacement during the T wave, and were found associated with stenosis locations in a subsequent study.

We extracted features from two aspects: values at the T-wave peak and dynamic changes during the TT interval. The TT interval was segmented into 24 sub-windows; for each sub-window, 18 time domain features were extracted.

We applied a Daubechies 4 (db-4) Discrete Wavelet Transform with 4 levels [18] on 36 channels. The low-frequency part (A4) of the 4th-level DWT was reconstructed using inverse DWT. Three frequency domain features were extracted per channel: percentage of energy in a4 components, power of the A4 reconstructed signal, and power ratio of A4 to the original signal, yielding 108 features per subject.

According to electro-physiology theory [26], [27], signal perturbation is higher in ischemic subjects during the ST segment. Three information theory measures were chosen: Shannon entropy per channel, multi-dimensional Gini index, and singular value decomposition entropy. A total of 38 features were extracted per subject. Shannon entropy was computed across all 36 channels to allow comparison between subjects given the relative constant sensor position to the heart [7]. The mean Shannon entropy of the Ischemic Heart Disease (IHD) group was considerably higher than the control group. The Gini index measurement of signal sparsity was smoothed using a window size of 3 time samples [28]; the standard deviation of the Gini index during the TT interval was computed as a feature. Control subjects showed one dominant singular value, whereas IHD subjects displayed several dominant singular values [Fig. 4(e)-(f)].

We compared four classifiers suitable for medium to small datasets: KNN (k=5), Decision Tree, SVM with radial basis function, and XGBoost [22]. Model selection was guided by suitability for medium to small datasets, ability to handle high dimensional data, and performance in previous related studies.

III. METHODS — B. Feature Extraction

1) Time Domain: We summarized 18 time domain features in Table II, describing the characteristics of (1) maximum cardiac current, (2) magnetic field map pattern, and (3) positive/negative magnetic poles distribution during TT interval. Ten of the features were defined in Lim et al. [17]. In addition, we proposed 6 magnetic poles related features describing: positive/negative pole area change during T wave and positive/negative pole displacement during T wave. These features were found to be associated with stenosis locations in the following study.

We were interested in features characteristics from two aspects: values at T-wave peak and the dynamic changes during TT-interval. To achieve this, the TT-interval was segmented into 24 shorter sub-windows. For each sub-window, we extracted the 18 time domain features.

2) Frequency Domain: We applied a Daubechies 4 (db-4) Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) with 4 levels [18] on each of the 36 channels. DWT decomposes the signal into time-frequency components. The low-frequency part (A4) of the 4th-level DWT (a4 component, corresponding to 0 to approximately 7.8 Hz) was reconstructed using inverse discrete wavelet transform (IDWT). Three frequency domain features were extracted for each channel: (1) the percentage of energy corresponding to a4 components, (2) the power of the A4 reconstructed signal, and (3) the power ratio of the A4 signal to the original signal. A total of 3 × 36 = 108 frequency features were obtained for each subject.

3) Information Theory: According to electro-physiology theory [26], [27], signal perturbation of ischemic subjects during ST segment is higher than that for healthy people. Three measures were chosen from information theory, including (1) Shannon entropy for each channel, (2) multi-dimensional Gini index, and (3) singular value decomposition entropy (SVD entropy). A total of 1 × 36 + 1 + 1 = 38 features were extracted.

The Shannon entropy measures the amount of signal complexity. Unlike [7], we used entropy values from all 36 channels instead of the mean. Because given the same sensor setup, the position of MCG sensors to adult heart is relative constant and it is possible to compare the entropy values from different subjects by channel. A plot of Shannon entropy values across 36 channels of all subjects is shown in Fig. 3. The horizontal axis is channel index. The distributions of Shannon entropy across channel among different subjects are similar. The mean Shannon entropy of IHD group (by channel) is considerably higher than that for control group.

The Gini index is a measurement of signal sparsity. To smooth out the result, we adopted a method developed by Banerjee [28] to calculate the multidimensional, using a window size of 3 time samples. After that, the standard deviation of Gini index during TT-interval was computed as another feature. Fig. 4(a) and (b) show the averaged MCG recordings for one control and one IHD subject during TT-interval. Fig. 4(c) and (d) plot the Gini index for each subject, respectively. The fluctuation of Gini index for IHD subject is higher compared to control group.

C. Classifiers

We compared the performance of four classifiers that are suitable for medium to small datasets, including KNN (k = 5), DT, SVM (with radial basis function) and XGBoost [22]. The guidelines to select machine learning model are: (1) suitable for medium to small datasets, (2) able to handle high dimensional data and (3) showing good performance in previous related studies.

input: We conducted experiments on 193 IHD subjects, excluding those with stenosis <35%. Using 18 time-domain features and an XGBoost model, we aimed to distinguish stenosis location via magnetic field distribution. Because most subjects had multi-artery blockages, we simplified the task into three independent binary classifications: LAD (129 cases vs. 64 controls), LCX (73 vs. 120), and RCA (77 vs. 116). Magnetic pole-Related Features

In ECG studies, clinicians use the appearance of ST elevation at different leads to localize ischemic area. Inspired by this theory, we were interested to know whether stenosis at different locations can be distinguished by magnetic field distribution. We conducted experiments on 193 IHD subjects, excluding those with coronary stenosis lower than 35%. For this part of study, we only used 18 time domain features and XGBoost classification model. One problem was that a majority of IHD subjects had multiple blockages at different arteries. Ideally, we either need to isolate enough cases with stenosis on a single artery, or have a much larger dataset to encode stenosis location as a 1 × 3 vector label and solve a multi-class classification problem.

To solve this, we simplified this quest of a multi-class classification into three binary classifications: to predict the occurrence of stenosis on each artery independently. For instance, within 193 IHD cases, we spotted 129 cases had stenosis on LAD vs. 64 cases with no stenosis on LAD, regardless of other stenosis locations. Therefore, we performed three independent predictions to predict: stenosis on LAD (129 cases) vs. no stenosis on LAD (64 cases), stenosis on LCX (73 cases) vs. no stenosis on LCX (120 cases), stenosis on RCA (77 cases) vs. no stenosis on RCA (116 cases). Data composition is shown in Table VII.

Table VIII shows the prediction results for each artery. Fig. 9 plots the top 5 representative features for the prediction of stenosis on each artery. The prediction accuracy for LAD, LCX and RCA are 0.74, 0.68 and 0.65, respectively. Due to higher occurrence, LAD has higher prediction accuracy compared to other two.

section: V. DISCUSSION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: This study compared four machine learning classifiers on a database of 347 healthy and 227 IHD subjects with 164 features. XGBoost outperformed other models, leveraging gradient boosting and regularization to handle common clinical null inputs. For IHD detection, 164 features were categorized and classified independently, then combined via ensemble learning; the SVM-XGBoost mix achieved the best accuracy of 94.03%. The dataset included 34 mild stenosis, 16 NSTEMI, and 27 post-surgical CAG-negative cases, rarely addressed previously. Engineering focused on time-domain, frequency-domain, and information theory features; 8 of the top 10 most important features related to T wave repolarization synchronicity, including magnetic pole dynamics, signal power, and entropy. Normal ventricular repolarization propagates from endocardium to epicardium; ischemia alters electrical conductivity, causing slower repolarization and impaired relaxation. Ischemic regions produce eccentric cardiac currents, consistent with observations of high Shannon entropy, high Gini index standard deviation, and multiple dominant singular values in IHD subjects. Previous ECG studies predicted ischemia location via ST elevation; this method can be extended to MCG using magnetic field maps. In the localization phase, three binary classifiers detected LAD, LCX, and RCA stenosis. Performance was relatively low, explained by: 1) features designed for IHD detection rather than localization; 2) multi-location stenosis requiring more data; 3) CAG being anatomical while MCG is functional, as stenosis does not always cause ischemia. Fig. 10 illustrates LAD, LCX, and RCA territories under right-dominant circulation; LAD occlusion affects anterior wall and septum, RCA affects inferior wall, and LCX affects posterior wall. An interesting finding was that LCX stenosis signal changes resemble RCA posterior wall infarction. ECG shows ST elevation in V7-V9 and depression in V1-V3 for this pattern, consistent with Fig. 9 findings. RCA and LCX stenosis correlate with positive magnetic pole distortion, while LAD stenosis correlates with negative distortion. Future work aims to apply the method to other PQRST-wave portions; recent ECG research links spatial QRS-T angle to left ventricular dysfunction. During the QRS period, rapid magnetic field rotation makes human annotation difficult, but the model can process the whole segment at once. This study proposes localizing coronary stenosis using only magnetic field maps, avoiding time-consuming source reconstruction routines suitable for clinical settings. The MCG technique is sensitive to NSTEMI patients where ECG fails. As a pilot study, improving accuracy is possible by designing more relevant magnetic pole features or analyzing whole field structures via deep learning (CNN, LSTM, 3D-CNN).
output:
V. DISCUSSION

In this study, we compared the performance of 4 machine learning classifiers on a well-documented database including 347 healthy subjects and 227 IHD subjects with a total of 164 features. XGBoost outperforms the other three models in all performance measurements. XGBoost takes the advantage of the gradient boosting method where new models are added to correct the errors made by previous models. It also uses a more regularized model formalization to reduce overfitting. In addition, it can handle null inputs, which is quite common in clinical settings. In the first part of the study for IHD detection, we divided 164 features into three categories after selecting three optimal classifiers. We then performed classification on each feature category independently and used ensemble learning to boost system performance further. The agreement of the results between different combinations of ensemble methods was excellent. The best performance of accuracy = 94.03% was achieved by the SVM-XGBoost mix model.

We aimed to develop a model suitable for IHD early detection. The dataset includes 34 cases with mild coronary stenosis (<35%), 16 cases with non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) and 27 post-surgical patients with CAG negative. These groups are rarely addressed by previous related studies. We engineered a large feature group including time domain, frequency domain and information theory. 8 out of top 10 most important features are related with T wave repolarization synchronicity: 4 features about magnetic pole dynamics, 1 feature about signal power and 3 features about signal entropy. In normal ventricles, the repolarization sequence propagates from endocardium to epicardium [29], [30]. When cardiac ischemia occurs, electrical conductivity within the ischemic region changes correspondingly, causing slower repolarization rate and impaired ventricular relaxation. From the signal processing aspect, ischemic region produces eccentric cardiac current sources. It is consistent with our observations that IHD subjects have high Shannon entropy, high standard deviation of Gini index, and multiple dominant singular values. Because cardiac ischemia leads to reduced repolarized synchronicity and increased signal perturbation.

Previous ECG studies used ST elevation at different leads to predict ischemia location [31]–[33]. This method can be extended to MCG to locate blocked arteries using magnetic field map pattern. In the second part of the study, we constructed three binary classification models to detect stenosis on LAD, LCX and RCA. Results indicate that stenosis at different locations are distinguishable, but at relatively low accurate score. Low model performance can be explained by several reasons: 1. the adopted features are designed for IHD detection. To solve localization problem, we need more descriptive features regarding field dynamics. 2. Coronary stenosis usually happens on multiple locations, and the more complicated the case is, the more data we need to build a robust prediction model. 3. CAG is an anatomical imaging tool, whereas MCG is a functional imaging technique. Coronary stenosis does not necessarily lead to cardiac ischemia. Functional imaging methods such as fractional flow reserve (FFR) or positron emission tomography (PET) can be better options of gold standard.

Fig. 10 plots the three arteries that we inspected in our study and their blood supply regions. Considering only right-dominant blood supply system, LAD occlusion causes anterior wall and interventricular septum infarction, RCA occlusion leads to infarction in inferior wall, and LCX occlusion causes posterior wall infarction. One interesting observation is that cardiac signal changes caused by LCX stenosis resemble those seen on posterior wall infarction due to occlusion in RCA. In ECG, it appears as ST-segments elevation in V7-V9 and depression in V1-V3 [34]. This is consistent with our finding in Fig. 9. RCA and LCX stenosis both have higher correlation with positive magnetic pole distortion, whereas LAD stenosis is more associated with negative magnetic pole distortion.

The continuation of this work includes two directions. First, we are interested in applying this method to other portions of the PQRST-wave. Recently publication on ECG suggested that spatial QRS-T angle is associated with left ventricular dysfunction [35]. During the QRS period, the magnetic field rotates rapidly, making it very difficult for human interpreter to annotate and analyze major cardiac events. With the help of proposed model, we can process the whole QRS segment at once.

Fig. 9. Top 5 representative features for the prediction of stenosis on three arteries. Red shaded blocks represent positive magnetic pole related features; blue shaded blocks represent negative magnetic pole related features.

Fig. 10. Illustration three coronary arteries (LCX, LAD, RCA) and their blood supply regions. The whole system is projected onto a magnetic field map.

We present the possibility of localizing coronary artery stenosis using only magnetic field map. Conventional MCG localization techniques involve cardiac source modeling and realistic volume conductor modeling [36], which is time-consuming and not suitable for large-scale clinical applications. The localization method proposed in this study avoids source reconstruction routine and demonstrates its potential in clinics. In addition, this MCG based technique is sensitive to NSTEMI patients, where ECG localization fails. As a pilot study, a lot of work can be done to improve localization accuracy. To achieve this, we can design more relevant features regarding magnetic pole pattern, or analyze the whole field structure at once following deep learning approaches, such as CNN, LSTM or 3D-CNN.

Abstract: The modeling of an efficient classifier is a fundamental issue in automatic training involving a large volume of representative data. Hence, automatic classification is a major task that entails the use of training methods capable of assigning classes to data objects by using the input activities presented to learn classes. The recognition of new elements is possible based on predefined classes. Intrusion detection systems suffer from numerous vulnerabilities during analysis and classification of data activities. To overcome this problem, new analysis methods should be derived so as to implement a relevant system to monitor circulated traffic. The main objective of this study is to model and validate a heterogeneous traffic classifier capable of categorizing collected events within networks. section: Background
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
Background

Machine learning algorithms are used for data classification, and their performances are analyzed. A subfield of machine learning is automatic classification, which uses algorithms to solve classification problems by grouping homogeneous classes of similar data objects. Classification is supervised learning that requires a training set to train the decision rule and construct a classifier. The training examples are regarded as complete because they contain variable values and their classification. Training is a developmental task in which behavior changes until a desired one is achieved through weight optimization. Preprocessing is often applied to the training data. The choice of a training algorithm depends on the problem specification. Data classification is the natural choice for prediction with discrete known outcomes, and it is commonly used to support data security issues, especially in anomaly detection. A classification model should be simple enough for all employees to execute properly.

Support Vector Machines (SVMs) are supervised training techniques designed to solve discrimination and regression problems. The principle is to transform input variables into a large characteristic space and then find a suitable hyperplane that models the data and separates them into two groups so that the linear boundary produces a maximum margin.

A Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) is a neural network composed of successive feedforward layers that connect neurons by weighted links. A formal neuron is a processing unit of several inputs performing complex logic, arithmetic, or symbolic functions. The output corresponds to a weighted sum of inputs. MLP learning is performed by the error gradient propagation algorithm. The training examples are shown successively to adjust the network weights by accumulating calculated gradients. Training is stopped when the calculated error is less than a certain threshold.

K-Nearest Neighbor (KNN) classification is a supervised learning algorithm that is mainly used when the attributes are continuous, but it can be modified to work with categorical attributes. The idea is to estimate the classification of new data examples on the basis of instances used in the training phase.

A novel binary classifier for anomaly detection is proposed. The work aims to propose a robust algorithm for the training and recognition of events collected and integrated from network traffic. The incorporation of a new machine learning method based on MLP is suggested. The proposed model is easy to implement, applicable to unstructured data, and presents high accuracy. For classification problems, the number of classes to which the inputs belong should be determined. Each class is set to receive an input. A binary value is predicted, and the classifier answers whether an event extracted from network traffic is an intrusive activity or not. Two databases are utilized: one for training and the other for testing and validation. In practice, no predefined rule exists regarding sharing a database quantitatively between training and validation. The validation of such a model requires static data with supervised methods or structured data presented in sequence. The architecture is a neural network consisting of three layers, each of which has neurons directly linked to the neurons of the next layer. No direct connection exists between the input layer and the output layer. A single hidden layer is added to achieve the goal. Traffic activities are collected using network sniffing tools. Heterogeneity is mainly represented at the level of the supported protocol, data source, version, and size. A packet may contain missing or noisy values. The total size of a package cannot exceed 65,535 bytes. Significant formatting is required before analyzing and classifying traffic. Normalization is conducted to establish patterns of activities that facilitate the distinction between activities and the extraction of useful fields. A particular coding for the enumeration of occurrences is realized and adapted to the model. The number of features must be fixed in advance. The input layer receives the preprocessed occurrences successively. An occurrence is subdivided into a set of fields. Each field is received by a neuron. section: Conclusion and Future Work
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: We present classification techniques for supervised learning applied to real problems. Most classifiers struggle with high-dimensional, heterogeneous data. We validate a new machine learning model using proposed solutions that enable efficient, fast analysis. Future work will design and validate an intrusion detection system using this classifier to improve network monitoring and ensure accurate decision making.
output: In this paper, we present a number of classification techniques used in supervised learning to solve different real problems. Most classifiers suffer from limitations due to the large dimensions and heterogeneity of data. The validation of the new classifier model based on the proposed machine learning algorithm is achieved on the basis of suggested solutions that guarantee an efficient and fast analysis. In our future work, we will design and validate an efficient intrusion detection system by using the proposed classifier to improve network monitoring and ensure accurate decision making.

input: Vapnik introduced statistical learning theory in 1999 to address the fundamental trade-off between model complexity and generalization error. The theory provides a framework for constructing learning machines that minimize the risk of misclassification. It establishes the Vapnik-Chervonenkis dimension as a measure of the capacity of a statistical learning system. The structural risk minimization principle is proposed as a method to select optimal learning machines by balancing empirical risk and structural risk. Lauer and Bloch applied support vector machine methods for system identification in their 2006 work.

Microaneurysms (MAs) are early indicators of diabetic retinopathy (DR), the most common cause of blindness before age 50. This study evaluated MA detectability using 25x25 pixel patches extracted from fundus images in the DIARETDB1 database. common cause of blindness before the age of 50. Microaneurysms (MAs), resulting from leakage from retinal blood
vessels,are early indicatorsof DR. In this paper, we analyzed
MA detectability using small 25 by 25 pixel patches

I. INTRODUCTION

Microaneurysms are the earliest clinical signs of diabetic retinopathy (DR), a leading cause of vision loss worldwide. The prevalence of DR is increasing in parallel with the global diabetes epidemic, underscoring the need for effective screening methods. Early detection of microaneurysms is critical, as timely intervention can prevent progression to more severe forms of the disease. Traditional screening relies on manual grading of fundus photographs by expert clinicians, a process that is time-consuming, subjective, and limited by the availability of trained personnel. Automated detection systems have the potential to improve accessibility, reduce costs, and increase consistency of diagnosis. However, developing robust algorithms that can accurately identify microaneurysms across diverse imaging conditions remains a significant challenge. This paper presents a novel approach for microaneurysm detection utilizing Principal Component Analysis (PCA) for dimensionality reduction and machine learning classifiers for pixel-wise classification. The proposed method aims to balance detection accuracy with computational efficiency, making it suitable for real-time clinical applications.

Early detection of MAs is critical for diagnosis and treatment of DR, which has led to a great deal of research towards automatic detection of MAs.

Ram et al. [6] created a clutter rejection strategy, in which successive stages of the algorithm eliminated more and more clutter, while passing most target MAs. One recent work [7] proposed a comprehensive grading system for DR based on classification of 16 features that captured shape, color, and intensity information and the features were extracted from candidate regions.

Many existing MA detection methods rely on hand-crafted features, which are often based on low-level information. Low-level information is easily susceptible to signal drift artifacts and thus prevent reliable generalization among different research sites. A recent method [1] leveraged the use of deep learning for MA detection using a Stacked Sparse Autoencoder (SSAE). Deep learning approaches often learn high-level and robust attributes directly from the raw signal input, and have been successfully applied to various classification and recognition tasks [8]–[10]. In [1], small image patches were generated from the original fundus images and used by the SSAE to learn high-level features from pixel intensities. These patches were then classified as either MA or non-MA using the high-level features learned by SSAE.

This work is inspired by the deep learning SSAE analysis performed in [1] and extends our previous MA analysis [23]. Our goal is to determine whether traditional machine learning methods can achieve similar or better performance on the same fundus image dataset by exploring the full context of the image information, especially when the size of the dataset may be too limited for reliably training deep learning networks. We explore the utility of raw data, extracted from the public DIAbetic RETinopathy DataBase - Calibration Level 1 (DIARETDB1) [11], and ROC [22] for MA classification using random forests (RFs) [12], neural networks (NNs) [13], and support vector machines (SVMs) [14]. In Section II, we describe the materials and methods used in this work, including data and features, cross validation strategy, classifiers employed for MA detection and evaluation metrics. In Section III and IV, we present and analyze the experimental results on DIARETDB1 and ROC datasets respectively. Finally, in Section V, we draw conclusions and discuss future work.

A. Data

We analyzed DIARETDB1 [11] images that were acquired from 89 patients, in which each image was manually annotated by multiple experts at Kuopio hospital. 84 of the 89 patients contained at least mild non-proliferative signs of DR, while the remaining five patients were healthy with no signs of DR. From each patient image, patches were extracted and labeled as H1 or H0, for locations in which MAs were present or absent, respectively, based on information provided in DIARETDB1 ground truth files. Each image patch had a size of 25×25 pixels, with an image resolution of approximately 0.015-0.02 mm/pixel. As in [1], 2182 H1 patches were directly extracted from locations manually labeled as MA and centered at the marked ground truth H1 locations, while 5963 H0 patches were extracted from uniformly random locations throughout the image. An example of DIARETDB1 fundus images is shown in Fig. 1, while examples of H1 and H0 image patches cut from the fundus image are shown in Fig. 2. Our analysis focused on the use of the green channel from the provided RGB images, since MA lesions have the highest contrast in the green plane compared to other color planes [4], [17].

The ROC dataset [22] contained 50 patients, 28 of whom had images with roughly the same resolution and size as those found in DIARETDB1. From this data subset, we extracted features (25×25 pixel patches centered on each location) based on the ground truth provided in the dataset reference. The 28 patients had a total of 201 MAs. In order to keep the balance of the dataset and make the dataset roughly consistent with the ratio of MA patches vs non-MA patches that we extracted from DIARETDB1, we randomly extracted 588 non-MA patches (21 patches/patient) from the ROC dataset.

B. Features

Classification of MA vs non-MA patches was performed using three sets of features. The first feature set consisted of raw pixel intensities, rasterized from the image patches. The dimensionality of the feature space was 25×25, i.e., 625. Although raw pixels yielded good discriminability between patch classes, feature space reduction may be valuable to reduce both classifier training time and concerns regarding the curse of dimensionality [18]. We used two dimensionality reduction techniques to process the original feature set.

We first employed principal component analysis (PCA) [19], a common feature dimensionality reduction method. PCA projects data onto a new space in which consecutive dimensions contain less and less of the variance of the original dataspace and compresses the most important information onto a subspace with lower dimensionality than the original space. As a preprocessing step, we whitened data to zero mean and unit variance. For both PCA and whitening, only training data was used to establish the mean, variance, and principal components of the original data. We tested the feature space with 5-100% of the projected subspace using leave-10-patients-out cross-validation to inspect how many principal components are needed to generate maximum performance.

We also explored the use of the RF feature importance for dimensionality reduction. Feature importance is a measure of the performance loss that would occur if a dimension of the original data space is removed using the RF as the classifier [12]. After sorting dimensions from highest to lowest feature importance, we selected data with top 5-100% of the original space to determine the point at which performance saturated.

section: V. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
We presented RF, NN, and SVM methods to detect microaneurysms in fundus images using the DIARETDB1 database. Our methods outperformed previous deep learning work on the same database using AUC and F-measure. Further validation on a different dataset showed similar results.

After PCA reduction to 625 dimensions, SVMs achieved near-maximum performance with 30% of data; performance plateaued for SVMs while RF and NN performance decreased. We hypothesize this drop is due to overtraining on uninformative dimensions; RFs use random subsets of dimensions per node, and if informative components are excluded, performance degrades. NNs may similarly overtrain on noisy dimensions, indicating SVMs are more robust to noisy features than NNs and RFs.

Reducing dimensionality using RF feature importance achieved high AUC with fewer dimensions and maintained this performance as more dimensions were included. This approach is more robust and generalizable than PCA, eliminating the need to fine-tune the number of principal components.

Training RF on DIARETDB1 and testing on ROC yielded similar performance to RF trained and tested on ROC via cross-validation, indicating our method has the potential to generalize across different datasets.

Future work will extract and classify features from all eye locations to generate a two-dimensional confidence map, scored using the RX anomaly detector [21]. We plan to report results as sensitivity versus number of false positives per eye, providing optometrists with an understandable metric and allowing developers to compare performance agnostic to database size.
output:
In this paper, we have presented several common machine learning methods to detect microaneurysms in fundus images for the diagnosis of diabetic retinopathy using the publicly available database DIARETDB1. The machine learning methods employed in this work include RF, NN, and SVM. Our methods outperformed previous work [1] that conducted deep learning using the same database, measured by both AUC and F-measure. Further validation of our method on a different dataset ROC showed similar results as we found on DIARETDB1. Our results yield a promising step towards automated early detection of microaneurysms and diabetic retinopathy.

Three interesting results were observed in our findings. First, after application of PCA to the original 625-dimensional dataspace, SVMs achieved near maximum performance using only 30% of data. With the incorporation of more principal components, the performance of the SVM plateaued, while the performance of the RF and NN both decreased. Upon further investigation, we hypothesized that this performance drop is due to overtraining on uninformative, or noisy, dimensions. PCA projects most information in signals onto a subset of dimensions, or the first few principal components, in a new subspace, rendering the remainder of dimensions largely uninformative. RFs create an ensemble of decision trees, each with a random subset of dimensions selected for each node of the tree. For experiments with inclusion of more than approximately 5% of principal components (see Fig. 6), if the random subset for a given node does not include one of the informative principal components, the data partition from this node may be meaningless and lead to poor generalization performance. The NNs may be similarly overtrained to these uninformative dimensions, yielding poor performance when more dimensions are included. This result indicates that SVMs are more robust and less sensitive to noisy features than NNs and RFs in classifying MA and non-MA patches.

Second, by reducing dimensionality using RF feature importance, we were able to achieve high AUC with fewer dimensions (see Fig. 8) and maintain this high AUC as more dimensions were included. This is an important difference from the PCA experiment in that performance results are more robust and generalizable to new data. With this approach, fine tuning of the number of principal components is no longer required for any of the classifiers.

Third, when we trained the random forest on DIARETDB1 and used ROC as the testing data, the performance was similar as that achieved by the random forest trained and tested on the ROC dataset using cross-validation. Such a finding indicates that our method has the potential to generalize across different datasets.

In the future, we plan to extract and classify features from all locations within an eye to generate a two dimensional classifier confidence map, which we will then score using algorithms such as the RX anomaly detector [21]. With this new processing protocol, we plan to use a different performance metric, with results reported in terms of sensitivity vs number of false positives (false MAs) per eye, rather than sensitivity vs false positive rate. This would both provide optometrists with a more easily understandable metric and allow algorithm developers to compare performance with a metric that is more agnostic to database size, sub-selection of patches within images, etc.

section: I. INTRODUCTION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: With data volume growing rapidly, distributed machine learning frameworks are needed to handle workloads exceeding single-machine capacity. We focus on the parameter server framework, where servers store globally shared parameters and workers process allocated data. During training, workers iteratively pull parameters, compute updates, and push results, with inter-machine communication via Ethernet typically causing the system bottleneck. We propose a data and parameter partition problem to minimize training time under the synchronous scheme. We investigate a two-step heuristic that first partitions data then parameters, analyzing a theoretical bound based on submodularity. We also adapt a multilevel graph partition approach for joint optimization. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate performance improvements.

Related Work

Classical distributed system design [20] provides several frameworks for distributed machine learning [5], [9]–[11], [13], [21], [22], including parameter server [5], [9]–[11], [13] for machine learning algorithms and MXNet [22] for deep learning. Our work uses the parameter server framework. Open source implementations include PS-lite [5], Petuum [11], and YahooLDA [9]. Industry deployments exist at Google [10] and Microsoft. The parameter server was first proposed for specific applications, such as YahooLDA [9] and DistBelief [10]. YahooLDA is optimized for Latent Dirichlet Allocation [23]. Petuum [11] built a general platform, and PS-lite [5] optimized communication and improved performance. However, communication cost remains inefficient [16], [17]. Prior work [11], [12] investigates stale synchronous schemes, focusing on the trade-off between model convergence and synchronous time consumption. [24] investigates communication volume optimization for geo-distributed jobs, focusing on online resource placement. section: III. MODEL — A. Distributed Machine Learning
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Let $D \triangleq \{d_1, d_2, \dots, d_n\}$ denote the data, where $d_i$ is an $m$-dimensional vector of features. Let $P \triangleq \{p_1, p_2, \dots, p_m\}$ denote the model parameters, which form the weight vector $W \triangleq [v_1, v_2, \dots, v_m] \in \mathbb{R}^m$. The prediction error is measured by a loss function $l(d_i, W)$, such as $l_1$ loss (least absolute deviations) or $l_2$ loss (least square errors). The risk function is defined as Loss$(W) \triangleq \sum_{i=1}^n l(d_i, W) + V(W)$, where $V(W)$ is the regularization term. To minimize this function, gradient descent iteratively updates $W$ as $W_{t+1} = W_t - h \nabla \text{Loss}(W_t)$, where $h$ is the learning rate. Because of the additive property of Loss$(W)$, the gradient $\nabla \text{Loss}(W_t)$ can be distributed across multiple workers. Specifically, the partial derivative $\frac{\partial \text{Loss}}{\partial w_i}$ is reorganized as $\sum_{j=1}^n \frac{\partial l(d_j, W)}{\partial w_i} + \frac{\partial V(W)}{\partial w_i}$, which is further partitioned across $k$ workers based on data indexes $n_1, n_2, \dots, n_k$ for parallel computation.
output:
Typical machine learning algorithms can be viewed as minimizing an objective function. The additive property of its objective function makes distributed machine learning possible. The objective function of supervised learning usually corresponds to a measure of the prediction error, such as the inaccuracy of classifying spam emails. Let $D \triangleq \{d_1, d_2, \dots, d_n\}$ denote the set of data, and $d_i$ be the $i$-th data which is usually a $m$-dimensional vector containing $m$ feature values. Let $P \triangleq \{p_1, p_2, \dots, p_m\}$ denote the set of parameters in the machine learning algorithms. These parameters form a weight vector $W \triangleq [v_1, v_2, \dots, v_m] \in \mathbb{R}^m$, which is used to adjust the weights of $m$ features in data. The prediction error of learning algorithms with parameter $W$ can be measured by a loss function $l(d_i, W)$, for example, $l_1$ loss - least absolute deviations, or $l_2$ loss - least square errors, etc. Learning algorithms iteratively update the parameter vector $W$ and try to minimize the risk function:

Loss$(W) \triangleq \sum_{i=1}^n l(d_i, W) + V(W)$; (1)

where $V(W)$ is the regularization term. It is usually used to penalize the learning model complexity and to avoid overfitting. The risk function value is aggregated from the losses of all data. The aggregation could be allocated to multiple machines if the data is allocated correspondingly.

To minimize the risk function, one common optimization algorithm is the gradient descent. For example, when training a logistic regression model, the gradient descent algorithm is used to minimize the cross-entropy loss. In gradient descent, we need to iteratively calculate the gradient of the loss function w.r.t. model parameters and update the parameters based on the gradient. Formally, let $\nabla \text{Loss}(W_t)$ denote the gradient of the loss function at iteration $t$. Then, we need to update parameters for iteration $t+1$ as $W_{t+1} = W_t - h \nabla \text{Loss}(W_t)$, where $h$ is the training rate. Because of the additive property of the loss function shown in Eq. (1), the calculation of the gradient $\nabla \text{Loss}(W_t)$ can be distributed to multiple workers. Specifically, $\nabla \text{Loss}(W_t) \triangleq [\frac{\partial \text{Loss}}{\partial w_1}, \frac{\partial \text{Loss}}{\partial w_2}, \dots, \frac{\partial \text{Loss}}{\partial w_m}]$, where $w_i$ is the $i$-th element of vector $W_t$. The calculation of $\frac{\partial \text{Loss}}{\partial w_i}$ can be reorganized such that multiple workers can run in parallel:

$\frac{\partial \text{Loss}}{\partial w_i} \triangleq \frac{\partial}{\partial w_i} \left( \sum_{j=1}^n l(d_j, W) + V(W) \right)$

$= \sum_{j=1}^n \frac{\partial l(d_j, W)}{\partial w_i} + \frac{\partial V(W)}{\partial w_i}$

$= \sum_{j=1}^{n_1} \frac{\partial l(d_j, W)}{\partial w_i} + \sum_{j=n_1+1}^{n_2} \frac{\partial l(d_j, W)}{\partial w_i} + \dots + \sum_{j=n_{k-1}+1}^{n_k} \frac{\partial l(d_j, W)}{\partial w_i}$; (2)

where $n_1, n_2, \dots, n_{k-1}$ are the indexes that partition the data samples. The calculation of partial derivatives of $\frac{\partial \sum_{j=1}^{n_1} l(d_j, W)}{\partial w_i}$, $\frac{\partial \sum_{j=n_1+1}^{n_2} l(d_j, W)}{\partial w_i}$, $\dots$, $\frac{\partial \sum_{j=n_{k-1}+1}^{n_k} l(d_j, W) + V(W)}{\partial w_i}$ can be assigned to worker $w_1; w_2; \dots; w_k$, respectively. Similarly, the calculation of other gradient elements can be reorganized for multiple workers. In this way, the training process is distributed to different machines.

section: III. MODEL — B. Parameter Server Framework
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
We integrate data and parameter partitioning into the parameter server framework [4]. The framework consists of servers, workers, and a scheduler. Servers maintain globally shared model parameters, while workers solve sub-problems using data subsets and update parameters. Each machine hosts one server and one worker. The scheduler allocates data and parameters to machines without duplication before training, and this assignment remains fixed throughout the process.

The communication is the primary bottleneck. Let $k$ denote the number of machines. Let $D_i$ and $P_i$ denote the data and parameters allocated to the worker and server on the $i$-th machine, respectively. The scheduler distributes data and parameters prior to training. In each round, workers fetch data, pull shared parameters from servers, compute updates, and push updates back to servers. Communication within a machine occurs via memory buses, while inter-machine communication uses network infrastructure like Ethernet. Inner-machine communication time is negligible compared to inter-machine communication; thus, analysis focuses on inter-machine volume.

The assignment is done by the scheduler before the actual training starts and it is known to all machines. Besides, the assignment is fixed during the training process.

section: III. MODEL — C. Data Sparsity in Inference Problems
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Inference problems benefit from data sparsity when solved in a distributed manner. When updating parameters with data $d_i$, only non-zero attributes change the parameter value [18], since zero elements bring no information. For example, in spam prediction, if a word does not exist in an email, it cannot be determined if the word is more frequent in spam or non-spam emails, and the prediction model cannot be updated accordingly. If a worker finds zero attributes in $d_i$, there is no need to pull corresponding parameters from servers. This reduces the communication volume for that worker. If major attributes in input data samples are zero, the communication volume of training inference learning models could be significantly reduced [5]. Workers can skip parameters corresponding to zero data attributes during training. The allocation of data samples and parameters is critical for balancing communication volume among machines and significantly affects training time.
output: Inference problems benefit from data sparsity when they are solved in a distributed manner. Specifically, when updating parameter values with data $d_i$, only non-zero attributes in the data change the parameter value [18], since zero elements bring no information for the interface. For example, in spam prediction, if a word does not exist in a spam e-mail, we cannot determine whether this word is more frequent in spam or non-spam e-mails, and cannot update the prediction model accordingly. If a worker finds that some attributes of its $d_i$ are zero, then there is no need to pull parameters corresponding to these attributes from servers. The communication volume of this worker is reduced correspondingly. Therefore, if major attributes in input data samples are zero, the communication volume of training inference learning models could be significantly reduced. In practice, the parameter server framework supports to push or pull part of the parameters during training [5]. Workers can skip parameters that correspond to zero data attributes during training. The allocation of data samples and parameters is critical for balancing the communication volume among machines, and significantly affects the training time.

section: III. MODEL — E. Problem Formulation
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
We propose minimizing training time on the parameter server by exploiting data sparsity. We assume synchronous parameter updates across all machines, as asynchronous updates may diverge for certain learning algorithms [12]. Training time is quantified by the number of synchronization rounds and inter-machine communication volume. We model the time per round as proportional to the maximum communication volume across machines. The number of rounds is determined by the worker with the most data samples, formally $\max_{i,j} D_{ij}$. An unbalanced data partition slows training; optimizing only communication or rounds cannot minimize time alone. For instance, assigning all data to one machine eliminates communication but leaves others idle. Our objective function is formulated as $\max_{i,j} D_{ij} \max_i \left( \frac{|N(D_i)|}{P_{ij}} + \sum_{j \neq i} |P_i \cap N(D_j)| \right)$. The first term bounds the number of iterations; the second bounds communication volume per iteration; their product bounds worst-case training time. While computation time per round contributes to total time, it is primarily determined by the input batch size, which is a fixed hyperparameter applied uniformly across workers. Thus, the partition policy hardly affects computation time, so we treat it as a constant and omit it from the formulation. The problem is formalized as:

$\min \max_i \left( D_{ij} \max_i \left( \frac{|N(D_i)|}{P_{ij}} + \sum_{j \neq i} |P_i \cap N(D_j)| \right) \right)$

subject to:

$|N(D_i)| \leq u$, $\forall i$,

$\sum_i D_{ij} = n$, $\sum_i P_{ij} = m$.

The objective minimizes the upper bound of overall training time, modeled by the upper bounds of iteration amounts and communication volume. $|N(D_i)| \leq u

output: The objective function of our problem is a function of both set Di and Pi. Optimizing the function is NP-complete even when assuming that the sets of Pi are given [26]. Therefore, we optimize the original problem via a two-step heuristic. In the first step, we partition the data set D. In the second step, we partition the parameter set P. Besides, the submodular property of function f could help the first step optimization. In this section, we first explain the submodular property, and then introduce the two steps of optimization.

The neighbor set cardinality function f over data set D is non-negative, monotone, and submodular [1].

The function f is defined as the cardinality of a neighbor set and is non-negative by definition [1]. For all subsets D0, D00 ⊆ D, f(D0) ≤ f(D00) when D0 ⊆ D00, establishing monotonicity [1]. Submodularity is defined by the diminishing returns property: for any D0, D00 ⊆ D and element d ∉ D00, f(D0 ∪ {d}) − f(D0) ≥ f(D00 ∪ {d}) − f(D00) [1]. This is proven by showing |N(D0) ∩ N(d)| ≤ |N(D00) ∩ N(d)|, which follows from N(D0) ⊆ N(D00) [1]. While the submodular property aids optimization, directly optimizing f is complex. To minimize training time, the dataset is first partitioned, which is NP-complete [18], followed by model parameter partitioning [1].

section: IV. TWO-STEP HEURISTIC PARTITION — C. Parameter Partition
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: After determining data partition D, we partition parameters P across servers to minimize inter-machine communication. The memory constraint from data partition is assumed satisfied; otherwise, the scenario is infeasible. We solve this with a greedy approach: servers start with empty parameter sets, and in each iteration, the server with the smallest current communication cost receives an unassigned parameter that increases cost the least. The process repeats until all parameters are assigned. Different data partitions yield different parameter partitions; sparser graphs reduce communication volume. The worst-case time complexity is O(m(n + m)), where n = |D| and m = |P|, though real-world graphs are typically sparse.
