IV. TWO-STEP HEURISTIC PARTITION — C. Parameter Partition

After the partition of D is determined, we partition P among servers. The objective is to minimize the inter-machine communication volume since the value of max_{i,j} P_{ij} has been determined, or formally, min_{max_i} (|N(D_i)|_{P_{ij}} + P_{j \neq i} |P_i \ N(D_j)|). Besides, the memory constraint could be removed for the parameter partition. It should have been satisfied in the data partition whose objective is min_{i,j} |N(D_i)|. Otherwise, the input scenario as infeasible. Also, the parameter partition would not change the value of |N(D_i)|. Therefore, the memory constraint can be omitted.

We solve the parameter partition with a greedy approach. Initially, servers are given empty parameter sets. Then, in each iteration, we choose the server on the machine that has the smallest cost which is the inter-machine communication volume |N(D_i) n P_{ij}| + P_{j \neq i} |P_i \ N(D_j)|, and then give it an unassigned parameter that would induce the smallest increase on the cost. The intuition is to balance the inter-machine communication while keeping the increase as low as possible. The procedures are shown in Algorithm 2. Specifically, lines 1-4 initialize the parameter partition and the cost. P^0 stores unassigned parameters. The initial cost is |N(D_i)| since P_i \ N(D_i) = ;, i.e. all communication is inter-machine. In line 6, the algorithm chooses the machine with the smallest cost. In line 7, an unassigned parameter p is greedily chosen. To reduce search space, we only consider p \in N(D_i), i.e., parameters that have correlation with data in the machine. Lines 8-9 update P_i, cost(P_i), and P^0. The allocation repeats until all parameters are assigned.

Different data partitions would impact the parameter partition. Figs. 4(b) and 5(b) illustrate the parameter partition results based on the different data partitions. Clearly, the example in Fig. 4(b) has less inter-machine communication, which is only one parameter p_3 transferring between two machines. In contrast, all six parameters need to be pulled/pushed between two machines.

Theorem 3: The worst-case time complexity of the parameter partition is O(m(n + m)), where n = |D| and m = |P|.

Proof: The initialization in lines 1-2 takes linear time. For the while loop, we first analyze the time cost in each iteration. Choosing P_i costs at most O(k). Choosing p in line 7 costs at most O(n + km). Specifically, calculating set D_i costs at most O(n) and the cardinality of D_i is O(m). The increase on cost function could be calculated by querying the correlation D_i \ p for i = 1; ...; k. Therefore, it costs O(km) time to find p from O(m) candidates. In lines 8-9, assigning and removing can be finished in O(1) time. The while loop has O(m) iterations. Consequently, the while loop costs O(m(k + n + km + 1)) = O(m(n + m)). The worst case time complexity of the parameter partition is O(m(n + m)).

A. Dataset
The dataset we use is summarized in Table IV. The first four are real-world datasets. Specifically, the news20 and rcv1.binary are text datasets. The CTRa is a click-through dataset from anonymous Internet companies. These datasets are stored in libsvm format [40]. The number of data corresponds to the size of set D in our model and the number of features corresponds to the size of P. The soc-liveJournal is a social network dataset. The social network dataset is a general graph G0 = (V0, E0) instead of a bipartite graph, but it can be easily converted. Specifically, we treat the nodes in the dataset as both set D and P, i.e. D = P = V0. If there is an edge between two nodes in G0, we connect the corresponding nodes in D and P. In this way, the original graph could be converted to a bipartite graph.

Besides the real-world dataset, we also build three sets of synthetic data with different data sparsity. Specifically, the number of correlations between data and parameters is represented by a matrix in the synthetic dataset, where rows represent data and columns represent parameters. The value of each element in the matrix could be either 0 or 1, showing whether there is a correlation between the corresponding data and parameter. The sparsity is controlled by a sparsity coefficient g, which is defined as the percentage of zero elements in the matrix. The sparsities of sparse, medium, and dense synthetic datasets are 0.999, 0.995 and 0.991, respectively. The synthetic dataset may have no meaning from the machine learning point of view. It is because the data does not contain any real-world meanings. The purpose of the synthetic dataset is used to test the partition algorithm. During experiments, we ignore the result of the machine learning algorithms. Instead, we set a threshold on the maximum number of iterations of training models, and want to compare the time used for training under different data or parameter partitions.

In both real-world and synthetic datasets, the scheduler of the parameter server would build the dependency graph by one round of traversal over data samples. The dependency graph represents the correlation between data and parameters. It starts from a bipartite graph with no edges. Two sets of vertices in the bipartite graph represent sets of data samples and parameters. During traversal, for each data sample, if there is a non-zero attribute, it adds one corresponding edge to the bipartite graph. After the traversal, the graph partition algorithms is called. After the partition, the scheduler would allocate the parameters and data samples to servers and workers, respectively, based on the partition result. The dependency graph and the partition result would be stored in a lookup table. In this way, the partition is also known to all workers. In each training round, workers can quickly acquire the graph and the partition. Therefore, they know where to pull/push the parameters of the learning model.

input: We implement graph partition on a local machine and deploy learning algorithms on an Amazon EC2 cluster. The local machine uses a 6-core i7-8700 CPU at 3.2 GHz with 32 GB RAM. The cluster consists of 16 t2.large instances, each with 8 GB RAM running Ubuntu 18.04, configured with OpenMPI and PS-lite. The partition instance acts as the scheduler; each instance hosts server and worker nodes. We compare graph partition schemes against a random baseline. Specifically, we test a two-step heuristic (TSH-1, adding one vertex per iteration; TSH-2, adding two vertices) and a multilevel bipartite approach (MBP). We also evaluate PaToH [41], a hypergraph partitioner supporting bipartite graphs. Performance is measured using relative improvement over random partition, defined as (Crandom - Ccomparison)/Ccomparison × 100%, where cost C represents inter-machine communication volume in Figs. 8–10 and total training time (partition + model training) in Fig. 11. Partition results are stored in recordio format.
output:
In our experiment, we implement the graph partition on a local machine and then the learning algorithms on a cluster which is deployed in Amazon EC2. Our local machine has a 6-core i7-8700 CPU running at 3.2 GHz with 32 GB RAM. The cluster on EC2 contains 16 t2.large instances. Each t2.large instance contains 8 GB RAM and runs on Ubuntu 18.04. The parallel computing environment is set up in all instances. Specifically, each instance is installed with the OpenMPI library and its dependent packages. We deploy PS-lite, an open-source parameter server framework that is available at https://github.com/dmlc/ps-lite, on the cluster as the platform to train machine learning algorithms. The instance where the partition algorithm is deployed is labeled as the scheduler. Each instance contains server and worker nodes. On the local machine, we compare the performance of graph partition. The baseline is the random partition scheme. In this scheme, data and parameters are uniformly and randomly allocated to each machine. We implement the two-step heuristic and investigate the trade-off between its time complexity and performance. Specifically, in the data partition, we compare the difference between adding one vertex to a machine in each iteration (denoted as TSH-1) and adding two vertices (denoted as TSH-2). The multilevel bipartite partition approach is denoted as MBP. We also test a popular graph partition algorithm, PaToH [41], which is a well-optimized hypergraph partitioner and supports taking a bipartite graph as the input.

The inter-machine communication volume and the training time are impacted by the partition algorithm and the number of partitions. To clearly show the improvement caused by graph partition algorithms under different numbers of partitions, we use relative improvement over the random partition as the metrics to evaluate the performance of different algorithms. This metric helps cancel out the effect of the number of partitions. The relative improvement is defined as (Crandom - Ccomparison)/Ccomparison × 100%, where Crandom represents the cost of random partition and Ccomparison represents the cost of partition found by comparison algorithms. The cost represents the inter-machine communication volume when we compare the performance of different partition algorithms in Figs. 8, 9, and 10. When comparing the training time in Fig. 11, the cost represents the overall time consumption of both the graph partition phase and the model training phase. The partition result on the local machine is stored in recordio format.

output:
In this paper, we investigate the potential speed-up of parameter server frameworks brought by the data sparsity, especially when training inference models. By partitioning the data among workers and parameters among servers, the intermachine communication volume could be reduced. We formulate a graph partition problem based on this observation. The partition problem is modeled by a bipartite graph. We investigate two approaches to solve the problem. In the two-step heuristic approach, we first solve the data partition by using the submodular property of the neighbor set cardinality function, and then partition the parameters among machines. In addition, we adapt the multilevel graph partition approach for general graphs to fit the optimization over the bipartite graph.

Both approaches are tested with synthetic and real-world datasets. Experiment results show that the two-step heuristic approach provides a trade-off between computational complexity and algorithm performance, which helps the algorithm adapt to different datasets. The multilevel partition approach has better performance except in a social network dataset.

Our scheme cannot be applied to all machine learning models. For deep learning models with millions or billions of parameters, the data-parameter correlation is complex. Build the correlation graph is not feasible. Instead, using hashing techniques to compress those models might be a better approach. For reinforcement learning models, data samples may not be available in advance. Reinforcement learning can explore the solution space during training and learns from the experience. For this case, our data partition scheme cannot partition the model parameters before training. It is an interesting topic to discuss the model placement problems to optimize the training time for reinforcement learning models. Additionally, our partition scheme can be extended by integrating some ideas from federated learning. For example, we can discuss the trade-off between communication latencies and learning accuracy level as indicated in [42]. Moreover, the asynchronous update can be investigated in future work.

ABSTRACT Machine learning for author name disambiguation is usually conducted on the training and test subsets of labeled data created for a specific task. As a result, disambiguation models learned on heterogeneous labeled data are often inapplicable for other purposes that either do not use the same labeled data or do not make use of any labeled data at all. This article explores the idea of transfer learning in a new context, author name disambiguation. We focus on cases where a disambiguation task lacking labeled training data uses models trained on labeled data generated for other tasks. For this purpose, two labeled source datasets are used for training of disambiguation models to be applied to three test target datasets that are deficient of labeled training data. Our results show that transfer learning can produce disambiguation performances similar to those achievable by traditional machine learning in which training and test datasets come from the same labeled data source. The good performance through transfer learning are possible when training source datasets have similar feature distributions as test target datasets. This study suggests that through transfer learning, rich disambiguation models in previous studies can be retained and reused across ambiguous bibliographic data from different fields and data sources, motivating further research on how to correct feature distribution differences between source and target datasets to expand the application of transfer learning in author name disambiguation beyond the model sharing explored in this research.

section: I. INTRODUCTION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Digital libraries rely on author name queries, but author names are frequently ambiguous due to synonyms and homonyms. This ambiguity can merge or split author identities, leading to flawed research findings if not controlled. While machine-learning-based approaches generally outperform rule-based methods for author name disambiguation (AND), creating labeled training data is time-consuming and does not guarantee accuracy. To address this, this article proposes that disambiguation models learned on training data for one task can be reused for others. If transfer learning works in AND, researchers can focus on reusing previous labeled data rather than creating new datasets for every task. This would allow rich models from previous studies to be retained and reused across different fields and data sources. Exploring transfer learning in AND offers a novel perspective and could make the field more cumulative by enabling strong replication and extension of existing work.
output:
Digital libraries are widely used for searching trends, references, and developments in science. In using digital libraries, author name is the most frequent query [1]. One of the biggest challenges for digital libraries in providing accurate author query results to users is that author names are ambiguous. The same author can be represented by different name strings (synonyms). For example, a renowned economist at the University of Michigan, Charlie Brown, is represented by several names in publication records: Charlie Brown, Charlie Charles Brown, Charlie C. Brown, C.C. Brown, and C. Brown. In contrast, different authors can have the same name (homonyms). For examples, there are more than 200 researchers named ‘Wei Wang’ in computer and information science according to the computing digital library DBLP. This name ambiguity can merge and/or split author identities in bibliographic data, possibly leading to flawed research findings if not properly controlled [2]. So, scholars in information retrieval and information systems have proposed a variety of methods to distinguish ambiguous author names in digital libraries, which has formed a research area called ‘author name disambiguation.’

Among many methods for author name disambiguation (AND), machine-learning-based approaches have been reported to produce better disambiguation results than rule-based algorithms or heuristics [3]–[5]. This might be because machine learning generates models adapted to each of diverse name ambiguity settings and scenarios by detecting sophisticated disambiguation patterns through training and validation on labeled data [6]. Although crucial in machine learning for AND, creating labeled data is time-consuming and costly. Also, it does not guarantee accuracy and representativeness [7], [8].

To address the issue of labeled data in machine learning for AND, this article proposes that disambiguation models learned on training data for one disambiguation task can be reused for others. If this transfer learning works in AND, researchers can focus more on reusing previous labeled data than creating new training, or ground truth, datasets for every task. This also means that rich AND models that supported previous studies can be retained and reused across ambiguous bibliographic data from different fields and data sources. As such, exploring the transfer learning in AND can motivate researchers to develop AND methods from a novel perspective, which will be a unique contribution of this article to this topic. Even more importantly, robust transfer learning approaches could help make work in the field more cumulative by enabling strong replication and extension of existing work.

section: II. BACKGROUND
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: About 60% of 200 cited papers on author name disambiguation use machine learning, divided into classification and clustering studies [3], [6], [9]. Classification studies train models on labeled pairwise comparisons to distinguish matching from non-matching author name instances [7], [10]–[12]. Clustering studies generate clusters of all and only instances belonging to the same author, outputting similarity scores instead of binary classifications [13]–[19]. Machine learning typically outperforms heuristic and rule-based methods [3]–[5], relying on labeled ground truth data to detect disambiguation patterns [20]. Creating labeled data is labor-intensive and prone to bias, especially for East Asian homonyms [21], [22]. Alternative methods using external authority data or automatic matching face scalability and bias issues [23]–[25]. This article explores transfer learning, which reuses models trained on other tasks to reduce labeling costs [26], [27]. If effective, rich prior models can be reused across diverse AND scenarios [28]. Despite promise, transfer learning approaches remain rarely tested in this context.
output:
When ‘author name disambiguation’ is searched on Google
Scholar, about 60% of the 200 papers that have received at
least one citation rely on machine learning techniques. AND
machine learning approaches can be divided into two general
groups – classiﬁcation studies and clustering studies - based
on the types of learning output they produce [3], [6], [9].
The ﬁrst is focused on producing disambiguation results at
a pair level. Such studies generate disambiguation models
trained on labeled data in which author name instances are
compared in a pairwise fashion over various dataset features
(e.g., coauthor names). Classiﬁcation algorithms assign any
given pair of name instances (for instance, ‘‘C.C. Brown’’ and
‘‘Charles C. Brown’’) an indicator that distinguishes between
pairs that match and thus represent the same author (i.e., positive set) and pairs that do not, indicating that they refer to
different people (i.e., negative set). Then, the learned models
are applied to test data to predict whether a pair of author
name instances that was not included in training data refer to
the same author (match) or not (non-match) [7], [10]–[12].
The latter group of studies disambiguates names at a cluster
level. They train and test models to generate clusters that
contain all (exhaustive; perfect recall) and only (pure; perfect precision) author name instances belonging to the same
authors [13]–[19]. Here, every variant of ‘‘Charles Brown’’
would be clustered by an effective algorithm. Like classiﬁ-
cation studies, clustering studies also train models on labeled
data for pairwise comparison of author name instances over
other dataset features. They, however, differ from the classiﬁcation studies in that models produce similarity scores -
instead of binary classiﬁcations - for instance pairs in test
data. In short, rather than asking whether or not two different
name strings are the same, clustering algorithms ask how
similar they are. Then, clustering algorithms decide which
instances in test data will be grouped into the same cluster
using the similarity scores as distances among instances.
A few studies use pre-deﬁned criteria (e.g., number of clusters) to guide the clustering process, but many others search
for optimal thresholds that produce best clustering results
using part of labeled data (development data).
Machine learning techniques – whether they emphasize
classiﬁcation or clustering – typically perform better than
heuristic- and rule-based methods in AND [3]–[5]. Such good
performances would be due to the fact that machine learning
detects distinct disambiguation patterns in labeled, ground
truth, training data. The learned patterns are then used to
generate disambiguation models that classify cases in test
data (supervised classiﬁcation) or that tune hyper-parameters
to produce the best clustering results (semi-supervised clustering). This contrasts to other AND approaches using heuristics (e.g., two author names with the same full surname and
initialized forename are assumed to refer to the same author)
or a set of pre-deﬁned rules based on disambiguation patterns
found in previous studies or empirical observations (e.g., two
author names that share coauthors are likely to refer to the
same author).
As such, labeled data is indispensable for generating high-performing classiﬁcation or clustering models in
machine learning for AND. A common practice in AND
using machine learning is to create labeled data for each
AND task. This is reasonable because each task deals with
different types and levels of name ambiguity [20]. Creating
labeled data for each task is, however, not an easy job. It is
often a labor-intensive, manual process that requires hiring
human coders for quite a long time even to produce even
relatively small labeled datasets. Despite the costs in time
and resources, recent studies have demonstrated that manual
labeling for AND can produce biased (especially toward
homonyms of East Asian names) and erroneously labeled
data [21], [22].
Alternative labeling methods have been proposed to overcome such problems. Two promising approaches involve
linking author names to external authority data [23], [24]
and automatic labeling by matching author names based on
a strong indicator of author identity (e.g., email address)
or triangulation of such indicators [13], [21], [25]. But the
alternative labeling approaches require advanced techniques
for large-scale, computationally intensive data processing and
record linking. They are also vulnerable to biased sampling
and labeling errors [21].
This article examines a new alternative, transfer learning,
which has been studied actively for use in text mining and
image processing applications [26], [27]. The basic idea
behind transfer learning is that tasks for which labeled data
are too costly or simply impossible to produce can reuse
(or transfer) models trained on labeled data developed for
other tasks. If transfer learning works in AND, researchers
can reduce resources spent on costly data labeling and focus
J. Kim, J. Owen-Smith: Model Reuse in Machine Learning for AND: An Exploration of Transfer Learning
more on developing and validating models. Most importantly,
rich disambiguation models in prior AND studies can be
reused across diverse disambiguation scenarios and datasets.
Despite their promise for addressing known challenges in
AND, transfer learning approaches have rarely been tested
in this context.
In the following sections, the usefulness of transfer learning in AND is demonstrated by disambiguating author names
in three test or ‘‘target’’ datasets using models learned from
two widely used labeled training datasets developed for AND
research.

section: III. METHOD — A. OVERVIEW OF TRANSFER LEARNING
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Transfer learning reuses a model from one name disambiguation task to another. Standard machine learning trains separate models for each task using distinct datasets. In contrast, transfer learning applies a model trained on a source task to test data for a target task. This study defines transfer learning in AND as learning a target task model using a source model, where source and target tasks share the same feature set but have disjoint source and target datasets.
output:
Model Reuse in Machine Learning for Author Name Disambiguation An Exploration of Transfer Learning

This article shows that an algorithmic model for a name disambiguation task can be reused to disambiguate a different set of name data for another purpose. Fig.1 compares the different workflows of traditional machine learning and transfer learning in AND. Standard machine learning is conducted separately for Task A and B using bespoke training and test datasets. In contrast, the transfer learning approach that is our focus in this study applies the model learned in Task B to test data developed for Task A.

FIGURE 1.
A visualized concept of transfer learning in author name disambiguation. A traditional machine learning (left) generates algorithmic models for each task using different training data, whereas a transfer learning (right) applies a model trained for one task (Task B) to the other task (Task A) for which training data are unavailable.

One common scenario where transfer learning could benefit AND research involves situations where it is necessary to conduct supervised machine learning in the absence of labeled data. More formally, we define transfer learning in AND as a process in which given a training source data (Ds), a source task (Ts), a test target data (Dt), and a target task (Tt), the learning of a disambiguation model for Tt is conducted using the disambiguation model obtained from Ds for Ts, where Ds ≠ Dt, Ts = Tt, and only Ds is labeled.

Here, ‘Ts = Tt’ means that both tasks aim to disambiguate author names using the same feature set. In computer and information science, many different types of transfer learning have been studied outside AND [26], [27]. As this article is the first attempt to explore the application of transfer learning to AND, the proposed definition would serve as a starting point for further elaboration in future research.

section: III. METHOD — B. SOURCE DATA AND TARGET DATA
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
We treat DBLP, MEDLINE, and APS as target datasets for testing, and KISTI and AMINER as source datasets for training. Author names in target data are linked to ORCID ids to label data for benchmark learning and evaluation.

DBLP (computer science) contains approximately 700K author name instances linked to ORCID ids. After converting names to lowercased ASCII strings and stripping 10% of forenames to initials, instances are filtered if they refer to multiple unique authors under the format of full surname plus first initial. Among the filtered instances, 13,635 instances in 600 blocks were selected for analysis.

MEDLINE (biomedicine) uses author names matched to ORCID ids from the December 2015 version, resulting in approximately 2M instances from 1991–2014. Instances are filtered if they belong to multiple unique authors when forenames are initialized. The analyzed dataset uses 36,948 name instances in 600 randomly chosen blocks.

APS (physics) is a collection of Physical Review papers. 198K author name instances are linked to ORCID ids; 26,217 instances belonging to multiple unique authors under name initialization serve as target data. All filtered instances are used for disambiguation due to the dataset's small size.

KISTI (computer science) includes 41,605 author name instances representing 6,937 computer scientists, semimanually labeled by researchers at KISTI and Kyungsung University.

AMINER (computer science) records 7,528 name instances for 1,546 unique computer science authors, labeled by an international research team.
output:
We treat three datasets (DBLP, MEDLINE, and APS – American Physical Society) representing three different science domains (computer science, biomedicine, and physics each) as target data for testing, and use two labeled datasets from computer science (KISTI and AMINER) as source data for training. Fig. 2 summarizes the process of transfer learning using the training source data and test target data. Note that author name instances in target data are linked to author ids in ORCID – an open-source researcher profile [28] - to label data for benchmark learning (i.e., baseline learning using standard methods that can be used to contextualize the performance of our transfer learning approach) and evaluation of test results (details are explained in Evaluation).

FIGURE 2.
An overview of transfer learning in this article. Machine learning algorithms are trained on two training source data (KISTI and AMINER recording publications in CS) to learn disambiguation models for TASK D. The learned models are used on test data for Task A (DBLP recording publications in CS), Task B (MEDLINE; Biomedicine), and Task C (APS; Physics) that cannot generate their own models because training data are unavailable.

1) DBLP (COMPUTER SCIENCE)
Author names in computer science publications have been the main target of disambiguation studies [3]. DBLP is a digital library that provides authorship information of computer and information science publications worldwide [29]. Author names in DBLP are already disambiguated with high accuracy through machine learning algorithms and manual correction [30]. For this article, about 700K author name instances that are linked to ORCID author ids are obtained from [31]. After deleting author identifiers, all names are converted into lowercased, ASCII strings and 10% of their forenames are stripped into their first initials to increase name ambiguity in the data. Then, name instances are filtered for disambiguation if they refer to two or more unique authors when their strings are simplified into the format of full surname plus their first forename initial. For example, three name instances – Mark Newman (Author X), M. Newman (Author Y), and M. E. Newman (Author Y) – are filtered because they share the same first forename initial (“M”) with the full surname (“Mark”) while they refer to two distinct authors (Author X and Author Y). In AND, groups of name instances that meet the same filtering criterion, e.g., sharing the same full surname and first forename initials, are called ‘blocks.’ This filtering of instances (‘blocking’) is a commonplace pre-processing step conducted by AND researchers to collate name instances to be disambiguated together. Among the filtered instances from the ORCID-linked DBLP data, 13,635 instances belonging to 600 blocks were randomly selected for analysis.

2) MEDLINE (BIOMEDICINE)
Biomedical researcher names have also received much attention from disambiguation scholars. The public MEDLINE database has been one of the most frequent target datasets for AND [6]. Maintained by the National Library of Medicine (NLM), MEDLINE contains the largest collection of publication records in biomedicine. We matched author names in MEDLINE (December 2015 version) to ORCID ids following the steps outlined in [21]. That process resulted in approximately 2M ORCID ids-linked instances in papers published between 1991∼2014. As was the case with DBLP, author names are filtered only if they belong to two or more unique authors when their first forenames are initialized. The final, filtered dataset we analyze uses 36,948 name instances in 600 randomly chosen blocks as target data.

3) APS (PHYSICS)
This dataset is a collection of papers published in Physical Review journals managed by the American Physical Society (APS). Many studies have used it for modeling complex networks [32]. For this study, 198K author name instances in the raw APS data (2017 version) are linked to ORCID ids. Among them, 26,217 instances were selected to serve as target data because they belong to two or more unique authors when first forenames are initialized. Unlike DBLP and MEDLINE, we use all name instances rather than a sample for disambiguation because the ORCID-linked APS dataset is relatively small.

These three target datasets are disambiguated by algorithms trained on two different source datasets – KISTI and AMINER – which are both commonly used in AND [20], [21], [33], [34].

4) KISTI (COMPUTER SCIENCE)
KISTI data includes 41,605 author name instances representing 6,937 computer scientists. The data are semimanually labeled by researchers at the Korea Institute of Science Technology and Information (KISTI) and Kyungsung University [35].

5) AMINER (COMPUTER SCIENCE)
This dataset is labeled by an international research team [36] for algorithmic AND in a computer and information science digital library, AMiner, maintained by the Tsinghua University in China [37], [38]. AMINER records a total of 7,528 name instances for 1,546 unique computer science authors.

section: III. METHOD — C. MACHINE LEARNING SET-UP
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
Section III.C. MACHINE LEARNING SET-UP

This study evaluates transfer learning using classification and clustering on author name disambiguation (AND).

1) INPUT FEATURES
Pairwise comparisons of author name instances from KISTI and AMINER generate similarity profiles using four features: author name, coauthor name, title words, and venue name [5], [11], [14], [21], [39]. Strings are lowercased and non-alphanumerical characters removed; title words are stopword-listed and stemmed. After preprocessing, 2∼4-gram vectors are compared using Cosine Similarity of Term Frequency (range: 0 to 1) per Equation 1 [1]. Similarity measures are calculated only among name instances sharing the same full surname and first forename initial to reduce computational load [1].

2) ALGORITHMS
Three algorithms—Logistic Regression (L2 Regularization, class weight=1), Naïve Bayes (Gaussian, maximum likelihood), and Random Forest (Gini Impurity, 500 trees)—represent baselines in AND [11], [13], [15], [40], [41].

For classification, models learn disambiguation patterns on training source data (KISTI, AMINER) to predict match/non-match for instance pairs. Scikit-Learn Python implements classifiers; models are then applied to test target data (DBLP, MEDLINE, APS) [1].

For clustering, the same features and algorithms train models on source data. Models assign probability scores to test instance pairs. A Hierarchical Agglomerative Clustering (HAC) algorithm groups instances with scores above a threshold. The optimal threshold is determined by applying trained models to development data (50% of source data) to find average probability thresholds yielding best-fit clustering per block [14], [15], [21]. Source datasets are split into 50% training and 50% development subsets. Training data supports both classification and clustering; development data supports clustering only. HAC uses average linkage implementation from reference [14].

2) ALGORITHMS
Pairwise, feature speciﬁc similarity scores for blocked name
instances are fed into three algorithms – Logistic Regression (LR), Naïve Bayes (NB), and Random Forest (RF) –
that represent the baseline and/or best performing algorithms
reported in multiple AND studies [11], [13], [15], [40], [41].
For classiﬁcation, ﬁrst, each algorithm is tasked to learn
disambiguation patterns on training source data (KISTI and
AMINER). Here, the learning target is to predict whether a
pair of instances refer to the same author (match) or not (nonmatch), given a set of similarity scores. So, when the learned
models are applied to test target data (DBLP, MEDLINE,
and APS), they produce binary decisions of whether instance
pairs in each test data refer to the same author or not. In this
study, Scikit-Learn packages in Python are used to implement
classiﬁers. L2 Regularization with class weight = 1 is used
for Logistic Regression. For Naïve Bayes, Gaussian Naïve
Bayes with maximum likelihood estimator is chosen. For
Random Forest, split quality is measured by Gini Impurity
and 500 trees are used after grid search.
Second, machine learning for clustering also uses the same
features, pre-processing, and algorithms (LR, NB, and RF) as
those for classiﬁcation in blocking and pairwise comparison
of instances. Unlike the classiﬁcation tasks in which models
are used for predicting binary classes, however, the learning target of clustering tasks is to produce groups of name
instances that refer to the same authors. For this, speciﬁcally,
the aforementioned classiﬁcation algorithms learn disambiguation patterns on training source data and assign a probability score to each pair of instances in test data quantifying
how much the pair is likely to represent the same author based
on their feature similarities.
The probability scores among instances in test data are
then used by a Hierarchical Agglomerative Clustering (HAC)
algorithm which collates into a cluster including all the
name instance pairs that have probability scores beyond a
certain threshold. To decide the best threshold for test data,
the trained models are applied (before test data) to development data (50% of source data) to ﬁnd the average probability
thresholds that produce the best-ﬁtting clustering results per
block [14], [15], [21]. This average score is used to guide
clustering decisions by the HAC algorithm on test target
data. To accomplish this, entire source datasets (KISTI and
AMINER respectively) are randomly split into 50% (training
data) and 50% (development data) subsets. The training data
are used for both classiﬁcation (2-step procedure: train →
test) and clustering, whereas the development data are only
used for clustering (3-step procedure: train →development
→test). The HAC algorithm is implemented by the code
in [14] using its average linkage function.

We evaluate classification algorithms using Recall, Precision, and F1 scores for positive (match) and negative (non-match) pairs, defined in equations 2-7. Recall Positive (RP) equals the number of correctly predicted matches divided by the number of true matches. Precision Positive (PP) equals the number of correctly predicted matches divided by the number of predicted matches. F1 Positive is the harmonic mean of RP and PP. Recall Negative (RN) equals the number of correctly predicted non-matches divided by the number of true non-matches. Precision Negative (PN) equals the number of correctly predicted non-matches divided by the number of predicted non-matches. F1 Negative is the harmonic mean of RN and PN. RP assesses how many true match pairs are correctly predicted, while PP measures how many predicted matches are actual matches. RN counts how many true non-match pairs are predicted, and PN checks how many predicted non-matches refer to different authors. F1 metrics serve as harmonized mean scores balancing recall and precision for both pair types. Further details are in [7].

Fig.4 reports classification performances of Logistic Regression (LR), Naïve Bayes (NB), and Random Forest (RF) on DBLP test data, comparing transfer learning (trained on KISTI and AMINER) against benchmark learning (ORCID). Upper subfigures show positive pair results; lower subfigures show negative pair results.

For positive pairs, transfer learning with LR and NB produces higher precision than benchmark learning (ORCID), indicating more accurate same-author predictions. However, this comes at the cost of lower recall, meaning some true positives are missed. Consequently, F1 scores for transfer learning are lower than benchmark learning in the upper-right subfigure.

For negative pairs, transfer learning from AMINER and KISTI yields lower precision but higher recall than benchmark models. This indicates that transfer-learning models correctly identify more distinct-author pairs but also produce more false negatives. As a result, F1 scores are lower than benchmark learning in the lower-right subfigure.

Across positive and negative pairs, transfer-learning F1 scores are close to benchmark scores for LR and NB but notably lower for RF models. This suggests transfer learning is more effective at detecting negative pairs than positive pairs in DBLP test data.

Fig.5 and Fig.6 extend these patterns to MEDLINE and APS datasets. Transfer learning generally shows higher precision and lower recall for positive pairs, and lower precision and higher recall for negative pairs compared to benchmark learning, with exceptions observed for RF on MEDLINE and NB on APS.

Overall, Fig.4∼6 indicate that models trained on KISTI labeled data can successfully classify author name pairs in DBLP, MEDLINE, and APS, producing F1 scores comparable to benchmark learning on labeled subsets. Performance gaps between transfer and benchmark learning are wider for RF models, likely because RF learns training data patterns well but is less generalizable to new data sources than LR and NB.

Fig.4 reports the performances of three classification algorithms – Logistic Regression (LR), Naïve Bayes (NB), and Random Forest (RF) – in predicting whether a pair of author name instances in test target data (DBLP) refers to the same author (positive; P) or not (negative; N). The gray bars (KISTI) and white bars (AMINER) represent performances obtained through transfer learning trained on the two training source datasets. Black bars (ORCID) represent performances obtained from benchmark learning processes using the same algorithms trained on a subset of ORCID-linked DBLP. Performances for positive pairs are shown in upper subfigures, whereas those for negative pairs are reported in the figure's lower panels.

Fig.4 demonstrates that transfer learning for classification by Logistic Regression and Naïve Bayes produce better disambiguation results than benchmark learning (ORCID) in terms of positive pair precision (upper-left subfigure). In other words, when these two algorithms predict that pairs of name instances refer to the same authors using transfer learning, those decisions are more accurate than those made using standard benchmark learning procedures. In this instance, transfer learning has benefits both for research efficiency and for accuracy.

This positive performance by KISTI and AMINER in terms of precisions, though, is offset by lower recall than ORCID's (upper-middle subfigure). This indicates that some true positive pairs are not successfully predicted by algorithms trained using transfer learning on KISTI and AMINER, but they are correctly predicted by the more standard benchmark-learning models. These high-precision and low-recall performances by the transfer learning lead to F1 scores lower than those by the benchmark learning (upper-right subfigure). Overall, then, Figure 4 suggests that transfer learning for classification performs better than benchmark methods in terms of correctly identifying positive pairs, but also has a tendency to report false negatives.

When it comes to disambiguating negative name instance pairs (those which truly refer to distinct authors), all the algorithmic models trained using transfer learning from AMINER and KISTI perform worse than the benchmark models in precision (lower-left subfigure) but do better in recall (lower-middle subfigure). This means that if algorithmic models trained by reliance on transfer learning predict that name instance pairs refer to different authors, their decisions are more accurate than the benchmark models when evaluated on the full list of true negative pairs (→higher recall). However, they also produce more false negative pairs than the benchmark models (→lower precision). The low-precision and high-recall performances by transfer-learning result in F1 scores lower than those by benchmark learning (lower-right subfigure).

Unlike the case of positive pairs, however, transfer learning produces F1 scores very close to the benchmark F1 scores for Logistic Regression and Naïve Bayesian algorithms, but less close for the Random Forest models. This means that the transfer learning models are better at accurately detecting negative pairs than they are at identifying positive pairs in the DBLP test target data. In addition, the high precision and low recall for positive pairs (upper subfigures) in combination with the low precision and high recall for negative pairs (lower subfigures) indicate that true positive pairs are misclassified by the transfer learning more frequently into false negative pairs than false positive ones compared to the benchmark learning.

Fig.5 and Fig.6 present performance indicators for pairwise classification by transfer learning in MEDLINE and APS, respectively. Overall, the presented patterns of performance of transfer learning compared to benchmark learning for these datasets are very similar to those we discussed in the case of DBLP. Transfer learning shows higher precision and lower recall in disambiguating positive pairs and lower precision and higher recall for negative pairs than benchmark learning, although exceptions are observed for Random Forest models on MEDLINE data and Naïve Bayes classifications on APS data.

Fig.4∼6 indicate that disambiguation models learned on KISTI labeled data can quite successfully classify author name pairs in DBLP, MEDLINE, and APS: their models produce F1 scores close to those by benchmark learning trained on the part of target data. This implies that when labeled training data are unavailable for one of three target data, KISTI can serve as a training data without degrading performance below the level that would be achievable if algorithms are trained on a labeled subset of DBLP, MEDLINE or APS. Another interesting observation is that performance gaps between transfer and benchmark learning are wider for Random Forest models than others. This might be because Random Forest is known to learn patterns representing training data better than the other two algorithms, LR and NB: the learned patterns are applied well to test data that come from the same data source as training data (benchmark learning) but less generalizable to test data from a new source (transfer learning).

section: V. RESULTS — B. CLUSTERING PERFORMANCE
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Clustering evaluates predicted groups by quantifying how well they contain only matching instances (precision) and all matching instances (recall). A baseline is used to measure transfer learning gains over blocking. Blocking groups all name instances matching on full surnames and first forename initials [44]–[46]. As blocking achieves near-perfect recall but low precision, transfer learning produces more fragmented but purer clusters. Fig.7 shows transfer learning achieves higher precision and lower recall than benchmark learning across DBLP, MEDLINE, and APS for all three algorithms, except NB's precision on APS. Compared to baselines, both transfer and benchmark learning outperform blocking in F1 scores. Transfer learning trained on KISTI produces better precision, recall, and F1 scores than AMINER-trained transfer learning and blocking, approaching benchmark learning performance on DBLP and APS.
output:
Unlike classification results in which positive and negative pairs are evaluated separately, clustering results are assessed by quantifying the extent to which predicted clusters contain only (perfect precision) and all (perfect recall) instances that should belong to the same authors. For clustering evaluation, especially, a baseline is added to gauge the performance gains obtained by transfer learning compared to blocking. The blocking (all name instances that match on full surnames and first forename initials refer to the same author) has been used as a disambiguation heuristic in several studies [44]–[46] as well as the standard author search format by many digital libraries.

According to Fig.7, transfer learning produces higher precision and lower recall than benchmark learning: precision bars for KISTI and AMINER are taller than those representing ORCID. Likewise, their recall bars are shorter. Combined, these observations indicate that transfer learning predicts more fragmented but purer clusters than benchmark learning. In other words, transfer learning tends to split name instances that should belong to the same cluster into other clusters more often than benchmark learning (lower recall), whereas its predicted clusters tend to contain name instances that should belong to other clusters less often than those predicted by benchmark learning (higher precision). This pattern is consistent across DBLP, MEDLINE, and APS data for all three algorithms (with the sole exception of NB's precision for APS data). This interpretation aligns well with classification results above (Fig.4∼6), suggesting that true positive pairs are misclassified by transfer learning more frequently into false negative pairs than false positive ones compared to benchmark learning results. Note that name instances for an author split incorrectly into different clusters create false negative pairs (false non-matches), whereas name instances of different authors merged into the same clusters create false positive pairs (false matches).

When compared with baselines (dotted lines in Fig.7), machine learning techniques – whether it be transfer or benchmark learning – outperform the heuristic (blocking) baseline in terms of F1 scores. As blocking collects all name instances that match on the full surname and first forename initial into the same cluster, its recall tends to be almost perfect (close to 1.0 in middle subfigures). But blocking-based clusters (= blocks) contain many false positive name instances of distinct authors, resulting in low precision. Considering precision and recall together, blocking produces contaminated (low precision) but consolidated (high recall) clusters. When precision and recall are weighed equally (F1 scores), blocking produces disambiguation results worse than machine learning: dotted lines in right subfigures in Fig.7 are positioned below bars.

A noticeable observation in Fig.7 is that transfer learning trained on AMINER produces only marginally better and sometimes worse performances than blocking depending on test target data and algorithms (e.g., see AMINER's F1 scores by RF in MEDLINE). Like classification, however, transfer learning for clustering trained on KISTI produces better results than the AMINER-trained transfer learning and blocking-based disambiguation. It even produces precision, recall, and F1 scores that are close to those produced by benchmark learning for DBLP and APS. This implies that transfer learning can work well or bad depending on the choices of training source data and algorithms.

output:
Performance gaps between KISTI- and AMINER-trained models indicate that the two training source data may have different feature characteristics for pairwise comparisons. To check this intuition, we compare distributions of feature-specific similarity scores for each data source.

As described in III. B. MACHINE LEARNING SET-UP, name instances in training and test data are compared for similarity over four features – author name, coauthor name(s), title words, and venue (conference or journal) names. For this, first, an alphabetical string of a feature is dissected into an array of 2∼4 grams (e.g., 'Smith' → 'sm-mi-it-th-smi-mitith-smit-mith'). Next, two arrays for a pair of instances are compared to quantify how they are similar by calculating the cosine similarity of n-gram's Term Frequency. This cosine similarity score is calculated for each of four features per instance pair. Table 2 illustrates this similarity calculation conducted on a few instances selected from the KISTI dataset.

**TABLE 2.** An example of per-feature similarity score calculation.

Clustering algorithms learn patterns from the lists of per-feature similarity scores and labels. So, if two training datasets have different distributions of per-feature scores, they may generate different disambiguation models. We suspect that differences in the feature distributions across AMINER and KISTI contribute to the overall patterns of performance we describe above.

Fig.8 presents the comparison of per-feature similarity score distributions between AMINER and KISTI. For visual simplicity, each score is rounded up into nearest bins with intervals of 0.1 (x-axis). Also, the ratios of the scores in the same bin over all scores are plotted (y-axis).

According to Fig.8, the two training source datasets have similar distributions of per-feature similarity scores for Title and Venue for both positive and negative pairs. Their differences are, however, noticeable for two other features, Author and Coauthor. First, in both KISTI (circle) and AMINER (cross), most positive pairs share the same arrays of string n-grams (x = 1.0), whereas a few pairs bear different n-grams (x < 1.0). In negative instance pairs, however, many AMINER pairs still share the same n-gram arrays (see the cross with x = 1.0 & y > 0.8), which means there are many authors who still share the same names (homonyms) in the AMINER data.

This is the case because AMINER data were created to disambiguate author names that share the same or very similar name strings [20], [36]. In contrast, pairs in KISTI show a different 'Author' distribution in which similarity scores are scattered across x values, indicating that different authors tend not to share many n-grams. Scores are centered around x = 0.5, not x = 0.0, because only pairs in the same block are compared for disambiguation and they share at least full surname and first forename initial, even if they refer to different authors.

Regarding 'Coauthor,' both KISTI and AMINER show similar distributions of similarity scores for positive pairs. But for negative pairs, AMINER has a distribution shape (crosses) moving toward right compared to KISTI's (circles). This means that authors in AMINER tend to share more similar coauthor names than those in KISTI.

How are such different distributions of feature similarity scores in the training source data related to those in the test target data? Fig.9 and Fig.10 shows the per-feature similarity score distributions of KISTI and AMINER, respectively, juxtaposed to those of three test target data – DBLP, MEDLINE, and APS.

Considering that previous studies have shown that author name and coauthorship play the most important roles in distinguishing authors [5], [18], [19], [47], disambiguation models learned on AMINER may have incorrectly assigned author name instances with similar author name strings and coauthor names to belong to different people, producing a greater number of false negatives and leading to the lower observed recall scores for transfer learning from AMINER described in our discussion of Fig. 4∼7 above. Put more simply, AMINER's focus on highly similar names led to different distributions of similarities on key matching features, which seems to describe the systematic differences in AMINER and KISTI based transfer learning we find.

FIGURE 10. Comparison of per-feature similarity score distributions between AMINER and three target data. Pairs of name instances in the same blocks are assigned a set of similarity scores over four features (Author, Coauthor, Title, and Venue). Each feature's similarity scores are rounded up into nearest bins with intervals of 0.1 (x-axis) and the ratios of the scores in the same bin over all scores are plotted on y-axis. The distributions are depicted separately for positive (left) and negative (right) pairs.

As such, comparing the feature similarity score distributions between training and test data illustrates that transfer learning can perform well if pairs in training source data have feature similarity patterns similar to those of pairs in test target data. In other words, models trained on AMINER would produce better disambiguation results than KISTI-trained models for tasks in which homonyms are prevalent. This suggests that successful transfer learning in the AND context requires close attention to the design features of training datasets and the particular patterns of feature similarity distributions across training and target data.

section: VI. DISCUSSION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Transfer learning shows promise in AND, though target data labeling remains necessary for model evaluation and source data selection. Performance depends on matching feature similarity distributions between source and target datasets, as demonstrated by comparisons across AMINER, KISTI, and other domains. Despite labeling requirements, transfer learning allows researchers to prioritize model building over data annotation. Models trained on computer science data can be effectively applied to biomedicine and physics, suggesting broad reusability. Furthermore, similar feature distributions across disparate fields indicate that hyper-parameter tuning could enable consistent high performance, motivating wider adoption of transfer learning techniques in the field.
output:
Model Reuse in Machine Learning for AND: An Exploration of Transfer Learning

This article provides an initial demonstration that transfer learning works well in the context of AND, a finding of potential value to help researchers who may face challenges in creating bespoke labeled data for their particular machine learning tasks. However, the issue of labeling still needs to be addressed, though in a different way, for the sake of transfer learning. First, the proposed transfer learning does not eliminate the need of labeling for target data. To test the performances of transfer-learning-induced models, for example, part of test data needs to be labeled. It would be an interesting topic to develop methods for labeling part of test data that are small but representative to properly evaluate learning performances.

Second, the systematic performance differences we identify for transfer learning from AMINER and KISTI suggest that labeling some representative part of test data is also required to identify appropriate labeled source data for transfer learning. As shown by the comparison of feature similarity score distributions (Fig. 8∼10), transfer learning performances in this article appear to be related to the match of feature similarity score distributions between training source data and test target data. For high-performing transfer learning, part of target data may be labeled to generate feature similarity distributions to be compared with those of candidate source data to find the best match. Another direction to address this issue would focus on correcting differences of feature distributions between source and target data, which has been actively researched for transfer learning in text classification [27].

Despite these problems, the transfer learning explored in this article has important implications for AND. The first and most important advantage of transfer learning would be that researchers can focus more on disambiguation model building and application development and less on time-consuming, expensive data labeling.

Second, appropriately specified transfer learning procedures can facilitate the application of disambiguation models across different studies increasing both the replicability and the extensibility of AND research as a whole. Many machine learning methods for AND have been validated on labeled data created from publication records in one specific field, computer science [3], [20]. So, those methods can be assumed to perform well, if reported so, on data representing authorship characteristics of the computer science field. What has been less clearly demonstrated is how disambiguation methods validated on CS-oriented labeled data can be applied to disambiguating author names in other fields like biomedicine, physics, engineering, and social sciences, where institutional and other differences may yield different patterns of feature similarity. This study demonstrated that disambiguation models trained on one CS-oriented labeled dataset, KISTI, can be used to effectively resolve name ambiguity in authorship data from biomedicine (MEDLINE) and physics (APS) as well as computer science (DBLP). This suggests that rich, high-performing methods in previous CS-field-focused studies can be validated and reused for application to other fields through transfer learning.

Third, the transfer learning results in this article can motivate disambiguation scholars to attend more closely to transfer learning. As shown in V.C.FEATURE SIMILARITY DISTRIBUTION, three test target data showed very similar distributions across features, despite representing widely disparate fields. As a result, enabling effective transfer learning through algorithms trained on KISTI but applied to other datasets with similar feature score distributions may prove useful as a means to speed and expand machine-learning based AND research. This might be because although authorship behavior (e.g., average number of coauthors) differs per field [45], patterns characterizing name pairs of matched or non-matched author identities tend to be similar across fields (e.g., non-matched pairs are likely not to share coauthors). This suggests that through hyper-parameter tuning and model modification, transfer learning for AND may consistently be able to hit performance benchmarks similar to or higher than those achieved through the more traditional approaches represented in our benchmark learning case.

section: VII. CONCLUSION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Transfer learning was evaluated for disambiguation tasks where labeled training data is unavailable. Results indicate that models developed via transfer learning can achieve performance comparable to traditional machine learning when source data closely represents target dataset features. However, transfer learning barely surpassed benchmark metrics on key disambiguation tasks. Despite this, the approach allows researchers to focus on modeling and application rather than costly labeling by enabling the reuse of prior methods. This study provides a foundation for researchers to explore transfer learning's potential in novel disambiguation contexts.

ABSTRACT

Today, predictive analytics applications became an urgent desire in higher educational institutions. Predictive analytics used advanced analytics that encompasses machine learning implementation to derive high-quality performance and meaningful information for all education levels. Mostly know that student grade is one of the key performance indicators that can help educators monitor their academic performance. During the past decade, researchers have proposed many variants of machine learning techniques in education domains. However, there are severe challenges in handling imbalanced datasets for enhancing the performance of predicting student grades. Therefore, this paper presents a comprehensive analysis of machine learning techniques to predict the final student grades in the first semester courses by improving the predictive accuracy. Two modules will be highlighted in this paper. First, we compare the accuracy performance of six well-known machine learning techniques namely Decision Tree (J48), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Naïve Bayes (NB), K-Nearest Neighbor (kNN), Logistic Regression (LR) and Random Forest (RF) using 1282 real student's course grade dataset. Second, we proposed a multiclass prediction model to reduce the overfitting and misclassification results caused by imbalanced multi-classification based on oversampling Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE) with two features selection methods. The obtained results show that the proposed model integrates with RF give significant improvement with the highest f-measure of 99.5%. This proposed model indicates the comparable and promising results that can enhance the prediction performance model for imbalanced multi-classification for student grade prediction.

input:
I. INTRODUCTION

In higher education institutions, student academic management systems record final examination marks and grades across courses and programs to generate performance reports. Repository data can reveal insights into academic performance. Determining student performance remains a crucial challenge [1]. Common influence factors typically rely on socioeconomic background, demographics, and learning activities, compared to final examination grades [2-5]. Consequently, predicting student grades is viewed as a solution to improve performance [6]. Predictive analytics has demonstrated benefits in higher education by identifying patterns in vast databases [7]. It addresses areas including performance, dropout prediction, early warning systems, and course selection [8]. Furthermore, its application in predicting academic performance has increased [9]. Predicting student grades is important for improving performance. While many machine learning techniques have been applied, methods to improve imbalanced multi-classification in grade prediction are difficult to find [10], [11]. This study performs a comparative analysis to find the best prediction model by addressing two research questions: (1) Which machine learning algorithm performs highest accuracy in predicting final course grades? (2) How can imbalanced multi-classification datasets be addressed using selected algorithms with oversampling SMOTE and feature selection methods? To answer these questions, student final course grades were collected from two core courses in the first semester final examination results at a Malaysian polytechnic. A descriptive analysis visualized grade trends to aid lecturer decision-making. Then, a comparative analysis was conducted using six well-known algorithms: LR, NB, J48, SVM, kNN, and RF. To address imbalanced classification, data-level solutions using SMOTE and feature selection were applied. The novel contributions of this paper are: (1) A proposed combination of SMOTE modification and two feature selection algorithms to automatically determine the optimal sampling ratio and feature set for improving imbalanced multi-classification in student grade prediction; (2) Findings that the minority class ratio in imbalanced datasets does not necessarily need to match the majority class ratio to achieve better performance; (3) Evidence that the proposed model impacts prediction performance differently based on the versatility of the feature selection algorithm after SMOTE implementation. This paper is organized as follows: Section II describes related research on grade prediction. Section III illustrates the methodology for developing predictive models. Sections IV and V present the descriptive analysis and prediction results, respectively. Section VI discusses the findings. Section VII highlights the main conclusions and future directions.

Our dataset contains records of 641 students who taken two core courses namely Computer System Architecture (CSA) and Introduction to Computer System (ICS). Based on the analysis performed, we found 362 students obtained distinction grade (A−, B+, B) in CSA course, followed by the pass grade (B−, C+, C, C−, D+, D) with 176 students, the excellent grade (A) with 80 students, failed grade (E, E−, F) with 19 students and finally exceptional grade (A+) with 4 students. input: We compared six machine learning algorithms on a student dataset using ten-fold cross-validation with stratification. Performance was measured using accuracy, precision, recall, and f-measure. Table 5 summarizes results showing J48 and RF achieved the highest precision at 0.989, followed by kNN at 0.985, LR at 0.983, and SVM at 0.981. NB had the lowest precision at 0.978. USING MACHINE LEARNING ALGORITHMS

Our main objective is to compare the predictive model based on the accuracy performance in this section. Here, six selected algorithms were used to train the student dataset and their prediction accuracy was evaluated. In order to analyze the differences, we compare the performance accuracy using the ten-fold cross-validation with stratification as a testing method to derive the best predictive model for optimal results. We measure the performance using various metrics including classification accuracy, precision, recall (Sensitivity) and f-measure to ensure the predictive model was fit to produce accurate results. Table 5 summarizes the prediction performance measures of different classifier on the student dataset. It can be seen from Table 4 that the results indicated J48 and RF achieves the best prediction performance with precision score of 0.989 whereas followed by kNN with 0.985. Meanwhile, LR and SVM obtained precision 0.983 and 0.981 respectively. The lowest model is achieved by NB with 0.978. However, because of the classes in our dataset were highly imbalanced, the prediction results were often lead to misclassification decisions of the minority class that was created while training the dataset. For generalizability purpose, another experiments in dealing with the issues were conducted to reduce the ratio of each classes which it is described in the next subsection.

This study increased the default parameter of nearest neighbors (k) in the sample SG in the minority class, randomly selected N samples, and recorded them as SG_i. section: VI. DISCUSSION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: This study addresses imbalanced multi-classification for student grade prediction using a real dataset from JTMK, Malaysia Polytechnics. To handle imbalance, SMOTE and two feature selection (FS) methods were compared across J48, NB, kNN, SVM, and RF using accuracy, precision, recall, and f-measure. Results show all models improved with SMOTE alone; however, wrapper-based FS only significantly improved kNN and NB, while SVM performance remained unchanged due to hyperplane computation limitations in high-dimensional imbalanced data. NB FS usage was supported by prior work [30] showing highest accuracy with wrapper-based selection. FS alone did not improve RF, likely due to the imbalanced dataset, though it enabled quicker model interpretation without reliance on few features [34]. Combining SMOTE with appropriate feature selection introduced the SFS model, which outperformed previous studies [12], [15]. The best accuracy of 99.5% was obtained by RF, slightly higher than kNN and J48, making RF the ideal algorithm; kNN was identified as the ideal solution working with the best k value and optimal features [35]. The proposed SFS model had a significant effect on kNN depending on the FS algorithm, similar to kNN's best performance in handling imbalanced data across case studies [36]. Overall, oversampling SMOTE benefits predictive models, but integrating accurate features with different FS algorithms influences effectiveness. Limitations include analysis on a single dataset, reliance on specific algorithms, and use of only SMOTE; thus, future work should test other datasets and algorithms, including SVM ensembles, which showed greater accuracy in prior work [37].

section: VII. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: This paper proposes a multiclass prediction model using six models to predict final student grades based on first-semester exam results. A comparative analysis of SMOTE oversampling combined with feature selection methods shows improved accuracy over feature selection alone. The proposed model performs more effectively than SMOTE and feature selection alone with certain parameter settings. These findings offer a practical approach for addressing imbalanced multi-classification through data-level solutions for student grade prediction. In higher education institutions, predictive analytics supports governance and decision-making. Future work should investigate emerging machine learning algorithms and ensemble methods to optimize prediction results. Additionally, analysis of multiple imbalanced datasets using appropriate sampling techniques and metrics suitable for imbalanced domains, such as Kappa and Weighted Accuracy, is recommended to enhance decision support systems and improve student academic performance.
output:
Predicting student grades is one of the key performance indicators that can help educators monitor their academic performance. Therefore, it is important to have a predictive model that can reduce the level of uncertainty in the outcome for an imbalanced dataset. This paper proposes a multiclass prediction model with six predictive models to predict final student’s grades based on the previous student final examination result of the first-semester course. Specifically, we have done a comparative analysis of combining oversampling SMOTE with different FS methods to evaluate the performance accuracy of student grade prediction. We also have shown that the explored oversampling SMOTE is overall improved consistently than using FS alone with all predictive models. However, our proposed multiclass prediction model performed more effectively than using oversampling SMOTE and FS alone with some parameter settings that can influence the performance accuracy of all predictive models. Here, our findings contribute to be a practical approach for addressing the imbalanced multi-classification based on the data-level solution for student grade prediction.

In HEI, predictive analytics plays a significant role in governance for improving valuable information and developing trusted decision-making that contributes to data science [38]. Determining the quality of the collected dataset to reduce the imbalance and missing values difficulties is part of the challenging issues that adhere to select the relevant and valuable predictive models [39]. Therefore, as for future works, further investigation on the use of appropriate emerging predictive techniques in such advanced machine learning algorithms [40] and more ensemble algorithms are recommended to optimize the result for predicting student grades. It is also essential to select several multi-class imbalanced datasets to be analyzed with appropriate sampling techniques and different evaluation metrics which suitable for the imbalanced multi-class domain such as Kappa, Weighted Accuracy and other measures. Thus, using machine learning in higher learning institutions for student grade prediction will ultimately enhance the decision support system to improve their student academic performance in the future.

In the last few years, ensembling techniques have shown power in data mining competitions such as the Netflix challenge; however, such methods have not found wide use in computational biology. This work shows how ensembling techniques can be applied to practical problems, including bioinformatics, and how they often outperform other machine learning techniques in both predictive power and robustness. Furthermore, a methodology of ensembling, Multi-Swarm Ensemble (MSWE), is developed by using multiple particle swarm optimizations and its ability to enhance the performance of ensembles is demonstrated.

input: The exponential growth of data in computational biology has transformed the field, making data extraction as critical as storage. While machine learning is widely applied across sub-fields like genomics and proteomics, the techniques used often lag behind advancements in machine learning itself, with simple, older methods remaining prevalent due to their ease of use. Ensembling methods, such as random forests and bagging, represent the leading edge of machine learning, offering improved accuracy and robustness. Ensemble learning combines multiple models to create a final model, often by manipulating training data through random sampling.

data availability. On one hand is the issue of how to store
and access the trove of information, and on the other hand

Machine learning has been used in many sub-ﬁelds of

microarrays, systems biology, evolution and text mining,
etc. It has been used in aiding gene prediction [1], identifying regulatory elements [2], [3], [4] and non-coding RNAs
[5], predicting protein structures, interpreting proteomics

While there is a good amount of machine learning being
utilized in the ﬁeld of computational biology, the level of
techniques being used lags behind what is being developed
in the ﬁeld of machine learning. Simple, older methods are
the most commonly used in computational biology. Often

in the evaluation of gene expression data from microarray

Ensembling methods have been on the leading edge of

input: Different ways to manipulate training data, such as assigning weights to samples or modifying features, create diverse models but risk reducing individual model performance. While combining different machine learning algorithms preserves information, existing ensemble methods like voting and grading either assign equal weights or rely on performance-based weighting, which may not optimize the ensemble effectively. Greedy hillclimbing methods improve on grading but risk local minima. To address this, this study proposes Multi-Swarm Ensemble (MSWE), which uses particle swarm optimization (PSO) to determine weights for machine learning algorithms and ensembles them to maximize AUC. Using combined weights from ten PSO ensembles increases robustness against overfitting and variance. Experiments demonstrate that MSWE achieves consistent superior performance over conventional algorithms and improves ensemble performance compared to greedy approaches.
