the training set is to assign weights to each training sample,
and after training a model with the training data, updating
the weights by increasing the weights of samples that were
incorrectly classiﬁed, and decreasing the weight of samples
that were correctly classiﬁed before training the next model.
This method will create models that are increasingly better at
predicting the more difﬁcult samples, AdaBoost [20]. Changes
in the features can be similarly performed. One example, as in
Cherkauer et al. [21], in which multiple artiﬁcial neural networks were constructed, each with a different subset of the
features available. Random forests [13] for example uses a
combination of manipulating both features and training samples. There are yet other methods of manipulating data to
achieve varying models, such as including randomness in the
data and manipulating output targets [18]. Besides data
manipulations, one can also achieve different models through
parameter tuning and the utilization of different models.
Ensembles that are generated by combining different
machine learning algorithms seem to be a logical choice,
according to [18] “A necessary and sufﬁcient condition for
an ensemble of classiﬁers to be more accurate than any of its
individual members is if the classiﬁers are accurate [deﬁned
as any improvement over random guessing] and diverse.”
While the methods of data manipulation explained above
do create diversity, the individual models might suffer in
performance from the removal of training samples and/or
features. Instead, by utilizing different algorithms, you can
achieve diversity without the cost of potentially reducing
information content for each individual model.
There are various different methods of combining multiple
models from different machine learning algorithms. One
method is grading [22], in this method the multiple models
are trained on the data and the ﬁnal model is simply a
weighted average of the individual predictions. The weights
are assigned based on the performance of each individual
model. This way a model that performed well has more say in
the ﬁnal results than a model that has performed poorly. A
second method of combining different models is voting [23],
[24]. This is a simpliﬁed version of the grading method. In this
method all models have the same weight, and the predictions
from each model can simply be used in a majority vote manner in order to decide how the ﬁnal model should predict a
particular instance. Stacking [25] is yet another method,
though slightly more involved. In stacking, the multiple models are combined by another model that takes in the outputs of
all the models as features. Finally, the method demonstrated
in Rich et al. [17] uses a greedy hillclimbing algorithm in order
to select which models to utilize in the ensemble. This model
is similar to the grading method in a way since they allow for
multiple copies of the same model, in effect, giving it more
weight. This method of greedy hillclimbing works simply by
ﬁrst selecting the very best performing model from the many
models trained on the data. Once this best model is selected, it
becomes part of the ensemble, which, at this point in the algorithm. consists only of the best method. The next step in this
algorithm is to choose which other model can be added to the
ensemble in order to produce the best overall result. The algorithm attempts all possibilities, and evaluates the ensemble by
simply averaging all the outputs from the models in the
ensemble (as in voting). Once the next best addition to the
ensemble is made, the algorithm continues to add models to
the ensemble until it is no longer beneﬁcial.
Each of the methods above has its advantages. The voting algorithm is simple, fast and performs very well; however, its downside is that it could be further optimized,
given the fact that all models have the same weight in this
ensemble. The Stacking method does achieve some of the
optimization; however, choosing which machine learning
algorithm to use to create the ensemble can have a signiﬁ-
cant impact on the ﬁnal results. Grading is a simple way of
optimizing on the voting method with a machine learning
algorithm bias, albeit not the best optimization technique.
The
ensemble
method
with
greedy
hillclimbing
[17]
improves on the grading technique by attempting to ﬁnd
the best combination of models with a greedy algorithm.
While the greedy hillclimbing ensembling method [17]
does obtain excellent results, the fact that a greedy method
is utilized is a potential area for improvement. Greedy algorithms, while very fast, are very simple and are very prone
to local minima [26]. Greedy algorithms are used due to
their incredibly fast speeds and despite the fact that these
algorithms will likely not output the global optimal solution, their solution should be improved from the worst possible solutions. In the ensembling case, it is assumed that a
greedy method will optimize and outperform a simple voting method. Jogen et al. [26] shows that the greedy algorithm will, under some conditions, output the very worst
possible solution in an optimization problem. Without prior
knowledge of when this occurrence will happen, it seems
unadvisable to rely on such a method. With this in mind,
we were compelled to analyze an ensemble algorithm that
relied on a better performing optimization algorithm.
The particle swarm optimization (PSO) is a popular
computational method to iteratively ﬁnd optimal solutions.
Thus, in this study we aim to use an ensemble of PSOs to
improve on the AUC of an ensemble of various machine
learning algorithms. Since PSO is a very good optimizer, it
is expected that the solutions will outperform those
obtained through greedy algorithms. However, in order to
avoid overﬁtting, and to improve robustness, we decided to
use the combined weights of ten PSO ensembles, in essence
creating an ensemble of ensembles. This will also increase
the consistency of the ensemble, given that PSO is an algorithm with a random element and every run has a degree of
variance, thus avoiding overﬁtting the weights for the
machine learning algorithms. Therefore, in this paper, we
propose a method, Multi-Swarm Ensemble (MSWE) that
utilizes multiple particle swarm optimizations to obtain the
weights of the machine learning algorithms, and then
ensembles them to maximize the AUC. We are able to show
the consistent superior performance of ensemble learning
over conventional machine learning algorithms; furthermore, we show the increased performance of ensembles
when using the MSWE methodology.

METHODS

2.1 Datasets
The datasets were collected from the UCI machine learning repository [30], [31] and from a breast cancer metastasis dataset obtained from van de Vijver [32]. The datasets were split into training and testing sets; for the breast cancer data, a 50/50 split was used due to small sample size. For other datasets, the training set was divided into three parts: 50% for training machine learning algorithms, 25% for estimating performance and training the ensemble, and 25% for estimating ensemble performance. Datasets with separate test sets were divided as described. The Connect-4 dataset was used twice to generate two binary classification problems (win vs. loss/draw and loss vs. win/draw) to demonstrate method stability. The letter recognition dataset was transformed into two problems: classifying "O" vs. others (easier, unbalanced) and classifying letters from the first or last 13 letters of the alphabet (harder, balanced) [17]. Only the breast cancer dataset underwent feature selection, using information gain [33] to select the top 80 genes from the training data.

2.2 Machine Learning Algorithms
Various machine learning algorithms were tested using the Weka software package [34]. The methods selected represented a wide array of methodologies including Bayesian, functions, nearest neighbors, simple rules, trees, and ensemble learners. Specific methods used were: BayesNet, Naïve Bayes, Logistic regression, SMO, IBK1, IBK5, KStar, LWL, Decision table, FURIA, JRip, PART, ADTree, BFTree, FT, LMT, NBTree, RepTree, J48, and VFI. Ensemble learning methods included Random forest, average, grading, and greedy ensemble. The average ensemble uses the average output of all algorithms. The grading ensemble multiplies the average output by each algorithm's AUC from training data. The greedy ensemble uses a greedy algorithm to optimize weights for each algorithm, as in Rich [17].

2.3 Particle Swarm Optimization
Particle swarm optimization (PSO) is a nature-inspired metaheuristic that makes few assumptions, applies to non-differentiable problems, and searches large spaces. PSO optimizes a function by particles exploring the solution space; each particle represents a possible solution. Particles move towards the best solution with added randomness to avoid local minima, such as in the Schaffer f6 function [27]. This process repeats until the best particle cannot be improved. Movement is determined by a random component and an optimization component, with coefficients that typically decrease over time. Different PSO variations define the "best solution" differently, sometimes using multiple best solutions.

2.4 Multi-Swarm Ensemble Method
The proposed Multi-Swarm Ensemble (MSWE) method utilizes multiple particle swarm optimizations to obtain weights for machine learning algorithms in an ensemble to maximize resulting AUC. First, conventional machine learning algorithms are trained. Then, a particle swarm algorithm optimizes the weights of each algorithm to maximize ensemble AUC. This process repeats ten times to obtain ten sets of weights. Finally, the weights for each algorithm are averaged into a single weight, used to combine predictions into the final ensemble. The final result is an ensemble of ensembles, as each set of weights from each PSO run forms an ensemble, and ten such ensembles are combined. The PSO algorithm used was from the Matlab toolbox: Another Particle Swarm Toolbox [36].

2.1 Datasets
The datasets were collected from the UCI machine learning repository [30], [31] and from a breast cancer metastasis dataset obtained from van de Vijver [32]. Table 1 contains information about these datasets.

The datasets were divided in the following manner. First they were divided into two, the first half used for training and the second half for testing. The training set was further divided into 3 parts (consisting of 50, 25 and 25 percent of the training data). The first part was used to train the machine learning algorithms, the second part was used to estimate the performance of those methods and to train the ensemble, and the third part was used to estimate the performance of the ensemble. Some of these datasets already contained a separate test set; in those cases, the provided training set was again divided into 3 parts as described above. For the breast cancer data, given its small sample size, the data was simply split into training and testing (50/50). The machine learning models were trained on the training set with 10-fold cross validation; the ensemble was then trained on the training data. Of all the datasets, the only dataset that had feature selection performed was the breast cancer dataset. This was performed to mimic the real use of these types of datasets where a small number of predictive genes are selected as genetic markers of a condition. The feature selection performed used information gain [33] to rank the genes, and the top 80 genes were selected. This was performed using the training data only. Information gain is a simple measure of the information content of a single feature; this is measured as the ability of the feature to separate instances from the different classes. The connect 4 datasets was used twice. The classification problem for this dataset is to separate a win, a loss and a draw. Two binary classification problems were generated from this dataset, one to predict a win versus a loss or draw, and one to predict a loss versus a win or draw. Given the nature of the game, these two problems are identical, and the purpose of using these two classification problems was to demonstrate the stability of methods, since there should be no difference expected in performance between these two datasets for a given method. The letter recognition dataset was also transformed into two separate problems in the same manner as in Rich et al. [17]. The first classification problem is to classify the letter “O” from all the other, creating an easier, but unbalanced problem. The second classification problem is to classify a letter as belonging from the first 13 letters of the alphabet or the last 13 letters; this creates a balanced but much harder problem.

2.2 Machine Learning Algorithms
Various machine learning algorithms were tested in this work. The methods tested in this study used the Weka software package [34]. The methods were chosen to represent a wide array of methodologies: Bayesian, functions, nearest neighbors, simple rules, trees and ensemble learners. The methods used were: BayesNet, Naïve Bayes, Logistic regression, SMO, IBK1, IBK5, KStar, LWL, Decision table, FURIA, JRip, PART, ADTree, BFTree, FT, LMT, NBTree, RepTree, J48, VFI. The ensemble learning methods used were: Random forest, average, grading, and greedy ensemble.

The average ensemble is simply an ensemble in which the average of the output of all machine learning algorithms is used as the output. The grading ensemble works in a similar manner, but in this case the average of the outputs of the machine learning algorithms in the ensemble are multiplied by their respective AUCs from the training data. The greedy ensemble uses a greedy algorithm to optimize the weights used for each machine learning algorithm in the ensemble, as in Rich [17].

2.3 Particle Swarm Optimization
The field of evolutionary computation offers various methods of optimization that can achieve great performance. Of these, a popular method is particle swarm optimization (PSO). Particle swarm optimization is within the field of nature inspired/swarm intelligence algorithm. PSO is a metaheuristic, and as such, makes few to no assumptions about a problem, can be applied to problems that are not differentiable, and can search very large spaces. PSOs can be used in extremely irregular problems with many local optima, such as Schaffer f6 function [27]; which is a function with many local minima. In PSO, a function is optimized by particles exploring the solution space of the problem. The first step is to define the solution space and randomly populate the solution space with particles; each particle represents a possible solution. The next step is to compute the solution for each particle, after which each particle moves towards the best particle in the solution space, with some added randomness to reduce the chances of local minima.

This process is repeated until the best particle in the solution space can no longer be improved. There are various algorithms determining the movement of particles in the field of PSO. In general terms there are 2 simple components that determine the movement of a particle. A random component and an optimization component. The simplest form of a random component is a random direction that is added to the movement of the particle multiplied by a coefficient that usually decreases with, similar to cooling in simulated annealing. The optimization component is the direction towards the best solution of the colony also multiplied by a coefficient. Different variations of PSO use different “best solution” definitions and some use multiple best solutions.

2.4 Multi-Swarm Ensemble Method
Our proposed method, Multi-Swarm Ensemble (MSWE), utilizes multiple particle swarm optimizations to obtain the weights of the machine learning algorithms in an ensemble to maximize the resulting AUC. In our methodology, the first step is to train the conventional machine learning algorithms. The next step is to use a particle swarm algorithm to optimize the weights of each machine learning algorithm to optimize the AUC of their ensemble. This process is repeated ten times in order to obtain ten sets of weights for the machine learning algorithms. Finally, the weights for each machine learning algorithm are averaged into a single weight; these weights are then used to combine the predictions of the machine learning algorithms into the final ensemble. The ensemble is a weighted average ensemble where the predictions from all machine learning algorithms are averaged together with their respective weights from the particle swarm optimization. The final result is in reality an ensemble of ensembles, since each set of weights from each particle swarm optimization run is in itself an ensemble, and ten of those are combined forming the final ensemble. The particle swarm optimization algorithm used was from the Matlab [35] toolbox: Another Particle Swarm Toolbox [36].

When selecting a machine learning algorithm for use, researchers tend to follow one of two approaches: relying on a preferred algorithm from the past or attempting many methods and choosing the one that performs the best for that particular problem. Unfortunately, one cannot know how well a method will perform on data meant to be predicted on; only how well it will perform on training data. From training data, researchers can obtain an estimate of how they expect the chosen method to perform. Fig. 2 compares both approaches of model selection. The blue bars represent the overall best method (LMT), while the red bars represent the best method for each dataset given the training data. This figure plots the loss in AUC between the AUC of these two choices of models for each dataset and the AUC of the method that actually performed the best in the test set. By taking the best performer in each individual dataset, one is making the best possible choice of a machine learning algorithm given the data at hand; however, this figure shows that even this approach is unreliable. This approach still underperformed in six out of nine cases; in two of these six cases, the best method underperformed the best method in the test set by 8 and 7 percent in AUC. This data shows that selecting a best overall method is not reliable, given that each dataset is different and might yield better performance under a different machine learning algorithm. section: CONCLUSION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Ensembles outperform individual machine learning algorithms in AUC, reliability, robustness, and consistency. The MSWE method outperformed the best individual algorithm across all 9 datasets, improving AUC and consistency. In the breast cancer dataset, where overfitting was an issue, MSWE improved robustness. In the connect-4 dataset, where AUC differences between algorithms were small, MSWE improved reliability. Ensembles leverage information from all available methods, increasing robustness by mitigating individual overfitting. The MSWE method optimizes algorithm weights using particle swarm optimization (PSOs), achieving better AUC fine-tuning than grading or greedy hillclimbing methods, while avoiding weight overfitting through an ensemble of multiple PSO runs. While conventional machine learning remains widely used, the scientific community should adopt newer methods. In the breast cancer microarray dataset, choosing a 40 percent precision threshold, MSWE achieved a recall of 82.5 percent compared to 44.5 percent for the best individual algorithm, enabling the identification of nearly twice as many patients with future metastasis.

Our work has shown that an ensemble approach outperforms
individual machine learning algorithms in AUC, reliability,
robustness and consistency. The improvement in AUC and
consistency was shown by the fact that the MSWE method
outperformed the best individual machine learning algorithm in all 9 datasets. The improvement in robustness was
shown in the breast cancer dataset on which overﬁtting
was an issue, and the improvement in reliability was
shown in the connect-4 dataset in which the difference in
AUCs was much smaller with ensembles. In general,
ensembles can outperform machine learning algorithms
because they use the information from all methods available. Ensembles also increase robustness and reliability
given the fact that if a method overﬁts in a dataset, it will
still be ensembled with other methods. We also show
how the MSWE method outperforms other ensembling
methods. Our proposed MSWE method improves on the
weights of machine learning algorithms within the ensembles with the use of PSOs. This increases the AUC by better
ﬁne tuning the weights than other methods in which different weights are assigned for each machine learning algorithm, such as grading or greedy hillclimbing. The MSWE
method also avoids the overﬁtting of the weights due to
the fact that an ensemble of multiple PSO runs are used.
Conventional machine learning algorithms are still widely
used and favored over newer, perhaps more unconventional
methods. As a scientiﬁc community it is important to adapt
and adopt newer methods and ideas. Perhaps, more signiﬁ-
cant than the 15 percent improvement in AUC between the
best machine learning algorithm and the MSWE method in
the breast cancer dataset is the difference in their recall. This
dataset is a microarray gene expression set obtained from
breast cancer tumors. The purpose of this dataset is to predict
future metastasis of the cancer. This type of dataset has been
used to aid healthcare professionals in deciding if further chemotherapy treatment should be administered, as in OncotypeDx [29]. When comparing the best machine learning
algorithm with the MSWE method for this dataset and choosing a threshold precision of 40 percent, the best machine
learning algorithm had a recall of 44.5 percent while the
MSWE method had a recall of 82.5 percent. This means that
with the same percentage of false positives, you can identify
almost twice as many patients with future metastasis. Hopefully, through this work, more bioinformaticians can be
aware of the power of ensembling, and increase its use in a
ﬁeld that is abundant in predictive problems.

section: I. INTRODUCTION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Numerous traffic accidents cause deaths and injuries, and patients often cannot reach medical facilities timely. Researchers proposed Intelligent Transport Systems (ITS) networks to improve road safety by standardizing communication protocols for smart and electrified vehicles [1]. Through ITS, smart automobiles and electric vehicles connect and share data to save human lives during pandemics [3] and enable sustainable mobility via technology [4], such as emission reductions from alleviated traffic volume [5]. The United States was the first regulatory body to recognize the promise of ITS, awarding Dedicated Short Range Communications (DSRC) 75 MHz of the 5.9 GHz spectrum. IEEE develops WAVE standards for Vehicular Ad Hoc Networks (VANET) based on DSRC standards. Mobile vehicles equipped with On-Board Units (OBUs) and fixed Road Side Units (RSUs) comprise the VANET. Smart vehicles support two communication forms: Vehicle-to-Vehicle (V2V) and Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) [6]. Until now, the communication network met the smart vehicle environment criteria [7], [8]. However, as the number of facilities and vehicles increases, the network cannot offer electric vehicle devices ultra-low latency, security, and high dependability. Because electric vehicles rely on connectionless transmission, they are susceptible to cyber-attacks, including Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks. DDoS attacks disrupt V2V and V2G connections, preventing smart vehicles from processing or transmitting critical information, thereby jeopardizing passenger safety. To counter this, researchers suggest the electric vehicle environment must be powered by machine learning security mechanisms. AI and machine learning-enabled electric vehicles provide benefits, including increased device reliability and security. However, when a dataset contains many irrelevant characteristics, machine learning algorithm accuracy decreases. Therefore, researchers seek the best technique to identify important features. Recently, graph-based machine learning [9]–[11] has been developed to select the best features of a dataset. The use of graph-based characteristics for detecting malicious nodes is documented in several research [9], [10], [13], [14]. If a good mix of critical and non-critical elements exists in the data, machine learning algorithms learn more successfully. Malicious node detection methods rely heavily on feature selection [12]. Finding optimal graph-based features to reveal hidden network structures and disclose malicious host communication patterns is key to flow-based characteristics [12]. Using graph-based machine learning and identity-based encryption (IBE), this study discusses a secure data exchange mechanism with a cyber-attack detection approach. The proposed technique guarantees no personal or private information is revealed using an identity-based encryption signature for electric car access control. Network irregularities are evaluated and dangerous packets are excluded using graph-based machine learning.

Related work

Intelligent transport systems (ITS) enable intelligent transportation, improving road safety [17], [18]. However, smart vehicles with limited computing capacity share private information, making them vulnerable to cyberattacks such as data leakage, DoS, and DDoS [19]–[24]. Researchers have suggested detection techniques for various cyberattacks in the ITS environment [26]–[28]. Most existing methods are ineffective for electric vehicles due to low vehicle resources. However, modern communication networks allow the use of sophisticated methods like machine learning, which extract features from raw data to improve detection reaction time [29], [30]. Conventional methods cannot be used in VANETs due to non-continuous topology. A graph-based attack detection method was presented previously [31]–[33], but no study exists on graph-based DDoS detection in VANET scenarios. Other disciplines have presented graph-based techniques; for example, authors in [31] proposed a distributed graph-based technique to monitor IoT devices, classifying traffic as normal or abnormal. Authors in [32] suggested a network graph intrusion detection technique to find malicious nodes. Author [33] proposed Graph-based Outlier Detection in IoT (GODIT) for real-time DoS detection, which analyzes real-time graph data to identify attacks; GODIT can outperform typical machine learning algorithms [33]. For botnet identification, authors in [12] suggest a graph-based ML model that first examines graph property relevance before building a generalized model using key features; this approach reduces training time and model complexity while increasing bot detection rates across two heterogeneous datasets [12]. Beyond graph-based ML, various access control (AC) and attack detection systems exist, but none consider electric vehicle benefits. FGAC has not been extensively studied in the context of electric vehicles [39]. Data leaking is also significant; access control measures ensure only authorized individuals access data, providing rule-based control for data generators [34]–[38]. Authors in [39] proposed a graph-based technique to analyze host communication, but it is not memory efficient as graph size increases with user count [39]. Authors in [12] proposed a graph-based botnet detection technique capable of detecting zero-day attacks, analyzing efficiency using different ML algorithms [12]. While effective, existing AC and attack detection systems do not account for electric vehicle environment benefits [12].

section: III. METHODOLOGY — B. Graph-Based Machine Learning Technique
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
The malicious node detection stage converts network traffic into a graph and uses graph features for detection. Network flow is collected over one time window from RSU-connected smart vehicles. Two tuples are calculated: source IP and packets sent, forming a tuple set T with n total vehicles. Destination IP and packets sent are omitted to reduce memory and increase speed.

A graph G(V,E) is generated using the tuple values. Vertex set V and edge set E represent the graph structure. At the RSU, the following features are extracted from G: in-degree of RSU, out-degree weight, out-degree centrality, betweenness centrality, local clustering coefficient, closeness centrality, eigen centrality, and Katz centrality. In-degree of RSU is calculated as the count of edges E(i) connected to RSU vertices. Out-degree weight measures total packets sent by smart vehicles to RSU. Out-degree centrality is the ratio of outbound connections to total nodes. Betweenness centrality counts shortest paths through a vertex divided by total shortest paths. Local clustering coefficient measures neighbor connectivity density. Closeness centrality is the reciprocal of the sum of shortest paths from a vertex to all others. Eigen centrality reflects node importance based on neighbor significance. Katz centrality estimates relative node significance considering immediate and non-immediate surroundings.

Six machine learning models are used for malicious user detection: SVM with kernel mapping, logistic regression, decision tree classifier, random forest, gradient boosting, and multinomial naive Bayes.

section: V. CONCLUSION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: In this work, we propose a security framework for Intelligent Transport Systems (ITS) that addresses the resource constraints of electric vehicles. The system integrates Identity-Based Encryption (IBE) for access control with entropy measurement and graph-based machine learning for cyberattack detection. Evaluation shows the framework communicates effectively within ITS environments while optimizing vehicle resources. This approach represents a critical first step toward securing ITS using graph-based machine learning, with future work focusing on incorporating additional machine learning technologies.
output: Intelligent Transport Systems (ITS) place a premium on passenger safety. The early work in this field was mainly focused on developing new methods and equipping vehicles with new devices that might improve their performance. However, when the number of cars increases, the limited resources available to Intelligent Transport Systems (ITS) are unable to meet the security needs. The majority of research on the evolution of electric car technology has glossed over this point. Few researchers have addressed this problem and developed AI, machine learning, and deep learning-based security frameworks. These methods, however, are inefficient owing to the resource-constrained nature of electric cars. In this regard, we propose a system for providing AC in an Intelligent Transport System environment while also safeguarding it against various cyber threats. Our system is built on methods from IBE signature scheme, entropy measurement, and graph-based machine learning technique. Access control is managed through IBE, and cyberattacks are detected via entropy measurement and graph-based machine learning techniques that analyze the characteristics of data flow. We got acceptable results showing that our suggested framework is capable of communicating effectively with Intelligent Transport Systems (ITS). Our work is distinguished by a development framework that makes effective use of the smart vehicle system's resources. Our suggested framework is a critical first step toward the development of methods for securing Intelligent Transport Systems (ITS) using graph-based machine learning techniques. Our future research should focus on enhancing the suggested framework via the incorporation of new machine learning technologies.

1 Introduction
Botnets represent networks of computers compromised with sophisticated bot
malware that puts them under the control of a remote attacker [1]. Bot malware
provides the attacker with the ability to remotely control behavior of the
compromised computers through specially deployed Command and Control
(C&C)communicationchannels.Computerscompromisedbythebotmalware
are popularly referred to as bots or zombies, while the attacker is referred to as
the botmaster. Controlled and coordinated by the botmaster, botnets represent
a collaborative and highly distributed platform for the implementation of a
wide range of malicious and illegal activities, such as sending SMAP e-mails,
DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service) attacks, Information theft, etc. Due
to their malicious potential botnets are often regarded as one of the biggest
security threats today [1, 2].
Over the course of the last decade, many botnet detection approaches have
been reported in the literature, with various goals, based on diverse technical
principles and varying assumptions about bot behavior and the characteristics
of botnet network activity [2–4]. As botnets rely on the Internet for both
communicating with the attacker as well as for implementing different attack
campaigns network trafﬁc analysis is one of the main means of identifying
existence of botnets. One of the latest trends in network-based botnet detection
is the use of machine learning algorithms (MLAs) for identifying patterns of
malicious trafﬁc. The main assumption of machine learning-based methods is
that botnets create distinguishable patterns within the network trafﬁc and that
these patterns could be efﬁciently detected using MLAs.This class of detection
approaches promises automated detection that is able to generalize knowledge
about malicious network trafﬁc from the available observations, thus avoiding
pitfalls of signature-based detection approaches that are only able to detect
known trafﬁc anomalies. Various detection methods have been developed
using an array of MLAs deployed in diverse setups [5–24]. These methods
employ diverse principles of trafﬁc analysis targeting various characteristics
of botnet network activity. Furthermore, contemporary detection methods
have been evaluated using different evaluation methodologies and data sets.
The great number of diverse detection solutions introduces the need for a
comprehensive approach to summarizing and comparing existing scientiﬁc
efforts, with a goal of understanding the challenges of this class of detection
methods and pinpointing opportunities for the future work.
A number of authors have tried to summarize the ﬁeld of botnet protection through series of survey papers [1, 2, 25, 26]. Although providing

state of the art on botnet detection, leaving the question of current trends

Abstract
This paper evaluates machine learning for identifying botnet traffic. It reviews background, analysis principles, and state-of-the-art comparative analysis of detection methods. It also outlines challenges, limitations, and future development possibilities for machine learning-based botnet detection systems. The paper is organized as follows: Section 2 presents background on botnet detection with focus on traffic analysis and machine learning. Section 3 presents analysis principles for evaluating existing methods. Section 4 presents a comparative analysis of the state of the art, analyzing prominent approaches by their characteristics, capabilities, and limitations. Section 5 discusses presented scientific efforts and possibilities for future improvements. Section 6 concludes the paper.

2 Botnet Detection
This section presents background on botnet detection focusing on network-based detection and the use of machine learning for identifying botnet network traffic. Depending on the point of deployment, detection approaches are generally classified as client-based or network-based. Client-based detection approaches are deployed at the client computer targeting bot malware operating at the compromised machine [28, 32–37]. These methods commonly detect the presence of bot malware by examining client-level forensics, such as API calls, file changes, application and system logs, active processes, key-logs, resource usage, etc. Some methods also include analysis of traffic visible on the computer’s network interfaces [22–24]. Network-based detection, on the other hand, provides botnet detection by analyzing network traffic at different points in the network. This class of methods identifies botnets by identifying network traffic produced in different botnet operational phases such as C&C communication, attack phase, and propagation [2].

There are conceptual differences between client- and network-based detection, making the latter often seen as more promising. Network-based detection targets the essential aspects of botnet functioning, i.e., network traffic produced as a result of botnet operation. Botnets could make their operation more stealthy by limiting the intensity of attack campaigns (sending SPAM, launching DDoS attacks, scanning for vulnerabilities, etc.) and by tainting and obfuscating C&C communication. However, this often contradicts the goal of providing prompt, powerful, and efficient implementation of malicious campaigns. On the other side, attackers invest great efforts in making the presence of bot malware undetectable at compromised machines through client-level resilience techniques such as rootkit ability and code obfuscation [38–40]. Attackers also try to deploy network-based resilience techniques such as Fast-flux, Domain-flux, and encryption, but these often introduce additional botnet traits usable for detection [17, 41]. Furthermore, network-based detection is primarily based on passive analysis of network traffic, making it more stealthy in operation and even undetectable to botnet operators compared to client-based detection, which could be detected by the malware at the compromised machine. Finally, depending on the point of traffic monitoring, network-based detection can have a wider scope than client-level detection systems. When deployed in core and ISP networks, network-based detection approaches are able to capture traffic from a larger number of client machines. This provides the ability to capture additional aspects of botnet phenomena, such as group behavior of bots within the same botnet [8,

within the same botnet [8, 42], time regularities of bots activity and diurnal
propagation characteristics of botnets [43].
2.1 Network-Based Detection
Network-based detection is based on the analysis of network trafﬁc in order
to identify presence of compromised computers. Network-based detection is
commonly classiﬁed based on the principles of functioning as signature- or
anomaly-based methods. Furthermore, methods can be classiﬁed as passive
or active depending on the stealthiness of their operation.
The passive detection approaches operate based on observation only thus
they do not interfere with botnet operation which makes them stealthy in their
operation and undetectable to the attacker.Active detection methods represent
more invasive methods that actively disturb botnet operation by interfering
with malicious activities or the C&C communication of the bots.Additionally,
these techniques often target speciﬁc heuristics of the C&C communication
or attack campaigns, arguably providing higher accuracy of detection. The
majority of contemporary botnet detection approaches are passive while only
a few such as BotProbe [44] are active.

input:
Abstract

Signature-based methods rely on predefined rules and deep packet inspection to match malicious payload signatures. These techniques detect known botnets with bounded false positives but fail against new threats due to reliance on static signatures and evasion techniques like encryption and DGA.

Anomaly-based detection identifies traffic deviations associated with botnet operation, ranging from rate changes to flow patterns. Unlike signature methods, it can detect novel malicious activity. However, it commonly produces false positives. Machine learning sub-classes improve this by enabling automated pattern recognition from traffic traces without prior knowledge of malicious characteristics.

Machine learning-based detection assumes botnets produce distinguishable network patterns detectable by specific algorithms. The core challenge is generalizing from limited prior experiences to new events. Algorithms are classified as supervised or unsupervised. Supervised methods, such as SVM, ANN, decision trees, and Bayesian classifiers, train on input-output pairs to classify traffic as malicious or benign. Unsupervised methods, such as K-means and hierarchical clustering, identify groups of similar observations without prior training. Traffic classification depends on the feature set extracted from network instances.
output:
Signature-based methods are based on recognizing botnet speciﬁc characteristics of trafﬁc, also known as “signatures” [45–48]. The signature-based
methods rely on a set of predeﬁned rules regarding anomalous trafﬁc and
packet level signatures. These approaches commonly performs packet level
analysis by using deep packet inspection (DPI) in order to match signatures of
malicious payloads. This class of detection techniques covers all three phases
of botnet life-cycle and it is able to detect known botnets with bounded number
of false positives (FP). The main drawback of signature-based approaches is
that they are only able to detect known threats, and that efﬁcient use of these
approaches requires constant update of botnet trafﬁc signatures. Additionally,
these techniques are liable of various evasion techniques that change signatures of botnet trafﬁc and malicious activities of bots, such as encryption and
obfuscation of C&C channel, Fast-ﬂux and DGA techniques, etc.
Anomaly-based detection is a class of detection methods that is devoted to
the detection of trafﬁc anomalies associated with botnet operation [5–24, 42,
49–53]. The trafﬁc anomalies that could be used for detection vary from easily
detectable as changes in trafﬁc rate and latency, to more ﬁnite anomalies in
ﬂow patterns. Some of the most prominent anomaly-based approaches detect
anomalies in packet payloads [45, 49], DNS trafﬁc [17, 51, 52], botnet group
behaviour [8, 42, 43], etc. The anomaly-based detection can be realized using
different algorithms ranging from the statistical approaches, machine learning
techniques, graph analysis, etc. In contrast to the signature-based detection,
the anomaly-based detection is generally able to detect new forms of malicious
activity that exhibits anomalous botnet related characteristics. However, one
of the main challenges of using anomaly-based detection is the fact that in
contrast to signature-based detection these approaches result in false positives.
One of the latest and the most promising sub-class of anomaly-based methods
are detection methods that rely on machine learning for detection of bot-related
trafﬁc patterns. The machine learning is used because it offers the possibility
of automated recognition of bot-related trafﬁc patterns.Additionally, machine
learning provides the ability of recognizing the patterns of malicious trafﬁc
without a prior knowledge about the malicious trafﬁc characteristics, but by
inferring knowledge from the available botnet trafﬁc traces.
2.2 Machine Learning for Botnet Detection
The basic assumption behind machine learning-based methods is that botnets
produce distinguishable patterns of network activity and that these patterns
could be detected by employing some of the MLAs [28, 29].
On the Use of Machine Learning for Identifying Botnet Network Trafﬁc
7
Machine Learning (ML), is a branch of artiﬁcial intelligence, that has the
goal of construction and studying of systems that can learn from data [54].
Learning in this context implies ability to recognize complex patterns and
make qualiﬁed decisions based on previously seen data. The main challenge of
machine learning is how to provide generalization of knowledge derived from
the limited set of previous experiences, in order to produce a useful decision
for new, previously unseen, events. To tackle this problem the ﬁeld of Machine
Learning develops an array of algorithms that discover knowledge from
speciﬁc data and experience, based on sound statistical and computational
principles. Machine learning algorithms can be coarsely classiﬁed based on
the desired outcome of the algorithm as supervised MLAs and unsupervised
MLAs.
Supervised learning [55] is the class of well-deﬁned machine learning
algorithms that generate a function (i.e., model) that maps inputs to desired
outputs. These algorithms are trained by examples of inputs and their corresponding outputs, and then they are used to predict output for some future
inputs. The supervised MLAs are used for classifying input data into some
deﬁned class and for regression that predict continuous valued output. In
the context of botnet detection, supervised MLAs are commonly used for
implementing network trafﬁc classiﬁers that are able to classify malicious
from non-malicious trafﬁc or identify trafﬁc belonging to different botnets.
Some of the most popular supervised MLAused for botnet detection are: SVM
(Support Vector Machines), ANN (Artiﬁcial Neural Networks), Decision tree
classiﬁers and Bayesian classiﬁer.
Unsupervised learning [56] is the class of machine learning algorithms
where training data consists of a set of inputs without any corresponding
target output values. The goal of unsupervised learning may be to discover
groups of similar examples within the input data, referred to as clustering, to
determine the distribution of data within the input space, known as density
estimation, or to project the data from a high-dimensional space down to two
or three dimensions for the purpose of visualization. In the context of botnet
detection, un-supervised MLAs are commonly used for the clustering of botrelated observations. The main characteristic of unsupervised MLAs is that
they do not need to be trained beforehand. The most popular unsupervised
learning approaches used for botnet detection are: K-means, X-means and
Hierarchical clustering.
In both learning scenarios trafﬁc is analyzed from a certain analysis
perspective that entails how do trafﬁc instances, that will be classiﬁed or
clustered by MLAs, look like. For each of trafﬁc instances a set of features

input: Stevanovic and Pedersen analyze machine learning methods for botnet traffic detection across TCP, UDP, HTTP, IRC, and DNS protocols. They categorize contemporary detection methods by the machine learning algorithms (MLAs) used, distinguishing between supervised and unsupervised approaches and noting that analysis perspective depends on targeted protocols. Regarding real-time operation, the authors note that timely detection requires efficient processing of large data quantities, though requirements vary by analysis principles and detection goals. For performance evaluation, the authors emphasize that reliable results depend on high-quality datasets with known "ground truth," distinguishing between malicious botnet traffic and benign "background" traffic. Labeled datasets are formed through four scenarios: labeling existing traces via IDS or signature systems, merging traces from researcher-deployed honeypots, merging traces from fully controllable test environments with available bot malware source code, and merging traces from semi-controlled environments with purposely infected machines under traffic filtering. Non-malicious traffic can be self-generated or captured from LAN, campus, enterprise, core, or ISP networks, though ensuring benign representativeness is challenging outside controlled networks and must match the monitoring point and network type of the malicious trace.

• MLAs – The contemporary detection methods rely on different MLAs employed in diverse setups in order to perform detection of malicious network traffic. Both supervised and unsupervised MLAs are used offering different levels of automation and resulting in different types of findings. Furthermore, traffic is analyzed by the MLAs from different perspectives depending on the targeted communication protocols. Finally, in order to capture anomalous characteristics of botnet traffic detection approaches rely on a diverse sets of traffic features extracted for each traffic instance analyzed by the MLAs. In this analysis we outline MLAs and traffic analysis perspective used by the detection methods. Furthermore, we briefly elaborate on the employed feature representation.

• Real-time operation – Timely detection is the preferred characteristic of detection systems defined as the ability of operating efficiently and producing the detection results in a “reasonable” time. The timely detection entails a need for a detection method to operate in real-time fashion, thus being capable of processing large quantities of data efficiently. However, it should be noted that the requirements of realtime operation vary depending on the used traffic analysis principles and the goal of detection. In this analysis we outline methods that are advertised as providing real-time detection and detection approaches that have potential of being used in real-time based on their operational efficiency.

3.2 Performance Evaluation

Performance evaluation is realized by analyzing evaluation practices used for experimenting with detection methods, quantitative and qualitative aspects of evaluation data and obtained detection performance.

One of the main prerequisites of reliable performance evaluation is the qualityoftrafﬁcdatasetsusedfortrainingandtestingoftheproposeddetection approaches [3, 31]. The evaluation data sets should include a substantial amount of traffic for which the “ground truth” is known i.e. traffic consisting of elements labeled as malicious and non-malicious. Correctly labeled data sets are one of the main requirements of deterministic evaluation of detection performance.The malicious traffic represent traffic produced by botnets, while non-malicious traffic, often refereed to as the “background” traffic originates from benign applications running on “clean” computers. The labeled data set On the Use of Machine Learning for Identifying Botnet Network Trafﬁc 11 is formed either by labeling previously recorded traffic trace or by combining malicious and non malicious data sets. Typical scenarios of obtaining labeled data sets are outlined bellow:

• Scenario 1 – Labeled traffic is obtained by performing labeling of a network trace using a variety of different labeling practices. The labeling of the traffic can be done by using some of the existing IDS systems [46, 47, 57] and signature-based botnet detection systems [45, 48] or by relying on domain name and IP address blacklists.

• Scenario 2 – Labeled traffic is obtained by merging a non-malicious traffic trace with a malicious traffic trace captured by Honeypots [58] deployed by researchers themselves or by some third party.

• Scenario 3 – Labeled traffic is obtained by merging a non-malicious traffic trace with a malicious traffic trace generated within fully controllable testing environments, where researchers have total control on both C&C servers and compromised computers. This scenario requires bot malware source code to be available. Having the source code, experiments can be realized in safe and totally controlled fashion.

• Scenario 4 – Labeled traffic is obtained by merging a non-malicious traffic trace with a malicious traffic trace generated in semi-controlled testing environments, by purposely infecting computers with a specific bot malware. Compromised computers are allowed to contact the C&C servers in order for bot-related traffic to be recorded. In order to limit any unwanted damage to the third parties on the Internet the traffic produced by infected machines is filtered using different rate and connection limiting techniques as well as matching of the malicious signatures of bot traffic [58].

Non-malicious traffic traces could be obtained in various ways: from self generated traffic using statistical traffic generators to the network traces recorded on LAN, campus/enterprise and in some cases even core and ISP networks. However, it should be noted that for the process of obtaining background traffic the primary concern is to make sure that the traffic traces are benign and “representable” for the particular point of traffic monitoring. While easily achieved on the controlled LAN networks, making sure that traffic obtained from other real-world networks is benign is a much more challenging task. Furthermore, as traffic from one network to another vary, background traffic should match the malicious trace in terms of the point of traffic monitoring and the type of network. 12

Evaluating methods across traffic traces from different botnet types indicates the ability to cope with new threats. Using separate traces for training and testing indicates generalization capability. Understanding performance metrics is crucial for assessing detection capabilities. Common metrics include true positive rate (TPR), true negative rate (TNR), false positive rate (FPR), false negative rate (FNR), accuracy, error rate, and precision. TPR is calculated as TP divided by TP plus FN. TNR is TN divided by TN plus FP. FPR is FP divided by FP plus TN. FNR is FN divided by FN plus TP. Accuracy is the sum of TP and TN divided by the total samples. Error rate is the sum of FP and FN divided by the total samples. Precision is TP divided by TP plus FP. TP represents positive samples classified as positive; TN represents negative samples classified as negative; FP represents negative samples classified as positive; FN represents positive samples classified as negative. However, detection approaches are commonly expressed using only a subset of these metrics, most commonly TPR and FPR.

for detection to be evaded botnets should severely limit the efﬁciency of implementing their malicious agenda. The vulnerability of detection approaches to

Background
Most methods were evaluated on campus or LAN networks using Scenario 1 data [8, 11, 13-17, 19-21]. DNS traffic analysis with domain/IP blacklists/whitelists was the dominant labeling method [8, 14-17, 19, 21], while others used commercial IDS [11, 13, 20]. Only 4 approaches used Scenario 2, requiring malware code execution (Scenario 3) or binaries (Scenario 4) [8, 11, 13, 20]. Performance was evaluated on traces from more than 5 bot samples for only 5 approaches [7, 18, 21, 23, 24], with a maximum of 188 samples [18]. Most methods tested with fewer than 4 bot malware samples. The diversity of malware samples is poor, as most rely on fewer than 3 botnet families. DNS-based approaches often have an unknown number of contributing botnet families. Reported performance indicates strong potential for identifying botnet traffic using MLAs. Several methods achieved 100% True Positive Rate (TPR) and low False Positive Rate (FPR) [11, 19, 20]. Many approaches have FPR below 1%, suggesting real-world operational viability.

Vulnerability to Evasion Techniques
Table 4 shows the strength of indication (SF – strong factor, WF – weak factor) of methods being evaded. These indications are guidelines, not precise measures. Most methods are resistant to encryption of botnet traffic; only four approaches [7, 12, 21, 22] relying on packet payload features are vulnerable. However, the majority are vulnerable to flow perturbation due to flow-level analysis. All techniques are more or less vulnerable to time-based evasion, especially those promising real-time operation. Client-based techniques [22-24] are vulnerable to evasion targeting host internal monitoring. This study does not address evasion complexities or their effect on botnet utility. Future work should analyze modern detection system vulnerability to evasion techniques and their effect on overall botnet utility.

Background — M. Stevanovic and J. M. Pedersen

5.1 Principles of Traffic Analysis
Detection methods target botnets from monitoring points, mostly local and campus networks. This is because machine learning approaches depend on evaluation data from captured botnet activity. Core and ISP network analysis is challenging due to high traffic volumes. Different monitoring points reveal different botnet portions, making detection methods complementary rather than competing. Methods target specific botnet types based on command-and-control technology to improve performance, but should be combined with other approaches to avoid evasion. Most methods target TCP, UDP, and DNS protocols. The analysis perspective is critical for practical machine learning use; it must encompass the targeted phenomena and be understandable to the system operator. For example, DNS traffic can be analyzed by domain names or domain-to-IP mappings. The latter provides more descriptive results and captures IP and domain flux strategies used by criminals. Table 2 shows that decision tree classifiers (C4.5, Random Forests, REPTree) and clustering methods (Hierarchical, X-means) are commonly used. These have proven capabilities in network traffic analysis. However, features introducing bias, such as IP addresses, or based on packet payloads should be avoided due to evasion risks and privacy violations.

5.2 Evaluation Challenge
The main challenge is obtaining reliable evaluation datasets capturing both malicious and non-malicious traffic. Existing studies use various strategies for ground truth, but each has drawbacks. Scenario 1 relies on domain and IP blacklists or signature-based intrusion detection systems, which can produce unreliable labeling. Efforts to eliminate false positives remain largely unsolved. Scenarios merging malicious and non-malicious traffic suffer from artificially merging diverse traces, which can introduce traffic anomalies and bias detection. Non-malicious background traffic used in datasets must be carefully selected.

input: The majority of botnet detection methods were evaluated using traffic from a limited number of botnets, highlighting the need for testing with more comprehensive malware samples to prove generalization to previously unseen threats. Evaluated methods report promising performance but are characterized by substantial false positives and false negatives. High false positives render methods unusable in operational networks, while false negatives carry a high cost due to potential technical and financial damage from compromised machines. An optimal approach requires false positives near zero and minimized false negatives, though only a few methods analyzed could meet this requirement. Future work should focus on developing operational network detection methods based on network traffic analysis with operator-understandable context, real-time operation, and evaluation using extensive traces from diverse botnets, with special attention to minimizing identification errors. Machine learning algorithms for identifying botnet network traffic have been of research interest for the last decade, resulting in numerous methods based on diverse traffic analysis principles and varying performance. This review outlines the opportunities and challenges of using machine learning for identifying botnet network activity, covering 20 methods proposed over the last decade analyzed by their operational principles, evaluation procedures, performance, and evasion vulnerabilities. While this class of approaches shows great potential, challenges must be thoroughly understood for effective use in network-based botnet detection.

Based on the analysis the majority of the detection approaches were
evaluated using trafﬁc from a modest number of botnets. This could be
explained due to many legal, ethical and practical limitations of obtaining the
botnet trafﬁc traces. However, the small number of used bot samples indicates
the need for more thorough testing where more comprehensive set of malware
samples would be used, in order to prove that the detection system is able to
generalize inferred botnet knowledge to previously unseen botnets.
5.3 Cost of Errors
The evaluated botnet detection methods report overall promising performances of identifying malicious trafﬁc. However, the majority of the
approaches are characterized with a substantial number of FP and FN. We
would like to elaborate on the cost of these errors by following Sommer
et al. [30] analysis of the cost of errors on intrusion detection use case. As in
the case of any other anomaly detection system botnet detection systems are
sensitive to number of FP. The high number of FP positives can easily deem
the detection method unusable from the perspective of the use in operational
networks. Furthermore, depending on the use case botnet detection can have a
high cost of FN as any compromised machine within the operational network
could cause a lot of technical and ﬁnancial damage. Therefore, an optimal
detection approach would have FPclose to zero and minimized number of FN.
However, based on the analysis presented in Section 4 only a few detection
methods could potentially fulﬁll this requirement opening the space for further
improvements.
5.4 Opportunities for Future Work
Future work should be devoted to the development of detection methods that
would ﬁnd their use within operational networks. These methods should rely
on the principles of network trafﬁc analysis that would encompass targeted
botnet network characteristics and would carry the context that is understandable to the operator of the system. Furthermore, one of the important goals
of future detection systems is to operate in real-time thus facilitating timely
detection. The future methods should be evaluated using an extensive set of
network traces originating from different types of botnets. Finally, special
attention should be placed on minimizing the number of errors in identifying
On the Use of Machine Learning for Identifying Botnet Network Trafﬁc
25
botnet network trafﬁc so the proposed methods would performance-wise be
suitable for being used in operational networks.
6 Conclusion
Theuseofmachinelearningalgorithms(MLAs)foridentifyingbotnetnetwork
trafﬁc has been the subject of interest within the research community during
the last decade resulting in numerous detection methods. The contemporary
detection methods are based on different principles of trafﬁc analysis, they
target diverse traits of botnet network activity using a variety of machine
learning algorithms and they consequently provide varying performance of
detection. This paper outlines the opportunities and challenges of using MLAs
for identifying botnet network activity and presents the review of the most
prominent contemporary botnet detection methods based on MLAs. The
presented study covers 20 detection methods, proposed over the last decade.
The methods have been analyzed by investigating principles of their operation,
the used evaluation procedures, obtained performance and vulnerabilities on
evasion techniques. The analysis indicates a great potential of this class of
approaches to be used for identifying botnet network trafﬁc. However, the
study also indicates some of the challenges of using MLAs in the context of
network-based botnet detection that should be thoroughly understood in order
for this class of detection methods to be effectively used.

The approach analyzes runtime behavior to identify malicious activity, reducing false positives compared to signature-based tools. Experiments on a 32-bit Windows testbed show the system detects known malware with 98% accuracy while maintaining low overhead. Detection relies on monitoring system calls and API invocations to build a behavior profile. The method successfully identifies polymorphic and obfuscated samples that evade static analysis. Nguyen and Armitage survey internet traffic classification using machine learning. Kührer et al. evaluate the effectiveness of malware blacklists. Dietrich and Rossow empirically research IP blacklists. Sinha et al. analyze the effectiveness of reputation-based blacklists. Sheng et al. empirically analyze phishing blacklists. Kheir et al. propose Mentor, using positive DNS reputation to filter benign domains from botnet C&C blacklists.

input: Online learning control using adaptive critic designs (ACDs) has been widely studied, but previous methods relying on neural networks with manually designed features require improved generalization and learning efficiency for continuous state and action spaces. This paper presents a novel ACD framework that integrates sparse kernel machines into the critic to address these limitations. A sparsification method based on approximately linear dependence analysis improves kernel machine generalization and computational efficiency. From this framework, two algorithms—kernel HDP (KHDP) and kernel DHP (KDHP)—are proposed and analyzed theoretically and empirically. Due to the representation learning and generalization capability of sparse kernel machines, KHDP and KDHP achieve significantly better performance than previous HDP and DHP with manually designed neural networks. Simulation and experimental results on a continuous-action inverted pendulum problem and a ball and plate control problem demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed kernel ACD methods.
output:
Online Learning Control Using Adaptive Critic Designs With Sparse Kernel Machines

Xin Xu, Senior Member, IEEE, Zhongsheng Hou, Chuanqiang Lian, and Haibo He, Senior Member, IEEE

Abstract—In the past decade, adaptive critic designs (ACDs), including heuristic dynamic programming (HDP), dual heuristic programming (DHP), and their action-dependent ones, have been widely studied to realize online learning control of dynamical systems. However, because neural networks with manually designed features are commonly used to deal with continuous state and action spaces, the generalization capability and learning efficiency of previous ACDs still need to be improved. In this paper, a novel framework of ACDs with sparse kernel machines is presented by integrating kernel methods into the critic of ACDs. To improve the generalization capability as well as the computational efficiency of kernel machines, a sparsification method based on the approximately linear dependence analysis is used. Using the sparse kernel machines, two kernel-based ACD algorithms, that is, kernel HDP (KHDP) and kernel DHP (KDHP), are proposed and their performance is analyzed both theoretically and empirically. Because of the representation learning and generalization capability of sparse kernel machines, KHDP and KDHP can obtain much better performance than previous HDP and DHP with manually designed neural networks. Simulation and experimental results of two nonlinear control problems, that is, a continuous-action inverted pendulum problem and a ball and plate control problem, demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed kernel ACD methods.

Index Terms—Adaptive critic designs, approximate dynamic programming, kernel machines, learning control, Markov decision processes, reinforcement learning.

input: Reinforcement learning (RL) is a machine learning framework for solving sequential decision-making problems modeled using the Markov decision process (MDP) formalism. In RL, an agent interacts with an initially unknown environment and modifies its action policies to maximize cumulative payoffs [1], [2]. Earlier RL research focused on tabular algorithms in discrete state and action spaces [3], but these approaches struggle with high-dimensional state spaces common in real-world applications. This work proposes a deep neural network approach to approximate the value function, enabling RL in continuous and large-scale domains. Reinforcement learning and approximate dynamic programming have received increasing research interest for solving optimal control problems in Markov decision processes with large or continuous state and action spaces. Despite empirical successes in real-world applications, existing algorithms are often slow to converge and require extensive training samples. This issue is closely related to the generalization capability of learning machines. Function approximation is a central topic for improving reinforcement learning efficiency. The main categories include value function approximation, policy search, and actor-critic methods. Actor-critic algorithms, which combine value function and policy search, are more effective for online learning with continuous spaces. Adaptive critic designs, including heuristic and dual heuristic programming, are widely studied; dual heuristic programming is the most popular. However, the learning efficiency of these methods greatly depends on the empirical design of the critic, including network structure and learning rates. Multilayer perceptron neural networks are commonly used but require manual selection. Additionally, robustness to uncertainties remains an open problem due to local minima in neural network training. Recent works have attempted to approximate optimal control using adaptive critic designs with or without a priori system models, but manual basis function design still limits performance. It is desirable to develop automatic feature representation and selection methods for critic learning in adaptive critic designs.

Feature representation and selection is critical for improving generalization performance, yet there are relatively fewer works in reinforcement learning compared to supervised learning. Recently, it was pointed out that the choice of basis functions for the critic should be studied to improve adaptive critic design performance. The motivation of this paper is to present a novel kernel-based feature representation method for adaptive critic designs and develop new online learning control algorithms with sparse kernel machines. Based on statistical learning theory, sparse kernel machines have better generalization capability than conventional multilayer perceptron neural networks with manually designed structures. The goal of this paper is to provide a new kernel-based feature representation method for adaptive critic designs, which is important for realizing efficient online learning control for uncertain dynamical systems.

Kernel machines have been popularly studied for nonlinear and nonparametric supervised and unsupervised learning. The main idea is that an inner product in a high-dimensional feature space can be represented as a Mercer kernel function, allowing existing learning algorithms in linear spaces to be transformed into kernel-based algorithms without explicitly computing the inner products; this is known as the kernel trick. In supervised learning, the most popular kernel machines are support vector machines and Gaussian processes, which have been applied to many classification and regression problems and often achieve state-of-the-art performance. In unsupervised learning, kernel principal component analysis and kernel independent component analysis have also been studied. Comprehensive reviews on kernel machines are available in comprehensive reviews.

The combination of kernel methods with reinforcement learning and approximate dynamic programming has received increased research interest. However, function approximation is more difficult in reinforcement learning than in supervised learning. Earlier work used kernel-based locally weighted averaging to approximate state value functions. Gaussian processes and support vector machines have also been studied in reinforcement learning, such as in temporal difference learning, for reinforcement learning, and in model-based approximate policy iteration. In batch learning of state value functions with discrete state spaces, support vector regression was applied, though there were no theoretical results on the obtained policies. Gaussian process-based policy iteration uses manually selected support points and approximated state transition models. Least-squares policy iteration offers reinforcement learning methods with good convergence, stability, and sample complexity properties, but approximation structures may degrade performance with improper feature selection. A kernel-based least-squares policy iteration algorithm was presented for Markov decision processes with large or continuous state spaces, though it is mainly restricted to discrete actions.

This paper presents a novel framework of adaptive critic designs with sparse kernel machines by integrating kernel methods into the critic learning of adaptive critic design algorithms. A sparsification method based on approximately linear dependence analysis is used to sparsify the kernel machines when approximating action value functions or their derivatives. Using the sparsified kernel machines, two kernel adaptive critic design algorithms, kernel heuristic dynamic programming and kernel dual heuristic programming, are proposed to realize efficient online learning control for dynamical systems. To the best knowledge, there are very few works on integrating kernel methods into online learning control based on adaptive critic designs. Simulation and experimental results on two nonlinear control problems, a continuous-action inverted pendulum and a ball and plate control problem, demonstrate that kernel adaptive critic designs obtain much better performance than previous adaptive critic design methods. The main contributions of this paper are twofold. One is automatic feature representation using kernels for value function approximation in adaptive critic designs. Due to the structure learning and nonlinear approximation ability of sparse kernel machines, kernel heuristic dynamic programming and kernel dual heuristic programming can obtain much better performance than previous heuristic and dual heuristic programming methods with manually designed neural networks. state/action spaces, approximation and generalization methods
for RL have received more and more research interest in
recent years. In the literature, there are several synonyms
used for RL, including approximate/adaptive dynamic programming (ADP) and neuro-dynamic programming [3]–[7].
One common goal of ADP and RL is to solve the optimal
control problem of MDP with large or continuous state and
action spaces. Until now, RL has been shown to be a very
promising framework to solve learning control problems which
are difﬁcult or even impossible for mathematical programming and supervised learning methods. However, despite
some successful empirical results in real-world applications
[8]–[11], realizing efﬁcient online learning control for MDPs
with large or continuous space is still a difﬁcult problem.
In such cases, many RL or ADP algorithms are slow to
converge and require a large amount of training samples
[12]. As indicated in [1], this problem is closely related
to the generalization capability of learning machines, which
is the ability of a learning algorithm to perform accurately
on new, unseen examples after having trained on a ﬁnite
data set.
In order to improve the generalization capability and learning efﬁciency of RL, function approximation has been a
central topic in RL. Currently, there are three main categories
of research work on function approximation for RL, that
is, value function approximation (VFA) [13], [14], policy
search [15], and actor-critic methods [16]. The actor-critic
algorithms, viewed as a hybrid of VFA and policy search,
have been shown to be more effective than standard VFA
or policy search in online learning tasks with continuous
state/action spaces [17]. In an actor-critic learning controller,
there is an actor for policy learning and a critic for VFA
or policy evaluation. One pioneering work on RL algorithms
using the actor-critic architecture can be found in [18].
In recent years, adaptive critic designs (ACDs) [19]–[23],
[28]–[30] were widely studied as an important class of
actor-critic learning control methods for dynamical systems.
Generally, ACDs can be categorized as the following major
groups: heuristic dynamic programming (HDP), dual heuristic programming (DHP), globalized dual heuristic programming (GDHP), and their action-dependent versions [17].
Among ACD architectures, DHP is the most popular one,
which has been proven to be more efﬁcient than HDP [19].
Although ACDs have been applied in various learning control problems [24]–[26], such as aircraft control, automotive
engine control, and power system control, there are still some
difﬁcult issues in the design and implementation of ACDs.
The ﬁrst issue is that the learning efﬁciency and convergence
