section: I. INTRODUCTION — C. Transfer Learning
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: An obstacle in automated sleep staging for wearables is the lack of training data. Transfer learning compensates by pre-training on a larger dataset and re-training on the target task. In sleep staging, in-hospital PSG data can boost wearable performance. A major impediment is the difference between source and target data; specifically, wearable devices use different EEG electrode locations than in-hospital recordings. Differing electrode locations pick up activity from different brain regions at different strengths, so models trained on clinical electrodes perform poorly on wearable electrodes. In previous work, we compared transfer learning algorithms including CORAL, Deep Domain Confusion, and subspace alignment on a fully-supervised sleep staging task and found that freezing several neural network layers and re-training the remaining layers was typically the most effective method. This work seeks to improve upon this baseline by incorporating domain knowledge of electrophysics.
output:
An obstacle in the development of automated sleep staging algorithms for wearable sensors is the lack of wearable-sensor data needed for training machine-learning models. One way to compensate for the lack of data is transfer learning—the process of pre-training a model on a similar but larger dataset and then re-training on the smaller dataset from the desired task (the target). In the case of sleep staging, standard in-hospital PSG’s can be retrieved from patient records and used to boost machine learning performance on wearable devices. An additional impediment to transfer learning, however, is differences between the source and target—the more dissimilarities between the source and target data, the less effective transfer learning will be. For sleep staging, a major difference between in-hospital and wearable sleep staging is the EEG channel locations, as wearable devices frequently utilize electrodes in different locations from in-hospital recordings. Electrodes in differing locations pick up on activity from different regions of the brain at different strengths (Fig. 1), and so machine learning models trained using electrodes in locations typical for clinical practice won’t perform as well when using electrodes in locations used by wearables (Fig. 2).

In our previous work [6], we compared a multitude of transfer learning algorithms—including CORAL [7], Deep Domain Confusion [8], and subspace alignment [9] on a fully-supervised sleep staging task and found that the most effective method was typically the simplest method of freezing several neural network layers and re-training the remaining layers as normal. In this work, we seek to improve on this method further by incorporating domain knowledge of electrophysics.

Physics-informed machine learning improves performance by incorporating known physical laws as data synthesis, additional objectives, or architectural biases [10]. Applications span data compression, fluid dynamics, plasma dynamics, quantum mechanics, materials science, and geophysics [11]–[23], yet the approach remains underexplored for sleep staging.

Low-resolution brain electromagnetic tomography (LORETA) uses scalp EEG to approximate point currents within the brain [24]. A forward model matrix L is constructed using boundary element methods (BEM) derived from MRI-segmented tissue types; a current of 1 unit is simulated at each grid location and orientation (x, y, z) to map potentials to m scalp electrodes [24]. The inverse problem computes point currents S via regularized least-squares (sLORETA), minimizing the difference between measured and modeled EEG while penalizing current magnitude [25]:

Here, L^⊺ is the transpose of L, λ is the regularization constant, H is the average-reference operator (I − (1/N)1_N), N is the number of EEG channels, I is the N×N identity matrix, and 1 is the N×N matrix of ones.

An additional method for improving machine learning performance is the incorporation of known physical laws to add additional information and constraints. Methods of incorporating physics into machine learning include synthesizing or modifying data, adding additional objectives ensuring the machine learning model learns rules which are consistent with known physics, and building biases directly into the model architecture [10]. Applications for physics-informed machine learning include data compression [11], fluid dynamics [12], plasma dynamics [13], quantum mechanics [14], [15], [16], materials science [17], [18], [19], and geophysics [20], [21], [22], [23], however very little research has attempted the application of physics-informed machine learning to sleep staging.

E. LORETA
Low-resolution brain electromagnetic tomography (LORETA) is a method of using scalp EEG to approximate the point currents within the brain which generate the EEG [24]. The first step is to use either finite element methods or boundary element methods (BEM) to create a ‘forward model’ which is a matrix mapping currents at various locations and orientations within the brain to the EEG measurements X ∈ R^{t×m} detected at the set of m real electrodes. The forward model is an n×m matrix L which maps currents S ∈ R^{t×n} at n locations and orientations within the brain to a set of m electrodes on the scalp. The BEM mesh is created from an MRI scan of a human brain. The skin, bone, and brain tissue combined with cerebro-spinal fluid are segmented according to intensity, after which a mesh simulating the shape and electrical properties of each tissue type is created. A grid of evenly spaced locations and orientations (3 orientations are used – one for each direction x, y and z in 3D space) for point currents within the brain is next created. To create the forward model matrix, a current of magnitude 1 unit is simulated at each point and each orientation one-at-a-time while the BEM simulation calculates the resulting electric potentials at the scalp electrodes. The elements of the i’th column of L are equal to the potentials detected at each electrode in response to a current at the i’th position and orientation within the brain: X = LS (1)

Once the forward model has been created, computing the point currents S is an inverse problem. One of several approaches is called sLORETA [25] - which computes the point currents from EEG measurements via regularized least-squares:
min_{S} ||HX − LS||_2^2 + λ||S||_2^2 (2)
⇒ S = L^⊺ H (H L L^⊺ H + λ H)^{-1} X (3)

Where L^⊺ indicates the transpose of L, λ is a regularization constant, H is the average-reference operator H = I − (1/N) 1_N, N is the number of EEG channels, I is the N × N identity matrix, and 1 is the N × N matrix of ones.

input: Synthetic data at target electrodes is generated from source dataset real data using a Boundary Element Method (BEM) model derived from the Colin27 MRI scan [28] and Fieldtrip [29]. Two forward models are computed: model Ls maps source electrodes Xs to point currents within the brain, and model Lt predicts EEG at target electrodes Xt using those point currents. The target prediction follows the equation X_t = L_t L^\top_s (H L_s L^\top_s + \lambda_H)^{-1} X_s [4], where \lambda_H is a regularization parameter. Since the target dataset uses the AF7–AF8 channel, EEG at AF7 and AF8 are computed independently and re-referenced to each other. The synthetic and real source EEG are pooled into a single dataset, which is used to pre-train a neural network.

section: III. METHODS — B. Adding Variation to the Synthetic Data
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Increased variety in training data results in more robust machine learning models. Additional variation is injected into synthetic data by introducing noise to boundary element model parameters: the number of vertices for brain, skull, and scalp meshes, and the resolution of the point current grid. This noise simulates real-world variation such as skull morphology or electrode placement. Five source datasets are used - the Wisconsin Sleep Cohort (WSC), [31], [32] the Computing in Cardiology Challenge 2018 dataset (CiCC), [33], [34] the Institute of Systems and Robotics, University of Coimbra dataset (ISRUC), [35] and the Osteoporotic Fractures in Men Study dataset (MrOS), [31], [36], and the Montreal Archive of Sleep Studies (MASS) [37].

CiCC was captured at 200 Hz and contains 994 healthy subjects or subjects with spontaneous arousals, sleep-disordered breathing, or periodic limb movement. ISRUC was captured at 200 Hz and contains 126 healthy subjects and subjects with REM sleep behavior disorder, sleep disordered breathing, periodic limb movement, insomnia, depression, epilepsy, or Parkinson’s. MrOS was captured at 256 Hz and contains 2900 healthy subjects and subjects with nocturnal hypoxemia or sleep disordered breathing. WSC was captured at 100 Hz and contains over 1100 subjects who are either healthy or have sleep disordered breathing. The MASS dataset was captured at 256 Hz and contains 200 subjects with apnea/hypopnea indices of up to 20. However, 85 subjects were excluded because their stages were scored using an epoch length of 20 seconds instead of 30, which made them inconsistent with the format used in all other datasets. Patient age and sex demographics are in Table I.

The CiCC dataset includes the F3, F4, C3, C4, O1, and O2 EEG channels. WSC includes the C3 and O1 channels. MASS includes the C3, C4, F3, F4, O1, O2, F7, F8, T3, T4, T5, T6, P3, P4, Fz, Cz, Pz, and A2 channels. ISRUC contains the F7, F8, F3, C3, O1, F4, C4, and O2 channels. MrOS contains the C3, C4, A1, and A2 channels. All channels in each source dataset were used in generating synthetic EEG. Either the C3–A2 or C3–M2 channel was used when pre-training on real source data, depending on which channel was present in the source dataset.

The C3 channel was chosen because of the channels which were present in all source datasets; the C3–A2 and C3–M2 channels were physically closest to the AF7–AF8 channels present in the target dataset. The WSC, CiCC, ISRUC, and MrOS datasets also had EOG channels which were referenced to the same location as the EEG channels, and so the EOG channels were assumed to be approximately equivalent to F7 and F8 channels and included as such when generating synthetic data. The MASS dataset however used a different EOG electrode scheme in which the EOG electrodes were placed in pairs vertically or horizontally across each eye; so the EOG electrodes in the MASS dataset were not used at all, as they differed greatly from EEG electrodes and provided less information about currents within the brain tissue.

To determine whether results were sensitive to different transfer learning conditions, the process was run with different numbers of re-trainable layers—one condition in which the single closest layer to the output was re-trained and another condition in which the four closest layers to the output were re-trained.

section: V. DISCUSSION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
Performance improved over training directly on the target dataset (77.0% [6]) in all transfer learning conditions. Augmenting real source datasets with synthetic data generated using electrophysiological models generally improved performance. This approach can improve automated sleep staging with wearable devices, making long-term at-home monitoring more feasible.

In previous work [6], re-training output layers generally outperformed other transfer learning methods (CORAL [7], Deep Domain Confusion [8], subspace alignment [9]) on a fully-supervised sleep staging task. This approach was used as the baseline for comparison. Synthetic data augmentation improved upon re-training without synthetic data. This improvement is suspected to be due to other methods being designed for semi-supervised scenarios and this method incorporating electrophysiology domain knowledge.

One case where synthetic data augmentation did not improve performance was when data was synthesized from the WSC dataset. This likely resulted from WSC using fewer channels (four total, two EEG and two EOG), making the inverse problem of approximating point currents highly underdetermined, reducing synthetic data realism.

A general limitation in sleep staging is scorer variation [4], though most large datasets use a single scorer; good performance is still achievable despite this.

Beyond sleep staging, this synthetic data approach opens possibilities for incorporating physical models into other medical machine learning tasks. Synthetic EEG could improve seizure detection, brain-computer interfaces, or simulate scenarios with little data (e.g., brain tumors or traumatic brain injury) by incorporating tissue abnormalities into boundary element models. Although experiments used forehead-worn wearables, the approach could apply to other wearable types, such as ear-worn sensors.

Potential improvements include using more MRIs to increase synthetic variety, using individual MRIs for personalized models, incorporating movement artifacts, and using more sophisticated head models (e.g., adding muscle tissue). Combining these physics-informed methods with other data augmentation or transfer learning techniques may further improve performance.

Other approaches to channel mismatch exist. U-Sleep [39] works across multiple channels but was trained on clinical datasets using randomly selected common electrode locations, making it unsuitable for wearable devices with rarely used locations; it also requires an EOG channel often unavailable in wearables. Heremans et al. [40] used a transfer learning approach for wearables requiring simultaneous source and target data, which is not always available. Phan et al. [41] used a pre-train and fine-tune approach similar to previous work [6]. Nasiri et al. [42] trained a model simultaneously on source and target datasets with an attention mechanism to select transferable features, showing improvements on large clinical datasets but not yet evaluated on small wearable datasets.

This method builds on pre-training and fine-tuning [6, 41] and poses a supplement to other transfer learning approaches. Adding synthetic data increases source-target similarity and can be incorporated into existing methods with little modification. More research is needed to determine the benefit of synthetic data with more elaborate algorithms.

Although the improvement from synthetic data is modest, it is statistically significant and intended as an easily incorporable method for improving transfer learning. Stronger gains may be achievable through personalized models. Differences between source and target datasets unrelated to channel location, such as age or pathology, may limit effectiveness, as the LORETA-based method cannot correct such differences. Effectiveness is also limited by available source channels; certain electrode location combinations may be more effective at producing realistic synthetic data, explaining performance variance across source datasets. More research is needed to determine the most effective channels and why.
output:
Performance in all transfer learning conditions was improved over training directly on the target dataset without pre-training, which we previously reported to be 77.0% [6]. Transfer learning performance was generally improved by augmenting real source datasets with synthetic data generated using electrophysiological models. Our approach can be used to improve automated sleep staging with wearable devices, thereby making long-term at-home monitoring of sleep disorders using wearable sensors more feasible.

In our previous work [6], we compared a multitude of transfer learning methods, specifically CORAL [7], Deep Domain Confusion [8], and subspace alignment [9] with the simpler and more widely used approach of re-training several output layers as normal and found that re-training output layers generally outperformed other methods on a fully-supervised sleep staging task. We therefore decided to use the approach of re-training output layers as the method to build on when developing our synthetic data-based transfer learning method, as well as use it for the basis of comparison. In this work, we developed and tested a method for augmenting the source data with synthetic data and found it improved on re-training without synthetic data. We suspect that this improvement over other transfer learning methods we tested is due to 1) many of the other methods were intended for use in a semi-supervised training scenario and 2) because this method incorporates additional domain knowledge of electrophysiology. See appendix for side-by-side comparison of our new results with the results from our previous research comparing other transfer learning methods.

One case in which synthetic data augmentation did not improve performance was when the data was synthesized from the WSC dataset. We can speculate that this results from WSC using fewer channels than other datasets, as it used only four channels, two of which were EEG and another two were EOG. It is likely that having so few channels made the inverse problem of approximating the point currents within the brain using measurements at the scalp highly underdetermined, thereby reducing the accuracy of the point current computations, which in turn reduced the realism of the synthetic data. This highlights one shortcoming of our approach, which is that a reasonably large number of EEG channels in the source dataset is necessary.

One limitation present in all sleep staging research is that sleep scorers display considerable variation in their scoring [4], but recordings in most large-scale datasets were scored by only one scorer. It remains possible however to achieve good performance in spite of this limitation.

In addition to improving performance in this particular use case, our synthetic data approach opens the possibility for incorporating physical models into other forms of machine learning for medical tasks. Synthetic EEG could be used for improving performance on other tasks such as seizure detection and brain-computer interfaces. Synthetic EEG could also be used to simulate scenarios for which there is very little data available (e.g., sleep staging on patients with brain tumors or traumatic brain injury) by incorporating the tissue abnormality into the finite or boundary element model. Furthermore, although we performed our experiments using forehead-worn wearables, our approach could be applied to other wearables, such as ear-worn sensors.

Some additional potential ways to improve performance include using a larger number of MRI’s to increase variety in the synthetic EEG, using an MRI from a specific individual to build personalized models, and incorporating movement or other artifacts into the synthetic EEG. The realism of the synthetic data could also potentially be improved by using more sophisticated head models, such as by incorporating additional tissue types such as muscle. It may also be possible to improve performance further by combining other data augmentation or transfer learning methods with physics-informed synthetic data generation.

There have been several other approaches to dealing with channel mismatch. U-Sleep [39] was developed to work for a multitude of channels, however it was trained on multiple large clinical datasets by randomly selecting samples from one of several channels used in the clinical datasets. Because such datasets only include commonly used clinical electrode locations, this technique would not work well for training a model to work on wearables with rarely used electrode locations. Furthermore, U-sleep requires the use of an EOG channel, which is also not available in many wearable devices.

Heremans et al. [40] used a transfer learning approach more specifically intended for wearables by adding an additional objective function incentivizing the model to learn similar feature representations between samples taken simultaneously from both the source and target modality. Unfortunately, simultaneous data from clinical polysomnography and the desired wearable device is not always available, which limits the practical feasibility of this approach.

Phan et al. [41] used a more conventional pre-train and fine-tune approach similar to the approach we found effective in our previous work [6]. A model was pre-trained on one large dataset before certain sections of the model were re-trained on data from differing channels on a smaller dataset.

Nasiri et al. [42] developed a novel transfer learning approach in which a model was simultaneously trained on both the source and target (even if the two datasets had differing numbers of channels) while an attention mechanism was trained to select the most transferable features to use for both. The approach led to substantial improvements when tested on a large target dataset of clinical polysomnograms, but has not yet been evaluated in smaller datasets of wearable recordings.

Our method builds on the pre-training and fine-tuning method described in our previous work [6] and Phan et al. [41] as well as poses a possible supplement to other transfer learning approaches, such as those described above. Our approach augments transfer learning by adding an additional mechanism to increase similarity between the source and target dataset via the addition of synthetic data. The addition of synthetic data can easily be incorporated into other transfer learning methods such as those described above with little to no modification of either the machine learning mechanism or synthetic data generation method. More research is needed to determine how much benefit can be provided by the addition of synthetic data when using more elaborate algorithms than the pre-train and fine-tune approach used in this paper.

Although the improvement provided by the addition of synthetic data is modest, it still achieves statistically significant improvement and again, is intended as an additional method for improving transfer learning performance which can be incorporated easily into existing transfer learning methods. Stronger gains may also be achievable through the usage of personalized models. Differences between the source and target datasets that are not related to channel location, such as age or pathology, may also limit the effectiveness of the synthetic data generation method, as the LORETA-based method would not be able to correct such differences. Again, more personalized models may achieve stronger improvements. The effectiveness may also be limited by the channels available in the source dataset - some numbers or combinations of electrode locations may be more effective than others at producing realistic synthetic data, hence the variance in performance across source datasets. More research is needed to determine which channels are most effective and why.

input: We developed a transfer learning method using electrophysiological models of the human head to generate synthetic EEG data. We applied this method to a sleep staging task with wearable at-home EEG sensors and found it outperformed other transfer learning methods that do not incorporate physical models. Our approach is useful for boosting performance when using EEG from infrequently used sensor locations. It also increases the feasibility of long-term sleep disorder monitoring using automated staging with at-home sensors. Other potential applications include personalized models and simulating EEG from patients with physiological abnormalities.

Tighter tolerances and expensive previous designs make computer-aided design (CAD) increasingly important. Various methods exist for designing medium- and high-power vacuum electronic devices (MVEDs), including linear and nonlinear models, particle-in-cell (PIC) methods for beam–wave interaction circuits, and finite-difference time-domain (FDTD), mode-matching (MM), method of moments (MoM), and multilevel fast multipole method (MLFMM) for waveguide components [4], [5].

Recent advances in computing have enabled global optimization algorithms, such as simulated annealing and particle swarm optimization, to explore parameter spaces for MVED components. However, these methods suffer from long computation times when the number of free parameters is large, and designs often require trade-offs between multiple requirements, such as gain, bandwidth, and frequency. Multiple objective optimization is possible but further increases computing time.

Recent leaps in machine learning have impacted many areas, including self-driving and image classification. AlphaGo’s 2016 victory over a world champion demonstrated that AI based on deep learning can make better decisions than humans in challenging games. Machine learning is a useful tool for MVED development as it helps explore relationships between coupled parameters, potentially reducing optimization complexity and time.

Various methods have been developed for the design of MVEDs, for example, the linear and nonlinear models and particle-in-cell (PIC) method [4] to simulate different beam–wave interaction circuits, the beam optics based on particle tracking or PIC for the electron gun and collector design, the finite-difference time-domain (FDTD), mode-matching (MM), method of moments (MoM), multilevel fast multipole method (MLFMM), and others that can be used to design the waveguide components such as the input/output couplers and microwave windows [5], [6].

Benefiting from the advances in computer science and the boost of the computing resources in recent decades, global optimization algorithms, such as the Simulated Annealing Algorithm, Evolutionary Algorithms, stochastic methods, particle swarm optimization, and others, have been used to explore the parameter space and search for the optimal design of different components in MVEDs [7]–[10]. However, one of the challenges is the long overall optimization time it needs when the free parameter number is large. Another challenge is the components to be designed normally have to satisfy multiple requirements, for example, the gain, bandwidth, and frequency for an interaction circuit. The optimal design is normally a trade-off between these parameters. Multiple objective optimizations are possible solutions; however, they require longer computing time.

In recent years, the huge leaps in machine learning and data mining make them revolutionary techniques and greatly impact many areas such as self-driving, finance, image classification, and so on [11]. AlphaGo, a computer program that combines advanced search trees with deep neural networks, beat a Go world champion in 2016 [12], [13]. It is a landmark achievement that shows artificial intelligence based on deep learning can make better decisions than humans in the most challenging classical game of Go. Machine learning can possibly be a useful tool in the development of MVEDs since it helps explore the relationships between coupled parameters. It is a powerful tool that enables the researcher to use them to investigate deeper into the problem and reduce the complexity and reduce the optimization time.

The functions and performance were studied via the case study of optimizing a magnetron injection gun (MIG) for gyrotron devices, as presented in Sections III and IV. Section V concludes the findings on the potential of machine learning technology in the MVED research field.

input:
Machine learning algorithms optimize task performance using examples [14]–[16]. They divide into supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning [14]–[16]. This article selects suitable methods for MVED development [1].

Supervised learning predicts outcomes from labeled data [1]. Unsupervised learning finds hidden patterns without labels [1]. Reinforcement learning finds optimal strategies through interactions, such as self-driving [1].

MVED component performance can be predicted using Maxwell equations, but the large boundary condition variations and long computing times make full parameter space exploration impractical [1]. Thus, machine learning sample data contains labeled outputs but is relatively small, on the scale of tens of thousands or smaller [1]. Supervised learning is therefore preferred [1].

Artificial neural networks and decision trees are common supervised learning algorithms [21]–[24]. Neural networks explore nonlinear input-output relations and function as black boxes; they are hard to interpret with large network sizes [21], [22]. Decision trees are white boxes that visualize decision-making and input connections [23], [24]. Regression trees handle continuous outputs but risk overfitting with complex relations [23], [24]. Neural networks support multiple outputs, unlike single-output regression trees [21], [22]. Both methods were used in this article [1].

Benefiting from deep learning progress, many convenient machine learning packages exist, such as Python Scikit-learn [25], the C++ library SHARK [26], and the MATLAB Statistics and Machine Learning Toolbox [27]. These allow researchers to process data without algorithmic details [25]–[27].

SUIT MVED DESIGN
Machine learning algorithms aim to optimize the performance of a certain task by using examples and/or experience [14]–[16]. They can be divided into three categories,
supervised learning, unsupervised learning, and reinforcement
learning. Each category includes different algorithms as brieﬂy
listed in Table I. New algorithms are been invented as a
result of rapid development in various research ﬁelds, and
they can be found in recent review articles [17]–[19]. This
article does not intend to dive deeply into each method as
this can be achieved by reviewing the referenced papers
but to select the suitable methods for MVED development.
Supervised learning is trained from data with labeled outputs.
After training and validation, it can be used to predict the
outcomes from unknown inputs. Unsupervised learning does
not have labeled outputs for training. The method tries to
ﬁnd the hidden pattern directly from the input data. It can
be used to ﬁnd the connections and clusters among the inputs.
Reinforcement learning is used to ﬁnd the optimal strategy
from interactions, for example, self-driving and games.
One of the common features in the design of MVED components is that their performances can be relatively accurately
predicted by solving Maxwell equations, or the coupled equations between Maxwell equations and Lorentz equation when
a beam–wave interaction is considered. However, the large
number of variations in the boundary conditions and the long
computing time for each parameter set make it not practical to
travel over the whole parameter space. As a result, the sample
data that can be used in machine learning contain labeled
outputs, and the number of sample data is relatively small,
on the scale of tens of thousands or smaller. Supervised
learning is therefore a better option as the labeled data can
be used for training and predicting performance.
Artiﬁcial neural networks [21], [22] and decision trees [23],
[24] are the two major supervised learning algorithms. Artiﬁ-
cial neural networks are inspired by biological neural networks
that are based on a collection of neurons. It naturally has
the advantage of exploring the nonlinear relations between
the inputs and outputs. The network can be trained to ﬁt (or
learn) any samples and predict the results from given inputs
after training. The artiﬁcial neural networks operate as a black
box. When the network size is large and a complicated neuron
connection model is used, it will be hard to interpolate the
relationship between the inputs and outputs. Decision tree
models are regarded as white boxes. They were initially used
to represent classiﬁcation rules on the input attributes. The
decision-making process can be visualized and provide more
information on the connections among the input data or features. A regression tree is a type of decision tree that can deal
with continuous output values. Its disadvantage includes over-
ﬁtting the training data to reduce the actual prediction accuracy
when the relations between the inputs and outputs are complicated. The regression trees are normally for single output
while artiﬁcial neural networks can deal with multiple-output
problems. In this article, both methods were used.
Beneﬁting from the rapid development of deep learning algorithms and architectures, many commercial and
open-sourced machine learning packages have been developed with excellent ﬂexibility and are convenient to use.
For example, the machine learning package in Python Scikitlearn [25], the C++ library SHARK [26], and the Statistics
and Machine Learning Toolbox in MATLAB [27]. This allows
the researchers to process their data without knowing every
detail of the machine learning algorithm.

Among the components in an MVED, the interaction circuit requires the most resource when the PIC method is used. The passive components require less computing resource since no electrons are needed in the simulations. The complexity of electron guns design lies between these two cases. The magnetic-field immersed guns, including the MIG [28] and cusp electron gun [29] for the gyrotron devices, are more complicated. In this article, the MIG gun was used as a case study. Although a theoretical model based on the conservation of angular momentum can be used to estimate some parameters, and a synthesis method was developed to provide a good starting point for the design, further optimization was still required as the electric and magnetic fields have to match well to achieve an optimal design.

A schematic of the standard triode-type MIG is shown in Fig. 1 [30]. Its geometry is to be determined by the parameters labeled in Fig. 1. Together with the parameters used to define the magnetic field, there were 15 parameters to be optimized. From the theoretical model and the experience in the electron gun design, the geometry parameters were strongly coupled with each other and the relations among them were complicated. The variation of one parameter could possibly be compensated by a combination of other parameters, which makes it more difficult to find a systematic way to achieve an optimal design by manual tuning.

The challenge in the optimization is the long computing time needed. Most computer resources are consumed by processes that calculate the particles' trajectories. An iteration process was used to consider the space charge effect. Fig. 1. Parameterized geometry of the triode-type MIG.

Normally, 12–20 iterations are needed until the solution converges, depending on the strength of the space charge force. When also considering the effect of thermal velocity spread and angular spread of the electrons emitted from the cathode, larger electron samples are needed to represent the distribution. To achieve a higher simulation accuracy, fine meshes are used because the trajectories can be sensitive to the magnetic field.

An MIG gun was simulated and optimized using the genetic algorithm for a high-power gyroklystron [30]. The genetic algorithm is inspired by natural evolution [31], [32]. It stimulates the natural selection process with a certain population generated by crossover, reproduction, and mutation from the initial individuals. Those individuals with higher fitness scores have a higher chance to be kept and used to generate the springs. To find a global optimal MIG gun geometry and to avoid trapping in a local minimum, the parameter ranges were set relatively large which leads to large parameter space. A large population size of 100 was used, and the mutation rate was set relatively high. The optimization was stopped after 400 generations. The computing time for the whole optimization process is three weeks on a PC with a 10-core Intel Core i9 CPU and 32-GB RAM. More details on the simulation setup and final optimized results can be found in [30].

During the optimization, it was found that many parameter sets were labeled as a "bad beam transportation rate" as the entire electron beam did not reach the interaction region, whose location was defined at the exit of the electron gun region. Multiple geometries and magnetic field parameters contribute to this after carefully examining the trajectories of the electrons. When the acceleration electric field strength at the radial direction is too high or the magnetic field at the emitter surface is too low, the electrons may not have enough axial momentum and will directly strike on the modulation anode. When the transverse-to-axial velocity ratio (beam alpha value) at the acceleration region is high, the axial velocities of the electrons will keep reducing at the magnetic field compression region and the electrons will eventually be reflected back to the cathode due to the magnetic mirror effect.

The genetic algorithm was not able to discover the physics inside the electron gun design and the connections among the parameters. It was unavoidable that a large computing resource was "wasted" to simulate the "bad" parameter sets. If the performance of these parameters can be predicted before the simulations, then it would significantly speed up the optimization process.

In this article, both the artificial neural networks and decision trees were used to explore the in-depth connections among the geometry parameter, magnetic field parameters as well as beam quality of the given parameter set. For both supervised learning processes, the inputs were those parameters used for the electron gun simulations. The 70% of the input data was used for training and 30% was used for validation. The regression trees were trained with least-squares boosting and a training iteration of 2000. The feedforward neural networks were chosen as the artificial neural networks with a hidden layer size of 50 and a delay layer size of 20, as shown in Fig. 2. The Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm was used as the training function.

section: IV. SIMULATION RESULTS — A. Identity of the “Bad” Parameter Sets
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Machine learning can identify poor-performing parameter sets without running full particle tracking simulations. In supervised learning, beam transportation rates from simulations served as labeled outputs for training and validation. After validation, artificial neural networks and regression trees predicted transportation rates for future genetic algorithm populations. Parameter sets predicted to have rates below 100% were classified as "bad," while those at 100% were "good." Prediction accuracy for both algorithms as a function of generation number is shown in Fig. 3. The sample data count equals generation number multiplied by population size (100). Both algorithms showed similar excellent performance, with accuracy exceeding 94% after 4 generations. This high accuracy using only 400 samples was surprising; accuracy stabilized only after 10,000 samples (100 generations), though the improvement was not significant. Using only parameters predicted to have unity transportation rates for particle tracking simulations saved 28% of simulations, significantly reducing optimization time.

The regression tree can visualize the tree been built and show the importance of the input parameters. Fig. 4(a) shows the importance of the input parameter on the transportation rate, and Fig. 4(b) shows the main branch of the regression tree. It showed the transportation rate was mainly determined by the gap distance of the cathode to modulation anode (X4), the magnetic field angle at the cathode (X10) which was not predicted from the theoretical analysis, magnetic field compression ratio (X12), and the voltage of the modulation anode (X13). The most significant parameter was the gap distance of the cathode to the modulation anode. A small gap distance would result in a strong radial electric field. The electrons might propagate straight across and strike the modulation anode surface if the magnetic field was too weak to bend the electrons.

The relation among the parameters was nonlinear. The regression tree can simplify the complicated relations and provides more suitable parameter ranges, which is useful to narrow down the parameter space during the optimization. A low beam loss can only be obtained by proper combinations of X4, X12, X13, and X10, which are marked as the branches in thicker wires in Fig. 4(b). The compression ratio should not be too big, and the suggested parameter range could also be obtained from the regression tree model. section: V. DISCUSSION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
V. DISCUSSION

Supervised learning algorithms, regression trees and artificial neural networks, were selected for MVED design. In a MIG optimization case study, these algorithms achieved high prediction accuracy with limited sample data, saving approximately 28% optimization time.

Regression trees provide parameter importance visualization, enabling parameter space narrowing and circuit discovery. However, artificial neural networks require approximately 8600 training samples for converged accuracy and outperform regression trees with the same data. Training data is specific to design conditions (e.g., fixed beam voltage and magnetic field), limiting applicability to other requirements. Increasing sample data tenfold across varied conditions could enable optimal design with approximately 1000 particle tracking simulations.

ZHANG AND CROSS: POTENTIALS OF MACHINE LEARNING IN VACUUM ELECTRONIC DEVICES
output:
Two supervised learning algorithms, regression trees and artificial neural networks, were down-selected as the machine learning algorithms in the design of MVEDs. Through the case study of optimizing a MIG for gyrotron devices, the functions of the machine learning algorithm were explored. They include the following.

Fig. 6.
Prediction accuracies of the goal function by regression trees and neural networks with different tolerate errors Δ.

1) Identify the “bad” parameter sets. Both regression trees and artificial neural networks can achieve high prediction accuracy for such classification problems at a small number of sample data. When integrating this feature into an optimization routine, a significant optimization time can be saved, ∼28% in the case study.

2) The regression trees can be visualized and show the importance of the input parameters. They are excellent tools to explore deep inside the importance of the initial input parameters and to gain knowledge on the components to be designed, to constrain the parameter ranges and narrow down the parameter space, and to discover novel beam–wave interaction circuits and advance the research in millimeter and submillimeter-wave MVEDs.

3) Predict the performance of the components under investigation. A relatively large number of training data is required to achieve a converged prediction accuracy. The training data size was ∼8600 in the case study and fewer data may be needed depending on the problem to be solved. With the same training data set, artificial neural networks have much better prediction accuracy than regression trees.

It should be noted that in the case study, the trained network is an assistant to the multiple-objective genetic optimization. The number of particle tracking simulations can be significantly reduced by further applying the knowledge learned. For example, if the importance of the parameters is known, the particle tracking simulations can be carried out more effectively on more important parameter sets, and the parameter range of the unimportant parameters can be narrowed.

The drawback is the data used for training is with specific design requirements, for example, the fixed beam voltage and peak magnetic field. It is difficult to offer a parameter set close to optimal design for other design requirements. However, this problem can be possibly solved by increasing the sample data number (ten times the size of the current sample data) at different design conditions, including different beam voltages, beam currents, magnetic fields, and others. The future target is to allow machine learning to achieve an optimal MIG design with arbitrary requirements at a minimum particle tracking simulation number of around 1000.

With the rapid progress of machine learning and data mining technologies, it is believed that more powerful features can be integrated into the current CAD tools for MVEDs, to significantly advance the research.

Abstract:

Recent power allocation algorithms for distributed antenna systems (DAS) maximize spectral efficiency (SE) and energy efficiency (EE). Traditional iterative methods suffer from high computational complexity, limiting practical implementation. This paper proposes a deep neural network (DNN) model to approximate the nonlinear mapping between user channel realizations and optimal power allocation schemes derived from traditional iterative algorithms. The DNN-based method maximizes SE and EE while significantly reducing online computational time. Simulation results show that the proposed scheme achieves performance comparable to traditional iterative algorithms with lower complexity.

In recent years, a lot of power allocation algorithms have been proposed to maximize
spectral efﬁciency (SE) and energy efﬁciency (EE) for the distributed antenna systems (DAS). However,
the traditional iterative power allocation algorithms are difﬁcult to be implemented in reality because of their
high computational complexity. With the development of machine learning algorithms, it has been proved
that the machine learning method has excellent learning ability and low computational complexity, which can
approximate the traditional iterative power allocation well and be easily to be implemented in reality. In this
paper, we propose a new deep neural network (DNN) model for DAS. From the perspective of machine
learning, traditional iterative algorithms can be regarded as a nonlinear mapping between user channel
realizations and optimal power allocation schemes. Therefore, we train the DNN to learn the nonlinear
mapping between the user channel realizations and the corresponding power allocation schemes based on
the traditional iterative algorithm. Then, a power allocation schemes based on DNN method is developed to
maximize SE and EE for DAS. The simulation results show that the proposed scheme can not only obtain the
almost similar performance as the traditional iterative algorithm, but also reduce much online computational
time.

section: I. INTRODUCTION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
In recent years, rapid growth in cellular data transmission has placed pressure on 5G systems [1], [2]. To provide high data rates, researchers have proposed distributed antenna systems (DAS) that reduce access distance between remote access units and user equipment [3], [4]. Existing work shows DAS advantages for spectral efficiency (SE) and energy efficiency (EE) [4]–[12].

Optimizing SE and EE power allocation is significant for high data rate transmission in DAS. Many algorithms have been proposed, but traditional iterative methods sacrifice substantial online computational time, making them unrealistic for systems with constantly changing channel state information [13]–[19]. Deep learning offers a solution, enabling real-time power allocation with lower complexity [15]–[19]. Specifically, deep learning has been applied to channel estimation and signal detection in OFDM systems, showing better performance in reducing time and complexity [15]. Neural networks have been trained to learn the nonlinear mapping of the weighted mean square error (WMMSE) algorithm, achieving similar performance with reduced computational time [16]. Deep learning has also been used for energy efficiency optimization through power control in interference networks [17] and for robust power control using ensemble networks with noise inputs [18]. Convolutional neural networks have solved device-to-device scheduling using user location instead of channel state information, saving the cost of channel measurement [19]. However, little work has studied deep neural network (DNN) based power allocation for DAS.

This paper investigates DNN algorithms for downlink DAS. We define iterative algorithms as traditional optimization methods and select the sub-gradient algorithm as the baseline [15]. We generate numerous channel realizations using the sub-gradient algorithm to obtain optimal power allocation schemes, which serve as input-label pairs for DNN training. The goal is to design a DNN structure and parameters that achieve performance close to the sub-gradient algorithm while significantly reducing online computation time. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: Section II presents the DAS model, system configuration, channel model, and formulations for maximum SE and EE optimization. Section III details the system architecture, network structure, data generation process, and DNN training stages. Section IV presents DNN parameter selection and simulation results. Section V concludes the paper.

instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: The maximum SE optimization can find optimal power allocation schemes using the sub-gradient algorithm [11]. When the objective is maximizing EE, the non-convex objective function must be transformed into an equivalent subtractive form using fractional programming. However, the sub-gradient algorithm has high time complexity without considering user interference, and combining it with fractional programming results in extremely high computational complexity. Due to this complexity, the algorithms cannot be used directly in actual systems.
output: According to [11], the maximum SE optimization can find the optimal power allocation schemes by using the sub-gradient algorithm. When the objective problem is maximizing EE, we should transform the non-convex objective function into an equivalent objective function with subtractive form by using fractional programming. However, the time complexity of using the sub-gradient algorithm is still high without considering the interference between users, and the time complexity is extremely high after combining fractional programming for maximizing the EE optimization. Therefore, we cannot use algorithms directly in the actual systems due to the high computational complexity.

A fully-connected deep neural network which contains five layers, one input layer with 15 nodes, three hidden layers with 50, 100, 50 nodes and one output layer with 15 nodes is proposed for DAS. section: V. CONCLUSION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: We exploited a DNN to solve the power allocation problem in DAS. We modeled the system with perfect channel state information and orthogonal channels, then used a sub-gradient algorithm to maximize spectral and energy efficiency, saving optimal schemes for training data. We trained the DNN using these channel realizations and corresponding power allocations, then tested its performance against the sub-gradient algorithm on new channel realizations. The DNN method achieved comparable performance with significantly reduced computational time. Future work will explore CNN using user location, migration learning for insufficient datasets, and ensemble learning to improve generalization in complex wireless environments.
output:
In this paper, we exploited the DNN algorithm to solve power
allocation problem in DAS. Firstly, we introduced a system
model and assumed that perfect channel state information is
known at both transmitter and receiver side and the channels
are orthogonal so there are no interference to each other.
Secondly, we randomly generated a large number of the
channel realizations and used the traditional sub-gradient
algorithm to maximize SE and EE optimization and save
the optimal power allocation schemes. Thirdly, we fed the
channel realizations and the corresponding power allocation
schemes into the DNN and used the loss function to train
the DNN. Fourthly, we generated other channel realizations
for testing dataset and fed into the DNN which had been
trained well and got the outputs of DNN. Otherwise, the same
testing dataset were fed into the traditional sub-gradient algorithm and calculate the optimal power allocation schemes.
Finally, we showed the performance and computational time
difference between the DNN method and the sub-gradient
algorithm, respectively.
In the future, we will explore more excellent machine
learning algorithms to solve the power allocation problem
in DAS. For example, we will try to use the CNN to realize
power allocation by using user geographic location instead
of user channel information. In addition, we will try to use
migration learning to deal with the problem of insufﬁcient
training dataset in wireless communication systems. What’s
more, we will try to use the ensemble learning to make the
generalization ability of the trained model stronger so that it
can cope with various complicated situations in actual wireless communication systems. Finally, we hope to ﬁnd more
machine learning methods with excellent performance and
low computational complexity to truly implement power allocation algorithms in actual wireless communication systems.

section: I. INTRODUCTION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: The task of stock prediction remains challenging due to market complexity and nonlinearity [5]. While fundamental and technical analysis provide baselines [1], [2], recent advances employ machine learning and deep learning to improve accuracy [3], [4]. Prior work combines Genetic Algorithms with neural networks [7], evaluates Support Vector Machines on indices like NIKKEI 225 [8], and compares ensemble methods such as Random Forest and XGBoost against single models [13]-[16]. Deep learning approaches, particularly LSTM networks, have shown strong performance for trend forecasting [17]-[22]. However, limitations persist regarding input data representation and feature selection [12]. Tehran's stock market, influenced by privatization under article 44, exhibits unique constraints like daily ±5% price limits [23]. Despite this, limited research applies novel algorithms to predict Tehran stock groups. Nabipour et al. [23] recently used tree-based and deep learning models for 1 to 30-day ahead prediction, finding LSTM superior. This study compares nine machine learning models (Decision Tree, Random Forest, Adaboost, XGBoost, SVC, Naïve Bayes, KNN, Logistic Regression) and two deep learning methods (RNN, LSTM) using ten technical indicators across continuous and binary input approaches. Experiments utilize ten years of historical data from four investor-critical groups (petroleum, diversified financials, basic metals, non-metallic minerals) on the Tehran Stock Exchange. The study aims to determine the best tuning parameters and evaluate preprocessing effects on prediction performance using classification metrics.
output:
The task of stock prediction has always been a challenging problem for statistics experts and finance. The main reason behind this prediction is buying stocks that are likely to increase in price and then selling stocks that are probably to fall. Generally, there are two ways for stock market prediction. Fundamental analysis is one of them and relies on a company’s technique and fundamental information like market position, expenses and annual growth rates. The second one is the technical analysis method, which concentrates on previous stock prices and values. This analysis uses historical charts and patterns to predict future prices [1], [2].

Stock markets were normally predicted by financial experts in the past time. However, data scientists have started solving prediction problems with the progress of learning techniques. Also, computer scientists have begun using machine learning methods to improve the performance of prediction models and enhance the accuracy of predictions. Employing deep learning was the next phase in improving prediction models with better performance [3], [4]. Stock market prediction is full of challenges, and data scientists usually confront some problems when they try to develop a predictive model. Complexity and nonlinearity are two main challenges caused by the instability of stock market and the correlation between investment psychology and market behavior [5].

It is clear that there are always unpredictable factors such as the public image of companies or political situation of countries, which affect stock markets trend. Therefore, if the data gained from stock values are efficiently preprocessed and suitable algorithms are employed, the trend of stock values and index can be predicted. In stock market prediction systems, machine learning and deep learning approaches can help investors and traders through their decisions. These methods intend to automatically recognize and learn patterns among big amounts of information. The algorithms can be effectively self-learning, and can tackle the predicting task of price fluctuations in order to improve trading strategies [6].

Since recent years, many methods have been improved to predict stock market trends. The implementation of a model combination with Genetic Algorithms (GA), Artificial Neural Networks and Hidden Markov Model (HMM) was proposed by Hassan et al. [7]; the purpose was transforming the daily stock values to independent groups of prices as inputs to HMM. The predictability of financial trend with SVM model by evaluating the weekly trend of NIKKEI 225 index was investigated by Huang et al. [8]. A comparison between SVM, Linear Discriminant method, Elman Backpropagation Neural Networks and Quadratic Discriminant method was their goal. The results indicated that SVM was the best classifier method. New financial prediction algorithm based on SVM ensemble was proposed by Sun et al. [9]. The method for choosing SVM ensemble’s base classifiers was proposed by deeming both diversity analysis and individual prediction. Final results showed that SVM ensemble was importantly better than individual SVM for classification. Ten data mining methods were employed by Ou et al. [10] to predict value trends of Hang index from Hong Kong market. The methods involved Tree based classification, K-nearest neighbor, Bayesian classification, SVM and neural network. Results indicated that SVM outperformed other predictive models. The value fluctuations by a developed Legendre neural network was forecasted by Liu et al. [11] by assuming investors’ positions and their decisions by analyzing the prior data on the values. Indeed, they examined a random function (time strength) in the prediction model. Araújo et al. [12] proposed the morphological rank linear forecasting approach to compare its results with time-delay added evolutionary forecasting approach and multilayer perceptron networks.

From the above research background, it is clear that each of the algorithms can effectively solve stock prediction problems. However, it is vital to notice that there are specific limitations for each of them. The prediction results not only are affected by the representation of the input data but also depend on the prediction method. Moreover, using only prominent features and identifying them as input data instead of all features can noticeably develop the accuracy of the prediction models.

Employing tree-based ensemble methods and deep learning algorithms for predicting the stock and stock market trend is a new area of research activities. In light of employing bagging and majority vote methods, Tsai et al. [13] used two different kinds of ensemble classifiers, such as heterogeneous and homogeneous methods. They also consider macroeconomic features and financial ratios from Taiwan stock market to examine the performance of models. The results demonstrated that with respect to the investment returns and prediction accuracy, ensemble classifiers were superior to single classifiers. Ballings et al. [14] compared the performance of AdaBoost, Random Forest and kernel factory versus single models involving SVM, KNN, Logistic Regression and ANN. They predict European company’s prices for one-year ahead. The final results showed that Random Forest outperformed among all models. Basak et al. [15] employed XGBoost and Random Forest methods for the classification problem to forecast the stock increase or decrease based on previous values. Results showed that the prediction performances have advanced for several companies in comparison with the existing ones. For examining macroeconomic indicators to accurately predict stock market for one-month ahead, Weng et al. [16] improved four ensemble models, boosting regressor, bagging regressor, neural network ensemble regressor and random forest regressor. Indeed, another aim was employing a hybrid way of LSTM to prove that the macroeconomic features are the most successful predictors for stock market.

Moving on using deep learning algorithms, a deep neural network algorithm with the transaction records and public market data was investigated by Long et al. [17] to assess stock price trends. Their final results indicated that bidirectional LSTM could forecast the future of market for investors, and the technique attained the greatest performance. The employment of RNN and CNN algorithms was examined by Rekha et al. [18] to compare the accuracy of those with real values from stock markets. LSTM with an automatic encoder and LSTM with an embedded layer were utilized by Pang et al. [19] to acquire better stock market estimations. The result of experimental works indicated that LSTM with an embedded layer outperformed for the Shanghai composite index with 57.2% accuracy. The deep convolutional LSTM algorithm was employed by Kelotra and Pandey [20] to efficiently calculate stock market movements. They used a model with Rider-based monarch butterfly optimization method and gained the RMSE and MSE of 2.6923 and 7.2487. A forecasting LSTM model and an overfitting prevention LSTM module were suggested by Baek and Kim [21] to predict stock market. They showed that using the overfitting prevention module make results more accurate. Using a hybrid method of LSTM and GA was presented by Chung and Shin [22] to develop a new stock market prediction method. Their results indicated that the method outperformed the benchmark model.

Overall, regarding the above literature, prior studies often concentrated on macroeconomic or technical features with recent machine learning methods to detect stock index or values movement without considering appropriate preprocessing methods.

Tehran’s stock market has been greatly popular lately due to the remarkable growth of the main index in the last decade. The important reason behind that is privatizing most of the state-owned in the Iranian constitution firms under the general policies of article 44. The shares of lately privatized firms can be bought by ordinary people under particular conditions. The market has some special features compared to other country’s stock markets; for example, dealing price limitation that is ±5% of opening price for every index in each trading day. This matter hampers scatter market shocks and irregular market fluctuations, political matters, etc. over a particular time and could form the market smoother. However, the effect of fundamental parameters on the market is considerable and the prediction task of future movements is not easy [23].

This study employed stock market groups (that are important for traders) to investigate the task of predicting future trends. In spite of remarkable progress in Tehran stock market in the recent decade, there has been not adequate papers on the stock price predictions and trends via novel machine learning algorithms. However, a paper has been published recently by Nabipour et al. [23] where they employed tree based models and deep learning algorithms to estimate future stock prices from 1 day ahead to 30 days ahead as a regression problem. The experimental results indicated that LSTM (as the superior model) could successfully predict values (from Tehran Stock Exchange) with the lowest error.

In this research, we concentrate on comparing prediction performance of nine machine learning models (Decision Tree, Random Forest, Adaboost, XGBoost, SVC, Naïve Bayes, KNN, Logistic Regression and ANN) and two deep learning methods (RNN and LSTM) to predict stock market movement. Ten technical indicators are utilized as inputs to our models. Our study includes two different approaches for inputs, continuous data and binary data, to investigate the effect of preprocessing; the former uses stock trading data (open, close, high and low values) while the latter employs preprocessing step to convert continuous data to binary one. Each technical indicator has its specific possibility of up or down movement based on market inherent properties. The performance of the mentioned models is compared for the both approaches with three classification metrics, and the best tuning parameter for each model (except Naïve Bayes and Logistic Regression) is reported.

All experimental tests are done with ten years of historical data of four stock market groups (petroleum, diversified financials, basic metals and non-metallic minerals), that are totally crucial for investors, from Tehran stock exchange. We believe that this study is a new research paper that incorporates multiple machine learning and deep learning methods to improve the prediction task of stock groups’ trend and movement.

This paragraph is organized to show the structure of our paper. Section 2 defines our research data with some statistical data, and two approaches supposed for input values. Eleven prediction models, including nine machine learning and two deep learning algorithms, are introduced and discussed in Section 3. The final results of prediction are presented in Section 4 with analyzing, and Section 5 concludes our paper.

input:
A new step converts continuous indicator values to binary data based on each indicator's properties. Figure 6 shows the process of stock trend prediction using binary data, where +1 indicates an upward trend and -1 indicates a downward trend.

Indicator calculations follow references [26]–[28]:

*   **SMA and WMA:** If the current value is below the moving average, the trend is -1; otherwise, it is +1.
*   **MOM:** If the MOM value is positive, the trend is +1; otherwise, it is -1.
*   **STCK, STCD, LWR, MACD, and ADO:** If the current value (time t) is greater than the previous price (time t-1), the trend is +1; otherwise, it is -1.
*   **RSI:** If the value exceeds 70, the trend is -1; if below 30, the trend is +1. For values between 30 and 70, if the current value (t) is larger than the prior value (t-1), the trend is +1; otherwise, it is -1.
*   **CCI:** If values surpass 200, the trend is -1; if below -200, the trend is +1. For values between -200 and 200, if the current value (t) is larger than the prior value (t-1), the trend is +1; otherwise, it is -1.
output:
In this approach, a new step is added to convert continuous values of indicators to binary data based on each indicator's nature and property. Figure 6 indicates the process of stock trend prediction with binary data. Here, binary data is introduced by +1 as the sign of upward trend and −1 as the sign of downward trend.

Details about the way of calculating indicators are presented here [26]–[28]:

The average of values in a particular range computes SMA indicator, and this helps investors to decide if a price will go further in the same trend. WMA indicator provides us a weighted average of the last n prices, where the weighting falls with every previous price.

• SMA and WMA: if current value is below the moving average then the trend is −1, otherwise it is +1.

MOM indicator computes the speed of the fall or rise in values and it is a handy indicator of strength (or weakness) in estimating prices.

• MOM: if the value of MOM is positive then the trend is +1, otherwise it is −1.

STCK indicator is a momentum to liken a specific closing price of a stock to its range over a certain period. The oscillator's sensitivity to market movements is decreased by adjusting that period or by a moving average of values.

The relative position of the closing values is calculated by STCD compared to the amplitude of price oscillations in a particular period. This is assumed that as prices grow, the closing price tends towards the prices which fit to the higher part of the area of price movements in the previous period and when prices drop, the reverse is true. LWR indicator is a kind of momentum indicator that estimates overbought and oversold levels. Occasionally LWR indicator is employed to discover entry and exit times for investors. MACD indicator demonstrates the association between two moving averages of a stock's price as another kind of momentum indicator. Investors regularly use this to buy the stock after the MACD indicator goes beyond its signal line and sell the shares in the opposite situation. ADO indicators is typically employed to observe the flow of money into or out of stock. Investors ordinarily use ADO line to find buying or selling time of stock or confirm the strength of a movement.

• STCK, STCD, LWR, MACD and ADO: if the current value (time t) is more than the previous price (time t-1) then the trend is +1, otherwise it is −1.

RSI indicator is another momentum that assesses the magnitude of recent price changes to evaluate oversold or overbought situations for stock values. RSI indicator is indicated as an oscillator (a line graph that moves between two extremes) and changes between 0 to 100.

• RSI: its value is between 0 and 100. If the RSI value surpasses 70 then the trend is −1, and if the value goes below 30 then the trend is +1. For values between 30 and 70, if the current value (time t) is larger than the prior value (time t-1) then the trend is +1, otherwise it is −1.

CCI indicator is utilized as a momentum-based oscillator to decide on what time a stock price is getting a condition of being overbought or oversold. CCI indicator also estimates the difference between the history of average price and the current value. This indicator defines the time of entry or exit for investors by computing special signals.

• CCI: if values surpass 200 then the trend is −1 and if values go below −200 then the trend is +1. For values between −200 and 200, if the current value (time t) is larger than the prior value (time t-1) then the trend is +1, otherwise it is −1.

AdaBoost is an ensemble model that sequentially trains weak learners, adjusting sample weights based on prior forecasting errors to focus on difficult instances [2]. XGBoost is a recent tree-based ensemble model using boosting rules. It offers benefits over other tree models, including regularization to prevent overfitting, in-built cross-validation, handling of missing data, parallelized tree building, and tree pruning [3].

Support Vector Machines (SVMs) are supervised learning approaches for classification and regression. The boundary is defined in Equation 1, mapping input vectors $x_i \in \mathcal{R}^d$ into a high-dimensional feature space $H$ via a kernel function $K(x_i, x_j)$ [4]. SVMs can perform linear or non-linear classification efficiently; for non-linear cases, a kernel trick maps inputs to high-dimensional spaces. Common kernel functions include radial basis function (RBF), polynomial, and sigmoid, defined in Equations 2-4, where $\gamma$ is the RBF constant and $d$ is the polynomial degree [5]. SVMs are effective in high-dimensional spaces, though care must be taken to avoid overfitting when the number of features exceeds the number of samples [6].

Naïve Bayes is a probabilistic classifier using Bayes' theorem with strong feature independence assumptions given the class variable [1].

The conditional probability of class y given features x1 to xn is defined as P(y) multiplied by the product of P(xi|y) for all i, divided by P(x1,...,xn) [1].

Naïve Bayes is highly fast due to class distribution separation, allowing independent one-dimensional evaluation that mitigates the dimensionality curse [1].

KNN is a lazy, non-parametric algorithm making no assumptions about underlying data distribution [2].

KNN finds targets by dividing data into training and test sets, selecting K, choosing a distance function, computing distances from a test sample to K training samples, sorting these distances, and assigning the test class via majority vote of the K nearest neighbors [2].

ANNs are single or multi-layer networks with fully connected nodes. Figure 11 illustrates an ANN with input, output, and two hidden layers, where each node connects to all nodes in the next layer. Deeper networks form with more hidden layers.

A node computes a weighted sum of inputs plus a bias, then applies a non-linear activation function to produce output for the next layer. The network processes data from input to output layer, with final output computed across all nodes. Weights and biases are trained via forward pass, target comparison, and gradient descent with backpropagation. Equation 6 defines the output $Z$ as $f(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i w_i + b)$, where $x$ are inputs, $w$ are weights, and $b$ is bias.

RNNs are significant neural networks used for sequential data, addressing the limitation of independent inputs by maintaining specific memory of prior computed values. However, practical RNNs are limited to looking back a few steps despite theoretical capability for long sequences. Figure 13 illustrates the RNN architecture.

LSTM is a specific RNN type used in document classification, time series analysis, and speech recognition. It solves RNN limitations by employing gates to forget old information and learn new ones. An LSTM layer consists of four interacting neural network layers, with a unit containing a cell, an output gate, and a forget gate. The cell recognizes values over time intervals, while gates control information flow.

IV. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS — A. CLASSIFICATION METRICS

F1-score, accuracy, and ROC-AUC metrics evaluate model performance. Precision and recall are calculated using true positives (TP), true negatives (TN), false positives (FP), and false negatives (FN) as defined in Equations 7 and 8. F1-score and accuracy are defined in Equations 9 and 10. Accuracy is insufficient for uneven class distributions; F1-score balances precision and recall [1].

Precision = TP / (TP + FP) (7)
Recall = TP / (TP + FN) (8)
Accuracy = (TP + TN) / (TP + FP + TN + FN) (9)
F1-Score = 2 × (Precision × Recall) / (Precision + Recall) (10)

B. RESULTS

Data was normalized and split into 70% training and 30% test sets. Models were fitted and validated using early stopping to prevent overfitting. Deep learning models (RNN, LSTM) required input reshaping into three dimensions (samples, time_steps, features). Weight regularization and dropout layers were applied. All code used Python3 with Scikit-Learn and Keras libraries [2].

In the first approach, continuous feature data was used. Tables 4-6 report results. Naive-Bayes and Decision Tree were least accurate (~68%), while RNN and LSTM were top predictors (~86%). Running time was higher for superior models [3].

Naive-Bayes and Decision Tree remained least accurate (~85%), and RNN and LSTM remained top predictors (~90%), but the performance gap narrowed. Prediction speed improved with binary data [4].

Deep learning methods (RNN, LSTM) showed technical skill in forecasting stock movement, especially with continuous data where machine learning models performed weaker. However, RNN and LSTM running time was always higher due to large epoch counts and multi-day price inputs. An extra layer converted continuous values at time t to binary based on the previous value at t-1, identifying up/down trends. This converted non-stationary values into trend-deterministic values, making prediction easier [5].

section: V. CONCLUSIONS
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: The study predicted stock market movement using machine learning and deep learning on four Tehran Stock Exchange groups, using ten years of data with ten technical features. Nine ML models (Decision Tree, Random Forest, Adaboost, XGBoost, SVC, Naïve Bayes, KNN, Logistic Regression, and ANN) and two DL methods (RNN and LSTM) were tested. Two input approaches were tested: continuous and binary data. Three classification metrics evaluated performance. Results showed a significant improvement when using binary data. RNN and LSTM were the superior models in both approaches.
output:
The purpose of this study was the prediction task of stock market movement by machine learning and deep learning algorithms. Four stock market groups, namely diversified financials, petroleum, non-metallic minerals and basic metals, from Tehran stock exchange were chosen, and the dataset was based on ten years of historical records with ten technical features. Also, nine machine learning models (Decision Tree, Random Forest, Adaboost, XGBoost, SVC, Naïve Bayes, KNN, Logistic Regression and ANN) and two deep learning methods (RNN and LSTM) were employed as predictors. We supposed two approaches for input values to models, continuous data and binary data, and we employed three classification metrics for evaluations. Our experimental works showed that there was a significant improvement in the performance of models when they use binary data instead of continuous one. Indeed, deep learning algorithms (RNN and LSTM) were our superior models in both approaches.
