section: IV. DISCUSSION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: This section reviews literature on machine learning and deep learning in online education. Most ML approaches rely on limited data despite requiring large volumes to function effectively; open-source datasets have been used to evaluate student performance using numerical, textual, visual, and video data collected via surveys and streaming [27], [43], [50], [52], [53]. However, classification of unstructured datasets remains ineffective without standardized parameters. Dropout and at-risk student studies often cover small percentages of on-campus datasets, and ML algorithms may yield unsatisfactory results on small datasets; preprocessing methods could improve accuracy [84], [85], [86], [87]. Some ML and DL algorithms provide probabilistic predictions without actual values, requiring human grading for reliable evaluation. Few studies address the temporal nature of at-risk indicators, though their dynamic fluctuation over time suggests temporal data could improve predictor performance [52]. Most research frames the issue as a binary classification task, with limited investigation into class identification or diverse classifications needed for management strategies. Feature engineering has received little attention; experiments predominantly use student demographics, TF-IDF, heuristics, and e-learning logs, with few examining deep learning algorithms like ANN, DNN, RNN, and CNN compared to classical methods like SVM, DT, NB, and KNN. Existing literature ignores the dynamic character of student performance, which fluctuates over time, and performance on real-time dynamic data remains unknown. Maintaining class balance is widely considered the most significant factor for high classification success [84], [85], [86], [87]. Properly implemented ML can accelerate educational development and substantially alter teaching, learning, and research, allowing educators to support at-risk students early to improve success and retention.
output:
In this part, we will describe the major findings of our literature review on the application of machine learning and deep learning in online education.

• The majority of machine learning approaches were taught utilizing limited quantities of data. It is true, however, that ML algorithms require massive volumes of data in order to work well. Studies [27], [43], [50], [52], [53] evaluated the online education performance of students using open-source datasets. Several research collects numerical, textual, visual, and video data via Google Forms, Online Survey, Online Questioner, Public opinion, and online streaming. Ineffective classification of unstructured and disorderly datasets by ML and DL algorithms. In order to create any type of dataset to measure the influence of online education and student performance, standard parameters must be established.

• Additionally, it was observed that the dropout and prediction of students at risk studies for on-campus students only covered a relatively small percentage of the dataset. This was a point of contention among the researchers. Machine learning algorithms might not yield satisfactory results when trained on relatively small datasets. In addition, the pre-processing data method has the potential to assist considerably in providing more accurate results.

• In some instances, machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) algorithms provided probabilistic predictions without an actual value, which was a critical task for the evaluation of students, necessitating random test human grading to assure fair and reliable ratings.

• There hasn’t been enough research on the temporal nature of the indicators used to predict at-risk and dropout pupils. Due to these properties’ dynamic nature, their values fluctuate over time. The performance of the predictors can be improved by using temporal data in the classification process. For example, article [52] computes temporal features.

• The majority of research papers approached the issue as a categorization challenge. The methods used to identify the classes of students in the dataset were the topic of very few investigations. Additionally, the aforementioned issues are classified as binary issues, but numerous other classifications would be included to assist management in creating more successful intervention strategies.

• Tasks involving feature engineering, where the features used might affect how well a predictor performs, have received less attention. In the experiments, features like student demographics, TF, IDF, Heuristics 1, 2, and 3, and e-learning interaction session logs were predominantly utilized. Additionally, it was found that only a small number of researchers examined the potential of deep learning algorithms like ANN, DNN, RNN, and CNN, instead of the more common classical machine learning algorithms like SVM, DT, NB, and KNN.

• The dynamic character of student performance is not considered in the existing literature. The performance of the pupils is a dynamic process that either improves or degrades with time. Predictor performance on real-time dynamic data is still unknown.

• There have been several different kinds of studies that have focused on the class, or data balance [84], [85], [86], [87]. Maintaining a good class balance is widely regarded as the most significant component in achieving high classification success.

ML has the ability to accelerate educational development, and it is evident that instructional effectiveness has increased dramatically. By properly and effectively implementing ML approaches in the educational sphere, teaching, learning, and research will all be substantially altered. To support difficult students early and take action to increase success and retention, educators who use ML will have a better picture of how their students are developing with their learning.

instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
We suggest the following research directions for predictive learning analytics of student performance:

*   Formalize a specific definition of the variable "learning outcomes" before developing prediction models to measure learning objective achievement.
*   Develop predictive models to improve teaching and learning in poor nations and for non-technical degrees, such as humanities; models must be tailored to specific educational contexts and settings to be effective across contexts.
*   After anonymizing sensitive student data, compile and share educational datasets with other academics for utilization.
*   Develop intelligent algorithms that can predict a cohort's academic achievement and program-level results; this would facilitate evaluation procedures and improve overall program quality for educational leaders.
*   Develop machine learning models that justify and explain student achievement levels and investigate how hybrid models might increase the precision of student outcome forecasts.
*   Future researchers may look into methods for refining educational datasets to increase accessibility; focus on making systems more practical, accommodating certain students' demands, and streamlining navigation.
*   Researchers can look into ways to lessen student mental health difficulties; specifically, address the difficulty some students have adjusting to the epidemic, which might result in stress, by tackling the socioeconomic and educational issues affecting these children.
*   It is essential to find strategies to increase stakeholder engagement to direct efforts toward supporting students; other academics may employ stakeholder engagement models and frameworks to describe how stakeholders collaborate to improve learning outcomes for deaf students.

input:
SSL-SoilNet: A Hybrid Transformer-Based Framework With Self-Supervised Learning for Large-Scale Soil Organic Carbon Prediction

Kakhani et al. introduce SSL-SoilNet, a framework combining Vision Transformers for satellite imagery and Transformers for climate data, trained via self-supervised contrastive learning and fine-tuned on labeled soil samples. Tested on two large-scale datasets (LUCAS and a European dataset), the model outperforms traditional supervised learning and conventional machine learning algorithms (random forest, gradient boosting) in soil organic carbon (SOC) prediction. Evaluation metrics include root-mean-square error (RMSE), mean absolute error (MAE), and concordance correlation coefficient (CCC). This approach advances digital soil mapping (DSM) and facilitates accurate land management decisions.

Index Terms— Contrastive learning, deep learning (DL), digital soil mapping (DSM), Europe, LUCAS, self-supervised model, soil organic carbon (SOC), spatiotemporal model.

like satellite imagery, topography, remote sensing indices, and
climate series. Within the domain of ML, self-supervised learning
(SSL), which exploits unlabeled data, has gained prominence
in recent years. This study introduces a novel approach that
aims to learn the geographical link between multimodal features

superiority over traditional supervised learning models, which

section: I. INTRODUCTION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Deep learning (DL) has become a popular field for modeling spatial and sequential data across various scientific domains [1]. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) excel at learning hierarchical data representations, enabling the integration of multimodal fusion, feature extraction, and inference into end-to-end frameworks [2]. The convergence of DL for spatial and sequence learning resembles many dynamic geoscience challenges [3]. Among geoscience applications, digital soil mapping (DSM) is prevalent for predicting soil properties [4]. DSM integrates multiple data types controlling soil formation, such as topography and climate, to produce high-resolution maps [5]. Soil organic carbon (SOC) is a critical component of the global carbon cycle, with two-thirds of terrestrial carbon stored in this form [10]. Predicting SOC via DSM is a regression problem effectively addressed by machine learning [11], [12]. The advent of remote sensing has led to widespread use of ML techniques using satellite imagery and vegetation indices at various scales [13]–[15]. However, classical ML faces limitations: it treats climate data as static values rather than time-series, limiting accuracy due to dynamic climatic conditions [16]. Furthermore, it overlooks spatial correlations present in remote sensing features [20]. Advanced DL techniques, such as transformers, address these issues by capturing long-term dependencies through self-attention mechanisms [18], [19]. The efficacy of transformers relies on large labeled datasets, but acquiring ground-truth soil data is often expensive and time-consuming, involving in situ surveys and laboratory analyses [27]. This scarcity poses challenges for training reliable DL models. Self-supervised learning (SSL) emerges as a promising alternative, where models are pre-trained on unlabeled data to learn robust feature representations before fine-tuning on limited labeled samples [28]. In SSL, contrastive learning is a widely employed technique that learns representations by differentiating similar (positive) and dissimilar (negative) samples [29]. However, these methods cannot be directly applied to multimodal data, as image-specific augmentations are unsuitable for temporal sequences [30]. The application of contrastive learning to soil property estimation remains relatively unexplored. This study presents SSL-SoilNet, a novel hybrid network for large-scale SOC prediction. The methodology comprises two phases: initially, self-supervised contrastive learning is applied to large unlabeled multimodal data (remote sensing and climate) to learn inherent structures [29]. Subsequently, the pre-trained model is fine-tuned using labeled ground reference samples for SOC prediction [29]. This framework extracts spatial information from remote sensing images while capturing time-series information from climate data. It uniquely establishes geographical linkages between image and climate data through similarity identification, enabling effective utilization of multimodal advantages. The main contributions are: 1) a hybrid multimodal model integrating remote sensing and climate data for SOC prediction; 2) a self-supervised contrastive learning framework leveraging unlabeled data for initial training and limited ground references for fine-tuning; 3) an innovative approach calculating similarities between climate and image data at specific locations, departing from traditional image augmentation techniques.

I
N RECENT years, deep learning (DL) has become an
increasingly popular field of study. It has been used to
model sequences and data with spatial context in computer
vision, speech recognition and control systems, as well as in
related scientific fields in physics, chemistry, and biology [1].
One of the primary benefits of DL models, specifically convolutional neural networks (CNNs), is their ability to learn
abstract hierarchical representations of the data, which enables
networks to uncover spatial, spectral, and temporal patterns
hidden in the data. This enables researchers and engineers
to streamline the information extraction processing chain,
potentially integrating multimodal data fusion, feature extraction, and inference duties into a single, holistic end-to-end
learning framework [2]. The convergence of DL approaches
for both spatial learning and sequence learning has generated
significant interest due to its remarkable resemblance to many
dynamic geoscience challenges (e.g., [3]).
There are a wide range of applications in geoscience that
can be addressed via DL among which we can mention
anomaly detection, dynamic modeling, semantic segmentation,
hyperspectral data analysis, and digital soil mapping (DSM)
[4]. DSM is one of the most prevalent methods for mapping soil properties, and its use continues to increase [5].
It refers to the process of producing high-resolution digital
maps of soil types and properties using statistical and ML
techniques to integrate multiple forms of data that largely
control soil forming processes, such as topography, vegetation,
climate, and parent material [6]. These maps can be used
for a variety of purposes, including precision agriculture,
land-use planning, environmental management, and natural
disaster risk assessment. As soil is essential for ecosystems
and plays a significant role in carbon cycling, food security,
biodiversity, and human activity, DSM enables a more efficient
and accurate characterization of soil variability and provides
a more comprehensive understanding of soil distribution and

properties over vast areas. In particular, DSM has proven to
be a valuable tool for mapping soil organic carbon (SOC)
content (e.g., [7], [8], [9]). SOC is a crucial component of the
global carbon cycle and plays a vital role in regulating climate
change. Two-thirds of the carbon in the terrestrial environment
is found in the form of SOC [10].
SOC prediction using DSM is an example of a regression
problem that can be effectively addressed by an ML approach
as proven by previous studies like [11] and [12]. With the
advent of remote sensing satellites and the development of
this technology over the past decade, methods based on ML
have become even more widespread in the field of DSM using
remote sensing images or other products such as vegetation
indices at local and global scales (e.g., [13], [14], [15]).
Yet, classical ML faces some criticisms due to its limitations. One significant limitation is its failure to consider the
dynamic nature of certain input data, notably climate data
utilized extensively in DSM, which ought to be treated as timeseries data. However, classical ML treats each observation
as a single value, disregarding the temporal relationships
between observations. Due to many inherent factors, such as
abnormal climatic conditions, the accuracy of monotemporal
data is basically limited [16]. To overcome these limitations,
advanced DL techniques, such as transformers [17], provide
a powerful solution. Transformers, originally developed for
natural language processing tasks, have shown exceptional
performance in time-series analysis due to their ability to
capture long-term dependencies within data [18]. Transformers
leverage self-attention mechanisms weigh the importance of
different points in the time series, here climate data, allowing
it to focus on relevant data points regardless of their position
in the sequence [19].
Classical ML also faces another drawback as it overlooks
spatial and neighborhood details, often referred to as conceptual or geometric information. This is a basic limitation,
as many remote sensing features exhibit spatial correlation, meaning that their values at one location are often
related to the values at nearby locations, and this information
can be highly beneficial for prediction [20]. In this case,
spatial autocorrelation in the residuals of spatial environmental models could be accounted for by using features
from multiple scales [21], and a variogram can be used to
determine an effective scale. Several studies in the DSM
field have attempted to address this issue using DL models.
Specifically, in [22], a CNN-based architecture with shared
layers was utilized to predict particle size fractions of clay,
sand, and silt across six standard layers. More recently,
Tziolas et al. [23] introduced a dual input DL architecture that
simultaneously combined Sentinel-2 data and environmental
covariates through two distinct neural network branches to
estimate SOC. Nowadays, with the emergence of vision transformers (ViT), Jagetia et al. [24] applied this method to soil
classification, demonstrating superior performance compared
to other models. Additionally, in a study by Lin et al. [25] and
Jin et al. [26], Vis-NIR spectra were leveraged in conjunction
with the Swin Transformer to predict soil properties.
The efficacy of transformers relies on the availability
of a large number of data samples for training a robust
model [27]. However, acquiring soil property information is
often expensive and time-consuming, involving in situ surveys
and extensive laboratory analyses. Consequently, groundtruth samples may be insufficient in certain regions, posing
challenges in training reliable DL models. To mitigate this
dependence on high-quality datasets, self-supervised learning
(SSL) emerges as a promising alternative. In SSL, a model
is initially pre-trained on unlabeled data, leveraging inherent
data structures or patterns to learn valuable representations or
features [28]. Subsequently, the pre-trained model undergoes
fine-tuning using labeled data samples to adapt to specific
downstream tasks, such as image classification.
Given the often easy accessibility of unlabeled data, such
as RS imagery and climate data, self-supervised pre-training
proves effective in enabling the model to acquire reliable
and adaptable feature representations [29]. This approach is
particularly advantageous when the downstream task lacks
sufficient labeled data, as pre-trained models can prevent overfitting and yield robust performance post-fine-tuning. In SSL,
contrastive learning stands out as a widely employed technique [30]. Contrastive learning aims to learn representations
shared among similar samples (positive pairs) while differentiating them from dissimilar samples (negative pairs) [29].
Typically, positive pairs consist of two random “views” of
the same sample through random data augmentation, while
negative pairs arise from other samples in the dataset. The
learning objective in contrastive learning is to minimize contrastive loss, promoting the closeness of representations for
positive pairs and pushing apart representations for negative
pairs. However, these methods cannot be directly applied to
multimodal data, as image-specific augmentation techniques
are not suitable for temporal sequences. The application of
contrastive learning to address soil property estimation remains
a relatively unexplored area.
Thus, in this study, we present a novel hybrid network
designed for SOC prediction on a large scale, leveraging
a substantial number of unlabeled samples during the pretraining phase, without requiring extensive laboratory analysis.
This network, called SSL-SoilNet, utilizes a self-supervised
contrastive learning approach. The methodology comprises
two main phases. Initially, self-supervised contrastive learning is applied to a large unlabeled samples that includes
both remote sensing and climate data. This phase focuses
on leveraging the inherent structure and patterns within the
multimodal data for unsupervised feature learning. Subsequently, the pre-trained self-supervised model is transitioned
into the supervised segment, where ground reference samples
are incorporated for fine-tuning. The second phase focuses on
refining the model for SOC prediction by using labeled data.

Self-supervised contrastive learning is a paradigm that entails the unsupervised pre-training of models using unlabeled data. This approach is characterized by the formulation of a task wherein the model endeavors to discriminate between positive pairs (representing similar instances, s+) and negative pairs (representing dissimilar instances, s−) within the given unlabeled data. The central idea, derived from the theoretical mathematical framework outlined in [31], involves optimizing the model through a contrastive loss function, which quantifies the divergence or convergence between the representations of input pairs. The general formulation of the contrastive loss ℓ is expressed as

ℓi, j = −log exp sim(si, sj)/τ / P2N k=1 1[k̸=i] exp(sim(si, sk)/τ) (1)

where si and sj positive pair, s+; sk negative (contrastive) pairs, s−; 1 indicator function; τ temperature parameter.

The temperature τ allows us to balance the influence of many dissimilar representations versus a similar one. This idea was introduced first in [30] as SimCLR. The similarity function, sim(·, ·), is cosine similarity as defined by sim(u, v) = u⊤· v / u · v. (2)

As depicted in Fig. 2, a pivotal departure from the classical SimCLR methodology is observed concerning positive pairs denoted as s+. In contrast to the conventional SimCLR approach where positive pairs involve augmented images, here, these pairs comprise representations derived from image-based inputs, (I), and temporal sequences, (T), originating from the identical spatial location. This distinction holds significance as it introduces a novel dimension to the concept of positive pairs within the SimCLR framework. Rather than relying solely on image augmentations to diversify positive pairs, the inclusion of temporal information alongside spatial representation enhances the model’s capacity to encapsulate both static and dynamic aspects inherent to the given spatial context. Consequently, the positive pairs, now comprising not only visual variations but also temporal dynamics, contribute to a more comprehensive and contextually rich feature extraction process. This adaptation of positive pairs aligns with the input data’s intrinsic nature, emphasizing the capture of spatiotemporal relationships in SimCLR. It represents a deliberate refinement catering to diverse data modalities, especially in soil properties prediction scenarios where both spatial and temporal cues collectively shape the underlying information structure. The pseudocode outlining the training procedure is detailed in Algorithm 1.

instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: The self-supervised model is fine-tuned for regression to predict soil organic carbon (SOC) values. Intermediate representations from image-based (I) and time-series (T) inputs are fed into a two-layer MLP trained on labeled data. Due to the skewed distribution of soil samples, root-mean-squared logarithmic error (RMSLE) is used as the loss function. RMSLE is defined as the square root of the mean squared difference between the natural logarithms of the observed (y_i) and predicted (ŷ_i) values plus one, which mitigates the impact of skewed data and avoids undefined logarithms for zero or negative values.

IV. EXPERIMENTS AND ANALYSIS — B. Evaluation Metrics

When evaluating predictive models, common metrics include mean absolute error (MAE), the coefficient of determination (R²), root-mean-square error (RMSE), ratio of performance to interquartile distance (RPIQ), and concordance correlation coefficient (CCC). MAE is the average of absolute differences between predicted and true values: MAE = 1/n ∑(|yi − ŷi|) [4]. R² represents the proportion of variance in the dependent variable explained by independent variables: R² = 1 − ∑(yi − ŷi)² / ∑(yi − ȳ)² [5]. RMSE is the square root of the average squared differences: RMSE = √(1/n ∑(yi − ŷi)²) [6]. RPIQ is calculated as (Q3 − Q1) / RMSE [7], where Q1 and Q3 are the 25th and 75th percentiles of true samples. CCC measures agreement between predicted and true values, accounting for mean and variance differences: CCC = 2ρσyσŷ / (σ²y + σ²ŷ + (µy − µŷ)²) [8], where ρ is the correlation coefficient, σ are standard deviations, and µ are means. These metrics provide quantitative measures of accuracy, correction, agreement, and calibration against observed values.

C. Results

The outcomes of the conducted experiments are consolidated in Tables III and IV. Experiment groups are discussed in Sections IV-C1–IV-C3.

1) Baselines: The study includes three network configurations for the LUCAS and RaCA datasets (Tables III and IV), denoted as ViT + Trans., ViT + LSTM, and CNN + Trans. These represent hybrid architectural approaches. ViT and ResNet-101 process image data; LSTM networks substitute Transformers for time-series analysis due to established efficacy with sequential information [48]. Across methods and input features, ViT + Trans. generally outperforms the other configurations across most evaluated metrics.

2) Contrastive SSL Versus Supervised Learning: Each configuration was evaluated using supervised training with ground reference samples and self-supervised contrastive learning with unlabeled samples. Approximately 70,000 unlabeled samples were used for LUCAS and 30,000 for RaCA. Irrelevant land-cover classes (e.g., built-up areas, water bodies) were excluded using ESA land-cover product [49]. In both datasets, SSL-SoilNet outperformed supervised SoilNet, demonstrating the pre-trained model’s effectiveness in linking image-based and climate-based information geographically, enhancing prediction accuracy. With the RaCA dataset, RMSE decreased by 8.38 Mg/ha, R² increased by 4%, and MAE was reduced by 8.39 Mg/ha. This improvement may be attributed to the model addressing severe data imbalance, particularly in upper SOC ranges. Notably, RPIQ did not improve, as its definition focuses on population spread rather than solely accuracy; a low RMSE can still yield a high RPIQ, suggesting these metrics should be analyzed together.

3) Ablation Study: Input features were categorized into four groups: Landsat images and derived indices, topographic information (elevation, slope), and primary and secondary climate variables. Testing across ViT + Trans., ViT + LSTM, and CNN + Transformer configurations revealed that excluding all climate information resulted in the lowest performance, underscoring the significance of time-series information as soil properties are influenced by climatic conditions. Incorporating secondary climate variables marginally improved RMSE, CCC, and R² compared to primary variables, indicating a contributory role. Topographic information consistently enhanced accuracy for both datasets. Omitting primary and secondary climate variables sometimes reduced MAE, for example in supervised ViT + LSTM (LUCAS) and supervised ViT + Trans. MAE = 1/n ∑(yi − ŷi) (4)

R2 (also known as the coefficient of determination) is a statistical measure that represents the proportion of the variance in the dependent variable that can be explained by the independent variables in a regression model. It is commonly used to assess the goodness of fit of a regression model. This value is calculated using the following equation:

R2 = 1 − ∑(yi − ŷi)² / ∑(yi − ȳ)² (5)

where n is the number of observations, yi is the observed value of the dependent variable for observation i, ŷi is the predicted value of the dependent variable for observation i based on the regression model, and ȳ is the mean of the observed values of the dependent variable.

RMSE is calculated by taking the square root of the average of the squared differences between the predicted values and the true values

RMSE = √(1/n ∑(yi − ŷi)²) (6)

RPIQ represents the spread of the population and is calculated using the following equation [47]:

RPIQ = (Q3 − Q1) / RMSE (7)

The values Q1 and Q3 represent the 25th and 75th percentiles of the true samples, respectively, defining the interquartile distance.

CCC is a measure of the agreement between the predicted values and the true values. It takes into account both the mean difference and the variance difference between the predicted and true values

CCC = 2ρσyσŷ / (σ²y + σ²ŷ + (µy − µŷ)²) (8)

where ρ represents the correlation coefficient between the predicted and observed values, σy and σŷ are the standard deviations of the observed and predicted values, respectively, and µy and µŷ are the means of the observed and predicted values, respectively.

These metrics provide quantitative measures to assess the accuracy, correction, agreement, and calibration of predictive models compared to the observed values.

C. Results

The outcomes of the conducted experiments are comprehensively consolidated in Tables III and IV. The details of each experiment group will be discussed in Sections IV-C1–IV-C3.

1) Baselines: Our study includes three primary network configurations for both the LUCAS dataset (see Table III) and the RaCA dataset (see Table IV), denoted as ViT + Trans., ViT + LSTM, and CNN + Trans. These configurations represent distinct hybrid architectural approaches we adopted for our analysis. Specifically, we utilized the ViT and a conventional CNN, here ResNet-101, to process image data. For the analysis of time-series data, we substitute long short-term memory (LSTM) networks over Transformers due to LSTM’s established efficacy in managing sequential information [48]. Irrespective of the selected method (supervised or SSL) and the type of input features, our findings generally indicate that the ViT + Trans. configuration outperforms the other two configurations across most evaluated metrics.

2) Contrastive SSL Versus Supervised Learning: Each network configuration introduced in Section IV-C1 was evaluated using two distinct methodologies. Initially, we conducted supervised training using only the ground reference samples available for each dataset. Subsequently, we integrated unlabeled samples into a self-supervised contrastive learning model, as described in Section II-B.

For the LUCAS dataset, approximately 70 000 unlabeled randomly selected samples were utilized, whereas for the RaCA dataset, around 30 000 were employed to prepare our pre-trained model. To guarantee relevance to soil, we evaluated the land-cover classes within each downloaded image patch. If the majority of a Landsat-8 image patch was identified as irrelevant land-cover classes such as built-up areas or permanent water bodies, that sample was excluded from our analysis. We have used ESA land-cover product [49] for this purpose.

In both datasets, the performance of SSL-SoilNet was superior to that of supervised SoilNet, demonstrating the pre-trained model’s effectiveness in linking image-based and climate-based information geographically. This integration of information contributed to enhanced prediction accuracy. A notable observation was made with the RaCA dataset results, where the improvement in evaluation metrics was substantial. Specifically, the RMSE decreased by 8.38 Mg/ha, the R2 increased by 4%, and the MAE was reduced by 8.39 Mg/ha. This marked enhancement may be attributed to the model’s ability to address severe data imbalance, especially in the upper quantiles of SOC ranges. Essentially, leveraging information from random samples allowed the model to better understand patterns in samples with high SOC levels. It is important to highlight that the RPIQ metric does not show improvement, which is attributed to its definition focusing on the population spread rather than solely on accuracy. A model exhibiting a low RMSE can still result in a high RPIQ, suggesting that RMSE and RPIQ metrics should be analyzed in conjunction.

3) Ablation Study: To evaluate the contribution of input features in our study, we conducted an ablation study by categorizing our input features into four groups: Landsat images and their derived indices, topographic information (i.e., elevation and slope), and two types of climate information (i.e., primary and secondary variables), as introduced in Section III-B4. We tested each feature group across different configurations, including ViT + Transformer, ViT + LSTM, and CNN + Transformer models in Tables III and IV.

As expected, the exclusion of all climate information resulted in the lowest performance across all configurations, underscoring the significance of using time-series information. This is because soil properties are influenced not only by surface information from satellite images but also by climatic conditions. Incorporating secondary climate variables yields marginally improved outcomes in terms of RMSE, CCC, and R2 compared to primary climate variables, indicating a contributory role of this feature group. Topographic information consistently enhanced prediction accuracy for both datasets. The omission of primary and secondary climate variables sometimes led to a reduction in the MAE, for example, in the supervised training of ViT + LSTM for the LUCAS dataset and supervised training of ViT + Trans. for the RaCA dataset. This is possibly due to the complex nature of time-series data, which may contain noisy information. Removing such noisy data can, in some instances, improve overall prediction accuracy.

section: IV. EXPERIMENTS AND ANALYSIS — D. Comparison to the Other ML Models
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
We evaluated our model against naive baselines and seven machine learning methods. For the LUCAS dataset, the mean served as the naive prediction; for the RaCA dataset, the median was used due to severe skewness. Although the naive model achieved zero R², it provided a baseline for comparison.

We compared our results against Random Forest, Deep Forest, XGBoost, GBDT, Extremely Randomized Trees, SVR, and Cubist. Hyperparameters were optimized using randomized grid search. On the LUCAS dataset, SSL-SoilNet achieved the highest accuracy across RMSE, R², MAE, CCC, and RPIQ metrics, outperforming all other models. Supervised SoilNet also surpassed other machine learning models. Low R² values for SVR and Extremely Randomized Trees were attributed to their inability to capture the nonlinearity inherent in the soil system.

On the RaCA dataset, results varied by metric. Random Forest recorded the highest RPIQ, indicating its capacity to generate wide prediction intervals despite lower precision. Deep Forest achieved the best MAE, and XGBoost secured the highest Concordance Correlation Coefficient. The disparity between the best and worst RMSE scores (between SSL-SoilNet and XGBoost) was 47.26 Mg/ha, with approximately a 20% difference in R² scores, highlighting the impact of skewed distributions on model consistency. Support Vector Regression and Cubist exhibited the lowest R² values among machine learning models, indicating a deviation from the data trend.

We illustrated the spatial distribution of observed and predicted Soil Organic Carbon (SOC) across the CONUS and Europe. In the RaCA dataset, regions with notable SOC variability included the northeastern area, west coastal area, and mountainous regions, where limited deep observations and shallow, coarse-textured soils influenced performance. Random Forest failed to capture this variability accurately, while SSL-SoilNet outperformed other models in matching reference data trends.

For the LUCAS dataset, all models captured continental-scale trends. In Europe, mountains and the Alps were of particular significance, with forest soils exhibiting the highest organic carbon concentrations and grasslands acting as specific biological hotspots. SSL-SoilNet demonstrated superior performance in Areas A, B, and C, particularly in accurately identifying samples with high SOC values in Area C. Supervised SoilNet showed marginal improvements over machine learning models in specific areas.

Challenging prediction areas were frequently associated with wetland land-cover classes, where decades of cold and anaerobic conditions resulted in significant soil heterogeneity and decelerated organic matter decomposition. Various factors control SOC dynamics, and the quality of input features significantly influences accuracy. We utilized satellite data with 30 m resolution and climate time-series data with ∼4 km resolution. Further improvements could be achieved by incorporating high-resolution satellite images and finer-resolution climate datasets (e.g., 1 km), particularly for regional-scale applications.

To comprehensively assess our model’s performance, we adopted a straightforward approach as the first step. We assumed the most basic scenarios for prediction models: for the LUCAS dataset, which exhibits a distribution close to normal, we used the mean as the simplest prediction for all available samples. Conversely, for the RaCA dataset, which demonstrates severe skewness, we employed the median of the available ground truth. Subsequently, we computed all evaluation metrics. Although the naive model is not expected to achieve high performance, as evidenced by the zero value for R2, it offers valuable insights into the efficacy of our proposed approach and other machine learning (ML) models when benchmarked against the most basic scenarios.

In the second step, we compared our results with those from seven commonly used ML models. The first model we evaluated was Random Forest (RF), a popular ML algorithm often applied to regression tasks, especially in the field of soil science (e.g., [50]). The second model, known as Deep Forest, is an advanced version of RF. It is a decision tree ensemble method that requires fewer hyperparameters than DL models [51]. Additionally, we explored two variations of gradient boosting: XGBoost [52] and Gradient Boosting Decision Tree (GBDT) [53]. XGBoost is an optimized distributed gradient boosting library known for enhancing efficiency and performance. GBDT is also a powerful technique that improves prediction accuracy by building decision trees sequentially, focusing on minimizing errors from previous trees. We also evaluated extremely randomized trees (ERT) [54], a variation of random forest that introduces additional randomness into the model, potentially increasing the diversity among the trees. The other ML models used for comparison were support vector regressor (SVR) and Cubist, which is a rule-based model that combines decision trees and linear regression [55]. The hyperparameters for all implemented models were determined using randomized grid search.

Tables V and VI present the analysis of two datasets, LUCAS and RaCA, providing insightful observations on the performance of various models. Across both datasets, SSL-SoilNet, the self-supervised contrastive learning model, achieved the highest accuracy as measured by RMSE and R2. This highlights the superiority of our proposed approach, largely due to the incorporation of additional information from unlabeled data during training. Additionally, for the LUCAS dataset, SSL-SoilNet surpassed other models in MAE, CCC, and RPIQ metrics, indicating that our approach excels in accuracy, provides more realistic prediction intervals (as calculated through RPIQ), and ensures greater concordance between predictions and observations (measured by CCC), all while maintaining the lowest mean average error. Supervised SoilNet also showed commendable performance, surpassing other ML models. It is important to note that the R2 values are low in certain cases, such as SVR and ERT, because these models struggled to capture the nonlinearity inherent in the data, which arises from the complexity of the soil system [56].

Fig. 7. Distribution of SOC (Mg/ha) measurements for test samples and the results from implemented models, SSL and supervised SoilNet, and RF, on the left side. Areas A–C highlight regions with data heterogeneity. On the right side, zoomed-in view sections compare the performance of different models against the ground truth across four rows, with SSL-SoilNet’s performance showing close alignment with the ground reference samples.

TABLE V
PERFORMANCE RESULTS FOR SSL AND SUPERVISED SOILNET, AND OTHER COMMON ML METHODS ON THE LUCAS DATASET

The scenario for the RaCA dataset was somewhat different, marked by significant positive skewness in value distribution, as detailed in Table I. Here, the RF model recorded the highest RPIQ, highlighting its capacity to generate wide prediction intervals, even though its predictions were less precise compared to those from SSL and supervised SoilNet. DeepForest, an improved version of RF, achieved the best MAE, while XGBoost secured the highest CCC. These findings illustrate the varied strengths of different ML methodologies in SOC prediction, suggesting no single approach dominates across all evaluation metrics. Despite this, DL models, especially SSL-SoilNet, have proven to offer the most accurate predictions.

The pronounced skewness of the RaCA dataset has also led to significant variability in performance metrics among all implemented methods. For example, the disparity between the best and worst RMSE scores (noted between SSL-SoilNet and XGBoost, respectively) was 47.26 Mg/ha, with a ∼20 % difference in R2 scores, highlighting the impact of skewed distributions on the consistency of model performance across various evaluation metrics. Furthermore, the SVR and Cubist models, exhibiting the lowest R2 value among the other ML models, indicated a deviation from the trend observed in the RaCA samples.

E. Discussion

We have illustrated the spatial distribution of observed SOC for test samples, alongside the predicted SOC from both SSL and supervised SoilNet, as well as the top-performing ML methods, RF for RaCA and GBDT for LUCAS datasets, across our study areas, which encompass the CONUS and Europe in Figs. 7 and 8. To enhance the visualization of the various model performances, we plotted the predicted values against the observed values in Supplementary Figs. S1 and S2. The map of residuals is also included in Supplementary Fig. S3.

In our analysis of the RaCA dataset, regions such as the northeastern area, west coastal area, and rocky mountain area exhibit notable variations in SOC values [57]. Specifically regarding mountainous regions, this variability can be partly ascribed to the limited availability of SOC observations at greater depths. The acquisition of samples from these deeper layers is resource-intensive and presents significant challenges [58]. Additionally, mountain soils within the CONUS are characterized by their tendency to be shallow, thin, and coarse-textured. Consequently, variations in these properties are anticipated to have a more significant influence on SOC dynamics in these areas [59]. A notable discovery from our study is the discrepancy between the output of RF and DL models. This indicates that RF failed to capture the variability within these areas accurately.

We focused on three distinct areas characterized by varying climatic conditions and land-cover classes to assess the performance of our implemented methodologies. Area A, located in the midwestern part of the United States, features land-cover classes predominantly consisting of wetlands and tree covers [60]. This region’s land cover is indicative of its ecological diversity and complexity. Area B, situated in the northeastern United States, is characterized by wetlands and forests, along with relatively high precipitation and low average temperatures [61]. Conversely, Area C is distinguished by its higher temperatures and above-average precipitation levels, with land cover primarily comprising wetlands, croplands, and developed areas in the southeastern United States. Despite the inherent differences among these areas, a commonality emerges in their heterogeneity concerning SOC values. Each area contains samples with both exceptionally low and high SOC values, presenting challenges for any ML/DL models in achieving accurate predictions. This variability underscores the complexity of SOC prediction and the necessity for sophisticated models capable of accommodating such diverse environmental conditions. The outcomes obtained from the RF model serve as evidence supporting this claim, as the final map generated by RF failed to accurately capture the data trends across Areas A–C. This inadequacy highlights the model’s limitation in reflecting the intricate spatial variations inherent to each area. In contrast, supervised-SoilNet demonstrated a marginally improved performance, particularly for Area A, as depicted on the right side of Fig. 7. Supervised-SoilNet’s slight improvement was not enough to accurately represent the correct data trends on a local scale. However, SSL-SoilNet outperformed the other models in accurately capturing the data trends across all designated areas. SSL-SoilNet demonstrates superior performance in dealing with the spatial complexity and variability of SOC values, offering a more precise and reliable prediction capability.

In the context of the LUCAS dataset, all models demonstrated the capability to capture data trends at a continental scale. In Europe, mountains, and specifically the European Alps, are of great significance. Forest soils within this region have the highest organic carbon concentrations [62], where low air temperatures slow down the decomposition of organic material, leading to significant accumulation of soil organic matter. Additionally, grassland soils are considered one of the most specific biological hotspots, abundant in organic carbon [63]. Due to the limited accessibility and extensive spatial heterogeneity of these regions [64], they could be among the most challenging areas. Utilizing a considerable quantity of unlabeled samples during the self-supervised training in SSL-SoilNet provides the model with an opportunity to acquire insights into these regions even in the absence of plentiful ground-truth samples. This facilitates more accurate predictions.

Detailed examinations were conducted for three distinct areas within Europe. Area A is situated in the northern part of Europe, specifically Finland, Norway, and Sweden, characterized predominantly by wetlands, high precipitation, and low temperatures. Area B, located in Germany and the Netherlands, is primarily composed of grassland, cropland, and wetlands, coupled with below-average temperatures and relatively high precipitation. Conversely, Area C in Spain experiences low precipitation and high temperatures, with its land-cover classes including cropland, grassland, and bareland.

For Area A, none of the implemented models were fully successful in accurately reflecting the trends observed in the ground reference samples. This difficulty in prediction for Area A aligns with previous studies that have identified it as a region with high uncertainty in SOC predictions [65]. However, the maps generated by SSL-SoilNet showed a closer resemblance to the reference samples than those produced by both supervised training and the GBDT model, indicating a relatively better performance. A similar observation was made for Area B, where SSL-SoilNet outperformed other models in matching the reference data trends. In the case of Area C, which presents a distinct environmental profile from Areas A and B, the only model that demonstrated proficiency in identifying samples with high SOC values was SSL-SoilNet. This finding underscores the effectiveness of SSL-SoilNet in dealing with the complex variability of SOC across different landscapes, particularly in areas where environmental conditions significantly differ.

An intriguing finding from both datasets is the association between challenging areas and the presence of land-cover class wetlands. Within these regions, soils have been influenced by decades of cold and anaerobic conditions, resulting in significant heterogeneity in composition [66]. This diversity, reflecting a range of soil microbial activities and decelerated organic matter decomposition rates [67], presents challenges in accurately assessing SOC and predicting its distribution in these areas.

Various factors control SOC, highlighting the complexity of its dynamics. Understanding the spatial distribution of these variables is crucial for predicting how ecosystems will adapt to changes in climate conditions. Therefore, it is essential to consider the primary predictive drivers across different regions, to effectively model SOC dynamics and ecosystem responses [58]. Wiesmeier et al. [68] suggested that regional approaches are needed to estimate the SOC storage capacity according to specific climatic conditions and vegetation characteristics. Moreover, another study suggested that SOC dynamics in more than 70% of topsoil in China were controlled by climate change and its coupled influence with environmental variation [69]. In light of these findings, we employed a comprehensive array of input features in our study, including satellite data with a spatial resolution of 30 m and climate time-series data with a spatial resolution of ∼4 km. Given that the quality of input features and the uncertainty within the data significantly influence prediction accuracy, further improvements can be achieved by utilizing high-resolution satellite images and/or climate datasets with finer resolutions (e.g., 1 km). This refinement could be particularly crucial for the application of our approach on a regional scale.

STRATA2.0: A Serverless Middleware for Machine Learning Training
Dimitrios Tomaras, Sebastian Buschjäger, Vana Kalogeraki, Katharina Morik, and Dimitrios Gunopulos

Serverless computing has gained interest for large-scale machine learning tasks, but training models in this setting faces challenges in data distribution, result aggregation, resource heterogeneity, failures, and container ephemerality. We propose STRATA2.0, a serverless middleware designed to support efficient training on serverless infrastructures. It addresses key challenges related to data communication, coordination, and synchronization using heterogeneous containers. Experiments show that STRATA2.0 achieves comparable accuracy with fewer data points, is on average three times faster than centralized approaches, reduces energy consumption by up to 50%, and remains resilient when up to 60% of training instances fail.

section: I. INTRODUCTION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
Serverless machine learning has emerged as a powerful way of building ML products on loosely coupled functions that provide compute and storage services [1]. The serverless model abstracts underlying infrastructure, allowing developers to focus on application code without managing servers [1]. These characteristics empower practitioners to iterate rapidly, decouple pipeline components, and leverage fine-grained parallelism without the overhead of managing infrastructure, compared to traditional server-based or VM-based solutions (IaaS) that require dedicated machine configuration [2], [3], [4]. The serverless model provides benefits including unlimited elasticity, automatic scaling, built-in high availability, a pay-per-use model that increases agility and optimizes costs, and lower set-up overhead, attracting growing interest. Its event-driven and modular nature enables scalable ML pipelines where components such as data ingestion, pre-processing, or model training can be independently deployed and triggered by events. Its automatic scaling capability makes it well-suited for parallelizing ML training tasks such as hyperparameter optimization and model evaluation. Furthermore, the pay-per-use pricing model reduces resource utilization, making it advantageous for sporadic or bursty training workloads. During inactivity, ephemeral containers stop running (scale to zero) to keep costs low. This feature has been proven beneficial for deep learning models (i.e., DNNs) for both training and inference, as shown in recent works [3], [4], [5], [6].

A notable constraint of serverless frameworks is the frequent assumption of homogeneity across incoming requests and the underlying hardware infrastructure. Consequently, autoscalers default to coarse metrics (e.g., queries per second, CPU utilization) and overlook application- and hardware-specific signals. In reality, incoming requests exhibit significant variability in task type and data volume, and functions may require diverse resource configurations. For example, while Random Forest inference is relatively lightweight and broadly supported, its training process is considerably more resource-intensive. It is dominated by data movement, memory management, and coordination efforts necessary to construct large and diverse trees, factors that directly affect model quality and impose distinct resource demands. When selecting container specifications and setting concurrency levels, developers must navigate a trade-off between deploying smaller containers with low concurrency and large containers with high concurrency. In homogeneous serverless container settings, naive task placement often results in resource fragmentation across cluster nodes, thereby impairing overall resource utilization [7]. In practice, resource demands within serverless architectures are highly dynamic, driven by time-varying workloads. This underscores the need for more agile, heterogeneity-aware and efficient resource allocation strategies.

Moreover, the ephemeral nature of serverless environments renders accurate ML training particularly fragile. Existing frameworks such as Apache MLlib [8] and XGBoost [9], built for long-lived executors, are ill-suited to serverless settings, especially for applications requiring high accuracy. In the serverless computing model, stateless retries and at-least-once semantics may lead to redundant or dropped gradient updates unless operations are strictly idempotent, thereby biasing optimization processes and impeding convergence. Additionally, preemptions can terminate containers mid-execution, introducing silent accuracy regressions upon resumption. Even "embarrassingly parallel" Random Forests suffer: retries and preemptions can disrupt bootstrap sampling, feature subset selection, and shard-level statistics, ultimately altering tree structure and degrading the integrity of the final model. While such conditions necessitate robust serverless execution mechanisms, prioritizing robustness exclusively by design, as in LambdaML [5], incurs significant time overhead, thereby hindering time-efficient training.

Consequently, enabling robust ML training (e.g., Random Forests and DNNs) in serverless settings demands a holistic approach that: (i) ensures model accuracy comparable to monolithic deployments despite the transient nature of serverless containers, (ii) minimizes resource fragmentation across worker nodes, particularly under high concurrency, (iii) exploits container heterogeneity to improve resource utilization, and (iv) satisfies developer-defined service-level objectives for cost-efficiency and latency, through appropriate system-level abstractions and primitives.

Contributions: We summarize our contributions below:

r We present STRATA2.0, a serverless middleware for machine learning training in serverless environments. STRATA2.0 comprises a comprehensive suite of mechanisms designed to enable efficient training of machine learning models in serverless infrastructures. Our mechanisms address key challenges in data communication, coordination and synchronization and scalable and time-efficient training of ML models using heterogeneous containers. By improving resource efficiency while maintaining model performance, our system addresses fundamental limitations in scaling ML workloads to large datasets and increasingly sophisticated model architectures.

r We prove both theoretically and confirm experimentally, that STRATA2.0 is fault-tolerant with respect to model accuracy. We employ a Rademacher-complexity analysis to demonstrate that failures of individual containers result in only minor deviations in predictive performance, with the resulting accuracy loss under failures being provably bounded (e.g. by O(1/M) for M trees in a Random Forest model).

III. A COMPREHENSIVE SUITE OF MECHANISMS FOR
SERVERLESS ML TRAINING TASKS

The proliferation of machine learning (ML) applications across diverse domains has exposed significant limitations in traditional cloud computing paradigms. While Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS) platforms provide substantial resources, they often introduce prohibitive operational overhead and cost inefficiencies for ML workloads characterized by dynamic resource demands and intermittent execution patterns. Serverless computing emerges as a compelling alternative, offering automatic scaling, pay-per-use pricing, and reduced administrative burden. However, applying serverless architectures to ML training introduces unique challenges. ML training jobs are typically compute-intensive, stateful, and require tight integration with specialized hardware accelerators (e.g., GPUs, TPUs). Furthermore, the iterative nature of training algorithms, involving frequent synchronization of model parameters and gradients, conflicts with the stateless, ephemeral execution model inherent in many serverless platforms. Existing solutions often address only isolated aspects of these challenges, such as function invocation or basic resource provisioning, but fail to provide a holistic framework for orchestrating the end-to-end lifecycle of ML training tasks in a serverless environment. There is a critical need for a comprehensive suite of mechanisms that bridges the gap between the capabilities of serverless platforms and the rigorous demands of ML training, enabling developers to harness the benefits of cloud-scale efficiency without sacrificing the performance and control required for effective model development.

Exposing multiple configurations mitigates resource fragmentation through finer-grained bin-packing and enables tiered autoscaling, where smaller containers absorb burstiness and larger ones sustain steady-state workloads.

STRATA2.0 generates samples of specific sizes and retrieves corresponding indices from a distributed storage system (e.g., S3), ensuring each sample fits within assigned container memory constraints rather than utilizing the whole raw dataset.

STRATA2.0 employs containers to serve as the host environment for the ML training process. Heterogeneous serverless containers are necessary to accommodate diverse ML training workloads so that resource configurations match per-workload demands and performance objectives are satisfied. Exposing multiple container configurations mitigates resource fragmentation through finer-grained bin-packing [10] and enables tiered autoscaling, where smaller containers absorb workload burstiness and larger ones sustain steady-state workloads.

In this work, we focus on Random Forest training, which assumes that training and test samples are independently and identically distributed (i.i.d.) according to an unknown distribution D over the input space X and labels Y. We are given a labeled sample S = {(xi, yi)|, i = 1, . . . , N}, where xi ∈ X ⊆ Rd is a d-dimensional feature-vector and yi ∈ Y ⊆ RC is the corresponding target vector, where C is the number of classes. Each decision tree (DT) in the forest is denoted as hi and its prediction for the observation x is given by hi(x). The forest is then given by a set of M trees {h1, h2, . . . , hM} and the RF’s prediction is given by f(x) = Σi=1M hi(x). Further, let θ = {θ1, . . . , θM} denote the set of all probability estimates associated with the leaves of all trees in the forest, and let fθ(x) represent the prediction of the forest with estimates θ.

STRATA2.0 generates samples of specific sizes (in terms of the number of data points) and retrieves the corresponding indices from the original dataset stored in a distributed storage system (e.g., S3), ensuring that each sample fits within the memory constraints of its assigned container [5], instead of utilizing the whole raw dataset.

Observation 1. Memory requirements vary significantly and can lead to substantial memory waste: We investigated the impact of input feature dimensionality and tree depth on per-worker memory consumption, and how this behavior varies under heterogeneous containers (with different CPU and memory capacities) for ML training tasks. Fig. 2 compares memory wastage between homogeneous and heterogeneous deployments for the same dataset and ML training task. Container selection is driven by the fraction of training samples used for tree construction, which serves as a threshold for assigning small or large container types. As the training data fraction increases, heterogeneous configurations improve efficiency, reducing memory wastage by up to 60% at 80% of the data. Based on these observations, we dynamically instantiate containers by jointly considering training sample size and model characteristics (e.g., tree depth), selecting the most appropriate heterogeneous container configuration.

We propose two efficient data communication mechanisms, GARF and MARF, to reduce the volume of data exchanged during training and lower communication costs. A key constraint of commercial serverless platforms is strict payload size limits (e.g., AWS 6 MB, IBM Openwhisk 1 MB, Google Cloud Functions 10 MB), which severely limit the volume of data transferable within a single invocation and constrain traditional ML training approaches relying on large datasets. Container parameters, defined by CPU and memory (e.g., tiers offering up to 10 GB [11]), significantly impact training performance; appropriate configuration can accelerate ML task convergence with minimal scheduling overhead [12]-[16]. In STRATA2.0, a naive communication strategy fetching all training data became a dominant straggler, particularly while scaling. STRATA2.0's MARF and GARF algorithms address these constraints by operating on smaller subsets of training data. We adopt a variant of the Random Forest algorithm known as leaf refinement [17],[18]. Given an already trained forest, this technique improves accuracy by minimizing a global loss function; it refines probability estimates in leaf nodes based on interactions across the ensemble without modifying underlying tree structures. The benefit of leaf refinement is that it is model-agnostic and can be applied to any tree ensemble, making it compatible with a wide variety of initial training methods. section: III. A COMPREHENSIVE SUITE OF MECHANISMS FOR — C. Distributed Training Mechanisms
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
The literature proposes parameter server (PS) or decentralized approaches for distributed training [2], [20], [21]. However, serverless infrastructures restrict direct function communication, requiring indirect interaction via a gateway [22], which increases synchronization overhead and developer burden. STRATA2.0 adopts a PS approach [2], [20], where the PS orchestrates training across worker nodes. Each worker returns local updates from the TrainDT function to the PS, which aggregates them to update and redistribute the global model. This relies on the intuition that workers maintain local model copies and periodically exchange information to ensure consistency.

Existing literature provides communication primitives such as Broadcast, AllGather, AllReduce, Scatter, Reduce, and ScatterReduce [8], [23], [24] for coordinating distributed training across models like DNNs and GBMs. While libraries like mpi4py [26] offer partial support, they depend on external orchestration, lack support for modern protocols like HTTP/gRPC, and offer limited integration with asynchronous messaging. STRATA2.0 implements these primitives; AllGather and AllReduce are identified as most suitable for training Random Forests. AllGather collects trained decision trees from all functions for gradient computation, while AllReduce aggregates trees and returns the result to each function.

STRATA2.0 adopts the AllGather primitive to enable seamless data exchange between the PS and serverless functions during training. Synchronizing local models across functions is critical; two state-of-the-art mechanisms are Bulk Synchronous Parallel (BSP) and Asynchronous Parallel (ASP) protocols [2], [5]. STRATA2.0 implements these via a gateway agent [22] and proposes a hybrid mechanism combining BSP and ASP. This hybrid mechanism adopts an asynchronous invocation strategy, allowing a fixed number of function instances to concurrently serve multiple TrainDT tasks to reduce delays from heterogeneous workloads. Despite asynchronous execution, a final synchronization step requires all TrainDT instances to complete before model updates.

Parameter Server: In the literature, two alternatives have been proposed for other machine learning models, such as deep neural networks: a) using a parameter server (PS) [2], [20] or b) adopting a decentralized approach [21]. However, current production serverless infrastructures do not support direct communication between functions, only indirect communication via a gateway [22]. This limitation increases synchronization overhead and burdens developers with managing the consistency of the global model. STRATA2.0 adopts a parameter server (PS) approach, similar to [2] and [20]. The PS, acting as a central node, orchestrates the training process across worker nodes. Each worker node returns its local updates (the result of TrainDT function) to the PS, which then updates the global model and propagates these updates back to the worker nodes. The core intuition is that many ML algorithms allow workers to maintain and update local copies of a global model in parallel. Periodically, after a fixed number of iterations, worker nodes exchange information (e.g., gradients or model parameters) to ensure global model consistency. The PS serves as a central coordination point, acting as a storage backend (e.g., a persistent or in-memory key-value store) responsible for aggregating, updating, and redistributing model parameters. In STRATA2.0, 1) each TrainDT function returns local updates to the PS, 2) the PS uses them to refine the global model, and 3) each UpdateDT/GradDT function subsequently pulls the latest model parameters from the PS.

Communication and Synchronization Semantics: While the PS is a widely adopted mechanism for coordinating distributed training, it does not suffice to ensure correct and efficient execution. Existing works in the literature have presented a set of primitives for data communication across worker nodes. Such state-of-the-art primitives are Broadcast, AllGather, AllReduce, Scatter, Reduce and ScatterReduce [8], [23], [24]. These serve as generic building blocks for training various machine learning models, including Random Forests, Gradient Boosted Machines (GBMs), and DNNs. By refining the leaf nodes of the trees we can further enhance predictive performance (for Gradient Boosted Machines) and support horizontal Federated Learning (FL) using the FedAvg methodology [25] (for Deep Neural Networks). Although state-of-the-art libraries like mpi4py [26] provide partial support for these primitives, they exhibit several constraints, such as: i) depend on external orchestration tools for deployment, ii) are not designed to operate over modern communication protocols such as HTTP or gRPC, and iii) offer limited or no integration with asynchronous messaging frameworks restricting their suitability for such applications. We have implemented these primitives in STRATA2.0 and more specifically, the AllGather and AllReduce are the most suitable to exploit for training Random Forests. When using the AllGather primitive for RFs, trained decision trees are collected from all serverless functions and redistributed for gradient computation. On the other hand, with AllReduce, the trees are aggregated from all functions, and the result is returned to each one of them.

STRATA2.0 adopts the AllGather communication primitive, as it enables seamless data exchange between the parameter server and serverless functions during training. However, synchronizing the trained local models among the different serverless functions is a critical task. Two common state-of-the-art mechanisms are the Bulk Synchronous Parallel (BSP) and the Asynchronous Parallel (ASP) protocols [2], [5]. We have implemented these communication protocols described above, and further proposed a hybrid synchronization mechanism that combines elements of the BSP and ASP paradigms. This hybrid mechanism, along with the ASP and BSP paradigms is implemented through the gateway agent [22], leveraging the exposed API and runtime mechanisms. The hybrid mechanism works as follows: When training Random Forests in a serverless infrastructure, we adopt an asynchronous invocation strategy for the serverless functions. This allows a fixed number of function instances to concurrently serve multiple TrainDT tasks, thereby reducing delays caused by heterogeneous processing capabilities or variable workloads across containers. However, despite asynchronous execution, all TrainDT instances must complete before model update, requiring a final synchronization step.

Serverless functions: The serverless functions run in Docker containers, created using the OpenFaas [27] OfWatchdog templates. The Watchdog contains an embedded HTTP server that receives function invocations as HTTP requests, invokes the function code within the container and returns the result. Similar to [7], STRATA2.0 opts for two distinct container configurations with different memory and CPU characteristics: small and large. A small container typically provisions a single vCPU core and 1 GB of memory, whereas a large container usually allocates at least twice those resources.
