section: VI. EMPLOYING ADDITIONAL EEG DATASETS TO
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: EEG fine-tuned contrastive models achieved higher accuracy than fully supervised baselines [43]–[49]. However, the SSL pretext task requires a semantically enriched data repository [44]. Since pretext training does not require labels, aggregating diverse EEG datasets can enrich the repository. EEG is recorded for various tasks, including abnormality detection [87], [88], sleep stage estimation [89], [90], affective state recognition [44], [91], and cognitive recognition [92]. Generating specific EEG records is expensive [93], [94]. Data aggregation and channel production are viable techniques to increase data volume for pattern recognition [93], [94].
output:
VI. EMPLOYING ADDITIONAL EEG DATASETS TO ENHANCE PRETEXT TRAINING

In EEG studies, some fine-tuned contrastive models showed higher accuracy than fully supervised models [43], [44], [48], [49]. However, the SSL pretext task requires a semantically enriched data repository to achieve accurate downstream results [44]. As the pretext task does not require labeled EEG, one might suggest aggregating different EEG datasets to enrich the pretext repository.

There are a variety of reasons that EEG is recorded, including, but not limited to, abnormality detection [87], [88], sleep stage/apnea estimation [89], [90], affective state recognition [44], [91], and cognitive recognition [92]. However, generating EEG records for a particular problem is expensive [93], [94]. Data aggregation and channel production are techniques to increase and enrich the required data for EEG-based pattern recognition problems.

input: If an EEG dataset has N channels, new channels can be created by treating each channel as a reference and computing the remaining channels relative to it. This produces N(N-1)/2 possible new channels for contrastive self-supervised learning pretext tasks [44]. Channel production benefits SSL techniques in two ways: it generates neurologically meaningful channels representing different data views, similar to augmentations, and it increases the data volume for more extensive SSL pretext learning.

section: VI. EMPLOYING ADDITIONAL EEG DATASETS TO — B. Data Aggregation
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Aggregating EEG data from open-source repositories enhances external validity by increasing data volume and minimizing setting-specific features. A tradeoff exists between repository size and similarity to downstream tasks; however, combining diverse datasets can improve downstream accuracy [44]. Several open-source datasets are suitable for pretext training. Affective recognition and cognitive assessment datasets include SEED [98], AMIGOS [116], DREAMER [149], DEAP [121], and the AMIGOS short and long video experiments [147]. Medical diagnosis datasets include ISRUC-Sleep [162], CHB-MIT [163], Physionet Sleep EDF, MASS, TUHab, and PC18 [169]–[170].
output:
More accurate model parameters can be derived when the
pretext task is trained using a large dataset. However, EEG
data acquisition is relatively expensive; a potential solution to
this challenge is to leverage previously collected EEG data
from open-sourced EEG repositories. Aggregating EEG data
from multiple sources for the pretext training task would
likely enhance the external validity of the computational
approach, as it markedly increases the volume of EEG being
analyzed and could minimize the inﬂuence of setting-speciﬁc
features. Adding more EEG data helps the pretext model to
observe more EEG samples, learning general EEG feature
representations. The pretext task only requires input data [36],
[43]. Thus, the downstream tasks employed during the various
experiments are irrelevant [95]. Hence, raw EEG data from
various studies, irrespective of the experimental paradigm,
can be preprocessed (e.g., resampled and denoised) using
consistent procedures and then aggregated to generate a larger
repository for any pretext task [44].
It can be presumed that there is a tradeoff between the
size of the data repository for the pretext task (i.e., how
many open-source EEG datasets are aggregated to train the
pretext model) and the similarity of the EEG traces in the
pretext repository to that being collected in the downstream
task. For example, aggregating EEG records of a sleep study
and an affective recognition study will boost the size of
the data repository for training the pretext model but also
might affect the internal validity of the pretext task negatively
as sleep EEG records would differ markedly from those of
awake individuals. In this example, one might hypothesize
that, due to these studies’ different nature, the aggregation
of the EEG records would impoverish the pretext model’s
feature representation, resulting in accuracy decay in the
downstream task. However, late evidence suggests otherwise.
Mohsenvand et al. [44] improved the accuracy of the downstream task in three different EEG studies (sleep apnea,
abnormality, and affective recognition) by combining the three
EEG data repositories in the pretext task.
Although data aggregation seems an effective technique to
enrich the pretext data points, the optimal balance between the
amount of data used to train a pretext model and the similarity
to the downstream task remains an open question ripe for
further investigation. Nevertheless, current best practices can
aggregate the available data repositories with other existing
physiologically “similar” EEG data for pretext training. In this
section, several open-source EEG datasets that have been
implemented in recent research are described. In addition,
Table I summarizes valuable facts about these data, such as
their availability, sampling frequency, and the total number of
EEG channels. In this article, EEG data are categorized into
two major categories: 1) affective recognition and cognitive
assessment and 2) medical diagnosis.
1) Affective
Recognition
and
Cognitive
Assessment: Mohsenvand et al. [44] employed the Shanghai Jiao
Tong University (SJTU), Emotion EEG Dataset (SEED)
[98], [137]–[139] for SSL learning. SEED is divided into
three subdatasets: 1) SEED I [138]; 2) SEED-IV [140];
and 3) SEED-VIG [141]. SEED I includes emotion-related
EEG records when each participant was watching emotional
videos. SEED-IV is an expansion of SEED I, where participants watched four types of emotion-related videos, and
in addition to EEG, their eye movements were recorded
as well. SEED-VIG was designed for vigilance estimation,
where the participant’s stimulation was via a virtual driving
system [142]–[146].
Sarkar and Etemad [147] applied SSL for affective recognition. Out of four datasets they used to illustrate their
model, Affect, Personality, and Mood Research on Individuals and Groups, abbreviated as AMIGOS [116], [148],
and Emotion Recognition Through EEG and ECG Signals
from Wireless Low-Cost Off-the-Shelf Devices, abbreviated
as DREAMER [149], were the repositories that include EEG
records. The AMIGOS dataset consists of two subdatasets.
One is called the short video experiment, where 40 participants watch affective-based videos and rate them as valence,
arousal, or dominance. The other one is called the long
video experiment, where 17 participants watch affective-based
videos alone and 20 participants watch the videos in groups
of a few participants. In addition to video rating, participants
were asked about their emotions on the second experiment’s
videos. The DREAMER dataset consists of EEG records for
self-affective state recognition after video stimuli. The records
were collected using the low-cost Emotiv EPOC wireless EEG
headset [45], [142], [150], [151].
Feradov [152] employed a publicly available dataset for
emotion analysis called EEG, physiological, and video signal
(DEAP) [121] to study the relationship between cognitive
brain activity and state of affect. DEAP includes self-assessed
EEG records from participants watching music videos. Each
participant scores his/her emotional levels regarding ﬁve
affective states of arousal, valence, dominance, liking, and
familiarity after each video, where, except the familiarity,
which is scored between 1 and 5, the rest are scored between
1 and 9 [35], [143], [153].
Seal et al. [96] developed an EEG database for emotion
classiﬁcation. Each participant watched three video patterns of
four emotions: natural, happy, sad, and fear (total of 12 videos
and 150 sec each). EEG was recorded while matching each
video pattern with emotion in a list. Since the frontal lobe
and temporal region have been shown to emit emotion-related
EEG information [154], [155], four frontal EEG channels,
referred to as FP2-F4, FP2-F8, FP1-F3, and FP1-F7 based
on the international 10/20 system [156], were employed.
Sengupta et al. [157] developed an EEG dataset for fatigue
and alertness recognition. Each individual was assigned to

Stroop tasks. The experiment was stopped either when the
individual performance drops below certain levels due to
fatigue or when the individual complains about extreme discomfort. After the experiment, each individual self-assessed
his/her level of cognitive fatigue.
Saba-Sadiya et al. [158] employed the EEG During Mental
Arithmetic Dataset [159], [160] for the SSL task. The data
include EEG records during a resting state and a mental arithmetic task. Klaproth et al. [161] proposed a pilot’s
adoptive cognitive assistance computational model based on
EEG records and ﬂight-dec interaction. Cognitive assistance
provides on-time helpful feedback by predicting an individual behavior regarding other individuals’ actions and the
environmental (e.g., the ﬂight simulator) factors/constraints.
Cognitive assistant addresses epistemically (due to lack of

as fuel pump failure and engine ﬁre) followed by air trafﬁc
control auditory messages. The experiment includes both standard and critical alerts; the goal was to study the EEG patterns
related to various alerts.
2) Medical Diagnosis: The Institute of Systems and Robotics (ISRUC) Sleep (ISRUC-Sleep) [162] and CHB-MIT Scalp
EEG dataset [163] is a potential EEG dataset for SSL pretraining. The ISRUC-Sleep is simply a sleep-scoring dataset. The
CHB-MIT Scalp EEG database includes pediatric participants
with intractable seizures [164]–[167].
Banville et al. [48], [49] employed four publicly available
datasets for sleep studies: Physionet Sleep EDF [100], Montreal Archive of Sleep Studies (MASS) [168], Temple University Hospital (TUH), Abnormal (TUHab) [169], and Physionet
Challenge 2018 (PC18) [170], for SSL EEG recognition. The
MASS and PC18 datasets are sleep studies. The TUHab
dataset is for pathological EEG detection [171], [172].

It remains unclear to what extent SSL can benefit from data aggregation and how the fusion of data from various EEG resources would improve the SSL pretext task for a particular problem. The SSL models of Mohsenvand et al. [44] performed better in the downstream task in all three studies, i.e., Sleep EDF [100], SEED [98], and TUHab [169], when all three repositories were aggregated for the pretext task. Although all the aggregated data were EEG records, the contexts of the studies were different, including the level of conscious awareness of participants (sleep versus awake). It remains unclear whether the results of downstream tasks of emotion and abnormality recognition would improve if one excluded the EEG data of the sleep study from Mohsenvand et al.’s model [44] and aggregated only EEG records from awake individuals, i.e., the ones corresponding to emotion SEED [98], and abnormality recognition TUHab [169].

Herein lies the potential to run EEG recognition experiments using data aggregation and sensitivity analysis. An improvement in the results, if sleep data is excluded from the pretext task, would indicate that data would not enrich the feature representations in pretext models, while a decrement would suggest that more data will continue to enhance the pretext model’s feature representation [43].

section: VII. IMPLEMENTATION CONSIDERATIONS

VII. IMPLEMENTATION CONSIDERATIONS AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS

SSL techniques have undoubtedly helped increase the accuracy of supervised EEG recognition problems, as shown in recent studies [44], [48], [49]. However, many unanswered or partially addressed questions exist, for example, how to select the optimal pretext augmentation or employ contrastive, generative, or hybrid EEG pretext. In this section, these relevant aspects of methodological decision-making are elucidated.

1) Optimum Augmentation Technique: The physiologically approved pretext augmentations maintain the informativity and fidelity of the EEG records, as was highlighted in Mohsenvand et al. [44]. However, the contrastive, generative, and unconventional/hybrid pretext tasks may appear arbitrary or irrelevant to the downstream task. In contrastive models, the augmented data (and their labels in supervised contrastive pretext) usually have no similarity/compatibility with the downstream task. For example, the pretext task may involve discriminating between whether Gaussian noise was added to the EEG trace or not. In contrast, the downstream task may include distinguishing whether a word is likely to be subsequently remembered or not based on the EEG power spectrum.

While learned features eventually assist the downstream task, it would be fruitful to discover the extent to which various augmentation techniques could be adapted in conjunction with downstream tasks to boost downstream accuracy/performance. For example, suppose that the literature/physiology suggests an association of alpha power with memory performance. In that case, the relevant augmentation of those bandwidths may produce pretext augmentations that are more relevant to a downstream task investigating memory performance. For example, if the downstream application seeks to identify oscillatory signatures of more successful memory encoding, a pretext augmentation of the frequency spectrum may be a more downstream-relevant pretext augmentation. Therefore, it is possible that the choice of pretext task could be enhanced by relying on the literature or empirically exploring the influence of the pretext task on downstream task performance. One might accomplish using machine learning feature selection or combinatory pattern recognition methods [173]–[175] on a few labeled data to shed light on how different data variables affect the downstream outputs (i.e., the original problem’s output) and, based on the variable “importance,” design downstream-relevant contrastive augmentation.

The current supervised contrastive pretext augmentations suggest developing negative and positive labels; hence, the pretext model usually has a two-class classification output layer. This output layer must be replaced with a brand new randomly initiated (instead of pretrained) output layer in the downstream task for fine-tuning (modification task in Fig. 2). For example, if the downstream task is a three-class problem (a regression problem), one would replace the usually two-class pretext SoftMax output layer with a three-class one (a regression output layer). Hence, all the pretext pretrained output layer’s information (i.e., pretrained weights, kernels, and biases that connect the last pretext hidden layer to the output layer) is replaced with randomly generated parameters (i.e., weights, kernels, and biases) for the downstream task.

As such, the SSL would benefit (in terms of downstream accuracy, ease of implementation, and maintaining learned pretext parameters) from contrastive augmentation techniques with identical output architecture and configuration as the downstream task (i.e., skipping the model modification task in Fig. 2).

2) Contrastive, Generative, or Hybrid EEG Recognition?: It is still unclear which pretext technique would be optimally effective for various EEG problems. A supervised contrastive model with a few pseudolabels would be less computationally intensive than an unsupervised contrastive model, such as autoencoder, where a whole “reconstruction” needs to be learned (rather than a few labels). However, there is some theoretical rationale for the unsupervised model’s consideration, such as its ability to extract complex EEG features and deeply encoded characteristics, giving the downstream model a chance of higher accuracy. For example, an autoencoder reconstructs the signal after augmentation, such as zero masking [see Fig. 7(a)], adding noise, and using a time shift, similar to the augmentations proposed by Mohsenvand et al. [44] and Banville et al. [48], [49]. In particular, zero masking is similar to image inpainting and reconstruction in image recognition studies [176]. In image recognition, one hybrid approach focuses on the closeness of clusters [27] of encoded representations of different views of an image [177]. A similar approach in EEG recognition is clustering feature representations of well-overlapped chunks of temporal records. Another approach is reconstructing high-resolution images from low resolution [178]. In EEG, a similar approach would require a signal to be reconstructed from its downsampled record or vice versa [see Fig. 7(b)]. Another approach would reconstruct the time domain from the frequency domain [see Fig. 7(c)], where the most important characteristics of a signal are embedded [66], [67]. Reconstructing an EEG channel from other channels can be another direction to be investigated, similar to image channel reconstruction [179]. Whether supervised or unsupervised, all these methods nonetheless find feature representations that work best for the downstream task. One area of investigation for future methodological research is to contrast the various supervised and unsupervised approaches discussed in this article.

Autoencoders are to “reconstruct” only, usually without any relevancy to the downstream task. Besides, in contrast to supervised contrastive models where the “learning” could be guided by pseudolabels that could have been potentially designed to be in conjunction with the downstream labels, an autoencoder’s feature representations and loss function convergence/learning performance very much depend on initial randomly generated parameters. For example, if a pretext contrastive autoencoder (supervised contrastive model) is trained twice, each time with different randomly selected initial parameters, i.e., weights, kernels, and biases, the trained encoder (model) would generate different (similar) feature representations in each try. To address this problem while benefiting from autoencoders’ profound encoding–decoding feature extraction advantage, one would recommend hybrid models [43], [79] where the autoencoders benefit from loss functions that are not just addressing reconstruction from any feature representation but representations relevant to downstream tasks. For example, an autoencoder would employ a loss function (to be minimized for machine learning) that reconstructs the original EEG from its augmented version. At the same time, the model would keep the cluster of augmented EEG encoded feature representations farther from the cluster of original EEG similar to Rafei and Adeli [27].

In contrast with autoencoders, unsupervised generative models, such as GANs, would lead to a trained discriminator enriched with feature representations sensitive to data authenticity (compared with contaminated/synthetic data). Note that, in GANs, no augmentation is required, which may produce a significant advantage over unsupervised contrastive models.

Nevertheless, supervised contrastive models surpass any generative, hybrid, or unsupervised contrastive models regarding computation efficiency, memory usage, and quick pretext convergence. Usually, with a few epochs (one or two), a supervised pretext model would yield near 100% pretext validation accuracy (similar to pretraining in [40]), mainly when augmentation intensity is relatively high (i.e., augmentations are easily distinguishable). However, the motivation to investigate techniques other than supervised contrastive models is for boosting downstream accuracy and efficiency.

3) Transfer Learning and Fine-Tuning Tips: In the standard transfer learning and fine-tuning process, an already trained model, referred to as the base model, is usually borrowed entirely or partially and modified to learn the current problem quickly using transfer learning and fine-tuning techniques. A base model usually includes hundreds of convolutional, recurrent, or dense (i.e., fully connected) layers. Using mighty/expensive resources, these layers have been trained (for days) on a different dataset than the current problem. Such datasets might have thousands of categories or include millions of data points. The base model is enriched with learned parameters, weights, filters, and kernels capable of identifying feature representation for any problem within the same data domain as the one base model was trained on.

The base model’s input and output layers are often modified to be compatible with the current problem. For example, nontrainable lower/upper scaling layers are added to the input layer for input data dimension compatibility. Output layer/s are substituted with trainable dense/SoftMax layers compatible with the current datasets output. The base model (or a portion of the base model) is frozen in transfer learning, meaning that its parameters are not updated. Instead, the newly added output layer is trained using a relatively large learning rate for many epochs. The base model already produced enriched feature representation from data; the only task is to learn from this representation to address the current problem using the new output layer. The base model (or a portion of the base model) is unfrozen in fine-tuning. Its parameters can now be updated using a relatively small learning rate for a few epochs to prevent overfitting, especially if the current dataset has few labeled data. Fine-tuning often boosts the accuracy of the model significantly [180], [181].

Despite the data domain, SSL techniques require careful transfer learning and fine-tuning implementation in the pretext and downstream stages. Regardless of the SSL type, there are two possible scenarios in pretext: 1) the pretext model is designed from scratch with various layers, including convolution, recurrent, and dense (i.e., fully connected) layers, all with randomly generated parameters and 2) the pretext model is the whole or a portion of a base model. Real-life industrial-level implementations usually fall in the second scenario, where a base model would make the pretext training computationally much more efficient. In that case, transfer learning does not help; the goal is not to solve the pretext task (e.g., learning pseudolabels or contrasts) but to enrich the feature representation layer of the pretext model with the information in the current data for the downstream task. As such, the base model (or a portion of it) is unfrozen and fine-tuned with a small learning rate only. However, in the downstream task, the procedure is similar to the standard transfer learning and fine-tuning, where the pretext model acts as a base model.

input: SSL enables learning from EEG records across variable experimental paradigms, allowing aggregation of multiple repositories to increase accuracy and reduce bias. This review examines how SSL techniques previously used in image processing [15], [36], [42]–[46] have been applied to EEG studies. It also summarizes datasets suitable for data fusion to support cost-efficient SSL pretext learning. The article proposes adapting image-processing solutions, such as generative models with enriched augmentations, to EEG problems. Future research should quantify the impact of tailoring pretext tasks to downstream applications and explore the advantages of generative, hybrid, or unsupervised contrastive models.
output: SSL enables learning from EEG records across trials with variable experimental paradigms, even when the trials explore different phenomena. It allows for aggregating multiple EEG repositories to increase accuracy, reduce bias, and mitigate overfitting in machine learning training. This article provided a thorough review of how SSL techniques, previously reviewed for their utility in image processing [15], [36], [42]–[46], have been employed in recent EEG studies. In addition, this article summarized available datasets for potential data fusion to help cost-efficient SSL pretext learning. Furthermore, this article proposes solutions that have been examined in mostly the image processing domain to be considered in EEG problems, such as generative models with potentially enriched augmentations (see Fig. 7). Finally, this article proposed future avenues to overcome challenges in SSL practice to exploit efficient EEG recognition. Future research should quantify the impact of tailoring the pretext task to the downstream application and explore the potential advantages of generative, hybrid, or unsupervised contrastive models.

Ning Liu

Abstract—Identifying drug-drug interactions (DDIs) is
a critical enabler for reducing adverse drug events and
improving patient safety. Generating proper DDI alerts during prescribing workﬂow has the potential to prevent DDIrelated adverse events. However, the implementation of DDI
alerting system remains a challenge as users are experiencing alert overload which causes alert fatigue. One strategy to optimize the current system is to establish a list
of high-priority DDIs for alerting purposes, though it is a
resource-intensive task. In this study, we propose a machine learning framework to extract useful features from the
FDA adverse event reports and then identify potential highpriority DDIs using an autoencoder-based semi-supervised
learning algorithm. The experimental results demonstrate
the effectiveness of using adverse event feature representations in differentiating high- and low-priority DDIs.
Additionally, the proposed algorithm utilizes stacked autoencoders and weighted support vector machine for boosting classiﬁcation performance, which outperforms other
competing methods in terms of F-measure and AUC score.
This framework integrates multiple information sources,
leverages domain knowledge and clinical evidence, and provides a practical approach for pre-screening high-priority
DDI candidates for medication alerts.
Index Terms—Semi-supervised learning, stacked autoencoder, classiﬁcation, drug-drug interactions, clinical decision support, adverse event reports.

section: I. INTRODUCTION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
output:
A DVERSE drug events caused by drug-drug interactions (DDIs) pose a major threat to patient safety, leading to increased morbidity and mortality, prolonged hospitalizations and higher healthcare costs [1] [2]. In general, DDI-related adverse drug events are largely preventable provided that proper warnings and interventions are implemented during provider's prescribing workflow [3]. To mitigate the risks of preventable DDIs, medication-related clinical decision support (CDS) is integrated into provider's electronic health record (EHR) system, aiming to generate DDI alerts and reduce errors during medication order entry. However, evidence [4] shows that CDS systems have not successfully reduced the risks of DDI exposure due to high override rates (as many as 98% [5]) caused by alert fatigue. Currently, most DDI alerting systems in the U.S. rely on the clinical contents from knowledge base vendors; and they are prone to include all possible DDIs to reduce legal liability [6]. The overwhelming number of DDI alerts, inaccurate and dubious information, and improper display during provider's workflow constitute the major reasons for poor acceptance of DDI alerts amongst clinicians [7], [8].

Recent studies suggest that tiering DDI alerts by severity and optimizing DDI notification mechanism represents a potential strategy to mitigate alert fatigue and establish better usability [6], [9], [10]. After reducing the volume of unnecessary DDI alerts, clinicians are able to pay more attention to the remaining clinically significant alerts. In an attempt to address this issue, early investigations [11] have been carried out by Phansalkar et al. under the sponsorship of the U.S. Office of the National Coordinator (ONC) for Health Information Technology, with the purpose of establishing a high-priority DDI list for alerting purposes. Through expert panel review, a list of 15 class-based DDIs were approved to be high-priority and should warrant interruptive alerting in CDS systems. In a later study [12], Phansalkar et al. approved a list of 33 class-based low-priority DDIs that can be made non-interruptive. These lists serve as an excellent starter for tiering DDI alerts, although they represent a small set. To assess additional high-priority DDIs is a resource-intensive task and requires endeavors from all healthcare stakeholders. Moreover, there is a substantial variation among various knowledge bases regarding the most severe DDIs [11], which makes it difficult to reach a consensus. Currently, there is no standardization on how to tier DDI alerts by severity, nor is there an implementation plan [5].

To facilitate DDI alert tiering processes and improve the list of established high-priority DDIs, we propose an evidence-based machine learning framework to pre-screen high-priority DDI candidates using the clinical evidences discovered from the FDA's Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS). Inspired by the DDI evidence evaluation approaches [13], we focus on the adverse drug events and outcomes associated with the high- and low-priority DDIs, aiming to identify useful features that help distinguish between these two DDI groups. High-priority DDIs exhibit different patterns in adverse events than that of the low-priority DDIs. To exploit these latent patterns enables machine learning models to learn the characteristics of the two classes of DDIs and make data-driven recommendations on the uncategorized DDIs.

Fig. 1 depicts the overview of the proposed machine learning framework. First, we perform a comprehensive analysis of FDA adverse event reports of the past three years and identify 110,495 unique drug pairs as experimental candidates. Next, we calculate the confidence measure of each drug pair and the corresponding adverse events to create a feature vector and subsequently construct a feature matrix of all drug pairs. Then, we utilize the knowledge bases of ONC High-Priority and Non-Interruptive Datasets to assign class labels to drug pairs with "high-priority", "low-priority", and "unlabeled". Last, we present an autoencoder-based semi-supervised learning algorithm that yields better classification performance by taking advantage of the unlabeled samples. The proposed algorithm exploits Stacked Autoencoders (SAE) [14] and Weighted Support Vector Machine (wSVM) [15] for performance boosting. In particular, a pair of stacked autoencoders are trained separately with the positive and negative labeled samples; the trained autoencoders serve as screening tools to identify reliable samples from unlabeled drug pairs via reconstruction errors; the reliable samples and their predicted class labels are added to original labeled samples to form an augmented training set for wSVM.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows.

r We present a machine learning framework that utilizes features extracted from adverse event reports to differentiate high-priority and low-priority DDIs. The feature engineering approach is shown to be effective for discovering clinical evidence from FDA adverse event reports or other similar case reports.

r We present an autoencoder-based semi-supervised learning algorithm that improves classification performance by utilizing both labeled and unlabeled samples. The proposed algorithm is a useful alternative in performing semi-supervised learning tasks.

r The proposed framework integrates multiple data sources, leverages domain knowledge and clinical evidence, and serves as a data-driven approach to improving the DDI alerting systems. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first machine learning framework to pre-screen high-priority DDI candidates.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. After reviewing the related work in Section II, we introduce the methodology in Section III. Experimental design, results and discussion are presented in Section IV, followed by research limitations in Section V. We conclude the paper and discuss the future work in Section VI.

section: II. RELATED WORK — A. Drug-Drug Interactions Discovery
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Researchers have explored machine learning for drug-drug interaction (DDI) discovery using diverse data sources. Features are generally divided into drug property features and post-marketing surveillance features, which include electronic health records, adverse event reports, social media, and search logs. Most literature treats DDI discovery as a classification problem. Tatonetti et al. developed a logistic regression algorithm using adverse event reports to identify novel interactions. Cheng et al. compared five supervised learning algorithms using similarity-based features within a DDI network. An ensemble of machine learning algorithms demonstrated improved prediction performance. Positive-unlabeled learning can facilitate DDI inference when no gold standard for non-interactions exists. Methods such as association rules and network analysis have also shown promise. Despite significant research efforts, there has been little discussion on using machine learning to pre-screen high-priority DDIs for medication alerts.
output:
The application of machine learning algorithms and the availability of multi-dimensional drug features present promising opportunities for discovering drug-drug interactions during pre- and post-marketing surveillance. Researchers have investigated a variety of information sources and non-conventional approaches to facilitate DDI discovery. Features used to predict DDIs can be summarized into two categories: drug property features and post-marketing surveillance features. The former feature group consists of the chemical, biological, physiological, and other features reflecting the intrinsic properties of drugs. The latter feature group represents drug information collected during post-marketing phase, including conventional information sources such as hospital EHR systems [16] and adverse event reports [17], and non-conventional information sources such as social media [18] and search engine log [19]. Previous work utilizing one or both feature groups to detect DDIs has varied application from new drug development [20] to post-marketing surveillance [21].

DDI discovery is viewed as a classification problem by most related literature. Tatonetti et al. [13] developed a signal detection algorithm based on logistic regression to identify novel DDIs from adverse event reports. Cheng et al. [22] constructed a DDI network and compared five supervised learning algorithms in DDI prediction using similarity-based features. An ensemble of machine learning algorithms [23] demonstrated an improved prediction performance. Besides, positive-unlabeled learning [24] can be utilized in making DDI inference provided that there is no gold standard for non-interacting DDIs. Other methods such as association rules [17] and network analysis [25] also demonstrated promising results. Despite a surprising amount of research efforts in DDI discovery, there has been little discussion on using machine learning to pre-screen high-priority DDIs for medication alerts.

section: II. RELATED WORK — B. Semi-Supervised Learning Algorithms
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.

In healthcare and other real-world application of machine
learning, it is always the case that good-quality labeled data are
rare or very expensive to obtain, while there usually exist abundant unlabeled data. Assigning labels to unlabeled data requires
lots of human efforts and domain knowledge. This study encounters the same issue. As mentioned earlier, the labeled highand low-priority DDIs were determined by expert panel review
processes and only reﬂect a small portion (15 and 31 classbased DDIs respectively). As a consequence, semi-supervised
learning algorithms that exploit unlabeled samples to improve
prediction performance have attracted considerable attention.
Following the taxonomy introduced by Zhu et al. [26], most
semi-supervised learning algorithms can be categorized into
four methodological groups: generative models, graph-based
methods, semi-supervised support vector machine and selflabeled methods. Generative models such as Gaussian mixture
models are based on the assumption that labeled and unlabeled
data follows a particular form of mixture distribution. However,
it is difﬁcult to verify the correctness of the distribution assumption [26], especially for the DDI dataset where there exists lots
of noisy and ambiguous samples. The graph-based methods [27]
utilize graph representations where vertices denote labeled and
unlabeled samples and edges reﬂect the similarity between samples, and then enforce label smoothness over the graph. Most
graph-based methods do not produce conﬁdence level for each
label prediction [28], and low-conﬁdence prediction may not
be beneﬁcial for boosting model performance. The same issue
exists with the semi-supervised support vector machine [29],
along with the computational complexity issue caused by vast
amount of unlabeled samples in our study.
Although the above-mentioned methods (i.e. generative models, graph-based methods, and semi-supervised SVM) have successful applications in various domains [30], the direct usage of
them in this study may not be useful and may even be problematic. In view of the nature and sources of the DDI data, there exist
many ambiguous samples in the unlabeled set that do not belong
to either positive class or negative class. Augmenting training
data with ambiguous samples and their inferred labels imposes
noises and errors and is less likely to improve model performance. Self-labeled methods [28] notably self-training [31], cotraining [32] and democratic co-learning [33] are better-suited
tools to handle the DDI data. In general, self-labeled methods
follow iterative procedures to enlarge the training set, through
which the unlabeled samples with the most conﬁdent predictions
are accepted into the training set incrementally. Stopping criteria
are built-in mechanisms for most self-labeled algorithms which
controls the self-labeling process and determines the amount of
unlabeled samples added to the training set. The proposed algorithm is a subclass of self-labeled techniques and represents an
effective alternative for tackling the DDI data of this study.

section: III. METHODOLOGY — B. Data Preprocessing
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
A total of 10 quarterly data files between 2016 Q1 and 2018 Q2 were downloaded from the FAERS database. Duplicate reports were removed by selecting only the most up-to-date version of each report, following the FAERS document [38]. Drug names were standardized using the RxNorm API [39] to map free-text names to generic drug concepts (RXCUI). After duplicate removal, 3,282,868 adverse event reports remained for processing.

Reports were narrowed down to 1,740,770 by including only those with at least one serious outcome (e.g., death, hospitalization) per [38]. Reports with exactly one drug were excluded as out of scope, leaving 936,865 reports.

Drugs with fewer than 50 reports were excluded. After codifying names with RxNorm, 2,891 unique generic drug concepts were identified. Among all pairwise combinations, drug pairs with at least ten reports were retained, resulting in a final list of 110,495 drug pairs.
output:
A total of 10 quarterly data files between 2016 Q1 and 2018 Q2 are downloaded from the FAERS database. An overview of data preprocessing is described in Fig. 2, and the following sections illustrate the details of each step.

1) Duplicate Reports Removal and Drug Names Standardization: Duplicate reports in the FAERS database introduce bias on the proportional reporting ratio of drug usages and adverse events, thus negatively impact data quality. The reports in the FAERS database follow a case and version mapping relationship where the same case may have multiple versions. The “primaryid” of each report is generated by concatenating the “caseid” and “versionid”. Following the suggestion in the FAERS document [38], we removed the duplicate reports by only selecting the most up-to-date version of each report. As we have mentioned earlier, the drug names in the FAERS database are reported arbitrarily by drug trade names, abbreviations or verbatim names which do not follow a standardized coding system. To codify the free-text drug names, we utilize the RxNorm API [39] to map each name to a generic drug concept denoted by a concept unique identifier (RXCUI). After removing the duplicates, a total of 3,282,868 adverse event reports is obtained for further processing.

2) Adverse Event Reports Selection: We narrowed down the number of reports to 1,740,770 by only including those who have at least one serious outcome [38] such as “death”, “life-threatening”, “hospitalization”, “disability”, “congenital anomaly” and “required intervention”. This study focuses on the interactions of drugs, thus the reports with exactly one drug listed are considered out of scope. A final list of 936,865 reports remains for further analysis.

3) Drugs Selection and Drug Pairs Generation: To ensure a reasonable drug reporting frequency, drugs with less than 50 reports in the FAERS database are excluded in the study. After codifying drug names with RxNorm, we obtained a list of 2,891 unique generic drug concepts. Among all pairwise combination of 2,891 drugs, we focus on the drug pairs that had at least ten reports. After removing the drug pairs with less than ten reports, we obtained a final list of 110,495 drug pairs.

section: III. METHODOLOGY — C. Feature Engineering and DDI Dataset Preparation
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
The FAERS database serves as the data source for investigating drug-adverse event relationships. Reports containing harmful interacting drugs reveal adverse event patterns that indicate potential high-priority drug-drug interactions (DDIs) retrospectively. Inspired by association rules learning, three-itemset rules of the form {Drug1 ∪ Drug2 ⇒ AdverseEventj} were considered, where the antecedent is a drug pair and the consequent is an adverse event. The support of a rule is the fraction of observations containing the drug pair and adverse event. The confidence of a rule is defined as the support of the rule divided by the support of the antecedent, serving as an estimate of the conditional probability P(AEj|D1, D2). Among all selected reports, 13,368 unique adverse events were identified, most with very low support. A subset of adverse events with support greater than 0.1% was selected, and confidences were calculated for their three-itemset rules. A confidence value matrix was constructed with drug pairs as rows and adverse events as columns. After removing highly correlated and low-variance columns, the matrix contained 247 features for all 110,495 drug pairs. Each drug pair is represented by a vector of non-negative confidence values. For example, the drug pair Ciprofloxacin and Fluconazole has calculated confidence values of 0.058 for "Acute kidney injury", 0.038 for "Atrial fibrillation", and 0.055 for "Diarrhea". Cells remain zero if no adverse event is associated with the drug pair.

All 110,495 drug pairs were looked up in DrugBank, and interacting pairs were selected to form the DDI samples (N = 36,632) for model development. Among these DDI samples, 288 are labeled "high-priority" by the ONC High-Priority Dataset and 356 are labeled "low-priority" by the ONC Non-Interruptive Dataset. The FAERS database provides a rich data source for investigating the relationships between drugs and adverse events. For the reports that contain harmful interacting drugs, the types and severity of the adverse events might reveal different patterns from others. These patterns contain critical information about DDIs and can be employed to detect potential high-priority DDIs retrospectively. Inspired by association rules learning [40], we consider the following three-itemset rules to investigate the relationship between drug pairs and adverse events {Drug1 ∪Drug2 ⇒AdverseEventj} or {D1 ∪D2 ⇒AEj}, where the left-hand side of the arrow (“antecedent”) denotes a pair of drugs, and right-hand side (“consequent”) denotes the adverse event j. For example, {Acetaminophen ∪Alcohol ⇒ Hepatotoxicity} means taking Acetaminophen and Alcohol together might be associated with Hepatotoxicity. The “support” of the rule Supp(D1 ∪D2 ⇒AEj) is the fraction of the observations in the union of the antecedent and consequent, which indicates the proportion of the reports where drug pairs Drug1 and Drug2, and AdverseEventj appear together. The “confidence” of the rules Conf(D1 ∪D2 ⇒AEj) is the support of the rule divided by the support of the antecedent Conf(D1 ∪D2 ⇒AEj) = Supp(D1 ∪D2 ⇒AEj) / Supp(D1 ∪D2), (1) which can be viewed as an estimate of the conditional probability P(AEj|D1, D2) [41], the probability of finding the AdverseEventj in reports under the condition that these reports also contain drug pairs Drug1 and Drug2.

Among all selected reports, there exist 13,368 unique adverse events (in preferred terms), most of which have very low support (or reporting frequency). We selected a subset of adverse events with support greater than 0.1% and calculated the confidences of their three-itemset rules using Eq. 1. We constructed a confidence value matrix (Fig. 3) with drug pairs as rows and adverse events as columns (features). After removing highly correlated columns and the columns with very low variance, we obtained a matrix with 247 columns for all 110,495 drug pairs. Each drug pair is represented by a vector of non-negative values across all 247 adverse events. For example, the drug pair - Ciprofloxacin and Fluconazole - is associated with more than 100 adverse events, of which the calculated confidence values are 0.058 for “Acute kidney injury”, 0.038 for “Atrial fibrillation”, and 0.055 for “Diarrhea”, etc. It is worth noting certain cells in the confidence matrix remain zero if there is no adverse event associated with the corresponding drug pair. To utilize the confidence values as features is a crucial step for enabling the application of machine learning algorithms.

The scope of this study is to identify a list of high-priority DDIs from the existing DDI candidates in order to reduce alert fatigue. For all 110,495 drug pairs, we are only interested in those pairs which are interacting with each other. Drug pairs which do not interact fall outside the scope. We looked up all 110,495 drug pairs in DrugBank and selected those interacting drug pairs to form the DDI samples (N = 36,632) for model development. Among all DDI samples, 288 are labeled “high-priority” by ONC High-Priority Dataset, 356 are labeled “low-priority” by ONC Non-Interruptive Dataset, and the severity levels of the remaining 35,988 drug pairs are not determined, thus they are considered as unlabeled samples. As shown in Fig. 3, we assigned the class labels “Yes” (or “positive”), “No” (or “negative”) and “Unlabeled” to indicate whether or not the drug pair belongs to the high-priority DDI category. We refer to the drug pairs with either positive or negative labels as the “original labeled samples” to differentiate the term “inferred reliable samples” used in the following section.

section: III. METHODOLOGY — D. Autoencoder-Based Semi-Supervised Learning
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
Section III.D: Autoencoder-Based Semi-Supervised Learning

The algorithm proceeds in three stages. First, stacked autoencoders are trained on original labeled positive and negative samples to learn data representations. Second, a screening algorithm evaluates reconstruction errors from both autoencoders on unlabeled samples; samples with a large error gap are selected as reliable positives or negatives. Third, these inferred reliable samples are combined with the original labeled data and used to train a weighted support vector machine, where original samples are weighted as 1 and reliable samples receive weights between 0 and 1 via a sigmoid function of their error gap.

Autoencoder preliminaries: An autoencoder is a feedforward neural network trained to reconstruct its input, enabling unsupervised representation learning. The structure includes an input layer, a hidden layer, and an output layer with matching dimensions. The encoder maps input x to a code h via activation function σ1, and the decoder maps h to reconstruction x̂ via σ2. Training minimizes the mean squared error between x and x̂, with optional regularization via dropout or L2 penalties. Optimization uses backpropagation with methods like SGD or Adam.

Stacked architecture: A stacked autoencoder consists of multiple autoencoder layers trained greedily. The code from one level becomes the input for the next. Proper depth reduces training data requirements and computational cost. Training involves pre-training each layer sequentially, followed by fine-tuning the full architecture via backpropagation.

DDI dataset construction and screening: Let P be positive DDI samples, N be negative samples, and U be unlabeled samples, all with dimension p=247 (adverse events). Separate stacked autoencoders are built on P and N. The screening algorithm reconstructs each unlabeled sample xi using both models, yielding errors errorPi and errorNi. The gap Δi = errorPi − errorNi determines class membership: xi is flagged as a reliable positive if Δi ≤ c1, or reliable negative if Δi ≥ c2. Thresholds c1 and c2 are set as the mth and (100−m)th percentiles of Δi to balance class addition. Reliable samples RP and RN are output for classifier training.

Weighted support vector machine: After augmenting the labeled set P ∪ N with reliable samples RP ∪ RN, a weighted SVM constructs the classifier. Original labeled samples xi receive fixed weight αi = 1. Inferred reliable samples xj receive weight αj = 1 / (1 + e−|Δj|), where |Δj| is the absolute error gap. This weights trustworthy samples higher. The optimization minimizes 1/2‖w‖² + C∑αiξi, subject to margin constraints yi(wTφ(xi) + b) ≥ 1 − ξi for all training samples. The regularization parameter C controls the margin-violation trade-off. The final algorithm is summarized in Algorithm 2.
output:
Algorithm
The overview of autoencoder-based semi-supervised learning algorithm is described as follows. First, stacked autoencoders are carried out to perform representation learning using the original labeled samples. Second, a screening algorithm is presented to determine the set of inferred reliable samples using autoencoder reconstruction errors. Third, after augmenting the original labeled samples with the inferred reliable samples, a classification model is constructed using weighted support vector machine, where the original labeled samples and the inferred reliable samples are weighted differently by a scoring function.

Fig. 4.
Structure of an autoencoder with one hidden layer. The input x is mapped to the internal representation (or “code”) h via an encoder f; the code h is subsequently mapped to the output (or reconstruction) x̂ via a decoder g. The objective is to have output x̂ to approximate input x as close as possible by minimizing the mean squared errors between x and x̂.

1) Autoencoder Preliminaries: Autoencoder [42] is a type of feedforward neural network and can perform representation learning in an unsupervised manner. It is trained to reconstruct its own input, through which the hidden layers can capture the useful feature representations. Traditionally, autoencoder is well-known for dimension reduction of high-dimensional data [43]. Recently, it is recognized as an emerging technique for data denoising [14], anomaly detection [44] and nonlinear feature fusion [45].

The general structure of an autoencoder includes an input layer, an output layer, and a hidden layer connecting them, in which the output layer has the same dimension as the input layer. Fig. 4 shows the simplest form of an autoencoder with one hidden layer. The input x is mapped to the internal representation (or “code”) h via an encoder, denoted as function f. The code h is subsequently mapped to the output (or reconstruction) x̂ via a decoder, denoted as function g. Let W(1) and W(2) denote the weight matrices, and b(1) and b(2) denote the bias vectors, then we have

h = f(x) = σ1(W(1)x + b(1))   (2)
x̂ = g(h) = σ2(W(2)h + b(2))   (3)

where σ1 and σ2 denote the activation functions, e.g., hyperbolic tangent function (tanh) and rectified linear unit (ReLU).

The aim of training an autoencoder is to have output x̂ to approximate input x as close as possible. We set up the objective function to minimize the average squared errors between x̂ and x:

J(W, b) = 1/|S| x∈S L(x, x̂) + Ω(W)
= 1/|S| x∈S ||x − (g ◦ f)(x)||2 + Ω(W)   (4)

where L is a squared loss function, S is a training set, f and g are the encoding and decoding functions parameterized by W and b provided that the activation functions are determined. To prevent overfitting of the training data, a regularization term Ω(W) is added to the objective function. Moreover, the regularization effects can be further strengthened by implementing the “dropout” techniques [46]. Autoencoder belongs to the feedforward neural network family. Some of the well-known optimization methods such as stochastic gradient descent (SGD) [47] and Adam [48] can directly come into play to optimize the weights and biases. Furthermore, backpropagation algorithm [41] can be applied to make efficient updates.

2) Stacked Architecture: A simple autoencoder is usually trained with only one hidden layer. If the dimension of the hidden layer (code) is lower than the input layer, we refer to this type of autoencoder as undercomplete autoencoder [42], e.g., Fig. 4. In other words, undercomplete autoencoder uses a bottleneck layer to compress the input into a lower-dimensional code. By limiting the amount of information flowing through the network, autoencoder is trained to learn the knowledge representations of the data, rather than copying the input to the output.

In this study, we do not limit the autoencoder structure to be exactly one layer, instead we use a stack of multiple hidden layers to form a stacked autoencoder. As illustrated in Fig. 5, a stacked autoencoder (SAE) consists of multiple simple autoencoders in which the resulting representation layer (“code”) of the first level autoencoder is used as the input layer of the second level autoencoder. Similar to other feedforward networks, proper depth in autoencoders reduces the amount of data needed for training internal functions, hence exponentially reduces the computational cost [42]. A general strategy to train a stacked autoencoder is to greedily pre-train a sequence of simple autoencoders starting from the layer of input data, then use the resulting “code” layer to train the successive layers, and finally apply backpropagation algorithm [41] on the stacked architecture to achieve fine-tuning [43].

3) Building Stacked Autoencoders on the DDI Dataset: Let P denote the high-priority DDI drug pairs in the training set, i.e., positive samples; and N denote the low-priority DDI drug pairs in the training set, i.e., negative samples. For the drug pairs without a known label, we use U to denote the set of these unlabeled samples. All samples in P, N, or U have the same dimension (p = 247) - the number of adverse events determined in Section III-C. We build two separate stacked autoencoders using the labeled samples P and N. After training, the stacked autoencoder built on P is expected to reconstruct the positive samples very well, while failing to reconstruct the negative samples; thereby it generates higher reconstruction errors on the negative samples than the positives. On the contrary, the stacked autoencoder built on N should have higher reconstruction errors on the positive samples than the negative samples. Samples with high reconstruction errors are flagged as anomalies and most likely belong to a different class. To use reconstruction errors as measures represents a strategy to determine reliable samples from set U.

4) Algorithm for Screening Reliable Samples: We develop a screening algorithm using autoencoder reconstruction errors to screen reliable positives (RP) and negatives (RN) from the unlabeled samples set U. The details of the screening algorithm are described in Algorithm 1.

After building autoencoders on sets P and N, we use the trained models (g ◦ f)P and (g ◦ f)N to reconstruct unlabeled samples in U, where (g ◦ f)P and (g ◦ f)N denote the stacked autoencoders built on labeled sample sets P and N. For each xi in U, we obtain two reconstruction errors from (g ◦ f)P and (g ◦ f)N respectively. Ideally, if xi is close to the positive class, it should have a small reconstruction error with (g ◦ f)P and a large reconstruction error with (g ◦ f)N, and vice versa.

For the purpose of screening reliable samples, we are interested in the unlabeled samples with a big gap between these two reconstruction errors. Let errorPi and errorNi denote the reconstruction errors obtained via (g ◦ f)P and (g ◦ f)N and Δi = errorPi − errorNi denote the gap, then xi is selected as a reliable positive if Δi is within the threshold c1 or a reliable negative if Δi is beyond the threshold c2. The values of both thresholds can be any values within [min(Δi), max(Δi)] and should satisfy the condition of c1 < c2. We denote the values of c1 and c2 using mth and nth percentiles of Δi, and set n = 100 − m to balance number of reliable positives and negatives added to the training set. For example, using 1th percentile for c1 is equivalent to adding the top 1% most reliable positives to the training set; which also implies that the top 1% most reliable negatives (i.e., using 99th percentile for c2) are added to the training set due to the n = 100 − m class balance constraint.

The choice of parameters c1 and c2 is data-driven and determined via sensitivity analysis.

5) Weighted Support Vector Machine (wSVM): After combining the reliable samples with the original labeled samples, we build a classifier on the augmented training set using weighted support vector machine (wSVM) [15]. The basic idea of wSVM is to assign weights to data samples in the training set such that the decision boundary is determined according to the relative importance and trustworthiness of the data samples. Typically, the weights of the original labeled samples should be larger than the inferred reliable samples.

Let xi be the ith sample in the original labeled set denoted as xi ∈ P ∪ N where the index i ∈ {1, 2, . . . , |P ∪ N|}, xj be the jth sample in the inferred reliable set denoted as xj ∈ RP ∪ RN where the index j ∈ {1, 2, . . . , |RP ∪ RN|}, and αi, αj be the corresponding sample weights for xi, xj. We re-weight all training samples through the following weighing system. For the original labeled samples xi, their weights are fixed to 1 (i.e., αi = 1, ∀i); for the inferred reliable samples xj, their weights are calculated by the sigmoid function and varied between 0 and 1 according to their |Δj| values:

αj = 1 / (1 + e−|Δj|)   (5)

where |Δj| is the absolute value of the difference between two reconstruction errors errorPi and errorNi, and 0 < αj < 1.

Following the same indexing rule, let yi ∈ {1, −1} denote the class labels for xi ∈ P ∪ N, and yj ∈ {1, −1} denote the class labels for xj ∈ RP ∪ RN. The reliable positives are assigned label yj = 1, and the reliable negatives are assigned label yj = −1. The wSVM is formulated as:

min w,b 1/2 wT w + C [ (|P ∪ N|) i=1 αiξi + (|RP ∪ RN|) j=1 αjξj ]   (6)

s.t.
(a) yi(wT φ(xi) + b) ≥ 1 − ξi xi ∈ P ∪ N
(b) yj(wT φ(xj) + b) ≥ 1 − ξj xj ∈ RP ∪ RN
ξi ≥ 0 ∀i
(d) ξj ≥ 0 ∀j   (7)

where the training samples xi and xj are mapped to a higher dimensional space through function φ. The regularization parameter C is a user-specified parameter which control the trade-off between margin and classification violation. Note that we assign the weights αi and αj to the corresponding data samples xi and xj in the formulation. We conclude the methodology section by presenting the autoencoder-based semi-supervised learning algorithm in Algorithm 2.

Algorithm 1: Algorithm for Screening Reliable Samples.
1: Input:
2: Stacked autoencoder built on P: (g ◦ f)P
3: Stacked autoencoder built on N: (g ◦ f)N
4: Set of unlabeled samples: U = {x1, x2, . . . , x|U|}
5: Lower threshold: c1
6: Upper threshold: c2
7: Output:
8: Set of reliable positives: RP
9: Set of reliable negatives: RN
10: Set of delta values: Δ
11: function SCREEN ((g ◦ f)P , (g ◦ f)N , U, c1, c2)
12: Initialization
13: RP := ∅
14: RN := ∅
15: Δ := ∅
16: for i := 1 to |U| do
17: errorPi := ||xi − (g ◦ f)P (xi)||2
18: errorNi := ||xi − (g ◦ f)N (xi)||2
19: Δi := errorPi − errorNi
20: if Δi ≤ c1 then
21: RP := RP ∪ xi
22: Δ := Δ ∪ Δi
23: else if Δi ≥ c2 then
24: RN := RN ∪ xi
25: Δ := Δ ∪ Δi
26: end if
27: end for
28: return RP, RN, Δ
29: end function

Algorithm 2: Autoencoder-Based Semi-Supervised Learning.
1: Input:
2: Set of positive samples: P
3: Set of negative samples: N
4: Set of unlabeled samples: U
5: Lower threshold: c1
6: Upper threshold: c2
7: Output:
8: Trained model: Classifier
9: function SEMI-SUPERVISED LEARNING P, N, U, c1, c2
10: (g ◦ f)P := Autoencoder(P)
11: (g ◦ f)N := Autoencoder(N)
12: RP, RN, Δ := Screen((g ◦ f)P , (g ◦ f)N , U, c1, c2)
13: αi := 1, ∀i ∈ {1, 2, . . . , |P ∪ N|}
14: αj := sigmoid(|Δj|), ∀j ∈ {1, 2, . . . , |RP ∪ RN|}
15: Classifier := weightedSVM(P, N, RP, RN, α)
16: return Classifier
17: end function

input: The autoencoder building and parameter tuning processes were implemented in TensorFlow using Keras. Constrained by input dimension (p = 247) and undercomplete structure, architectures with layer sizes ranging from 4 to 128 were tested for single and stacked layer scenarios. Models were trained using the Adam optimizer with normalized input data. Hyperparameter configuration was tuned by varying activation functions, learning rates, and dropout rates to maximize validation performance. This supports the idea that the gap between the two reconstruction errors can help determine reliable samples of the two classes.

input:
We compared the proposed algorithm against other state-of-the-art self-labeled semi-supervised methods on the DDI dataset. A fully-supervised SVM trained on labeled samples P and N served as the baseline. Unlabeled samples U were then added for semi-supervised learning. Besides the proposed method, compared algorithms included self-training [31], co-training [32], and democratic co-learning [33]. All methods used radial SVM as the base classifier, with a maximum of 30 iterations for self-training and co-training, and radial SVM, k-NN, and C5.0 for co-learning. Parameters were tuned for optimal performance, and results were averaged over ten data partitioning runs.

All semi-supervised methods outperformed the fully-supervised SVM across all metrics, demonstrating that incorporating unlabeled samples improves generalization. The proposed method achieved the best performance in AUC and F-measure, indicating stacked autoencoders effectively screen reliable samples from the high-dimensional DDI dataset. While self-training and co-training are computationally expensive due to their iterative nature, the proposed method is a reasonable choice for analyzing large volumes of unlabeled data. Additionally, co-training relied on the assumption of split-view features, which does not hold for the DDI dataset as shown by the evaluation results.

Section IV. EXPERIMENTS AND RESULTS — F. Performance Comparison of the Proposed Algorithm

With Other Methods on the DDI Dataset

Following the discussion in Related Work (Section II), we utilized several other state-of-the-art self-labeled semi-supervised learning methods for performance comparison. In the experimental design, we first built a fully-supervised SVM as baseline with the original labeled samples (P and N only), and then added the unlabeled samples U to the training set for performing semi-supervised learning. Besides the proposed algorithm, methods used for semi-supervised learning include self-training [31], co-training [32] and democratic co-learning [33]. In the experimentation, we used radial SVM as the base classifier for both self-training and co-training algorithms, and the maximum iteration is set to 30 for both algorithms. For co-learning, the three base classifiers are radial SVM, k-NN [41] and C5.0 [41]. All model parameters were properly tuned for the best performance. We repeated the data partitioning, training, and testing processes ten times for evaluating model performance of all methods.

Table II shows the summarized results (mean ± standard deviation) of the experiments. All semi-supervised learning methods including the proposed algorithm outperformed the fully-supervised SVM in every performance metrics, which demonstrates that the unlabeled samples, when properly used in conjunction with the labeled samples, can produce considerable improvement in model's generalization capability. The proposed method has the best evaluation performance in both AUC and F-measure metrics, which reflects the fact that stacked autoencoders are superior tools to screen the reliable samples from the high-dimensional DDI dataset. Meanwhile, self-training and co-training algorithms are computationally expensive due to the iterative nature of the algorithm; the proposed method is a reasonable choice provided there is a necessity to analyze an enormous amount of unlabeled samples. Moreover, co-training algorithm relies on the abundance of features as well as the assumption of two split views of features. As is demonstrated in the evaluation results, the assumption of split-view does not hold for the DDI dataset.

IV. EXPERIMENTS AND RESULTS — G. Performance Comparison on a Benchmark Dataset

To show the effectiveness and scalability of our approach, we extended the experiments using a high-dimensional benchmark dataset - Epilepsy EEG dataset [52] - from the UCI Machine Learning Repository [53]. The dataset consists of EEG recording information used for epileptic seizure detection. Each data point has 178-dimensional input vector representing the EEG signal values from brain electrical activity. The response variable has five classes representing different EEG signal categories. We transformed the dataset into a binary classification format by selecting two out of the five classes, namely the “eyes open” and “eyes closed” classes while removing data points of the other three classes.

The remaining data was then split into an 80% training set and a 20% testing set. For assessing the performance of semi-supervised learning methods, we assume that only a certain percentage of training samples (e.g. 10%) have class labels; while the rest do not, and their class labels were removed. After removing partial class labels, we obtained a mix of labeled and unlabeled samples for model training. As shown in Table III, we incrementally adjusted the percentage of the labeled samples from 10% to 90% to evaluate model performance under different scenarios. Similar to the experiments with the DDI samples, each scenario was repeated ten times for comparing the performance of all competing methods.

The benchmark dataset has balanced class labels (50% vs. 50%); for this reason we evaluated the model performance using the AUC score. The comparison results of all competing methods are reported in Table III and also visualized in Fig. 10. In general, the semi-supervised learning methods outperformed the SVM in terms of the average AUC score. As the percentage of visible labels increased from 10% to 90%, the performance improvement became smaller. It is also noted that the proposed algorithm outshines its competitors when the percentage of visible labels is located between 20% and 50%.

We trained a classifier using original and inferred samples to flag high-priority drug-drug interactions (DDIs). The classifier outputs a probability of a drug pair being high-priority based on adverse event features. We evaluated inferred DDIs against Drugs.com, noting that "Major" and "Moderate" interactions listed there serve as external opinions rather than confirmed alerts. Inferred DDIs are highly associated with Drugs.com's "Major" and "Moderate" labels.

Among the top 100 flagged DDIs, 20% were marked "Major" and 64% "Moderate" by Drugs.com. Without inferred samples, only 17% were "Major" and 59% "Moderate." output:
The experimental results have demonstrated the effectiveness of using post-marketing surveillance features in pre-screening high-priority DDIs. Under the proposed framework, we trained a classifier using the original labeled samples and inferred reliable samples to flag potential high-priority DDIs. Depending on the adverse event feature input, the classifier outputs a numeric value indicating the probability of the unlabeled drug pair being a high-priority DDI. To further assess the discriminative capability of adverse event features, we utilized an independent knowledge base—Drugs.com to evaluate the inferred high-priority DDIs. It should be noted that the “major” and “Moderate” drug interactions listed in Drugs.com are not the confirmed high-priority DDIs for use in medication alerts, but can serve as external opinions on evaluating the predictive performance. The inferred high-priority DDIs are highly associated with the major and moderate drug interactions in Drugs.com.

Among the top 100 potential high-priority DDIs flagged by the proposed framework, 20% are marked as “Major” interactions and 64% are marked as “Moderate” by Drugs.com; while only 17% “Major” and 59% “Moderate” can be flagged without using the unlabeled samples. In Table IV, we listed some of the major DDIs flagged by the framework.

Although the predictive results are satisfactory, the application of data-driven methods in predicting high-priority DDIs should always be considered as a complementary approach to supporting knowledge-based expert decisions. The established results are solely based on the utilization of post-marketing surveillance features. As we have discussed in Section II, drug property features are proven effective features in predicting DDIs and should be incorporated into the framework for producing more accurate and comprehensive results. The utilization of drug property features is not yet covered in this study and serves as one direction of future work.

section: VI. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
VI. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK

Identifying high-priority drug-drug interactions (DDIs) is crucial for optimizing EHR medication alerts and reducing alert fatigue. This paper introduces a machine learning framework and a semi-supervised algorithm to pre-screen high-priority DDI candidates using clinical evidence from adverse event reports. Experimental results show that features derived from adverse events contain effective information about DDI severity levels and demonstrate the desirable performance of the proposed algorithm in predicting high-priority DDIs.

Future work will incorporate chemical, biological, and other drug property features to improve model performance. The weighted SVM classifier can be replaced by other methods, such as random forest, gradient boosting, or ensemble classifiers. Additionally, the list of high-priority DDIs and the mechanism for displaying alerts can be continuously improved by analyzing retrospective data from user responses.
output:
Identifying high-priority DDIs is a crucial step to optimize medication alerts in EHRs. Proper tiering and displaying DDI alerts by severity levels represents a proven approach to reduce alert fatigue and improve patient safety. In this paper, we introduce a machine learning framework and a semi-supervised learning algorithm to pre-screen high-priority DDI candidates utilizing clinical evidence from adverse event reports. The experimental results show that features derived from adverse events contain effective information about the severity levels of DDIs; also demonstrate the desirable performance of the proposed algorithm in predicting high-priority DDIs.

Several lines of research and investigations have been emerged for future work. Besides the post-marketing surveillance features, there is a need to incorporate the chemical, biological, and other drug property features for improving model performance. The proposed method employs the weighted SVM as the final classifier, which can be replaced by other classifiers such as random forest [41], gradient boosting method [41], or an ensemble of different classifiers. Furthermore, the list of high-priority DDIs and the mechanism to display DDI alerts can be continuously improved through analyzing the retrospective data collected from user responses.

output: Most of the existing SemiHAR methods concentrate on solving annotation scarcity and rely on the covariate assumption stating that the input data are collected from similar distributions [10]. Nevertheless, this assumption does not always hold since people have diverse behavior patterns, and data from different participants are distributed variously [5]. Notably, when limited activity labels are present, the user labels are easily available during the data collection process and thus one could independently assign the user labels to the raw samples irrespective of the corresponding activity labels [11]. As shown in Fig. 1(c) and (d), the labeled data and unlabeled data are drawn from two different subjects user-1 and user-2, respectively. The distributions of the lying activities of labeled user-1 and unlabeled user-2 are almost identical. However, the walking class exhibits distinct distributions, as user-1 may walk slowly, while user-2 tends to walk faster [5]. This triggers the distribution discrepancy problem between the labeled and unlabeled data derived from different users. To tackle this problem, some researchers employ transfer learning to transfer the model trained on the labeled data collected from user-1 to the unlabeled data received from user-2 [12], [13], [14]. Although transfer learning is effective in solving the distribution shift problem, it cares most about its performance on the target unlabeled data [15]. In our setting, we aim to achieve high performance on both labeled and unlabeled data when they are distributed differently during training.
