section: I. INTRODUCTION — C. Dynamic Task Relations
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
HAR performance can improve by learning from extra tasks, specifically by capturing underlying dimension relations and reducing distribution shift. However, accuracy may degrade when learned tasks are less related [16]. Fig. 1(c) shows that discovering underlying sequence relations is more important than reducing distribution discrepancy for the lying class, while both are crucial for the walking class. Therefore, dynamically aggregating information through different task types is important. Most existing methods treat related tasks equally [17]–[19]. This problem can be alleviated by a task relation learner (TRL). Fig. 1(e) shows the model achieves a clear decision boundary for identifying lying and walking classes, and labeled and unlabeled walking activities from different users are well merged after training.

We propose a novel SemiHAR framework that trains multiple tasks together and dynamically learns task relations. Main contributions are as follows:

1) We propose a dimension-based Markov transition field (DMTF) technique to capture inherent interactions among multiple dimensions.

2) To mitigate distribution discrepancy, the user recognition (UR) task and activity recognition (AR) task are simultaneously handled by sharing parameter spaces.

3) We propose a TRL to dynamically learn task relations, which aims to balance multiple tasks for better recognition.

4) A novel generalization bound with a fast convergence rate is proven for SemiHAR. Comprehensive experiments and case studies on four real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of SemiHAR.
output:
The performance of HAR can be improved by learning knowledge from extra tasks. Specifically, the tasks of learning the underlying relations among different dimensions and reducing the distribution shift can improve a model's generalization. However, the accuracy of HAR may degenerate when the learned tasks are less related [16]. For example, as shown in Fig. 1(c), the task of discovering the underlying relations among sequences is more important than the task of reducing the distribution discrepancy of the lying class, while both are crucial for the walking class. Therefore, it is important to dynamically aggregate information through different types of tasks. Nevertheless, most of the existing methods treat each related task equally [17], [18], [19]. This problem can be alleviated by a task relation learner (TRL), which is designed in our model. As shown in Fig. 1(e), our model achieves a clear decision boundary for identifying the lying and walking classes, and the labeled and unlabeled walking activities from different users are well merged after training.

To address the above problems, we propose a novel SemiHAR framework, which trains multiple tasks together and dynamically learns task relations. Our main contributions are given as follows.

1) We propose a dimension-based Markov transition field (DMTF) technique to capture the inherent interactions among multiple dimensions.

2) To mitigate the distribution discrepancy problem, the user recognition (UR) task, identifying the current user for the labeled and unlabeled data, and the AR task, identifying the current activity for the labeled data, are simultaneously handled by sharing parameter spaces.

3) We propose a TRL to dynamically learn task relations, which aims to balance multiple tasks for better recognition.

4) A novel generalization bound with a fast convergence rate is proven for SemiHAR. In addition, comprehensive experiments and case studies on four real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of SemiHAR.

The rest of this article is organized as follows. First, the related work is introduced in Section II. Then, the problem statement, the details of the SemiHAR algorithm, and the theoretical analysis are provided in Section III. In Section IV, we conduct experiments on real-world datasets, analyze the effects of different parameters, perform ablation experiments, and provide case studies. Finally, Section V concludes this article.

input: We propose TRL, a hard-parameter multitask learning framework that dynamically determines positive parameter sharing based on target activity. Unlike existing methods that treat all tasks equally, TRL captures shared structures to improve performance. The approach shares hidden layers across tasks while maintaining task-specific output layers. Specifically, TRL trains forecasting and classification tasks simultaneously under hard-parameter sharing, dynamically learning which parameters to share to mitigate conflicting information across tasks.
output: Multitask learning aims to jointly learn multiple related tasks so that the similarity information or shared structures can be captured with the hope of achieving improved model performance [23]. In the context of deep learning, multitask learning approaches can be categorized into hard- and soft-parameter methods [24]. The former shares hidden layers across all the tasks and keeps a few task-specific output layers [17]. For example, Saeed et al. [18] employed a hard-parameter multitask learning framework to recognize eight transformations for HAR. Jawed et al. [19] proposed a novel multitask learning method, named MTL, which trains forecasting and classification tasks simultaneously under hard-parameter sharing settings. Unlike hard-parameter methods, each task of a soft-parameter method has its own model, and then, these task-specific models are regularized during training. For instance, Chen et al. [25] introduced a deep multitask learning method to softly share parameters between the corresponding convolutional layers. Most existing hard- and soft-parameter methods for HAR treat all tasks equally. Thus, conflicting information across multiple tasks may degrade the model's performance. To alleviate this problem, we propose the TRL based on the hard-parameter scheme, which can dynamically learn positive sharing according to the target activity.

section: methods — C. Distribution Discrepancy
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Transfer learning and multitask learning have been proposed to reduce distribution discrepancy from user heterogeneity [12]-[14], [25]. Transfer learning trains a model on source participant data and fine-tunes it for target users [15], but prioritizes target users over source users [15], [23]. Multitask learning addresses this by learning auxiliary and main tasks simultaneously [23], improving performance for all individuals [17]. However, these approaches are supervised and require annotated user-specific data, which is difficult to obtain in real-world applications [17]. Our method minimizes distribution discrepancy via a shared block and provides enhanced improvements for semisupervised learning.
output: To reduce the distribution discrepancy arising from user heterogeneity, transfer learning [12], [13], [14] and multitask learning [5], [25] techniques have been proposed in the literature. Transfer learning aims to train a learning model with the source data collected from a number of participants and then fine-tune it with the target users [15]. For example, Ragab et al. [13], Ganin et al. [26], and Chen et al. [27] are committed to tackling the distribution shift by transferring knowledge. One backward with these transfer learning methods is that they care most about the target users, and hence, the target users play a more important role than the source users [15], [23]. In practical scenarios, the goal of HAR is to improve the model's performance on both the target users and the source users. In contrast with transfer learning, multitask learning can tackle this problem by learning the auxiliary task and the main task simultaneously [23]. For instance, Shen et al. [17] tried to align distribution across multiple tasks and improve the performance of all individuals. However, these works are supervised learning approaches, which require the collection and annotation of user-specific training data, and the activity labels are difficult to obtain in many real-world applications. To fill this gap, our method not only minimizes the distribution discrepancy via a shared block but also provides enhanced improvements for semisupervised learning.

section: methods — D. Semisupervised Learning
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
output: According to the way in which unlabeled data are utilized, the semisupervised approaches in HAR can be classified into self-training, co-training, and unsupervised feature extraction methods. Tang et al. proposed SelfHAR, which combines the self-training and self-supervised learning tasks to increase the diversity of training data. The co-training approach extends self-training to two or more supervised classifiers that are iteratively built on each other's most confident predictions. For example, Bi et al. proposed the ActSemiCNN, which incorporates activity learning and semisupervised learning into a single framework to improve the model's performance. Chen et al. proposed a pattern-balanced co-training framework for semisupervised and imbalanced HAR. However, the misclassification of several unlabeled data is always inevitable in the self-training and co-training methods. To tackle this problem, unsupervised feature extraction methods try to capture useful features in an unsupervised manner. Tang et al. explored a contrastive learning framework, called SimCLR, and then illustrated its adoption in HAR. Nevertheless, most of the existing semisupervised methods focus on data scarcity and ignore shifted distributions. Furthermore, their generalization bounds are not discussed.

section: III. METHODOLOGY
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: The proposed model architecture, SemiHAR, integrates one unsupervised and two supervised tasks. An unsupervised DMTF task reconstructs 2-D data transformed from input signals to capture inter-dimensional interactions. Two supervised tasks, UR and AR, are trained simultaneously to reduce distribution discrepancy via parameter sharing. A TRL module connects the tasks and automatically assigns dynamic weights to balance their contributions.
output: In this section, we present the proposed model in detail. Fig. 2 shows the general architecture of SemiHAR. It consists of one unsupervised task and two supervised tasks. The unsupervised DMTF task reconstructs a series of 2-D data transformed from the whole set of input signals to capture the interactions among different dimensions. The UR task and the AR task (two supervised tasks) are simultaneously trained to reduce the distribution discrepancy between them by sharing parameters. The TRL connects these three tasks and automatically assigns weights for them.

output: In HAR, raw multivariate sensory data are preprocessed and segmented to produce equal-sized time series. Given a multivariate signal T = < t1, . . . , td > ∈ R^{d×n}, where tk = (t1,k, t2,k, . . . , tn,k), n is the series length, and d is the multivariate dimension, we denote the jth value of the ith instance of dimension k as a scalar ti,j,k. In our HAR setting, the training data contain two parts: a labeled set P and an unlabeled set G. A labeled domain is defined as a joint distribution P_o(T, y) on T × Y, where T, Y, and o denote the space of all labeled instances, the activity class space, and o participant(s) with activity labels, respectively. The labeled set is drawn from the labeled domain distribution, i.e., P = {(T_i, y_i)}_{p}^{i=1} ∼ P_o. Considering a set of individuals in P, each sample can be written as (T, y, o), which consists of a labeled sample T, an activity label y, and a corresponding user label o. An unlabeled domain is represented as G̃_o(T) on T̃, where T̃ is the unlabeled data space and the unlabeled samples are received from ̃o participant(s) without activity labels. Then, we are given unlabeled data from the unlabeled domain G = {(T_i)}_{g}^{i=1} ∼ G̃_o. In G, each sample (T, ̃o) consists of an unlabeled instance T and a user annotation ̃o. Under the distribution shift between the labeled and unlabeled data, we assume that P_o ≠ G̃_o, o ≠ ̃o where o, ̃o ∈ {o1, . . . , oz}. In addition, N signals are contained in both the labeled and unlabeled sets, i.e., p + g = N. Our goal is to construct a generalizable classifier from P and G. The Nomenclature summarizes the major notations used in this article.

section: III. METHODOLOGY — B. Dimension-Based Markov Transition Field

input: A Markov transition field converts a univariate time series into an image [35]. To represent dimension-based transitions in multivariate sensory data, we randomly select two dimensions, tm and tv, from the time series T. Each dimension is discretized into Q quantile bins. A Q×Q weighted transition matrix is constructed by counting first-order Markov chain transitions between the bins of tm and tv. This matrix is normalized to produce the dimension-based Markov transition matrix. Repeating this procedure d2 times generates multiple DMTF representations, which are averaged to capture multi-dimensional interactions. Inspired by MTF [35], the DMTF can be downsampled by averaging nonoverlapping c×c patches using a 1/c² blurring kernel to improve efficiency. The input data for the DMTF task are Mk1 = DMTF(Ti)Ni=1 ∈ ℝN×c×c, where k1 denotes the task. The encoder I outputs the latent hidden state hr = fi(Mk1) ∈ ℝN×e.

A Markov transition field (MTF) is a technique that converts a univariate time series into an image [35]. Given a time series Ti, the corresponding MTF is constructed by considering all continuous numerical values from ti,1,k to ti,n,k. Each cell in the Markov transition matrix can be interpreted as the likelihood of transition in a time-based axis. However, how to build this matrix to represent the dimension-based transition probabilities for multivariate sensory data is still a challenge in HAR.

In this section, we created a novel representation (i.e., DMTF image) by considering the dimensional information from t1 to td. Two dimensions tm = (t1,m, t2,m, . . . , tn,m) ∈Rn and tv = (t1,v, t2,v, . . . , tn,v) ∈Rn are randomly selected from T. tm and tv are first discretized into Q quantile bins, and thus, each signal value is associated with one of the quantiles qj (j ∈[1, Q]). Then, a Q × Q weighted transition matrix is constructed by counting the transitions among the quantile bins from tm to tv according to a first-order Markov chain. Finally, the dimension-based Markov transition matrix can be computed by normalizing the weighted transition matrix. The DMTF data are defined as

w_{i, j}|t1,m ∈qi, t1,v ∈qj
w_{i, j}|t1,m ∈qi, tn,v ∈qj
...
...
...
w_{i, j}|tn,m ∈qi, t1,v ∈qj
w_{i, j}|tn,m ∈qi, tn,v ∈qj

where w_{i j} represents a point in quantile qi of tm followed by a point in quantile qj of tv and DMTF(T) ∈Rn×n indicates the interactions from tm to tv derived by sequentially computing the transition probabilities between different dimensions.

Repeating the above procedure d2 times, we can obtain all DMTF representations of the signal T, and the final DMTF data are acquired by averaging the whole set of 2-D data to capture the interactions among multiple dimensions. Furthermore, inspired by the MTF [35], the DMTF can be reduced by averaging the pixels in each nonoverlapping c × c patch with the blurring kernel 1/c2 to improve the computational efficiency. Fig. 2 shows the procedure used to encode a multivariate time series into DMTF data. Therefore, the input data of the DMTF task are Mk1 = DMTF(Ti)N i=1 ∈RN×c×c, where k1 represents the DMTF task. Then, the encoder I outputs the latent hidden state hr = fi(Mk1) ∈RN×e.

output: Following the data splitting strategy used in [27], we simulate distribution discrepancy scenarios by drawing the labeled set P and the unlabeled set G from two distinct subjects o and ˜o. The data of o are evenly separated into two subsets: one is the labeled set P and the other is the test set. Considering that the labels are imbalanced, the accuracy metric that always evaluates the performance of a classifier with regard to frequent classes may lead to false positive results while keeping high accuracy [43]. As stated in [44], F1-score is an informative evaluation metric that considers both precision and recall. Therefore, referring to [25] and [29], we use both accuracy and weighted macro F1-score (abbreviated as F1-score) as the performance metrics in our evaluation. We utilize stochastic gradient descent with Adam to minimize the loss functions at a learning rate of 1e−3. All models are trained at most 2000 epochs with a batch size of 100 to monitor the validation results and stop the training process when no improvement is detected. Results are achieved by fivefold cross validation.

instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: SemiHAR is compared against state-of-the-art baselines across three groups: multitask learning (MTL), domain adaptation (DANN), and semisupervised learning (SelfHAR, ActSemiCNN, SemiTime, SimCLR, and a regular CNN). SemiHAR achieves the best performance on all datasets and is significantly better than the baselines in 26 out of 56 comparisons. DANN shows competitive results on Opportunity and Mhealth datasets, suggesting distribution discrepancies exist there. On the remaining datasets, semisupervised methods like SelfHAR, SimCLR, and ActSemiCNN perform similarly to DANN despite data collected from various users.
output:
IV. EXPERIMENTS — D. Comparison With the Baselines

To further verify the performance of our model, we compare SemiHAR with other state-of-the-art methods. Three groups of baseline methods are included for comparison.

1) Multitask Learning Model: MTL [19] joins an auxiliary forecasting task and a main time series classification task to boost the performance of the classifier, especially in a semisupervised setting.

2) Domain Adaptation Model: The adaptation of domain-adversarial neural network (DANN) [26] is achieved through aligning the distributions of features of the labeled data in the source domain and the unlabeled data in the target domain.

3) Semisupervised Learning Models: We include SelfHAR (the self-training method) [29], ActSemiCNN (the cotraining method) [30], and the unsupervised SemiTime [32] and SimCLR [34] feature extraction methods. In addition, we also employ a regular CNN [45] as a supervised baseline that is trained with the labeled dataset.

The overall results are presented in Table I. The bold text indicates the best value and the suffix star represents the best result significantly better than a value (t-test at 1% risk), the rest of the values that have not bold and nor suffix star are statistically equivalent to the best one, and the underline indicates the best baseline. We can observe that SemiHAR performs best on all datasets, and it is significantly better than the others on 26 out of 56 comparisons. In addition, DANN achieves competitive results on the Opportunity and Mhealth datasets, indicating that certain degrees of distribution discrepancies exist. For the other two datasets, the semisupervised methods, e.g., SelfHAR, SimCLR, and ActSemiCNN, obtain similar results to those of DANN even though the labeled and unlabeled data are collected from various users.

section: IV. EXPERIMENTS — E. Ablation Study
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: To understand task contributions, ablation studies were conducted. The variants are: SemiHAR without UR, without DMTF, and without TRL; DMTF+AR without UR and TRL; UR+AR without DMTF and TRL; and a single-task AR model trained on labeled samples. Results show that accuracy increases with more tasks, verifying each component's contribution. AR+UR+TRL outperforms AR+UR, DMTF+AR, and DMTF+UR+AR across all datasets, verifying TRL's role in task balancing. On Opportunity and Mhealth, AR+UR+TRL is superior, indicating noticeable discrepancies. On PAMAP2 and UCI-HAR, DMTF+AR+TRL achieves better performance than other variants, demonstrating that capturing inter-dimensional interactions improves HAR in various scenarios. SemiHAR achieves the best overall performance when combining all benefits.
output:
To gain a better understanding of the contributions of different tasks, we conduct ablation studies in this section. The settings are summarized as follows: 1) DMTF+AR+TRL is a variant of SemiHAR without the UR task; 2) AR+UR+TRL is a model without the DMTF task; 3) DMTF+AR+UR is a setting without the TRL; 4) DMTF+AR represents SemiHAR without the UR task and the TRL; 5) UR+AR indicates the method without the DMTF task and the TRL; and 6) AR is a single-task version of SemiHAR that only learns the AR task based on the labeled samples.

The results in Table II show the following tendencies.

1) The accuracy increases with the increment of task numbers, indicating the contribution of each task/component to SemiHAR.

2) AR+UR+TRL, DMTF+AR+TRL, and DMTF+UR+AR+TRL (SemiHAR) outperform AR+UR, DMTF+AR, and DMTF+UR+AR on all datasets, respectively. These results verify that the TRL is powerful for balancing tasks and thus brings better performance.

3) AR+UR+TRL is superior to other variants on datasets Opportunity (−0.89% and −0.07%) and Mhealth (−1.38% and −1.47%), which implies that their discrepancies are noticeable.

4) DMTF+AR+TRL achieves better performance than the other variant models on datasets PAMAP2 (−0.34% and −0.36%) and UCI-HAR (−0.10% and −0.80%).

section: V. CONCLUSION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
output:
In this article, we propose SemiHAR, a novel semisupervised human activity recognition model that focuses on capturing discriminative features contained among dimensions and reducing the distribution discrepancy between labeled and unlabeled data. In addition, we introduce a simple and effective attention mechanism TRL in the multitask setting to dynamically learn task relations. Theoretical and experimental analyses demonstrate the effectiveness of our SemiHAR.

Our future research will involve enhancing the accuracy of semisupervised classification by leveraging more related tasks, such as sensor placement recognition or sensor orientation recognition, to obtain high-level complex representations. Another interesting issue worth investigating is to concentrate on the real-time implementation of the HAR system for diverse application scenarios using unlabeled data, including fall detection and eldercare. Moreover, we are planning to explore human activity datasets based on images or videos and apply representation learning techniques to extract meaningful features effectively.

ABSTRACT A network intrusion detection system (NIDS) is an important technology for cyber security.
Recently, machine learning based NIDSs are being actively researched as various machine learning techniques are proposed. However, existing NIDSs have limitation in terms of generality because they have
been designed based on speciﬁc characteristics obtained from analyzing some partial datasets. Moreover,
in reality, the NIDS datasets have a signiﬁcantly imbalanced ratio between normal and abnormal data.
It causes the minority class problem, which needs to be addressed for developing robust and reliable
NIDSs working in various environments. This paper proposes a novel technique using service-aware dataset
partitioning, which provides high scalability to handle huge and rapidly growing network data ﬂexibly, and
helps the classiﬁer to improve the classiﬁcation performance in terms of accuracy and speed. We evaluated
our approach with the Kyoto2016 dataset, which is a well-known dataset for highly imbalanced data,
using various classiﬁcation algorithms and parameters for achieving the best performance and compared it
with existing state-of-the-art approaches. Our experimental results indicated that our approach can classify
network trafﬁcs rapidly and accurately with huge imbalanced datasets. We conclude that it can relieve serious
existing issues of imbalanced datasets for modern machine learning based NIDS solutions.

I. INTRODUCTION

Network intrusion detection system (NIDS) is a core technology in modern networks that detects anomaly activities on the network by analyzing traffic. It is essential for providing stable services on various networks, ranging from legacy networks to latest networks such as 5G and Internet of Things networks. Furthermore, the importance of NIDSs increases with vehicle-to-everything emerging, which requires very strict QoS requirements. Such technology is directly related to the daily lives of people, so any network attack threatening networks is seriously threatening their lives.

The associate editor coordinating the review of this manuscript and approving it for publication was Shadi Aljawarneh.

Misuse detection and anomaly detection are well-known approaches for implementing an NIDS. Misuse detection classifies the incoming traffic by comparing them with patterns extracted from past anomaly traffic. Therefore, it is also called signature- or knowledge-based detection. Essentially, misuse detection can detect known attacks with high accuracy and high speed. However, it can barely detect any unknown attack. In contrast to misuse detection, anomaly detection can detect both unknown and known attacks because it exploits statistical characteristics of attack traffic. Owing to the high and steady performance of anomaly detection, it is being mostly used nowadays, and is becoming more strengthened in combination with machine learning.

section: I. INTRODUCTION — Y. Uhm, W. Pak: Service-Aware Two-Level Partitioning for Machine Learning-Based Network Intrusion Detection
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
output:
I. INTRODUCTION — Y. Uhm, W. Pak: Service-Aware Two-Level Partitioning for Machine Learning-Based Network Intrusion Detection

Various machine learning techniques have been used for implementing an NIDS, such as random forest (RF) and decision tree (DT), which is simple but has high classification performance, or a deep neural network (DNN), which has been actively researched recently due to the growth of neural network (NN) technology. However, these methods have three critical issues to be used in NIDSs as follows.

First, the performance of existing NIDS cannot be guaranteed in real environments because most of these studies are based on a balanced and shortened dataset with modification rather than a large and unbalanced original dataset [1]–[6]. Thus, many technical issues arise in adopting unmodified real datasets, such as high resource requirements for processing time and memory. They usually fail to catch all issues persisting in only original datasets using such refined samples of dataset.

Second, the existing studies are vulnerable to minority class problem, which refers to the issue that most minority class data are misclassified as majority ones for the unbalanced dataset with high skewness. A few existing studies have attempted to resolve the minority class problem, have faced critical problems of low classification accuracy and poor classification speed [9]–[11], [30]. In fact, we can say that there is no practical solution for the minority class problem in the field of NIDS research so far.

Third, very few NIDS solutions have been able to handle the issue of increasing network traffic data efficiently. The researchers face the problem of network traffic data increasing at a significant speed. Most NIDS solutions inevitably take a very long time to process such large network traffic. If an NIDS cannot provide any efficient solution for supporting high scalability in terms of data size, it cannot be adopted in real networks. However, very few studies have focused on huge and increasing size of datasets, and processing speed.

This paper proposes a novel anomaly detection-based NIDS that is robust against these problems. Our contributions are as follows.

• We propose a service-aware partitioning algorithm to mitigate the minority class problem.
• We suggest an NIDS classifier that greatly improve the overall classification performance and scalability.
• We also show a new partitioning approach to provide partitioning in an incremental manner to support the rapidly increasing dataset.

We develop a service-aware partitioning algorithm to process the growing network data with high efficiency. This unique partitioning algorithm boosts classification accuracy and speed, and can sustain almost the same performance regardless of the various and dynamic network attacks.

Refining and partitioning of datasets are a common preprocessing method for machine learning in NIDS. However, our approach is different from existing works. First, our approach does not use refined and partial dataset but uses the original dataset without any modification. Second, partitioning is done by application service type, not partitioning size.

To implement service-based partitioning, we have developed sophisticated algorithms for service-based static and dynamic partitioning.

We should note that many NIDS solutions suffer from fluctuating performance according to different attack types. This characteristic is very important in developing a secure and robust NIDS. Our approach can provide a fundamental resolution for the low and fluctuated detection rate, and low scalability.

There are many studies on the issue of minority classes such as SMOTE [9]. However, the proposed method offers a different approach from these studies. It utilizes the actual protocol and session state information to make sub-partitions. Each sub-partition created in this way contains similar types of attack classes, and this homogeneousness improves learning efficiency and enables accurate detection on machine-learning. The proposed method has a completely different approach from existing work, so it can be used in conjunction with other methods and can achieve higher classification performance. It has a limit to effectively solve problems in all situations and environments using only one solution. Therefore, using the proposed methods individually or together with other methods will be of great help in solving the minority class problem.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. In Section II, we introduce the related work, and in Section III, we describe the minority class problem and our motivation behind conducting this study. In Section IV, we specifically explain our approach and its design, and in Section V, we show the experimental results. Finally, in Section VI, we summarize and conclude our research.

As mentioned earlier, misuse detection-based NIDSs have very powerful features but also have serious technical issues. So far, various approaches have been proposed to overcome the limitation of misuse detection-based NIDSs. Of these, the single machine learning algorithm-based NIDS is the most common and popular approach. The NN algorithm has been also introduced for NIDSs because it has achieved noticeable performance in areas such as image classification and voice recognition.

Recently, some researchers have attempted to combine multiple machine learning algorithms to further improve NIDS performance. This approach adopts multiple supervised machine learning algorithms or unsupervised and supervised algorithms simultaneously. Some researchers have tried to improve an NIDS by modifying and optimizing the training data, to achieve better classification.

According to the NIDS approach, we classify machine learning-based NIDS research into the following categories: single machine learning-based NIDS, hybrid machine learning-based NIDS, and data optimization-based NIDS.

In the research, usually, the performance between the proposed and other single machine learning-based NIDSs or conventional NIDSs is compared to evaluate the machine learning algorithm. The performance obtained using multiple datasets is also analyzed as the classification results highly depend on machine learning algorithms and datasets.

Ahmad et al. evaluated and analyzed NIDS performance in terms of precision and recall with the NSL-KDD dataset, using some selected algorithms such as multilayer perceptron, support vector machine (SVM), RF, and extreme learning machine [1], [7]. They also conducted experiments to show the effect of data size, i.e., full, half, and quarter sizes. Sahu et al. evaluated the suitability of J48 on an NIDS using 130,000 datasets selected from the Kyoto2006+ dataset [2], [8]. Cheong et al. also evaluated various algorithms such as SVM, DT, RF, Naive Bayes (NB), DNN, and k-nearest neighbor (kNN) using the Kyoto2006+ dataset [3], [12] to find the best classifier for an NIDS. They selected 1,800,000 data with 1% anomaly traffics from the Kyoto2006+ dataset to simulate real network circumstances. Furthermore, they conducted an extended experiment using 3,600,000 data extracted from the original dataset to analyze the effect of data size on the performance [8]. Yin et al. proposed an NIDS based on the recurrent neural network (RNN) algorithm, which is one of the most well-known DNNs. They evaluated the NIDS performance according to various combinations of learning rates and total neuron sizes in each layer with the NSL-KDD dataset. Park et al. proposed an NIDS using six labels expanded from the original three labels for the Kyoto2006+ dataset [5]. They developed additional labels using some features tightly coupled with the class in the dataset, and then, evaluated the classification results of the modified dataset using the RF algorithm. Lin et al. attempted to develop an NIDS using the convolutional neural network (CNN) algorithm, which is frequently used in image classification, and as a result, suggested an NIDS based on LeNet, which is a CNN variation for an NIDS.

In general, single machine learning-based NIDS shows high accuracy for most datasets, but cannot overcome the minority class problem entirely. Some researchers tried to resolve this problem using class weight, but found only the trade-off between the accuracies of multiple classes, thus just achieving a marginal effect on the overall performance.

In the latest NIDS research, hybrid approaches using two or more machine learning algorithms have been proposed to increase the classification performance of an NIDS. Semi-supervised learning is a well-known hybrid approach, using both unsupervised and supervised learning algorithms simultaneously [18]–[21], [29]. Such hybrid approaches show higher performance than single machine learning-based approaches.

Yuan et al. proposed a new hybrid approach that splits the KDD99 dataset into 10 sub-datasets; generates a prediction model for each subset using C5.0, one of latest DT algorithm; and determines the final class using NB with results obtained from the prediction models [18].

Li et al. suggested another semi-supervised learning that constructs as many C4.5-based binary classifiers as the total number of classes in the training dataset. When each binary classifier estimates the same class for the input data, the estimated class becomes the final output. Otherwise, the input data are treated as uncertain data. The kNN algorithm is trained with such uncertain data and used to choose the final class [19].

Soheily-Khah et al. proposed a semi-supervised learning model and evaluated it using the ISCX 2012 dataset [20], [25]. It uses the k-means algorithm, which is an unsupervised learning algorithm, as the first-level classifier. It finds the optimal k and makes clusters based on normal data, and then, removes the p (<k) farthest clusters from the attack data to decrease the size of the training data. Next, it trains the second-level classifier using the RF algorithm with the data. For performance evaluation, the proposed algorithm is compared and analyzed with various algorithms such as SVM, NN, NB, DT, and 1-NN through the Wilcoxon test [22].

Wang et al. proposed two hybrid algorithms, called HAST-I and HAST-II, using CNN and RNN. They use raw packet dump as a training dataset, instead of a dataset generated according to a pre-designed feature set [21]. HAST-I uses CNN to extract features from 2D data constructed by the first n bytes of the network flow or packet data. HAST-II adopts RNN to deal with time-series features in addition to CNN. They achieve very high classification accuracy from the evaluation using ISCX 2012 and DARPA 1998 [23], [24].

The main advantage of NIDS based on multi-supervised or semi-supervised learning is the higher classification performance compared to using single machine learning. As each classifier compensates the weakness of the other classifier, the classification performance can be increased significantly. This approach requires an efficient solution to find an optimal combination of multiple classifiers, which is still unknown and under research.

Yan et al. proposed region adaptive-SMOTE (RA-SMOTE) as an extended SMOTE [10], where the region around the minority class data is classified into independence point region, safety point region, and danger point region, and a different sampling policy is applied for each region. They evaluated RA-SMOTE using various classification algorithms such as SVM, RF, and backpropagation neural network (BPNN), with the NSL-KDD dataset, and compared it with SMOTE. Sun also proposed SMOTE-NCL based on SMOTE, which calculates an imbalance coefficient from the ratio of each class size to dataset size and continues to apply SMOTE to the data until the coefficient exceeds the threshold [11]. Then, it removes noisy data using the neighborhood cleaning rule [15]. For evaluation, the proposed algorithm was applied to the KDD99 dataset using DT, C4.5, and SVM [16]. Ambusaidi et al. evaluated various feature selection algorithms such as flexible mutual information-based feature selection, flexible linear correlation coefficient-based feature selection, and mutual information-based feature selection. They chose NB and SVM to develop NIDS classification algorithms, and evaluated the performance of each pair of feature selection and classification algorithms to find an optimal combination. Shah et al. compared the results with and without feature selection based on the information obtained using the KDD99 dataset and BPNN [13], [16]. Qazi et al. compared the results of various algorithms such as DT, NB, RF, and radial basis function by combining SMOTE, undersampling, and feature selection [14].

The abovementioned studies indicate that data optimization is very effective for significantly improving the classification accuracy by directly modifying the training dataset. However, it still has some open problems, such as how to determine tuning parameters, i.e., the size of data sampling and sampling algorithm. If we choose unoptimized algorithms, the classification performance can be rather degraded. Moreover, over-sampling inevitably increases the dataset size, leading to a long training time. If the sampling data do not reflect the overall characteristics of the original dataset, the increasing data can behave as noise, so the overall performance can decrease. On the contrary, under-sampling can lead to loss of characteristics of the original dataset, causing the training model to be biased and dependent on the sampling data. NIDS using such a model cannot guarantee high classification performance and the performance can fluctuate according to the traffic. Most feature selection algorithms remove features with low importance, but previous studies have shown that even features with low importance can improve the overall performance [17]. Thus, we still need to develop feature selection algorithms to find the best combination of features.

section: III. MOTIVATION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
output:
In this section, we discuss in depth the limitations of existing approaches, especially for the minority class problem occurring in large-scale datasets. We often find the occurrence of a serious imbalance between the amounts of attack and normal traffics in a real network dataset. In unfiltered network traffics, most traffics are normal and only a few are attack traffics as shown in Figure 1 (a). On the contrary, when we analyze network traffics filtered by the network security equipment, we find that the majority traffic is attack traffic as shown in Fig. 1 (b). In any case, the imbalance problem exists.

FIGURE 1. The ratio for each class in CIC-IDS2017 and Kyoto2016 datasets.

The Kyoto2016 dataset was built by gathering traffics from 2006 to 2015 using honeypots, so it is not a synthesized dataset but a real one, in contrast to the KDD99 or NSL-KDD datasets. KDD99 and its variants have been widely used in most existing studies, but they are outdated and provide insufficient information about the latest attacks. Moreover, compared to Kyoto2016, they are too small to include the various malicious data that have occurred [26]. These limitations lead us to select the Kyoto2016 dataset for analyzing the problems of modern NIDS and creating a solution for them. For an exact analysis, we use a dataset whose duplicate data are removed. Table 1 shows the feature list composed of the Kyoto2016 dataset. Because it contains session-specific information, we only use some selected features indexed to 1 to 14, 20, 22, and 24 in Table 1.

First, we analyze the Kyoto2016 dataset collected in February 2015 for better understanding the issues of the NIDS dataset. Table 2 depicts the high imbalance in terms of size between normal and attack traffics. We use some selected metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. Table 3 presents the classification result for the dataset in Table 2 using RF. As seen, most minority class data are miss-detected. A serious class imbalance causes biased training of a machine learning model to majority class data, so most minority class data can be misclassified as majority class if the model is used for classification. This phenomenon is called the minority class problem. Even if the minority class problem occurs and all minority class data are misclassified, some classification metrics, such as accuracy, may still appear to be very high because a minority class data with a very small size has little impact on the metrics. For an accurate analysis of the minority class problem, we should evaluate the classification results using the confusion matrix or by calculating the precision, recall, and F1-score for each class, as shown in Table 3.

instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: The proposed approach uses two partitioning stages. First, static agglomerative partitioning removes duplicate data and partitions the dataset by service, destination port, and session flag in a fixed order to enable fast incremental updates. Each sub-dataset contains homogeneous traffic for one service, which improves machine learning training under the minority class problem, as attacks are service-specific. Second, if sub-datasets remain too small, similar ones are merged based on shared abnormal classes or common destination ports. If large sub-datasets persist, dynamic divisive partitioning selects features dynamically. For example, a dataset with services SSH, HTTP-SSH, DNS and flags S1, SF, REJ, SHR partitions into 12 subsets; small subsets merge with similar ones using shared ports or session states to mitigate the minority class issue.
output:
IV. PROPOSED APPROACH — Y. Uhm, W. Pak: Service-Aware Two-Level Partitioning for Machine Learning-Based Network Intrusion Detection

In this study comprises two partitioning parts, i.e., static agglomerative partitioning and dynamic divisive partitioning as shown in Fig. 3. In the static partitioning, any duplicate data are removed from the training dataset. Then, the dataset is partitioned into small sub-datasets according to service, destination port, and session flag in static order. This fixed order of partitioning features helps the NIDS to increase partitioning speed, and above all, enables the NIDS to handle partial incremental partitioning for increasing dataset efficiently without repartitioning from the scratch. This feature allows us to apply new training data to NIDS classifier in a short time. As the service feature is used for the first partitioning, each sub-dataset contains only data related to one service or similar services.

FIGURE 3. Overall structure of two-level partitioning, where Smax is a control parameter for deciding the partitioned sub-dataset size. An NIDS always recognizes the service type of incoming traffics, so such service-based partitioning can be adopted in any NIDS without a technical implementation burden. Each sub-dataset generated from service-based partitioning contains almost homogeneous service traffic data. We also note that the type of attack is closely related to a specific service. For example, network attacks such as DoS Slowloris and DoS SlowHTTPtest generally target only a web service. Thus, each partition generated by service-based partitioning has mostly only attack data for the corresponding service. This characteristic also applies to normal data of the partition. Such homogeneity can have great advantage for better training of machine learning algorithms; therefore, we can increase the classification accuracy effectively under the minority class problem.

Similar attacks show similar session level behaviors. For example, every port scanning generates a large number of half open sessions. Thus, it is a good idea to split dataset using session state, which is analyzed and represented by 'flag' in IDS.

Now, we will describe the entire partitioning algorithm using an example. Let us assume that we have a dataset including normal and abnormal classes for three services, i.e., 'SSH', 'HTTP, SSH', and 'DNS', and for four flags, i.e., 'S1', 'SF', 'REJ', and 'SHR'.

We can easily partition it into 12 sub-datasets based on service and flag. If some partitions are too small, we need to merge them into larger sub-datasets in order to avoid the minority class problem. We need to merge similar sub-datasets which include common abnormal classes.

We can use destination ports used for each service to find the most similar services. For the example, 'SSH' and 'HTTP, SSH' are basically the same SSH, so the most similar ones in this example. In other prospects, we can choose these two services since they use the common destination port, 22. If too small sub-datasets still exist, it will be reasonable to merge two sub-datasets, S1 with SF, or REJ with SHR because S1 and SF include normal sessions, but REJ and SHR include abnormal ones.

If we still have large sub-datasets after static agglomerative partitioning, we perform additional partitioning, called dynamic divisive partitioning, which selects the partitioning feature dynamically. Now, we will describe the proposed algorithm in detail.

The dataset is first partitioned statically by predefined feature order, enabling fast updates. If any partition exceeds a maximum size threshold, dynamic partitioning using selected features refines only those sub-datasets. This hybrid approach balances update speed and partitioning efficiency.

When a new dataset with a new attack is available, the NIDS should train machine learning using the dataset to defend the new attack. If partitioning takes long, the NIDS becomes defenseless against the new attack for a long partitioning time at least.

To achieve such goals, we partition the dataset according to the predefined order of some selected features. Such a static partitioning can be deteriorated over the dynamic one in terms of partitioning quality but static partitioning can be simple and fast enough to handle the increasing dataset. However, we may still have a sub-dataset larger than Smax. As the number of such sub-datasets is small, we can apply dynamic partitioning to them for achieving high partitioning efficiency. If we have any sub-dataset larger than ρSmax after static agglomerative partitioning, we need additional partitioning. Unlike static partitioning, we dynamically find the best feature to be used in the next partitioning. To evaluate the quality of the feature, f, for partitioning, we consider the number of unique values in the feature, Uf, and their standard deviation, σf. A feature with larger Uf and smaller σf is effective for partitioning. Obviously, the field f with the larger Uf is better for partitioning. If σf is smaller, we can perform the more even partitioning. Therefore, the ratio of these two values can play an important role in choosing a proper field for partitioning. For example, Fig. 4 shows distribution for two features of a dataset: session duration time and packet count. From the distributions, we can easily conclude that the packet count is more favorable than duration time for partitioning a dataset. Thus, we suggest a partitioning coefficient for a feature f, i.e., pf, by combining Uf and σf, as shown in (3).

pf = σf / Uf (>0) (3)

For each sub-dataset larger than ρSmax, we calculate the coefficient of each feature except for features used in previous partitioning, such as service, destination port, and flag. Then, we choose a feature with the smallest non-zero pf as a partitioning feature and perform partitioning of the sub-dataset using the chosen feature. This procedure is repeated until all sub-datasets are smaller than ρSmax. The divisive partitioning algorithm using (3) is described in Algorithm 2.

input:
VI. CONCLUSION

This paper proposes a new two-level partitioning algorithm combining agglomerative and divisive partitioning to minimize attack type size per partition. Unlike most existing studies, we used very large unbalanced datasets, CIC-IDS2017 and Kyoto2016, to analyze the minority class problem. We confirmed that the proposed partitioning significantly increases classification performance using RF classifier. Compared to existing approaches, it achieves higher accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. It maintains high performance for both large and small datasets. The proposed algorithm also achieves higher classification speed than competitive algorithms regardless of dataset size. However, it cannot support inline intrusion prevention. Future work will extend the algorithm for real-time intrusion prevention. The algorithm exploits network traffic characteristics but can be extended to other classification problems suffering from minority class issues, such as unreliable telecommunication customers, fraud detection, or medical image classification.

Mahsa Bahrami and Mohamad Forouzanfar

Sleep apnea is a common sleep breathing disorder defined by airflow cessation or reduction exceeding 10 seconds. This study analyzes machine learning and deep learning algorithms for sleep apnea detection using 70 recordings from the PhysioNet ECG Sleep Apnea v1.0.0 dataset. ECG signals were pre-processed and segmented, then conventional machine learning methods (including linear/quadratic discriminant analysis, logistic regression, support vector machines, random forest, and AdaBoost) and deep learning methods (convolutional, recurrent, and hybrid networks) were implemented. Data were split into training, validation, and test sets, with model performance evaluated via fivefold cross-validation. The best detection performance was achieved by hybrid deep models, yielding 88.13% accuracy, 84.26% sensitivity, and 92.27% specificity. Developed algorithms are publicly available on GitHub.
output: 4003011 Sleep Apnea Detection From Single-Lead ECG: A Comprehensive Analysis of Machine Learning and Deep Learning Algorithms Mahsa Bahrami and Mohamad Forouzanfar, Senior Member, IEEE Abstract—Sleep apnea is a common sleep breathing disorder (SBD) in which patients suffer from stopping or decreasing airflow to the lungs for more than 10 sec. Accurate detection of sleep apnea episodes is an important step in devising appropriate therapies and management strategies. This article provides a comprehensive analysis of machine learning and deep learning algorithms on 70 recordings of the PhysioNet ECG Sleep Apnea v1.0.0 dataset. First, electrocardiogram signals were pre-processed and segmented and then machine learning and deep learning methods were applied for sleep apnea detection. Among conventional machine learning algorithms, linear and quadratic discriminate analyses, logistic regression, Gaussian naïve Bayes, Gaussian process, support vector machines, k-nearest neighbor, decision tree, extra tree, random forest, AdaBoost, gradient boosting, multi-layer perceptron, and majority voting were implemented. Among deep algorithms, convolutional networks (Alex-Net, VGG16, VGG19, ZF-Net), recurrent networks (LSTM, bidirectional LSTM, gated recurrent unit), and hybrid convolutional-recurrent networks were implemented. All networks were similarly modified to handle our biosignal processing task. The available data were divided into a training set to adjust the model parameters, a validation set to adjust hyperparameters, avoid overfitting, and improve the generalizability of the models, and a test set to evaluate the generalizability of the models on unseen data. This procedure was then repeated in a fivefold cross-validation scheme so that all the recordings were once located in the test set. It was found that the best detection performance is achieved by hybrid deep models where the best accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity were 88.13%, 84.26%, and 92.27%, respectively. This study provides valuable information on how different machine learning and deep learning algorithms perform in the detection of sleep apnea and can further be extended toward the detection of other sleep events. Our developed algorithms are publicly available on GitHub. Manuscript received December 19, 2021; accepted January 30, 2022. section: I. INTRODUCTION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: Sleep accounts for roughly one-third of the human lifespan and plays a critical role in health. Two main stages, rapid eye movement (REM) and non-REM (NREM), exist; REM sleep is associated with increased sympathetic activity and cardiovascular instability compared to NREM, where oxygen consumption, heart rate, and blood pressure decrease. Sleep apnea is most dominant during REM due to upper airway muscle relaxation. The prevalence of sleep disorders is increasing, with an estimated 70 million U.S. adults affected, increasing morbidity and mortality. Sleep-disordered breathing (SDBs), including obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) and central sleep apnea (CSA), are prevalent, with approximately one billion people suffering from OSA globally. CSA occurs mostly in NREM, while OSA severity is higher in REM. Accurate, affordable, and portable technologies are required to detect and monitor sleep events to prevent related health issues. Automatic algorithms for sleep apnea detection from physiological signals have been extensively researched, with ECG showing the most promise for convenience and precision due to its potential for single-sensor wearable devices. While conventional machine learning was an early approach, the focus has shifted to deep learning for automatic feature extraction. Given the variety of algorithms, datasets, and evaluation metrics, comparing performance is difficult. This study provides a fair comparison of 14 conventional machine learning and 19 deep learning algorithms for sleep apnea detection from single-lead ECG. Experiments use separate training, validation, and test sets to ensure generalizability, unlike studies that tune hyperparameters on test data. This extends previous work by analyzing significantly more models and performing feature importance analysis to identify effective ECG features. Algorithms are publicly available on GitHub.

LEEP accounts for about one-third of the human life
span and plays an important role in health and quality of life. Two main stages of sleep are called rapid eye
movement (REM) and non-REM (NREM) [3]. REM sleep
compared with NREM sleep is associated with increased
sympathetic activity, cardiovascular instability, and hemodynamic variations. During NREM, oxygen consumption and
heart rate decrease as well as the blood pressure, while in
the REM stage, blood pressure and heart rate surge. Sleep
apnea may occur during any stage of sleep, but it is most
dominant during the REM. This is mainly because the muscles
in the upper airway are further relaxed during the REM stage
of sleep.
The rate of people suffering from sleep disorders is increasing [6]. In the United States, it is estimated that about
70 million adults have sleep disorders [8]. The rate of morbidity and mortality increases in patients suffering from sleep
disorders [10]. Insomnia, sleep breathing disorders (SBDs),
central disorders of hypersomnolence, circadian rhythm sleepwake disorders, parasomnias, and movement disorders are the
main types of sleep disorders. Among different sleep disorders,
SBDs are more common. SBDs are divided into obstructive
sleep apnea (OSA), central sleep apnea (CSA), hypoventilation
in sleep, and hypoxia disorders. Upper airway obstruction
leads to OSA, whereas CSA occurs when the brain cannot
send proper signals into muscles responsible for breathing.
It is estimated that one billion people in the world are suffering
from OSA [12]. CSA occurs less than other types of apneas.
CSA mostly occurs in the NREM cycle, while OSA occurs in
both REM and NREM cycles but the severity of OSA in the
REM cycle is higher [14].
To prevent and manage cardiovascular, mental, and other
health issues related to sleep apnea, accurate, affordable, and
portable technologies are required that can detect and monitor
sleep events.
There has been considerable research on the development of automatic algorithms for the detection of sleep
apnea from a variety of physiological signals [15]–[22]
among which ECG has shown the most promising results
in terms of both convenience and precision [2], [4], [5],

section: II. BACKGROUND
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
Accurate sleep apnea detection is critical for managing side effects. Questionnaires, image processing, and signal analysis are the main monitoring approaches. Questionnaires are low-cost patient identification methods [24]. Medical image analysis is capable, especially for severe cases [25], and provides a unique opportunity for anatomical screening. Polysomnography (PSG) remains the gold standard [26], utilizing biological signals such as ECG, EEG, airflow, pulse oximetry, and nasal flow. However, these techniques require specialist settings and cannot be performed at home [27], [28]. Wearable and noncontact technologies are required for unobtrusive monitoring without expert presence [27], [28]. ECG provides a better possibility for wearable implementation among physiological signals.

Conventional machine learning relies on expert-defined features, while deep learning relies on automatic extraction. In [15], ECG signals were decomposed via Fourier transform, and statistical features were extracted for SVM classification. In [2], machine learning methods were compared using heart rate variability and ECG-derived respiration features; ANN achieved the best accuracy and sensitivity, though augmented naïve Bayes regression had higher specificity. Recently, deep learning has revolutionized detection. In [4], continuous wavelet transformation and Alex-Net were used for feature extraction from single-lead ECG, showing improved performance with time-frequency features. In [5], a two-layer CNN improved accuracy. In [7], LSTM provided an accurate, real-time OSA detection method from single-lead ECG. In [9], unsupervised feature learning was performed using a frequential stacked auto-encoder with HMM classification. In [11], a multiscale dilation attention convolution module combined with a weighted-loss time-dependent classifier improved performance. In [1], a hybrid CNN-LSTM achieved superior results compared to other deep networks.

In [29], a real-time method based on motion detection using quadrature microwave Doppler radar was proposed. In [30], a single-lead ECG wearable device was proposed to improve home monitoring. In [31], a phase-modulated continuous radar system could detect apnea events under predefined situations. Wearable devices for automatic sleep and health monitoring are important for future healthcare systems. Therefore, further research is required to evaluate AI models under the same settings and datasets to discover potentials and limitations for smart wearable algorithms.

Accurate detection of sleep apnea is an important step for the management of apnea side effects. Questionnaires, image processing techniques, and signal analysis methods are the main approaches for sleep apnea monitoring. Questionnaires are low-cost methods for the identification of patients with sleep disorders [24]. Medical image analysis is a capable method for analyzing sleep apnea especially in severe sleep apnea [25]. Medical image analysis also provides a unique opportunity for screening anatomical changes during sleep apnea. Polysomnography (PSG) is a gold standard for sleep apnea monitoring [26]. PSG consists of various biological signals, such as ECG, electroencephalogram, airflow pulse oximetry, arterial blood oxygen saturation, and nasal flow. However, none of these techniques can be performed in non-specialist settings, such as in home. Wearable and noncontact sleep technologies are required that can unobtrusively monitor and manage sleep without the need for direct expert presence [27], [28]. Different physiological signals have been analyzed for the detection of sleep apnea among which ECG provides a better possibility for implementation in wearable monitors.

Conventional machine learning and novel deep learning are two main automatic approaches for sleep apnea monitoring from physiological signals. The performance of conventional machine learning algorithms relies on expert-defined extracted features. In [15], ECG signals were decomposed to frequency bands by Fourier transform, and statistical features were extracted. A support vector machine (SVM) with Gaussian kernel function was then used to detect sleep apnea. In [2], the performance of different machine learning methods was compared. For this purpose, after extracting different time-domain features of heart rate variability (HRV) and ECG-derived respiration, artificial neural network (ANN), SVM, linear discriminate analysis (LDA), partial least-square regression, and augmented naïve Bayes regression were applied for the detection of sleep apnea events. The best accuracy and sensitivity were achieved by ANN; however, the specificity of augmented naïve Bayes regression was higher than other methods.

Recently, deep learning methods have revolutionized sleep apnea detection. Despite conventional machine learning approaches, deep learning methods rely on automatic feature extraction. Deep recurrent neural networks (DRNNs) and convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are two main types of deep learning models that have been used for sleep apnea monitoring. In [4], continuous wavelet transformation and Alex-Net were used for feature extraction and then different machine learning methods were used for the classification of sleep apnea episodes from single-lead ECG signals. It was shown that extracting time-frequency features improves the performance of sleep apnea detection. In [5], it was shown that the accuracy of sleep apnea detection can be improved by a two-layer CNN. In [7], a long short-term memory (LSTM) was used for OSA detection from single-lead ECG that provided an accurate and real-time method for sleep apnea detection. In [9], unsupervised feature learning from ECG signal was done by a frequential stacked auto-encoder, and a hidden Markov model was used for classification. In [11], a multiscale dilation attention convolution module was used and was shown that the combination of a multiscale attention convolutional module and a weighted-loss time-dependent classifier improves the performance of sleep apnea detection. In [1], we performed a comparison between a few deep networks and found that a hybrid CNN-LSTM achieves superior results.

In [29], a real-time sleep apnea detection method based on motion detection was proposed by using quadrature microwave Doppler radar. In [30], a wearable device based on single-lead ECG was proposed for improving the performance of home monitoring devices. In [31], a phase-modulated continuous radar system was proposed that could detect stop breathing events under predefined situations. Sleep wearable devices that can automatically monitor and manage sleep and health issues will form an important component of future healthcare systems. Therefore, further research is required on the evaluation of different artificial intelligence models under the same settings on the same datasets to discover their potentials and limitations to choose the appropriate algorithms that can perform well in smart wearables.

output:
A. Dataset

In this article, PhysioNet Apnea-ECG Database v1.0.0 [32] was used to build our models and to compare their performances. The database contains 70 recordings from 32 individuals (seven females, age: 44 ± 11, apnea–hypopnea index, AHI: 24 ± 25, height: 175 ± 6, weight: 86 ± 22) divided into four groups: A, B, C, and X. Thirteen individuals in this dataset have AHI ≤5 and are categorized as normal, 13 individuals have AHI > 30, and are categorized in the severe sleep apnea class, and six individuals have 5 < AHI < 30 and are categorized in the mild and moderate apnea class. The length of the 70 recordings is 8.2 ± 0.52 h. ECG signals are digitized at 100 Hz. The annotation of the presence of sleep apnea is provided for every 1 min by a sleep expert.

B. Preprocessing

ECG signals were segmented into 1-min intervals. To extract the R–R Intervals from the ECG signal, the Hamilton R-peak detection method based on an open-source code was employed [33]. A median filter proposed by Chen et al. [34] was used for removing physiologically uninterpretable points. The extracted R–R Intervals were then presented to the developed machine learning algorithms after appropriate processing as is discussed in Section IV.

In addition to the R–R Intervals, the amplitudes of R-peaks were also extracted and presented to the deep models. Cubic interpolation at 3 Hz was applied to sample R–R intervals and R-peak amplitudes at an equal rate. Finally, the interpolated R–R Intervals and R-peak amplitudes were fed to the deep models. To capture the time pattern of the input data when using DRNNs, the input data were segmented into n segments of 60/n s and n-cell DRNNs were designed to learn from the input data (here, n was set to 2).

output:
The most important features of ECG for apnea detection are HRV parameters [35]. In this article, a comprehensive set of time-domain, frequency-domain, and nonlinear features of HRV were extracted and presented to different machine learning models for sleep apnea detection.

1) Time-Domain Features: Time-domain features of HRV are mainly divided into statistical, long-term, and short-term features [36]. Minimum, range, median, mean, standard deviation (SDNN), skewness (third momentum), and kurtosis (fourth momentum) were the main statistical features extracted from R–R intervals. The standard deviation of successive differences between adjacent R–R intervals (SDSD) was the main long-term extracted feature of HRV. Short-term features of HRV consisted of the number of R–R intervals that differ from each other by more than 50 ms (NN50), the number of R–R intervals that differ from each other by more than 20 ms (NN20), percentage of successive R–R differences greater than 50 ms (pNN50), and the percentage of successive R–R differences greater than 20 ms (pNN20). In addition, the root mean square of successive differences between normal heartbeats (rMSSD) was extracted from the HRV signal. In total, 13 features were extracted from each ECG segment in the time domain.

2) Frequency-Domain Features: HRV has three predominant frequency bands [36]. Very low-frequency (VLF) band, that is, frequencies between 0.0033 and 0.04 Hz, exhibits the thermoregulation mechanisms. Low-frequency (LF) band, that is, frequencies between 0.04 and 0.15 Hz, exhibits mostly the sympathetic activity, and the high-frequency (HF) band, that is, frequencies between 0.15 and 0.4 Hz, exhibits parasympathetic activities.

Total power, VLF power, LF power, HF power, LF to HF ratio, normalized HF power (HFnu), and normalized LF power (LFnu) were extracted. In total, seven features were extracted from each ECG segment in the frequency domain.

3) Nonlinear Features: Nonlinear features are mainly used for modeling and analyzing ECG patterns before, during, and after sleep apnea. Poincaré plot features including SD1 and SD2, and their ratio (SD2/SD1) [37], cardiovagal index (CVI) [38], cardio sympathetic index (CSI) [38], and modified CVI [38] were extracted from the ECG signal. Permutation entropy [39] explaining the complexity of the HRV time series was also calculated. In total, seven nonlinear HRV features were extracted.

In total, 27 HRV features were extracted.

IV. Conventional Machine Learning — B. Dimension Reduction

Irrelevant features cause the curse of dimensionality and degrade classifier performance. Feature selection is applied prior to classification to identify the most effective variables. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was used for dimension reduction [19].

IV. Conventional Machine Learning — C. Classification

Multiple machine learning algorithms were compared for sleep apnea detection from single-lead ECG. Hyperparameters for each algorithm are summarized below.

Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) uses a linear decision boundary fitted via Gaussian densities and Bayes’ rule [16]. Main hyperparameters are the solver algorithm and a tolerance parameter defining the singular value significance threshold.

Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (QDA) uses a quadratic decision boundary [17]. The solver is set to SVD; tolerance is the main hyperparameter.

Logistic Regression (LR) models binary dependent variables using a logistic function [20]. Main hyperparameters are solver algorithm, tolerance, regularization strength (1/C), and penalty norm.

Gaussian Naïve Bayes (GNB) is a probabilistic method applying Bayes’ theorem with a naïve independence assumption between features [41]. The main hyperparameter is the portion of the largest feature variance added to all variances for stability.

Gaussian Process (GP) classification is a nonparametric approach using a kernel function to assign labels [20]. Main hyperparameters are kernel, optimizer algorithm, and the maximum number of Newton’s method iterations.

Support Vector Machine (SVM) maps data into higher dimensions using a kernel function and solves the problem via Lagrange equations [21]. Main hyperparameters are kernel type and kernel parameters.

K-Nearest Neighborhood (KNN) classifies samples based on nearest neighbors [22]. Main hyperparameters are distance metric, metric parameters, number of neighbors, and leaf size.

Decision Tree (DT) is a nonparametric classifier learning simple decision rules from extracted features [18]. Main hyperparameters are maximum tree depth, split strategy, and split criterion.

Random Forest (RF) extends DT using multiple DTs trained via bootstrapping [20]. It largely prevents overfitting. Main hyperparameters are maximum depth, minimum samples to split a node, split criterion, and number of estimators.

Extra Tree (ET) is an evolved DT model similar to RF but uses the whole original sample and random split points rather than bootstrapping and optimal cut points [20]. It is computationally more efficient than RF. Main hyperparameters are maximum depth, minimum samples to split a node, split criterion, and number of estimators.

AdaBoost (AB) combines weak learners (decision stumps) into a stronger classifier [20]. Unlike bagging, it upweights misclassified samples at each iteration. Main hyperparameters are number of estimators, boosting algorithm, and learning rate.

Gradient Boosting (GB) generalizes AB as an optimization problem minimizing loss via gradient descent [20]. Main hyperparameters are loss function, number of estimators, maximum depth, learning rate, sample fraction for base learners, and split criterion.

Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) is a feed-forward neural network modeling complex, nonlinear relationships [20]. Main hyperparameters are number of layers, number of nodes, learning rate, activation function type, optimization method, and loss tolerance. The number of hidden layers was set to 1.

Majority Vote (MV) is an ensemble method combining all conventional machine learning algorithms via majority voting [20].

Different CNNs and DRNNs [42] were employed to build standalone and hybrid deep models for the detection of sleep apnea. The flowchart of the proposed approach for sleep apnea detection using deep learning is shown in Fig. 2. CNN provides a unique opportunity for automatic feature extraction and classification of images, signals, and other biological data. Fig. 2. VGG16, VGG19, ZF-Net, and Alex-Net are well-known CNN architectures that have led to numerous successful applications in image processing. Here, we similarly modified these networks, based on the dimension of our input data, to be applied in the detection of sleep apnea.

A. ZF-Net
The developed ZF-Net comprised of 96 kernels of size 7 × 1 stacked to a 3 × 1 max-pooling followed by a batch normalization in the first layer, a convolution layer with 256 kernels of size 5 × 1 followed by a 3 × 1 max-pooling and batch normalization in the second layer, and three convolution layers with 512 kernels of size 3 × 1, 1024 kernels of size 3 × 1, and 512 kernels of size 3 × 1 stacked together followed by a 3 × 1 max-pooling in the third layer. B. Alex-Net
The developed Alex-Net comprised of a convolution layer with 96 kernels of size 11 × 1 stacked to a batch normalization layer followed by a 3 × 1 max-pooling operation in the first layer, a convolution layer with 256 kernels of size 5 × 1 stacked to a batch normalization layer followed by a 3 × 1 max-pooling operation in the second layer, and two convolution layers with 384 kernels of size 3 × 1, and a convolution layer with 256 kernels of size 3 × 1 each stacked to a batch normalization layer followed by a 3 × 1 max-pooling in the third layer. Data were then flattened and fed to two fully connected layers with 209 and two nodes.

C. VGG16
The developed VGG16 comprised of two convolution layers with 64 kernels of size 3 × 1 stacked together followed by a 2 × 1 max-pooling operation in the first layer, two convolution layers with 128 kernels of size 3 × 1 stacked together followed by a 2 × 1 max-pooling operation in the second layer, two convolution layers with 256 kernels of size 3 × 1 stacked together followed by a 2 × 1 max-pooling operation in the third layer, and two convolution layers with 512 kernels of size 3 × 1 stacked together followed by a 2 × 1 max-pooling operation in the fourth layer. Data were then flattened and fed to two fully connected layers with 512 and two nodes.

D. VGG19
The developed VGG19 comprised of two convolution layers with 64 kernels of size 3 × 1 stacked together followed by a 2 × 1 max-pooling operation in the first layer, two convolution layers with 128 kernels of size 3 × 1 stacked together followed by a 2 × 1 max-pooling operation in the second layer, four convolution layers with 256 kernels of size 3 × 1 stacked together followed by a 2 × 1 max-pooling operation in the third layer, four convolution layers with 512 kernels of size 3 × 1 stacked together followed by a 2 × 1 max-pooling operation in the fourth layer, and a convolution layer with 512 kernels of size 3 × 1 in the fifth layer. The developed LSTM comprised of a three-layer two-cell stacked architecture where each cell received a 2D structure of 90 × 2. The output dimension was set to 13 × 2. Data were then flattened and fed to two fully connected layers with four and two nodes.

The developed BiLSTM comprised of a three-layer two-cell stacked architecture where each cell received a 2-D structure of 90 × 2. The output dimension was set to 26 × 2. Data were then flattened and fed to two fully connected layers with four and two nodes.
