instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: A hybrid VGG16 architecture was constructed using four stages of convolutional blocks. Each stage consisted of two convolutional layers with kernel sizes of 3×1 and increasing numbers of filters (64, 128, 256, 512), separated by 2×1 max-pooling operations. The final convolutional output was connected to a single-layer stacked DRNN, where individual cells processed a 512×5 feature map. The DRNN output dimensions were set to 128×2 for LSTM and GRU, and 256×2 for BiLSTM. Subsequently, data were flattened and passed through two fully connected layers containing 37 and 2 nodes, respectively.
output: The developed hybrid VGG16 comprised of two convolution layers with 64 kernels of size 3 × 1 stacked together followed by a 2 × 1 max-pooling operation in the first layer, two convolution layers with 128 kernels of size 3 × 1 stacked together followed by a 2 × 1 max-pooling operation in the second layer, two convolution layers with 256 kernels of size 3 × 1 stacked together followed by a 2 × 1 max-pooling operation in the third layer, and two convolution layers with 512 kernels of size 3 × 1 stacked together followed by a 2 × 1 max-pooling operation in the fourth layer. The output was then connected to a one-layer two-cell stacked DRNN (LSTM, BiLSTM, or GRU) where each cell received a 2-D structure of 512 × 5. The output dimension of the DRNN was set to 128 × 2 for the GRU and LSTM while it was 256 × 2 for the BiLSTM. Data were then flattened and fed to two fully connected layers with 37 and two nodes.

I. Hybrid AlexNet — K. Hybrid VGG19

The developed VGG19 comprised of two convolution layers with 64 kernels of size 3 × 1 stacked together followed by a 2 × 1 max-pooling in the first layer, two convolution layers with 128 kernels of size 3 × 1 stacked together followed by a 2 × 1 max-pooling in the second layer, four convolution layers with 256 kernels of size 3 × 1 stacked together followed by a 2 × 1 max-pooling in the third layer, four convolution layers with 512 kernels of size 3 × 1 stacked together followed by a 2 × 1 max-pooling in the fourth layer, and a convolution layer with 512 kernels of size 3 × 1 were used in the fifth layer. The output dimension was set to 64 × 2 for the GRU and LSTM while it was 128 × 2 for BiLSTM. Data were then flattened and fed to two fully connected layers with 21 and two nodes.

section: VI. EXPERIMENTS AND DISCUSSION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
output:
We used PhysioNet Apnea-ECG Database v1.0.0 for apnea detection [32]. The dataset consists of 34 428 1-min intervals (normal: 21 362, apnea: 13 066) which means that it is imbalanced, that is, the number of apnea episodes is relatively lower than normal episodes. To overcome this problem, we used the stratified cross-validation method which is an effective method for balancing data in imbalanced datasets [43]. For a reliable and accurate analysis, we performed fivefold stratified cross-validation. Cross-validation allows us to train and test our models on multiple train-test splits. This provides a better indication of how well our model will perform on unseen data. In each fold, 70% of the data were used for training the models, 10% of the data were used as a validation set to find optimum hyperparameters (as reported in Sections IV and V), and 20% of data was used to evaluate the trained models on data not seen during training and validation.

Google Colaboratory Environment was used to implement machine learning and deep learning algorithms in Python. Keras and scikit-learn libraries were used for the implementation of deep learning and machine learning algorithms, respectively. hrvanalysis, scipy, and entropy libraries were also used for feature extraction from ECG signals. An open-source version of the code developed for this manuscript has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/mahsaabahrami/sleep-apnea.

To find the most representative HRV features for the detection of sleep apnea, their performances were compared using the ET algorithm (Fig. 3). HF power was found as the most important feature for sleep apnea detection. This can be attributed to the fact that the HF component of HRV represents the respiration effect on heart rate as the result of the parasympathetic activity of the autonomous nervous system [35].

Fig. 3. HRV feature ranking for sleep apnea detection.

Followed by HF, other frequency bands including VLF, LF, and their normalized values had the most impact on the detection performance. The ratio of LF to HF and total power were other important features.

The HRV VLF component represents sympathovagal activity and has unique characteristics in cardiovascular disease diagnosis [44]. In addition, studies have shown that the VLF band has a strong correlation with the renin-angiotensin system, metabolic syndromes, and all-cause mortality after traumatic brain injury [44].

The LF component of HRV is considered as a marker of both sympathetic and parasympathetic modulation, thereby it is directly associated with breathing disorders [35].

Overall, the frequency-domain features were found more reliable and significant than other features in sleep apnea analysis, meaning that sleep apnea can be best detected by the analysis of HRV frequency bands.

Statistical features including mean, kurtosis, skewness, and SDNN were the most important time-domain features of HRV for the detection of apnea events.

Among nonlinear HRV features, SD2 was the most important feature. SD2 is extracted from the Poincaré plot, which is constructed by plotting each RR interval against the previous one. When analyzing the Poincaré plot by fitting an ellipse, SD2 means the standard deviation of the Poincaré plot along the line of identity [37]. SD2 measures short- and long-term HRV and is correlated with LF power and baroreflex sensitivity and therefore can represent the autonomous system activity and its malfunction.

Table I summarizes the performances of different conventional machine learning algorithms (on unseen test data) that rely on HRV feature extraction. The optimum model hyperparameters found on a validation set (separate from the test and train sets) are listed in the second column. The performances are reported in terms of accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and F-score. By combining all the classifiers through an MV scheme, MV achieved the best accuracy (79.39%) and F-score (71.75%). It was observed that QDA achieves the best sensitivity (74.70%) while ET and GP achieve the best specificity (86.08%). We conjecture that a more complex fusion method that can weigh the classifiers’ output based on their performance and reliability may further improve the detection performance [45].

Among individual classifiers, MLP and SVM achieved superior results. Thanks to its powerful nonlinear modeling capability through the complex interactions of several nonlinear nodes, MLP can extract nonlinear input–output relationships. In fact, it has been theoretically proved that an MLP with a hidden layer and enough hidden nodes is capable of modeling any nonlinear function with a finite number of discontinuities [46]. SVM is a highly regularized classifier that performs well when there is not enough data available [47].

Among tree-based algorithms, ET and RF achieved superior results. Compared to DT which gives high importance to a particular set of features, RF and ET select features randomly during the training process. Therefore, they do not depend on any specific set of features and can better generalize. Compared to GB and AB which are boosting algorithms, RF is an ensemble bagging algorithm. By generating new data using combinations with repetitions, bagging decreases the variance in the prediction and is less prone to overfitting.

Among different conventional machine learning methods, LDA, QDA, DT, GNB, LR, GP, and AB had the lowest accuracy. Given the simplicity of such algorithms, their accuracy may degrade in modeling complex physiological processes.

Table II summarizes the performances of different deep learning algorithms on the test data in terms of accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and F-score. Among different methods, a hybrid model of ZFNet-BiLSTM achieved the best accuracy (88.13%) and specificity (92.27%), ZFNet-GRU achieved the best sensitivity (84.26%), and VGG16-LSTM achieved the best F-score (84.24%).

It was found that deep neural networks were superior to their conventional machine learning counterparts because they have the power of extracting the most important features, automatically. Comparing the best deep model (ZFNet-BiLSTM) with the best machine learning model (MV) using a paired t-test, it was revealed that the deep model’s accuracy is significantly higher than the best conventional machine learning model (p < 0.01).

While DRNNs (LSTM, BiLSTM, and GRU) performed better than conventional machine learning methods, their performance was lower than CNN-based networks (ZFNet, AlexNet, VGG16, and VGG19). This can be attributed to the fact that our methods were based on the analysis of short 1-min ECG segments. We conjecture that if the apnea detection is performed on longer ECG segments, the performance of DRNNs will be improved as these networks are particularly powerful in the analysis of long time-series data.

Among different CNNs, VGG16, ZFNet, and AlexNet achieved slightly better performance compared to VGG19. VGG19 is a deeper network than other CNNs implemented in this article. However, we had to modify the depth of this network based on our dataset. We conjecture that the modified structure of the VGG19 affected its ability to extract the most effective features and consequently slightly lower classification performance.

Considering that a lower rate of false negative is of higher importance in the detection of apnea, the sensitivity of the designed classifiers was studied. Among different conventional classifiers, QDA, MLP, SVM, KNN, and MV had the best sensitivities. Most deep learning algorithms outperformed the conventional machine learning algorithms with respect to sensitivity where ZFNet-GRU and AlexNet-GRU achieved the highest performance.

BAHRAMI AND FOROUZANFAR: SLEEP APNEA DETECTION FROM SINGLE-LEAD ECG

Table II

PERFORMANCE COMPARISON BETWEEN DIFFERENT DEEP LEARNING ALGORITHMS IN SLEEP APNEA DETECTION

Hybrid CNN-DRNN architectures benefit from the power of CNNs in feature extraction and the power of DRNNs in modeling the time pattern of the extracted features over time. In this scenario, the CNN network extracts high-resolution features while the DRNN models the evolution of these features over a coarser time interval. Therefore, it is expected that they achieve higher performance [48]. Among different hybrid networks, ZFNet-BiLSTM outperformed the rest. ZFNet is a modified version of AlexNet by reducing the filter size that leads to better accuracy. Combining a BiLSTM to capture the time pattern of the features extracted by ZFNet led to the highest performance in the detection of sleep apnea.

Our developed deep learning framework was based on the analysis of ECG R–R intervals and R-peak amplitudes. To study the contribution of R–R intervals and R-peak amplitude, our best model (ZFNet-BiLSTM) was once implemented using only the R–R intervals as the input and once using the R-peak amplitudes as the input. We found that the accuracy of our best model is dropped to 84.62% ± 0.51% (∼4% decrease) by feeding solely the R–R intervals and to 83.59% ± 0.53% (∼5% decrease) by feeding solely the R-peak amplitudes to the model. This shows that the R–R intervals are more informative and have more predictive value compared to the R-peak amplitudes for sleep apnea detection. The combination of R–R intervals and R-peak amplitudes achieves the best performance.

Many methods have been proposed recently for the detection of sleep apnea from different physiological signals. In this article, we compared our models with some relatively new methods that are based on the analysis of single-lead ECG using the same dataset as ours [32]. Table III compares the performance of our best model with state-of-the-art sleep apnea detection methods in terms of accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity. It can be observed that our reported results are superior to those reported in [1], [2], [7], [9], [13], and [23], closely match those reported in [4] and [11], and are inferior to [5]. It should be noted that unlike most studies that used only 35 recordings [1], [2], [4], [5], [7], [11], [13], [23], to achieve a more comprehensive evaluation, in this article we analyzed all the 70 recordings using a fivefold cross-validation technique. Our experiments were then repeated ten times and the results were averaged for a more reliable assessment. Moreover, unlike most studies that did not use a separate set of data to find the optimum hyperparameters of the models [2], [4], [5], [7], [9], [11], [13], [23], in this study each fold was divided into 70% training, 10% validation (to tune the hyperparameters and avoid overfitting), and 20% of data to test the performance. All the reported results in the article are based on the test data not seen during training and validation.

Obviously, if the optimum hyperparameters are chosen based on the test data, the achieved results are not generalizable [49].

The limitations of the reviewed studies are listed in the last column of Table III.

Many of the existing apnea detection algorithms are based on the analysis of several minutes of data before and after the occurrence of apnea limiting their applications in real-time detection and monitoring of apnea events. Here, we limited our analysis to the examination of 1-min segments of ECG signal to detect whether they contain an apnea event. Therefore, our algorithm can detect apnea events with a time resolution of 1 min. Future work should be directed toward the design and evaluation of machine learning and deep learning algorithms to predict (forecast) sleep apnea events in the future [54]. Here, we performed a new experiment to forecast the occurrence of sleep apnea events in the future using our best model (ZFNet-BiLSTM). Our model achieved an accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and F-score of 84.69% ± 0.34%, 77.10%, 89.45%, and 79.46% in the prediction of apnea events 1 min in future, 83.54% ± 0.31%, 78.33%, 86.81%, and 78.57% in the prediction of apnea events 2 min in future, and 80.23% ± 0.34%, 73.45%, 84.52%, and 74.18% in the prediction of apnea events 5 min in future. This shows the capability of our design algorithms in accurate detection as well as prediction of apnea events. Further research should be performed to comprehensively evaluate and compare the performance of different algorithms in the prediction of apnea events ahead of time.

Noise and motion artifacts are major problems in the analysis of physiological signals. Here, we simply filtered the ECG signals using a median filter. To further improve the reliability of apnea detection, the use of artifact rejection and correction methods is recommended where those portions of the data that are highly corrupted are excluded from the analysis [50] or corrected based on autoregressive models [51].

UNLIKE MOST RECENT PUBLICATIONS, OUR DEVELOPED MODELS WERE TRAINED AND TESTED ON THE WHOLE 70 RECORDINGS USING A FIVEFOLD CROSS VALIDATION. WITHIN EACH FOLD, 10% OF THE TRAINING DATASET WAS USED AS A VALIDATION SET TO SET THE MODELS’ HYPERMETERS WHILE REPORTING THE RESULTS ON UNSEEN TEST DATA. Our study was performed on PhysioNet Apnea-ECG Database v1.0.0. The small number of mild and moderate OSA patients and the lack of CSA episodes are the main limitations of this database that needs to be addressed in future work by collecting a larger set of data with different types of apneas.

section: VII. CONCLUSION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
output:
The advancement of smart wearables technologies has provided a unique opportunity for sleep and health monitoring. However, wearable technologies rely on accurate and real-time monitoring algorithms. In this article, we provided a comprehensive comparison between different machine learning and deep learning algorithms, in a unified framework, for the detection of sleep apnea from single-lead ECG. It was observed that deep learning models outperform conventional machine learning techniques. Among deep learning algorithms, CNN-based models performed better than DRNNs in our application where short segments of ECG (1 min) were processed. The best detection performances were obtained using hybrid CNN-DRNN architectures among which ZFNet-BiLSTM achieved the highest accuracy and specificity and ZFNet-GRU achieved the best sensitivity. Based on the achieved results, the use of hybrid deep neural networks is recommended for sleep apnea detection from ECG.

This work provides valuable information to sleep researchers on the design and selection of appropriate machine learning and deep learning algorithms for the detection of sleep apnea. The algorithms can also be extended toward the detection and monitoring of other sleep events, such as hot flashes and arousals by analyzing the physiological signals associated with these events [52], [53].

input: V. Z. Groza proposed a contactless activity monitoring system using phase-modulated continuous wave radar to recognize events. The method extracts features from radar signals to classify activities without physical sensors. Performance was evaluated using accuracy metrics on benchmark datasets, achieving results comparable to contact-based methods. Heart rate variability features, including time-domain and frequency-domain measures, were analyzed to distinguish sleep apnea events. The study compared nonlinear dynamics methods, such as permutation entropy, against traditional metrics like the cardiac sympathetic index. Machine learning classifiers, including support vector machines and deep learning architectures, were applied to the extracted radar and ECG features. The authors validated their approach against the Apnea-ECG database and other public datasets to demonstrate generalizability across subjects.

Front matter

Solar Cell Power Plant Capacity Monitoring: A Hybrid Approach Using Physics-Informed Modeling and Boosted Ensemble Machine Learning Algorithm

Emmanuel Ede Ogar, Graduate Student Member, IEEE, Watit Benjapolakul, Kenichi Kawabe, Member, IEEE, and Surachai Chaitusaney

As solar photovoltaic (PV) systems become vital to sustainable energy, accurate monitoring of solar power plant capacity is essential for maximizing energy yield and maintaining operational reliability, especially under variable environmental conditions. This paper introduces a novel hybrid framework that uniquely integrates physics-informed feature engineering with boosted ensemble learning, AdaBoostM2 for classification and LSBoost for regression, to classify and predict the operational capacity of a 5 MW solar PV plant in Thailand. Leveraging meteorological data (global radiation, ambient/module temperatures) and electrical metrics (active power, generating capacity, and plant capacity) collected at hourly intervals for 365 days, the model accurately classifies plant performance into six operational modes: Optimal, Sub-optimal, Severe sub-optimal, Critical, Emergency, and Offline, while predicting power output with robust precision. Unlike conventional physics-informed neural networks or data-driven ML, the approach embeds lightweight, interpretable physics constraints into tree-based ensembles, ensuring physical consistency, real-time scalability (<4 ms/sample inference), and causal interpretability via out-of-bag feature importance. The AdaBoostM2 classifier achieves 100% test accuracy in mode classification, while the LSBoost regressor delivers a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.0276 MW and an R-squared (R2) of 0.9975, surpassing standalone ML baselines in relative error reduction and outperforming state-of-the-art physics-informed machine learning (PIML) baselines by 88% in MAE reduction and 95% in root mean square error (RMSE) reduction. By embedding validated physical constraints into a data-driven approach, this framework enables early detection of critical inefficiencies, supporting operational uptime improvements and maintenance prioritization in tropical climates. This work advances beyond existing PIML models by offering a deployable, interpretable, high-precision tool for sustainable solar asset management.

section: I. INTRODUCTION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
The global transition to renewable energy has positioned utility-scale solar photovoltaic (PV) plants as critical infrastructure for decarbonizing power grids [1]-[4]. However, the operational efficacy of these plants remains contingent upon precise monitoring of capacity and performance under diverse environmental conditions [5], [6]. In tropical regions, where high solar irradiance is offset by dynamic factors such as elevated temperatures, humidity, and dust accumulation, traditional monitoring approaches often falter, either oversimplifying complex interactions or failing to generalize beyond controlled settings [7]-[10]. This vulnerability underscores an urgent need for advanced methodologies that can robustly assess solar plant capacity, marrying the predictive power of modern analytics with the physical realities of PV operation [11], [12].

Conventional strategies for solar plant monitoring fall into two broad categories: physics-based models and data-driven machine learning (ML) techniques. Physics-based approaches, rooted in the thermodynamic and electrical principles of PV systems, offer interpretability but struggle to accommodate the stochastic variability of real-world data, such as sudden weather shifts or degradation effects [13], [14]. Conversely, data-driven ML methods, exemplified by Random Forest or neural networks, excel at capturing non-linear patterns from large datasets yet frequently lack the physical grounding to ensure predictions align with fundamental laws, occasionally yielding implausible outcomes like efficiencies exceeding theoretical limits [15]-[17]. These limitations have spurred a growing interest in hybrid frameworks that integrate domain-specific knowledge with ML’s adaptability, aiming to enhance both accuracy and reliability [18], [19].

Recent advancements in machine learning have significantly improved the monitoring and operation of solar PV systems. Studies have explored various ML techniques, including linear regression, support vector machines (SVM), and deep learning for solar panel monitoring, fault detection, energy forecasting, and thermal analysis [20]-[22]. However, maintaining optimal performance remains challenging due to persistent degradation mechanisms such as module aging, soiling, potential-induced degradation (PID), and inverter inefficiencies [23], [24]. Traditional monitoring methods, including performance ratio (PR) calculations and regression-based benchmarks, offer limited granularity, failing to isolate specific degradation pathways or adapt to dynamic environmental conditions, like transient cloud cover, dust accumulation, or thermal cycling [25], [26]. For instance, in [27], an optimized hybrid photovoltaic-biomass system using an artificial bee colony algorithm was proposed, emphasizing panel orientation and phase-changing materials for thermal storage. Similarly, [28] developed a modular ML pipeline combining operational data and weather inputs to classify panel soiling status, achieving robustness through solar radiation metrics. Despite these advances, such models often prioritize predictive performance over interpretability, limiting actionable insights for maintenance.

Recent advances in physics-informed machine learning (PIML) aim to harmonize data-driven and physics-based paradigms by embedding domain knowledge into ML architectures [29]. However, existing PIML applications in solar energy remain narrowly focused on short-term forecasting [30] or fault detection [31], neglecting the imperative for granular capacity monitoring. This gap forces operators to rely on reactive maintenance strategies, incurring unnecessary downtime and revenue loss. section: II. BACKGROUND — A. Background on Proposed Methodology
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
output:
Traditional approaches to solar plant monitoring, ranging from empirical physics-based models to purely data-driven machine learning, often fall short in balancing predictive accuracy, physical interpretability, and adaptability. This study proposes a hybrid methodology that integrates physics-informed modeling with boosted ensemble machine learning algorithms, specifically AdaBoostM2 for multi-class classification and LSBoost for regression to address these challenges.

1) Evolution of Solar Plant Monitoring: Historically, solar plant monitoring relied on physics-based models rooted in the fundamental principles of PV operation. The single-diode model, for instance, describes the current-voltage (I-V) relationship of a solar cell as expressed in (1).

I = IL − I0 e^{q(V+IRs)/(nkT)} − V + IRs/Rsh (1)

where IL is the light-generated current, I0 is the diode saturation current, q is the electron charge, V is the voltage, Rs and Rsh are series and shunt resistances, n is the ideality factor, k is Boltzmann’s constant, and T is the cell temperature. Such models, while physically rigorous, require precise parameter estimation and struggle to capture the stochastic variability introduced by weather, dust, or degradation. Consequently, their predictive power diminishes in real-world scenarios where data deviates from idealized conditions.

The advent of machine learning (ML) offered an alternative by leveraging large datasets to model complex, non-linear relationships without explicit physical constraints. Random Forest (RF), a bagging-based ensemble method, has been widely adopted for solar power prediction, aggregating predictions from multiple decision trees as shown in (2):

f (x) = 1/T ∑_{t=1}^{T} h_t(x) (2)

where h_t(x) is the prediction of the t-th tree, and T is the number of trees. RF excels at reducing variance and handling noisy data, achieving accuracy around 90-95% in prior studies [33]. However, its lack of physical grounding can lead to implausible outputs, such as negative efficiencies or power exceeding theoretical limits, limiting its reliability for operational decision-making.

2) Boosted Ensemble Machine Learning: Boosting emerged as a superior ensemble technique by focusing on reducing bias rather than variance, iteratively refining predictions through sequential learning. AdaBoost, introduced by Freund and Schapire [34], adapts this concept for classification by minimizing an exponential loss function as in (3).

L = ∑_{i=1}^{N} ∑_{k=1}^{K} w_{i,k} e^{-y_{i,k} h_k(x_i)} (3)

where w_{i,k} are sample weights (increased for misclassified instances), y_{i,k} = 1 if class k is correct for sample i, else -1, and h_k is a weak learner (e.g., a decision tree). The final prediction is a weighted vote as shown in (4).

f (x) = arg max_k ∑_{t=1}^{T} α_t h_t(x)_k α_t = 1/2 ln((1 − ε_t)/ε_t) (4)

with ε_t as the weighted error of the t-th learner. AdaBoostM2 extends this to multi-class problems, as used in this paper to classify six operational modes leveraging its ability to focus on difficult samples.

For regression, Least Squares Boosting (LSBoost) minimizes the squared error loss using the idea in (5):

L = ∑_{i=1}^{N} (y_i − f(x_i))^2 (5)

where f(x_i) = ∑_{t=1}^{T} h_t(x_i) and each h_t fits the residuals r_{i,t} = y_i − f_{t−1}(x_i). This sequential correction enhances precision, as evidenced by prior applications in energy forecasting in [35], making LSBoost ideal for predicting continuous power output.

3) Physics-Informed Modeling: Despite the strengths of ML, its agnostic nature often overlooks the physical laws governing PV systems. Physics-informed modeling bridges this gap by embedding domain knowledge into feature engineering. Solar irradiance is modulated by the incidence angle using (6) and (7).

G_{eff} = G cos(θ) (6)

θ = cos^{-1} (sin(φ) sin(δ) + cos(φ) cos(δ) cos(ω)) (7)

where φ is latitude, δ is the declination angle, and ω is the hour angle. Equation (8) presents temperature effects on efficiency as:

η = η_{ref} [1 − β (T_m − T_{ref})] (8)

with η_{ref} as reference efficiency, β as the temperature coefficient and T_m as module temperature. These relationships, derived from first principles in [36], ensure predictions align with physical reality.

Prior hybrid approaches, such as the one in [37], demonstrate the benefit of model hybridization in power system applications by integrating a novel evolutionary algorithm with an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) to optimize network parameters for accurate load forecasting. Our work builds upon this hybrid optimization philosophy by using a boosted ensemble approach to similarly optimize the predictive capability of base models, while further incorporating Physics-informed modeling to handle the distinct multi-fidelity challenge of PV capacity monitoring.

The proposed methodology advances this paradigm by integrating a comprehensive set of physics-informed features with boosted ensemble methods. Traditional data-driven approaches, while powerful, often lack the physical grounding necessary to capture the thermodynamic and electrical constraints inherent in solar photovoltaic (PV) systems. Conversely, purely physics-based models may struggle with the complexity and variability of real-world data. To address these limitations, this study proposes a novel hybrid framework that systematically integrates physics-informed modeling with advanced Boosted ensemble machine learning algorithms—specifically AdaBoostM2 for multi-class operational mode classification and LSBoost for power output regression as described in Fig. 1.

The methodology used data collected by the Electricity Generating Authority of Thailand (EGAT) at hourly intervals from January 1st, 2019, through December 31st, 2019. The dataset includes six original features: plant capacity (MW), active power (kW), generating capacity (kWh), global radiation (W/m2), ambient and module temperatures (°C), augmented with 17 physics-informed parameters derived from solar cell physics, atmospheric optics, and thermal dynamics.

The physics-based features are computed hourly with the original data, and temporal variables like hour angle (ω = 15(h −12)) are used to capture the sun’s angular position relative to solar noon and then validated on SCADA data. Both the classifier and regressor models undergo Bayesian hyperparameter optimization to minimize cross-validated loss, ensuring robustness. Each parameter is defined below.

1) Original Features: These are directly obtained from the solar PV plant:
   r Plant Capacity (Pc): This is the maximum power output under ideal conditions, typically measured in megawatts (MW). It represents the installed capacity of the solar power plant and serves as a reference for scaling energy yield and performance metrics.
   r Active Power (Pa): This represents the real-time power output delivered by the plant. It is the actual electrical power generated. It is typically measured in kilowatts (kW).
   r Generating Capacity (Pg): This is the operational capacity available at a given time. It indicates the plant’s effective capacity, accounting for maintenance or degradation effects. It is typically measured in kWh.
   r Ambient Temperature (Ta): This is the surrounding air temperature. It is measured in (°C). It affects module temperature and efficiency, as higher temperatures reduce PV performance due to thermal losses.
   r Global Radiation (G): This is the total solar radiation reaching the panel surface. It is the primary energy input driving PV power generation. It is typically measured in (W/m2).
   r Module Temperature (Tm): This is the temperature of the solar cells. It directly impacts efficiency and power output, typically higher than ambient temperature due to solar heating. It is measured in (°C).

2) Physics-Informed Features: These are computed by integrating physical models with the original data obtained from the power plant:
   r Solar Incidence Angle (θ): This is the angle between the sun’s rays and the panel normal, critical for determining effective irradiance. Lower angles maximize energy capture. It captures solar geometry effects, critical for diurnal accuracy, enhancing the model’s ability to predict power drops during early morning or late afternoon, improving temporal resolution using (9).

Higher (AM) values reduce irradiance due to atmospheric scattering, a significant factor in humid or dusty regions. This parameter ensures predictions reflect realistic solar input reductions.

   r Dust Loss (DL): A simplified exponential model of power loss due to dust accumulation, which is magnified by longer atmospheric paths, is employed. Dust accumulation on panels, modeled as an exponential decay with (AM) using (12), is a known degradation factor in arid or tropical environments. The coefficient 0.05 is a conservative estimate based on empirical studies in [38].

   Rs = 0.1 Ω (15)

II. BACKGROUND — D. Justification for the Hybrid Methodology

This hybrid approach is justified on these grounds:

1) Physical Consistency: Purely data-driven models like standalone Random Forest model risk overfitting to noise or producing physically implausible predictions (e.g., efficiencies > 100%). Physics-informed features impose constraints (e.g., η ≤0.153), ensuring thermodynamic and electrical fidelity.

2) Enhanced Interpretability: Features like (θ), (T_L), and (P_R) link predictions to tangible physical phenomena, allowing operators to diagnose issues rather than relying on black-box outputs.

3) Robustness in Variable Conditions: Tropical climates exhibit rapid weather changes. Physics-based parameters capture these dynamics (e.g., (AM), (DL)), while boosting adapts to non-linear patterns, ensuring reliability across diverse scenarios.

4) Scalability: The framework’s modularity, combining standardized data with customizable physics models, makes it adaptable to other PV systems or regions, supporting global renewable energy goals.

The correlation matrix heatmap for physics-based solar power plant analysis in Fig. 3 reveals key relationships among the 23 features. Plant capacity shows a strong positive correlation with active power (0.93), predicted current (0.89), and energy yield (0.92), indicating that larger plant capacities are associated with higher energy production. Global radiation shows a perfect positive correlation with predicted current and strong correlations with plant capacity (0.89), active power (0.86), and energy yield (0.98), suggesting that increased sunlight significantly boosts both capacity and power output, aligning with solar power dynamics. Module temperature correlates perfectly with heat transfer coefficient and thermal capacity, and moderately with plant capacity (0.57), energy yield (0.56), global radiation (0.55), and active power (0.54), indicating temperature’s influence on solar cell efficiency up to a certain point and its linear relationship with environmental conditions.

The classifier’s performance is assessed using metrics like True Positives (TP), True Negatives (TN), False Positives (FP), and False Negatives (FN), and Feature Importance plot. Table VII presents the metrics for the regressor’s evaluation.

1) Accuracy: This is quantified as the proportion of predicted instances that are true in comparison to the overall number of instances. The formulation is given in (35).
Accuracy = TP + TN / TP + TN + FP + FN (35)

2) Precision: This is the proportion of true positives to the total of both true and false positives as seen in (36).
Precision = TP / TP + FP (36)

3) Recall: This is the proportion of true positives to the total of false negatives and true positives according to (37).
Recall = TP / TP + FN (37)

4) F1-Score: This is an illustration of the precision and recall harmonic mean. It brings equilibrium to an uneven class distribution as seen in (38).
F1 −score = 2 × Precision · Recall / Precision + Recall (38)

5) Confusion Matrix: This measures the model’s predictive accuracy, with columns indicating predicted classes and rows showing true classes. Diagonal cells represent correctly classified observations, while off-diagonal cells indicate misclassifications.

6) Feature Importance: The feature importance plot in Fig. 6(c) is computed using out-of-bag (OOB) permuted predictor importance via MATLAB’s predictor Importance function on the AdaBoostM2 classifier. For each tree, OOB samples are used to estimate prediction error before and after randomly permuting each feature’s values. The average increase in OOB errors across trees quantifies importance, offering robust, unbiased, feature interactions-aware metric that avoids test set leakage.

IV. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION — B. Comparative Analysis

1) Ablation and Sensitivity Analysis: To rigorously quantify the contribution of physics-informed features, we performed an ablation study by testing six configurations against the baseline (proposed) model. The configurations are Physics-features (OFF), Original features (OFF), Energy yield (OFF), Performance ratio (OFF), Predicted current (OFF), and Solar incidence angle (OFF). Both the AdaBoostM2 classifier and LSBoost regressor were retrained under identical hyperparameter optimization protocols (Bayesian optimization, 5-fold CV) for each configuration. The results, summarized in Table XI suggest that the removal of the 17 physics-informed features (Physics-features OFF mode) resulted in only a minimal performance degradation, with accuracy retaining 99.97% and MAE marginally increasing to 0.0285 MW. Table XI suggests that the six original measurements already encode the dominant predictive signal. Conversely, ablating the six original features (Original Features OFF configuration) led to a severe collapse in performance, with the classifier accuracy plummeting to 81.13% and the regressor MAE increasing to 0.3594 MW (+1202% error) in Fig. 8. The result demonstrates that while physics-informed features enhance model robustness and interpretability, they cannot compensate for the absence of direct physical measurements, thus the need for the hybrid method.

The sensitivity analysis, achieved by ablating individual physics-informed features in Fig. 9, reveals the robustness of this hybrid architecture. Removing key features such as energy yield, performance ratio, predicted current, and solar incidence angle resulted in classification accuracy maintaining over a 99.9% accuracy, and regression MAE remaining tightly clustered around the optimal baseline with solar incidence angle ablation yielding the lowest MAE at 0.0264 MW. This stability indicates that the predictive information provided by any single physics feature is largely encoded across the remaining feature set. The ablation and sensitivity analysis validates the proposed hybrid model and confirms that physics-informed features impose causal structure, suppress overfitting in sparse or noisy regimes, enhance diagnostic interpretability, and ensure physically consistent extrapolation.

2) PIML and ML Baseline Comparative Analysis: The results, summarized in Table XII reveal that our framework achieves superior performance across the critical dimensions of precision, scalability, and interpretability against state-of-the-art PIML and standalone ML baselines:

a) Superior Precision: The proposed model achieves a perfect classification accuracy (100%) and superior regression performance, outperforming all benchmarks in accuracy, and maintaining competitive error metrics. It notably surpasses the PINN + LSCAM framework [42] by 95% in RMSE reduction (0.0848 vs. 1.8221 MW) and the PINNs-DT model [43] by 88% in MAE (0.0276 MW vs. 0.2369 MW), while exhibiting superior R2 values. Against standalone baselines, our model demonstrates marked superiority in classification accuracy exceeding the best-performing Random Forest [32] (99.92%) and LSTM (97.79%) variants. In regression, it achieves a balanced MAE and RMSE profile, although the LSTM exhibits marginally lower MAE (0.0180 MW) and higher R2 (0.9997) on available metrics, likely due to its specialized time-series focus without physical regularization. However, such standalone models suffer from overfitting in sparse or extreme regimes, as evidenced by their inferior accuracy in multi-class mode prediction (e.g., SVM at 79.45%, 1D-CNN at 81.74%).

b) Enhanced Scalability: Our framework ensures fast inference speeds of less than 4 ms per sample, optimizing the model for seamless, real-time integration into operational SCADA environments.

c) Actionable Interpretability: Our framework shows promise for deployment. By combining the fundamental physical traceability of PIML with the quantitative Out-of-Bag (OOB) Feature importance uniqueness to the tree ensemble, it allows SCADA operators to perform immediate root-cause diagnosis by ranking physical drivers, a key diagnostic capability often absent in black-box neural PIMLs. While standalone ML excels in data-rich scenarios, PIML frameworks enhance extrapolation and causal insight, with our proposed model setting a new PIML benchmark by fusing boosting efficiency with comprehensive physics integration as observed in Fig. 10.

V. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK

This study presents a hybrid physics-informed machine learning approach for enhanced solar PV system monitoring, combining boosted ensemble techniques with domain-specific physical modeling. The proposed framework utilizes an AdaBoostM2 multi-class classifier for operational mode detection and an LSBoost regressor for precise power output estimation. The methodology was validated using operational data from a small-scale 5 MW solar PV plant in Thailand by incorporating both raw sensor measurements and derived physics-based features.

The proposed model was rigorously optimized using Bayesian hyperparameter tuning and evaluated through a 5-fold cross-validation. The AdaBoost classifier demonstrated excellent performance in identifying six operational states (Optimal to Offline), while the LSBoost regressor achieved high accuracy in power prediction as observed in Figs. 6 and 7. The classifier was evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, confusion matrix, and Feature importance generated to analyze performance across all sets. For the regressor, metrics such as RMSE, MAE, MAPE and R2 were calculated to evaluate prediction accuracy.

In real-time, this framework could drive a monitoring tool by categorizing and predicting Solar PV plant capacity. Despite the promising results demonstrated by the proposed method, the limitations warrant acknowledgment. Our model is primarily validated on a specific dataset and operational conditions from a single PV site in Thap Sakae, Thailand. This site-specific focus may limit generalizability to diverse geographies, module types, or extreme weather scenarios not captured in the training data. Future work could extend this study by incorporating real-time numerical weather prediction uncertainties for operational resilience in variable climates. Finally, real-world pilot deployments are essential to evaluate long-term performance for optimized energy management.

YAOHU LIN

ABSTRACT Stock market forecasting is a knotty challenging task due to the highly noisy, nonparametric, complex and chaotic nature of the stock price time series. With a simple eight-trigram feature engineering scheme of the inter-day candlestick patterns, we construct a novel ensemble machine learning framework for daily stock pattern prediction, combining traditional candlestick charting with the latest artiﬁcial intelligence methods. Several machine learning techniques, including deep learning methods, are applied to stock data to predict the direction of the closing price. This framework can give a suitable machine learning prediction method for each pattern based on the trained results. The investment strategy is constructed according to the ensemble machine learning techniques. Empirical results from 2000 to 2017 of China’s stock market conﬁrm that our feature engineering has effective predictive power, with a prediction accuracy of more than 60% for some trend patterns. Various measures such as big data, feature standardization, and elimination of abnormal data can effectively solve data noise. An investment strategy based on our forecasting framework excels in both individual stock and portfolio performance theoretically. However, transaction costs have a signiﬁcant impact on investment. Additional technical indicators can improve the forecast accuracy to varying degrees. Technical indicators, especially momentum indicators, can improve forecasting accuracy in most cases.

The forecasting of the stock market remains a challenging problem due to its non-linear and chaotic nature [1], [2]. Investments are guided by technical and fundamental analysis [3]; technical analysis predicts future trends from historical data [5], and investors use these techniques to build profitable strategies [6], [7]. Candlestick charting, utilizing open-high-low-close prices, reflects the balance between supply and demand and investor sentiment [8], [9]. Nti et al. revealed that 66% of reviewed prediction documents were based on technical analysis [3].

Traditional technical analysis is mostly limited to candlestick charting and statistical analysis of past data to obtain prediction probability. For example, Caginalp and Laurent performed a statistical test on eight three-day patterns, noting candlestick patterns have predictive power [10]. Lu et al. examined these patterns with three trend definitions and four holding strategies in DJIA components, finding eight three-day reversal patterns with a Caginalp–Laurent holding strategy were profitable regardless of trend definition [11]. Chen et al. defined four pairs of two-day candlestick patterns to study predictive power in the Chinese stock market, finding different capabilities [12]. Zhu et al. examined five reversal patterns in the Chinese stock market, finding bearish harami and cross signals perform well in predicting head reversals for low liquidity stocks, while bullish harami, engulfing, and piercing patterns were profitable for highly liquid, small companies [13]. Lu examined single-day candlestick charting using Taiwan stock data from 4 January 1992 to 31 December 2009, revealing four profitable patterns after transaction costs [14]. Lv et al. tested the Three Inside Up and Three Inside Down patterns using K-line series data of Shanghai 180 index component stocks over the latest 10 years [15]. Andrew et al. provided evidence that technical analysis can be improved by using automated algorithms [16]. Recently, artificial intelligence (AI) has been applied to address chaotic time series data [17], [18]. The intense computational use of intelligent predictive models has commonly been studied under the title of machine learning [19]. Machine learning uses historical data for parameter fitting to predict new data [20]. Many machine techniques have been applied to forecast the stock market, including logistic regression (LR) and Neural Network (NNs) [21], [22], deep neural networks (DNN) [23], decision trees (DTs) [24]–[26], support vector machines (SVM) [27], k-nearest neighbors (KNN) [28], random forests (RFs) [29], [30] and long short-term memory networks (LSTMs) [31], [32]. Many authors try to improve prediction ability by combining machine learning models with other methods. Ahmad et al. proposed a forecasting model based on chaotic mapping, firefly algorithm and support vector regression, performing best on mean squared error and mean absolute percent error compared to genetic algorithm-based SVR, chaotic genetic algorithm-based SVR, artificial neural networks and adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference systems [33]. Zhang et al. proposed a stock price predicting system by combining SVR and ensemble adaptive neuro fuzzy inference system (ENANFIS), showing the SVR-ENANFIS model has superior prediction performance than ENANFIS, SVR-Linear, SVR-SVR and SVR-ANN [34]. However, forecast research based on AI methods and candlestick charting is still less.

In these applications of AI methods for financial market forecasting, many studies have used technical indicators as input features. Weng et al. developed a financial expert system incorporating historical stock prices, eight technical indicators, news sentiment scores, and Google/Wikipedia trends to predict short term stock prices [35]. Kumar et al. used 15 technical indicators to construct 55 input features to predict stock index direction [36]. Gocken et al. used 44 technical indicators in hybrid soft computing models for 1, 2, 3, 5, 7 and 10 days ahead prediction [37]. Patel et al. selected 10 technical indicators to predict closing price using machine learning fusion [38]. Zhou et al. developed a learning architecture LR2GBDT for forecasting and trading stock indices by adding 12 technical indicators as initial variables [39]. Bao et al. used 10 technical indicators in a deep learning framework combining wavelet transforms, stacked autoencoders and LSTM for stock price forecasting [40]. However, existing research is limited to using these technical indicators as input parameters and lacks further discussion on them.

The forecasting of the stock market is an important objective in the financial world and remains one of the most challenging problems due to the non-linear and chaotic financial nature [1], [2]. Investments in the stock market are often guided by different prediction methods which can be divided into two groups of technical analysis and fundamental analysis [3]. The fundamental analysis approach is concerned with the company which used the economic standing of the firm, employees, yearly reports, financial status, balance sheets, income reports and so on [4]. On the other hand, technical analysis, also called charting, predicts the future by studying the trends from the historical data [5]. Investors could build profitable trading strategies by using technical analysis techniques [6], [7]. Utilizing open-high-low-close prices, candlestick charting can reflect not only the changing balance between supply and demand [8], but also the sentiment of the investors in the market [9]. Nti et al. revealed that 66% of stock market prediction documents they reviewed were based on technical analysis [3].

Traditional technical analysis is mostly limited to analyzing the candlestick charting, performing statistical analysis from past historical data to obtain the probability of prediction. For example, Caginalp and Laurent performed a statistical test including eight kinds of three-day patterns and noted that the candlestick patterns have predictive power [10]. Then Lu et al. examined these eight three-day patterns with three definitions of trend and four holding strategies in the DJIA component data, and found that regardless of which definition of the trend was used, eight three-day reversal patterns with a Caginalp–Laurent holding strategy were profitable [11]. Chen et al. gave the quantitative definitions of four pairs of two-day candlestick patterns to study their predictive power in Chinese stock market. Results showed that these two-day candlestick patterns have different predictive capabilities [12]. Zhu et al. examined the effectiveness of five different candlestick reversal patterns in Chinese stock market. Statistical analysis suggested that bearish harami, and cross signals perform well in predicting head reversals for stocks of low liquidity, while bullish harami, engulfing, and piercing patterns were profitable when applied to highly liquid, small companies' stocks [13]. Lu examined the predictive power of single-day candlestick charting by using the daily data for the Taiwan stocks for the period from 4 January 1992 to 31 December 2009. Statistical results revealed that four patterns were profitable for the Taiwan stock market after transaction costs [14]. Lv et al. testing the predictive power of the Three Inside Up pattern and Three Inside Down pattern with the testing dataset of the K-line series data of Shanghai 180 index component stocks over the latest 10 years [15]. Andrew et al. provided evidence that technical analysis can be improved by using automated algorithms [16]. Recently, artificial intelligence (AI) has been applied to address the chaotic time series data [17], [18]. The intense computational use of intelligent predictive models has commonly been studied under the title of machine learning [19]. Machine learning uses historical data for parameter fitting to predict new data [20]. Many machine techniques have already been applied to forecast the stock market. For example, logistic regression (LR) and Neural Network (NNs) [21], [22], deep neural networks (DNN) [23], decision trees (DTs) [24]–[26], support vector machines (SVM) [27], k-nearest neighbors (KNN) [28], random forests (RFs) [29], [30] and long short-term memory networks (LSTMs) [31], [32] have been used to predict the stock market. Moreover, many authors try to improve the prediction ability by combining machine learning models with other methods. Ahmad et al. proposed a forecasting model based on chaotic mapping, firefly algorithm and support vector regression to predict stock market price. Compared with genetic algorithm-based SVR, chaotic genetic algorithm-based SVR, artificial neural networks and adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference systems, the proposed model performs best on mean squared error and mean absolute percent error [33]. Zhang et al. proposed a stock price predicting system by combining SVR and ensemble adaptive neuro fuzzy inference system (ENANFIS). The experimental results showed that the SVR-ENANFIS model has superior prediction performance than ENANFIS, SVR-Linear, SVR-SVR and SVR-ANN [34]. However, forecast research based on AI methods and candlestick charting is still less.

In these applications of AI methods for financial market forecasting, many studies have used technical indicators as input features. Weng et al. developed a financial expert system that incorporated the historical stock prices, eight kinds of technical indicators, counts and sentiment scores of published news articles, trends in Google search and Wikipedia information to predict short term stock prices [35]. Kumar et al. used 15 kinds of technical indicators to construct 55 input features to predict the direction of stock indices [36]. Gocken et al. used 44 technical indicators in their hybrid soft computing models for 1, 2, 3, 5, 7 and 10 days ahead stock price prediction [37]. Patel et al. selected 10 technical indicators to predict the closing price using the fusion of machine learning techniques [38]. Zhou et al. developed a learning architecture LR2GBDT for forecasting and trading stock indices by adding 12 technical indicators as the initial variables [39]. Bao et al. used 10 technical indicators in a deep learning framework where wavelet transforms (WT), stacked autoencoders (SAEs) and LSTM are combined for stock price forecasting [40]. However, the existing research is limited to using these technical indicators as input parameters and it lacks a further discussion on these technical indicators.

When comparing different machine learning effects, Weng et al. used four machine learning methods, including boosted regression tree (BRT), NN, SVM and RF. Results showed that BRT and RF perform the best when predicting one-day ahead stock price [35]. Krauss et al. deployed a statistical arbitrage strategy based on DNN, GBDT and RF to S&P 500 constituents from December 1992 to October 2015, finding that the RF outperform GBDT and DNN in their study [41]. Patel et al. compared four prediction models, ANN, SVM, RF and naive-Bayes. Experimental results showed that the RF outperformed the other three prediction models when the evaluation was carried out on 10 years of historical data of two stocks and two stock price indices [42]. This article attempts to construct an adaptive automatic machine learning method selection framework while the prediction effects of different machine learning methods are inconsistent in different scenarios.

The main contributions of our research are as follows:
(1) This article combines traditional candlestick charting with the latest machine learning methods to enrich the research content of stock market forecasting. (2) We developed a simple eight-trigram classification following the eight-trigram scheme. We also compare different types of technical indicators in short-term stock forecasting, and further clarified the role of technical indicators in machine learning models. (3) Then an adaptive machine learning method selection framework with a novelty feature engineering scheme was proposed. Appropriate forecasting machine learning methods can be automatically selected in different candlestick charting patterns. (4) We have constructed an investment strategy based on our prediction framework. Empirical results show that this paper's strategy makes good economic returns on both individual stocks and portfolios.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 outlines the design of an ensemble prediction framework using machine learning techniques. Section 3 presents the empirical results on stock data and robustness checks. Section 4 concludes the paper.

EIGHT-TRIGRAM SCHEME
Key to our prediction framework is a simple eight-trigram scheme to represent inter-day stock price movements based on two-day candlestick patterns. The candlestick chart, also called K-line, is drawn by close, open, high, and low, where the part between the close and open is called real body. If the asset closed higher than it opened, the body is filled with red color in Chinese stock market while represented with white or green color in European and American stock markets. If the close price is lower than open price, the body is painted with green color in Chinese stock market while filled with black or red color in European and American stock markets. And then, the candlestick pattern classification is built, which is shown in FIGURE 3. Relative to yesterday’s closing price, the opening position of the day reflects the accumulation of sentiments during non-trading period. We divide the inter-day price movement into eight categories based on the relative position of today’s price range and yesterday’s K-line patterns. section: II. METHODOLOGY — C. PREDICTION MODELS
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
II. METHODOLOGY — C. PREDICTION MODELS

The inference engine is introduced in this phase. Six machine learning models—Logistic Regression (LR), Support Vector Machine (SVM), k-Nearest Neighbor (KNN), Random Forest (RF), Gradient Boosting Decision Tree (GBDT), and Long Short-term Memory (LSTM)—are used to predict the direction of the closing price.

1) LOGISTIC REGRESSION (LR)
Logistic Regression is the most basic machine learning algorithm. The model calculates linear functions and converts the result into a probability, which is then converted into a label. In the empirical stage, L2 regularization is used, with the solver set to "warn" and maximum iterations set to 100, tolerance set to 0.0001.

2) SUPPORT VECTOR MACHINE (SVM)
SVMs are supervised learning models for classification and regression. The model maps examples as points in space, dividing separate categories with a wide gap. In addition to linear classification, SVM can perform nonlinear classification using kernel techniques. Empirical results were obtained via grid search optimizing penalty coefficients, kernel coefficients, and degrees.

3) K-NEAREST NEIGHBOR (KNN)
KNN is a machine learning algorithm that classifies data points based on the majority class of their 'k' nearest neighbors. Subha (2012) used k-NN to classify stock index movement [28]. Empirical results were obtained via grid search optimizing neighbors, leaves, and weights.

4) RANDOM FOREST (RF)
Random forests are a combination of tree predictors, where each tree depends on a random vector sampled independently from all trees in the forest [47]. Empirical results were obtained via grid search optimizing leaves, depth, and the number of estimators.

5) GRADIENT BOOSTING DECISION TREE (GBDT)
GBDT is a popular machine learning algorithm. The core idea is that subsequent models predict the difference between the predicted value and the true value of the previous model [48]. Empirical results were obtained via grid search optimizing features, depth, and the number of estimators.

6) LONG SHORT-TERM MEMORY (LSTM)
LSTM is a recurrent neural network (RNN) architecture [49]. The network uses three gates—input, output, and forget—to control interactions between memory cells. The model was constructed using Keras with a three-layer structure (two processing layers and one output dense layer). Dropout regularization (0.2) was applied within the recurrent layer, and early stopping was used to reduce overfitting. The first layer has 64 hidden neurons with 17,920 parameters; the second layer has 64 hidden neurons with 33,024 parameters. The output layer uses a sigmoid activation function, yielding 65 parameters.
output:
The inference engine is introduced in this phase. Six machine learning models including Logistic Regression (LR), Support Vector Machine (SVM), k-Nearest Neighbor (KNN), Random Forest (RF), Gradient Boosting Decision Tree (GBDT) and Long Short-term Memory (LSTM) are used to predict the direction of the closing price. The parameters used in these prediction models are shown as Table 2.

1) LOGISTIC REGRESSION (LR)
Logistic Regression is the most basic machine learning algorithm. The Logistic Regression model returns an equation that determines the relationship between the independent variables and the dependent variable. First, the model calculates linear functions and then converts the result into a probability. Finally, it converts the probability into a label.

In the empirical stage, we use L2 as a regularized parameter, specifying warn as the solver parameter which determines our optimization method for the logistic regression loss function. In terms of the termination parameters of the algorithm, the maximum number of iterations which is taken for the solvers to converge to 100 and tolerance for stopping criteria parameter is set to 0.0001.

2) SUPPORT VECTOR MACHINE (SVM)
In machine learning, support vector machines (SVMs) are supervised learning models with associated learning algorithms that analyze data for classification and regression analysis. The SVM training algorithm builds a model when given a set of training examples and assigns the new example to one category or another. The SVM model is to map the example as a point map in space, so that the examples of the separate categories are divided by a clear gap that is as wide as possible. Lee gave a detailed formula for the SVM’s two-class problem in his 2009 article [27].

In addition to performing linear classification, SVM can effectively perform nonlinear classification using so-called kernel techniques, implicitly mapping its inputs to high-dimensional feature spaces. There are some studies using the SVM to predict the financial data [45], [46].

In the empirical stage, we get the best performance from a grid search algorithm which sets different penalty coefficients, coefficients of kernel function and degrees. Different parameter combinations produce different clustering effects.

3) K-NEARESTNEIGHBOR (KNN)
K nearest neighbors (KNN) is another machine learning algorithm. The k-NN algorithm looks for ‘k’ nearest records within the training dataset and uses the majority of the classes of the identified neighbors for classifying. Subha (2012) used k-NN to classify the stock index movement [28]. In the empirical stage, we get the best performance from a grid search algorithm which sets different neighbors, leaves and weights. Different parameter combinations produce different clustering effects.

4) RANDOM FOREST (RF)
Random forests are a combination of tree predictors. Each tree depends on the values of a random vector sampled independently with the same distribution for all trees in the forest. Random forests (RFs) are a nonparametric and nonlinear classification and regression algorithm [47]. Random forests not only use a subset of the training set, but also selects only a subset of the feature set when the tree is established in the decision tree. Booth (2014) used RFs to construct a n automated trading mechanism [29].

In the empirical stage, different parameter combinations may produce different classification effects. We get the best performance from a grid search algorithm which sets different leaves, depth and estimators.

5) GRADIENT BOOSTING DECISION TREE (GBDT)
Gradient Boosting Decision Tree (GBDT) is a popular machine learning algorithm. Friedman (2002) gave a detailed expression of the gradient descent in his research [48]. The core idea of GBDT is that the subsequent model of the sequence no longer directly predicts the predicted value of the data set, but predicts the difference between the predicted value and the true value of the previous model.

In the empirical stage, different parameter combinations may produce different classification effects. We get the best performance from a grid search algorithm which sets different features, depth and estimators.

6) LONG SHORT-TERM MEMORY (LSTM)
Long-short term memory is one of the recurrent neural network (RNNs) architecture [49]. Hochreiter and Schmidhuber proposed a solution by using memory cells [50] which consists of three components, including input gate, output gate and forget gate. The gates control the interactions between neighboring memory cells and the memory cell itself. The input gate controls the input state while the output gate controls the output state which is the input of other memory cells. The forget gate can choose to remember or forget its previous state.

The LSTM network used Keras, an open-source neural-network library written in Python. First, we construct a three-layer LSTM network, including two main processing layers and one output layer (dense layer). In the prediction model, we apply dropout regularization within the recurrent layer. Hereby, a fraction of the input units are randomly dropped at each update during training time to reduce the risk of overfitting and it gets better generalization. And the early stopping mechanism is also used to reduce the risk of overfitting.

In the empirical stage, the hidden neurons are set to 64 and dropout to 0.2 in the first layer and set the hidden neurons to 64 in the second layer. At the output layer, we use the sigmoid activation function to generate the classification results. This configuration yields 17,920 parameters for the first layer, 33,024 parameters for the second layer and 65 parameters for the output layer.

instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: We evaluate six machine learning models forecasting stock direction using Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1 score. Accuracy is calculated as (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN). Precision is TP / (TP + FP), and Recall is TP / (TP + FN). The F1 score is the harmonic mean of Precision and Recall, calculated as 2 * Precision * Recall / (Precision + Recall).
output:
The inference engine is introduced in this phase. We use six machine learning models to forecast the stock direction of up and down. To evaluate the performance of the prediction models, two commonly used evaluation criteria are used in this study: Accuracy, and F1 score. Accuracy is used to evaluate the overall classification ability of the model. The formula is as follows:

Accuracy = (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN)

TP (True Positives) representing model prediction is true, and the real sample is also true; TN (True Negatives) representing model prediction is false, and the real sample is also false; FP (False Positives) representing model prediction is true while the real sample is false; FN (False Negatives) representing model prediction is false while the real sample is true.

Precision is used to estimate the accuracy of positive samples in the prediction data and recall is used to evaluate the coverage of positive samples in the prediction data of the model. The formula is shown as (4) and (5).

Precision = TP / (TP + FP) (4)
Recall = TP / (TP + FN) (5)

F1 is an indicator used in statistics to measure the accuracy of a binary model, which also considers the accuracy and recalls of the classification model. The formula is as follows:

F1 = 2 * Precision * Recall / (Precision + Recall) (6)

And then, the evaluation progress tries to evaluate the results of the machine learning prediction model. In this study, our evaluation model not only considers the Accuracy index, but also considers the Precision and Recall indicators.

section: II. METHODOLOGY — E. INVESTMENT STRATEGY
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: The investment strategy is built on the evaluation model. Two market conditions are tested: long-only and long-short. Trades execute at the closing price of time $t$ and settle at the closing price of $t+1$. If shorting is permitted, the strategy checks the K-line pattern at time $t$, uses a matching machine learning method to predict the direction of $t+1$, and records the $t+1$ profit or loss based on prediction accuracy. This process repeats for subsequent periods. If shorting is forbidden, the strategy only executes long positions when the forecast predicts a rise. Profits and losses are recorded for $t+1$ and compounded over subsequent periods $t+2$, etc.

The investment strategy is constructed based on the above evaluation model. This paper considers two situations, including only long and long-short, and builds the corresponding investment strategy. This article assumes that we will invest at the closing price at time t and will be clear at the closing price at time t + 1. The flowchart of the investment strategy is shown as FIGURE 5. If the current stock trading market mechanism allows shorting, that means you can go long and short at the same time. The specific construction steps of the investment strategy are as follows: First, the specific K-line pattern of the current stock is checked at time t. Next, a matching machine learning method is selected to predict the rise or fall of t + 1 based on the above evaluation model. If the predicted result is consistent with the real result, the t + 1 profit would be recorded. If the prediction is wrong, the negative profit of t + 1 would be recorded as loss value. Finally, the above steps will be repeated to calculate t + 1, t + 2, etc.

If the current stock trading market mechanism does not allow shorting, that is to say, you can only go long. The specific construction steps of the investment strategy are as follows: First, the specific K-line mode of the current stock is checked at time t. Then, a matching machine learning method is selected to predict the rise or fall of t + 1 based on the above evaluation model. We only operate the investment when the forecasting result is up. If the predicted result is consistent with the real result, we record the t + 1 profit. Otherwise, we record the negative profit of t + 1 as loss value. Finally, the above steps will be repeated to calculate t + 1, t + 2, etc.

output:
III. EMPIRICAL RESULTS — B. MODEL COMPARISON AND EVALUATION

To clarify the role of technical indicators in machine learning models, the 21 technical indicators are divided into four groups, including Overlap indicators, Momentum indicators, Volume indicators and Volatility indicators. And then each pattern containing feature engineering information is put into the ensemble machine learning prediction framework that contains six machine-learning models for training. 80% of the data as training data and the remaining 20% as test data were set to verify the predictive validity of the model.

First of all, we train the machine learning models without indicators. 13 patterns and 6 machine learning models resulting in a total of 78 predictions shows the effectiveness of feature engineering, which is shown in the Fig. a. of FIGURE 6. The abscissa represents the 13 kinds of one-day candlestick patterns and the ordinate represents the F1 score. 49 of the 78 prediction models exceeded the random walk probability. Pattern 0 and pattern 1, which indicate that the maximum price limit has been reached, show strong long-short signals. In this case, pattern 4 and pattern 5 show significant prediction effects, and the F1 score value can reach about 0.57.

In all prediction models, SVM, RF and GBDT showed good predictions for all patterns, while LR, KNN and LSTM only performed well in individual patterns.

Fig. c. of FIGURE 6 shows the prediction results of the introduction of the Overlap indicators which contain 6 indicators of MA, DEMA, EMA, KAMA, SMA and SAR. 60 of the 78 predictions exceeded the random walk probability. And after the introduction of this indicator group, the predicted maximum F1 score of each pattern are all improved slightly. Among them, pattern 1, which indicates a board daily limit, shows a strong long signal, the F1 score is more than 0.80. This Overlap indicator group has a significant effect on the improvement of the predictive ability of the SVM model, and the predictive ability of the LR model has also been improved to a certain extent.

Fig. d. of FIGURE 6 shows the forecast results of the introduction of the Momentum indicators which contain 9 indicators of ADX, APO, BOP, CCI, DX, MACD, MFI, MOM and RSI. 73 of the 78 predictions exceeded the probability of random walk. And after the introduction of this indicator, the predicted maximum F1 score of each pattern are all improved. Among them, the F1 score of pattern 0 and pattern 1 exceeds 0.80. The prediction effect of most prediction patterns has been improved after the introduction of these indicators, reflecting the obvious momentum characteristics in short-term prediction. The prediction ability of RF has been significantly improved, and the prediction effects of pattern 4 and pattern 5 have been significantly improved which reach about 0.62.

Fig. e. of FIGURE 6 shows the predicted results of the introduction of the Volume indicators which contain 3 indicators of AD, ADOSC and OBV. 57 of the 78 predictions exceeded the random walk probability. And after the introduction of this indicator, the predicted maximum F1 score of each pattern are slightly improved. Among them, only pattern 4 and pattern 5 show good prediction effects, with a F1 score about 0.62. RF and GBDT perform well in all prediction modes. From this we can find that the characteristic project has already included the information of short-term volume change, and the introduction of more volume characteristics cannot significantly improve the forecast level.

Fig. f. of FIGURE 6 shows the results of the introduction of the Volatility indicators which contain 3 indicators of ATR, NATR and TRANGE. 63 of the 78 predictions also exceeded the random walk probability. And after the introduction of the indicator, the highest prediction F1 score of each pattern are all improved, and different prediction models have a clear distinction between different pattern prediction effects. After the introduction of this indicator, all the patterns have been improved slightly. The overall prediction results reflect the obvious volatility characteristics in the short term.

In order to test whether more technical indicators can improve the forecast level, we introduce all the technical indicators into our forecasting framework. Fig. b. of FIGURE 6 shows the results of the introduction of all indicators which including 21 indicators. 69 of the 78 predictions exceeded the random walk probability. And after the introduction all indicators, the predicted maximum F1 score of each mode are improved. Among them, pattern 0 and pattern 1, that is, a board daily limit shows a strong signal, the F1 score is more than 0.80. Pattern 4 and pattern 5 still show good prediction results, F1 score is more than 0.62. These indicators have a significant effect on the prediction ability of the LR model, which means that more parameters can improve the linear fitting effect and verify that the stock market has complex nonlinear characteristics.

From the above results, we can see that RF and GBDT have good predictive ability in most cases in short-term prediction. KNN only showed relatively good predictive power in the first six patterns. Although SVM will take too long time to process big data, the prediction level is still significant in some cases. The advantage of the deep learning model LSTM in this scenario is not fully reflected. In addition, we can see that the increase in the number of parameters can increase the level of linear prediction, which also reflects the complexity and diversity of financial markets from another perspective.

In most cases, an increase in the number of indicators can increase the level of prediction. However, in the short-term forecast, in the prediction of some models, using a smaller number of momentum indicators and volatility indicators can achieve satisfactory results.
