section: IV. CONCLUSION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
This paper develops an ensemble machine learning model that automatically selects prediction methods for daily k-line patterns. Empirical results show the framework has predictive power, and the investment strategy based on the model generates superior returns.

This study contributes in four aspects. First, it combines traditional candlestick charting with latest AI methods to enrich stock market forecasting research. Analyzing all 13 one-day candlestick patterns under various machine learning methods, the study concludes that pattern 4 and pattern 5 have apparent predictive effects. Second, a feature engineering approach is introduced. It develops an eight-trigram classification of two-day k-line patterns, alongside the 13 daily patterns and volume change features. Four sets of technical indicators—overlap, momentum, volume, and volatility—are introduced as auxiliary variables. Empirical testing finds momentum indicators are significantly better than others for short-term forecasting, though additional indicators generally improve results, a smaller set of momentum or volatility indicators can be satisfactory for some patterns. Third, a framework is proposed for assembling multiple machine prediction models to select the optimal method for different feature modes. The ensemble includes six models (RF, GBDT, LR, KNN, SVM, LSTM) with optimized parameters. Results show RF and GBDT have good predictive ability for short-term prediction in most cases; LR needs feature improvements; KNN and SVM fit only some patterns; and LSTM’s advantage is not fully reflected here. Finally, based on prediction results, an investment strategy is constructed. Empirical results show the strategy generates good economic returns on individual stocks and portfolios theoretically. The predicted maximum drawdown, Sharpe Ratio, and Sortino Ratio are better than buy-and-hold, though transaction costs significantly impact actual returns. The framework has predictive power, though profiting from certain patterns is difficult due to Chinese market stop-trading rules. SVM is deemed unsuitable for large-scale stock data. Future work aims to incorporate more suitable methods, such as reinforcement learning, and additional predictive factors like news events and market sentiment.

input: Phishing is a worldwide cybercrime that tricks users into downloading malware or revealing sensitive information via disguised websites. As AI advances, researchers increasingly use machine learning and deep learning to classify phishing sites. Experiments in this study compare various methods, showing that ensemble machine learning algorithms outperform others in both detection accuracy and computational cost. These architectures also maintain strong performance when feature counts drop significantly. This makes ensemble methods particularly suitable for binary phishing classification in training and real-time detection settings.

performances of various machine learning and deep learning methods, several experiments are conducted in
this study. According to the experimental results, ensemble machine learning algorithms stand out among
other candidates in both detection accuracy and computational consumption. Furthermore, the ensemble
architectures still provide impressive capability when the amount of features decreases sharply in the dataset.
Subsequently, the paper discusses the factors why ensemble machine learning methods are more suitable for
the binary phishing classiﬁcation challenge in up-date training and real-time detecting environment, which
reﬂects the sufﬁciency of ensemble machine learning methods in anti-phishing techniques.

section: I. INTRODUCTION — Y. Wei, Y. Sekiya: Sufficiency of Ensemble Machine Learning Methods for Phishing Websites Detection
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: This study evaluates traditional machine learning (ML) algorithms for phishing URL detection, contrasting their performance against deep learning (DL) methods. We implemented and compared a 3-layer fully connected neural network (FCNN), a long short-term memory (LSTM) model, and a convolutional neural network (CNN) on a published dataset. Empirical results show that conventional ML methods achieve higher accuracy and lower false-positive rates than DL techniques, which are limited by computational constraints and time complexity. Based on these findings, this paper provides suggestions for phishing feature selection and discusses the sufficiency of ML-based approaches for detecting phishing websites.
output:
A typical AI-based phishing detection procedure is shown in FIGURE 1, in which AI techniques can learn and extract features to classify phishing attacks effectively and efficiently. Existing phishing detection methods usually choose ML or DL to detect unknown attacks. Due to its ability to automatically extract features, DL has recently been seen as a promising phishing detection tool [4]. However, our research found that based on some generally recognized phishing websites features [5], conventional ML methods achieve higher accuracy and lower false-positive rate. Besides, DL techniques always suffer from deficiencies in computational constraints and time complexity. This study is intended to indicate the sufficiency of traditional ML algorithms for phishing URLs detection.

In summary, this paper makes the following contributions:
• We evaluated multiple ML algorithms for phishing detection empirically and contrasted their performances.
• We implemented and evaluated a 3-layer fully connected neural network (FCNN) model, an LSTM model, and a CNN model on a dataset.
• We analyzed the performances of ML-based methods and DL-based methods. Moreover, we discussed the sufficiency of ML-based methods for phishing detection and provided suggestions for the phishing feature selection approach.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows: Section II presents the previous research employing, respectively, ML and DL. Section III introduces and compares three published datasets and features. Section IV provides the detection results by utilizing conventional ML algorithms. In section V, we build several DL models and compare the results with ML. Finally, Section VI discusses ML methods’ sufficiency for phishing detection and proposes future works in phishing detection field.

ML-based phishing detection primarily uses supervised learning, extracting features from URLs, hyperlinks, webpage content, and hybrids [10]–[17]. Performance depends on dataset quality, feature characteristics, and algorithm selection [18].

A URL-feature engine by Butnaru et al. [13] outperformed Google Safe Browsing and maintained accuracy against phishing URLs after one year, though authors noted robustness concerns against adversarial attacks [13]. Jain and Gupta [14] proposed six new hyperlink features that reduced processing time and worked across languages, but the method fails if attackers alter source code references. K. L. Chiew et al. [19] introduced a Hybrid Ensemble Feature Selection (HEFS) framework using a Cumulative Distribution Function gradient method to optimize feature subsets, integrating with Random Forest to improve detection accuracy.
output:
There are supervised, semi-supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement methods in Machine Learning, the most popular one used to detect phishing acts is the supervised method, where machines try to make intelligent decisions by learning certain features of phishing and legitimate sample dataset [10]. These kinds of solutions always extract features like URLs [11], [12], [13], hyperlinks information [14], webpage content [15], [16], hybrid features [17], and other resources. The performance of these methods typically depends on the quality of the dataset, the characteristics, and the algorithm employed in the approach [18]. The following are typical ML algorithms used in phishing detection methods: Support Vector Machine, Classification and Regression Tree, Random Forest, AdaBoost, Light Gradient Boosting Machine...etc.

A phishing detection engine using the features extracted from URLs was proposed by A. Butnaru et al. [13]. They also assessed how well phishing detection performed over time without model training. As a result, their solution works better than Google Safe Browsing (GSB), which is the default security tool in most popular web browsers. It is worth mentioning that the model performs well against phishing URLs even after one year. Although the methodology achieves good performance, the authors are concerned about the robustness against adversarial attacks, which are frequently exploited by malevolent entities even when the system produces good performance.

Jain and Gupta [14] presented a novel method that analyzes hyperlinks included in the HTML source code of websites to identify phishing assaults. In their feature selection process, six new features were proposed to increase the detecting performance, which is also the key contribution in this work because both processing time and response time were thus reduced. Moreover, their approach is language-independent to detect any textual language webpage. However, the approach has certain restrictions because it is totally dependent on the website’s source code. If the attackers change all the page resource references, their method will make a false prediction.

section: II. LITERATURE REVIEW — B. DL-BASED PHISHING DETECTION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
output:
It is precisely because of its capability to find hidden information in complicated datasets, DL has recently emerged as a viable substitute for traditional ML techniques. In order to enhance the effectiveness of phishing detection solutions, various DL-based approaches have been applied. Popular DL algorithms used in phishing detection include Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) [21], [22], Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) [23], Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) [24], [25], Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) [26], [27], and hybrid [28]...etc.

Yerima and Alzaylaee [25] presented a DL-based approach with high detecting accuracy, where CNN is utilized to distinguish legitimate websites from phishing websites. A 1D-CNN model with two convolutional layers, two max-pooling layers, and one fully connected layer was constructed in their method. The model surpassed several popular machine learning classifiers, according to testing on a benchmarked dataset of 4,898 examples from phishing websites and 6,157 instances from reliable websites. However, to fine-tune the important impacting parameters (i.e. number of filters, filter lengths, and the number of fully connected units), they conducted a series of experiments. This time-consuming and labor-intensive procedure is frequently observed in DL-based methods [29], [30].

Li et al. [23] proposed an LSTM-based phishing detection method for big email data which consists of two important stages: sample expansion stage and testing stage. To suit the needs of in-depth learning, sufficient training samples should be provided, they merged KNN with K-Means in the sample expansion stage. Prior to testing, they preprocessed the data by generalizing, word segmenting, and creating word vectors. The LSTM model was then trained using the preprocessed data. Finally, they categorized phishing emails. The accuracy rate of their proposed phishing email detection method can approach 95%, according to experimental results. In their research, to make the detection system more efficient, they labeled a small amount of data manually. Based on this small dataset, they used KNN and K-Means to expand it into the final samples. It is commonly known that DL can manage large amounts of data and when the size of the dataset increases, DL performs better. However, it is difficult for researchers to find abundant and appropriate datasets to work with. At the same time, using a single processor to train DL models on such a significant dataset is also a challenge.

In a recent comprehensive DL-based review in the phishing detection field [4], Do et al. indicated that each DL algorithm has unique properties that make it ideal for a specific application. For example, RNN is more appropriate for processing sequential data such as natural language and text. When analyzing two-dimensional data, such as images and videos, CNN produces better results. In addition, the main drawback is that supervised DL requires a massive amount of labeled instances, which adds a high level of computational complexity to the detection system [31]. Additionally, DL models are unable to justify the inference they draw. It would be tough to comprehend the relationship between input attributes and output decisions [32].

input: Deep Learning is the state-of-the-art for various problems due to its ability to handle big data and automatic feature generation. However, prevalent issues include model architecture design, manual parameter tuning, high training time costs, computational complexity, and deficient accuracy. Ensemble ML techniques, represented by Random Forest, are regarded as a crystallization of wisdom from various ML methods. By combining different models, the risk of selecting an improper decision is reduced, improving forecast performance. In experiments, CART, Random Forest, and Boosting methods obtained better performance in phishing classification. This is potentially due to these ensemble methods benefiting from the dynamic changing of assigned weight to each instance during iteration, making them more robust and stable than traditional ML algorithms. For instance, AdaBoost’s basic principle is to concentrate on cases previously incorrectly classified when training a new inducer [40]. In the initial iteration, each instance is given the same weight; subsequently, the weights of incorrectly categorized instances increase and those of correctly identified examples decrease. Additionally, based on their total prediction performances, individual basic learners are given voting weights. Hence, ensemble ML methods decrease both bias and variance of variable techniques while increasing the variance for stable classifiers, making them more suitable for classification tasks.

ABSTRACT One of the critical aspects in the mining sector is energy, being of great importance for the
operation since if it were to stop, one of the consequences would be the loss of large amounts of money. The
research objective is to predict the State of Charge of Batteries of equipment powered by photovoltaic solar
panels in the mining sector based on automatic supervised learning techniques. A monitoring system records
each energy variable programmed in the photovoltaic system, for which an analysis of the data extracted
from the monitoring system was carried out. The data were evaluated using automatic supervised learning
techniques using the RapidMiner tool, whose prediction average was 90.12%. The technique of automatic
supervised learning of artiﬁcial neural networks was chosen to predict the state of charge of batteries for
photovoltaic systems. A software tool was built with the neural network. The analysis and discussion of the
results of the training of the model were carried out, the contribution of this research being to determine the
prediction of the state of charge of batteries in photovoltaic systems in the mining sector using techniques
of supervised machine learning which was the neural network. Finally, with the model correctly trained,
validation was carried out that allowed comparing the predictive data with the data in real-time, obtaining a

section: I. INTRODUCTION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: The energy sector is vital for daily life, yet many regions lack reliable access. Photovoltaic (PV) systems are a viable technical and financial solution for meeting energy needs. These systems convert solar radiation into electricity via interconnected cells, panels, and modules, often incorporating batteries for energy storage. Accur estimating the state of charge (SOC) of these batteries is critical for battery energy storage systems. This research proposes a novelty in the field: using supervised machine learning techniques to evaluate battery SOC specifically within PV systems in the mining sector.
output:
The energy sector is essential for human beings in such a way that its absence would cause inconveniences such as the performance of different activities in daily life. However, they do not have this service in several parts of the world. Today one of the most viable solutions, technically and financially, to meet energy use needs is designated to those generated by photovoltaic (PV) energy systems.

Photovoltaic energies are technologies that, over time, have decreased maintenance costs, creating emissions that are harmful to the environment with great ease and linking to existing energy sources at the installation site. [1]

The associate editor coordinating the review of this manuscript and approving it for publication was B. Chitti Babu.

The interconnection of several photovoltaic cells is called a photovoltaic panel, which transforms solar radiation into electrical energy. A group of panels gives rise to a module, which, together with the batteries that reserve the electrical energy, the inverter, the switch, and the cables, make up the photovoltaic system.

Solar batteries store the electrical energy generated by photovoltaic solar panels so that they can be used at night and even on cloudy days; however, it is essential to accurately estimate the charge state in the batteries (SOC).

SOC estimation is a crucial link for the development of battery energy storage systems; in recently reviewed studies, no works like what is being proposed have been found, so the novelty of the proposal in this research is to use supervised machine learning techniques to evaluate the state of charge of batteries in PV systems in the mining sector.

Machine Learning is one of the fastest growing areas of computing, with wide-ranging applications. It refers to the automated detection of significant patterns in data. Machine Learning tools are concerned with providing programs with the ability to learn and adapt [2]. The more data is supplied to a machine learning framework, the more it can be trained, and the consequences of the higher value of insights will be considered. Machine Learning is intelligent to discover and show the hidden patterns in the data [3].

Shanthamallu et al. [4] indicate that supervised learning techniques focus on using a labeled combination of data to train an algorithm that serves the purpose of the best function to describe the selection of input data. The supervised learning technique can be used to predict different aspects of human activity, such as sentiment analysis [5], classification for bone health [6], and in different emerging technologies [7], as well as in the monitoring of photovoltaic panels [8].

According to Rahimi-Eichi et al. [9], SoC estimation technology is essential for developing lithium-ion battery energy storage systems. An accurate SoC is the main element for the safe operation of battery packs. It is also a baseline for cell EQ control. The role of a cell balancer is to keep all cells equalized during charging and discharging to maximize pack capacity and protect cells from overcharging or discharging. It can cause permanent damage when a cell is overcharged or over-discharged. Therefore, improving the accuracy of the estimated SoC makes a difference in mitigating cell damage, prolonging the life cycle, and lowering the cost of maintenance [10].

This research will be focused on developing the prediction of the state of charge of batteries for photovoltaic systems using Supervised machine learning techniques and integrating it into a web computer module. The data collection of the energy variables for the equipment that provides radio coverage in the mine can be handy to estimate the prediction of the state of charge of the batteries using Supervised machine learning techniques having the voltage as input data of the batteries, temperature of the batteries, current consumption, current charge, and current panels.

According to Rodríguez [11], a Photovoltaic system is a set of equipment that uses solar energy for power generation and consists of the following components: a) Photovoltaic Panel, Formed by solar cells, which generally receive the sun’s rays and which uses the photoelectric effect, the direct conversion of energy from the sun to continuous electrical energy is obtained b) Batteries, They operate as storers of the generated energy, which is distributed to their loads when the generation is low or when it does not exist in this case would be the absence of the sun. c) Regulator, an electronic device that works with the batteries to control their state of charge and ensure an optimal filling of energy. d) Inverter, this device allows the conversion of Direct Current (DC) into Alternating Current (AC), allowing loads that work with AC to work without any problem.

Gyu Gwang Kim et al. [12] presented a method to detect faults in a photovoltaic system based on the power ratio (PR), the voltage ratio (VR), and the current ratio (IR). Each ratio’s lower control limit (LCL) and upper control limit (UCL) were defined using data from a test site system under normal operating conditions.

Cook, Luo, and Weng [13] studied the constant resource-intensive re-evaluation of active residential PV locations, so they proposed to model solar sensing in a machine learning setup based on labeled data with supervised learning.

Karimi et al. [14] analyzed the photovoltaic cells from 5,400 cell images. From the data set, two unique degradation categories, “cracked” and “corroded,” were observed, while cells that were not degraded were classified as “good.” Cell images were classified into these three classes for supervised machine learning modeling, yielding 3,550 images. Using stratified sampling, a training and testing frame with a sampling ratio of 80:20 was generated. Three machine learning algorithms: support vector machine, random forest, and convolutional neural network.

Spyros Theocharides George et al. [15] evaluated the performance of different machine learning models to predict the power output of photovoltaic systems. Specifically, a variety of methods were explored, including artificial neural networks (ANNs), support vector regression (SVR), and regression trees (RT), with varied hyperparameters and features. Each model’s power output prediction performance was tested on real PV production datasets acquired over one year and compared to an existing persistence model (PM).

Ümit Agbulut et al. [16] designed and fabricated four layers of different sizes for a lumped PV system. The power outputs measured in the study were predicted with four machine learning algorithms, namely support vector machine, artificial neural network, kernel, nearest neighbor, and deep learning. To assess the success of these machine learning algorithms, coefficient of determination (R2), root mean square error (RMSE), mean bias error (MBE), t-statistics (t-stat), and mean absolute bias error (MABE) have been discussed in the document.

Kabilan R. et al. [17] presented a power prediction of a building-integrated photovoltaic system concerning various building orientations based on machine learning data science tools. The results showed that the application of linear regression coefficients to the forecast results of the developed PV power generation neural network improved the PV power generation forecast result. Jidong Wang et al. [18] used the Gradient Boost Decision Tree to make the prediction.

Dimd et al. [19] reviewed machine learning-based PV power output forecast models in the literature in the context of the Nordic climate. Ordoñez-Palacios et al. [20] predicted solar radiation in photovoltaic systems using Machine Learning techniques. Chen et al. [21] applied a random forest ensemble learning algorithm to detect and diagnose Photovoltaic array faults. Antunes Campos et al. [22] developed a machine learning application for temperature forecasting solar photovoltaic modules.

Kamarov and Susvoc [23] describe Autonomous Photovoltaic Systems with great applicability at different scales, from small photovoltaic systems that power lamps to networks capable of supplying electricity to entire populations. They usually have an energy storage system that allows them to function when there is no solar resource, at which time there is usually a greater demand for energy [24].

Ma, Hu, and Cheng [25] investigated a new data-driven method that can estimate SOC and SOE simultaneously based on a deep short-term memory (LSTM) neural network. The proposed algorithm is validated with two dynamic, driven cycles under various working conditions, such as different temperatures, different battery materials, and noise interference. Furthermore, the performance of the proposed method is compared with other popular algorithms, including support vector regression (SVR), random forest (RF), and simple recurrent neural network (Simple RNN). The results show that the proposed method obtains greater precision and robustness.

Tian et al. [26] indicate that recent development in deep learning provided an emerging solution for SOC estimation and proposed incorporating two types of domain knowledge in deep learning-based methods. First, the voltage and current sequences are decoupled into open circuit voltage (OCV), ohmic response, and bias voltage to augment the input of deep neural networks (DNN). Second, since conventional DNNs ignore the time dependency in SOC estimation results, they proposed a combination framework to adaptively merge DNN SOC estimation results from the DNN and short-term Ampere-hour predictions. The results show that the proposed method can drastically reduce the mean square error of the SOC estimate and the maximum absolute error.

In another work by Tian et al. [27], they propose a flexible method that uses only short chunks of load data to estimate maximum and remaining capacities to address state-of-health and state-of-charge estimation problems simultaneously. The proposed method is based on a convolutional neural network that only requires short-term load data to estimate two states. The results offer a flexible and easy-to-implement approach to accurate multi-state estimation over battery life.

The main objective is to correctly monitor the charge of batteries in solar-powered mining equipment. A grid-connected photovoltaic system (GCPS) uses a photovoltaic generator and a conventional power grid as a backup. The system includes a solar panel, battery bank, and regulator to control charging intensity and extend battery life. While Lead Acid batteries are most common due to cost, Nickel-Cadmium batteries are used in professional applications where cost is not decisive.

Mobile repeaters provide coverage for fixed and fleet equipment in open-pit mine areas, powered by solar energy accumulated in batteries. Repeaters became de-energized, causing communication failures in equipment across pit areas. The solution required field personnel to manually recharge batteries, but the process took hours, halting mine operations during recharge.

III. METHODOLOGY — C. DATA PREPARATION

1) DATA SELECTION
The analysis focused on Voltage, Current, and Consumption fields to predict battery State of Charge (SoC). An additional SoC field was added using the formula: SoC(t) = SOC0 + (1/C) * ∫ I(t) dt, validated by a Field Engineer [Ref 1].

2) DATA CLEANING
Fields (Voltage, Current, Consumption, SoC) were converted from General to Numeric data types. Erroneous symbols and blank spaces were removed.

3) MODELING
The dataset contains 19,062 records with four attributes (Voltage, Current, Consumption, SoC). Given the numerical nature of the data, regression was selected. Supervised machine learning techniques compared include Decision Tree, Random Forest, Gradient Boosted, Neural Network, and Support Vector Machine, using RapidMiner Software [Ref 2].

In this phase, the final database that will feed the modeling tool will be built; the Spreadsheet was migrated to a Comma Delimited CSV File.

1) DATA SELECTION
Through the data section, it was possible to highlight those fields that would contribute any value to the analysis of the State of Charge of the Batteries, which were Voltage, Consumption, and Current; thus, omitting the other fields exported from the Victron Energy System. However, it was considered to add one more field whose name would be SoC, to which we would add a formula to find the state of charge, refer to (1). This formula was applied through the values of the Voltage, Consumption, and Current fields mentioned above.

SoC (t) = SOC0 + n / C · ∫_{t0}^{t} I(t) · dt (1)

where: SOC0: the initial state of charge, n: battery performance, I(t): battery current, t0: initial instant, SoC: state of charge, C: battery capacity. The formula and the results obtained were validated by the Field Engineer, who would oversee the maintenance of the equipment’s solar panels.

– Decision Tree

Data is read from a CSV file (19,062 records) containing Voltage, Consumption, Current, and SoC using Pandas. section: V. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
Our results show that supervised learning techniques can predict the state of charge of batteries in photovoltaic mining systems acceptably, validated by test results.

These results align with Henri and Lu [31], who state that machine learning can predict and program the operation mode in real time for residential battery/photovoltaic systems. This relates to Henri, Lu, and Carreio [32], who state that machine learning can predict the optimal operating mode of the battery in real time for residential photovoltaic applications. Rehman et al. [33] show that machine learning can investigate monitoring data and simulate and optimize case studies.

This study contributes to the prediction of the state of charge of batteries; however, a limitation was not having sufficient resources to achieve greater coverage of companies in this area. Although not the study's purpose, this could have generated a baseline on the load status prediction of photovoltaic batteries.

All fundamental data were collected via the Victron Energy System, which monitors solar panel energy variables. Data preparation revealed that only three exported fields provide no value for state of charge analysis, an observation corroborated by the field engineer responsible for maintaining the equipment's solar panels. However, a fourth field, state-of-charge [34], was added using a formula to determine the State of Charge, similar to studies on the recovery of the energy storage system adaptive with the regulator ANFIS [35].

The most appropriate supervised machine learning technique was established as Neural Networks, used in works such as [36] and other cases with Deep Neural Networks [37]. In the present study, an average prediction of 90.12% was found with an execution time of 0.02 seconds; this best suited the prediction type since neural networks create their interpretation of information inside and are more robust to fault tolerance and flexible when input data presents insignificant changes. Despite this, some works use Non-supervised machine learning techniques for the electronic discovery of novel technology that presents detailed reviews and analyzes of solar energy technology [38].

The effectiveness of the neural network model training for predicting the state of charge of batteries was verified, observing that from iteration 282, 100% success is achieved for both trained and validation data. Model training metrics were also evaluated, choosing (MAE) as the most robust and less sensitive to outliers than mean square error.

It was shown that training and validation error approach each other as learning continues. To avoid overfitting, the "EarlyStopping" function was used, which stops training when the validation score does not improve; if a certain number of "Epochs" elapse without showing improvement, training stops automatically.

Thanks to the chosen automatic supervised learning technique, it was possible to predict the state of charge of the batteries by comparing predictive data and real-time data, obtaining a good relationship and satisfactory results. Additionally, the model and its weights were imported to the web computer module proposed for the research's specific objectives, consisting of a form where the user can enter monitored energy variables and predict the state of charge of their batteries.

In addition, it was possible to import the model together with its weights from the neural network to the web computer module proposed in part for the specific objectives of the research, consisting of a form where the user can enter the data of the monitored energy variables and predict the state of charge that dumps your batteries.

In future work, it is recommended to expand the determining attributes, such as the temperatures of the batteries, among others, in order not only to be able to find the state of charge of the batteries but also to be able to find the life cycle of the batteries. As well as carry out the construction of the application of other regression algorithms to compare the results and check the efficiency, as well as Deep Learning. To identify if the model is presenting problems such as underfitting or overfitting, it is recommended to divide the input data set into two subsets with the distribution of training and evaluation percentages varied.

Based on the results and the software tool built, it can be applied in companies dedicated to determining the state of charge of photovoltaic batteries and personnel interested in knowing their state.

ABSTRACT Since the COVID-19 pandemic, teachers and students have started using online and hybrid
learning in education. There might be several obstacles to adopting hybrid learning in theory classes or
lab practice sessions. Based on student opinions, deciding what is appropriate for theoretical class and lab
practice is challenging. We employed machine learning approaches to forecast the hybrid learning mode for
theory classes and lab practices. We introduce a framework that utilizes machine learning to automate the
identification of hybrid learning for Theory Class and Lab practice (TCLPI). Four machine learning models
form the foundation of this framework: Random Forest (RDT), Support Vector Machine (SVN), Logistic
Regression (LGR), and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XBT). In the context of Theory Class Identification
(TCI), the SVN achieves a maximum test accuracy of 0.93, whereas the LGR achieves a minimum accuracy
of 0.90. On the other hand, the Lab Practice Identification (LPI), XBT, RDT, and SVN achieved a test
accuracy of 0.80. The outcome of trained algorithms is assessed using the Shapley Additive Explanation
(SHAP), an explainable Artificial intelligence (AI) approach. This research found that student-teacher
interaction decreased during lab practice, which is crucial. Internet disconnections, a lack of support during
technological malfunctions, and the likelihood of cheating in exams without monitoring are also issues.
We also found that students were accepting of hybrid learning for theory classes. Each model’s intrinsic
feature relevance and SHAP values helped prove this. Research shows that hybrid learning works more for
theory classes; it is less needed for lab practice for students.

Learning involves procuring memories, skills, knowledge, and wisdom through experiences and education. Higher learning via internet technologies has transformed modern education, with many universities offering online courses or switching to fully online programs. Incorporating information, communication, and technology is crucial for promoting student participation and facilitating online, independent, or hybrid learning [1]. Previous research indicates online learning threatens conventional methods by offering flexibility and fostering social interaction [2]. During the pandemic, students and UAE residents were positive about online education, and remote access showed enhanced effectiveness with 81.25% of students favoring Web-lab, supported by assessment results indicating a 27.69% average grade increase [7]. However, the abrupt switch to remote learning presented challenges including connectivity issues, socioeconomic disparities, and declining motivation [7]. Evaluating cost-effectiveness and directing investments in hybrid learning depends on learner satisfaction and experience, which are closely connected to cognitive engagement [6]. Adapting learning environments to individual variances can lead to better long-term results [8]. In Jordan, teachers are happy with new restrictions requiring some courses online while others use hybrid methods [9]. Portugal’s educational system proposes online and hybrid learning pedagogy instruction [10]. A hybrid learning strategy with gamification worked well for programming classes at a Croatian university [11]. Mobile learning was used in Abu Dhabi to maintain classroom education during the pandemic [12]. Online learning affected the satisfaction of Egyptian university students towards hybrid learning [13]. Amid the COVID-19 pandemic, scholars investigated obstacles experienced by EFL students in online education, including a need for technological proficiency, assignment completion challenges, and internet connectivity problems [14]. A study highlighted the rise of virtual learning and increased online program enrollment, discussing advantages and drawbacks [15]. Issues with the pandemic-related shift to virtual learning included effects on soft skills, the necessity for creative teaching strategies, cheating on online tests, teacher stress, and impacts on social skills [16]. Considering resource competition and student retention, it is wise to assess how technology impacts learning thoroughly [17]. Researchers highlighted the need to synchronize learning objectives between traditional and ICT-based programs, emphasizing collaborative and social learning, and the vital role of social affordances in crafting productive settings [18]. The authors suggested using hybrid learning spaces for curriculum enhancement, emphasizing technology’s value in enhancing student skills, especially for mobile learners [19]. Hybrid learning gained traction during the COVID-19 pandemic, leading the University of Sciences and Humanities to introduce strategies for continuous education following a transition from a virtual setup to a hybrid model that experienced a 35% dropout rate and inadequate teacher preparation [19]. The swift switch to online instruction during the pandemic disrupted the educational landscape, posing challenges for students and educators, prompting a comprehensive assessment of hybrid methodologies [20]. Namyssova et al. underscored the necessity of thorough teacher training before introducing blended learning, noting obstacles from inadequate infrastructure and restricted technology access, including policy gaps, insufficient faculty support, and a shortage of technological resources [21]. Students have widely acclaimed hybrid learning for its accessibility, integrating online platforms like Blackboard with face-to-face elements, and for the flexibility provided by the online component’s scheduling [22]. Engaged students demonstrated a well-distributed allocation of time between in-person and virtual tasks, preferred outdoor activities, and prioritized measures to prevent musculoskeletal problems [23]. A previously developed and validated blended learning experiment was successful for Bangladeshi students, revealing positive associations with attitudes toward online learning and openness to technology, and negative correlations with technology skills, learning flexibility, and study management [24].

To investigate critical features for precise predictions, this research presented a hybrid machine-learning architecture called SHAP, which uses various algorithms and an explainable AI method. Eight significant sections organize the rest of the paper. Section II outlines the study’s methodology and materials, including the TCPLI framework and sections on dataset descriptions, statistical features of factor analysis, preprocessing, testing of datasets, training, and tuning of machine learning algorithms. The experiments conducted using machine learning techniques present their results in Section IV. Section V delves into the significance of trained algorithms with SHAP features and discusses the most significant features with SHAP values. In Section VI, we offer the study’s discussions, and in Section VII, we explain its findings as conclusions. Major future initiatives take up the final section VIII.

section: II. PROBLEM STATEMENT
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: A previous study lacked a fully automated AI framework for hybrid learning prediction. This research presents the first hybrid framework using Theory Class Identification (TCI) and Lab Practice Identification (LPI) with supervised machine learning algorithms to predict hybrid learning features. Additionally, current research has not applied explainable AI (SHAP) to investigate hybrid learning characteristics. Therefore, this study also investigates the benefits of SHAP methodology with machine learning algorithms. The primary performance metrics of each algorithm determine its effectiveness. After identifying novel key features and confirming their presence, a hybrid learning style for theory and practical labs was identified.
output: A previous study did not provide a fully automated AI-based framework that predicts hybrid learning for theory classes and lab practices. Because of this, we showed the first hybrid framework with Theory Class Identification (TCI) and Lab Practice Identification (LPI), along with supervised machine learning algorithms that correctly predicted the features of hybrid learning. Further, the current research did not use the explainable artificial intelligence approach SHAP to investigate the characteristics of hybrid learning. As a result, we also investigated the benefits of using the SHAP methodology to apply machine learning algorithms. The primary performance metrics of each algorithm determine its effectiveness. After investigating novel key features and confirming their presence, we identified a hybrid learning style for theory classes and practical labs.

VI. DISCUSSION

This study uses machine learning and explainable AI to predict informatics students’ hybrid learning for theoretical class and lab practice. All the algorithms achieved training scores of 0.90 and cross-validation scores higher than 0.82, while the sample size was approaching 100—the process of identifying the theory class accomplished this. For the lab identification task, 90 samples are sufficient to train 0.95 to 0.80 accuracy scores. Hence, more samples can reduce this gap between test and train scores. All models estimated more than 0.90 AUC values to identify the theoretical class while retaining 0.81-0.84 AUC ratings to identify lab practice. In theory class identification, XBT and SVN did better than others, explaining 80% of samples and having a cumulative actual positive rate of 87%. In lab practice identification, XBT and RDT were 100% accurate, with a cumulative true positive rate of 50%. For theory class prediction, SVN, XBT, and RDT had the same most excellent mean accuracy, f1-score, and recall of 0.94; for lab practice prediction, it was 0.80. In theory class prediction, LGR, RD, XBT, and SVN algorithms correctly identified 156, 157, 160, and 163, respectively. However, these algorithms misinterpreted records 18, 17, 14, and 11, respectively. The algorithms LGR, RD, XBT, and SVN accurately determined the total number of records as 77, 80, 80, and 80, respectively, for lab identification. However, these algorithms wrongly identified records as 23, 20, 20, and 20, respectively.

When making predictions in theory class, factors such as gender, course, future hybrid learning mode, and long-term solutions are essential. Additionally, my parents’ valuable perspective also plays a significant role. It is crucial to consider factors such as reduced quality of interaction with teachers, hurdles encountered, isolation from a natural study environment, lower stress levels, ease of communication, and university assistance when predicting laboratory outcomes. Significant features emerge from these factors. The SVN model’s SHAP scores in theoretical class prediction, teacher interaction quality, and absence reduction were substantial. Other noteworthy aspects included time management, the convenience of attending two classes at once, the ability to turn on mic video camera interrupts, the encouragement of website learning, and the isolation of a natural study environment. The XBT, RDT, and SVN model SHAP values forecast lab practice, which isolates university initiatives and support within a genuine study environment. Lower teacher interaction quality, less stress, and more accessible communication were all essential features.

section: VII. CONCLUSION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: This study evaluated machine learning for hybrid learning in informatics education. Models were trained and validated using explainable AI (SHAP) to identify key factors. The SVN algorithm achieved the highest test accuracy of 93% for theoretical classes, while XBT, RDT, and LGR followed with 92%, 90%, and 90% accuracy, respectively. For lab practice, RDT, XBT, and SVN scored homogeneous accuracy of 80%, with LGR performing lowest at 77%. Students and parents readily accept hybrid theory classes, citing reduced stress and flexibility. However, hybrid lab practice is less viable, resulting in decreased student-teacher interaction, concentration, and engagement, alongside technical issues like internet instability and exam monitoring risks.
output: In this study, we employed machine learning techniques to identify the possibilities of incorporating hybrid learning into the education of informatics students, whether in lab practice or theory classes. Furthermore, we evaluate the explanatory power of the proposed models using an explainable AI approach (SHAP). We also presented a combined framework that identifies the applicability of hybrid learning with significant accuracy. The factor analysis technique created novel and essential factors for the experiments. The SVN algorithms achieved a test accuracy of 0.93% in predicting hybrid learning for theoretical classes, while XBT achieved the second-greatest accuracy of 92%. RDT and LGR achieved an identical accuracy rate of 90%. We demonstrated that students and parents eagerly accept hybrid learning for theory classes. Each model’s intrinsic feature importance and SHAP values proved this. While a viable solution for theory classes, hybrid learning lacks significance for lab practice. Using hybrid learning makes students less stressed and makes it easy to join two different classes simultaneously. They also believed the hybrid learning mode separated them from the natural study environments. To predict the hybrid learning for lab practice, RDT, XBT, and SVN scored a homogeneous accuracy of 80%, and LGR scored the lowest accuracy of 0.77%. During the lab practice, there was a decrease in the quality of interaction between the students and the teachers, which is an important aspect. Furthermore, students face challenges, including intermittent Internet access, inadequate assistance in the event of technical difficulties, and the risk of exam cheating as a result of insufficient monitoring. They experience a decrease in their ability to concentrate and engage with people.

MAYANK GULATI, KOEN ZANDBERG, ZHAOLAN HUANG, GERHARD WUNDER, CEDRIC ADJIH, EMMANUEL BACCELLI

TDMiL is a framework for distributed training and transfer learning on microcontroller-based IoT devices. It combines logical components such as CoAPerator, a central aggregator, and embedded runtimes tailored for heterogeneous, resource-constrained hardware. Experiments evaluate schemes addressing computational variability among distributed learning microcontroller devices (stragglers). The implementation is released as open-source, compatible with commercial IoT hardware and a public IoT testbed.

ABSTRACT More and more, edge devices embark Artificial Neuron Networks. In this context, a trend is to simultaneously decentralize their training as much as possible while shrinking their resource requirements, both for inference and training—tasks that are typically intensive in terms of data, memory, and computation. At the edge’s extremity, a specific challenge arises concerning the inclusion of microcontroller-based devices typically deployed in the IoT. So far, no general framework has been provided for that. Such devices not only have extremely challenging resource constraints (weak CPUs, slow network connections, memory budgets measured in kilobytes) but also exhibit high polymorphism, leading to large variability in computational performance among these devices. In this paper, we design and implement TDMiL, a versatile framework for distributed training, and transfer learning. TDMiL interconnects and combines logical components including CoAPerator (a central aggregator) and various tiny embedded software runtimes that are specifically tailored for networks comprising heterogeneous, resource-constrained devices built on diverse types of microcontrollers. We report on experiments conducted with the TDMiL framework, which we use to comparatively evaluate several schemes devised to address computational variability among distributed learning microcontroller-based devices, i.e., stragglers. Additionally, we release the code of our implementation of TDMiL as an open-source project, which is compatible with common commercial off-the-shelf IoT hardware and a well-known open-access IoT testbed.

input: Machine learning (ML) has transformed across sectors, shifting from powerful PCs and clusters to edge devices like smartphones and single-board computers. The TinyML community now targets even smaller microcontrollers, which operate in the milliwatt range despite limited computing capacity. These devices perform inference effectively after off-device training and optimization. Federated Learning (FL) emerges as a decentralized technique training models across collaborating devices without centralizing raw data, safeguarding privacy and enabling local customization. The typical FL workflow involves selecting devices, distributing a global model, local training, sending updates to a central server, and aggregating for a new global model until convergence. Throughout this process, communication protocols play a pivotal role, addressing challenges including system heterogeneity from differences in hardware and network availability, and statistical heterogeneity from varying data distributions. Solutions like FedProx mitigate heterogeneity under less constrained conditions, though they necessitate tracking both global and local models, posing challenges for direct applicability in tiny distributed ML.
output: Machine learning (ML), particularly when leveraging deep neural networks (DNNs), has undergone a significant transformation over the last decade, making an indelible impact across various sectors. The standard deployment of ML involves a data pipeline that utilizes a model—a sophisticated framework of algorithms that process and interpret data to make informed decisions. Such models are initially subjected to an intensive training phase, equipping them for subsequent inference operations and their eventual production use. Initially requiring powerful PCs and clusters, machine learning has been adapted to less powerful edge devices such as smartphones, or single board computers in the category of Jetson Nano or RaspberryPi, which are based on relatively cheap microprocessors with a power consumption in the range of a few Watts. Some prior work on distributed learning on such machines can be found for instance in [1] and [2]. However, pushing further, the TinyML [3] community is now targeting even smaller devices based on microcontrollers. Despite their very limited computing capacity and a much lower power consumption in the range of milliWatts, microcontrollers can perform model inference effectively once they have been adequately trained and optimized off-device (this training phase usually demands considerable data and more computing resources). The pioneering efforts of the TinyML community have spearheaded the investigation into on-device learning such as MCUNet [4], etc., especially focusing on extremely resource-constrained microcontrollers. As discussed in [5], addressing memory and power constraints in microcontroller units for Internet of Things (IoT) has been a driving force behind TinyML applications. The TinyML-as-a-Service (TMLaaS) architecture supports on-device learning, as demonstrated through a practical case study. Additionally, [6] explores the potential of reformable TinyML, emphasizing adaptability and cognition in IoT devices. The survey paper categorizes solutions, outlining their autonomous self-enhancement capabilities and highlighting the roles of distributed TinyML and over-the-air approaches. Altogether, these works underscore the utility of TinyML in providing lightweight ML solutions for resource-constrained IoT environments. Among these advancements, Federated Learning (FL) emerges as a decentralized ML technique that trains models across numerous collaborating devices without centralized training, thereby safeguarding privacy and enabling local customization. By leveraging such decentralized strategies, the ML landscape is witnessing a transformative shift, enabling global model training without any exposing, transmitting (centralizing) of raw data. This influential approach initially introduced in a seminal paper on Federated Averaging [7], with subsequent research such as [8] focusing on communication efficiency and enhanced privacy via strategies such as sub-sampling and quantization. The typical FL workflow involves selecting participating devices, distributing a global model, training locally, sending updates to a central server, aggregating for a new global model, and iterating until convergence. This collaborative learning process ensures that the resulting model is refined and suitable for inference across all participating devices. Throughout the FL process, communication protocols play a pivotal role. In addition to the general challenges encountered in FL, such as heterogeneity stemming from differences in client systems, including hardware resources and network availability (system heterogeneity), as well as variations in data distributions across these devices (statistical heterogeneity), tiny distributed ML must confront the overarching problem of resource constraints. Moreover, solutions like FedProx [9], aimed at mitigating heterogeneity under less constrained conditions, raise questions. They necessitate the tracking of both global and local models during a client’s update, posing challenges in terms of its direct applicability.

I. INTRODUCTION — A. CHALLENGES IN DISTRIBUTED LEARNING WITH INTERCONNECTED MICROCONTROLLERS

Current research into FL for edge devices often glosses over a critical aspect—the in-depth analysis of computational and communication costs—imperative for devices with limited resources. Additionally, EdgeML’s [10] work on multi-hop wireless network-based learning underscores the need for a robust communication stack for collaborative learning, emphasizing that much of the existing research primarily focuses on optimizing computational performance, neglecting the importance of the communication layer. More loosely related work on Gossip Learning (GL) aims to further decentralize model aggregation, in a peer-to-peer fashion. However, studies such as [11] point towards the limitations of the GL framework, notably in terms of delayed convergence, especially when dealing with diverse data distributions. Further work on GossipFL [12] focused on improving the convergence rate and accuracy in constrained IoT environments.

Considering the diverse nature of wireless networks, differences in hardware specifications among edge devices, and varying data distributions across these devices, we can make two key observations:

• The presence of computational variability entails the occurrence of slow-performing workers, commonly termed “stragglers”. If not dealt with effectively, these stragglers have the potential to significantly impact the overall convergence of the training process, as indicated in FedProx [9].

• Communication protocols need to be optimized not only for resource constraints but also to be adaptable across a diverse range of link layers. This includes typical wireless technologies like Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE), IEEE 802.15.4, and LoRa, as well as various network technologies, including wired options such as BACnet, PLC as specified in [13], and local bus communications (USB, Inter-Integrated Circuit (I2C), etc.). Ensuring the use of secure protocols is crucial, especially when handling the exchange of (privacy) sensitive information among tiny devices reliably.

It’s important to note that existing studies in the domain of low-resource distributed machine learning have not been specifically designed to tackle these particular challenges. Additionally, certain methodologies are limited by wired setups [14], which poses scalability challenges and diminishes the overall effectiveness and the applicability of the implementation.

Conversely, current approaches that handle heterogeneous networks, like FedProx [9], [15], have not been explored within the context of resource-constrained devices. Commonly employed communication stacks for federated learning, such as Google’s Remote Procedure Call (gRPC) [16], Websockets [17], etc., lack adaptability for highly constrained microcontroller-based IoT devices. These devices, operating under stringent resource limitations, require specialized and lightweight communication frameworks. The challenges arise from unique constraints such as limited processing power, communication bandwidth, memory, and energy resources. Addressing these challenges necessitates the development of tailored protocols that consider resource constraints, and intermittent connectivity. This adaptability is crucial for the practical deployment of distributed learning on edge devices, ensuring that the advantages of FL, such as enhanced privacy and rapid local inference, are not overshadowed by unaddressed scalability and resources concerns. This paradigm shift, leveraged through the TDMiL framework, is essential for extending FL methodologies effectively to IoT devices, to unlock their full potential in this evolving ecosystem.

In light of the challenges outlined above, there arises a compelling need for a dedicated communication stack tailored to meet the constraints of IoT devices, thus enabling on-device learning. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. First, section II delves into existing research on distributed learning with interconnected microcontrollers, then section III explores available IoT communication protocols. A selection thereof is presented, which is tailored to provide a protocol stack facilitating efficient exchange of model updates within the distributed tiny device landscape. Then, a foundational scenario is presented to illustrate the interplay of different components involved in distributed learning in section IV. Through algorithms thereafter detailed in section V, several distributed learning schemes are introduced, and implemented in section VI. A comparative analysis across different data distributions, model architectures, and varying workloads, demonstrate on-board learning with simple neural networks and transfer learning using deeper neural networks on diverse datasets across multiple IoT devices. Further, section VII and section VIII offer a comprehensive experimental analysis of the communication and computational aspects of experimental results based on these, concluding with discussions on implications and avenues for future research.

Related Work — Inference & Model Optimization for Microcontrollers

Inference optimization is categorized at the algorithm and system levels. At the algorithm level, model compression techniques such as pruning, low-rank decomposition, efficient architectures, and quantization reduce resource consumption on microcontroller-based devices. At the system level, emphasis is placed on computation and memory resource allocation, and operator scheduling. Prior work caches intermediate results like activations for gradient calculation. Other efforts integrate model optimization and transpilers, such as TVM, with embedded platforms like RIOT to support diverse Microcontroller Units.
output:
MICROCONTROLLERS

Inference optimization strategies can be coarsely categorized in two levels: the algorithm level and the system scheduling level [18]. At the algorithm level, the main focus is typically model compression techniques, including pruning [4], [19], low-rank decomposition of weights [20], [21], efficient model architecture [4], [19], and quantization [20], [22] in order to decrease resource consumption of models and inference on-board microcontroller-based devices. On the other hand, at system scheduling level, emphasis is put on the allocation of computation and memory resources [4], [23], or on scheduling between model operators, in prior work such as [24]. In particular, intermediate results required for the training stage (e.g., activations) can be cached in the memory for subsequent gradient calculation. Another domain of prior work such as [25] aims at integrating model optimization and transpilers for diverse model architectures (such as TVM) with common low-power embedded software platforms (such as RIOT [26]) to support a wide range of Microcontroller Units (MCUs).

Meta-learning, akin to transfer learning, facilitates fast
adaptation to new but similar tasks using limited data samples. It promotes collaborative learning by adjusting neural
network initialization. TinyReptile pioneers meta-learning
on resource-constrained devices, introduces a novel audio
classification dataset, and reduces resource consumption,
offering practical insights.
Similarly, TinyMetaFed [34] streamlines collaborative
neural network initialization training. It optimizes communication, safeguards privacy, enhances computational efficiency, and ensures robustness through selective transmission
of weight parameters. These advancements significantly
enhance TinyML, making it more adept for resourceconstrained IoT environments.
One observes that much of the aforementioned prior
research has primarily focused on computational aspects, [31]
brought attention to a bandwidth limitation in communication
between MCUs and the server, resulting from the use of a
serial port. This limitation leads to increased latency when
transferring from the server to the client compared to the
client-to-server direction. Likewise, [32] emphasized the
critical necessity of enhancing communication costs. The
TinyFL approach [14] proposes an alternative network protocol using a hybrid primary-subordinate I2C configuration
to address these challenges. However, this wired approach
raises significant scalability concerns and cannot effectively
leverage cross-device FL with a substantial number of
connected tiny devices. Other prior work such as [35]
propose efficient model serialization to aiming to decrease
network load due to model transfers over the network. On the
other hand, TinyMetaFed [34], takes a different approach to
alleviate communication costs in FL. Specifically, it suggests
transmitting a selective portion of model weights significant
for the overall training objective.
We observe that none such prior work addresses the
inherent issue of distributed learning asynchronicity, which
stems from slow-performing clients i.e. stragglers. This
observation highlights a notable gap in the existing literature,

section: II. RELATED WORK — D. OUR CONTRIBUTIONS
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
We present a principled approach to distributed learning on microcontroller-based IoT, addressing wireless constraints and stragglers. Our method complements existing meta-learning solutions like TinyReptile [33] and TinyMetaFed [34]. Our specific contributions are:

*   We introduce a framework using CBOR and CoAP for efficient model and parameter transfer across arbitrary architectures, enabling synchronous and asynchronous FL.
*   We introduce strategies for integrating asynchronous stragglers with varying workloads into the learning process.
*   We design an embedded software platform for on-board training and transfer learning on model families including MLP, LeNet-5, and MobileNetV3-M.
*   We evaluate straggler strategies using standard TinyML FL benchmark datasets, analyzing computation, communication costs, latency, and memory footprint on microcontroller devices.
*   We released open-source code built upon the RIOT embedded platform [36], providing a practical basis for future research.
output:
II. RELATED WORK — D. OUR CONTRIBUTIONS

The work we present provides a principled approach to distributed learning in the context of microcontroller-based resource-constrained IoT environments, tackling its fundamental challenges, including constraints stemming from typical wireless communication and the issue of stragglers. Our approach can complement aforementioned meta-learning solutions, such as TinyReptile [33] and TinyMetaFed [34]. More in detail, our contributions are the following:

• Generic Resource-Constrained Communication for Model & Parameter Transfer: We introduce a framework utilizing Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) and Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) for efficient exchange of model updates (weights and gradients) from arbitrary model architectures, facilitating various distributed learning approaches such as synchronous and asynchronous FL.

• Handling Asynchronous Resource-Constrained Stragglers: We introduce strategies for managing asynchronous stragglers with varying workloads in distributed networks, ensuring their effective integration into the learning process.

• On-Board Training & Transfer Learning: We design an embedded software platform enabling on-board training and transfer learning on several families of models: simple neural network Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) architectures and for deeper networks like LeNet-5, MobileNetV3-M, etc.

• Comparative Performance Evaluation: We evaluate the straggler strategies using various standard FL benchmark datasets from the TinyML domain. We experimentally analyze computation, communication costs, latency, and memory footprint on microcontroller-based IoT devices.

• Open Source Implementation: We released our code, which builds upon a popular microcontroller-based embedded software platform (RIOT [36]) thus providing a practical basis for future experimental research in this domain.

section: III. BACKGROUND ON IoT DEVICES & PROTOCOLS
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
Microcontrollers in smart appliances operate with limited processing power, featuring CPU clock frequencies of 10–100 MHz and memory budgets of 32–512 KiB [37]. Network links on these devices are often inadequate for the low latency and high throughput required by standard protocols. The conventional stack combining TCP and HTTPS places a significant burden on resource-constrained devices [37].

Common FL frameworks like TensorFlow Federated [38] and Flower [39] rely on gRPC [16] as a core communication element. gRPC uses Protocol Buffers [40] for efficient data serialization but deploying it with TCP and HTTPS creates communication bottlenecks on typical IoT devices.

Alternative protocols like WebSockets and MQTT are considered for resource-constrained FL scenarios. WebSockets enable bidirectional, efficient data transfer, while MQTT operates on a publish-subscribe model suited for low bandwidth and unreliable networks [39]. However, even these protocols can be resource-intensive and may not suit severely constrained devices. Hence, other IoT-tailored protocols must be surveyed.
output:
Microcontrollers in smart appliances operate within extremely limited processing capabilities. For instance, as analyzed in [37], low CPU clock frequencies from 10 MHz to 100 MHz and total memory budgets as small as 32 KiB to 512 KiB are not uncommon. Additional hurdles must be faced too: for instance, network links used by these devices are often inadequate for the low latency and high throughput required by most communication protocols. The conventional stack, for instance combining TCP and HTTPS, places a significant burden on these devices, making it inadequate for resource-constrained environments.

Common FL frameworks like TensorFlow Federated [38] and Flower [39] often rely on Google’s Remote Procedure Call (gRPC) [16] as a core element in their communication stack. gRPC, an open-source framework, enables language-agnostic communication between distributed systems using Protocol Buffers (protobuf) [40] for efficient data serialization and transmission. However, deploying gRPC, which entails using TCP and HTTPS, leads to communication bottlenecks on typical resource-constrained devices.

Alternative protocols like WebSockets, which enable lightweight, real-time communication between devices, and Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT), designed to minimize network bandwidth and power consumption, are commonly considered for resource-constrained environments in FL scenarios. WebSockets facilitate bidirectional, efficient data transfer, while MQTT operates on a publish-subscribe model, particularly suited for scenarios with low bandwidth and unreliable networks. However, it’s important to note that even these protocols, while effective, can be resource-intensive and may not be suitable for severely constrained devices with limited processing capabilities. Hence, other protocols tailored for IoT must be considered. We next survey the landscape of such protocols.

section: III. BACKGROUND ON IoT DEVICES & PROTOCOLS — A. IoT COMMUNICATION PROTOCOL LANDSCAPE
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: IP protocols from the IETF dominate the IoT landscape [41]. 6LoWPAN adapts IP for constrained link layers like 802.15.4 and BLE. Transport protocols above IP include UDP, TCP, and QUIC; DTLS secures UDP, while TLS is required for TCP and QUIC. These features trade off constrained device support against convenience, as TCP manages parallel packets and QUIC multiplexes streams, requiring RAM buffering and complex state machines. Web transfer protocols vary by resource constraints; HTTP/TLS and MQTT run on less constrained machines, while microcontrollers use CoAP (secured with OSCORE/DTLS) and MQTT-SN. For highly dynamic clients with asynchronous events and large payloads in lossy environments, CoAP Pub/Sub is recommended over MQTT-SN due to inherent application layer fragmentation [42]. Management protocols on microcontrollers favor lightweight alternatives like LwM2M, which can use CoAP as a transfer protocol. Application data serialization on microcontrollers uses lightweight formats like CBOR or protobuf to minimize airtime overhead, unlike JSON or XML used on less constrained devices.
output:
Constrained IoT devices require optimizations of all the components of the system, including communication protocols at different layers of the protocol stack. While the IoT communication protocol landscape is still very polymorphic and fragmented, there has been some solidification around IP protocols standards from the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF), depicted in Figure 1. Let’s overview this landscape, keeping in mind potential applicability to distributed learning on microcontrollers.

• Convergence Layer: The Convergence Layer begins with the Internet Protocol (IP), either IPv4 or IPv6, which serves as a universal protocol. In order to ensure compatibility with various IoT technologies, there are adaptations made for constrained link-layer connections, such as 802.15.4 through 6LoWPAN [41] which enables to abstract away the variety of MAC layers (for instance low-power radios such as IEEE 802.15.4, BLE, LoRa, etc.).

• Transport Protocols: Above IP, one finds transport protocols such as UDP, TCP, and QUIC. DTLS provides security for UDP, while TLS is an option on top of TCP and is mandatory in QUIC. At this level, there are clear tradeoffs between supporting very constrained devices and providing convenient features. For instance, TCP automatically manages multiple packets in parallel, while QUIC (on top of UDP) allows for multiplexing of streams. These features, however, require buffering (RAM) and a more complex state machine (CPU).

FIGURE 1. Communication protocol landscape for IoT.

• Web Transfer Protocols: On top and along the transport protocols, web transfer protocols are used for named data exchanges. While on the less resource-constrained machines protocols such as HTTP (secured with TLS) or MQTT are used, on microcontroller-based IoT devices more lightweight equivalents are used such as, respectively, CoAP (secured with OSCORE or DTLS) and MQTT-SN. Work such as [42] suggests that in scenarios with highly dynamic clients, especially during asynchronous events, the recommendation is to utilize CoAP Pub/Sub rather than Message Queuing Telemetry Transport-Sensor Networks (MQTT-SN), for applications handling large payloads in environments prone to high packet loss, which matches our scenario. This preference is rooted in CoAP’s inherent support for application layer fragmentation, effectively preventing message drops caused by exceeding the allowed number of retransmissions.

• Management Protocols: Above web transfer protocols, another layer of protocols may be used to provide remote management of devices, over the network. While the less resource-constrained machines use protocols such as gPRC, Websockets (or NetConf, SNMP, etc), on microcontroller-based IoT devices more lightweight alternatives are used such as Light-weight Machine-to-Machine (LwM2M). For instance, LwM2M can use CoAP as a transfer protocol and extend its capabilities to unify management tasks, offering a standardized, foundational IoT device management framework.

• Data Representation & Serialization Tools: Actual application data transferred from one machine to another (potentially based on different hardware!) must be represented and serialized in a convenient and interoperable format. While the less resource-constrained machines use serialization schemes such as JSON and XML, on microcontroller-based IoT devices more lightweight alternatives are used to incur fewer bits-over-the-air, such as with Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) binary formats or protobuf.

We now transition towards solution space, considering the following simple yet generic scenario.

The scenario involves a PC server with ample resources connected via an arbitrary network to N microcontroller-based machine learning clients. instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: In our scenario, client network paths to the orchestrator are assumed free from significant external, internal, or cross-interference. We assume standard IoT network and node fault tolerance mechanisms, such as CoAP confirmable retransmissions [43] and IEEE 802.15.4 retransmissions [44], can handle most failures. Prior work confirms that typical TinyML model transfers, approximated at 100 kB, transmit successfully over comparable low-power links [25, 45]. While significant follow-up work is needed to optimize fault handling for FL, this scenario provides a solid base. We consider only a handful of clients; since client transmissions do not significantly interfere, the bottleneck shifts to the orchestrator's unconstrained link and processing power, so scalability is not further addressed here.
