In our scenario, we consider that individual network paths (including their low-power segments) from a client to the orchestrator are not significantly impacted by external, internal or cross-interference or side-traffic.

Basic network & node fault tolerance: We assume network and node fault tolerance mechanisms typically at work within the IoT network stack can handle most cases. Such mechanisms include for e.g., CoAP confirmable message retransmissions at the application layer (see [43] section II-A), while complementary mechanisms are provided in the routing protocol and in the lower layers of the stack (e.g., IEEE 802.15.4 retransmissions [44]). Indeed, prior work (see [45] Table 4) confirms that large network transfers such as firmware updates of size ≈100 kB are transmitted without significant issues over a comparable low-power link (IEEE 802.15.4 using the 6LoWPAN and CoAP). Other related work (see [25] Table 3) indicates that models in typical TinyML model zoos, incur comparable transfer load over the network, i.e., ≈100 kB. Hence, while significant follow-up work should be dedicated to develop additional mechanisms to optimize specifically for FL the handling of network disruptions and node failures, our work on the above basic scenario should serve as solid base for such follow-up work.

Number of clients: In the scenario we consider, and in our experiments below, we tackle only a handful of clients. However, since we assume that clients’ data transmissions do not significantly interfere with one another, the bottleneck is essentially shifted to the orchestrator’s (unconstrained) link to the network and its (unconstrained) processing power. Therefore, we do not further address this scalability issue in this paper. Conversely, in cases where significant external interference or cross-interference are observed for data transmission from clients to the orchestrator, specific additional mechanisms would be required to handle these appropriately. Nevertheless, our work on the simple scenario we describe should serve as a solid base for such follow-up work.

LEARNING ON MICROCONTROLLERS
We design our communication stack on top of CoAP and CBOR for serialization, which offers specific advantages in addressing challenges posed by resource-constrained environments. We leverage CoAP capabilities for reliable asynchronous communication and blockwise transfer, which cater both for dynamic settings and large payloads in face of small maximum packet size, and packet loss typical in IoT. Additionally, we leverage CoAP support for Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS), securing efficiently IoT client-server communications. We chose CBOR over protobuf for serialization because prior work such as [35] hints that, for arbitrary model sizes, best-case CBOR outperforms best-case protobuf, which makes it favorable for optimal data representation. The combination of CBOR and CoAP thus streamlines IoT client-server data exchanges, and caters to the unique needs of communication of heterogeneous, low-power network links. The stack further allows seamless integration with established FL frameworks like Flower [39], TensorFlow Federated [38], etc. The shift we propose here stems from our realization that these frameworks, in their current configurations, primarily cater to unconstrained server setups. In contrast, our framework takes a progressive step forward and opens the door towards accommodating even more diverse configurations, such as (in future work) hosting the orchestrator/aggregator on constrained devices too, or designing and implementing model aggregation without a central agent at all (e.g. Gossip Learning).

instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: The orchestrator controls the distributed FL process and requires multiple CBOR-encoded messages to manage client learning. CBOR is used for serialization to minimize message size; it has comparable overhead to protobuf but integrates well with IETF protocols like CoAP. A communication stack of messages is designed between clients and the central server. A key requirement is efficient ML model serialization that supports partial updates without transferring full models. Models are split into logical operators with associated parameter sets; operators reference their used parameters, which can be shared. A full model update transfers all parameters and operators, while a partial update only transfers the necessary operators and parameters, useful for transfer learning. V. SYSTEM DESIGN — B. MODEL SERIALIZATION

As the orchestrator is in full control of the distributed FL process, it requires multiple types of messages exchanged to fully control the learning process on the clients. We define multiple CBOR encoded messages for this purpose. By using CBOR as message serialization format the message size is minimal. CBOR has a comparable serialization when compared with protobuf, however CBOR is used frequently in the IETF and integrates well with other protocols such as CoAP.

As part of the communication stack, we design a number of messages passed between clients and the central server. A key part of this is the efficient serialization of the ML models. Part of the requirements is that the message must allow for partial updates of the ML model, without the need to transfer the full ML models over the network.

To achieve this, we split a ML model into a logical set of operators used within the model. Each operator has one or more sets of parameters, or weights. Our serialization contains both the set of parameters and the operators, with the operators containing a reference to which parameters are used by the operator. Note that parameters can be shared between different operators where possible. A full model update contains the full set of parameters and operators in the model, while a partial update only transfers the set of operators and parameters required for the update useful in case of transfer learning task.

The ML models contain a Universally Unique Identifier (UUID) as handle, used in the communication messages. Together with the layer and parameter identifiers, a client is able to request an individual set of parameters from the server for the purpose of partial model updates.

Our implementation addresses systems and data handling aspects. The system comprises multiple components spread across different layers.

A central model aggregator combines locally trained client models. A. SYSTEM

Our implementation consists of multiple components spread across different systems.

1) MODEL AGGREGATOR

The model aggregator is a central entity responsible for combining locally trained models from participating clients. One common aggregation method is weighted averaging applied in [7], where the updates from each client are weighted based on the ratio of local data points to the total data points across all clients.

In asynchronous setups, this weighting considers the fraction of local points used in training relative to the overall points in the FL round, ensuring that even partially completed work from slower clients is incorporated, rather than discarding their contributions entirely. This adaptive approach addresses variations in client device speeds, promoting efficient model aggregation in FL scenarios. The global update weight (Wglobal) is computed using the formula:

Wglobal = (P(ni · εi · Wlocali)) / P ni

(1)

where ni, εi = eE denote the number of data samples and completed epochs over assigned epochs by client i respectively. Wglobal, Wlocali denote global model parameters and local model parameters for client i respectively.

2) ORCHESTRATOR

Our custom orchestrator, “CoAPerator”, is a key actor in our distributed learning setup. It manages CoAP-enabled client devices and provides the interface for the Model Aggregator to facilitate the FL algorithms. Developed with FastAPI [49] and aiocoap [50], CoAPerator is a Python-based application that seamlessly integrates robust functionality, providing streamlined device management within the CoAP ecosystem. It allows clients to register themselves with the orchestrator, through a CoAP resource directory service. From there on the orchestrator sets up a bidirectional communication channel over CoAP to manage the registered clients by providing RPC-style commands to the clients. Furthermore, it provides the endpoints for providing ML models to the clients. As previously mentioned the orchestrator exposes these services via CoAP.

Interaction with the orchestrator by administrators and by the model aggregator does not occur via the constrained network used by the clients. To ease interaction with this interface, it is provided via a REST-like API using HTTP and JSON. This interface is used to upload new models to the orchestrator, for example by the Model Aggregator when a new round is to be started.

3) FL CLIENTS

The FL clients run on constrained devices with firmware consisting of: RIOT [36] as an embedded operating system; an IPv6-enabled network stack; a CoAP stack; and the necessary primitives for FL and ML.

The clients are pre-provisioned with the location of the orchestrator and on start-up contact the orchestrator for registration. After registration, the clients expect a channel to be established, and initiated by the orchestrator in response to the completed registration process.

The clients are able to update the parameter and configuration of the FL process on the fly, based on instructions from the orchestrator. However, updating the structure of the deployed models is not possible without resorting to a firmware update.

Tabular Dataset – We implemented min-max scaling to normalize features within the range of 0 to 1. Given the relatively small size of the original tabular datasets (iris [51], wine [52], and breast cancer [53]) shown in Table 1, comprising a few hundred data samples, we employed a data augmentation technique. This involved applying Gaussian noise with a mean of zero and a standard deviation ranging from 0.05 to 0.25, effectively expanding the size of the original dataset.

The augmented dataset was subsequently utilized for both training and validation purposes, employing an 80-20% split. This divided dataset was then further partitioned among five clients. The data distribution among these clients could either be independent and identically distributed (IID) or non-IID, and we will showcase results for both scenarios. The original dataset remained unchanged and was utilized as the test set for the final evaluation (presented in Table 6) of the model trained in a distributed manner.

To analyze the impact of varying levels of diversity across clients, we employed the widely recognized technique of Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) [54]. By adjusting the hyperparameter α, we could control the diversity among clients, thus creating local datasets that maximally capture real-world variations. Specifically, we set α to a low value, 10−6, to depict an extreme scenario where diversity across clients is high. This approach results in clients receiving data points with imbalanced label classes in the non-IID case, as opposed to balanced labels in the IID case. This is evident when examining the class distributions across clients within our experiments: in the IID case, the height of the bars in histograms is relatively comparable across classes, while in the non-IID case, the heights vary significantly, indicating statistical heterogeneity among clients. This variation is illustrated in Figure 4, Figure 5, and Figure 6. The data used in the experiments can be accessed through our code repository.

MNIST Dataset – This dataset is a widely used collection of handwritten digits (28 × 28 pixel, grayscale) that serves as a benchmark in the field of ML and computer vision. We standardized the grayscale features, originally ranging from 0 to 255, to a normalized scale of 0 to 1 through min-max normalization. Each client received a pre-allocation of 125 samples for both local training and validation, divided in an 80:20 ratio. The data distribution among clients was IID. VII. EXPERIMENTAL SETUP — D. METHODOLOGY FOR STRAGGLERS

To simulate stragglers, deliberate delays were introduced between local epochs, leading the orchestrator to potentially direct clients to cease local training. In this context, incomplete work from paused clients undergoes one of two variants, outlined in subsection V-D: either it is discarded entirely (Algorithm 1), or it is effectively weighed by the aggregator (Algorithm 2).

1) IMPLEMENTED MODELS & ON-BOARD TRAINING

In order to test our design on relevant models, we picked the one that had a few "toy" models based on a basic Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) architecture, and on the other hand, LeNet5 and MobileNetV3-M models, which are more complex models used in TinyML literature (e.g., see model zoo used in [25]).

• MLP models: We have implemented a three-layer MLP with a variable number of neurons tailored to different tabular datasets with input, hidden and output dimensions as [4, 2, 3], [13, 10, 3] and [30, 10, 2] for the respective iris, wine, and breast cancer datasets. For the classification tasks with a cross-entropy loss, the number of trainable parameters for the respective datasets are as follows: 19, 173, and 332 parameters. In this straightforward configuration, we have manually crafted the gradient computation. The model's weights and biases are updated using a stochastic gradient descent (SGD) approach, and the computations are performed in an Eigen [59] C++ based library. For a more in-depth understanding of the implementation, the code can be accessed through the provided link.

• LeNet5 [60]: This representative early model with about 44.6K parameters specialized in classifying handwritten digits is a simple convolutional neural network with two convolutional layers and three fully connected layers. It consumes 28 × 28 grayscale image and produces likelihoods over 10 digit classes.

• MobileNetV3-M: This model is based on MobileNetV3 [61], an advanced backbone focuses on optimizing mobile and embedded vision applications efficiently. It leverages depth-wise separable convolution to achieve significantly higher efficiency compared to standard convolution (roughly 8 to 9 times less computation) with only a slight decrease in accuracy. In this study, we tailored it to mirror the input, output and classifier structures of LeNet5, yielding approximately 112.8K parameters. The classifier contains 84 and 10 neuron units in the last two fully connected layers, respectively. This customization of MobileNetV3 decreased drastically the resource consumption of tiny devices with slightly degradation of model accuracy on MNIST dataset. For the sake of clarity, we use the name "MobileNetV3-M" for this tailored model in this work.

Transfer learning setup – Both LeNet5 and MobileNetV3-M were pre-trained on the MNIST dataset, then transpiled and deployed on constrained devices using U-TOE [25]. For purpose of experiments, only the weights of the final layer (classifier) were reinitialized on uniform distribution and federated fine-tuned on devices. We also used cross-entropy for loss calculation and SGD optimizer with a learning rate of 0.01 and a weight decay of 0.01 for model training.

We now compare Algorithm 1 and Algorithm 2 when facing stragglers as specified in Section VII-D.

1) BITS OVER-THE-AIR
The primary payload, encoded in CBOR, comprises mostly float-represented model parameters during over-the-air transmission. Control data makes up the remaining portion (Figure 10), transmitted via CoAP in 64-byte blocks. FETCH requests are employed to request models, and the corresponding responses include CBOR encoded payloads, with the associated costs elaborated in Table 5. We conducted a controlled experiment involving two stragglers in each round. Algorithm 1 minimizes communication overhead by leveraging the orchestrator's ability to execute fetch requests exclusively on clients that have completed local training, as determined by the status of all clients. This results in a notable reduction in the number of fetch requests, decreasing from 5 to 3 in comparison to Algorithm 2. The total number of requests and responses between all clients and the orchestrator remains constant at 5 for both algorithms. Notably, Algorithm 1 achieves a lower exchanged bits per round by strategically excluding stragglers from contributing their model updates for aggregation.

2) MODEL PERFORMANCE
Both algorithms yield similar results in average metrics, computed by weighting based on the fraction of local client data during validation and testing, as depicted by the red (Algorithm 1) and purple (Algorithm 2) curves in Figure 11 to Figure 14, and further detailed in Table 6 for the IID setting. For all models shown in these figures (MLP-based models), performance peaks after just 15 rounds of training for IID data distribution. This indicates that even discarding the contributions of slow-performing clients (stragglers) does not adversely affect the performance on average metrics. On the other hand, including the contributions from stragglers adds little to the overall metric since the IID distribution is statistically similar across clients.

However, in the case of Non-IID data, Algorithm 2 (black curves) outperforms Algorithm 1 (blue curves), demonstrating stable convergence by intelligently aggregating the contributions of stragglers. It is evident that Algorithm 1 faces challenges when dealing with a Non-IID distribution, as it fails to converge, resulting in unsatisfactory outcomes. This is because discarding updates from slow clients with statistically important data points can lead to poor performance and the high fluctuations observed in the blue curve for Algorithm 1 under Non-IID data.

section: IX. DISCUSSION & FUTURE WORK
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
The single FL server represents a critical limitation, creating a point of failure that threatens reliability and scalability in dynamic IoT settings. To address this, we propose transitioning to a peer-to-peer aggregation model, such as Gossip Learning, to distribute processing across nodes and enhance resilience. While our CoAPerator Linux implementation is unsuitable for microcontrollers due to resource constraints, the TDMiL clients on RIOT provide a foundation for developing fully decentralized aggregation schemes on wireless microcontroller-based IoT devices. This approach would enable comparative evaluation of decentralized learning performance and scalability in resource-constrained environments.

A critical privacy vulnerability exists within TDMiL: while raw data remains on devices, model parameters remain sensitive and vulnerable to leakage by compromised aggregators. Currently, no mechanism ensures parameter confidentiality. In future work, we plan to integrate privacy-enhancing techniques, specifically Differential Privacy (DP) and homomorphic encryption, to protect model updates. Implementing these layers on microcontroller devices presents significant computational challenges; however, successful deployment would broaden TDMiL's applicability to privacy-sensitive domains and contribute to the field of privacy-preserving machine learning on edge devices.

section: X. CONCLUSION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input:
We introduced TDMiL and CoAPerator as integral components of a framework designed for distributed training and transfer learning on resource-limited IoT devices operating over low-bandwidth, lossy wireless networks.

A critical challenge for fleets of microcontroller-based IoT devices is the computational disparity among distributed learning nodes, commonly referred to as the "straggler" problem. Through rigorous experimentation with TDMiL, we conducted a comparative analysis of multiple novel schemes devised to mitigate this issue. These experiments yield valuable insights into optimizing distributed learning processes within heterogeneous IoT ecosystems, paving the way for more efficient and robust AI deployments in resource-constrained environments.

To foster innovation and collaboration, we released our TDMiL implementation as open-source, portable software. This empowers researchers and practitioners to reproduce our findings and extend our work to diverse hardware configurations and application scenarios. The community can build upon this foundation using proprietary setups or established open-access IoT testbeds, accelerating progress in distributed AI for IoT systems.

Our work represents a significant stride towards harmonizing the demands of AI with the inherent limitations of IoT deployments. As these technological domains evolve and converge, the framework serves as a robust platform for future innovations in distributed learning on resource-constrained devices. By addressing the unique challenges at the intersection of AI and IoT, we contribute to the broader vision of ubiquitous, intelligent systems that can operate efficiently at the edge of networks.

The concurrent acceleration of AI advancements and IoT proliferation presents a complex landscape of intersecting yet sometimes conflicting requirements. Addressing these challenges, we introduced TDMiL and CoAPerator, integral components of an innovative framework meticulously designed for distributed training and transfer learning. Our solution is specifically engineered to operate efficiently within the constraints of low-bandwidth, lossy wireless networks, facilitating seamless interconnection among resource-limited devices built on diverse microcontroller architectures.

At the core of our research lies a critical challenge inherent to fleets of microcontroller-based IoT devices: the computational disparity among distributed learning nodes, commonly referred to as the "straggler" problem. Through rigorous experimentation with TDMiL, we conducted a comprehensive comparative analysis of multiple novel schemes devised to mitigate this issue. These experiments yield valuable insights into optimizing distributed learning processes within heterogeneous IoT ecosystems, paving the way for more efficient and robust AI deployments in resource-constrained environments.

To foster innovation and collaboration in this rapidly evolving domain, we have released our TDMiL implementation as open-source, portable software. This strategic decision empowers researchers and practitioners to not only reproduce our findings but also to extend and adapt our work to diverse hardware configurations and application scenarios. By leveraging either proprietary setups or established open-access IoT testbeds, the community can build upon our foundation, accelerating progress in the field of distributed AI for IoT systems.

Our work represents a significant stride towards harmonizing the ambitious demands of AI with the inherent limitations of IoT deployments. As these technological domains continue to evolve and converge, the framework we've developed serves as a robust platform for future innovations in distributed learning on resource-constrained devices. By addressing the unique challenges at the intersection of AI and IoT, we contribute to the broader vision of ubiquitous, intelligent systems that can operate efficiently at the edge of networks.

SOURCE CODE
Our code is accessible in this repository for testing and to encourage experimentation with various model architectures and datasets: https://github.com/TinyPART/TDMiL-artifact.

Abstract—This letter presents a tactile sensing glove based on piezoelectric sensors, embedded electronics, and a machine learning (ML)-based approach for texture discrimination. Various time and frequency features were extracted and evaluated through ML algorithms, including support vector machines (SVM), single-layer feed-forward neural networks, and 1-D convolution neural networks. Six naturalistic surface textures were explored by simply sliding the index finger of seven participants on the surfaces with and without the tactile glove. Results showed that by employing an SVM classifier trained on both time and frequency features, a discrimination accuracy of 87% is achieved while utilizing only two sensors. Furthermore, this discrimination behavior was found to exceed the participants (76.79%) when attempting to discriminate the textures using their somatosensory system. This study demonstrated the capability of the tactile sensing glove in extracting tactile information, opening up interesting perspectives for wearable feedback systems for post-stroke rehabilitation.
Index Terms—Sensor systems, machine learning (ML), tactile sensing glove, textural features, texture discrimination, wearable sensing systems.

Humans can grasp, feel, and explore diverse objects and surfaces, and simultaneously infer their material properties—a challenging set of tasks for post-stroke patients characterized by motor injuries associated with sensory deficits. These sensory deficits can affect different modalities of sensation and control, including pressure and proprioception [1]. Different technologies have been proposed for sensory restoration and post-stroke rehabilitation [2], [3]. However, it remains challenging to simulate human tactile perception as the sense of touch not only reflects the tactile response to external physical stimuli (e.g., temperature and pressure) but also includes neural processing based on extraction and analysis of information, such as recognition of texture and roughness through tactile sensation [4]. It has been proved that sensory restoration with repetitive detection of various textures improved proprioceptive, tactile discriminative, and object recognition senses along with postural control [5], [6], [7]. Exposing patients to different textures, the sensory pathways that process tactile information are continuously stimulated, refining the sensory receptors and neural circuits responsible for detecting and interpreting tactile stimuli. This is strongly related to the fact that surface texture is an important object property that significantly affects the wear resistance and fatigue life of components [8]. To this end, texture perception and learning methods for embodiment intelligence can be designed by developing large-scale tactile sensing arrays [9] and machine learning (ML) techniques [10].

Soft sensors improve the performance, reliability, and biocompatibility of human–machine interface with human bodies [11], [12]. In particular, tremendous efforts have been made to recognize the material’s properties (e.g. Hardness [13]) using intelligent tactile sensors [4]. For instance, various types of artificial tactile sensors combined with ML techniques have been developed to capture the surface texture [8]. For example, researchers in [14] utilized a finger cap equipped with triboelectric sensors and convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for the identification of artificial textures and materials. Similarly, Qu et al. [15] integrated triboelectric sensors into a rigid finger and used a linear discriminant analysis algorithm to identify the textures and material. Piezoelectric sensors exhibit a high-frequency range similar to that of mechanoreceptors in human skin [16], making them well-suited for surface texture detection. In [17], it has been demonstrated that combining piezoelectric sensors and support vector machines SVMs or k-nearest neighbors is useful for texture exploration. However, most of the works in the literature proposed bulky texture classification systems and methods that are computationally demanding. Moreover, these approaches were validated in a controlled manner, in which the sliding velocity and force were controlled and used to identify artificial textures and materials. This is important as the sliding action is crucial for the discrimination of textures [18]; therefore, the touch force and velocity affect the perception of its roughness since they may alter the intensity and frequency content of the vibrations it elicits in the skin [19]. For that reason, it is crucial to consider the sliding velocity and force while developing a tactile sensing system for texture identification. Based on this, this letter attempts to develop a sensing system capable of restoring texture perception for post-stroke rehabilitation. The sensing system is composed of a piezoelectric-based tactile glove, embedded electronics, and ML algorithms. Unlike the existing approaches, the proposed one was tested on a dataset collected from naturalistic textures under uncontrolled experimental conditions. Subsequently, its performance was validated by comparing it to the ability of healthy users to perceive those textures.

output: Fig. 1 shows the structure of the tactile sensing glove. It is composed of eight piezoelectric sensing arrays attached to the volar side of a fabric glove and embedded electronics attached to a passive PCB on the backside of the hand. The sensing arrays are based on poly(vinylidene fluoride triﬂuoro-ethylene) sensors screen-printed on a transparent and ﬂexible (175 µ thick) DIN A4 plastic foil (MelinexST 725) substrate [20]. The arrays were shielded using conductive tapes (Model tesa 60262) and then protected using a thin ﬂexible protective layer (Art. 5500 Dream, Framisitalia). The intrinsic ﬂexibility of the sensing arrays together with its wide frequency bandwidth (0.5 Hz–1 kHz) makes it a good candidate as an electronic skin measuring dynamic contacts. The sensor distribution is based on allocating most sensors to the center of the ﬁngertip, which is the most active area for texture perception. The embedded electronics is composed of a BL600 microcontroller (Laird Connectivity, USA) and two 16 -channels daisy-chained DDC232 (Texas Instruments, USA) current-input analog-to-digital converters [20]. It can acquire, process, and send the tactile signals of the 64 sensors to a host PC through a USB connection. In the present study, the embedded electronics was conﬁgured to collect and process tactile signals of the eight sensors of the glove’s index ﬁnger at 2KSamples/s.

input:
II. MATERIALS AND METHODS — B. Experimental Setup and Protocol

This study evaluates the tactile glove's ability to detect textural features in healthy subjects. Seven participants (3 female, 4 male, ages 24-32) completed two experiments using six naturalistic textures (Carpet, Soft-PVC, Plastic Mesh, Paperboard, Wood, Foam) attached to a rigid plate.

Experiment 1 collected tactile data from the glove. Participants wore the Text-Glove and slid their index finger randomly on specified textures for 5 seconds in forward (25 times) and backward (25 times) directions. A total of 2100 trials were recorded (50 trials × 6 textures × 7 subjects).

Experiment 2 assessed human texture perception. The same participants were blindfolded and slid their bare finger on shuffled textures in forward and backward directions. The experiment comprised learning, reinforced learning, and validation phases. Participants performed 50 sliding actions per texture per phase. Informed consent was obtained prior to testing.
output:
II. MATERIALS AND METHODS — B. Experimental Setup and Protocol

This study aims to assess the ability of the developed tactile glove to detect textural features. One of the main applications of tactile gloves is the sensory restoration for post-stroke patients. For that reason, it is crucial to compare the performance of the developed tactile glove along with the discrimination methods to the texture perception of the somatosensory system in healthy subjects. To that aim, seven healthy participants (three females and four males, ranging in age from 24 to 32) were asked to participate in two experiments. In both experiments, a set of six materials with different naturalistic textures were selected: “Carpet,” “Soft-PVC,” “Plastic Mesh,” “Paperboard,” “Wood,” and “Foam.” The textures were attached to a rigid plate and placed in front of the participants as shown in Fig. 1 (top).

1) Data Collection Using Tactile Glove (Text-Glove): This experiment aims to collect a tactile dataset from the developed tactile sensing glove. During the experiment, participants were asked to wear the tactile glove and slide their index finger on the texture specified by the experimenter as shown in Fig. 1 (top). The participants slid the finger randomly without controlling the sliding force and velocity. However, they were asked to act within 5 s and in two directions—forward (25 times) and backward (25 times). In total, 2100 trials were recorded, consisting of 50 trials × six textures × seven subjects. Fig. 1 (Bottom) shows the response of the eight sensors to sliding on the “Plastic Mesh” texture.

2) Texture Perception (Text-Subject): The target of this experiment is to assess the subject’s ability to perceive and discriminate naturalistic textures. For that aim, participants of the Text-Glove experiment were requested to participate in the Text-subject experiment. During the experiment, participants were blindfolded and guided by the experimenter to the textures. Similar to the experiment Text-Glove, participants were asked to slide in the two directions with their bare index finger on the texture. The textures were shuffled and randomly presented so that the participants did not build a map of the texture location in the surrounding space. The experiment comprised three phases: learning, reinforced learning, and validation. In the learning phase, participants were informed beforehand, which texture would be presented. During reinforced learning, the textures were randomly presented, while the subjects were asked to guess the texture. The experimenter then provided verbal feedback on the correct answer by saying “correct” or “incorrect” and, in the latter case, disclosing the correct texture. During the final phase, the textures were again presented randomly, and the subject verbally indicated the texture, but no verbal feedback was given. The subject performed 50 sliding actions on each texture during each of the three phases. Before the experiments, all the participants were informed of the experimental procedure and signed an informed consent.

The dataset acquired in the Text-Glove experiment was processed and analyzed to train and test the models presented in Section II-D. The acquired data for each sliding action is presented as a 2-D tensor $X_i$. The collected dataset can be formulated as $D = \{(X_i, y_i)\;|\; X_i \in \mathbb{R}^{N_c \times N_s}, y_i \in \{\text{six textures}\}, i = 1, \dots, 2100\}$, where $N_c = 8$ is the number of sensors, and $N_s = 10^4$ is the number of samples ($2K\text{Samples/s} \times 5\text{ s}$). For each $X_i \in D$, a zero-calibration was applied by subtracting the median of each $X_i$.

Inspired by the work done in [17] and [21], two types of features were extracted from the tactile data using the following procedures:

1) **Time Features:** Since the dataset was collected in an uncontrolled experimental condition, which might result in different sensor activity for each texture and within each $X_i \in D$, the energy of each sensor was used to determine the two most active sensors. This procedure results in $\hat{X}_i \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times N_s}$, thus generating a new dataset $\hat{D}$. Then, four features were computed along the two sensors of $\hat{X}_i$. Specifically, the features are defined as the energy of the signals and three statistical moments, i.e., the standard deviation, skewness, and kurtosis. As a result, each $X_i \in D$ was transformed into a 1-D array $X_{\text{time},i} \in \mathbb{R}^{8 \times 1}$, where eight represents the four features for the two most active sensors. This step generates a new dataset representing the time features of all sliding trials and textures. The new dataset is expressed as $D_{\text{time}} = \{(X_{\text{time},i}, y_i)\;|\; X_{\text{time},i} \in \mathbb{R}^{8 \times 1}, y_i \in \{\text{six textures}\}, i = 1, \dots, 2100\}$.

2) **Frequency Features:** For each $\hat{X}_i \in D$, the power spectral density (PSD) for each sensor was computed, normalized, and then used to calculate the cumulative sum. From the normalized PSD, the frequency of the mode was extracted as the first feature. The cumulative sum was then used to compute the frequency indices of the median, first quartile, and third quartile. As a result, each $X_i \in D$ was transformed into a 1-D array $X_{\text{freq},i} \in \mathbb{R}^{8 \times 1}$, where eight represents the four frequency features for the two most active sensors. The output of this step is a new dataset representing the frequency features of the sliding trials and textures and it is expressed as $D_{\text{freq}} = \{(X_{\text{freq},i}, y_i)\;|\; X_{\text{freq},i} \in \mathbb{R}^{8 \times 1}, y_i \in \{\text{six textures}\}, i = 1, \dots, 2100\}$.

After feature extraction, the resulting datasets were normalized along the features to have zero mean and a standard deviation value of 1 and then used to train the ML algorithms.

Three discrimination algorithms are evaluated: SVM, a single-layer feed-forward neural network (SLFNN), and a 1-D CNN.

The SVM classifier is a supervised ML algorithm that computes the hyperplane maximizing the margin to the nearest samples of the two classes; only the linear kernel was implemented due to efficiency constraints [21].

In this letter, we assessed the texture discrimination sensing system using discrimination accuracy. Furthermore, the discrimination behavior of the ML algorithms was compared to that of the subjects in the Text-subj experiment. Table 1 summarizes the average discrimination accuracy for each dataset and algorithm with two sensors on the fivefolds. IV. CONCLUSION

This letter presents a tactile sensing glove combined with ML algorithms for naturalistic texture discrimination. The tactile glove is based on PVDF sensors and embedded electronics. A set of time and frequency features were extracted from tactile signals. The features were then used to train three classification algorithms (SVM, SLFNN, and 1-D CNN). The best discrimination accuracy is (87.19 ± 1.23)%, which can be obtained using the SVM classifier and a combination of both types of features. The performance of the proposed system was compared to the ability of blindfolded participants to discriminate the texture using their bare index finger. Results proved that the performance of the proposed system surpassed human tactile perception, which enabled accurate discrimination of the textures. All the experimental data were collected by randomly sliding the sensorized or the bare fingertip on the textures without controlling the sliding speed or the load making the developed approach suitable for real-time surface texture discrimination. For example, it is useful for sensory restoration in post-stroke patients or as a high-fidelity rehabilitation system.

A key issue is how to address the inherent nonlinearity of classical deep learning, a problem in the quantum domain due to the fact that the composition of an arbitrary number of quantum

of unitary transformations. In this article, we introduce the quantum path kernel (QPK), a formulation of
quantum machine learning capable of replicating those aspects of deep machine learning typically associated

dynamics of classical and quantum machine learning models. The QPK exploits the parameter trajectory,
i.e., the curve delineated by model parameters as they evolve during training, enabling the representation of
differential layerwise convergence behaviors, or the formation of hierarchical parametric dependencies, in
terms of their manifestation in the gradient space of the predictor function. We evaluate our approach with
respect to variants of the classification of Gaussian xor mixtures: an artificial but emblematic problem that
intrinsically requires multilevel learning in order to achieve optimal class separation.

section: I. INTRODUCTION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.

Bridging classical deep neural networks and quantum computing represents a key research challenge in quantum machine learning [1], [2]. The potential for improvement offered by quantum computing may be characterized in terms of its impact on algorithmic efficiency, generalization error, or its capacity for treating quantum data [3].

A notable recent result has been the introduction of variational quantum algorithms and the related neural network analog referred to as the quantum neural network (QNN) [4]. This consists of a feature map encoding data into a quantum Hilbert space upon which parameterized unitary rotations are applied prior to final measurement to obtain a classification or regression output. The system is optimized by classical methods. Such models provably lead to a computational advantage over classical models on certain artificial tasks [5], and in respect to the analysis of specific physical systems [6]. It has been quantitatively shown that QNNs can be trained faster than their classical analogues [4]. However, QNNs remain problematic. One limitation arises from the so-called barren plateau problem [7], in which the variance of the gradient vanishes exponentially with system size as the parameterized transformation becomes increasingly expressive [8]. A number of approaches, including layerwise training of QNNs [9], have been proposed to mitigate the issue.

A second problematic aspect of QNNs, and the principal focus here, is the linearity of quantum system dynamics. Concatenations of linear unitary transformations remain unitary, and thus "stacked" quantum transformations collapse to a single linear transformation, ruling out hierarchical feature learning of classical deep neural networks, which relies on nonlinearities. This property makes the QNN essentially a kernel machine [10]. In terms of the predictor function, the QNN is composed of multiplications of rotation operators parameterized by both feature and model weights. The nonlinearity of projections of rotation operators can be exploited to replicate a constrained form of nonlinearity for feature learning [11], [12]. Another strategy is to introduce nonlinearity via the measurement operation, i.e., a dissipative QNN [13]. Both approaches involve projection of the quantum state into a subspace of the original Hilbert space.

Much of the recent study of classical deep neural network dynamics has focused on the neural tangent kernel (NTK) [14], which represents the network in terms of training gradients in model parameter space. The NTK approximates predictor behavior via a linear model and is often applied to study neural networks in their asymptotic, infinite-width limit. In this regime, the network exhibits lazy training, i.e., parameter gradients remain at their initial values. The NTK accurately characterizes the dynamics of infinite-width neural networks but is otherwise only an approximation [16]. The difference in test error between the predictor and its linearized version depends on problem structure, with hierarchical feature learning capability being crucial to obtaining superior performance [18]. The first explicit application of NTK to QNNs, the quantum neural tangent kernel (QNTK), was given in [19].

Bridging classical deep neural networks and quantum computing represents a key research challenge in the field of quantum machine learning [1], [2]. The potential for improvement offered by quantum computing in the machine learning domain may be characterized in terms of its impact on algorithmic efficiency, generalization error, or else its capacity for treating quantum data [3].

A notable recent result in the field has been the introduction of the concept of variational quantum algorithms and the related neural network analog referred to as the quantum neural network (QNN) [4]. This, in essence, consists of a feature map encoding data into a quantum Hilbert space upon which certain parameterized unitary rotations are applied prior to final measurement in order to obtain a classification or regression output. The system as a whole is then optimized by classical methods. Such models provably lead to a computational advantage over classical models on certain artificial tasks [5], and in respect to the analysis of specific physical systems [6]. It has been quantitatively shown that QNNs can be trained faster than their classical analogues [4]. However, QNNs remain problematic in various respects. One limitation arises from the so-called barren plateau problem [7], in which the variance of the gradient vanishes exponentially with the system size as the parameterized transformation becomes increasingly expressive [8]. A number of approaches, including layerwise training of QNNs [9], have been proposed to mitigate the issue.

A second problematic aspect of QNNs, and the one that constitutes our principal focus here, is the linearity of the dynamics of quantum systems. Concatenations of linear unitary transformations remain unitary, and thus, “stacked” quantum transformations, in effect, collapse to a single linear transformation, appearing to rule out de facto the hierarchical feature learning of classical deep neural networks, which relies on nonlinearities to separate feature layers. This property makes the QNN essentially a kernel machine [10]. In terms of the predictor function, however, the QNN is composed of multiplications of rotation operators parameterized by both the feature and model weights. The nonlinearity of projections of rotation operators can be exploited to replicate a very constrained form of nonlinearity for feature learning [11], [12]. Another strategy is to introduce nonlinearity via the measurement operation, i.e., a dissipative QNN [13]. Both approaches involve the projection of the quantum state into a subspace of the original Hilbert space.

Much of the recent study of the dynamics of deep neural networks in the classical realm has focused on the neural tangent kernel (NTK) [14] which represents the network in terms of the corresponding training gradients in the model parameter space. The NTK hence approximates the behavior of predictors via a linear model. It is often therefore applied to study neural networks in their asymptotic, infinite-width, limit. In this regime, the network exhibits lazy training [15], i.e., parameter gradients remain at their initial values during the entirety of the training. The NTK thus accurately characterizes the dynamics of such infinite-width neural networks, but is otherwise only an approximation [16]. The difference in test error between the predictor and its linearized version depends on the problem structure [17], with hierarchical feature learning capability being crucial to obtaining superior performance [18]. However, the kernel nature of the NTK means that it shares with quantum computing a ready interpretation within a Hilbert space, and is thus of considerable interest within quantum machine learning. The first explicit application of NTK to QNNs, the quantum neural tangent kernel (QNTK) was given in [19].

In this article, we propose a method for overcoming the de facto lack of hierarchical feature learning capability in QNNs. We propose the application of path kernels [20] to QNNs, which we call the quantum path kernel (QPK). Such an approach generalizes the QNTK so that the resulting kernel is representative of the ensemble of NTKs calculated over the full parameter path trajectory, i.e., the function describing the evolution of model parameters over time, including implicitly any parametric evolutions corresponding to hierarchical feature learning. We show experimentally an increased expressivity of the resulting model relative to linearized equivalents, evaluating our method on the Gaussian xor mixture classification problem. For this problem, finite-width neural networks have both theoretically and empirically shown to be close-to-optimal performance, whereas linear NTK models fail [21], suggesting that it cannot be effectively resolved without implicating multilevel learning behavior. Furthermore, we discuss possible improvements for the proposed approach, which can be obtained by considering only the contribution of the parameter gradient path that gives rise to the most decorrelated feature representation. These specifically corresponds to the contributions associated with the maximally nonlinear point of the parameter path, corresponding to the largest (positive or negative) eigenvalues of the Hessian of the predictor function [22]. We further enhance the decorrelation between feature representations via a stochastic, noisy, or nongradient-descent-based training algorithm in which the averaging operation between decorrelated representations allows us to interpret the model as an ensemble technique.

The rest of this article is organized as follows. In Section II, we briefly review the necessary conceptual background. In Section III, we present the QPK and discuss the hierarchical feature learning of the induced model. In Section IV, we demonstrate how this leads to superior performance in solving the Gaussian xor mixture classification problem. Finally, Section V concludes this article.

A. CONTRIBUTIONS

1) We propose the QPK as a mechanism for building hybrid classical/quantum machine learning models which are able to emulate the hierarchical feature learning structure of deep neural networks without violating the underlying linearity of the quantum dynamics. We conjecture such a kernel can lead to improved performance of the kernel machine on tasks involving feature learning.

2) We provide numerical evidence of the superior performance of the QPK compared to the QNTK on the Gaussian xor mixture problem, which is Bayes optimally soluble only through implicating layerwise nonlinear separability.

3) We consider the importance of the extraction of noncorrelated feature representations corresponding to maximally varying portions of the parameter gradient path.

The introduction of the NTK by [14] has marked a significant step in the theory of machine learning, shedding new light on discussions regarding the relative performance of linear and nonlinear models. For example, Ghorbani et al. [17] suggested that tasks in which kernel methods (including NTK) perform worse than neural networks are those in which the kernel suffers from the curse of dimensionality, whereas neural networks, in learning some useful lower dimensional representation, do not. One example of such a problem is the Gaussian xor mixture classification task [21]. Furthermore, linearized models have been shown to perform slightly worse than wide (i.e., large, but noninfinite) neural networks on a CIFAR-10 benchmark [23], with the gap between the approaches increasing for finite width networks [24].

In relation to quantum computation, researchers have spent substantial effort on the limitations imposed by the linear dynamics of quantum systems. Authors in [25] review early approaches to the formulation of nonlinear quantum machine learning models: some have focused on developing a quantum perceptron equivalent or quantum neuron, i.e., a candidate building block for the quantum analog of neural networks; Schuld et al. [26] used phase estimation to implement the functioning of a step function; the authors in [27] and [28] proposed to exploit the repeat until success (RUS) policy to mimic the behavior of tangent and sigmoid activation functions, while Gili et al. [29] used RUS to construct a Born machine; Tacchino et al. [30] emulated the nonlinearity of perceptrons using measurements. Regarding QNNs, Sharma et al. [13] proposed dissipative QNNs in which the nonlinearity is obtained via intertwining measurements between unitary gates; the authors in [31] and [32] proposed the use of a larger Hilbert space to implement the nonlinear transformation, while Daksin [33] exploited the exponential form of unitary gate to achieve periodic activation functions. Finally, nonlinear models of quantum mechanics have been conjectured by [34], although these violate some computational complexity assumptions [35].

Regarding QNTK literature, authors in [36] have quantified the benefic effect of introducing handcrafted symmetries in the QNN using tools derived from the QNTK. Authors in [37] and [38] investigated lazy training in the quantum machine learning context.

This mapping is achieved via an implicit feature map φ : X → H, enabling the use of potentially infinite-dimensional spaces, such as those implied by the Gaussian radial basis function. II. BACKGROUND — C. NOTIONS OF NONLINEARITY IN CLASSICAL AND QUANTUM LEARNING MODELS

With respect to kernel machines and deep learning, the concepts of linear model, nonlinear model, and feature learning are formalized in [41]. A linear model is a function of the form

f(x; θ) = ∑_{j=1}^p θ_j φ_j(x) (6)

where {φ_j: X → R}^p_{j=0} are the feature functions. An additional feature φ_0 ≡ 1 incorporates the bias. This formula is linear in the parameter space R^p; it can be interpreted as an inner product, i.e., f(x; θ) = ⟨θ, φ(x)⟩_{R^p} (7). However, it behaves nonlinearly with respect to the original feature space X due to the feature functions; thus, kernel machines are linear models.

A nonlinear model is a function of the form

f(x; θ) = ∑_{j=1}^p θ_j φ_j(x) + ε ∑_{j,k=1}^p θ_j θ_k ψ_{j,k}(x) + ε^3/3! ∑_{j,k,ℓ=1}^p θ_j θ_k θ_ℓ ψ_{j,k,ℓ}(x) + · · · (8)

The higher-order terms are characterized by their own feature sets, e.g., {ψ_{j,k}: X → R}^p_{j,k=1} for the second-order term. The elements of such sets are unique up to a permutation of their variables; thus, the terms 1/2!, 1/3!, . . . compensate for multiple counting. The term ε ≪ 1 adjusts the contribution of the nonlinear terms. If the model is truncated to the second term, it is denoted a quadratic model [41], [42]. THE NEURAL TANGENT KERNEL

The output f (x; θ) of a machine learning model trained via (possibly stochastic) gradient descent can be approximated as a first-order Taylor expansion f (x; θ) ≈ f (x; θ0) + ∇θ f (x; θ0)(θ − θ0). Such an approximation allows the representation of machine learners as linear (kernel) models via the NTK ([14])

κntk(x, x′; θ) = ∇θ f (x; θ) · ∇θ f (x′; θ).

(14)

This is widely used to characterize the dynamics of infinite-width neural networks [15], in which the NTK is independent of the random initialization and constant in time. On a coarse level of detail, we can assert that model training that takes place in the lazy-training regime, i.e., when the evolution of θ(t) during the training of the model f (x, θ) closely follows the tangent path, can be decently approximated by the NTK.

A more detailed analysis in [16] has revealed that the NTK is constant if and only if the model is linear (in its parameters). Such a result allows us to quantify the nonlinearity of a model through its Hessian norm of the predictor function: if ∥Hf ∥ ≪ ∥∇w f∥ then the model is nearly linear. This has been used in [11] to analyze the behavior of the QNNs in the lazy training regime.

III. QUANTUM PATH KERNEL FRAMEWORK

Existing quantum methods fail to capture deviations from gradient path linearity seen in optimal classical learners during hierarchical feature learning, where lower-level features converge before higher-level ones utilize them. To incorporate this behavior into the implicitly kernel-based quantum machine learning regime, we introduce path kernelization, a key idea from Domingo [20].

The path kernel, denoted κpk, is defined as the line integral of the neural tangent kernel (NTK) over the multidimensional curve representing parameter evolution θ = γ(t) during training:

κpk(x, x′; γ) = γ ∇θ f(x; θ) · ∇θ f(x′; θ) dθ  (15)

For linear models trained with vanilla gradient descent on a convex loss, the parameter path is linear, the gradient ∇θ f is θ-independent, and the NTK remains constant. For nonlinear models, the loss landscape may be nonconvex, causing γ to deviate from a linear trajectory. Consequently, both ∇θ f and the NTK vary over time.

The path kernel was originally introduced in [20] to establish functional equivalence between gradient-trained nonlinear models and path kernel machines. Here, we do not focus on approximation capabilities but instead seek to exploit the intrinsic potential of path kernels to capture implicit feature hierarchy formation implementable within a quantum neural network (QNN) setting. Specifically, we investigate whether incorporating quantum path construction into kernel machines, such as the support vector machine (SVM), can enhance performance in feature learning settings.

The construction is depicted in Fig. 1. As parameters evolve, they generate a sequence of distinct NTK matrices, representing distinct data representations stacked hierarchically. As training converges, these matrices become similar, correlating their representations. The path kernel constitutes the average over these representations:

κqpk(x, x′; γ) ≈ (1/T) Σ_{i=0}^{T-1} ∇θ ⟨0|V†(x)U†(θt)OU(θt)V(x)|0⟩ · ∇θ ⟨0|V†(x′)U†(θt)OU(θt)V(x′)|0⟩  (17)

where T is the number of sampled points from the curve γ, and t = i/T ∈ [0, 1]. Equation (16) defines the quantum NTK (QNTK) as the classical analog. Equation (17) is the discretized version suitable for gradient descent-trained models. The corresponding kernel machine model is given by:

f(·) = Σ_{i=1}^n αi κqpk(xi, ·)  (18)

where coefficients αi are determined during training (as with SVMs), and xi are training set elements; these coefficients do not depend on x. The resulting QPK acts as both a quantized version of Domingo’s path kernel and a generalization of the QNTK. It is implicitly capable of embodying complex parametric interactions, such as transient coevolutions, during learning to arrive at the final trained model, including those implicated in hierarchical feature learning.

III. QUANTUM PATH KERNEL FRAMEWORK

Extant quantum methods hence do not fully capture the deviations from gradient path linearity exhibited by empirically optimal finite-width learners in the classical domain during hierarchical feature learning (where, of necessity, lower level features reach learning convergence prior to the higher level features that utilize them). Thus, in order to encompass this learning behavior within the (implicitly kernel-based) quantum machine learning regime, we introduce into the quantum domain a key idea of Domingo [20], namely, path kernelization

κpk(x, x′; γ) = γ ∇θ f (x; θ) · ∇θ f (x′; θ) dθ

(15)

where kpk is the path kernel, i.e., the line integral of κntk over the multidimensional curve representing the evolution of the parameters θ = γ (t), t ∈ [0, 1] during training, with θ̄ = γ̄ (1). Appendix A1 gives a proof that the path kernel is effectively Mercer, and sets out the pseudocode for its construction.

In general, chain rule dependencies arising from the specifics of the architecture of the classical deep networks will imply that hierarchical dependencies develop among the parameters during learning. The result holds even for stochastic gradient descent optimization, in which case (15) is a stochastic integral. It is thus key to our argument to consider the parameter path γ and its morphological evolution. For linear models, assuming a vanilla gradient descent training over a convex loss function L, the parameter path is described by a linear vector {(1 − t)θ0 + tθf | t ∈ [0, 1]}, where θ0 ∈ Rp are the parameters at their initialization, and θf ∈ Rp are the parameters at their convergence on the (ideally global) minima of L. In this case, it is immediately possible to check that the derivative of the linear model ∇θ f is independent of θ, and thus, that the NTK is constant. For nonlinear models, the loss function L may become nonconvex and γ is not constrained to have a linear trajectory. In this latter case, both the ∇θ f and the NTK will vary over time during learning.

The path kernel was originally introduced in [20] in terms of a direct functional equivalence between nonlinear models trained with gradient descent and path kernel machines (cf Appendix A2). We do not, however, here, focus on the potential of path kernels in approximating nonlinear models. Instead, we seek to exploit the intrinsic potential of path kernels to capture implicit feature hierarchy formation in a manner capable of implementation on a hybrid deep machine learning model within a QNN setting. We thus seek to establish whether incorporation of a quantum version of path construction into kernel machines, such as the support vector machine (SVM), can yield performance enhancements in a feature learning setting: Section IV will seek to quantify this directly.

We depict the construction of the path kernel in Fig. 1. The parameter trajectory for a nonlinear model is described by a complex, nonstraight curve. Each point of the parameter path θt = γ (t) may be used to define a new kernel representation for the training data, namely, κntk(x, x′; θt). We can then define a sequence of kernels stacked in a hierarchical way (whose structure, in passing, resembles the layers of a deep neural network, though this observation is peripheral to the argument being made here). Thus, each new “layer” is a source of representation learning: the new representation (i.e., kernel matrix) is the result of an optimization process that further adapts the previous representation to the given data discrimination problem (which resembles, though is again not equivalent to, classifier boosting).

QUANTUM NEURAL TANGENT KERNEL

The primary motivation for introducing the QPK is to enhance the performance of kernel machines in the quantum domain. As such, it represents a departure from the typical focus of the QNTK theory, which primarily aims to predict specific properties of the underlying quantum model. Nevertheless, it is possible to interpret the QPK as a generalization of the QNTK with corresponding insights into the dynamics of the training process. In particular, it may be seen that the QNTK is constant only when it is fully independent of θ, in which case

κqpk(x, x′; γ) = γ ∫ κqntk(x, x′; θ) dθ = κqntk(x, x′; 0).

That is, the QPK becomes identical to the QNTK. However, as set out in Section II-C, the particular structure of QNNs will, of itself, give rise to a nonlinear predictor. Thus, in principle, the QNTK would not be expected to be constant in output terms in the finite width regime [11]. However, a close-to-constant behavior can be expected for quantum machine learning models whose training is lazy (i.e., lazy training induced via overparameterization of the QNN, such that a large number of parameters result in a simplified loss landscape [44], [45], leading to rapid convergence to a global minima).

section: III. QUANTUM PATH KERNEL FRAMEWORK — B. DECORRELATION IN FEATURE REPRESENTATION
instruction: Rewrite the supplied research notes into clear, coherent IEEE-style academic prose. Preserve the scientific meaning, technical terminology, numbers, units, citations, equations, and limitations. Do not add facts.
input: The QPK kernel matrix depends on training initialization, including parameter values, optimization algorithms, and learning rates. Vanilla gradient descent with a fixed number of epochs introduces bias, as rapid convergence causes later contributions to dominate the aggregated kernel stack, outweighing earlier ones. More sophisticated algorithms, such as ADAM, adaptively adjust the learning rate in convex loss regions, reducing contribution similarity. Alternatively, perturbing parameter paths via noisy or non-gradient descent techniques decorrelates contributions, allowing the QPK to be interpreted as an ensemble method analogous to bagging for bias-variance tradeoff control. Multiple Kernel Learning may weigh individual kernel contributions optimally, though at the cost of path interpretability.
output:
The QPK clearly exhibits dependency on the training initialization: different initial parameter values, optimization algorithms, or learning rates may lead to differing QPK kernel matrices. In particular, the utilization of "vanilla" gradient descent optimization algorithms, with a fixed number of training epochs, may introduce subtle biases in the QPK.

For example, if training were to converge rapidly, any contribution between the instance of convergence and the end of the training will be effectively identical and oversampled: this contribution will hence outweigh the others, biasing the "stack" of aggregated kernel matrices toward its final layer, as per Fig. 1.

To avoid this, more sophisticated optimization algorithms can be considered. For example, the ADAM optimizer adaptively increases the learning rate in locally convex portions of the loss landscape, leading to fewer similar contributions within the path kernel. Furthermore, it is possible to perturb parameter paths via stochastic, noisy, or non-gradient descent-based optimization techniques in order to decorrelate subsequent contributions to the QPK. Having different, highly decorrelated contributions would allow us to interpret the QPK as an ensemble technique analogous to bootstrap aggregation (bagging) often used for tuning the bias/variance trade off in classical machine learning. (Multiple Kernel Learning [46] might also be used to optimally weigh individual contributions over the kernel at the expense of interpretability in path terms.)

Appendix A3 discusses implementation details for the QPK and its tested variants. We, therefore, now turn to an examination of the test regime.

We generate the dataset and train Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) to fit the data. Using the trained QNNs, we construct the Quantum Neural Tangent Kernel (QNTK) and QPK matrices to train Support Vector Machines (SVMs) for final classification. We analyze convergence across increasing QNN layer counts to highlight architectural effects. Finally, we compare QNTK and QPK performance in terms of training and testing accuracy [21].

The ground truth dataset is defined by feature dimensionality d, nonzero features d', noise variance ε̄, and n data points. It consists of samples [x₁ + ε₁, ..., x_d' + ε_d', 0, ..., 0]ᵀ with labels yᵢ = Σᵢ₌₁ᵈ' xᵢ, where xᵢ ∈ {±1} and εᵢ ~ N(0, ε̄). Optimal classification is performed by the oracle function f_oracle(x) = Σᵢ₌₁ᵈ' xᵢ.

Quantum neural networks (QNNs) process datasets using a parameterized circuit f(x; θ) = Tr[ρ_x,θO], with data encoding U_φ(x) = ⊗ⱼ₌₁ᵈ exp(−i xⱼ σʸⱼ/2). The trainable ansatz V(θ) consists of L layers of parameterized rotations. Each dataset is processed with QNNs having layers L = 1 to 20, trained via ADAM for 1000 epochs with initial learning rate η = 0.1, using binary cross-entropy or MSE loss with batch size equal to the training set size.

Depthwise convergence is evaluated regarding QPK and QNTK accuracies under SVM classification. Models are assessed for proximity to the lazy training regime by monitoring training loss and parameter norm deviation ||θ⁽ⁿ⁾ − θ⁽⁰⁾|| / ||θ⁽⁰⁾||. Results show no models reach the interpolation threshold even at maximum depth (40 parameters). Increasing layer count decreases loss and increases parameter proximity, but substantial parameter variation persists, particularly in smaller models, indicating non-lazy training characteristics and divergence from the QNTK.

Test accuracy comparisons between QPK and QNTK reveal similar performance at low noise, but QPK outperforms QNTK at high signal-to-noise ratios. Training accuracy plots show QPK achieves lower loss than QNTK across all noise levels, with the gap widening at higher noise, consistent with QPK's lower bias. These results indicate QPK's superior ability to replicate classical multilayer feature learning in the Gaussian xor mixture setting.

commonly used for classification and regression tasks, which
differs from the loss functions used in the works related to the
QNTK theory.
In the experimental setup described above, we study, both
epochwise and depthwise, the effect induced by different
initialization parameters on the convergence of the loss
function during training.
B. RESULTS
We evaluate the depthwise convergence characteristics of the
respective f (x; θ) models in terms of the corresponding accuracies of the QPK and QNTK under SVM final classification.
Of particular interest is evaluating the closeness of models to
the lazy training regime, indicative of the model being near to
linear. Lazy training, in classical machine learning, typically
occurs for very wide neural networks with the loss decreasing
to zero exponentially rapidly, while network parameters stay
close to their initialization values throughout training. In the
current context, this would correspond to the QPK collapsing
to the QNTK, and we would anticipate convergent classification performances for the two approaches.
We, therefore, evaluate training loss for each of the QNN
models over the respective training epochs with an increasing
number of QNN layers L = 1, . . . , 20. This will be used to
determine proximity to the lazy training regime (i.e., identifying if the QNN converges exponentially fast to zero loss).
We additionally plot the norm difference between the parameters during training compared to their initialization values.
These will be used to determine the extend to which parameters vary from their initialization, indicating the training
richness of models in the nonlazy training regime.
We are also interested in determining the robustness of
the classifiers to stochastic noise influences during training
and their corresponding resilience to overfitting (or the extent
to which benign overparameterization [44] effects exists),
measured in terms of generalization performance. Therefore,
the above evaluations are repeated for datasets additively
noise-perturbed in an increasing signal-to-noise ratio.
Finally, we are interested in comparing the generalization
performances of our approach to that of the QNTK. For this,
we evaluate test accuracy score for the QPK and QNTK,
against the oracle. Superior performance of the QPK, in
solving the Gaussian xor mixture problem, will be taken
to be indicative of superior ability to replicate the layerwise
feature-learning capability of classical multilayer networks.

In this work, we introduce the QPK as a mechanism to incorporate hierarchical feature learning into QNNs via kernelization of the training process. We evaluate this approach on the Gaussian xor mixture classification problem, a multilayer benchmark requiring a minimum two-layer solution to approach Bayes optimality. Experiments show superior generalization performance compared to the QNTK, especially in high-depth, low signal-to-noise settings.

Theoretically, the QPK converges to the QNTK only in the lazy training regime, where loss decreases exponentially while parameters remain near initialization. This behavior is characteristic of infinite-wide neural networks, which behave as linear models. Our experiments indicate QNNs do not operate in this linear regime.

We discuss the potential for using noisy or non-gradient descent optimization to perturb parameter paths within the QPK, thereby implicating more decorrelated feature representations. We also propose extending the QPK via heuristic weighting of individual kernel representations, such as multiple kernel learning. We additionally refer to the QPK as an ensemble method due to kernel matrix averaging, a topic for future investigation.

In this article, we have introduced the QPK as a mechanism for incorporating key complex classical multilayer network learning behaviors, in particular hierarchical feature learning, within QNNs via an appropriately expressive kernelization of the training process. We evaluate our approach on the Gaussian xor mixture classification problem, a straightforward benchmark of multilayer learning capacity that requires a minimum two-layer solution in order to approach Bayes optimally. The experimental results indicate superior generalization performance relative to the QNTK, an advantage which is especially pronounced in high-depth, low signal-to-noise settings.

We have shown theoretically that the QPK converges to the QNTK only in the lazy training regime, i.e., when the training loss decreases to zero exponentially fast whilst model parameters stay close to their initializations across training. Such behavior is classically seen in infinite-wide neural networks, whose behavior is then close to that of a linear model. Our experiments, by contrast, indicate that QNNs do not operate in the linear regime.

We have discussed, though do not evaluate in the current article, the potential for using stochastic, noisy, or non-gradient descent-based optimization techniques to artificially perturb parameter paths within the QPK in order to implicate more decorrelated feature representations. We furthermore propose in future to extend the QPK approach via weighting of individual kernel representations in a more heuristic way, for example via multiple kernel learning. We have also referred in passing to the interpretation of the QPK as an ensemble method due to the averaging operation over its kernel matrices. This will be explored more fully in future investigations.

The path kernel was introduced in [20] as a means of replicating arbitrary gradient descent-based machine learning models in the form of kernel machines, under some weak assumptions. The path kernel is consequently of inherent interest in the theory of classical machine learning in that it grants a further layer of interpretability to models, including those, such as the neural networks, that often lacks this [54]. In Section III-B, we have discussed the potential significance of decorrelated features; here, we propose a numerical implementation of the effective path kernel. APPENDIX B
NUMERICAL EVIDENCE FOR THE INABILITY OF RANDOM FEATURE KERNEL TECHNIQUES IN SOLving THE GAUSSIAN XOR MIXTURE CLASSIFICATION

In [21], the authors demonstrate that a two-layer-depth neural network with only a small number of neurons can easily outperform kernel methods on the Gaussian mixture classification problem, under the assumption that the number of training data points n →∞ is linearly proportional to the dimensionality of the data d →∞.

We modify Refinetti’s experiment for the current purpose to show the same result in a more straightforward way.

For each dataset, we compare the performances of the oracle with the performances of the best of ten randomly initialized neural networks and the best of ten random feature kernels. For each dataset specification, we repeat this procedure ten times.

In Fig. 10, we set out the results of the above described experiments. It may be observed that neural networks outperform the kernel approach in each case, with the differential in accuracy increasing with the number of zero-valued features.

Refinetti et al. [21] suggested that this difference in performance is accounted for by the fact that random feature kernels in high dimension behave as linear transformations [56]. Here, we have suggested a complementary interpretation of the results of such experiments. We have shown that the difference of performance between the two models is not uniquely determined by the failure of kernel methods per se. In fact, it is determined also by the feature learning capabilities of neural networks; inspecting the evolution of the W1 parameters during the training of a neural network reveals that elements in W1 related to the zero-features do indeed go to zero (Fig. 11). This results in having all of the hidden neurons (whose number is proportional to √d, and thus, increasing with the number of features) working adaptively to classify the three discriminatively informative components or features, thereby improving overall performance in contrast to the random feature kernel approach, for which adding feature (and parameters) drastically decreases performance (which is to say the path model outperforms the random feature kernel in this problem by being able to discharge junk features candidates, thus performing feature learning).

The Role of Machine Learning in Identifying Students At-Risk and Minimizing Failure

REYHAN ZEYNEP PEK
1, SIBEL TARIYAN ÖZYER2, TAREK ELHAGE3, TANSEL ÖZYER2,
AND REDA ALHAJJ

ABSTRACT Education is very important for students’ future success. The performance of students can be supported by the extra assignments and projects given by the instructors for students with low performance. However, a major problem is that students at-risk cannot be identified early. This situation is being investigated by various researchers using Machine Learning techniques. Machine learning is used in a variety of areas and has also begun to be used to identify students at-risk early and to provide support by instructors. This research paper discusses the performance results found using Machine learning algorithms to identify at-risk students and minimize student failure. The main purpose of this project is to create a hybrid model using the ensemble stacking method and to predict at-risk students using this model. We used machine learning algorithms such as Naïve Bayes, Random Forest, Decision Tree, K-Nearest Neighbors, Support Vector Machine, AdaBoost Classifier and Logistic Regression in this project. The performance of each machine learning algorithm presented in the project was measured with various metrics. Thus, the hybrid model by combining algorithms that give the best prediction results is presented in this study.

The data set containing the demographic and academic information of the students was used to train and test the model. In addition, a web application developed for the effective use of the hybrid model and for obtaining prediction results is presented in the report. In the proposed method, it has been realized that stratified k-fold cross validation and hyperparameter optimization techniques increased the performance of the models. The hybrid ensemble model was tested with a combination of two different datasets to understand the importance of the data features. In first combination, the accuracy of the hybrid model was obtained as 94.8% by using both demographic and academic data. In the second combination, when only academic data was used, the accuracy of the hybrid model increased to 98.4%. This study focuses on predicting the performance of at-risk students early. Thus, teachers will be able to provide extra assistance to students with low performance.
